### [1] [NLP-Driven Knowledge Extraction and Thematic Classification of Translated Ancient Indian Medical Texts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.28608)
*M. S. Rajeevan,B. Mini Devi,V. S. Anoop,C. Mallikarjuna*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper applies modern NLP techniques to translated Sushruta Samhita texts to extract and structure medical knowledge from ancient Ayurveda, making it computationally searchable and analyzable.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Ancient Indian medical texts such as Sushruta Samhita contain rich clinical and surgical knowledge, but their archaic format, complex vocabulary, and lack of structure make them hard to access, search, and analyze systematically using modern methods. There is a need to bridge the gap between these conventional narrative texts and contemporary data-driven research in medical informatics and digital humanities.

Method: The study uses several NLP and data modeling techniques on translated versions of the Sushruta Samhita: (1) BERTopic for topic modeling and thematic classification of passages into underlying medical topics; (2) Named Entity Recognition to identify and label key entities like diseases, treatments, researchers, and medicinal plants; and (3) construction of a knowledge graph in Neo4j to represent entities and their semantic relationships. Graph-based network analysis is then applied to explore and visualize the resulting knowledge structure.

Result: Using BERTopic, the authors derive coherent medical themes from the text. NER successfully extracts and categorizes entities such as diseases, treatments, and medicinal plants. The Neo4j knowledge graph links these entities into a semantic network that can be queried and visualized, enabling graph-based analysis of relationships and patterns within the ancient medical corpus. These results demonstrate that the chosen NLP and graph techniques can effectively structure and organize the content of Sushruta Samhita in a machine-readable, searchable form.

Conclusion: The paper concludes that combining topic modeling, NER, and graph databases is an effective strategy for computationally organizing ancient Ayurvedic medical knowledge. This approach enhances accessibility and interpretability of historical texts, supports knowledge retrieval and digital preservation, and contributes to fields like historical text analysis, medical informatics, and digital humanities. It helps bridge traditional Ayurvedic literature and modern data-driven research, making ancient Indian medical wisdom more usable for contemporary scholars and practitioners.

Abstract: Ancient Indian medical texts like Sushruta Samhita have extensive information on diseases, treatments, and surgical techniques. Yet, their ancient format and use of intricate vocabulary pose difficulties in accessibility and systematic ordering. The research here utilizes Natural Language Processing (NLP) methods like Named Entity Recognition (NER), BERTopic modeling, and Knowledge Graph development in Neo4j to extract, categorize, and visualize important concepts based on translated versions. Thematic classification with BERTopic allows for the identification of the underlying medical topics, whereas NER supports the structured entity recognition of diseases, treatments, researchers, and medicinal plants. Graphbased network analysis with Neo4j also allows for the semantic representation of relationship among extracted entities, supporting knowledge retrieval and digital preservation. The findings illustrate how graph databases, topic modeling, and entity recognition facilitate the computational organization of Ayurveda's historical medical wisdom, closing the gap between the conventional texts and contemporary data-driven inquiry. The suggested method promotes historical text analysis, medical informatics, and digital humanities to make ancient Indian medical wisdom more accessible and understandable.

</details>


### [2] [Parametric Multimodal User Memory: Storing What Captions Cannot Carry](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.28609)
*Bojie Li,Noah Shi*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper argues that current text-based user memories in personalized agents miss crucial perceptual information (voice, face, etc.), proposes a hybrid perceptual memory architecture combining vision-language grounding with dedicated identity encoders, and shows this design significantly improves recall of user identity across modalities and conditions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Personalized AI agents today primarily store user memories as text (transcripts, captions, notes). This works for explicitly nameable facts (e.g., “my cat is named Bibi”) but fails to capture rich perceptual aspects of identity such as what a user looks and sounds like across age, lighting, or fatigue. Existing systems often approximate perceptual memory by captioning everything and retrieving those captions by similarity, implicitly assuming textual descriptions are sufficient proxies for perception. The authors suspect large amounts of information are lost in this reduction to text, especially for non-nameable or hard-to-describe perceptual features. They aim to quantify how much identity information is lost when perception is funneled into text captions, and to design a memory system that preserves and utilizes this perceptual identity for more human-like, persistent personalization.

Method: First, the authors empirically measure information loss when using caption-based text re-identification vs. dedicated perceptual encoders across five modalities (including faces, voices, multi-speaker scenes, and audio/video). They build a strong caption-based re-identifier that converts perceptual input into text, then retrieves by text similarity, and compare its recall to modality-specific encoders. They report recall values and how close performance is to chance, especially for non-nameable perceptual cues.

Next, they propose a new perceptual memory architecture decomposing recall into two subproblems: (1) a vision-language model (VLM) to ground the referent in context (what and where in a scene), and (2) a dedicated identity encoder to extract a compact identity key (who). This identity key is stored as a single inline token that the language model reads via attention during generation, without external database lookups. They test configurations: VLM-only, encoder-only (ungrounded), and the combined system.

They evaluate recognition performance across scenarios such as cross-age face recognition, two-person scenes, and multi-speaker audio/video. Importantly, the recognition mechanism is training-free: it works with frozen base models, with O(1) registration cost per identity (constant-time, lightweight addition of new identities). They introduce the PerceptMem benchmark (12 domains, 1,080 tasks) to systematically study capacity limits and binding behavior of perceptual identity vs factual text memories.

Result: Caption-based text re-identification performs poorly compared to dedicated encoders, recovering as little as 0.11 of the encoder’s recall and approaching chance on non-nameable perceptual signals. This quantifies the severe loss from reducing perception to text captions.

In the proposed hybrid system, neither component alone is sufficient: the VLM alone achieves only 0.54 recall for cross-age face recognition where a face encoder reaches 0.81, while an ungrounded identity encoder obtains only 0.05 recall in two-person scene disambiguation. When combined (VLM grounding + identity encoder token), the system reaches near-oracle performance on correct-region recognition (0.96 recall) and generalizes to multi-speaker audio and video tasks.

The recognition core matches the recall of a standalone encoder on any frozen model without additional training, with constant-time registration of new identities. On the PerceptMem benchmark, they find that perceptual identity storage is capacity-limited (you can only store so many identity keys effectively), whereas exact factual memories are limited by binding and retrieval mechanisms. This supports a design separation: store perceptual identity in a compact parametric bank, and store exact facts in a conventional text memory store.

Conclusion: Text-only user memories fundamentally underrepresent a person by discarding much of the non-verbal, perceptual information that defines their identity. The paper demonstrates that caption-based approximations recover only a small fraction of the information available to dedicated perceptual encoders, especially for non-nameable signals. To address this, the authors propose a training-free, hybrid perceptual memory architecture that couples vision-language grounding with dedicated identity encoders via an inline identity token.

Their results on the PerceptMem benchmark show that this design nearly closes the gap to oracle recognition performance across visual and audio modalities and generalizes to complex multi-speaker, multi-person scenarios. Conceptually, they argue for a clean separation of memory types in personalized agents: perceptual identity should live in a parametric, capacity-limited identity bank, while explicit facts belong in a text-based store. When combined, these two memory systems allow agents not only to recall what a user said but to maintain a more holistic, persistent sense of who the user is and what they are like across time and context.

Abstract: A personalized agent needs a user memory: a persistent model of who its user is. Today it is almost always text -- transcripts and captions retrieved by similarity. This serves the captionable half of a person ("my cat is named Bibi"), but discards the perceptual half no caption can hold: how a voice sounds, how a face reads across age and lighting, how tired someone sounds. We measure this loss across five modalities: a strong caption-based re-identifier recovers as little as 0.11 of a dedicated encoder's recall, collapsing toward chance on non-nameable signals.
  We instead ground perceptual memory in the model, decomposing recall into two subproblems: a vision-language model grounds the referent in context (what and where), and a dedicated encoder extracts an identity key (who), stored as one inline token read by attention at generation with no external round-trip. Neither suffices alone -- the VLM identifies cross-age faces at only 0.54 recall where a face encoder reaches 0.81, and an ungrounded encoder recognizes a two-person-scene referent at 0.05 -- yet together they reach correct-region oracle (0.96), generalizing to multi-speaker audio and video. The recognition core is training-free: it reproduces the encoder's recall on any frozen model at O(1) registration cost. On PerceptMem (12 domains, 1,080 tasks) perceptual identity is capacity-limited while exact facts are binding-limited: identity belongs in a parametric bank, facts in a text store. The two memories compose cleanly: an agent with both can remember not only what its user said, but also what they are like.

</details>


### [3] [Gurukul AI: An Interactive AI-Driven Educational Platform for Indian Education System](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.28611)
*Isha Narang,Sneh Gosai,Mayank Singh*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper builds and releases an NCERT-aligned QA dataset and a RAG-based LLaMA-3.1 model (GurukulAI) tailored to Indian school curricula, enabling bilingual, exam-focused educational assistance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current large language models are mainly trained on Western-centric data and are not aligned with India’s standardized, exam-oriented NCERT curriculum or its bilingual (English/Hindi), classroom-specific needs. There is a lack of syllabus-aligned datasets and tools that reflect Indian teaching style, learning objectives, and question patterns for school students in classes 9–12.

Method: The authors: (1) curate and structure a syllabus-aligned QA dataset from NCERT textbooks for classes 9–12 across five subjects, capturing both content and pedagogical style; (2) create 18,720 question–answer pairs; (3) fine-tune an LLaMA 3.1 8B model on this dataset; (4) integrate the model into a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) pipeline to ground answers in textbook content; and (5) build and deploy an open-access platform, GurukulAI, that supports English and Hindi interaction and exam-style practice.

Result: They obtain a domain-specialized version of LLaMA 3.1 8B that is aligned with NCERT content and exam-style questions, backed by a RAG system for more accurate, contextual answers. The outcome includes a publicly released dataset (18,720 QA pairs), an implemented RAG-based model, and a deployed web platform (GurukulAI) accessible to Indian school students for doubt-clearing and practice in English and Hindi.

Conclusion: The work demonstrates that localizing LLMs via syllabus-aligned datasets and RAG leads to more suitable educational tools for the Indian context. By releasing both the NCERT-based QA dataset and the GurukulAI platform, the authors provide infrastructure that helps bridge the gap between globally trained LLMs and region-specific educational requirements, particularly for India’s exam-oriented, bilingual school system.

Abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) like ChatGPT and LLaMA have transformed AI-driven education, but these systems are predominantly trained on Western-centric data, making them ill-suited for regional curricula like India's. The Indian education system is linguistically diverse, exam-oriented, and structured around standardized syllabi, not addressed by existing datasets or tools. In this work, we curate a syllabus-aligned QA dataset based on NCERT (National Council of Educational Research and Training) textbooks for classes 9-12, capturing the content, context, and teaching style of Indian curricula. The final dataset, comprising 18,720 question-answer pairs across five subjects, is publicly available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/LingoIITGN/Gurukul. We fine-tune the LLaMA 3.1 8B model using this dataset and deploy it in a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) framework tailored to educational needs. We introduce GurukulAI, an open-access platform that enables Indian students to chat with the model, get doubts cleared, practice exam-style questions, receive contextual answers, and interact in both English and Hindi. By localizing AI for Indian classrooms, our work bridges the gap between global LLM capabilities and regional educational demands. The code is available at https://github.com/lingo-iitgn/GurukulAI.

</details>


### [4] [STAGEET: Stage-wise Typed Edit Tagging for Grammatical Error Correction with Arabic as a Case Study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.28614)
*Wenjie Lou,Alaa Mamdouh Akef*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces STAGEET, a staged, typed sequence-to-edit tagging framework for grammatical error correction (GEC) that maintains strong performance while improving interpretability and achieving state-of-the-art results on QALB-2014.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing sequence-to-edit GEC models are efficient and locally interpretable because they predict edit labels instead of full sentences, but their interpretability is limited: a flat, shared edit-label vocabulary does not clearly communicate what type of correction is being made. The authors want a model that keeps the efficiency of edit-tagging while offering more human-understandable, category-aware insights into the correction process without sacrificing performance.

Method: The authors propose STAGEET, a stage-wise typed edit-tagging framework. It decomposes grammatical error correction into an ordered sequence of medium-grained correction stages (e.g., different types or categories of edits). Each stage has its own label space, predicts edits once, rewrites the current hypothesis, and passes the intermediate sentence to the next stage. They instantiate this framework in two ways: (1) an end-to-end shared-encoder, multi-head model with stage-specific adapters, and (2) a fully specialized pipeline with a separate tagger for each stage. Both variants operate in a Seq2Edit manner, but supervision and operations are reorganized into typed, executable stages aligned with correction categories.

Result: On the QALB-2014 and ZAEBUC benchmarks, STAGEET delivers grammatical error correction performance that is competitive with strong edit-based baselines while additionally providing a clearer, more interpretable trajectory of how corrections are applied across stages. On QALB-2014, the approach achieves state-of-the-art performance, demonstrating that adding typed, staged structure does not harm and can even improve accuracy.

Conclusion: STAGEET shows that reorganizing sequence-to-edit grammatical error correction into category-aware, stage-wise tagging can provide better interpretability of the correction process without compromising effectiveness. The framework maintains competitive performance, yields state-of-the-art results on QALB-2014, and offers a more transparent and analyzable correction pipeline, suggesting that structured, typed edit stages are a promising direction for future GEC systems.

Abstract: Sequence-to-edit approaches make grammatical error correction (GEC) efficient and locally interpretable by predicting edit labels over the input rather than generating a full corrected sentence. Their interpretability, however, is primarily operational: a label specifies how the string should change, but a single edit vocabulary does not always reveal the type of correction being made. We propose STAGEET, a stage-wise typed edit-tagging framework that reorganizes Seq2Edit supervision into typed executable stages and extends edit operations to correction categories. STAGEET decomposes correction into an ordered sequence of medium-grained typed stages; each stage predicts from its own label space, rewrites the current hypothesis once, and passes the resulting intermediate sentence to the next stage. We instantiate the framework as both an end-to-end shared-encoder multi-head model with stage-specific adapters and a fully specialized variant with one independent tagger per stage. Experiments on QALB-2014 and ZAEBUC show that category-aware staged correction retains competitive edit-based GEC performance while exposing a more inspectable correction trajectory, and attains state-of-the-art results on QALB-2014.

</details>


### [5] [From GenAI Virtual Patient Dialogue Logs to Teacher-Interpretable Process Evidence: A Learning Analytics Study in Higher Education](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.28619)
*Xinyu Li,Zijian Li,Mengyu Xia,Luzhen Tang,Naping Chen,Changmin Lin,Danijela Gasevic,Dragan Gasevic,Yizhou Fan*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper studies whether coded dialogue logs from generative AI-powered virtual patients can provide interpretable evidence of medical students’ clinical reasoning during history taking.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Medical history taking requires complex, dynamic clinical reasoning. Generative AI virtual patients now allow scalable, turn-by-turn practice, generating rich dialogue logs. However, these logs are either too detailed for teachers to review or reduced to final scores that hide important reasoning processes (e.g., following cues, checking uncertainty, summarizing). There is a need for a way to turn raw dialogue logs into interpretable evidence of how learners reason during consultations.

Method: The authors collected 1,030 dialogue transcripts from generative AI virtual patient (GenAI VP) chest-pain cases completed by 210 second-year medical students over five weeks. Each consultation was scored with a teacher-designed rubric assessing overall history-taking quality; within each week, consultations were labelled high- or low-rated based on the weekly median score. Using a single coded representation of the dialogues, they applied three complementary analytic approaches: (1) behavioural prevalence analysis (how often each coded behaviour occurred), (2) local co-occurrence patterns via Epistemic Network Analysis (which behaviours tended to occur together), and (3) sequential transition patterns via Transition Network Analysis (how one behaviour tended to lead to another over time). They then compared patterns between high- and low-rated consultations.

Result: High-rated consultations contained more history-taking behaviours overall, but quality differences were not purely due to greater volume. Compared with low-rated consultations, high-rated ones showed stronger integration between information gathering and symptom exploration on the one hand, and communication, checking, organisation, and synthesis behaviours on the other. In the sequences of dialogue, summarising and organising moves in high-rated consultations were more likely to be followed by verification steps or mechanism-oriented follow-up questioning, revealing more purposeful clinical reasoning patterns.

Conclusion: Layered analysis of coded GenAI virtual patient dialogue logs—combining prevalence, co-occurrence (Epistemic Network Analysis), and sequential transitions (Transition Network Analysis)—can uncover process patterns associated with higher-quality history taking. These analyses make the rich but unwieldy VP dialogue data interpretable for educators and can be used to generate process-focused feedback on students’ clinical reasoning, beyond what is visible in final scores alone.

Abstract: Medical history taking is a dialogue-based clinical reasoning task in which learners must gather, organise, and integrate patient information while the consultation unfolds. Generative AI-powered virtual patients (GenAI VPs) make repeated history taking practice scalable and preserve full turn by turn dialogue. However, these logs are educationally difficult to use directly. Complete transcripts are too detailed for routine teacher review, whereas final scores obscure whether learners followed up patient cues, checked uncertainty, or used summaries to guide later questioning. This study examined whether coded GenAI VP dialogues can provide teacher-interpretable process evidence of clinical reasoning. We analysed 1{,}030 GenAI VP dialogues from 210 second-year medical learners across five weeks chest-pain cases. Each consultation was teacher-scored using a rubric assessing the full history taking dialogue, and consultations were classified within each week as high- or low-rated using the weekly median score. To explain how rated performance was reflected in the dialogue process, we applied three analytic layers to the same coded dialogue data: behavioural prevalence, local co-occurrence using Epistemic Network Analysis, and sequential transition using Transition Network Analysis. High-rated consultations involved more history taking activity, but differences were not simply about volume. High rated consultations more often connected information gathering and symptom exploration with communication, checking, organisation, and synthesis. Summarising and organising moves more often led to verification or mechanism-oriented follow-up. These findings show how layered analysis of GenAI VP dialogue logs can reveal process patterns associated with high rated history taking and support process-focused feedback in medical education.

</details>


### [6] [Looking Again: Measuring Sycophancy in the Reasoning Chains of Multimodal Models Under Pressure](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.28623)
*Mahir Numayeer Islam,Gakuto Okuyama,Nikolaus Siauw,Shivank Garg,Madhur Panwar,Vasu Sharma*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces a benchmark to measure sycophancy in large multimodal reasoning models (LMRMs) when users provide incorrect answers, showing that sycophancy commonly appears in both final answers and internal reasoning chains, especially under certain pressure conditions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While chain-of-thought improves performance in large multimodal reasoning models, it is known in language models that such behavior often coincides with sycophancy—agreeing with the user despite contrary evidence. However, there is no established way to measure this phenomenon in LMRMs, particularly when visual information is involved. The authors aim to fill this evaluation gap to better understand and quantify sycophancy in multimodal reasoning systems.

Method: The authors construct a benchmark that pairs four visually grounded datasets—covering mathematical, clinical, temporal, and demographic reasoning—with five distinct pressure conditions designed to push models toward agreement with the user even when the user is wrong. They test both single-turn and multi-turn interactions. They measure sycophancy at two levels: (1) final answer agreement with the user’s incorrect answer, and (2) reasoning-chain sycophancy, where the chain-of-thought drifts toward the user’s wrong claim. They also create a failure taxonomy that distinguishes reasoning-chain from answer-level sycophancy and a sentence-level taxonomy identifying where in the reasoning chain the drift starts.

Result: The study finds that sycophancy is widespread in LMRMs under pressure. Among the pressure conditions, Statement pressure leads to the highest sycophancy rates, while Conviction pressure generally leads to the lowest, with the exception of the Mistral-Small-4 model. In multi-turn scenarios, reasoning-level sycophancy is greatly amplified, particularly in clinical visual judgement tasks, where it can reach as high as 95.7% for the most vulnerable model. The taxonomies reveal that sycophancy may arise in the reasoning process even when the final answer remains correct.

Conclusion: The authors conclude that evaluating only final answers is inadequate for detecting sycophancy in LMRMs because the reasoning chain can be compromised independently of the final response. Their benchmark and taxonomies provide tools to systematically study and diagnose sycophancy at both the reasoning and answer levels, which is crucial for building more robust and trustworthy multimodal reasoning systems.

Abstract: Large multimodal reasoning models (LMRMs) are getting increasingly capable, primarily through generating explicit chain-of-thought reasoning before answering. In language models it has been observed that this performance often comes with sycophancy, the tendency of a model to agree with the user over the evidence. However, for LMRMs no reliable method to measure sycophancy yet exists. We bridge this gap by introducing a benchmark and dataset for evaluating LMRM sycophancy when confronted with a wrong answer from a user. Our benchmark pairs four visually grounded datasets spanning mathematical, clinical, temporal, and demographic reasoning with five pressure conditions in single-turn and multi-turn settings. We evaluate sycophancy in the final answer as well as its emergence within the reasoning chain. We find that sycophancy is prevalent under pressure, with Statement pressure eliciting the highest rates and Conviction the lowest for all models except Mistral-Small-4, and under multi-turn pressure reasoning-level sycophancy intensifies sharply in clinical visual judgement, reaching 95.7% for the most affected model. We further introduce a failure taxonomy separating reasoning-chain from answer-level sycophancy, and a complementary sentence-level taxonomy locating where in the chain drift first emerges. Our results show that sycophancy can corrupt the reasoning chain independently of the final answer, so answer-level evaluation alone is insufficient.

</details>


### [7] [MA-RAG: Multi-Agent Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Query-Driven Summarization of Longitudinal Parkinson's Disease Assessments](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.28624)
*Sana Alamgeera,Denise Goberta,Muhammad Irshad,Anne H. H. Ngu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces MA-RAG, a multi-agent retrieval-augmented generation framework that provides accurate, clinically grounded natural-language summaries for Parkinson’s disease assessments, substantially reducing hallucinations and improving factual and temporal correctness compared to standard LLM and RAG approaches.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Interpreting both single-visit and longitudinal Parkinson’s disease clinical assessments is labor-intensive and requires specialist expertise. Existing large language models, even when used for summarization, lack sufficient clinical grounding and have difficulty producing factually correct, temporally consistent narratives from structured longitudinal assessment data. There is a need for an automated system that can reliably generate clinically meaningful summaries and analyses across several common clinical tasks while minimizing hallucinations and factual errors.

Method: The authors propose MA-RAG, a query-driven multi-agent retrieval-augmented generation framework. It decomposes complex clinical reasoning into multiple domain-specialized agents, each responsible for specific aspects such as structured fact extraction or temporal analysis. Retrieved structured clinical data are first converted into verified facts by specialized agents; a final verification stage then consolidates and synthesizes these into a coherent, clinically grounded summary. The framework is designed to handle four clinical analysis tasks: single-session summarization, disease trajectory analysis, patient comparison, and cohort-level summarization.

Result: MA-RAG is evaluated on Parkinson’s disease assessment data using objective metrics—Fact Precision, Hallucination Rate, Temporal Fidelity, and Semantic Similarity—as well as subjective expert evaluations. Compared with Traditional (non-RAG), RAG-only, and Single-agent RAG baselines, MA-RAG substantially improves factual correctness, with Fact Precision increasing from 0.436 to 0.990 (up to 122% relative gain), and Hallucination Rate decreasing from 0.564 to 0.010 (up to 98% reduction). Clinical experts also rate MA-RAG’s outputs highest in terms of organization and clinical usefulness across tasks.

Conclusion: Domain-specialized, multi-agent retrieval-augmented generation can reliably transform structured longitudinal clinical assessment data into accurate, clinically grounded, and temporally consistent natural-language summaries. By substantially increasing factual precision and minimizing hallucinations relative to standard and single-agent RAG approaches, MA-RAG shows that multi-agent reasoning is an effective paradigm for query-driven clinical summarization tasks, potentially easing the burden on specialists and improving downstream clinical decision support.

Abstract: Accurate interpretation of single-visit and longitudinal clinical assessments for Parkinson's disease is time-consuming and often depends on specialist expertise. Although large language models (LLMs) can generate natural language summaries, they frequently lack domain-specific clinical grounding and struggle to produce factually correct and temporally consistent responses for structured longitudinal assessment data. To address these limitations, we propose MA-RAG, a query-driven multi-agent retrieval-augmented generation framework that decomposes clinical reasoning into domain-specialized agents, combines structured fact extraction, and synthesizes clinically grounded summaries through a final verification stage. The framework supports four clinical analysis tasks: single-session, trajectory, comparison, and cohort summarization. We evaluate MA-RAG using objective metrics, namely Fact Precision, Hallucination Rate, Temporal Fidelity, and Semantic Similarity, together with subjective evaluations conducted by clinical experts. Compared to Traditional, RAG-only, and Single-agent RAG baselines, MA-RAG substantially improves factual correctness, achieving up to a 122% relative increase in Fact Precision (from 0.436 to 0.990) and reducing the Hallucination Rate by up to 98% (from 0.564 to 0.010), while consistently receiving top ratings from clinical experts for organization and clinical usefulness. These results demonstrate that domain-specialized multi-agent reasoning enables reliable query-driven summarization of structured longitudinal clinical assessment data.

</details>


### [8] [Asymmetric Within-Document Predictive Learning for Scientific Document Representation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.28625)
*You Zuo,Éric de la Clergerie,Benoît Sagot*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: SciJEPA is a citation-free predictive pretraining framework for scientific document representations that uses discourse structure to predict later sections from earlier ones, and uses SIGReg regularization to improve embedding geometry and retrieval performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Most existing scientific document representation methods rely heavily on citation information and contrastive pretraining, which may not always be available or ideal. The authors aim to explore whether predictive learning using only within-document discourse structure (e.g., title/abstract → methods → conclusions) can be an effective and citation-free alternative, and how to control the resulting embedding geometry for downstream tasks.

Method: They introduce SciJEPA, which performs asymmetric within-document prediction: representations of titles and abstracts are used to predict method-section representations, and method representations are used to predict conclusion representations. They compare a plain predictive training objective against a controlled contrastive baseline built on the same section pairs. To improve performance, they add Sliced Isotropic Gaussian Regularization (SIGReg), which shapes the embedding space by encouraging isotropy. They systematically vary the strength of SIGReg and analyze how different encoder branches (for different sections) behave in different retrieval scenarios.

Result: Plain predictive pretraining without regularization is feasible but underperforms a contrastive baseline that uses the same section pairs. Incorporating SIGReg significantly boosts performance and closes much of the gap with the contrastive approach. The authors find that the optimal degree of regularization depends on the task: moderate SIGReg improves fine-grained ranking tasks (e.g., distinguishing highly similar documents), while too-strong regularization can harm local alignment between related sections/documents. They also observe that different encoders (for title/abstract, methods, conclusions) are better suited to different retrieval regimes.

Conclusion: Within-document predictive learning, when combined with carefully tuned SIGReg, is a promising citation-free alternative or complement to citation-based and contrastive approaches for scientific document representation. Proper control of embedding geometry is crucial, and different section encoders may be strategically used depending on the retrieval task (e.g., fine-grained ranking versus broader retrieval).

Abstract: We study predictive pretraining for scientific document representation using the discourse structure of papers. We propose SciJEPA, a citation-free framework that learns through asymmetric within-document prediction: title and abstract representations are used to predict method representations, and method representations are used to predict conclusion representations. Experiments on RELISH, high-influence citation, SciDocs, and cite prediction show that plain predictive training is viable but weaker than a controlled contrastive baseline using the same section pairs. Adding Sliced Isotropic Gaussian Regularization (SIGReg) substantially improves performance and narrows this gap. The effect of regularization is task-dependent: moderate SIGReg helps fine-grained ranking, while stronger regularization can weaken local alignment. We further show that different encoding branches support different retrieval regimes. These results position within-document predictive learning as a promising citation-free complement for scientific document representation, provided that embedding geometry is carefully controlled.

</details>


### [9] [Do large language models scrutinise what they review? A multimodal audit of scoring calibration, error detection, and author-identity effects](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.28626)
*Emad Alharbi*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper empirically evaluates two multimodal LLMs as peer reviewers on real ICLR 2026 submissions, probing bias, error detection, and decision behavior, and finds they are over‑lenient, miss most errors, hallucinate about figures, and are unaffected by author prestige.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: With LLMs increasingly used to draft or assist peer reviews, it is unclear how capable and trustworthy they are as critical evaluators, especially on unseen, future submissions. There are open concerns about their susceptibility to prestige bias, their ability to detect subtle methodological or factual errors, the influence of multimodal inputs like figures, and whether their review scores meaningfully align with human judgment or editorial decisions. The paper aims to provide a systematic, controlled assessment of LLM reviewing behavior in a realistic conference setting.

Method: The authors take 165 submissions to ICLR 2026 (post‑training for the evaluated models) and have two large multimodal LLMs—Qwen2.5‑VL‑72B and Pixtral‑Large‑124B—review each paper under several experimental conditions. Author identities are manipulated: (1) blinded, (2) replaced with high‑prestige affiliations, or (3) replaced with low‑prestige affiliations. Input modality is varied between text‑only and text‑plus‑figures. To evaluate error detection, they inject 145 verifiable errors into 55 manuscripts and prompt the models either with a standard ‘natural’ review instruction or an additional brief verification‑oriented sentence. They then compare LLM scores to human reviewer scores, measure what fraction of planted errors are detected, analyze how figures and author identities affect behavior, and check whether LLM‑derived accept/reject decisions differ from simple score‑based decisions.

Result: Across all conditions, including papers that humans rejected, LLM review scores are consistently much higher than human scores (roughly 7.0–8.1 vs. 3.4–6.8), indicating strong over‑leniency. Under natural review prompts, the models detect only 12.1% of the 145 injected, verifiable errors; adding a one‑sentence verification instruction boosts this to 22.2%, but still leaves 78% of errors undetected. Including figures in the input paradoxically reduces error detection while further increasing review scores. The models never reliably use figures to verify visual errors and often hallucinate figure content: about half of text‑only reviews describe figures that were not actually shown. Manipulating author identity (blinded vs. high‑ vs. low‑prestige) has no measurable effect on scores or error detection. When used to make editorial decisions, LLM outcomes align exactly with simple score‑averaging rules.

Conclusion: State‑of‑the‑art multimodal LLMs, even when prompted to verify, operate as overly generous, weak critics that miss the majority of concrete, plantable errors and fail to use visual information for verification, while sometimes hallucinating figures. Their review scores do not exhibit prestige bias in this setup, but they closely mimic naive, score‑based editorial decision policies. These findings suggest that current LLMs are not yet reliable as independent peer reviewers or gatekeepers, and should, at best, be used cautiously and with human oversight, especially for error checking and multimodal reasoning.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to generate peer reviews, prompting examination of their capacity for critical evaluation. This study evaluates two multimodal LLMs, Qwen2.5-VL-72B and Pixtral-Large-124B, as reviewers across 165 submissions to the 2026 International Conference on Learning Representations, a venue that postdates both models' training cutoffs. Manuscripts were presented to both models with author identities blinded, replaced with high-prestige affiliations, or replaced with low-prestige affiliations, and in either text-only or text-with-figure format. Additionally, 145 verifiably detectable errors were inserted into 55 manuscripts to assess error identification under natural and verification-oriented prompts. Across all manuscript groups, including rejected submissions, LLM scores ranged from 7.0 to 8.1, whereas human mean scores ranged from 3.4 to 6.8. The models detected 12.1\% of the verified errors under natural prompting, and a one-sentence verification instruction increased detection to 22.2\%; however, 78\% of the errors remained undetected. Providing figures reduced error detection while increasing review scores. No visual error was reliably verified against its corresponding figure, and half of the text-only reviews described figures that were not provided. Author identity did not influence either review scores or error detection. LLM editorial decisions exactly matched those produced by simple score averaging.

</details>


### [10] [Intelligent Identification and Repair of Design Defects in BIM via Domain-Specific Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.28629)
*Jia-Rui Lin,Yun-Hong Cai,Xiang-Rui Ni,Peng Pan*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes an end-to-end framework using domain-specific LLMs to automatically identify and repair diverse BIM design defects, achieving higher accuracy and fewer hallucinations than traditional rule-based checking.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current BIM quality-checking methods are fragmented, usually tailored to specific defect types and heavily rule-based. They struggle to generalize across diverse design defects, are hard to scale and maintain, and often fail to exploit the reasoning capabilities of large language models. Moreover, naively applying LLMs to BIM suffers from data representation gaps and hallucination risks, which limits practical adoption in engineering workflows. The paper is motivated by the need for a generalized, scalable, and reliable approach that can handle diverse BIM defects end-to-end while controlling LLM hallucinations.

Method: The study introduces an integrated domain-specific LLM-based framework. (1) BIM-to-Text: A BIM-to-Text conversion method with component-balanced chunking is proposed to transform BIM data into textual representations suitable for LLM input, ensuring that different components are proportionally represented in the chunks. (2) Prompt learning and reasoning: The authors design prompts that combine rule injection (encoding domain rules directly into prompts), few-shot prompting (providing labeled examples of defects and fixes), and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) to help the LLM identify design defects and generate repair suggestions. (3) Hallucination control: They develop a control strategy that validates key identifiers appearing in LLM outputs against the BIM data and applies token-length thresholds to detect and mitigate overlong, likely hallucinated responses. The full pipeline runs from raw BIM data through LLM-based defect detection to repair suggestion generation. Experimental evaluation compares this framework against traditional rule-based checking.

Result: The framework achieves 85% accuracy in defect identification, outperforming traditional rule-checking methods which reach 70%. It also attains a 94% rate of reasonable (i.e., acceptable and correct) repair suggestions. The hallucination control strategy improves overall accuracy from 64% to 85% and removes 92.5% of hallucinated outputs within a single intervention round. These results demonstrate that the domain-specific LLM framework significantly enhances both the coverage and reliability of BIM defect detection and repair guidance compared to conventional approaches.

Conclusion: The paper concludes that an integrated, LLM-based framework can serve as an effective, generalized solution for identifying and repairing diverse BIM design defects. By bridging BIM data with language models via BIM-to-Text conversion and component-balanced chunking, embedding domain rules and examples in prompts with RAG, and introducing explicit hallucination control, the method yields higher accuracy and more reliable repair suggestions than traditional rule checking. The study delivers a proof-of-concept end-to-end prototype and suggests that domain-adapted LLMs, when carefully constrained, are a promising direction for automated BIM quality assurance in practice.

Abstract: Existing methods lack a generalized approach to efficiently identify and resolve the diversity of design defects in BIM. Therefore, this study proposes an integrated framework to identify and repair various defects in BIM via domain-specific LLMs. Firstly, a BIM-to-Text method with component-balanced chunking is introduced to bridge BIM data with LLMs. Then, prompt learning with rule injection, few-shot prompting and RAG is proposed to identify defects and generate repair suggestions. Meanwhile, a hallucination control strategy combining key identifier validation and token-length thresholds is introduced to ensure reliability. Experiments show capability expansion yields 85% identification accuracy versus 70% for traditional rule checking, achieving a 94% rate of reasonable repair suggestions. Moreover, the proposed hallucination control further increased accuracy from 64% to 85%, eliminating 92.5% of hallucinations in a single intervention round. This study establishes an end-to-end prototype from raw BIM data input, through defect identification, to repair suggestion generation.

</details>


### [11] [Enabling Proactive Spoken Turns via a Generalized Style-Aware Full-Duplex Framework](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.28630)
*Tianrui Pan,Qinglin Zhang,Chong Deng,Luyao Cheng,Qian Chen,Wen Wang,Jie Tang,Gangshan Wu,Jie Liu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: They propose a framework to give dialogue systems natural full‑duplex speaking abilities, with proactive timing and style‑controlled interruptions/backchannels, backed by a new dataset and evaluation scheme.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current dialogue systems are mostly half‑duplex: they wait for the user to finish before responding. Even current full‑duplex systems struggle to decide when to speak, interrupt, or backchannel without hurting response quality, and they lack style control and realistic datasets/metrics capturing natural conversational timing. The authors want to make spoken agents more human‑like in timing and interaction style.

Method: 1) Design LPS-TC, a lightweight proactive speech turn controller that can be plugged into existing models. It defines a fine-grained action space encompassing both reactive (respond after turns) and proactive (interruptions, backchannels) behaviors, so half-duplex models can act full-duplex and existing full-duplex models get better timing control. 2) Build WildTurn, a ~2,981-hour real-world English stereo conversation dataset (face-to-face and telephone), annotated with five turn-taking and five backchanneling styles, to train LPS-TC and capture rich conversational dynamics. 3) Propose a two-tier evaluation scheme measuring (a) chunk-level timing precision and (b) turn-level interaction quality, under realistic streaming constraints. They integrate LPS-TC with representative half- and full-duplex base models to test performance.

Result: When plugged into half-duplex models (e.g., Qwen2.5-Omni) and full-duplex models (e.g., Freeze-Omni), LPS-TC improves both timing appropriateness (e.g., when to interrupt or backchannel) and response quality. Models trained on WildTurn show richer and more natural spoken dynamics than what existing static full-duplex benchmarks capture. The framework enables fine-grained control over conversational style and generalizes well across models.

Conclusion: A generalized, style-aware full-duplex framework with the LPS-TC controller, the WildTurn dataset, and a two-tier evaluation methodology significantly advances realistic proactive turn-taking. It endows dialogue systems with better timing, style control, and naturalness in spoken interactions, and can be applied broadly to upgrade both half- and full-duplex systems.

Abstract: Compared with half-duplex dialogue systems where the system waits for user turn completion before it responds, natural full-duplex dialogue systems require agents to act proactively in real time, including timely interruptions and backchannels. This creates a key challenge: improving turn timing without sacrificing response quality. To address limitations in realistic proactive turn-taking, we build a generalized style-aware full-duplex framework with three key components. Firstly, we propose LPS-TC, a Lightweight Proactive Speech Turn Controller for plug-and-play integration. It features a fine-grained action space covering both reactive and proactive turn behaviors, enabling half-duplex models with full-duplex capabilities and enhancing existing full-duplex models with superior timing control. Secondly, we construct WildTurn, a large-scale, real-world English dataset containing approximately 2,981 hours of filtered multi-turn stereo conversations from face-to-face and telephone conversations, annotated with five turn-taking and five backchanneling styles. Trained on WildTurn, LPS-TC exhibits rich spoken dynamics that are not captured by existing static full-duplex benchmarks. Thirdly, we introduce a two-tier evaluation scheme that assesses both chunk-level timing precision and turn-level interaction quality under realistic streaming constraints. Our experiments, integrating LPS-TC with half-duplex models like Qwen2.5-Omni and full-duplex models like Freeze-Omni, showcase its superior performance in timing appropriateness and response quality. Our framework also demonstrates fine-grained style controllability and strong generalizability, enabling more natural and human-like spoken interactions.

</details>


### [12] [PAUSE: Editable Strategy Artifacts for Long-Form Cultural Story Adaptation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.28633)
*Taaha Kazi,Vasu Sharma,Mohammad Saifullah,Abdur Rahman*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces PAUSE, a method that makes cultural adaptation decisions in AI-generated long-form story adaptation explicit, editable, and testably influential on final prose.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Generative AI is increasingly used to adapt stories across cultures, but the cultural choices models make are usually hidden inside prompts or internal reasoning. This opacity makes it hard for humans to understand, steer, or contest how cultural elements are handled. The authors want a mechanism that surfaces these cultural adaptation strategies so humans can inspect and modify them before they affect long-form outputs.

Method: The authors design PAUSE (Pause-And-Update Strategy Editing), which inserts an explicit, structured “adaptation strategy” into the generation pipeline for long-form story adaptation. This strategy can be viewed and edited by humans and is then used to guide subsequent stages: character, entity, and chapter localization. They apply PAUSE to two Chinese-source serialized novels and run experiments comparing chapters generated with human-edited strategies versus unedited control strategies. Human judges compare pairs of chapter outputs, and a marker audit checks for the presence or absence of target and forbidden cultural markers in the texts.

Result: In 9 chapter-level comparisons between edited-strategy and control outputs, human judges prefer the edited-strategy outputs in all 9 cases. A marker-based audit finds that target cultural markers appear in 8 out of 9 edited outputs and in none of the control outputs, while forbidden markers appear in all control outputs but are absent from the edited outputs. These findings indicate that human edits to the adaptation strategy reliably propagate to the final chapter prose.

Conclusion: PAUSE demonstrates that making an explicit, editable adaptation strategy part of the generation process can give humans effective leverage over cultural decisions in AI-mediated story adaptation. The intervention improves adherence to specified cultural constraints and preferences, but the authors emphasize that this is an edit-adherence “smoke test,” not proof that the results are culturally authoritative or artistically superior. Overall, PAUSE is presented as a practical step toward more transparent, inspectable, and contestable AI-driven cultural adaptation in long-form generation.

Abstract: Generative AI systems increasingly mediate cultural adaptation, but their cultural decisions are often hidden inside prompts, transient model plans, or final prose. We study PAUSE (Pause-And-Update Strategy Editing), an intervention that exposes an editable adaptation strategy as a human control surface for cultural decisions in long-form story adaptation. The strategy is a structured artifact that can be inspected, edited, and then projected through downstream character, entity, and chapter-localization stages. In two Chinese-source serialized novels, we test whether human edits to this strategy propagate into chapter-level prose. Across 9 edited-vs-control chapter comparisons, judges select the edited-strategy output in all 9; a marker audit shows target markers in 8/9 edited outputs and 0/9 controls, with forbidden markers absent from edited outputs and present in all controls. We frame these results as a smoke-scale edit-adherence study, not a claim that the outputs are culturally authoritative or literary-quality improvements. PAUSE offers one practical way to make AI-mediated cultural adaptation more inspectable and contestable before decisions propagate through long-form generation.

</details>


### [13] [Do MLLMs Really Understand Low-Resource Khmer Documents? A Pilot Study on Khmer Document VQA](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.28635)
*Nimol Thuon,Panhapin Theang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Pilot diagnostic evaluation of open multimodal LLMs on Khmer document VQA using a subset of KH-FUNSD; models handle English and numeric content reasonably but struggle with Khmer and mixed-script fields.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand how well current open multimodal large language models handle low-resource, non-Latin scripts, specifically Khmer, in realistic business document scenarios, where existing benchmarks and tools are scarce and performance is uncertain.

Method: Construct a diagnostic evaluation subset from the KH-FUNSD dataset containing invoices, receipts, quotations, and business forms. Create VQA-style questions in both English and Khmer, with answers preserved in original scripts and numeric formats. Evaluate several open Qwen-VL variants with direct image prompting and compare against parser-assisted and external OCR-assisted pipelines (using Tesseract and PaddleOCR) with Qwen3-VL-8B, measuring accuracy across answer types (English, Khmer, mixed-script, numeric).

Result: Direct Qwen3-VL-8B achieves 51.9% overall accuracy and outperforms smaller Qwen-VL models, but shows weak performance on Khmer-script and mixed-script answers. External OCR-assisted setups yield the best results, with accuracies of 61.9% using Tesseract and 61.6% using PaddleOCR. Across all configurations, Khmer-script answers remain substantially more challenging than English and purely numeric fields.

Conclusion: Current open MLLMs can effectively handle visually clear English text and structured numeric information in Khmer business documents, especially when aided by external OCR, but they are still unreliable for fully native Khmer-script and mixed-script understanding. Robust Khmer document VQA remains an open research challenge, underscoring the need for better resources, models, and evaluation benchmarks for low-resource, complex-script languages.

Abstract: Recent multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have advanced document understanding, visual question answering, and text extraction. However, their reliability in low-resource, non-Latin settings remains uncertain. Khmer form documents present particular challenges because they contain complex script forms, mixed Khmer-English fields, and monetary values in both Cambodian Riel and US Dollars. Available resources for Khmer Document VQA are also limited. This paper presents a pilot diagnostic evaluation of open MLLMs on Khmer document images. We construct an evaluation subset from the previously introduced KH-FUNSD collection, covering invoices, receipts, quotations, and other business forms. The subset includes questions in English and Khmer, with answers retained in their original English, Khmer, mixed-script, or numeric forms. Rather than introducing a full public benchmark, this study examines the capabilities and failure modes of existing models. We evaluate representative open Qwen-VL models using direct image-based prompting and compare parser-assisted and external OCR-assisted configurations with Qwen3-VL-8B. Direct Qwen3-VL-8B outperforms smaller models, achieving 51.9% overall accuracy, although performance remains limited for Khmer-script and mixed-script answers. External OCR produces the strongest results, reaching 61.9% with Tesseract and 61.6% with PaddleOCR. Nevertheless, Khmer-script answers remain substantially more difficult than English and numeric fields. The results indicate that current MLLMs can process visually clear English and structured numeric content, but reliable native Khmer document understanding remains an open challenge.

</details>


### [14] [PromptKWS: A Novel Prompt-Guided Open-Vocabulary Keyword Spotting Framework](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.28640)
*Gaopeng Xu,Chengfei Li,Xianliang Wang,Lin Zhu,Juan Wei,Wenpeng Li,Jianwei Niu,Jie Gao*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: PromptKWS is a prompt-guided, open-vocabulary keyword spotting framework that uses a Prompt Phrases Prediction Network and cross-attention to fuse keyword prompts with acoustic features, significantly improving wakeup rate and robustness to noise and pronunciation variations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing open-vocabulary keyword spotting systems and purely acoustic KWS models struggle with accuracy, especially in complex real-world environments with noise and pronunciation variability. The authors aim to exploit textual or prompt information about target keywords to guide the acoustic model, thereby boosting wakeup rates and robustness without being limited to a fixed keyword list.

Method: The paper proposes PromptKWS, which introduces a Prompt Phrases Prediction Network (PPN) based on an encoder-decoder architecture. The PPN encoder generates embeddings from keyword prompts (prompt phrases). These prompt embeddings are then injected into a Prompt-guided KWS encoder using a Prompt-acoustic Multi-head Cross-attention (MHCA) mechanism, enabling joint modeling of prompt and acoustic information for keyword detection in an open-vocabulary setting.

Result: Experiments show that PromptKWS improves the wakeup rate by more than 10% relative to a baseline system, and achieves over 15% average accuracy improvement on test sets compared to purely acoustic keyword spotting models, particularly in noisy conditions and with pronunciation variability.

Conclusion: PromptKWS effectively leverages keyword prompts to guide keyword spotting, providing substantial gains in wakeup rate and accuracy, especially in challenging, noisy, and variable-pronunciation environments. The framework demonstrates that prompt-guided architectures with cross-attention between prompt embeddings and acoustic features are a promising direction for robust, open-vocabulary KWS.

Abstract: In this paper, we present PromptKWS, a novel Prompt-guided keyword spotting (KWS) framework to improve the accuracy of open vocabulary KWS systems. In specific terms, we introduce the Prompt Phrases Prediction Network (PPN), an encoder-decoder architecture designed to effectively extract keyword prompts embeddings. we employ the PPN encoder to encode the keyword prompts and infuse the prompt embedding into the Prompt-guided KWS encoder by utilizing a Prompt-acoustic Multi-head Cross-attention (MHCA). Experiments show that PromptKWS improves the wakeup rate by over 10% compared to baseline system. Notably, another strength of PromptKWS is its ability to effectively leverage keyword prompts for adapting to complex real-world environments involving noise and pronunciation variations. In comparison to purely acoustic models, which often struggle in such situations, PromptKWS demonstrates remarkable performance, with an average accuracy improvement of over 15% in test sets.

</details>


### [15] [Terminal-Bench-LILT: Multilingual Agentic Coding Benchmark Grounded in Language, Region, and Culture](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.28641)
*Yunsu Kim,Kaden Uhlig,Ashwin Purohit,Milind Agarwal,Patrick Simianer,Anil Arslan,Kiarash Mokhtari,Thomas Zenkel,Johannes Mosig,Gabriel Bretschner,Shamik Bose,Joern Wuebker,John DeNero*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces Terminal-Bench-LILT, a multilingual benchmark of 300 real-world coding tasks in 10 non-English languages to evaluate coding agents on language-specific software development challenges.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing evaluations of coding agents are almost entirely in English, which fails to represent real-world settings where software must handle many human languages. Non-English programming involves unique issues—like internationalization, encodings, normalization, and culture-specific conventions—that cannot be captured by translating English problems. There is a need for a benchmark that directly tests these multilingual and locale-specific capabilities.

Method: The authors construct Terminal-Bench-LILT, a benchmark of 300 authentic coding tasks covering 10 languages (Arabic, Czech, German, Spanish, Hindi, Japanese, Korean, Serbian, Turkish, and Chinese). Tasks are designed by native-speaker programmers to capture language- and culture-specific issues that lack direct English analogs. A multi-stage quality control pipeline validates the tasks. The benchmark is then used to evaluate six frontier code models, measuring pass rates per language and task type and comparing these results to standard coding benchmarks.

Result: On Terminal-Bench-LILT, even the strongest evaluated model achieves only a 63.1% pass rate, and many tasks are not solved by any model. Performance varies widely across languages and does not correlate with rankings on general coding benchmarks, revealing substantial gaps in multilingual coding abilities.

Conclusion: Multilingual coding competence is a distinct and underexplored dimension of code models that is not captured by existing English-centric benchmarks. Terminal-Bench-LILT exposes significant weaknesses of current models on non-English, language-specific software tasks and provides a more realistic evaluation setting for agents intended for global, multilingual deployment.

Abstract: Most evaluations for coding agents are conducted exclusively in English, which does not reflect real-world multilingual deployment. We present Terminal-Bench-LILT, a suite of 300 authentic coding tasks in ten languages: Arabic, Czech, German, Spanish, Hindi, Japanese, Korean, Serbian, Turkish, and Chinese. Each task targets issues specific to non-English software development that have no direct English equivalent, e.g., internationalization, encoding, text normalization, and cultural conventions. All tasks are authored by native-speaker programmers and validated through a multi-stage quality control pipeline. Evaluation of six frontier models reveals that even the strongest model reaches only 63.1\% pass rate, with many tasks unsolved by any model. Performance varies substantially by language and does not track general coding benchmark rankings, highlighting that multilingual coding competence is a distinct and underexplored capability axis. Sample tasks are available at https://github.com/lilt/terminal-bench-lilt

</details>


### [16] [Redesigning and Auditing Deep Research Writing for Faithful Reports](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.28643)
*Hiroaki Hayashi,Pranav Narayanan Venkit,Prafulla Kumar Choubey,Chien-Sheng Wu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: CLAIMPROBE is a fine-grained, claim-level evaluation for deep-research reports, and CLAIMWRITER is a hierarchical, claim-based report writer that greatly reduces hallucinations and improves factual coverage while keeping report quality and cost efficiency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing rubric-based evaluations of deep-research systems are too coarse and can hide specific factual problems like hallucinations, missing key facts, and bad citations in generated reports. There is a need for an evaluation that operates at the claim level and for generation methods that directly optimize factual grounding and updatability of reports when sources change.

Method: The authors first build CLAIMPROBE, an auditing methodology that decomposes deep-research reports into individual claims, then checks each claim against retrieved evidence for hallucination, misattribution, citation hygiene, and recall of necessary facts. They apply CLAIMPROBE to existing DR pipelines to reveal hidden weaknesses. Next, they design CLAIMWRITER, a hierarchical claim-based writer: it extracts atomic source facts, aligns them to a query-derived outline, constructs a source-linked claim representation, and generates each section of the report from these grounded claims. They plug CLAIMWRITER into three existing DR frameworks, changing only the report-writing component, and measure factuality, recall, report quality, and update behavior when sources change.

Result: Using CLAIMPROBE, the authors show that even strong DR systems with good rubric scores still omit important evidence and misattribute claims. With CLAIMWRITER substituted in as the writer, hallucination rates drop by 2.6–4.5× and necessary-fact recall increases by 1.2–1.7× across three prior DR frameworks, while overall report quality is mostly unchanged. In update experiments where sources are modified, CLAIMWRITER propagates changed source facts into revised reports more reliably than alternative update methods and does so at lower cost.

Conclusion: Claim-level evaluation reveals factual weaknesses that rubric-based assessment misses in deep-research systems. A hierarchical, claim-grounded generation process (CLAIMWRITER) substantially improves factuality and coverage without sacrificing report quality and offers better, more cost-effective support for updating reports when underlying sources change. This suggests future DR systems should be built and evaluated around explicit claim representations and claim-level grounding to evidence.

Abstract: Rubric-based evaluations of deep-research (DR) systems often obscure fine-grained factual failures in generated reports. We introduce CLAIMPROBE, a claim-level audit that decomposes DR reports into claims and measures hallucination, misattribution, citation hygiene, and necessary-fact recall against retrieved evidence. Using CLAIMPROBE, we find that strong DR pipelines can omit key evidence and misattribute claims even when their rubric scores remain stable. We then propose CLAIMWRITER, a hierarchical claim-based writer that extracts source facts, maps them to a query-derived outline, and drafts each section from a source-linked claim representation. Across three prior DR frameworks, replacing only the report writer with CLAIMWRITER reduces hallucination by 2.6 to 4.5 times and improves necessary-fact recall by 1.2 to 1.7 times, while largely preserving overall report quality. CLAIMWRITER also enables localized revision: when sources change, it propagates changed source facts into revised reports at the highest rate among update methods, while also being more cost-effective.

</details>


### [17] [Cross Lingual Transfer in Tulu Legal Comprehension: Script-Dependent Improvement and RAG-Induced Knowledge Conflict](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.28645)
*Sindhu Shetty,Spurthi Setty,Natan Vidra*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper evaluates how current LLMs handle cross-lingual legal complaint classification in a very low-resource Dravidian language (Tulu), showing that performance is strongly script-dependent, that adding Kannada RAG gives mixed gains, and that main failures stem from reasoning (fact substitution and confabulation) rather than corpus gaps; it also proposes analysis tools for low-resource multilingual RAG evaluation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Low-resource languages like Tulu lack large training corpora, so practitioners often scaffold understanding via related higher-resource languages, but rigorous, domain-specific evaluation methods for such cross-lingual settings—especially in legal NLP—are missing. The authors want to know when and how LLMs fail in these environments, whether simple transliteration across related Dravidian scripts plus Kannada RAG actually helps comprehension, and how to systematically characterize reasoning failures in low-resource multilingual RAG systems.

Method: The authors use the legal domain and frame the task as classifying legal complaints written in Tulu. They evaluate three LLMs (Llama3, Hex-1, Sarvam) under different input-script and retrieval conditions. First, they transliterate Tulu complaints into multiple Dravidian scripts to test script-dependent comprehension without additional training, measuring classification performance and error patterns. Second, they add a Kannada legal corpus into a RAG pipeline and assess how retrieval affects model answers and reasoning. They perform qualitative reasoning-trace analysis to identify recurring failure modes (fact substitution vs. confabulation) and deploy a “statistical-honesty” evaluation framework to quantify when answers remain grounded in the query/corpus, using this to compare robustness across scripts and models.

Result: Transliteration across Dravidian scripts allows the tested LLMs to achieve some comprehension of Tulu complaints without large-scale training, but performance is strongly script-dependent: inputs written in Kannada script provide the clearest performance gains, despite Kannada itself being relatively low-resource. Incorporating Kannada legal documents into a RAG setup yields mixed effects: some models show modest improvements in certain settings, but others develop new failure patterns. When errors occur, they cluster along two axes: (1) fact substitution, in which the model latches onto specific retrieved passages and distorts overall reasoning, and (2) confabulation, where content is hallucinated without grounding in either query or corpus. Analysis shows that these failures are better explained by the models’ parsing and reasoning limitations than by insufficiencies in the underlying Kannada corpus. Moreover, better script-level comprehension tends to correlate with greater robustness under RAG, as confirmed by the reasoning-trace and statistical-honesty analyses.

Conclusion: The study concludes that, in cross-lingual low-resource legal NLP, script choice significantly shapes LLM comprehension, with Kannada script giving the most reliable understanding of Tulu complaints among those tested. Simple RAG over a related-language legal corpus has only weak and inconsistent benefits; reasoning failures often persist and manifest as fact substitution and confabulation. These errors primarily reflect limitations in model reasoning and information integration rather than corpus quality. The authors argue that script-dependent comprehension and RAG robustness are closely linked, and they demonstrate that reasoning-trace analysis plus a statistical-honesty framework provide practical, generalizable tools for evaluating multilingual RAG systems in low-resource settings.

Abstract: Low-resource languages without an adequate training corpus often use a related, higher-resource language as a scaffold for comprehension. Still, there is a need to develop rigorous evaluation methods to identify when models fail in cross lingual low-resource environments. Using the legal domain as a backdrop, three models (Llama3, Hex-1, Sarvam) were tested on the ability to classify legal complaints written in a low resource Dravidian language (Tulu). Transliterating queries across Dravidian scripts allowed models to gain a preliminary understanding of speakers' complaints without the use of wide scale training, though the level of comprehension was heavily script dependent (with Kannada - another relatively low-resource language - producing the strongest positive trend). Retrieving from a corpus of Kannada legal papers across a RAG framework caused mixed results. Some models had a weak positive trend in comprehension under certain conditions, but when models failed, it was often across two axes: fact substitution (fixating on specific passage excerpts that skewed reasoning) and confabulation (hallucination that had no basis in either query or corpus). Within low resource domains, results identify the model's parsing of information and subsequent reasoning as the source of reasoning failure, rather than corpus contents. Script-dependent comprehension and RAG robustness also seem to travel together. This is further supported by the reasoning-trace analysis and a statistical-honesty framework deployed - techniques that are more broadly applicable to low-resource multilingual RAG evaluation.

</details>


### [18] [Can Large Language Models Identify Meaningful Touchpoints in Conversion Attribution?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.28649)
*Jinqi Wu,Sishuo Chen,Zhangming Chan,Yong Bai,Chao Yi,Han Zhu,Shuodian Yu,Lei Zhang,Sheng Chen,Chenghuan Hou,Jian Xu,Chaoyou Fu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper studies how well large language models (LLMs) can identify meaningful, semantically relevant user touchpoints for conversion attribution, finding they reveal many hidden associations but are still imperfect, and shows that LLM-based labels can significantly boost industrial CVR model training.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing touchpoint selection for conversion attribution mostly relies on collaborative-filtering heuristics, which focus on co-occurrence patterns and often miss semantically related but implicitly connected touchpoints that humans would consider relevant. This semantic gap undermines both the quality of attribution and downstream models relying on these labels, motivating an investigation into whether LLMs can better capture human-aligned semantic intent in attribution tasks.

Method: The authors first perform human annotation of user journeys to expose the mismatch between current rule-based/collaborative-filtering touchpoint selection and human-perceived semantic relevance. They then systematically evaluate different LLMs on the task of identifying implicitly related, semantically relevant touchpoints within conversion paths, varying prompting strategies and foundation model choices. They analyze LLM reasoning patterns and selection performance and finally use the LLM-generated attribution labels as supervision to retrain or enhance an industrial conversion rate (CVR) prediction model, measuring offline performance gains.

Result: The evaluation shows that LLMs can successfully uncover many implicitly related, semantically relevant touchpoints that existing heuristic methods miss, partially bridging the semantic gap. However, performance is still far from perfect, with substantial room for further improvement. The study also finds that prompting strategy and base model choice significantly affect identification performance and reasoning behavior. When LLM-attributed labels are used to train industrial CVR models, the models exhibit significant offline performance improvements, demonstrating practical value of LLM-based attribution.

Conclusion: LLMs are promising tools for upgrading conversion attribution from rigid rule-based matching to more human-aligned semantic reasoning. While current LLMs do not fully solve the problem, they already capture many hidden semantic associations between touchpoints and conversions that traditional methods overlook. Careful choice of prompting and model can materially influence performance. Leveraging LLM-generated attribution labels can substantially enhance downstream CVR models, indicating a viable path to more accurate, semantically grounded attribution in real-world e-commerce and advertising systems.

Abstract: Touchpoint selection in conversion attribution, namely identifying meaningful touchpoints contributing to conversions, is essential for e-commerce recommendation and online advertising. Current selection methods rely heavily on collaborative-filtering-based heuristics, which fail to align with user-perceived semantic intent. Through human annotation, we reveal a significant semantic gap: many implicitly-related, semantically relevant touchpoints remain undetected by existing rules. Therefore, we systematically evaluate the capability of Large Language Models (LLMs) in identifying these hidden associations. Our evaluation shows that while LLMs effectively uncover a substantial portion of implicitly-related touchpoints, significant room for improvement remains in their selection performance. Furthermore, we analyze the impact of different prompting strategies and foundation model choices on identification performance, providing valuable insights into their reasoning patterns and effectiveness. These insights offer a new roadmap for transitioning conversion attribution from mechanical rule-matching to human-aligned semantic reasoning. Moreover, we leverage the LLM-attributed conversion labels for enhancing industrial CVR model training and achieve significant offline performance gains, showing the potential of LLMs in conversion attribution.

</details>


### [19] [Test-Time Scaling for Scientific Equation Discovery](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.28660)
*Haowei Lin,Hubert Lim,Xiangyu Wang,Letian Huang,Di He*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper studies how to best allocate test-time compute (“test-time scaling”) for LLM-based automated equation discovery, showing that search width is the key factor for performance and efficiency when a good verifier is available.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While test-time scaling has improved reasoning for closed-ended tasks like math and coding, it is unclear how to leverage extra test-time compute for open-ended problems such as discovering equations from data. Automated equation discovery with LLMs requires searching a large space of candidate equations guided by feedback from datapoints, and existing methods (Best-of-N, tree search, evolutionary search, etc.) lack a unified perspective on how to allocate compute effectively.

Method: The authors formulate LLM-driven equation discovery as an iterative search process that encompasses Best-of-N sampling, sequential refinement, tree search, and evolutionary-style algorithms under a unified compute-allocation framework.
