They introduce minimal parallel controllers that hold prompt engineering and other heuristics fixed, varying only how test-time compute is allocated—especially search width, population/branching trade-offs, and controller type—under fixed compute budgets. They then evaluate these configurations on LLM-SRBench equation-discovery tasks using an informative verifier derived from observed datapoints.

Result: Experiments show that search width is the primary factor governing performance: as the available compute budget increases, the optimal search width also tends to increase, leading to better equation-discovery performance. In contrast, how compute is split between population and branching, as well as the specific choice of controller, has comparatively minor impact. Properly tuning width also improves wall-clock efficiency by taking better advantage of parallelism.

Conclusion: For LLM-based equation discovery with a strong verifier, effective scaling primarily depends on how exploration versus exploitation is controlled through search width. A wider search, appropriately matched to the compute budget, yields better solutions and more efficient parallel use of resources, whereas more intricate controller designs or population/branching schemes matter less. This highlights that test-time scaling for open-ended equation discovery is largely an allocation problem focused on search breadth rather than complex search heuristics.

Abstract: Test-time scaling (TTS) improves language model reasoning by allocating additional test-time compute, but prior work mainly studies closed-ended tasks such as math and coding. We study TTS for automated equation discovery, an open-ended setting where models search over candidate equations and rely on observed datapoints for feedback. We formulate LLM-driven equation discovery as an iterative search process that unifies Best-of-N, sequential refinement, tree search, and evolution-style methods under a common compute-allocation view. To isolate allocation effects from prompt engineering and other heuristics, we compare minimal parallel controllers under fixed budgets. On LLM-SRBench equation-discovery tasks, we find that search width is the dominant allocation parameter: the best width in our sweep generally increases with the compute budget, while the population--branching split and controller choice matter less. Appropriate width selection also improves wall-clock efficiency by increasing parallelism. These results suggest that, given an informative verifier, controlling exploration and exploitation is central to scaling LLM-based equation discovery.

</details>


### [20] [GreenBench: Benchmarking Energy Efficiency and Carbon Footprint of Open-Source LLM Inference on Apple Silicon](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.28667)
*Rajeswari Kannan,Raj Firke,Shreya Bengle,Srushti Deshmukh*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: GreenBench benchmarks energy use, throughput, and carbon footprint of several 3–9B LLMs on Apple M4 Pro, showing highly efficient, low-power inference and model-size trade-offs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Despite concern over the environmental impact of LLMs, most Green AI work focuses on datacenter GPUs and embedded devices. The energy behavior of LLM inference on Apple Silicon, especially with unified memory, is not characterized, leaving practitioners without data-driven guidance on efficiency and carbon trade-offs when using Macs for LLM inference.

Method: Develop GreenBench, a benchmarking framework that runs five open-source LLMs (3–9B parameters) on three NLP tasks on an Apple M4 Pro (48 GB unified memory). Use macOS powermetrics to directly measure CPU+GPU and system power, and Ollama’s nanosecond-resolution timing to get precise throughput. Evaluate energy per token, throughput, and estimated CO2 emissions, and perform Pareto analysis to find accuracy–efficiency trade-offs across models and sizes.

Result: On the M4 Pro, sustained LLM inference draws about 0.47 W at the CPU+GPU package level and 8–12 W total system power. This yields roughly 30–40× better energy efficiency per token than datacenter GPUs in a single-user deployment. Smaller 3–3.8B models achieve 2.6–4.2× higher throughput and up to 62% lower energy per token compared to 7–9B models. Pareto analysis highlights Qwen 2.5 (7B) as a good balance of accuracy and efficiency (57% MMLU, 59 tokens/s) and Llama 3.2 (3B) as ideal for low-latency use cases (175 tokens/s). The framework reports per-token energy at package and system levels and converts these to CO2 estimates for India and US electricity grids.

Conclusion: Apple M4 Pro offers extremely energy-efficient LLM inference for small to mid-size models, far outperforming traditional datacenter GPUs on a per-token basis in single-user scenarios. Model size strongly affects both throughput and energy per token, enabling practitioners to select models based on accuracy, latency, and energy constraints. GreenBench provides a practical methodology and reference data for quantifying and comparing the environmental footprint of LLM inference on Apple Silicon.

Abstract: The rapid proliferation of Large Language Models (LLMs) has raised concerns about their environmental impact during inference. While Green AI research has focused on datacenter GPUs and embedded platforms, the energy profile of LLM inference on Apple Silicon, with its unified memory architecture, remains unstudied. This paper presents GreenBench, a benchmarking framework that evaluates the energy efficiency, throughput, and carbon footprint of five open-source LLMs (3-9B parameters) across three NLP tasks on an Apple M4 Pro with 48 GB unified memory. Using macOS powermetrics for direct power measurement and Ollama's nanosecond-precision timing, we find that the M4 Pro draws only 0.47 W of CPU+GPU package power during sustained inference, with total system power of 8-12 W, achieving 30-40x better energy efficiency per token than datacenter GPUs in single-user deployment. Smaller models (3-3.8B) deliver 2.6-4.2x higher throughput and up to 62% less energy per token than larger models (7-9B). Pareto analysis identifies Qwen 2.5 (7B) as the optimal accuracy-efficiency trade-off at 57% MMLU and 59 tokens/s, while Llama 3.2 (3B) suits latency-critical applications at 175 tokens/s. We provide per-token energy at package and system levels with CO2 estimates for India and US grids.

</details>


### [21] [ReVA: A Region-Aware Visual Assistant for Visually Grounded Question Answering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.28707)
*Anoop Senthil*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: ReVA is a region-aware VQA model that adds explicit region tokens from detected bounding boxes, alongside global image tokens, to reduce hallucinations and improve spatial and fine-grained reasoning in multimodal LLMs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing multimodal LLMs for VQA perform well overall but fail on tasks requiring precise spatial reasoning and fine-grained visual understanding, leading to hallucinated objects, attributes, and relations. These errors stem from weak region-level grounding when only global image embeddings are aligned with the language model, so the authors aim to strengthen the visual grounding at the region level to improve factual consistency.

Method: ReVA uses a frozen CLIP ViT-L/14 as the vision encoder and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct as the LLM, connected by a dual bridge. The image bridge converts the final ViT block features into global image tokens, while the region bridge crops and aggregates intermediate ViT features (capturing both low-level textures and higher-level object cues) into K region tokens per detected bounding box. Automatic bounding boxes are generated zero-shot via a detector stack: RAM++ to recognize candidate objects, spaCy to parse question text, and Grounding DINO to localize both question-agnostic and question-dependent regions. The resulting image and region tokens are concatenated as a prefix to the LLM prompt so that the model conditions its answers jointly on scene-level context and fine-grained region evidence.

Result: On VQAv2, MMBench, POPE, and SEED-Bench, ReVA outperforms an image-token-only baseline. Specifically, on the POPE hallucination benchmark it achieves 82.85% mean F1 versus 81.14% for the baseline, indicating reduced object hallucinations and better grounding. Performance gains on other benchmarks further support improved visual reasoning and factual accuracy.

Conclusion: Explicit region-aware visual representations, realized via a dual image–region token bridge and automatic region proposal pipeline, significantly reduce hallucinations and improve the factual grounding of multimodal LLMs for VQA. Combining global scene tokens with fine-grained region tokens yields better spatial reasoning and visual understanding than relying on global image features alone.

Abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have achieved remarkable progress in Visual Question Answering (VQA), yet they continue to struggle with questions requiring precise spatial reasoning and fine-grained visual understanding. These limitations often manifest as object, attribute, and spatial hallucinations, where models generate confident but visually unsupported responses due to insufficient region-level and fine-grained visual grounding. To address this challenge, we propose ReVA, a region-aware VQA model that employs a frozen CLIP ViT-L/14 Vision Transformer (ViT) and a Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct large language model (LLM) connected through a dual bridge that aligns both whole-image and region-level representations with the LLM's embedding space. The image bridge maps final transformer block features into image tokens. The region bridge maps cropped features from enriched intermediate features across ViT blocks so early texture and later object cues are more evident, into K region tokens for every bounding box. ReVA uses a detector stack that supplies automatic zero-shot bounding boxes that are both question-agnostic and question-dependent, using RAM++ (Recognize Anything Model), spaCy, and Grounding DINO. The image tokens and region tokens are concatenated as an LLM prompt prefix to jointly encode scene-level context and fine-grained regional evidence when answering questions. Evaluated on VQAv2, MMBench, POPE, and SEED-Bench, ReVA achieves 82.85% mean F1 on POPE, compared with 81.14% for an image-token baseline without region tokens. These results demonstrate that explicit region-aware visual representations reduce object hallucination and improve the factual grounding of MLLMs.

</details>


### [22] [Evaluating Multilingual Sentence Embeddings for Translation Error Detection:An English--Greek Contrastive Study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.28776)
*Eleftherios Kalogeros,Athanasios Ntalakas,Manolis Gergatsoulis,Paschalis Nikolaou,Sotiria-Lito Alexaki*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper tests whether popular multilingual sentence-embedding models can reliably tell correct English→Greek translations from very similar but wrong ones, showing they work reasonably well but miss subtle errors and are best used inside larger evaluation systems rather than alone.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multilingual sentence embeddings are widely used for cross-lingual semantic similarity and as building blocks for MT evaluation, but we do not know how sensitive they truly are to specific, fine-grained translation errors. Without this understanding, practitioners might overtrust similarity scores that actually ignore important factual, grammatical, or discourse-level mistakes. The authors want to systematically measure which types of translation errors these models can and cannot detect.

Method: The authors create a contrastive English–Greek dataset from FLORES+ reference translations. For each English sentence, they include the correct Greek translation and minimally modified erroneous variants, manually checked by two translation experts. The errors are grouped into 10 core and 5 exploratory categories spanning factual, lexical-semantic, grammatical, relational, referential, and discourse phenomena. They then compute cosine similarity between English sentences and (a) correct Greek translations and (b) erroneous alternatives using five multilingual embedding models: BGE-M3, Multilingual E5, Multilingual MPNet, LaBSE, and Jina Embeddings v3. They also evaluate COMETKiwi, a reference-free quality estimation model, as a baseline. Performance is measured by contrastive accuracy (preferring the correct over the incorrect translation) and by similarity/score margins, broken down by error category.

Result: On the contrastive task, BGE-M3 is the best embedding model with 89.30% accuracy, while COMETKiwi reaches 94.49%. All embedding models are comparatively strong at detecting explicit factual and lexical changes but noticeably weaker on tense-aspect issues and pronoun/coreference errors. COMETKiwi improves over embeddings on several hard categories, including tense-aspect, pronoun/coreference, and semantic-role errors, but is less sensitive to date/time errors and worse than embeddings on numerical inconsistencies. Overall, the models show complementary strengths and weaknesses across error types.

Conclusion: General-purpose multilingual sentence embeddings contain useful signals about semantic adequacy and can distinguish many correct vs. incorrect translations, especially when errors are explicit and lexical or factual. However, they are not consistently sensitive to more subtle grammatical, referential, or discourse-level issues. Because of these gaps and their varied error profiles, such embeddings should not be used as standalone MT evaluation metrics; instead, they are better integrated as components within richer, multi-signal translation-evaluation frameworks that can capture a broader range of error phenomena.

Abstract: Multilingual sentence embeddings are increasingly used to estimate semantic similarity across languages, yet their sensitivity to fine-grained translation errors remains insufficiently understood. This study investigates whether general-purpose multilingual embedding models can distinguish correct English-Greek translations from minimally modified erroneous alternatives. A contrastive dataset was developed from FLORES+ sentence-aligned reference translations and reviewed by two translation experts. It contains 1,850 examples across ten core and five exploratory error categories, covering factual, lexical-semantic, grammatical, relational, referential, and discourse-level phenomena.
  Five multilingual sentence-embedding models (BGE-M3, Multilingual E5, Multilingual MPNet, LaBSE, and Jina Embeddings v3) were evaluated using cosine similarity between each English source sentence and its correct and erroneous Greek translations. A reference-free COMETKiwi model was also evaluated as an MT quality-estimation baseline. Performance was assessed through contrastive accuracy and score margins for category-specific sensitivity. BGE-M3 achieved the highest accuracy among embedding models at 89.30 percent, while COMETKiwi achieved 94.49 percent. Embedding models detected explicit factual and lexical changes more reliably than tense-and-aspect and pronoun-coreference errors. COMETKiwi improved performance on several difficult categories, including tense and aspect, pronoun and coreference, and semantic-role errors, but showed lower sensitivity to date-and-time errors and underperformed the embedding models on numbers. The results show complementary error-sensitivity profiles: multilingual sentence embeddings provide useful semantic adequacy signals but are better suited as components of broader translation-evaluation frameworks than as standalone metrics.

</details>


### [23] [A rigor-matched audit of periodic-step layer skipping for efficient llm inference: conflayers versus swift, with a supplemental analysis of trained routing alternatives](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.28846)
*Prateek Kumar Sikdar,Arpan Ghosh*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper audits and compares different layer-skipping methods for speeding up LLM inference, finding that SWIFT generally outperforms a confidence-based early-exit baseline in both accuracy and true inference speed once search overhead is accounted for, while trained-routing methods give only modest speedups and can severely hurt accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs are expensive to run because every token requires executing all transformer layers. Layer-skipping methods promise faster inference by running only a subset of layers per input or per step, but prior work often lacks rigor-matched comparisons, clear separation of search overhead from actual compute savings, and fair baselines. The authors aim to rigorously evaluate and compare several prominent layer-skipping approaches across models and tasks, clarifying their real accuracy–efficiency trade-offs and providing a template protocol for future work.

Method: The authors perform a controlled, three-seed audit of multiple layer-skipping strategies against standard autoregressive decoding. They evaluate two periodic-step, online search-based methods—ConfLayers (a confidence-gated early-exit baseline) and SWIFT (self-speculative decoding)—which dynamically decide which layers to run and can revise that decision every few generation steps. Experiments are run on two Qwen2.5 model sizes (0.5B and 1.5B) and two benchmarks (GSM8K for reasoning and CNN/DailyMail for summarization). They disentangle pure inference cost from online-search overhead to measure true inference speed. As a supplemental analysis, they also test two trained-routing, coarser-granularity methods (LayerRoute and LayerDrop) under a strict protocol that ensures per-input gating, a strong full-model baseline, and actual inference-time compute skipping.

Result: SWIFT achieves the best accuracy in three of the four model–task combinations, while ConfLayers is consistently worse, especially on GSM8K with the 1.5B model. When search overhead is factored out, SWIFT has lower true inference cost than ConfLayers in all settings, with 5–21% faster effective inference, even though naive wall-clock timing can misleadingly favor ConfLayers in some cases. ConfLayers has low, stable search overhead (1–2% of total cost), whereas SWIFT’s overhead is larger and more variable, reaching up to 28.7%. The trained-routing methods (LayerRoute and LayerDrop) provide only modest speedups (1.08–1.33×) and suffer substantial accuracy loss relative to periodic-step methods; LayerRoute nearly collapses on GSM8K at 1.5B with a mean exact match of 0.003 across three seeds.

Conclusion: Periodic-step, online search-based layer-skipping—especially SWIFT—offers a better accuracy–efficiency trade-off than a simple confidence-based early-exit baseline, once true compute cost is properly measured. In contrast, coarser trained-routing approaches yield limited speed benefits and can drastically degrade accuracy on challenging reasoning tasks. The authors provide a fully specified audit protocol intended as a standard for rigor-matched efficiency evaluations of future layer-skipping and compute-reduction techniques.

Abstract: Layer-skipping methods for efficient LLM inference decide, at some granularity, which transformer layers to execute for a given input. We present a rigor-matched, three-seed audit of two periodic-step, search-based methods that make this decision online at inference time and re-evaluate it every few generation steps: a confidence-gated early-exit baseline (ConfLayers) and genuine self-speculative decoding (SWIFT, Xia et al. 2024), together with vanilla autoregressive decoding, across two model scales (Qwen2.5-0.5B and Qwen2.5-1.5B) and two tasks (GSM8K reasoning and CNN/DailyMail summarization). SWIFT is the strongest method on accuracy in three of four cells; ConfLayers is dominated everywhere, with particularly large deficits on GSM8K at 1.5B. Once online-search overhead is separated from pure inference cost, SWIFT's true inference speed is faster than ConfLayers's in all four cells (5-21%), reversing the naive wall-clock ranking in three of them. ConfLayers's search overhead is small and stable (1-2% of cost), while SWIFT's is larger and more variable (up to 28.7%). We additionally examine two trained-routing methods, LayerRoute (Sikdar, 2026) and LayerDrop (Fan et al. 2020), as a supplemental analysis because they operate at coarser decision granularities. Under a verified protocol with genuine per-input gating, a genuine full-model baseline, and genuine inference-time compute skipping, both show modest speedups (1.08-1.33x) but accuracy well below the periodic-step methods, including a near-total collapse for LayerRoute on GSM8K at 1.5B (0.003 mean exact-match across three seeds). We release the full audit protocol as a template for rigor-matched efficiency comparisons.

</details>


### [24] [Latent-Space Intervention for Cross-Lingual Factual Consistency: Consistency Improvements without Accuracy Drops](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.28860)
*Faeze Ghorbanpour,Constanza Fierro,Alexander Fraser,Anders Sogaard*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces a latent-space intervention method to make LLM factual answers more consistent across languages without hurting accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs often give different factual answers to the same question depending on the language, undermining reliability and fairness in multilingual use. The authors want a general, model-agnostic way to align cross-lingual behavior without retraining the base model.

Method: They train layer-specific autoencoders on parallel multilingual hidden representations of an LLM. At inference time, they encode and reconstruct these representations to better align languages in the latent space, and optionally combine this with PCA projection and mean-shift interventions. They then apply these corrected representations when the model answers factual QA prompts in multiple languages, comparing open-ended and multiple-choice settings.

Result: Latent-space intervention increases geometric alignment between languages and yields higher cross-lingual answer consistency with English. In open-ended QA, Spearman rank correlation between English and Arabic answers improves by 0.16 and between English and Russian by 0.20. In multiple-choice QA, answer agreement with English improves on KLAR and mParaRel benchmarks. Ablations show autoencoder reconstruction alone gives consistent consistency gains without hurting factual accuracy, PCA adds little, and mean-shift gives larger consistency gains in open-ended QA but slightly hurts accuracy.

Conclusion: Cross-lingual latent-space intervention via autoencoders can systematically improve how consistently an LLM answers factual questions across languages, aligning multilingual outputs with English while largely preserving accuracy. Simple reconstruction-based interventions are especially attractive because they improve consistency at essentially no accuracy cost.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) often answer the same factual question differently across languages. We study whether cross-lingual latent-space intervention can reduce this inconsistency. We train layer-specific autoencoders on parallel multilingual representations and apply inference-time corrections to factual QA prompts. We find that latent intervention improves geometric alignment between languages, and that this improvement translates into consistent gains in cross-lingual consistency with English across both open-ended and multiple-choice QA formats, without degrading factual accuracy. In open-ended QA, Spearman's rank correlation between English and non-English languages improves substantially, with gains of 0.16 for English-Arabic and 0.20 for English-Russian pairs. In multiple-choice QA, answer agreement with English improves consistently across both KLAR and mParaRel. Ablations show that AE reconstruction yields consistent gains at no accuracy cost, while PCA projection contributes marginally, and mean-shift produces substantially larger consistency gains in open-ended QA at the cost of some accuracy.

</details>


### [25] [No Detectable Change in Side-Level WER from Prompt-Level Context: A Preregistered Ablation on a Production Oral-History Corpus](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.28875)
*Theodore O. Cochran,Stephanie Dodson,Keith Nore*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper tests whether providing rich prompt context improves transcription accuracy in a production oral-history system using large multimodal models, and finds no meaningful WER gains under realistic deployment conditions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Earlier work on smaller models suggested that adding domain or conversation context in prompts could significantly improve speech transcription accuracy, especially for specialized domains like oral history with degraded audio and distinctive vocabulary. As large multimodal models are deployed in production, it is important to verify whether this inexpensive adaptation lever still works at scale and in realistic settings, rather than relying on idealized or lab-only benchmarks.

Method: The authors run a preregistered within-item paired ablation study using a real production oral-history transcription pipeline. Nineteen cassette sides (10.6 hours) of noisy 1970s–1980s interview audio are reprocessed under three prompt conditions (full context, reduced context, and no context) crossed with two commercial LMM configurations (gpt-4o-transcribe and gemini-2.5-flash). Transcripts are scored against operator-corrected verbatim references using side-level word error rate (WER). The study design includes preregistration, frozen analysis code (by hash) prior to confirmatory scoring, and an implementation audit to verify that prompt manipulations were active. They also perform sequence-alignment analysis on context-listed phrases and examine post-hoc run-to-run variability of the pipeline.

Result: For gpt-4o-transcribe, adding full prompt context compared to no context resulted in a median paired WER difference of +0.6 points, with a resampled confidence interval of [-1.1, +1.0], indicating no reliable improvement and possibly a slight degradation. Gemini-2.5-flash produced results too unstable to support strong negative conclusions. A post-hoc rerun showed that run-to-run variability in the production pipeline exceeds the small observed differences between prompt conditions. Sequence-alignment analysis detected a modest benefit on fully context-listed phrases, but the effect was too small to materially change overall side-level WER, and for Gemini it coincided with higher errors on tokens not included in the context list.

Conclusion: Under realistic production conditions for an oral-history transcription system using large multimodal models, supplying extensive prompt-level context does not yield detectable improvements in aggregate WER, contrary to earlier gains reported for smaller models. This suggests that prompt conditioning as currently implemented may offer only localized benefits (e.g., on explicitly listed phrases) that are washed out at the side level and that may trade off against other kinds of errors. The authors argue that evaluating context mechanisms requires fine-grained, sequence-aligned metrics—covering term-level accuracy, insertions, and speaker labels—rather than relying solely on aggregate WER, and that production pipelines must account for run-to-run variability when assessing small effect sizes.

Abstract: Supplying context at inference time to a large multimodal model is an inexpensive lever for adapting speech transcription to a domain, and earlier results on smaller models reported large gains. This work tested that mechanism where it ships, in the prompt-conditioning layer of a production oral-history transcription tool, on a sample from its own production corpus. Full prompt-level context did not detectably change side-level word error rate (WER), and none of the four preregistered hypotheses was supported. The design was a within-item paired ablation, preregistered with the analysis code frozen by hash before the confirmatory batch was scored; two disclosed gpt-4o pilot sides had been scored earlier, during scorer development. Nineteen cassette sides, about 10.6 hours of degraded 1970s-80s interview audio, were reprocessed through the production code path under three prompt arms, crossed with two deployed commercial configurations, gpt-4o-transcribe and gemini-2.5-flash, and scored against operator-corrected verbatim references. For gpt-4o-transcribe the median paired difference between the full-context and no-context arms was +0.6 WER points, with a side-resampled interval of [-1.1, +1.0]; the Gemini estimates were too unstable to support a comparable negative inference. A post-hoc rerun found run-to-run pipeline variability larger than the confirmatory differences, so effects of that size cannot be resolved from one transcription per cell. An implementation audit verified the manipulation was live, and sequence-alignment analysis found a small improvement on complete context-listed phrases, too small to materially change side-level WER, and for Gemini coexisting with worsened unlisted-token error. Evaluating context mechanisms therefore requires sequence-aligned term-level, insertion, and speaker-label measures alongside aggregate accuracy.

</details>


### [26] [Moving the Mean Toward the Known Good, Not Beyond It: What Inference-Time Interventions and Weight Consolidation Buy in Open-Ended Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.28886)
*Roberto I. Ono Filho*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper studies whether a generate–verify–select–consolidate training loop can improve a model’s performance on online bin packing by learning from its own verified good solutions. It finds that consolidation reliably shifts average outputs toward a strong classic heuristic but does not surpass it: the model’s best observed solutions converge exactly to heuristic-level performance and never go beyond.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The authors want to understand what is actually gained when a model is trained on its own verified successes in an iterative loop, as is common in modern LLM self-improvement methods. They observe in practice that adding verifiers and recap mechanisms at inference time seems to change behavior but not reliably improve development of better solutions. This motivates a controlled empirical study on a concrete combinatorial task, online bin packing, to see if self-training on high-value generations leads to genuine algorithmic improvement beyond a known classic heuristic benchmark.

Method: They use an iterative cycle on an online bin packing task: (1) generate candidate solutions, (2) verify and score them by value (bin-packing excess), (3) select value-filtered candidates, and (4) LoRA-consolidate the model on these filtered outputs. They compare this consolidation loop against controls: random-consolidation (training on randomly chosen candidates), and a supervised SFT-only control that anchors the model to the classic heuristic solutions. They repeat the full experimental pipeline three times with fresh random seeds and a never-before-used held-out test set read once, measuring both mean excess and the best observed candidate per instance, and they track the frequency of solutions that beat the classic heuristic.

Result: Training on value-filtered candidates systematically shifts the model’s average outputs on held-out variants towards higher value: mean excess improves by about 1.7–3.1 points relative to baselines, with statistically significant p-values (0.008 and 0.004). Across three independent replications, mean improvements are stable (around -2.0 in excess), and all evaluable held-out variants favor consolidation (p=0.008). However, the best observed candidate per instance converges exactly to the classic heuristic’s performance (0.021028 excess) and does not surpass it; this happens equally for the consolidation and random-control lineages. The SFT-only control shows that the classic heuristic acts as an attractor: 96% of candidates land exactly at its level, indicating that the supervised anchor, rather than explicit avoidance of bad candidates, drives concentration. Consolidation reduces the per-candidate rate of better-than-classic solutions (from 10% to 3.9%) but, because it generates more candidates overall, it still produces more above-classic solutions in absolute terms (5 vs. 1, though on small counts). Additional observations show that adding a verifier into the generation stream leads the model to mimic verifier-style outputs (e.g., fabricating about 16.4 verdict lines per notebook) and that schematic recaps mainly improve document integration rather than genuine problem-solving development.

Conclusion: Iterative self-training via generate–verify–select–LoRA-consolidate can reliably improve the mean quality of a model’s outputs on online bin packing, pulling them toward a strong classic heuristic baseline. However, this process does not yield clear evidence of surpassing the underlying heuristic: the best solutions plateau exactly at the heuristic’s performance across replications and controls. The behavior appears dominated by attraction to the supervised heuristic anchor, not by discovery of genuinely superior algorithms, and self-imitation of verifiers affects style more than it advances solution quality. Overall, the loop buys predictable improvements in average quality and concentration around a known baseline, but, in this setting, does not yet deliver open-ended algorithmic progress beyond the classic heuristic.

Abstract: What does a generation loop gain from learning on its own verified successes? In cycles of generate, verify, select and LoRA-consolidate on online bin packing, training on value-filtered candidates shifts what the model writes on held-out variants toward value (-1.7 points of excess, p=0.008; -3.1 against a random-consolidation control, p=0.004) while the best observed candidate converges to the classic heuristic's level and no further. A confirmation battery replicates the whole procedure three times, with fresh seeds and a never-consulted held-out set read exactly once: the mean was nearly identical in all three lineages (-2.0, -1.8, -1.9), and after aggregating within held-out variant all seven evaluable variants favored consolidation (p=0.008). The best observed candidate moved to the classic heuristic's level, exactly (0.021028 in all three lineages, for attract and for the random control alike), and never beyond it. A matched SFT-only control shows the supervised anchor, not repulsion from bad candidates, does the concentrating (96% of candidates land exactly at the classic heuristic's level). The tails cut both ways: consolidation lowers the per-candidate rate of better-than-classic candidates (10% to 3.9%) while its larger production yields more such candidates absolutely (5 against 1, on few events). As motivation we report the inference-time ledger that led here: a model-written schematic recap buys judged document integration and nothing buys development; a verifier written into the stream is imitated, 16.4 fabricated verdict lines per notebook. Mean quality among valid candidates can be bought and replicated; the observed best goes to the classic and, so far, never beyond it.

</details>


### [27] [VoiceCodeBench: Evaluating Exact Structured-Token Recovery in Automatic Speech Recognition](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.28916)
*Tyler Baumgartner,Brandon Tai,Lisa Kaelin-Martin,Candice Fan,Luc Debaupte,Bill Wang,Yi Zhong*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper presents VoiceCodeBench, a benchmark for evaluating how well ASR systems recover exact structured tokens (like IDs, paths, and quantities) beyond traditional word error rate (WER).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Conventional ASR evaluation with word error rate overlooks whether transcripts preserve exact values (identifiers, file paths, numeric quantities) that downstream applications must parse or execute. A system can be fluent and have low WER yet corrupt workflow-critical tokens, potentially breaking real-world pipelines. There is a need for a benchmark and metrics that focus specifically on exact recovery of such structured tokens in realistic workplace audio.

Method: The authors build VoiceCodeBench, a dataset of 300 human-recorded English workplace speech segments across eight workflow domains. They annotate 1,482 target entities spanning 26 entity types, each with a canonical written form that can be recovered from the audio. Under a strict raw-audio-only setting, ASR systems receive only audio bytes, without extra context or metadata. They propose and compute several evaluation metrics: Canonical Token/Entity Match (CTEM), Task Success Rate (TSR), and per-entity-type exact recovery, along with standard WER. They then evaluate 12 baseline ASR systems on this benchmark and analyze correlations between WER and the new entity-sensitive metrics.

Result: Experiments with 12 baseline ASR systems show that while lower WER tends to improve structured-token recovery, it is not a sufficient predictor: Spearman correlations between WER and CTEM and between WER and TSR are both -0.73, indicating only partial alignment. The best system by Task Success Rate achieves 68.7%, meaning that nearly one-third of recordings still contain at least one unrecovered workflow-critical value. Per-type exact recovery reveals remaining weaknesses on certain entity categories.

Conclusion: The study demonstrates that traditional WER-based evaluation is inadequate for assessing whether ASR outputs preserve exact structured values needed for downstream workflows. VoiceCodeBench and the associated entity-centric metrics (CTEM, TSR, per-type recovery) provide a more appropriate way to measure ASR performance in settings where precise token recovery is critical for parsing, routing, storage, comparison, or execution. Entity-sensitive evaluation should complement or, in some applications, supersede WER when selecting or optimizing ASR systems.

Abstract: Automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems are commonly evaluated with word error rate (WER), yet many voice workflows depend on exact written values for identifiers, paths, and measured quantities. A transcript can appear fluent and achieve low WER while corrupting a value that a downstream system must parse, store, or execute.
  We introduce VoiceCodeBench, a benchmark for evaluating exact structured-token recovery in English ASR. It contains 300 human-recorded workplace segments spanning eight workflow domains and 1,482 audited target entities across 26 entity types, each with a canonical written form recoverable from the audio. Under a raw-audio-only protocol, systems receive audio bytes without additional context or metadata. Alongside WER, we evaluate Canonical Token/Entity Match (CTEM), Task Success Rate (TSR), and per-type exact recovery.
  Across 12 baseline ASR systems, lower WER generally corresponded to better structured-token recovery but did not fully determine it: Spearman correlations were -0.73 for both WER versus CTEM and WER versus TSR. The strongest baseline by TSR reached only 68.7%, leaving nearly one third of recordings with at least one unrecovered workflow-critical value. These results show that entity-sensitive metrics are needed to assess whether ASR output preserves exact values that production systems must parse, route, store, compare, or execute.

</details>


### [28] [Causal Interventions Reveal Typologically Organized Syntactic Mechanisms in Multilingual Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.28924)
*Sasha Boguraev,Toshiki Nakai,Kyle Mahowald,Julius Steuer*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper uses mechanistic interpretability on multilingual language models to test whether similar syntactic structures across languages rely on shared internal mechanisms, and finds consistent, graded cross-lingual transfer that correlates with typological similarity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Linguistic theory posits that cross-linguistic syntactic regularities are underpinned by similar cognitive processing mechanisms, but this has been hard to test directly because human processing mechanisms are not easily accessible or manipulable. With the advent of multilingual language models and mechanistic interpretability tools, it becomes possible to inspect and intervene on internal model computations, offering a new empirical window into questions about shared syntactic mechanisms across languages.

Method: The authors apply mechanistic interpretability techniques to multilingual language models. They first identify and isolate the internal mechanisms responsible for particular syntactic phenomena within a single language, then attempt to transfer these identified mechanisms to other languages within the same models. They conduct experiments across four different multilingual LMs and focus on three syntactic constructions: subject–verb number agreement, anaphoric pronoun gender agreement, and filler–gap object extraction, analyzing whether mechanisms found in one language support performance in others.

Result: They observe consistent cross-lingual transfer of the isolated mechanisms: mechanisms discovered for a syntactic construction in one language can be applied to other languages in the same model and still support accurate processing of that construction. Moreover, the degree of successful transfer is graded, with stronger transfer occurring between typologically more similar language pairs, indicating the model’s internal structure reflects linguistic typology to some extent.

Conclusion: The findings suggest that multilingual language models implement shared, partially language-agnostic mechanisms for core syntactic phenomena, and that these mechanisms align with typological similarity across languages. This offers concrete, testable hypotheses about how cross-linguistic syntactic structures might be organized and processed and illustrates that mechanistic interpretability of language models can provide useful evidence for, and constraints on, linguistic theory and models of multilingual processing.

Abstract: Linguistic theory has long recognized cross-linguistic syntactic regularities, leading to claims that these similar structures are processed by similar mechanisms. However, this hypothesis has been difficult to test empirically due to our lack of fine-grained, manipulable access of human processing mechanisms. In this work, we take advantage of techniques from mechanistic interpretability to study such a question in multilingual LMs. We first isolate language-internal mechanisms before attempting to transfer them cross-lingually. Across four models and three well-studied constructions (subject--verb number agreement, anaphoric pronoun gender agreement, and filler--gap object extraction) we find consistent cross-lingual mechanism transfer. We further find transfer to be graded, with more transfer between more typologically similar languages. We believe our work provides novel hypotheses about cross-linguistic syntactic structures and multilingual processing, and more broadly shows how the study of language models can help inform linguistic theory.

</details>


### [29] [Leveraging Turn-taking Dynamics for Intent Recognition in Multi-party Conversations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.28926)
*Galo Castillo-López,Alexis Lombard,Gaël de Chalendar,Nasredine Semmar*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: They improve multi-party dialogue intent recognition by adding a self-supervised auxiliary task based on how predictable speaker turns are, which boosts performance over prior methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing intent recognition methods for multi-party dialogue largely treat utterances in isolation or only use basic context, ignoring the rich interaction structure encoded in who speaks when. Turn-taking behavior carries information about roles, engagement, and conversational dynamics that can be useful for intent recognition but is typically not modeled explicitly. The authors aim to exploit this underused signal to improve performance without needing extra annotation, by using a self-supervised formulation.

Method: They design a multi-task learning framework where the main task is intent recognition in multi-party dialogue, and the auxiliary task is predicting a continuous value called turn-transition entropy. This entropy is computed in a self-supervised way from the sequence of speaker transitions in the dialogue and measures how predictable the speaker changes are. Multiple pre-trained language models serve as backbones, and the model is trained jointly on intent labels and the entropy target, encouraging representations that encode turn-taking dynamics. They also test training on the entropy target alone to assess whether it is a meaningful signal.

Result: Across experiments using several pre-trained models, adding the turn-transition entropy auxiliary task consistently improves intent recognition accuracy compared with baselines that do not use explicit multi-party interaction dynamics. The method outperforms previous state-of-the-art approaches. Furthermore, the continuous entropy target can be learned as a standalone objective, indicating it is non-trivial and encodes useful information rather than noise.

Conclusion: Modeling turn-taking dynamics via a self-supervised turn-transition entropy objective is an effective way to enhance multi-party dialogue intent recognition. The auxiliary task both improves performance when combined with the main task and proves learnable on its own, suggesting that interaction predictability is a valuable, general signal. This opens up a direction for leveraging conversational structure in multi-party dialogue systems without requiring extra labeled data.

Abstract: We propose a multi-task learning approach for multi-party dialogue intent recognition that leverages an auxiliary task that models turn-taking dynamics. Specifically, we introduce turn-transition entropy, a self-supervised target computed from the sequence of speaker transitions, which quantifies the predictability of interaction patterns. Experiments on multiple pre-trained models demonstrate that incorporating this auxiliary task improves intent recognition performance, outperforming existing approaches which ignore multi-party interaction dynamics. We find that our proposed continuous target can be learned as a single-task objective, suggesting that it is an actual signal carrying useful information.

</details>


### [30] [The Hallucination Signal Is a Mean Shift: Why Simple Probes Suffice](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.28930)
*Jungseob Lee,Jaehyung Seo,Heuiseok Lim*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper shows that hallucination-detection signals in LLM hidden states are largely one-dimensional mean shifts, making simple linear probes with good covariance handling nearly as effective as complex architectures. It introduces LayerMix, a layer-aggregation method that matches oracle-layer performance without needing oracle layer selection.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Many recent works use hidden-state probes to detect hallucinations in large language models, but they increasingly adopt complex probe architectures without a clear understanding of what signal these probes are exploiting. It is unclear whether the signal requires non-linear modeling, sophisticated attention across layers, or if it is largely a simpler geometric phenomenon. The authors aim to characterize the geometry of hallucination-related signals in representation space across models and datasets, to clarify how much complexity in probe design is actually necessary.

Method: The authors study three 7B-scale language models and three datasets within a paired-example setup (likely contrasting hallucinated vs correct responses). They analyze the hidden-state representations to identify dominant directions that separate hallucinated from non-hallucinated cases, focusing on mean shifts and covariance structure. They remove the top discriminative direction to test its importance, and compare a spectrum of classifiers: one-dimensional linear probes, full-dimensional linear models, shrinkage linear discriminant analysis, L2-regularized logistic regression, and a variety of more complex architectures (including cross-layer attention probes like CLAP). They also investigate how the hallucination signal is distributed across layers, and propose LayerMix, a simple aggregation strategy over a contiguous band of layers, and compare it to oracle layer selection and CLAP under matched experimental paradigms.

Result: They find that a single mean-shift direction explains most of the hallucination-detection signal in hidden states; when this direction is removed, detection performance drops to chance. Shrinkage LDA recovers about 73% of the performance gap between a one-dimensional classifier and a full-dimensional linear classifier, attributing the remaining performance differences primarily to difficulties in high-dimensional covariance estimation, not to genuine non-linear structures. A simple L2-regularized logistic regression achieves strong performance (AUROC 0.952) and matches or outperforms twelve more complex probe architectures. Their multi-layer aggregation approach outperforms CLAP cross-layer attention probing under the same paradigm. They also find that the useful signal spans a contiguous band of layers rather than being isolated to a single layer, enabling effective aggregation without oracle knowledge.

Conclusion: Hallucination detection signals in LLM hidden states are predominantly linear and low-dimensional, manifesting mainly as a single mean-shift direction, so complex non-linear probe architectures offer little additional benefit in the studied paired-example setting. The main challenge is accurate high-dimensional covariance estimation rather than modeling non-linearity, which allows simple linear models with appropriate regularization—like L2-logistic regression and shrinkage LDA—to perform near optimally. Because the signal is spread over a contiguous range of layers, a simple aggregation strategy (LayerMix) can closely match oracle-layer performance and exceed sophisticated cross-layer attention methods, indicating that future work should prioritize understanding and exploiting this geometric simplicity rather than increasing architectural complexity.

Abstract: Hidden-state probes effectively detect LLM hallucinations, but the geometry of the signal remains poorly characterized, driving increasingly complex probe architectures. Across three 7B-scale models and three datasets in a paired-example paradigm, we find the signal overwhelmingly dominated by a single mean-shift component, and removing this direction collapses detection to chance. Shrinkage linear discriminant analysis closes about 73% of the gap between 1D and full-dimensional classifiers, so apparent architectural complexity largely reflects high-dimensional covariance estimation difficulty rather than exploitable non-linearity. A simple L2-regularized logistic regression (0.952 AUROC) bounds or outperforms twelve controlled architectural alternatives, and our multi-layer aggregation exceeds CLAP cross-layer attention probing under matched paradigm. Because the signal spans a contiguous layer band, LayerMix aggregates it to match oracle-layer performance without oracle access. Our claims characterize the geometry within the controlled paired-example paradigm. Our code is available at https://github.com/js-lee-AI/LayerMix.

</details>


### [31] [VocalAffectBench: Evaluating Vocal Emotion Recognition in AI Audio Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.28932)
*Models Luc Debaupte,Tyler Baumgartner,Brandon Tai,Candice Fan,Bill Wang,Yi Zhong*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces VocalAffectBench, a test-only benchmark to evaluate how well AI audio models can recognize emotions from raw speech, showing that current models capture some affective cues but perform poorly at robust, discrete emotion recognition.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Voice agents and audio-based AI systems increasingly need to understand affective cues in speech that are not present in text transcripts. However, there is a lack of standardized, public benchmarks that specifically test whether audio models can recognize expressed emotions directly from raw audio, without relying on text or metadata. The authors aim to fill this gap and provide a common evaluation ground for emotion recognition in speech.

Method: The authors construct VocalAffectBench, a curated benchmark of 273 English WAV clips (1.95 hours) from 51 speakers with seven emotion labels (angry, disgusted, fearful, happy, neutral, sad, surprised), each with 39 clips. They evaluate six baseline AI audio models on this dataset, constraining them to use only the raw audio signal (no transcripts or contextual metadata). In addition to the 7-way classification, they perform a secondary analysis by grouping emotions into three valence buckets—positive, neutral, negative—excluding ‘surprised’ due to its ambiguous valence, and compute performance metrics such as accuracy and recall by class.

Result: On the 7-way emotion classification, the six baselines achieve an average accuracy of 35.5%, with the best model (gemini_3_5_flash) reaching 46.5%, compared to a 14.3% random baseline. In the coarse-grained valence classification (positive/neutral/negative, excluding surprised), aggregate accuracy improves to 50.9%. Performance varies substantially across emotion classes: neutral achieves the highest recall at 75.6% on average, while surprised and fearful are much lower, at 10.7% and 15.4% recall, respectively.

Conclusion: The benchmark reveals that current AI audio models can pick up some affective signals from speech but are far from achieving robust, discrete emotion recognition, especially for non-neutral emotions. Neutral states are recognized relatively well, but more nuanced or intense emotions like fear and surprise are often misclassified. This indicates that emotion understanding in voice agents remains fragile and underscores the need for better models and methods for affective speech processing, particularly for the non-neutral emotions that are most critical in real-world voice interaction workflows.

Abstract: Voice products increasingly need affective cues that are present in speech but absent from transcripts. We introduce VocalAffectBench, a public, test-only benchmark for evaluating whether AI audio models can identify expressed vocal emotion from raw audio. The benchmark contains 273 human-recorded English WAV clips from 51 speaker accounts totaling 1.95 hours across seven labels: angry, disgusted, fearful, happy, neutral, sad, and surprised, with 39 clips per class. All baselines are evaluated from audio alone, without transcripts or contextual metadata. Across six released baselines, average accuracy is 35.5%. The strongest baseline, gemini_3_5_flash, reaches 46.5% on the seven-way task, above the 14.3% random baseline but far from robust emotion recognition. A secondary valence-bucket analysis maps labels into positive, neutral, and negative classes, excluding surprised because its valence is ambiguous. Aggregate accuracy under this coarser view is 50.9%. Performance is highly uneven across classes. By recall, neutral is identified most reliably at 75.6% averaged across baselines, while surprised and fearful reach only 10.7% and 15.4%, respectively. These results show that the evaluated baselines can extract some affective signal from speech, but discrete expressed-emotion recognition remains fragile, especially for non-neutral emotions that are often most important in voice agent workflows.

</details>


### [32] [CoVA-SFT: A Large-Scale Dataset for Chain of Visual Abstractions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.28958)
*Tsung-Han Wu,Heekyung Lee,Anya Ji,Haoming Chen,Trevor Darrell,Joseph E. Gonzalez,David M. Chan*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: They build and release a large structured multimodal chain-of-thought dataset and benchmark (CoVA-SFT and CoVA-Bench) to teach models to interleave text and visual reasoning, and show it improves multimodal CoT but still lags strong text-only CoT.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard chain-of-thought reasoning in LLMs is purely textual, which is awkward and limiting for problems that are naturally visual or require internal visual workspaces (e.g., layouts, diagrams, tables). Existing multimodal models can process images, but there is no large, high-quality, multi-step dataset that explicitly trains them to construct, manipulate, and verify such internal visual abstractions while solving complex reasoning tasks expressed in text. The authors aim to fill this dataset gap so multimodal LMs can learn richer, mixed text–visual reasoning procedures rather than only linear verbal chains.

Method: They create CoVA-SFT, a supervised fine-tuning corpus with 51.9K examples and over 222K multimodal reasoning steps. Each example includes (1) explicit rationales, (2) “agentic renderings” that translate reasoning steps into visual/layout operations over structured canvases, and (3) verification loops that check or refine intermediate results. The data spans 5 layout families (i.e., types of visual workspaces or canvases) and 17 complex tasks, all designed so that solving them requires interleaving linguistic reasoning with visual abstraction and manipulation. In parallel, they construct CoVA-Bench, a 1,700-example held-out benchmark covering the same task types for standardized evaluation. They then fine-tune multimodal LLMs on CoVA-SFT and compare their performance on CoVA-Bench against existing interleaved CoT baselines and strong text-only CoT models.

Result: Models fine-tuned on CoVA-SFT significantly outperform all prior interleaved multimodal CoT baselines on CoVA-Bench, achieving more than a 2× average improvement. This demonstrates that the structured, multi-step, self-corrected CoVA-SFT data effectively teaches models to use mixed text–visual reasoning. However, even with these gains, CoVA-trained multimodal models still underperform strong text-only CoT models on the same tasks, indicating that the current multimodal reasoning approach is not yet competitive with mature textual CoT pipelines.

Conclusion: A large, structured multimodal CoT dataset with explicit visual workspaces, agentic actions, and verification loops can substantially improve interleaved text–visual reasoning in multimodal LLMs relative to previous multimodal CoT approaches. Nevertheless, the fact that these models still trail robust text-only CoT baselines shows that building truly competitive multimodal reasoning systems remains an open challenge. Future work needs better methods or data to close this performance gap and more fully exploit visual abstraction for complex reasoning.

Abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning has dramatically improved large language models (LLMs) by allowing them to decompose problems into intermediate steps. While CoT is widely effective for linguistic tasks, text-only CoT forces models to serialize visual problems into awkward prose. Although architectural solutions exist to process visual inputs, the community lacks a massive, multi-step, self-corrected dataset to teach models how to build and maintain internal visual workspaces when solving purely textual reasoning problems. To address this limitation, we introduce CoVA-SFT, a highly structured corpus of 51.9K samples containing over 222K multimodal reasoning steps across 5 distinct layout families and 17 complex tasks, and CoVA-Bench, a companion benchmark of 1,700 held-out test samples spanning the same tasks for reproducible evaluation. By providing explicit rationale formulations, agentic renderings, and verification loops, CoVA-SFT teaches multimodal language models to interleave text and visual abstractions. We validate the dataset by demonstrating that models fine-tuned on CoVA-SFT outperform all interleaved CoT baselines by more than 2x on average on CoVA-Bench, though they still fall short of strong text-only CoT baselines, highlighting open challenges for future work.

</details>


### [33] [The Illusion of Replacement: Rethinking Specialized Machine Learning Models in the Foundation Model Era](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.28980)
*Kiyan Rezaee*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper surveys whether language-based models can replace traditional specialized architectures for structured data across multiple modalities.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To investigate the growing trend of using language models as a universal interface for varied data types and tasks, and to assess if they can truly supplant structure-aware models rather than just match task accuracy in specific benchmarks.

Method: A systematic review of 159 papers (2016–2026) spanning nine data modalities, categorizing approaches into eight representational regimes from pure language models to fully specialized architectures, and comparing them in terms of predictive accuracy, structural representation, and computational handling of structure.

Result: Language-mediated models are often competitive and sometimes superior in specific settings such as extreme few-shot prediction, symbolic tasks that can be discretized, text-annotated knowledge graphs, and large-scale single-modality pretraining. Yet, when evaluation focuses on explicit structural representation and computation rather than task accuracy alone, these models do not show evidence of fully replacing specialized architectures. Instead, researchers frequently reintroduce structure via graph modules, structural tokens, specialized attention mechanisms, or other non-linguistic components.

Conclusion: Current evidence does not support a general architectural replacement of structure-aware models by language-based systems. Specialization tends to be relocated into auxiliary components rather than eliminated, and although scaling improves language-based models, it remains unknown whether they can ever close the gap to architectures that explicitly encode and compute over structure.

Abstract: Can the specialized architectures that machine learning has traditionally built for structured data be replaced by language-based models? This question is examined through a review of 159 papers (2016--2026) across nine modalities, with predictive accuracy considered alongside structural representation and computation. A distinction is made between performing a task and preserving and computing the structure that makes the task tractable, and existing approaches are organized into eight representational regimes, ranging from language-only systems to fully specialized architectures. Language-mediated models are found to be highly competitive in specific settings, including extreme few-shot prediction, discretized symbolic tasks, textually annotated knowledge graphs, and large-scale single-modality pretraining. However, whenever structural representation or computation is directly evaluated rather than accuracy alone, no evidence of general architectural replacement is found. Instead, a recurring pattern is observed across independent research communities: when language alone is insufficient, the missing structure is reintroduced through a graph module, structural tokens, specialized attention, or another non-linguistic component. In this sense, specialization more often relocates than disappears. Moreover, although performance of language-based models is improved by scaling, whether the gap to a structure-aware architecture can eventually be eliminated remains untested.

</details>


### [34] [Detecting and Guiding LLM-Generated Korean Poetry with Interpretable Form-level Features](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.28986)
*Keunhyeung Park,Seunguk Yu,YoungBin Kim*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper studies why LLMs write Korean poems like broken prose, proposes simple linguistic features to distinguish human vs. LLM poems, and uses the same features to guide LLMs to write more human-like poetry.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Modern Korean poems generated by LLMs often lack core formal properties of human poetry, instead resembling prose split into lines. There is a need both to detect machine-generated poems reliably and to systematically steer LLMs toward human-like poetic form using interpretable, linguistically grounded criteria rather than opaque neural signals.

Method: The authors define four form-level linguistic dimensions—Volume, Structure Variation, Rhythmic Irregularity, and Normative Adherence—and instantiate them as five interpretable, automatically computable features over poem texts. They train a logistic regression classifier on these features to distinguish human from LLM-authored poems and evaluate it zero-shot on poems from seven unseen LLMs, comparing against the KatFishNet baseline. For generation, they condition or guide LLMs (e.g., GPT-5.2, Gemini-3) using target values of these features, then obtain expert evaluations and statistical analyses of how closely the guided outputs match human distributions on length, rhythm, and line-ending patterns.

Result: The five-feature logistic regression classifier achieves an average AUC-ROC of 83.60 on zero-shot out-of-distribution detection across seven unseen LLMs, outperforming the prior best method KatFishNet (75.84 AUC) by 7.76 absolute points, or 10.23% relative improvement. However, a particular punctuation-related pattern from one generator falls outside their feature taxonomy and remains hard to classify. For generation, expert judges prefer poems produced under feature guidance over unconstrained GPT-5.2 outputs. Quantitative analyses show that, when guided, GPT-5.2 and Gemini-3 outputs shift their length, rhythmic irregularity, and line-ending statistics toward human distributions.

Conclusion: Simple, interpretable, language-specific features capturing poetic form can serve as a unified tool both for diagnosing whether a poem is LLM- or human-written and for steering LLMs toward more human-like poetic style. This dual use suggests a promising alternative to complex, black-box detectors and generic decoding tricks, especially for languages like Korean where poetic norms are distinct and underrepresented in current LLM training.

Abstract: LLMs often struggle with modern Korean poetry, producing outputs that resemble "line-broken prose." We address two coupled tasks: detecting whether a Korean poem is human- or LLM-authored, and guiding LLMs to generate poetry closer in form to human writing. We quantify the human-LLM gap along four form-level linguistic dimensions: output length (Volume), the diversity and connective use of line-final forms (Structure Variation), the irregularity of line lengths (Rhythmic Irregularity), and adherence to standard orthography (Normative Adherence). We operationalize these dimensions as five interpretable features. For detection, a logistic regression classifier over these five features attains an average AUC-ROC of 83.60 in zero-shot out-of-distribution detection across seven unseen LLMs, versus 75.84 for the strongest baseline in our comparison, KatFishNet, an absolute gain of 7.76 AUC points and a 10.23% relative improvement; one generator-specific punctuation pattern outside our taxonomy remains a boundary case. For generation, expert evaluation on GPT-5.2 prefers feature-guided poems over the unconstrained baseline, and analyses across GPT-5.2 and Gemini-3 show that targeted length, rhythm, and ending statistics move toward the human distribution. These results suggest that interpretable, language-specific features can bridge the diagnosis and guidance of LLM-generated poetry.

</details>


### [35] [A Unifying Perspective on Language Model Representations: From Filler-Role Structure to Mechanistic Interpretability](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29034)
*Zhang Enyan,R. Thomas McCoy*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes Tensor Product Representations (TPRs) as a unified framework to explain several existing interpretability methods for language models, and shows both mathematically and empirically that these methods can be derived from and instantiated via TPRs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing interpretability methods for language models—such as linear probing, activation patching, sparse autoencoders, and analogy-style vector arithmetic—offer fragmented insights that are not clearly connected by a common theory of how models represent compositional structure. The authors want a principled, unified account of the internal structure of language models that can explain why these different tools work and how they relate to each other.

Method: The authors adopt Tensor Product Representations (TPRs), where compositional structures are encoded as bindings between fillers and roles in vector space. They formally derive how popular interpretability tools (additive analogies, linear probes, sparse autoencoders, activation patching) can be understood as operations over TPRs. Then, using a range of models from small toy setups to large language models, they construct versions of these interpretability methods explicitly based on the TPR derivations and compare their performance to standard implementations.

Result: They find that the TPR-based derivations of each interpretability method can be instantiated in practice and that these TPR-constructed variants perform comparably to the standard versions across different model scales. This supports the claim that TPRs can serve as a common underlying structure explaining why these interpretability methods work.

Conclusion: Tensor Product Representations provide a plausible unifying hypothesis for the internal structure of language models that underlies multiple existing interpretability methods. By showing both theoretical derivations and empirical parity between TPR-based and standard methods, the work moves toward an interpretability paradigm that not only explains isolated phenomena but also the systematic relationships between different analysis tools.

Abstract: A wide range of methods have been proposed for interpreting language models, delivering important insights into their inner workings. However, different methods and their resulting insights stand in relative isolation: what could the underlying structure of language models be, such that they give rise to all our interpretations? In this work, we propose using Tensor Product Representations (TPRs) as a unifying hypothesis. TPRs give a concrete proposal for how compositional structure could be represented in vector space --- as filler-role bindings. We show, both mathematically and empirically, that TPRs can unify several prior interpretability methods: additive analogies, linear probing, sparse autoencoders, and activation patching. Mathematically, we show that these methods can all be derived from TPRs. Empirically, we apply the derivations to a range of different models --- from small toy models to LLMs --- to construct instances of each of the above interpretability methods; these constructed variants perform comparably to their standard variants. We view this work as a step toward what interpretability will ideally provide: a unified account of the nature of neural networks, corroborated not just by individual observations but also by an explanation of the connections between them.

</details>


### [36] [RouteSparse: Input-Conditional Pattern Routing for Budgeted Long-Context Prefilling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29058)
*Chao Zhang,Yifan Ji,Ziyan Zhang,Kai Song,Fei Lin*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: RouteSparse dynamically routes each attention head and prompt segment among a small set of sparse attention patterns to accelerate long-context prefilling while tightly controlling accuracy loss.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing dynamic sparse attention methods like MInference fix one sparse pattern and sparsity budget per head, assuming they remain suitable for all prompts. This leads to suboptimal quality–latency tradeoffs because different inputs and segments may benefit from different sparsity patterns or densities. The authors aim to retain the speedups of dynamic sparsity for very long contexts while adaptively choosing patterns per input to minimize accuracy loss under hardware constraints.

Method: They introduce RouteSparse, which maintains a small library of GPU-efficient sparse attention patterns. For each head and prompt segment, a lightweight probe estimates the utility and uncertainty of each pattern. A latency-aware router then selects both the pattern and its sparsity budget, formulating the decision as a constrained risk minimization problem. For cases with high uncertainty, the method selectively falls back to denser attention masks. The approach also derives an error certificate for attention outputs based on the probability mass omitted by sparsification, and it incorporates hardware profiling so that the router’s choices align with actual GPU efficiency characteristics.

Result: On Llama 3.1-8B-Instruct with 128K-token prompts, RouteSparse attains a 6.5× speedup over dense prefill with only a 0.2-point drop on the RULER benchmark. In contrast, a fixed per-head routing baseline achieves a slightly higher 7.3× speedup but with a substantially worse 1.6-point RULER drop. Additional ablation studies show that input-conditional routing, hardware-aware profiling, and selective dense fallback each significantly improve the overall quality–latency tradeoff.

Conclusion: RouteSparse demonstrates that input-conditional routing among a small, hardware-efficient library of sparse attention patterns can deliver substantial long-context acceleration with minimal accuracy degradation. By framing routing as constrained risk minimization and using both uncertainty-aware fallback and error certificates from omitted probability mass, the method outperforms fixed-pattern baselines and clarifies which design components are most critical for balancing speed and quality in sparse attention systems.

Abstract: Dynamic sparse attention can reduce the quadratic cost of long-context prefilling without changing model weights. MInference assigns each attention head one pattern offline and estimates that pattern's sparse indices for every prompt. This design is efficient, but it assumes that a head's preferred pattern and sparsity budget remain suitable across inputs. We introduce RouteSparse, which routes each head and prompt segment among a small library of GPU-efficient sparse patterns. A low-cost probe estimates pattern utility and uncertainty; a latency-aware router then selects a pattern and budget, while uncertain cases fall back to a denser mask. We formulate routing as constrained risk minimization, derive an attention-output error certificate from omitted probability mass, and evaluate the method on long-context retrieval, question answering, summarization, and language modeling. On Llama 3.1-8B-Instruct with 128K-token prompts, RouteSparse achieves $6.5\times$ dense prefill speed with a 0.2-point RULER drop relative to dense attention, compared with $7.3\times$ speed and a 1.6-point drop for fixed per-head routing. Ablations confirm that input-conditional routing, hardware profiling, and selective dense fallback each contribute to the quality--latency tradeoff.

</details>


### [37] [Not All or None: Dynamic Construction of Target-aware Memory Graph for Conversational Stance Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29066)
*Yifan Xiang,Bin Liang,Yuqi Huang,Ruifeng Xu,Kam-Fai Wong*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes TamGraph, a target-aware memory graph model that selectively uses historical conversational context to improve conversational stance detection, significantly boosting LLM performance on English and Chinese benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Conversational stance detection in real-world social media is difficult because it must infer a user’s attitude toward a target using long, noisy conversational histories. Existing methods either rely on all prior turns (introducing noise and inefficiency) or ignore conversation history (missing useful target-related cues). The authors aim to design a mechanism that can dynamically exploit only the target-relevant parts of the conversation history for accurate stance detection.

Method: The authors introduce TamGraph (target-aware Memory Graph), which dynamically leverages target-related historical statements. Instead of feeding all previous utterances, TamGraph uses a stepwise, entropy-guided backtracking process to selectively activate memory from historical conversation turns. It then builds a target-aware graph over utterances, where edges model stance relations. This graph structure conditions the stance prediction on only the most relevant prior context, integrating memory selection and relational modeling in a unified framework.

Result: On both English and Chinese conversational stance detection benchmarks, TamGraph outperforms baseline methods, including large language models without such a memory-graph mechanism. The experiments show substantial gains in stance classification accuracy/metrics, demonstrating the effectiveness of selective memory activation and target-aware graph modeling.

Conclusion: Selective, target-aware use of conversation history via a memory graph can significantly improve conversational stance detection. By using entropy-guided backtracking to activate only relevant historical utterances and modeling their relations in a graph, TamGraph effectively captures target-specific stance dynamics while reducing noise, leading to strong performance across languages.

Abstract: Stance detection is crucial for understanding the underlying attitude of an expression towards a target. Conversational stance detection is a more challenging stance detection task in real-world social media scenarios, as it involves detecting the user's stance by leveraging the target-related historical statements across conversational sessions. In this paper, we propose target-aware Memory Graph TamGraph, a novel method that dynamically leverages target-related statements for conversational stance detection. Instead of considering all preceding historical conversations or using no prior conversation information for stance detection, our TamGraph employs a stepwise, entropy-guided backtracking mechanism to selectively activate memory from historical conversations and dynamically constructs a target-aware graph to model the stance relations among utterances. This allows the exploitation of target-related information from the conversation history for stance detection while preventing the introduction of noise. Experimental results on both English and Chinese benchmarks demonstrate that our TamGraph substantially improves LLM performance on conversational stance detection.

</details>


### [38] [Recognition-Refusal Misalignment in LLMs: Why Models Answer Structurally Unanswerable Questions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29109)
*Yucheng Du,Xiyang Hu*

Main category: cs.CL
