TL;DR: The paper shows language models internally recognize when math/code questions are structurally unanswerable, but this signal is not aligned with their safety/refusal mechanisms, causing them to confidently answer impossible questions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand why large language models often produce confident answers to structurally impossible questions instead of abstaining, and whether this is due to lack of internal recognition of impossibility or a failure to route that recognition to a refusal response.

Method: Analyze hidden states of instruction-tuned LLMs (1.7B–70B) to find a linear direction separating answerable from structurally impossible math and code prompts; compare this "recognition" direction with a safety-refusal direction and an invalidity-aware direction; perform generation-time steering along these directions; compare base vs. instruct models.

Result: A single linear direction in hidden states predicts structural (im)possibility, demonstrating that models encode a "no admissible answer" signal. This recognition direction is almost orthogonal to the safety-refusal direction but partially aligned with an invalidity-aware direction. Steering along the recognition direction modulates invalidity-aware behavior in a dose-responsive way, unlike random directions. The misalignment geometry already exists at the pretraining stage.

Conclusion: LLMs' tendency to answer structurally impossible questions stems from a routing failure, not an encoding failure: they internally represent that no valid answer exists, but this signal is not aligned with the safety-refusal pathway, so the model does not abstain despite recognizing impossibility.

Abstract: Large language models often answer structurally unanswerable questions, such as computing cot(-540°) or evaluating (1).startswith("1"), instead of abstaining. We ask whether this failure reflects missing recognition or failed routing from recognition to abstention. Across instruction-tuned models from 1.7B to 70B parameters, a single linear direction in the hidden state separates answerable from structurally impossible math and code prompts, showing that models represent impossibility before generation. Yet this recognition direction is nearly orthogonal to the canonical safety-refusal direction that mediates trained harmful-content refusal. An in-domain behavior-defined invalidity-aware direction is closer to recognition, but only partially aligned with it, and remains near-orthogonal to safety refusal. Generation-time steering along the recognition direction changes invalidity-aware behavior bidirectionally and dose-responsively on structural math and code cells, while random directions do not. Base/instruct comparisons further show that the low-cosine geometry is already present at the pretraining endpoint. The confident-on-impossible failure is therefore better explained as a routing failure than as an encoding failure: the model has a usable "no admissible answer" signal, but the safety-refusal pathway is not aligned to use it.

</details>


### [39] [HEAR Who Said What: Unlocking Speaker-Attributed Reasoning via Counterfactual Voice Grounding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29120)
*Dongwook Lee,Sangkwon Park,Eunwoo Song,Che Hyun Lee,Youngho Cho,Junho Kim,June Young Yi,Heeseung Kim,Sungroh Yoon*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces HEAR, a benchmark to test whether Speech Language Models can correctly attribute speech to speakers and reason about them, and A2R, a new model trained to rely on vocal cues rather than semantics, achieving strong performance and generalization on multi-speaker tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing Speech Language Models are used in multi-speaker settings but it is unclear whether they can accurately attribute speech to the right speaker and perform higher-level reasoning over speaker identities. There is a need for a systematic diagnostic benchmark to probe these abilities and for training approaches that make models truly use acoustic speaker cues instead of shallow semantic patterns.

Method: The authors create HEAR, a hierarchical benchmark with 2.4K human-verified samples from 887 multi-party audio clips, specifically designed to test foundational skills of speaker attribution and speaker-aware reasoning. They evaluate 20 state-of-the-art SLMs on HEAR, then propose A2R, a 30B-parameter model trained on CASH (Counterfactual Audio with Speaker-level Hard negatives), where counterfactual and hard-negative examples force the model to attend to acoustic vocal characteristics instead of purely linguistic content.

Result: On HEAR, existing leading SLMs perform poorly and appear to rely more on semantic priors than on actual vocal evidence for speaker identity. The proposed A2R model significantly improves performance on HEAR and, without task-specific fine-tuning, shows strong zero-shot generalization to a range of multi-speaker downstream tasks, indicating improved robustness and speaker awareness.

Conclusion: Speaker attribution and reasoning are weak points for current SLMs, which tend to exploit semantic cues rather than true speaker information. By introducing HEAR and training with the CASH strategy, the authors demonstrate that a model (A2R) can be guided to genuinely leverage acoustic speaker cues, unlocking latent capabilities for robust, speaker-aware reasoning in multi-speaker audio scenarios.

Abstract: Speech Language Models (SLMs) are increasingly deployed in multi-speaker environments, yet their ability to attribute speech to the correct speaker and reason over speaker identities remains unclear. Hence, we introduce HEAR, a conceptually hierarchical benchmark diagnosing the foundational capabilities of speaker-attributed reasoning, comprising 2.4K human-verified samples from 887 diverse multi-party audio clips. Evaluating 20 leading SLMs on HEAR reveals they struggle with these foundational tasks, often relying on semantic priors rather than actual vocal cues. To address this, we present A2R, a 30B model optimized on Counterfactual Audio with Speaker-level Hard negatives (CASH), a dataset designed to guide the model to prioritize acoustic vocal cues over linguistic signals. A2R achieves strong performance on HEAR and exhibits zero-shot generalization to diverse multi-speaker downstream tasks, demonstrating that learned speaker attribution unlocks the model's latent capacity for speaker-aware reasoning. All resources are available at https://attributetoreason.github.io/AttributeToReason/

</details>


### [40] [AI Historian: Helping historians organize and verify person-centred temporal clues from dispersed historical narratives](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29133)
*Yifeng Lu,Zijie Yang,Jie Li,Qingkai Min,Yue Zhang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces AI Historian (AIH), an AI agent system for organizing person-centered timelines from dispersed historical narratives, achieving higher accuracy and much faster annotation than humans and naive LLM prompting.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Historical information about a person is scattered across many texts, chapters, and perspectives, making it hard and time-consuming for historians to reconstruct accurate, source-traceable timelines of people’s activities, relationships, and contexts. Existing workflows require manual extraction, cross-text linking, and temporal reasoning, which does not scale to large corpora such as the Twenty-Four Histories. There is a need for tools that can systematically extract and align person-time evidence while preserving verifiable links to original sources.

Method: The authors design AI Historian (AIH), an AI agent system that operates on source sentences as basic evidence units. AIH automatically identifies named persons and temporal cues in text, proposes cross-text associations for events and time references, verifies these associations, and infers comparable temporal ranges, all while preserving explicit traces back to the source sentences. They evaluate AIH on six biographical cases from Sima Qian’s Shiji involving Liu Bang, Xiang Yu, and Xiao He. They compare three conditions: AIH agent, human-only annotation, and direct LLM prompting. They then scale AIH to larger corpora, including the Twenty-Four Histories, other ancient Chinese, Japanese, and Korean histories, and modern historical materials, and publish the processed outputs via the Westlake Historian platform.

Result: On the Shiji test cases, the AIH agent achieved a temporal-localization MicroIoU of 86.2%, outperforming human-only annotation at 81.3% and vastly exceeding direct LLM prompting at 17.1%. In terms of efficiency, AIH required about 14 minutes for annotation, compared to 1 hour 32 minutes for human-only work. The system was successfully applied to large-scale corpora, including major East Asian historical works and modern materials, producing structured outputs released through Westlake Historian.

Conclusion: AI Historian can substantially reduce the time and effort required to organize person-centered historical timelines from fragmented narratives while maintaining or improving accuracy relative to traditional manual annotation. By preserving explicit links from inferred timelines back to original sentences, AIH turns previously obscured, chapter-dispersed connections into transparent, revisable hypotheses that historians can collaboratively examine and test. The system shows promise as an infrastructure for large-scale, source-traceable historical research across diverse corpora.

Abstract: History is not preserved in complete, continuous form. Accounts of a person's activities, relationships and historical contexts are scattered across texts, chapters and narrative perspectives; historians must retrieve, identify and compare these materials to reconstruct temporal sequences and verify them against sources. Here we present AI Historian (AIH), an AI agent system that helps historians organize person-time evidence from dispersed biographical narratives. It takes source sentences as evidence units, identifies people and temporal cues, verifies candidate cross-text associations and infers comparable temporal ranges while preserving traceable source-text evidence. We evaluated AIH on six Shiji cases concerning Liu Bang, Xiang Yu and Xiao He. AIH Agent achieved a temporal-localization MicroIoU of 86.2%, compared with 81.3% for human-only annotation and 17.1% for direct large-language-model prompting; it required about 14 min, versus 1 h 32 min for human-only annotation. We further applied AIH to the Twenty-Four Histories and other ancient Chinese histories, ancient Japanese and Korean histories, and modern and contemporary historical materials, and released the results through Westlake Historian. These results indicate that AIH can reduce the cost of organizing historical materials at scale while turning connections obscured by chapter-based narration into traceable, revisable research questions for collaborative testing.

</details>


### [41] [Quantifying Error Tolerance in Synthetic Data: An Atomic-level Operand vs. Operator Perturbation Study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29144)
*Jiaxiang Liu,Chenhao Yuan,Shuwen Xu,Boxuan Xing,Xiusheng Huang,Yinhao Xu,Hao Liu,Wenhao Teng,Xiangwen Liao,Pengfei Cao,Jun Zhao,Kang Liu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes a new framework, ATOM, to analyze and improve synthetic data quality for training large language models by separating harmless input (operand) noise from harmful function (operator) errors, leading to better performance than strong baselines like LIMA.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Synthetic data is vital for scaling large language models, but current data filtering methods are poorly calibrated: they either remove too many potentially useful samples or keep too many flawed ones. A key missing piece is a quantitative understanding of what kinds of errors models can tolerate. Without this, practitioners do not know which imperfections in synthetic data truly harm model performance and which are acceptable or even beneficial for diversity.

Method: The authors introduce Atomic Tree Operation Modeling (ATOM), which decomposes each data sample into atomic functional units of the form f(x) → y, where f is an operator that maps an input x (operand) to an output y. They then explicitly distinguish perturbations to the operand x (e.g., changes in input content) from perturbations to the operator f (e.g., changes in the underlying task, instruction, or reasoning function). Experiments compare model robustness under these two perturbation types and construct synthetic datasets that preferentially preserve operator correctness and diversity while allowing more flexibility/noise in operands.

Result: Empirically, the authors find a double dissociation: language models remain robust when operands x are perturbed but suffer severe performance degradation when operator f is perturbed. Leveraging this insight, they design ATOM-based synthetic data that focuses on ensuring operator correctness and diversity rather than strict operand precision. Training on this ATOM-synthesized data yields performance gains, including a reported +3.1% improvement over a strong baseline such as LIMA.

Conclusion: The study concludes that not all synthetic data errors are equally harmful: operator-level errors are fatal to model performance, whereas operand-level noise is comparatively tolerable. Therefore, filtering and generation strategies should prioritize operator quality and diversity over aggressive cleaning of operand details. The ATOM framework operationalizes this distinction and produces synthetic datasets that outperform rigorous baselines, highlighting that operator diversity is a more critical driver of model improvement than fine-grained operand precision.

Abstract: Synthetic data generation has become a cornerstone for advancing large language models. However, the lack of the quantitative analysis for error tolerance became a critical bottleneck. Consequently, current filtering strategies fluctuate between two extremes: they are either overly aggressive, risking the exclusion of potentially valuable samples, or overly permissive, failing to eliminate erroneous samples effectively. To bridge this gap, this paper introduces Atomic Tree Operation Modeling (ATOM), a framework that decomposes data into functional units ($f(x)\rightarrow y$). ATOM distinguishes benign Operand $x$ perturbations from fatal Operator $f$ perturbations. The former are needlessly discarded by aggressive filtering, while the latter slip through permissive filtering. Our experiments reveal a double dissociation: models are robust to operand perturbations but collapse under operator perturbations. By prioritizing operator over aggressive operand precision, our ATOM-synthesized data outperforms rigorous baselines (e.g., +3.1% gain over LIMA), suggesting that operator diversity matters more than operand precision. Our code is available at https://github.com/Lut-hub/ATOM.

</details>


### [42] [Toward a Cross-Lingual Romanization Ecosystem for Sinitic Languages: A Paired Mandarin-Cantonese Case Study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29170)
*Zijie Zhang,Tan Lee,Yong Cao,Benyou Wang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: They propose a unified, cross-lingual romanization framework and infrastructure for multiple Sinitic languages, show how to design several coordinated romanization schemes, and demonstrate that this alignment improves speech-to-text performance in low-resource settings.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing romanization systems for Sinitic languages (e.g., Mandarin Pinyin, Cantonese Jyutping) were developed independently, so there is no systematic cross-lingual alignment between them. This makes it harder to transfer models and resources across related languages, which is especially problematic for low-resource Sinitic varieties. The paper aims to create a principled, shared design framework that aligns romanization across Sinitic languages to enable better technological interoperability and transfer learning.

Method: They define a cross-lingual romanization design framework based on four principles: (1) phonetic correspondence (similar sounds share similar symbols), (2) historical-phonological correspondence (cognates have similar romanized strings), (3) one-phoneme-one-symbol, and (4) use of basic Latin letters, with explicit balancing of trade-offs between them. Using this framework, they design paired Cantonese and Mandarin schemes (CantRomZJ1 and MandRomZJ1) and additional schemes for Meixian Hakka, Shanghai Wu, and Nanjing Jianghuai Mandarin. They then build open-source digital infrastructure for storing, converting, parsing these romanizations, building dictionaries, and generating input methods. Finally, they fine-tune Meta’s Massively Multilingual Speech (MMS) models for speech-to-romanization and compare performance of their aligned MandRomZJ1+CantRomZJ1 against a Pinyin+Jyutping baseline on Cantonese recognition tasks.

Result: Their aligned MandRomZJ1+CantRomZJ1 setup reduces Cantonese word error rate (WER) by 7.80% and character error rate (CER) by 10.61% compared with the Pinyin+Jyutping baseline when using MMS-based speech-to-romanization. This empirical result shows that using cross-lingually aligned romanization schemes improves transfer from higher-resource Mandarin to lower-resource Cantonese in speech technology.

Conclusion: A systematically aligned cross-lingual romanization framework for Sinitic languages is both feasible and beneficial. By designing romanization schemes that share phonetic and historical-phonological correspondences and by providing supporting open-source infrastructure, the authors can measurably improve low-resource speech technology performance (here, Cantonese) via better transfer. This suggests that careful romanization design is an important lever for improving multilingual and low-resource NLP and speech applications within the Sinitic language family.

Abstract: This paper proposes the Sinitic Romanization Ecosystem, a cross-lingual Sinitic romanization design framework with supporting digital infrastructure and a community-driven open-source workflow. The design framework addresses the lack of systematic cross-lingual romanization alignment among Sinitic languages through four design principles: phonetic correspondence for representing similar sounds with similar romanized symbols, historical-phonological correspondence for aligning cognate romanization strings, one-phoneme-one-symbol, and basic Latin-letter use, with a balancing consideration recognizing trade-offs among these principles. For the main paired case study, we devel-op CantRomZJ1 and MandRomZJ1, Cantonese and Manda-rin romanization schemes following the design framework, respectively. We also develop schemes for several other Sinitic languages, including Meixian Hakka, Shanghai Wu, and Nanjing Jianghuai Mandarin, following the same de-sign framework. To bring the romanization schemes into practical use, we develop open-source infrastructure for structured romanization storage, conversion, parsing, dic-tionary construction, and input-method generation. Finally, we evaluate the design framework through speech-to-romanization experiments based on Meta's Massively Mul-tilingual Speech (MMS) fine-tuning. Compared with the Pinyin+Jyutping baseline, our Man-dRomZJ1+CantRomZJ1 condition reduces Cantonese WER and CER by 7.80% and 10.61%, respectively. These results suggest that cross-lingual romanization alignment can improve transfer in low-resource Sinitic speech technology.

</details>


### [43] [Toward Cultural Alignment: Human-Centered Evaluation of Multimodal AI Stories Across Five African Communities](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29209)
*Millicent Ochieng,Felermino D. M. A. Ali,Elizabeth A. Ankrah,Najeeb Gambo Abdulhamid,Migisha Boyd,Stephanie Nyairo,Mercy Muchai,Samuel Chege Maina,Aditya Vashistha,Anja Thieme,Jacki O'Neill*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper evaluates how well AI-generated multimodal stories reflect the real cultures of five African communities, builds a taxonomy of cultural (mis)alignment, and tests automated LLM judges against community judgments.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As multimodal generative AI systems are increasingly used to tell stories about real-world communities, there is a risk that they may misrepresent or stereotype those communities. Existing evaluations usually rely on superficial cultural markers or automated metrics, rather than on the perspectives of the people being represented. The authors are motivated to understand what true cultural alignment requires and whether automated judges can reliably stand in for community members in large-scale evaluation.

Method: The authors run a community-grounded mixed-methods study with 19 cultural representatives from five African communities. Participants evaluate AI-generated multimodal stories using both quantitative annotations and qualitative focus group discussions. From these data, the authors derive a taxonomy of cultural alignment, consisting of five types of cultural markers and eight mechanisms through which misalignment tends to occur. They also evaluate five multimodal LLM-based judges by comparing their scores with community judgments across the five communities to assess reliability and calibration.

Result: The study shows that cultural alignment cannot be reduced to surface-level or recognizable cultural markers; instead, alignment depends on how those markers are embedded in social, linguistic, procedural, and visual contexts. The authors identify five broad cultural marker categories and eight recurring misalignment mechanisms. In the automated evaluation component, the five multimodal LLM judges exhibit strong variability in reliability and calibration across different communities—no single judge consistently matches community-grounded assessments everywhere.

Conclusion: Culturally accurate AI storytelling requires context-aware alignment, going beyond token cultural symbols to how they function within lived practices, relationships, language, and visual norms. Automated multimodal LLM judges are not yet trustworthy as universal proxies for community evaluation, given their inconsistent performance across communities. The authors argue for community-calibrated evaluation pipelines in which automated judges are explicitly validated against community judgments and selectively deployed, with human review remaining essential where judges fail to align.

Abstract: In this paper, we examine how well AI-generated multimodal stories align with the lived practices, relationships, language, values, and visual expectations of the communities they represent. We conduct a community-grounded mixed-methods evaluation with 19 culture representatives across five African communities, combining quantitative annotations with qualitative focus group discussions. We find that cultural alignment depends not simply on recognizable cultural markers, but on how those markers fit social, linguistic, procedural, and visual context. From these evaluations, we develop a taxonomy of cultural alignment comprising five broader cultural marker categories and eight recurring mechanisms of misalignment. We additionally evaluate five multimodal LLM judges to examine whether automated evaluation can approximate community-grounded judgments at scale. Judge reliability and score calibration vary substantially across communities, with no single judge performing consistently across all five settings. These findings motivate community-calibrated evaluation pipelines in which automated judges are validated against community judgments to determine where they can be trusted and where human review remains necessary.

</details>


### [44] [Attribute-Based Activation Steering of LLMs for Group-Specific Explanation Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29215)
*Leandra Fichtel,Janek Prange,Henning Wachsmuth*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes an activation-engineering method to steer LLMs so they generate explanations tailored to specific audience groups, outperforming prompting and other steering baselines while preserving factuality.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: People have diverse backgrounds, prior knowledge, and abilities, so one-size-fits-all explanations from LLMs are often ineffective. Simply prompting models for audience adaptation has proven insufficient, and there is a lack of computational techniques that can reliably tailor explanations to specific user groups while remaining factually correct. The paper aims to fill this gap by developing a systematic way to adapt explanatory style and assumed knowledge level for particular target groups.

Method: The method has two main steps. First, the authors identify group-specific attributes related to explanation style and knowledge level for a chosen target group (e.g., domain experts vs. laypersons). Second, using activation engineering, they compute steering vectors corresponding to these attributes and inject them into the internal activations of an LLM during inference. This enables fine-grained control of the generated explanations with respect to the target group. They then empirically evaluate steering effectiveness using automatic metrics for specificity and factuality, and run a human study with experts from different target groups.

Result: The proposed activation-steering approach produces explanations that are more specifically tailored to the intended target group than explanations obtained via prompting or existing steering baselines. At the same time, it largely preserves factual correctness, as measured by automatic and human evaluations. Human experts from different groups judge the tailored explanations as better aligned with their needs and backgrounds.

Conclusion: Activation-based steering can effectively control LLMs to generate explanations adapted to particular audience groups, outperforming prompt-only and prior steering methods in terms of tailoring while maintaining factuality. This suggests that internal activation manipulation is a promising direction for building explanation systems that account for users’ backgrounds and knowledge levels.

Abstract: To effectively enable people to understand new topics, explanations should be tailored to their backgrounds and abilities. So far, prompting alone has been shown to be insufficient for creating such explanations and other computational methods are missing. Therefore, this paper investigates whether LLMs can be steered to generate explanations that are tailored to a specific group of people. To this end, we propose an approach that first identifies group-specific attributes in terms of explanatory style and knowledge of a specific target group. Building on activation engineering, it then computes attribute-based steering vectors and adds them to the internal activations of an LLM during inference to enable a fine-grained steering. In our experiments, we assess the steering effectiveness of our approach in terms of specificity and factuality of the generated explanations. Additionally, we evaluate the explanations in a study with human experts from different target groups. Compared to prompting and state-of-the-art steering baselines, our approach tailors the explanations significantly better to the target group while largely maintaining factuality.

</details>


### [45] [Anchoring Speech with Semantics: A Multimodal Adapter Mechanism for Automatic Speech Recognition in Low-Resource Languages](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29239)
*Kuan-Tang Huang,Cheng-Yeh Yang,Chien-Chun Wang,Hung-Shin Lee,Hsin-Min Wang,Berlin Chen*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes SAMA-ASR, an adapter that injects semantic and acoustic anchor embeddings into an encoder–decoder ASR model to improve low-resource speech recognition, showing gains on Taiwanese Hokkien and Hakka.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Low-resource ASR suffers from scarce transcriptions, limiting supervised learning for accurate target-side generation. However, related tasks like speech-to-text translation can provide additional semantic information about utterances. The paper is motivated by leveraging these richer semantic signals and acoustic cues to better guide the decoder in low-resource ASR, without requiring heavy model changes or large resources.

Method: The authors introduce SAMA-ASR, a lightweight adapter module added to an encoder–decoder multitask speech model. The module injects two types of anchors into the decoder states via cross-modal adaptation: (1) semantic anchors from auxiliary text translations represented as embeddings capturing utterance-level meaning, and (2) an acoustic anchor derived from the input speech. These anchors are fused with decoder hidden states before token prediction. During training, oracle translations are used; at test time, anchors are generated automatically by an upstream speech-to-text translation model. The approach remains plug-and-play for similar multitask speech architectures, and the authors analyze performance under different translation model capacities.

Result: On two 30-hour low-resource Sinitic datasets (Taiwanese Hokkien and Hakka), SAMA-ASR consistently outperforms several baselines, including purely acoustic ASR, prompt-based approaches that use translations, and systems using only semantic translation guidance without the proposed adapter structure. The method maintains strong performance even when the semantic anchors come from automatically generated translations rather than oracle ones. Experiments varying the speech-to-text translation model show that even a relatively compact translator can provide anchors that yield meaningful ASR improvements.

Conclusion: SAMA-ASR demonstrates that explicitly anchoring the ASR decoder with both semantic information from translations and an acoustic summary of the speech can significantly improve recognition in low-resource conditions. The approach is lightweight, compatible with encoder–decoder multitask setups, and robust when using automatically generated semantic anchors from modest-capacity speech translation models, making it practical for deployment in low-resource language scenarios.

Abstract: Low-resource ASR remains difficult because scarce transcripts provide limited supervised evidence for target-side generation. To address this gap, we propose SAMA-ASR, a lightweight adapter mechanism that augments the decoder with semantic anchors from auxiliary translations and an acoustic anchor from speech; in principle, the mechanism can be applied to similar encoder--decoder multitask speech models. Through cross-modal adaptation, SAMA-ASR conditions decoder states on translation-derived semantic embeddings and a speech embedding, combining utterance-level meaning with speech-grounded evidence before token prediction. At evaluation time, these semantic anchors can be generated automatically by an upstream speech-to-text translator rather than supplied as oracle translations. Experiments on two 30-hour datasets covering the low-resource Sinitic varieties Taiwanese Hokkien and Hakka show that SAMA-ASR improves over acoustic, prior prompt-based, and semantic-only translation-guided baselines and remains effective in practical automatic semantic-anchor settings; translator-capacity analyses show that useful semantic anchors can be produced by a compact ST model.

</details>


### [46] [When Patients Cut In: Extending Clinical Conversational AI Safety to Interruptions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29241)
*Zachary Ellis,Spencer Hazel,Adam Brandt,Yajie Vera He,Ernest Lim,Jared Joselowitz*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Study evaluates how clinical voice agents recover from patient interruptions and finds large, configuration-specific failures in preserving required clinical content.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Clinical voice agents are increasingly used in real care, where patients often interrupt the system mid-utterance. Existing benchmarks assume cooperative turn-taking, so they miss a critical failure mode: interruption-induced loss of clinically required content. The authors aim to expose and quantify this overlooked problem.

Method: The authors design a transcript-based evaluation that simulates patient interruptions using three overlap types from conversation analysis: recognitional, competitive, and transitional sub-unit. They create four experimental cells (history-taking vs FAQ; information gathering vs provision) and test four practical, non-reasoning LLM configurations in cascaded speech-agent style. Performance is scored on whether the agent still delivers or elicits the clinically required content after being interrupted.

Result: Target-question failures vary between models in history-taking (gathering) tasks. In FAQ-style (provision) tasks, interruption increases failure rates for all models, with rankings changing across cells. Competitive FAQ interruptions are particularly harmful: all four models fail to cover the required information in all 30 trials (Wilson 95% CI 88.6–100.0%), while baseline (no interruption) failures are 0/30 for three models and 4/30 for Llama.

Conclusion: Interruption robustness is highly context- and configuration-dependent and cannot be captured by a single aggregate score. Reliable assessment must be grounded in the specific clinical content, reported separately for different task/overlap cells, and aligned with the interruption patterns expected in deployment. Even minor conversational markers (like an apology for interrupting) can shift recovery rates substantially and inconsistently across models.

Abstract: Clinical voice agents are now deployed in routine care, where real patients do not wait their turn: they interrupt. These systems typically use a cascaded architecture (speech-to-text -> LLM -> text-to-speech), so when a patient cuts the agent off mid-utterance, clinically required content can be lost even when the model handles cooperative transcripts well. Yet clinical conversational-AI benchmarks almost universally assume patients wait for the agent to finish, missing interruption-induced loss of required content. We present a transcript-based evaluation of interruption recovery, adapting conversation-analytic overlap categories into three operational types (recognitional, competitive, transitional sub-unit) and testing four deployment-oriented, non-reasoning LLM configurations across four cells spanning history-taking (information gathering) and FAQ (information provision), scored on whether the agent preserves the clinically required content. In the gathering cells, target-question failure varied across models; in the provision cells, where arms are directly comparable, failure rose for every model. Rankings differ across cells, and competitive FAQ interruption produced 30/30 provision-coverage failures for all four models (Wilson 95% CI: 88.6-100.0%; baseline 0/30 for three, 4/30 for Llama). A brief apology marker ("sorry to interrupt") shifts recovery by tens of percentage points, inconsistently across models, and for one it reduces recovery. Interruption robustness therefore cannot be a single score: evaluation must be content-grounded, reported per cell, and matched to the deployment's interruption profile.

</details>


### [47] [Large Language Models Systematically Favor Popular Options: Evidence and Mitigation Across MCQs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29257)
*Abdelrahman Abdallah,Mohammed Ali,Bhawna Piryani,Mahmoud Abdalla,Adam Jatowt*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper identifies and analyzes a 'popularity bias' in LLM multiple-choice question answering, introduces a controlled benchmark (PopMCQ) to measure it, and proposes an inference-time debiasing method (PopDebias) that substantially improves accuracy when popular options are misleading.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard MCQ benchmarks for LLMs can be confounded by how frequently answer options appear in training data or general text, making models prefer popular options regardless of correctness. This undermines evaluation validity and real-world reliability, especially when correct answers are less frequent or less salient in the training distribution. The authors aim to rigorously isolate and quantify this popularity bias and to provide practical tools to mitigate it without costly retraining.

Method: 1) Empirically observe that LLMs over-select popular but incorrect MCQ options and remain highly confident in these wrong choices, indicating miscalibrated confidence. 2) Construct PopMCQ, a benchmark where answer option popularity is systematically manipulated via six controlled strategies while holding the correct answer fixed, enabling causal analysis of popularity effects. 3) Design PopDebias, an inference-time calibration procedure that estimates a popularity prior over options (from a small calibration split) and subtracts it from model scores/logits at test time. 4) Evaluate 22 open-source LLMs (0.5B–32B parameters) on PopMCQ with and without PopDebias to measure impact on accuracy under varying levels of popularity pressure.

Result: On PopMCQ, models frequently choose popular but incorrect options, especially when all distractors are more popular than the correct answer; in the most adversarial setting, they pick such wrong answers 66% of the time, revealing strong popularity bias and confidence miscalibration. Applying PopDebias leads to consistent improvements across 22 open-source LLMs, with maximum accuracy gains of up to 54.1 percentage points under strong popularity pressure, while incurring negligible computational overhead and requiring no fine-tuning or labels at test time.

Conclusion: LLMs evaluated with standard MCQs are systematically biased toward popular answer options, which can severely distort both accuracy and calibration, particularly when correct answers are comparatively rare in the training distribution. The PopMCQ benchmark offers a controlled way to measure this bias, and the PopDebias method shows that a simple inference-time correction can substantially mitigate popularity effects, strengthening both evaluation reliability and practical robustness without retraining models.

Abstract: Multiple-choice questions (MCQs) are a standard format for evaluating large language models (LLMs), yet the popularity of answer options can confound evaluation. Modern LLMs systematically prefer popular but incorrect options over less popular correct ones, a vulnerability we call \textbf{popularity bias}. This pattern aligns with confidence miscalibration: model confidence remains high even as accuracy collapses for popular options. To systematically isolate this phenomenon, we introduce \textbf{PopMCQ}, a benchmark with six controlled strategies that vary option popularity while keeping the correct answer fixed. In our most adversarial setting, where all distractors are more popular than the correct option, models choose popular but wrong answers 66\% of the time. To mitigate this bias, we propose \textbf{PopDebias}, a lightweight inference-time correction that estimates and removes a popularity prior from model predictions. It requires no fine-tuning, is label-free at test time (using only a small calibration split for parameter fitting), and adds negligible computational cost. Experiments on 22 open-source LLMs (0.5B to 32B parameters) show consistent improvements, with accuracy gains up to 54.1 percentage points under strong popularity pressure. The code and data are available https://github.com/DataScienceUIBK/PopMCQ

</details>


### [48] [SHADOWBENCH: Toward Reliable Automatic Evaluation of Semantic Alignment in Autoformalization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29270)
*Hojae Han,Jongyoon Kim,Sanghyuk Park,Dongwook Cheon,Myungjae Jeon,Sunjong Choi,Soonho Kong,Wonseok Heo,Seung-won Hwang,Donghoon Hyeon*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: They introduce SA-Pass, a semantic evaluation protocol for autoformalized theorems that checks logical equivalence with target statements via shadow lemmas, and release ShadowBench, a Lean 4 benchmark where SA-Pass closely matches expert judgment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing autoformalization metrics for translating informal math to proof-assistant code are weak: they may reward type-correct but semantically wrong theorems or penalize correct but differently-formulated ones. The field needs an automatic, scalable way to evaluate whether generated formal statements really capture the intended informal theorem, without relying on humans for each instance.

Method: They define SA-Pass (Semantic Alignment Pass), inspired by Pass@k, which uses a set of auxiliary shadow statements that encode the intended meaning of a target theorem. For a generated formal statement to get full credit, it must (1) compile in Lean, (2) imply every shadow (forward check), and (3) be implied by the conjunction of all shadows (backward check), thereby approximating logical equivalence. They instantiate this protocol in ShadowBench, a Lean 4 benchmark of 178 nontrivial problems across eight mathematical domains, and evaluate different autoformalization agents, including Claude Code with a Lean-specific agentic wrapper.

Result: On ShadowBench, Claude Code (Opus 4.8) with the Numina-Lean-Agent attains a 61.8% compile rate but only 11.2% SA-Pass, indicating that most type-correct outputs are semantically misaligned. Over solutions produced by six distinct agentic setups, SA-Pass decisions agree with expert human judgments 98.8% of the time in a binary correct/incorrect sense, demonstrating that the protocol is a highly reliable proxy for expert assessment.

Conclusion: SA-Pass provides a robust, semantics-aware automatic metric for evaluating autoformalized mathematical statements, substantially improving over naive compile-based or syntactic checks. ShadowBench shows that current systems are far from reliably capturing theorem semantics despite decent compile rates, and the high agreement with experts suggests SA-Pass can support large-scale benchmarking and competitions such as the ICML 2026 AI4Math Challenge without intensive human labeling.

Abstract: Autoformalization translates informal mathematical theorems into code for proof assistants such as Lean. A central challenge is that current evaluation metrics can accept type-correct but misaligned statements or reject correct statements written in a different formulation. Inspired by Pass@$k$, we propose SA-Pass (*Semantic Alignment Pass*), which tests formal statements using auxiliary statements called *shadows* that characterize the intended statement. A generated statement receives full credit only when it compiles, implies each shadow (forward check), and is implied by their conjunction (backward check). We instantiate SA-Pass in ShadowBench, a Lean 4 full autoformalization benchmark of 178 postgraduate- to research-level problems spanning eight mathematical areas. Claude Code (Opus 4.8) with Numina-Lean-Agent reaches $61.8\%$ compile rate and $11.2\%$ SA-Pass. Across outputs generated by six agentic configurations, SA-Pass achieves $98.8\%$ binary agreement with expert judgments. An early version of ShadowBench served as the benchmark for Track 4 of the ICML 2026 AI4Math Challenge.

</details>


### [49] [Modality Fault Lines: Structural Corruptions Reveal Fragile Omni-Modal Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29278)
*Zhaolu Kang,Meixin Wu,Yu Xue,Yingjie He,Qiming Shi,Lei Wei,Yidi Wang,Richeng Xuan,Zhichao Hu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces SCEval, a benchmark that tests omni-modal LLMs under structured corruption of text, vision, and audio inputs to reveal where their cross-modal reasoning breaks down.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing evaluations of omni-modal large language models mostly use clean, fully intact text, vision, and audio inputs. High scores on such tasks are often interpreted as strong cross-modal fusion and robustness. However, these tests cannot distinguish whether models truly rely on stable, shared cross-modal structure or merely exploit superficial cues that only work when all modalities are clean and perfectly aligned. There is a need for an evaluation framework that probes how models behave when one or more modalities remain present and human-interpretable, but their internal evidence structure is perturbed, revealing hidden brittleness in multi-modal reasoning.

Method: The authors define the concept of a modality fault line: a point at which a model’s behavior becomes unstable when a modality is structurally perturbed while still being visible and interpretable to humans. To operationalize this, they propose SCEval (Structure-Corruption Evaluation), a diagnostic protocol that keeps the question, answer space, and modality channels (text, vision, audio) fixed while applying controlled structural corruptions to each modality individually and in combination. They construct SCEval from 273 human-verified tri-modal question-answering examples drawn from Social-IQ, OmniBench, and VALOR. Using these, they systematically corrupt the structure of text, visual, and audio inputs and evaluate how model accuracy changes. They run SCEval on 15 different omni-modal systems, including both proprietary and open-source models, comparing performance across clean and corrupted conditions and across different types of modality damage.

Result: Across the 15 evaluated omni-modal systems, structural corruption of the inputs consistently reduces accuracy relative to clean conditions, indicating that models are sensitive to disruptions in modality structure. Text–vision corruptions in particular form the most stable shared modality fault line, suggesting that the interaction between language and images is a key locus of instability. Additionally, when multiple modalities are corrupted together, the resulting performance degradation is non-additive: the drop in accuracy cannot be explained as a simple sum of the individual modality corruptions. This complex interaction pattern shows that models’ multi-modal fusion is more fragile and entangled than clean performance suggests.

Conclusion: The study concludes that high omni-modal accuracy on clean inputs does not guarantee reliability when the structure of cross-modal evidence is degraded, even if the modalities remain present and understandable to humans. The SCEval framework and the notion of modality fault lines reveal that current omni-modal LLMs often rely on brittle cross-modal cues rather than robust, shared representations. Therefore, future model development and evaluation should explicitly test behavior under structured modality corruptions to assess and improve true cross-modal robustness, rather than relying solely on clean-input benchmarks.

Abstract: Omni-modal large language models are increasingly evaluated on clean text--vision--audio inputs, where every channel is present, synchronized, and readily interpretable. Such scores are often taken as evidence of robust cross-modal fusion, but clean evaluation cannot tell whether success depends on stable cross-modal structure or on cues sufficient only in intact inputs. To address this gap, we define a modality fault line: a boundary at which model behavior becomes unstable when a modality remains present and human-interpretable, but its internal evidence structure is perturbed. We introduce SCEval (Structure-Corruption Evaluation) a diagnostic evaluation protocol that keeps the question, answer space, and modality channels fixed while applying controlled structural corruptions to text, vision, and audio individually and jointly. Built from $273$ human-verified tri-modal examples from Social-IQ, OmniBench, and VALOR, SCEval evaluates $15$ proprietary and open-source omni-modal systems. The results show that structural corruption lowers clean accuracy, text--vision damage forms the most stable shared fault line, and multi-modal degradation is non-additive rather than a simple function of the number of corrupted modalities. Clean omni-modal accuracy therefore does not establish that a model will remain reliable when cross-modal evidence becomes structurally unreliable.

</details>


### [50] [Cloud and On-Premises Deployment of Uzbek Legal RAG via Targeted Retriever Fine-Tuning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29284)
*Tatul Danielyan,Mariam Avetisyan,Hrant Davtyan*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper presents the design, evaluation, and deployment lessons of an Uzbek legal RAG system under both cloud and on-prem constraints, introducing new benchmarks and a strong open Uzbek embedder (UTE-1), and showing that heavy LLM fine-tuning is often unnecessary and impractical.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: General-purpose LLM leaderboards do not reflect the real constraints of legal QA in low-resource languages like Uzbek, especially under strict cost, privacy, and latency constraints. There was also no appropriate evaluation benchmark for such a setting, making model and system choices hard to justify and optimize.

Method: The authors build a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) legal assistant for Uzbek in two deployment regimes: cost-constrained cloud with access to proprietary models, and on-prem with only open-weight models and limited hardware. They construct two expert-based benchmarks: a retrieval benchmark with 178 queries and gold spans, and an end-to-end benchmark with 504 Q&A pairs scored by an LLM judge (validated against humans and another-family judge). They compare open vs proprietary models for both retrieval and QA, develop and train UTE-1, an Uzbek text embedding model, and run a QLoRA fine-tuning experiment for long-context legal QA, analyzing performance, practicality, and maintainability.

Result: (1) The performance gap between proprietary and open models in this Uzbek legal RAG setting is small and can be closed cheaply via fine-tuning, especially on the retrieval side. (2) UTE-1 achieves state-of-the-art open-model performance for Uzbek text embedding. (3) Attempts to close remaining gaps through heavy QLoRA fine-tuning for long-context legal QA yield negative or impractical results under real hardware and maintenance constraints. (4) The benchmarks, LLM-judge evaluation pipeline, and UTE-1 embedder are successfully created and released.

Conclusion: For low-resource legal QA systems like Uzbek Legal RAG, careful system and retrieval design, plus light fine-tuning of embedding models, are generally more impactful and sustainable than extensive LLM fine-tuning. Open models, when properly tuned and evaluated under realistic benchmarks, can nearly match proprietary systems, even under strict privacy and latency constraints. The released benchmarks, code, and UTE-1 embedder provide a foundation for future research and practical deployments in low-resource legal NLP.

Abstract: Deploying large language models for legal question answering raises challenges that general-purpose leaderboards do not capture, particularly for low-resource languages and under hard operational constraints. We report on building and operating a retrieval-augmented (RAG) legal assistant for Uzbek that must run in two regimes: a managed cloud service that maximizes answer quality within a per-token cost ceiling, and an on-premises deployment for clients whose legal data may not leave their infrastructure, restricting us to open-weight models on limited local hardware under latency constraints. Because no evaluation existed for this setting, we build two domain benchmarks: a retrieval benchmark of 178 expert-annotated legal queries with gold provision spans, and an end-to-end benchmark of 504 expert-curated question--answer pairs scored by an LLM judge whose ratings we validate against human judgments and against an independent-family judge. Applying these benchmarks under each regime, we find the open-versus-proprietary gap is small and cheaply closed by fine-tuning. Therefore, we train UTE-1, which is a state-of-the-art text embedder among open models for Uzbek. We also demonstrate that closing the performance gap via fine-tuning is both impractical due to the intensive hardware demands of long-context legal Q\&A and unnecessary, given that legal acts change frequently. We support this by reporting a negative result from a QLoRA experiment. We distill practical guidance for similar deployments, drawn from a system serving real users in production. We release our benchmarks, evaluation code and the fine-tuned embedder (UTE-1) \href{https://metric-ai-lab.github.io/Uzbek-Legal-RAG/}{at this https URL} to support future work on low-resource legal NLP.

</details>


### [51] [Learning Simple Test-Time Environments for LLM Web Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29305)
*Junxuan Li,Zijun Liu,Ziyi Huang,Peng Li,Yuzhou Liu,Ming Yan,Yang Liu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes Test-Time Environment Decomposition (TTED), a label-free learning framework that lets LLM web agents decompose and learn from complex environments during inference to improve compositional generalization and real-world web automation performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM agents that work well in manually constructed, simple environments often fail in complex real-world settings. Existing explanations focus on compositional generalization gaps across combinations of simple environments, but they usually assume agents cannot learn about the environment during deployment. The authors are motivated to enable LLM web agents to adapt online to complex observations by learning structure (decomposition) of the environment at test time, thereby making them more robust in real-world use.

Method: The authors introduce trial steps where the agent actively decomposes a complex environment observation into simpler sub-modules or sub-environments before executing the main task. They then propose Test-Time Environment Decomposition (TTED), a label-free test-time training procedure that updates or adapts the agent’s behavior based on experience gathered in these sub-environments, without requiring explicit supervision. The method composes the learned behaviors from simpler sub-environments to handle the full complex environment, effectively performing environment structure discovery and adaptation during inference.

Result: Empirical evaluations on both synthetic and realistic web benchmarks show that (1) experience gained by the agent in simpler sub-environments can be successfully composed to yield better performance on the overall complex environment, and (2) applying test-time training to these sub-environments substantially improves the agent’s compositional generalization and success rate on real-world web automation tasks. Additional analysis gives design insights into how the label-free learning component should be implemented for effectiveness.

Conclusion: The paper concludes that enabling LLM agents to decompose and learn from environment structure at test time is a powerful way to close the performance gap between controlled benchmarks and complex real-world tasks. TTED demonstrates that label-free test-time environment decomposition can significantly enhance compositional generalization and robustness of LLM web agents, suggesting that such online environment learning mechanisms will be crucial for reliable real-world deployment as task environments become more complex.

Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents have demonstrated remarkable proficiency in manually constructed environments, yet their performance frequently collapses when transitioned to complex real-world settings. Existing research largely attribute this degradation to the compositional generalization gaps in LLMs on combinations of multiple simple, well-structured environments. In this work, we propose that LLM web agents can learn simple environment observations at test time. Specifically, we introduce trial steps for agents to decompose a complex environment observation into sub-modules, and implement a label-free learning method, Test-Time Environment Decomposition (TTED), to adapt agent behaviors with experience during inference. Our empirical evaluations demonstrate the framework's efficacy across both synthetic and realistic benchmarks, showing (1) experience gains acquired within simpler sub-environments can be effectively composed to improve performance in the full one, and (2) test-time training on sub-environments can significantly enhance the compositional generalization of agents in real-world web automation tasks. We also provide key insights in the design of the label-free learning algorithm. As more complex environments are accessed by LLM agents, we believe learning environment decomposition skills at test time will be critical for robust real-world deployment.

</details>


### [52] [Detecting and Repairing Hallucinations in Retrieval-Augmented Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29307)
*Sai Krishna Reddy Mulakkayala,Niki van Stein,Aske Plaat*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper studies how to automatically repair hallucinations in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) answers, comparing several strategies that modify unsupported factual claims and quantifying their impact on grounding and answer preservation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Retrieval-augmented language models still produce unsupported (hallucinated) statements, and current work largely focuses on detecting these problems instead of fixing them. For end users, merely flagging an answer as unreliable is not enough; they need the answer to be repaired into something trustworthy, yet it is unclear what automatic post-processing strategies are effective or how they trade off factual grounding versus preserving the original answer’s content.

Method: Using the RAGTruth benchmark with human-annotated unsupported passages, the authors first decompose each flagged answer into atomic factual claims. Each claim is then automatically checked against the retrieved documents to determine support. For claims identified as unsupported, they apply three distinct repair strategies: (1) delete the unsupported claim, (2) replace the claim directly with relevant source text from the retrieval, or (3) rewrite the claim in a way intended to align it with the retrieved evidence. This yields 916 repaired answers. Three language models from different model families are used as judges to evaluate the repaired answers, focusing on whether they still contain unsupported content and how much of the original text is preserved.

Result: All three repair strategies lower the proportion of answers judged to contain unsupported content compared to leaving answers untouched, and the three LLM judges agree on the ranking among strategies. Deletion leads to the greatest reduction in unsupported content but keeps the least of the original answer, preserving about 64.3% of the text. Rewriting preserves the most original content (about 80.1%) but yields the smallest reduction in unsupported content. Replacement lies between these two in both grounding improvement and text preservation. Interestingly, editing is applied not only to faulty answers: 83.5% of answers that were originally annotated as clean are modified by the repair pipeline as well.

Conclusion: There is no single best repair strategy; instead, deletion, replacement, and rewriting occupy different positions on a trade-off between factual grounding and preserving the original answer. Deletion is best for maximizing factual reliability at the cost of answer completeness, while rewriting is best for maintaining the original content but offers the least improvement in grounding. Because these strategies optimize different goals, selecting among them requires additional evidence about downstream answer usefulness that current automatic metrics cannot provide. Thus, hallucination mitigation in RAG systems should be framed as choosing among alternative repair policies, not as finding a universally superior fix.

Abstract: Language models increasingly answer questions by consulting retrieved documents rather than memory alone, a design now common in search assistants and enterprise knowledge tools. Grounding a model in retrieved text reduces unsupported statements but does not eliminate them, and a reader cannot tell a grounded sentence from an invented one. Most research on this problem stops at detection, yet flagging a faulty answer changes nothing for the person reading it, and little is known about which action should follow. Using RAGTruth, a benchmark whose unsupported passages are annotated by hand, we split each flagged answer into individual factual claims, check each against the retrieved source, and compare leaving the answer untouched with three repair strategies of increasing richness: deleting an unsupported claim, replacing it with source text, and rewriting it. Three language models from different families judge the 916 repaired answers. Every strategy reduces the proportion of answers judged to contain unsupported content, and all three judges agree on the ordering. Deletion achieves the largest reduction while retaining least of the original answer, at 64.3% of the text, whereas rewriting retains 80.1% and reduces least. Repair is not confined to faulty answers: 83.5% of answers annotated clean are edited too. The strategies occupy different points on a grounding preservation trade-off rather than forming a quality ranking, and choosing between them needs evidence about answer usefulness that automatic metrics cannot supply.

</details>


### [53] [All You Need Is Non-Commutative Words](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29314)
*Carla M. Quispe Flores,Stanley Salvatierra,Renan Cabrera*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Paper encodes words as unitary matrices and sentences as their products, enabling efficient, order-aware text classification with a compact representation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Transformer models rely on large embeddings and positional encodings; bag-of-words ignores order. The authors seek an order-sensitive, mathematically principled, and compact representation of text that reduces parameters and attention cost while supporting continual learning.

Method: Map each lexical token to a unitary matrix. Represent a sentence as the ordered matrix product of its token matrices, leveraging noncommutativity to encode word order without positional encodings. Develop an attention mechanism arising from the same algebra, using antisymmetric self-attention without separate query/key/value projections. Introduce a parallel-composition mechanism for variable-length chunks at reduced attention cost. Design a canonical-coset readout layer that parameterizes all relevant unitary degrees of freedom and supports continual learning through nested group extensions that expand the operator space per task while keeping existing representations unchanged.

Result: On standard text-classification benchmarks, this unitary-matrix representation matches or beats bag-of-words baselines, with better accuracy on IMDB and comparable results on AG News. It replaces a typical ~30k-dimensional sparse vocabulary space with a dense 64-parameter real-valued encoding per token, showing strong expressive power relative to dimensionality.

Conclusion: Encoding tokens as unitary matrices and sentences as their ordered products offers a compact, order-aware alternative to conventional text representations. This algebraic framework yields simplified attention, efficient composition, and a continual-learning-friendly readout while maintaining or improving performance over bag-of-words on key benchmarks, demonstrating the expressive efficiency of the proposed parameterization.

Abstract: We represent lexical tokens as unitary matrices and encode each sentence as their ordered product. The noncommutativity of matrix product captures word order without positional encodings (PEs). The same algebra yields several capabilities, including antisymmetric self-attention with no query, key, or value projections, and parallel composition of variable-length text chunks at a reduced attention cost. Furthermore, it provides a canonical-coset readout layer that encodes all true unitary degrees of freedom compactly, while supporting continual learning through nested group extensions that enlarge the operator space with each new task preserving prior representations exactly. Across standard text-classification benchmarks, the method matches or exceeds bag-of-words baselines. Achieving higher accuracy on IMDB and comparable performance on AG News. Notably, this is accomplished by replacing the conventional $\sim$30,000-dimensional vocabulary space with a dense, 64-parameter real-valued encoding, highlighting the expressive efficiency of our parameterization.

</details>


### [54] [Padārtha: Ontology-Grounded Fine-Grained NER Benchmark for Classical Sanskrit](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29324)
*Sujoy Sarkar,Pretam Ray,Paramhans Shah,Manoj Balaji Jagadeeshan,Akash Gairola,Arjuna S R,Pawan Goyal*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces Padārtha, an ontology-grounded, fine-grained NER benchmark for Sanskrit based on the Mahābhārata, evaluates generative and traditional NER models, and shows major performance drops at fine granularity and on unseen entities.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing NER tag sets, typically designed for modern journalistic text, are not culturally or historically neutral and impose inappropriate source-culture categories when applied to classical literature like Sanskrit epics. There is a need for an annotation schema grounded in the indigenous ontological tradition of the text, as well as for a large, fine-grained NER benchmark to study model performance, especially at fine granularity and for unseen entities.

Method: The authors design a fine-grained NER tag set derived from the Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika ontological system, defining 18 categories under 10 ontological nodes, which are also mapped to five standard coarse NER tags. Expert annotators label more than 12.6K entries from a scholarly index of named entities and align them with mentions in the Mahānāma corpus of the Mahābhārata, resulting in fine-grained labels for over 108K entity mentions across 73K+ verses, plus a curated 5K-verse test set focusing on rare mentions. They then benchmark fine-tuned generative NER models against traditional task-specific NER architectures on both coarse and fine-grained tagging, and evaluate generalization to unseen entities and ambiguous mentions.

Result: Padārtha provides a large-scale, ontology-grounded NER resource for Sanskrit, with 108,335 annotated mentions and a stress-tested evaluation set. Generative NER models, when fine-tuned, achieve performance comparable to conventional NER systems on this benchmark. Nonetheless, all evaluated systems experience a steep performance drop when moving from coarse to fine-grained categories and perform poorly on out-of-entity mentions that did not appear in training data. Fine-tuned models especially struggle with unseen entities and frequently assign the majority sense in cases of lexical ambiguity.

Conclusion: Ontology-grounded, tradition-specific schemas like Padārtha can more appropriately capture the semantics of classical texts while remaining interoperable with standard NER frameworks. Current NER models, including strong generative ones, are not yet robust at fine-grained categorization or handling unseen entities in such settings, and the challenges cannot be explained by data scarcity alone. This benchmark exposes systematic weaknesses in existing architectures and highlights the need for methods that better leverage ontological structure and handle ambiguity and rare entities.

Abstract: Annotation schemas are not neutral. When applied to classical literature, tag sets developed for modern journalistic texts impose source-culture definitions on texts they were never designed to describe. We instead ground a schema in the tradition of the text itself introducing \textit{Padārtha}, the first ontology-grounded fine-grained Named Entity Recognition (NER) benchmark for Sanskrit, built on the \textit{Mahābhārata} epic. Our tag set derives from \textit{Nyāya-Vaiśesika}, a classical Indian ontological system, yielding 18 fine-grained categories organized under 10 ontological nodes and mapped onto five standard coarse tags, ensuring interoperability with existing benchmarks. Expert annotators label over 12.6K entries from a scholarly index of named entities, linked to corresponding mentions in the \textit{Mahānāma} corpus, producing fine-grained annotations for 108,335 entity mentions across 73,632 verses, along with a 5,000-verse expert-verified test set sampled to stress rare mentions. We present the first systematic benchmarking of generative NER against traditional architectures for Sanskrit, finding that fine-tuned generative models perform comparably to task-specific systems. However, all systems show a sharp decline from coarse to fine granularity and struggle with out-of-entity mentions unseen during training. The limitation is not due to data scarcity alone, as fine-tuned models recall unseen entities far worse than seen ones and tend to default to the majority sense under lexical ambiguity.

</details>


### [55] [StageWell: A Process-Aligned Chinese Corpus for Positive-Psychology Support Dialogue](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29326)
*Yuxiong Wang,Ziwei Lin,Bo Wang,Yu Zhang,Shiguang Ni*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper presents StageWell, a Chinese corpus and framework for modeling positive psychology dialogues as a structured six-stage, multi-turn support process, along with a protocol (HQS) for constructing and evaluating data that improves LLMs’ process control, response quality, and safety.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing positive psychology dialogue resources mainly supervise at the single-turn level (e.g., labeling strategies per reply or giving holistic dialog-level preferences) without explicitly encoding where in the support process a turn occurs, what support function it serves, or how to locally repair flawed responses. This makes it hard for models to manage coherent, staged, multi-turn support rather than just generating isolated empathetic replies. The authors want to build a dataset and protocol that make the support process structure explicit and provide high-quality signals for both supervised fine-tuning and preference optimization.

Method: They design StageWell, which organizes positive psychology support into a six-stage process. Using a multi-agent workflow, they rewrite whole dialogues to align them with this process and generate: (1) 12,445 supervised fine-tuning instances, (2) 1,849 DPO preference pairs, and (3) a GroundTruth subset of 120 expert-revised dialogues plus 977 QA pairs. They also propose HQS, a structured protocol guiding data construction and evaluation. For DPO, they create process-localized repair pairs: each pair consists of a flawed model output (rejected) and a targeted rewrite (chosen) under the same context and stage constraints, making preferences local to specific process positions and support functions. They then train several 9B–14B open-source LLMs with this data and evaluate process control, response quality, and safety using automatic and human metrics.

Result: Training four 9B–14B open-source LLMs with StageWell and HQS supervision leads to consistent improvements: average BERTScore increases by 0.037, Q-Overall by 1.32 points, S-exact by 0.236, while the rate of highly critical safety issues (H-critical) decreases by 0.167. These gains hold across models, indicating that the process-aligned data and localized DPO repairs enhance both supportive-dialogue competence and safety.

Conclusion: Explicitly modeling supportive dialogue as a structured, multi-turn, six-stage process and using process-localized preference pairs for DPO yields better process control, higher response quality, and improved safety in positive psychology dialogue systems. The StageWell corpus and HQS protocol provide a practical framework and resource for building more reliable, process-aware supportive dialogue models, rather than treating the task as independent single-turn response generation.

Abstract: Positive psychology dialogue aims to support emotional distress and positive resource building, requiring models to produce not only empathetic replies but also coherent progression through a multi-turn support process. Existing resources often reduce supervision to turn-level strategies or holistic preference labels, leaving process position, support function, and local repair targets implicit. We introduce StageWell, a process-aligned Chinese corpus for positive psychology dialogue, together with HQS, a structured protocol for data construction and evaluation. StageWell organizes support into a six-stage support process and uses a multi-agent whole-dialogue rewriting workflow to construct 12,445 SFT instances, 1,849 DPO preference pairs, and a GroundTruth subset of 120 expert-revised dialogues and 977 QA pairs. Guided by HQS, DPO pairs are built as process-localized repairs: flawed model outputs are used as rejected responses, and targeted rewrites under the same context and stage constraint are used as chosen responses. Across four 9B-14B open-source LLMs, this supervision yields robust gains in process control, response quality, and safety. Averaged across models, BERTScore improves by 0.037, Q-Overall increases by 1.32 points, S-exact increases by 0.236, and the H-critical rate decreases by 0.167. These results highlight the value of modeling supportive dialogue as a structured multi-turn support process rather than as single-turn response generation.

</details>


### [56] [When to Adapt: Conditional Memory Adapters for Retention-Preserving Domain Specialization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29327)
*Jiayu Hou,Lei Wang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes Engram Adapter, a conditional, memory-based adapter for LLMs that boosts in-domain performance while nearly preserving out-of-domain capabilities.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning approaches often harm out-of-domain performance because their modifications are always active, even for inputs outside the target domain. The authors want a way to specialize large language models to new domains without losing their broad, general capabilities.

Method: They repurpose conditional memory mechanisms from pretraining as a post-hoc adapter for frozen LLMs. The adapter performs multi-channel matching over local n-gram patterns with explicit occupancy tracking, so it selectively injects residuals mostly for in-domain inputs. A learned scalar gate further suppresses incoherent or noisy retrievals on OOD inputs. The base model weights remain frozen, and the adapter is lightweight and conditionally activated.

Result: On Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B adapted to AG-News and MedMCQA, Engram Adapter increases in-domain accuracy while retaining 99.4%–100.1% of average performance on a variety of OOD tasks (reasoning, translation, code, legal). On LegalBench it slightly surpasses the frozen base model, whereas comparable always-on adapters substantially degrade OOD performance. Mechanistic probes show that, for OOD inputs, activation norms after gating and projection are reduced to about 0.08% of the hidden-state norm, resulting in minimal KL divergence and negligible accuracy changes vs. the base.

Conclusion: Conditional, memory-based adapters can yield modular domain specialization that keeps the original model’s general skills largely intact. The Engram Adapter’s selective activation and strong attenuation on OOD inputs allow parameter-efficient domain adaptation with negligible negative side effects, suggesting a promising direction for future modular LLM design.

Abstract: Large language models deployed in specialized domains must improve in-domain performance without sacrificing general capabilities. Existing parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods are typically always on: their learned perturbations are applied to every input, which can degrade out-of-domain (OOD) performance. We propose Engram Adapter, a framework that repurposes pretraining-time conditional memory as a post-hoc adapter for frozen LLMs. It uses multi-channel matching over local n-gram patterns with explicit occupancy tracking as a lightweight selectivity prior, making residual injection more likely on in-domain inputs while a learned scalar gate suppresses incoherent OOD retrievals. We evaluate on Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B with AG-News and MedMCQA as adaptation tasks and OOD benchmarks spanning reasoning, translation, code generation, and legal reasoning. Engram Adapter improves in-domain accuracy while preserving 99.4%--100.1% of average OOD performance; on LegalBench it slightly exceeds the frozen base model on average, whereas comparable always-on baselines degrade sharply. Mechanistic analyses show that although OOD activations are non-zero, gate and projection attenuation reduce residuals to approximately 0.08% of hidden-state norm, yielding small KL drift and negligible accuracy change. These results suggest conditional activation is a promising route toward modular, retention-preserving domain specialization over frozen backbones.

</details>


### [57] [Arabic Safety Alignment as Selective Refusal: An Empirical Study of SFT, DPO, and Guard Calibration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29378)
*Mohamad Zbib,Ammar Mohanna*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper evaluates how Arabic large language models balance refusing harmful prompts versus over-refusing benign ones, showing that refusal-only SFT leads to blanket refusal, mixed SFT can hit high harmful refusal with modest benign refusal, DPO and guards have model-specific effects, and transfer to Arabizi is limited, so deployment should use model-specific operating-point tuning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Safety evaluation for Arabic LLMs is underexplored, and a single refusal score hides the trade-off between avoiding harmful outputs and not blocking benign or sensitive content. The authors aim to create a clearer, quantitative view of this trade-off for Arabic-capable models, including script variants like Arabizi, and to understand how different alignment techniques (SFT, DPO, inference-time guards) affect safety behavior.

Method: They introduce two metrics, benign refusal rate B and harmful-prompt refusal rate H, and evaluate five Arabic-capable LLMs on the human-written AraSafe dataset across 130 runs. They compare configurations with refusal-only SFT, mixed SFT, DPO, and inference-time guards, and also test generalization to Arabizi prompts. Additionally, they run a blinded human audit of 300 responses to quantify annotator agreement and compare it to automated guards like Qwen3Guard and Aya Expanse 32B.

Result: Refusal-only SFT drives models toward nearly blanket refusal. Carefully chosen mixed-SFT configurations achieve H ≈ 90–93% while keeping B ≈ 14–23%, with four configurations consistently surpassing the H = 90% target across runs and Fanar doing so in most runs. DPO and guards do not act as uniform improvements but shift B and H differently per model.
