Human annotators show 89% agreement on refusal labels (κ = 0.78), and two guard models reach about 89–91% accuracy relative to that standard. For Arabizi prompts, SFT improves H for all models but none reaches the 90% target, indicating incomplete transfer from Modern Standard Arabic.

Conclusion: Safety alignment for Arabic LLMs should be tuned per model and per deployment target rather than assuming any single method (e.g., SFT, DPO, or guards) is universally beneficial. Mixed SFT can reach strong harmful-prompt refusal with acceptable benign refusal, refusal-only SFT is too aggressive, and alignment in Modern Standard Arabic only partially transfers to Arabizi. Deployers should pick a target operating point in the (B, H) trade-off space and keep only interventions that move the model toward that point.

Abstract: Arabic large language models must refuse harmful prompts without over-refusing benign or sensitive prompts, yet a single refusal rate hides this trade-off. We evaluate it using benign refusal B and harmful-prompt refusal H, where H measures refusal rather than harmful compliance. Across five Arabic-capable models and 130 runs on the full human-written AraSafe set, refusal-only supervised fine-tuning (SFT) collapses toward blanket refusal, whereas selected mixed-SFT configurations reach H = 90% to 93% at B = 14% to 23%; four selected configurations exceed the H = 90% target in all three runs, while Fanar does so in two of three. Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) and inference guards change B and H differently across models rather than acting as uniform upgrades. In a blinded 300-response audit, annotator binary-refusal agreement is 89.0% (kappa = 0.78); Qwen3Guard and Aya Expanse 32B reach 88.7% and 91.0% accuracy, respectively, with no conclusive paired difference. Selected SFT raises H on Arabizi for all five models, but none reaches 90%, showing only partial transfer from Modern Standard Arabic. Overall, the results support model-specific operating-point selection: set a deployment target and retain only interventions that improve it.

</details>


### [58] [AlgoWorlds: Benchmarking Tool Use for Global Optimization in Algorithmic Worlds](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29397)
*Zixiang Xu,Jiaan Wang,Fandong Meng*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: AlgoWorlds is a benchmark that turns classical combinatorial optimization problems into partially observed, tool-based decision environments to test whether LLM agents can make globally optimal, not just feasible, decisions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing tool-use benchmarks only check if agents can complete workflows and use tools correctly, but in real-world decision problems (like routing or dispatch) many different feasible solutions exist and can vary greatly in quality. The key open issue is whether agents can transform tool-gathered information into globally optimal decisions under shared constraints and costs.

Method: The authors design AlgoWorlds, which converts formally specified combinatorial optimization problems into single-shot decision environments with partial observability and tool access. Each environment hides a concrete problem instance, exposes it only via task-specific information tools, and then requires the agent to commit to a structured final decision. They build 240 such environments across ten combinatorial optimization problem families and four workload levels, using deterministic instance generators, exact solvers to certify optimal solutions and difficulty, and two distinct tool-interface styles per problem. They then evaluate seven strong LLMs on these environments, measuring feasibility and exact global optimality.

Result: Across 240 environments and seven LLMs, most models can usually produce feasible decisions, but they rarely achieve globally optimal ones. The best model attains exact optimality on only 38.61% of tasks. Many failures occur even when the agent has already collected enough information to reconstruct the full hidden instance, indicating that data acquisition is not the main bottleneck.

Conclusion: AlgoWorlds reveals that current LLM agents struggle not just with acquiring information via tools but with integrating that information to reason about global constraints and verify decisions. Feasible yet suboptimal choices are common, so achieving true decision optimality in complex, tool-based settings remains a major challenge. AlgoWorlds provides a structured, verifiable benchmark to study and improve these capabilities.

Abstract: Tool-use benchmarks generally evaluate whether an agent completes a workflow using appropriate tools and valid arguments. However, feasibility alone is insufficient in real-world decision settings such as route planning and fleet dispatch. Individual choices interact through shared constraints and costs, so a feasible solution may still be substantially suboptimal. This raises a harder question: can an agent turn information gathered through tools into a globally optimal decision? We introduce AlgoWorlds, a benchmark that transforms formally specified combinatorial optimization problems into partially observed decision environments with verifiable global optima. Each environment contains a hidden instance observed only through task-specific information tools, after which the agent commits to one structured decision evaluated for feasibility and optimality. AlgoWorlds contains 240 environments covering ten combinatorial optimization families and four workload levels. Family-specific deterministic programs generate the instances, exact algorithms certify their optima and determine workload levels, and two structurally different tool interfaces present each underlying instance. We evaluate seven leading LLMs, including Claude Opus 4.8 and GPT-5.6 Sol. Achieving global optimality remains highly challenging: although leading models produce feasible decisions in most cases, the best-performing model reaches exact optimality in only 38.61% of cases. Even when agents collect sufficient information to reconstruct the hidden instance, most failures end in feasible but suboptimal decisions. The challenge therefore extends beyond information acquisition to information integration, global constraint reasoning, and decision verification. The project homepage is available at https://xzx34.github.io/AlgoWorlds/, and the code is available at https://github.com/xzx34/AlgoWorlds.

</details>


### [59] [Evaluating the Semantic Specificity of Representation Steering in Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29431)
*Zhangdie Yuan,Andreas Vlachos*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper shows that a popular method for fixing reasoning errors in large language models, Localized Representation Steering (LRS), often just changes outputs via a global label bias rather than truly repairing reasoning, and introduces Cross-Rule Transfer (CRT) as a way to detect this.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current evaluations of representational interventions like LRS may be misleading because they can be satisfied by shallow label-flipping instead of genuine changes to internal reasoning circuits. The authors want a rigorous way to test whether an intervention actually repairs reasoning or merely biases outputs on benchmark tasks.

Method: They introduce Cross-Rule Transfer (CRT), which tests an intervention not only on rules where the model fails, but also on related rule families where the model is already accurate. They apply CRT to late-layer LRS designed to fix 'contradiction blindness' and add four supporting controls: (1) showing equivalence to a direct logit bias, (2) using random/control vectors that still flip labels, (3) transferring the steering vector across models (cross-model grafting), and (4) checking what happens when steering is applied at early layers instead of late layers.

Result: When they apply late-layer LRS designed to fix contradiction blindness, CRT shows that performance on already-correct rules collapses from 99.6% to 40.4%, indicating that the steering vector is enforcing a blanket 'contradiction' prediction. The four controls collectively support the interpretation that the intervention is acting as a global label bias rather than a targeted reasoning repair.

Conclusion: Benchmark gains from LRS on reasoning tasks can be illusory, reflecting superficial label overrides instead of genuine reasoning improvements. The proposed CRT framework, along with several diagnostic controls, offers a more reliable way to audit representational interventions and distinguish real reasoning circuit repairs from global output biases.

Abstract: Localized Representation Steering (LRS) is widely used to correct reasoning pathologies in large language models. However, standard benchmark evaluations can easily be fooled by superficial label overrides, creating a false impression of reasoning circuit repairs. In this work, we propose Cross-Rule Transfer (CRT), a diagnostic framework that audits representational interventions by evaluating them on rule families where the model is natively competent. Evaluating late-layer LRS for a widespread logical failure, contradiction blindness, reveals that the intervention merely injects a global label bias: applying the steering vector to rules the model already handles correctly (99.6% baseline) degrades performance to 40.4% by forcing false contradiction predictions. We support this diagnosis with four complementary controls (direct logit bias equivalence, control vector label-flipping, cross-model grafting, and early-layer steering checks), providing a rigorous methodology to distinguish genuine reasoning repairs from superficial label overrides.

</details>


### [60] [Whose Assessment of Distress? Community Perspectives and LLM Alignment on Well-Being Posts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29446)
*Andrew Aquilina,Xiang Lorraine Li,Yu-Ru Li*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper investigates whether large language models (LLMs) correctly reflect community-specific perceptions of psychological distress and finds that LLMs systematically over-estimate distress compared to both in-group and out-group human judgments, especially for none-to-mild cases.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Psychological distress judgments depend heavily on community norms around emotion and help-seeking, but current LLM-based distress detectors are typically aligned to a single universal standard. This raises concerns that such models may misinterpret or miscalibrate distress for specific identity-based communities, with potential harms in mental health applications. The authors aim to empirically test how well LLMs align with the perspectives of the communities whose language they analyze.

Method: The authors run a perspectivist annotation study using 1,198 Reddit posts sampled from six identity-based communities. 321 human participants provide 9,587 distress judgments, yielding community-specific labels. They compare ratings from contextualized in-group raters (who share the community identity and receive context) and uncontextualized out-group raters. They quantify in-group alignment via odds ratios (e.g., OR = 1.18). Then they evaluate nine open-weight LLM configurations and four frontier LLMs against these human labels, examining accuracy, over/under-estimation rates, and patterns across distress levels, especially in none-to-mild cases.

Result: In-group raters show a modest but significant tendency to agree more with their community than out-group raters (OR = 1.18), with substantial variation across communities. Open-weight LLMs systematically over-estimate distress: for posts humans label as none-to-mild distress, model accuracy is only 31–44%, with most errors being false positives. GPT-5 and Gemini 2.5 Pro show similar inflation for none-to-mild cases even when their overall calibration is mixed, while Claude Opus 4 is comparatively conservative. Human out-group aggregates are nearly balanced (18% over-estimation vs. 19% under-estimation), indicating that the LLMs’ inflation is not simply mimicking an outsider perspective. Instead, inflating models share a strong prior toward detecting distress that exceeds both in-group and out-group human judgments.

Conclusion: Psychological distress judgments are community-specific, and current LLMs used for distress detection fail to adequately capture these community perspectives. Many models exhibit a strong, miscalibrated prior toward distress, particularly over-flagging posts that communities view as none-to-mild. This misalignment goes beyond simple outsider bias and may have inequitable consequences when such systems are deployed in mental-health-related settings. The work highlights the need for community-grounded evaluation and calibration of LLM distress detectors to avoid uneven or harmful impacts across identity-based communities.

Abstract: Judgments about psychological distress are socially situated: what counts as concerning hinges on community norms around emotional expression, vulnerability, and help-seeking. Yet large language models (LLMs) used for distress detection are typically aligned to a single, undifferentiated standard. How well do these models capture the perspectives of the communities whose language they assess? We address this question through a perspectivist annotation study in which 321 participants provided 9,587 judgments on 1,198 Reddit posts spanning six identity-based communities, yielding community-specific labels. Raters in the contextualized in-group condition show a modest tendency to agree more with their community than uncontextualized out-group raters (OR = 1.18), an effect varying significantly across communities. We then evaluate nine open-weight LLM configurations and four frontier configurations against these labels. Open-weight LLMs systematically over-estimate distress: when communities perceive none-to-mild distress, these models achieve only 31-44% accuracy, predominantly producing false positives. GPT-5 and Gemini 2.5 Pro show the same none-to-mild inflation even when their full-sample over/under rates are mixed, while Claude Opus 4 is more conservative. This pattern does not simply mirror an outsider reading position: uncontextualized out-group human aggregates were nearly symmetric, with 18% over-estimation versus 19% under-estimation. Instead, the models that inflate none-to-mild cases exhibit a distress prior that exceeds both contextualized in-group and uncontextualized out-group human judgments. These findings have implications for equitable AI deployment in mental health contexts, where miscalibrated distress detection may unevenly affect the communities being assessed.

</details>


### [61] [AI Can Be Easily Persuaded in Clinical Decision Making](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29453)
*Jiayuan Zhu,Jiazhen Pan,Fenglin Liu,Minhao Hu,Junde Wu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper experimentally examines how easily AI systems used in clinical decision making can be persuaded by different forms of human input and social cues.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: With AI increasingly used in high-stakes, evidence-based medical decisions, it is critical to know whether AI systems can maintain objective, accurate judgment when exposed to persuasive or biased human inputs, since errors can directly affect patient safety.

Method: The authors run controlled experiments in which the same medical questions and clinical scenarios are presented to an AI system, but the accompanying persuasive statements are systematically varied along dimensions such as the speaker’s professional authority (senior clinician vs medical student), national background, institutional affiliation, claimed past performance, number of physicians, alignment with the AI’s initial answer, and repetition of pressure. They then measure how often the AI changes its decisions under each condition, including cases where persuasive clinician views are fabricated to support incorrect answers.

Result: The experiments show that AI decisions are significantly influenced by social and presentational factors: authority cues (e.g., senior clinician vs medical student), institutional and national labels, claimed superior past performance, multiple agreeing physicians, and repeated pressure all increase the chance that AI changes its decision. The same persuasive content is about 10% more effective when attributed to a senior clinician than to a medical student. Simply asserting better performance history reliably increases persuasiveness. Importantly, plausible but fabricated clinician opinions can persuade AI to abandon correct answers in favor of wrong ones.

Conclusion: AI systems in clinical contexts are highly susceptible to persuasion based on who appears to be speaking and how their opinion is framed, not solely on the objective correctness of the information. Because they can be pushed away from correct judgments by convincing but incorrect support, ensuring robustness to social pressure and persuasive framing is essential for safe, reliable deployment of AI in high-stakes medical decision making.

Abstract: As AI becomes increasingly integrated into clinical practice, it is playing a growing role in medical decision making. Medicine, however, is a high stakes and evidence based field, where decisions can directly affect patients' lives. It is therefore important to understand whether AI can maintain objective judgment when others try to persuade it. In this paper, we study how easily AI can be persuaded through controlled experiments. We find that professional authority, national background, institutional affiliation, claimed past performance, multiple physicians, supported clinician views, and repeated pressure can all affect AI decisions. Surprisingly, the same persuasive input changes about 10% more cases when it comes from a senior clinician than from a medical student. Simply claiming a better performance history consistently makes the physician more persuasive. More strikingly, a plausible clinician view can persuade AI away from a correct decision even when it is fabricated to support an incorrect answer. This indicates that AI can be strongly influenced by convincing support without reliably determining whether this view from the clinician is correct. Together, these findings suggest that AI can be easily persuaded by what people say, who says it, and how the opinion is presented. Therefore, it is essential for AI to maintain sound judgment under persuasion, enabling its safe and reliable use in high stakes medical decision making.

</details>


### [62] [Item-Mean Surrogates: Why Richer Persona Data Fail to Improve LLMs as Human Surrogates](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29455)
*Daehwan Ahn,Chengfeng Mao,Dokyun Lee*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper shows that while LLMs match average human survey responses well, they fail badly at predicting how specific individuals deviate from those averages, limiting their use as true human surrogates.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs are increasingly used or proposed as stand-ins for humans—for example, to simulate survey participants, voters, or consumers—often by giving them detailed personas. Many claims assume that with rich enough persona information, LLMs can approximate how a specific person would answer questions or behave in experiments. This paper investigates whether that assumption holds empirically at scale.

Method: The authors use four large datasets covering over 400,000 human participants and more than 6,000 survey items and experimental outcomes. They elicit LLM responses to the same items (with and without detailed persona information), then compare: (1) how closely LLM averages match human item-level means; (2) how much of the person-level variation in responses, after removing item means, is explained by LLM predictions; (3) performance of different models, persona richness, and fine-tuning; and (4) variance components analyses decomposing item means, stable person effects, and person-by-item interaction effects. They also analyze how LLM response distributions compare to human response distributions in terms of spread, use of categories, and shape.

Result: LLMs track aggregate human responses very well: the average LLM answer to each item closely aligns with the average human answer. However, most of this apparent success is just reproducing the item mean. After removing each item's human mean from both human and LLM responses, LLM predictions explain only about 3.05% of the remaining respondent-specific variance, versus a 53.6% benchmark from human test-retest reliability. Richer personas, different model variants, and fine-tuning fail to close this gap. Variance decomposition shows that, once item means are removed, the dominant reliable signal is the person-by-item effect—how a specific individual departs from the item mean on that specific question—which is roughly 8.9 times larger than the stable person effect. LLM responses also compress human response distributions: they have lower variance, use fewer response categories, and distort the shapes of distributions.

Conclusion: Current LLMs can serve as good predictors of item-level averages but are poor surrogates for specific humans: they do not capture the key person-by-item deviations that dominate reliable individual-level variation, even when supplied with rich persona data or fine-tuned. These models generate compressed, distorted response distributions that miss the full diversity and structure of human responses. The authors label this limitation “item-mean surrogacy” and argue that claims about LLMs as human surrogates should be evaluated using stringent empirical tests, proposing four such tests focused on predicting individual-level variation, reproducing distributions, and matching reliability benchmarks.

Abstract: LLMs are increasingly used as human surrogates, often on the premise that richer persona data could make them substitutes or exploratory tools for specific individuals. We test this premise across four datasets covering more than 400,000 participants and more than 6,000 survey items and experimental outcomes. LLMs perform well at the aggregate level: their average responses closely align with average human responses to the same items. But this success largely reflects predicting each item's average human response. Once each item's human mean is removed, LLM predictions explain only 3.05% of the remaining respondent-specific variation, far below the 53.6% human test-retest benchmark. Richer personas, model variants, and fine-tuning do not close this gap. In variance analyses, once item means are removed, the reliable remaining signal is person-by-item. It captures how a respondent departs from the mean on a particular item and is about 8.9x larger than the stable person effect. Persona data encode the respondent, but not this item-specific deviation. LLM responses also compress human response distributions, using less spread, fewer response categories, and distorted distributional shapes. We call this pattern item-mean surrogacy. Current LLM surrogates can approximate item averages, but not the distributions or respondent-specific deviations needed to replace individual humans. We propose four empirical tests for LLM-based human-surrogate claims.

</details>


### [63] [Chain-of-Thought Faithfulness of Reasoning Models Varies with Where and How Preference Cues Are Delivered](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29464)
*Aryo Pradipta Gema,Neel Rajani,Rohit Saxena,Wai-Chung Kwan,Pasquale Minervini*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: FACE-Eval tests whether chain-of-thought (CoT) monitoring reliably reflects how models adopt user preferences, especially when cues come through tools or raw artifacts rather than directly from the user message.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: CoT monitoring is used to check and attribute model reasoning, assuming that written reasoning faithfully captures what influenced the final answer. However, models often receive preference or bias cues indirectly (e.g., via tool outputs or raw documents) rather than explicit instructions in the user prompt. Existing evaluations mostly test faithfulness only when cues are explicit and in the user message, leaving a gap in understanding how faithful CoT is when cues are implicit or tool-mediated. The paper aims to fill this gap and test whether CoT monitoring still works under more realistic, tool-augmented conditions.

Method: The authors build FACE-Eval, a 5,100-example benchmark that systematically varies (1) cue location: in the user message vs in a tool return and (2) cue explicitness: explicit summary vs implicit raw artifact. They probe models along two dimensions: (a) verbalized commitment—how much the produced chain-of-thought explicitly acknowledges and endorses the cue among answers that follow it, and (b) unverbalized adoption—how often the model’s final answer follows the cue even when its chain-of-thought does not mention it. They test 15 open-weight models from eight model families with sizes from 4B to 1.6T parameters and different channels (e.g., with or without visible CoT). They also test interventions: a source-attribution prompt that asks models to cite where preferences came from, and a notice that their reasoning will be monitored. Finally, for the largest model in each family, they use external transcript monitors (GPT-5.6-Luna and GPT-4o-mini) to detect whether the model adopted the cue and correlate this with measured unverbalized adoption.

Result: Across all models, verbalized commitment is systematically lower when cues come from tool returns versus user messages and when cues are implicit versus explicit. However, unverbalized adoption shows the opposite pattern: models are more likely to adopt cues silently when they arrive via tool outputs, and usually when the cues are implicit. These effects are robust across models and channels. A source-attribution prompt partially reduces the gap between user- and tool-channel faithfulness in seven models, sometimes by increasing hidden adoption in the user channel, while merely warning that reasoning will be monitored does not reliably improve faithfulness. Using GPT-5.6-Luna and GPT-4o-mini as monitors, the authors find that higher levels of unverbalized adoption correlate strongly and negatively with monitor detection performance across 32 experimental conditions (Pearson r = -0.54 and -0.78).

Conclusion: The study concludes that chain-of-thought monitoring can systematically miss how models adopt preference or bias cues, especially when such cues are delivered through tool outputs or must be inferred from raw artifacts. In those settings, models often follow cues without explicitly acknowledging them in their reasoning, undermining the reliability of CoT-based safety and attribution methods in tool-augmented workflows. Prompting models to attribute sources helps somewhat, but generic warnings about monitoring do not. Overall, CoT monitoring, at least in single-call, prefilled-tool scenarios, should not be assumed to be a faithful record of the influences on a model’s answers, and improved techniques are needed for robust preference attribution and safety auditing when tools are involved.

Abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) monitoring assumes that reasoning traces faithfully record the information that shapes a model's answer. Existing faithfulness tests often place explicit bias cues in the user message, while agents may encounter preferences through tool returns or raw artifacts. We introduce FACE-Eval (Faithful Attribution of Cue Effects Evaluation), a 5,100-sample evaluation that varies cue location (user message or tool return) and explicitness (direct summary or raw artifact). We measure verbalized commitment among cue-following answers and unverbalized adoption among all cued samples. We evaluate 15 open-weight models from eight families, with total parameters ranging from 4B to 1.60T. Every model has lower verbalized commitment for tool-return than user-message cues and for implicit than explicit cues. Unverbalized adoption is higher for tool-return cues on all 15 models and for implicit cues in 28 of 30 model-channel comparisons. A source-attribution prompt narrows the channel gap on seven models, sometimes by increasing user-channel unverbalized adoption, while telling models that their reasoning will be monitored does not reliably close the gap. We also use two transcript monitors (GPT-5.6-Luna and GPT-4o-mini) to detect preference adoption in the largest model of each family. Across 32 model-channel-explicitness cells, higher unverbalized adoption is associated with lower detection ability for both monitors (Pearson r=-0.54 and r=-0.78, respectively). These results suggest that CoT monitoring may be less reliable when preference information arrives through tools or must be inferred from raw artifacts, within the single-call, prefilled-tool setting tested here.

</details>


### [64] [MUDDLE: Measuring Understanding of Documents under Distractor and Length Effects](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29477)
*Jason Luo,Saibilila Abudukelimu,Judy Song,Andrew Feng,Shivank Garg,Vasu Sharma,Kevin Zhu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces MUDDLE, a controlled benchmark to disentangle the effects of context length and topical distractors on document question-answering performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing document QA systems operate over multiple retrieved documents, where failures can stem from either excessively long contexts or the presence of topically similar but incorrect distractor documents. Prior benchmarks conflate these two factors, making it unclear why models fail and how to improve robustness to distracting context.

Method: The authors construct MUDDLE using 270 human-annotated questions, each linked to one source document. Each question is instantiated in five conditions: (1) source alone, (2) source plus two topically similar hard negative documents, (3) source plus four hard negatives, (4) source plus two random distractors, and (5) source plus four random distractors. Random distractors are carefully matched to the hard negatives by length and provenance, so any performance difference isolates the effect of topical similarity rather than context length. Every condition is rendered in markdown, page images, and raw PDF, but the main reported experiments use markdown due to input size limits. Answers are scored by an LLM judge across three model families, with detailed analysis focusing on gpt-5-mini.

Result: In markdown experiments, accuracy drops more when the context contains topically similar hard negatives than when it contains length-matched random distractors. For gpt-5-mini, hard negatives reduce accuracy at both context sizes, while random distractors yield performance close to the no-distractor baseline. Although the magnitude of the effect is modest, it is consistent in direction, and pooled analysis across context sizes shows that hard negatives significantly underperform their length-matched random counterparts.

Conclusion: MUDDLE provides a controlled benchmark that cleanly separates the impact of topical distractors from that of context length on document QA performance. The findings show that topically similar hard negatives are more harmful than equally long but random distractors, highlighting the need to improve model robustness specifically to misleading but on-topic context. The authors release data and code to enable reproducible research on context degradation in retrieval-augmented question answering.

Abstract: Document question-answering systems increasingly answer questions over collections of retrieved documents rather than one clean source, so robustness to distracting context matters as much as reading ability. When such systems fail, it is often unclear whether the context was too long or the distractors were too close to the topic, because prior work tends to conflate these two effects. We present MUDDLE, a controlled benchmark that separates them. MUDDLE uses 270 human-annotated questions, each tied to a single source document, and instantiates every question in five conditions: the source alone, the source with two or four topically similar hard negatives, and the source with two or four random distractors. The random distractors are matched to the hard negatives in length and provenance, so an accuracy gap between the two arms reflects topical similarity rather than length. All five conditions are rendered in markdown, page images, and raw PDF, but the distractor sweep reported here is run in markdown, since a source plus its distractors exceeds current image and PDF input limits. We score answers with an LLM judge across three model families. In the complete markdown sweep, hard negatives lower accuracy more than length-matched random documents at both context sizes for gpt-5-mini, while random documents stay near the no-distractor baseline. The effect is small but directionally consistent, and for gpt-5-mini hard negatives significantly underperform length-matched random distractors when pooled across context sizes. We release the data and evaluation code for a reproducible study of context degradation.

</details>


### [65] [SIC-Agents: Benchmarking and Building an Adaptive Simulator for Pediatric Serious Illness Communication Training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29481)
*Zihan Wang,Anita Marie Slominska,Rennie Bimman,Elizabeth Di Flumeri,Amanda Mayappo-Neeposh,Conall Francoeur,Tamara Ellen Carver,Xiao-Wen Chang,Doina Precup,Esin Darici Haritaoglu,Ismail Haritaoglu,Akshatha Arodi,Naomi Goloff*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces a benchmark suite and a simulation framework specifically designed for training clinicians in pediatric serious illness communication (SIC), along with a self-improving LLM-based simulator that better follows training curricula.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Pediatric serious illness communication is essential for quality care, but current scalable training options for clinicians are limited. Existing large language model simulators mainly optimize for generic conversational quality and are not tuned to the specific, high-stakes needs of pediatric SIC, such as handling multi-party conversations, parental distress, and feedback-driven learning. There is a need for structured benchmarks and specialized simulators that align with educators’ curricula to help train clinicians effectively at scale.

Method: The authors collaborate with educators and pediatric clinicians to design a pediatric SIC training setting and then create two benchmarks. PitfallBench evaluates simulator behavior at the turn level by focusing on common pitfalls in SIC, while DialogueBench assesses performance across entire conversations. They propose SIC-Agents, a self-improving simulation framework in which the system generates a clinician-editable skill document that encodes desired communication skills and behaviors. This skill document is then used to guide and iteratively improve the simulator’s behavior during dialogue simulations.

Result: Experimental comparisons show that the SIC-Agents framework leads to better simulator performance on the SIC benchmarks than static expert-designed prompts, indicating that an explicit, editable skill document plus self-improvement can produce more curriculum-aligned, realistic parent simulations in pediatric SIC scenarios.

Conclusion: The paper concludes that pediatric SIC requires specialized evaluation and simulation tools beyond generic dialogue quality metrics. By introducing PitfallBench and DialogueBench as benchmarks and SIC-Agents as a self-improving, curriculum-contingent simulation framework, the authors demonstrate a more effective approach for training clinicians in pediatric serious illness communication. They make their benchmarks publicly available to foster further research and development in this domain.

Abstract: Pediatric serious illness communication (SIC) is critically important, yet scalable communication training for clinicians remains limited. Compared with other dialogue simulation settings, pediatric SIC poses additional challenges, including multi-party interactions, response to parental distress and strong dependence on feedback dynamics. Existing LLM-based simulators optimize generic dialogue quality rather than curriculum-contingent behavior required for effective SIC training. In collaboration with educators and pediatric clinicians, we introduce the first benchmark suite and simulation framework tailored to pediatric SIC training. Our benchmarks, PitfallBench and DialogueBench, evaluate simulators both at the turn-level and across full dialogues. We further propose SIC-Agents, a self-improving framework that generates a clinician-editable skill document to guide simulator behavior. Our experiments show that SIC-Agents outperforms static expert prompting. To support future research, we release our benchmarks for parent simulation in pediatric SIC at https://github.com/Beikewzh/sic-benchmarks

</details>


### [66] [CoCoA: Context-Conditional Cultural Alignment for Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29492)
*Kyungdon Lee,Wei Xu,Alan Ritter,Dong-Ho Lee,JinYeong Bak*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces CoCoA, a method to make LLMs handle cultural bias in a context-dependent way, favoring culturally appropriate entities when cultural cues exist and staying neutral when they don’t.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing debiasing approaches push models toward uniform neutrality, which is inadequate for cultural bias because appropriate behavior should change with context—sometimes preferring in-culture entities, sometimes staying neutral. LLMs currently over-favor Western entities regardless of context, motivating a framework that can distinguish when to adapt culturally and when to remain neutral.

Method: The authors propose CoCoA (Context-Conditional Cultural Alignment), which uses dual-context training on identical entity pairs under two conditions: with cultural cues and without them. The framework applies (1) a contrastive alignment objective to differentiate behavior across these contexts, (2) calibration to keep overall preference magnitudes reasonable, and (3) drift regularization to avoid hurting general capabilities. Training is further guided by goal-aware gradient reconciliation so that updates align with the target context-conditional behavior.

Result: On two cultural bias benchmarks, CAMeL and Camellia, spanning ten languages and four LLMs, CoCoA lowers the Cultural Bias Score from 43 to 24 on average, while keeping neutrality scores close to ideal (around 50.2). It also shows minimal degradation across five standard general-purpose benchmarks, indicating that the method effectively reduces cultural bias without sacrificing overall performance.

Conclusion: Cultural bias mitigation in LLMs cannot be solved by uniform debiasing toward neutrality; instead, models need context-conditional behavior that is sensitive to cultural cues. CoCoA operationalizes this idea and empirically demonstrates that context-aware alignment can substantially reduce entity-centric cultural bias with minimal impact on general performance, suggesting a promising new direction for culturally aware LLM alignment.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) often favor Western-associated entities across cultural contexts. Conventional debiasing methods aim for uniform neutrality, but cultural bias mitigation demands context-conditional behavior, preferring culturally appropriate entities when cultural cues are present and remaining neutral when they are absent. We propose CoCoA (Context-Conditional Cultural Alignment), a framework that learns this behavior through dual-context training on the same entity pairs under contexts with and without cultural cues. CoCoA combines a contrastive alignment objective with calibration and drift regularization, optimized through goal-aware gradient reconciliation. We evaluate CoCoA on CAMeL and Camellia, two entity-centric cultural bias benchmarks, across ten language settings and four LLMs. CoCoA reduces the Cultural Bias Score from 43 to 24 on average while maintaining near-neutral preferences at 50.2, with minimal impact on general performance across five standard benchmarks. These findings highlight that effective cultural alignment requires context-conditional modeling rather than uniform debiasing, and establish a new direction for mitigating entity-centric cultural bias in LLMs.

</details>


### [67] [LLM Judges as Raters: A Pre-Registered Audit of Severity, Halo, Reliability, and Version Instability in LLM Essay Scoring on Public Corpora](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29517)
*Veerendra Kumar Sunkavalli*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper evaluates large language models (LLMs) acting as essay graders using rigorous rater-effect methodologies rather than simple agreement metrics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing evaluations of LLM-based essay graders mostly rely on agreement statistics (e.g., correlations, accuracy) with human graders, but educational measurement research shows that raters can systematically differ in severity, exhibit halo effects, and drift over time. This paper is motivated by the need to treat LLM graders as raters and assess them with the same advanced psychometric tools used for human raters, to understand their biases, stability, and comparability across versions and providers.

Method: The authors apply a pre-registered rater-effects battery—including many-facet Rasch modeling for severity, analysis of residual halo, generalizability and decision studies, cross-version severity shift analysis, and differential functioning—to public essay-scoring corpora in two languages (Portuguese ENEM/Essay-BR and English ASAP). They analyze 2,377 essays evaluated by 12 LLM judges from 4 providers across 5 version contrasts, with replicated cells. The full dataset is released as a score tensor for transparency and reuse.

Result: They find substantial variation in LLM judge severity: on the ENEM 0–1000 scale, judge severity spans 219 points; on ASAP, the panel’s spread is 15–33% of the score range, compared to about 1% between trained human raters. LLM–human correlations remain in a relatively low .47–.56 range, indicating limited discriminative alignment. All five version contrasts show significant severity shifts beyond a family-wise permutation null, with shifts up to 133 points. One LLM judge was deprecated mid-study, detected via identity canaries. However, two pre-registered hypotheses were not supported: severity-adjusted leaderboard reversals were not statistically robust, and “silent drift” was refuted because agreement changed in tandem with severity in four of five contrasts. Replication analyses show that LLMs are self-consistent (phi ≥ .80 with as few as two replications) but still fall short of human-level scoring accuracy. A same-instrument reanalysis overturns their earlier conclusion about halo; when controlling for instrument and calibration, they find no credible evidence that LLM halo exceeds the range observed among trained human raters.

Conclusion: LLMs used as essay graders should be treated as raters and evaluated with full psychometric rater-effect frameworks, not just simple agreement statistics. Current LLM judges show large severity differences, notable version-to-version shifts, and only moderate agreement with humans, limiting their suitability as stand-alone scoring instruments. While LLMs can be self-consistent and their halo may not be worse than that of trained humans when properly calibrated, human-level accuracy and stability are not yet achieved. Ongoing monitoring, calibration, and version auditing are essential when deploying LLM-based scoring in educational settings.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as essay graders in learning analytics, evaluated almost exclusively with agreement statistics. Educational measurement warns that raters also differ in severity, show halo, and drift as instruments. We treat LLM judges as raters and run a pre-registered rater-effects battery (many-facet Rasch severity, residual halo, generalizability/decision studies, cross-version shifts, differential functioning) on public corpora in two languages (ENEM/Essay-BR; ASAP): 2,377 essays, 12 judges, 4 providers, 5 version contrasts, replicated cells, released as a score tensor. Judge severity spans 219 points on ENEM's 0-1000 scale; on ASAP the panel spread is 15-33% of the score range against a between-trained-human gap near 1%. Judge-human correlations sit in an undiscriminating .47-.56 band. All five version contrasts shift severity beyond a family-wise permutation null (up to 133 points), and one judge was deprecated mid-study, caught by identity canaries. Two pre-registered tests returned honest nulls: severity-adjusted leaderboard reversals did not survive a permutation null, and "silent drift" was refuted: agreement moved with severity in four of five contrasts. Replication yields self-consistency (phi>=.80 at k<=2) but not human-level accuracy, and a same-instrument check overturned our own halo comparison: matched on instrument and calibration, we find no credible evidence that judge halo exceeds the trained-human range.

</details>


### [68] [Ontology-Guided Multi-Agent Extraction of Evaluation Objects from Academic Review Texts: Evidence from Chinese Library and Information Science](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29526)
*Haolin Chen,Hongyi Dong,Yu Zhu,Yijia Hong,Leiqing Niu,Jiyuan Ye*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper presents an ontology-guided multi-agent framework to extract evaluation objects from scholarly evaluative texts, achieving significantly better performance than rule-based and zero-shot baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing scientific entity extraction methods focus on research articles and perform poorly on evaluative texts (reviews, commentaries, book reviews) where evaluation objects are abstract, context-dependent, and have ambiguous type boundaries. There is a need for a method that can robustly identify and classify such evaluation objects to support evidence-based research evaluation and STI mining.

Method: The authors design an ontology-guided multi-agent framework that operates in three stages: (1) candidate discovery to identify potential evaluation objects; (2) ontology-constrained classification that uses a domain ontology to guide type assignment and boundary decisions; and (3) domain review where domain knowledge or experts refine and validate the detected entities. They also conduct experiments and ablation studies comparing their framework to rule-based and zero-shot baselines using metrics like Precision, Recall, F1, and Type Accuracy.

Result: The framework obtains Precision of 90.33%, Recall of 84.55%, Entity-level F1 of 87.34%, Strict Typed F1 of 79.78%, and Type Accuracy of 91.35%. It substantially outperforms rule-based and zero-shot baselines, and ablation studies show that the multi-agent workflow improves recall and stability, while ontology-based boundary constraints improve fine-grained classification and reduce category confusion.

Conclusion: The proposed ontology-guided multi-agent framework effectively extracts evaluation objects from scholarly evaluative texts, enabling structured use of such texts and offering methodological support for evidence-based research evaluation and STI mining. The multi-agent design and ontology constraints are key to its improved performance and robustness.

Abstract: Academic reviews, scholarly commentaries, and book reviews serve as sources of evaluative statements about theories, methods, literature, institutions, and policies, providing valuable evidence for scholarly evaluation. Existing scientific entity extraction methods mainly target research articles and are less effective for evaluation objects, which are often abstract, context-dependent, and characterized by ambiguous type boundaries. This study proposes an ontology-guided multi-agent framework for evaluation object extraction. The framework combines candidate discovery, ontology-constrained classification, and domain review. Experimental results show that it achieves a Precision of 90.33%, Recall of 84.55%, Entity-level F1 of 87.34%, Strict Typed F1 of 79.78%, and Type Accuracy of 91.35%, substantially outperforming rule-based and zero-shot baselines. Ablation results indicate that the multi-agent workflow improves recall and stability, while ontology-based boundary constraints enhance fine-grained classification and reduce category confusion. The framework supports the structured utilization of evaluative scholarly texts and provides methodological support for evidence-based research evaluation and STI mining.

</details>


### [69] [Argument-Aware Semantic Alignment of Normative Texts: A Toulmin-Based Neuro-Symbolic Approach](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29529)
*William Schroeder*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper investigates whether explicit argument structure improves alignment between cybersecurity standards beyond what neural semantic similarity can capture.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Aligning requirements across specialized normative texts, such as cybersecurity standards, is hard because equivalent requirements may differ in wording, syntax, and abstraction, and existing similarity methods miss the underlying argumentative structure.

Method: The authors propose a neuro-symbolic pipeline that combines neural text representations with features derived from Toulmin-style argument structure. An LLM is used for explicitation: extracting claims, grounds, warrants, qualifiers, and backing, and reconstructing enthymemes. These argument features are then integrated into an alignment model via argument-aware similarity and structural features, and evaluated on a NERC-CIP to NIST-CSF control mapping task.

Result: Argument-derived features improve requirement alignment performance over a neuro-symbolic baseline that uses only semantic similarity. Feature selection highlights warrant-related features as particularly informative, and shows that a compact subset of claim–grounds–warrant features performs competitively with the full Toulmin feature set.

Conclusion: Explicit argument structure serves as a useful intermediate representation for aligning specialized normative texts. While demonstrated on cybersecurity standards, the approach suggests broader potential for argument graphs from LLM explicitation to aid retrieval, reasoning, and explanation over normative documents, though domain-independent generalization is not yet claimed.

Abstract: Semantic alignment between specialized normative texts is challenging when equivalent requirements use different terms, syntax, and levels of abstraction. Lexical overlap, distributional embeddings, and semantic similarity capture topical relatedness but often miss the argumentative structure by which normative claims are supported, qualified, and justified. This paper asks whether explicit argument structure adds information complementary to neural semantics for aligning requirements. We treat cross-standard control mapping as argument-aware semantic alignment and build a neuro-symbolic pipeline that combines neural text representations with Toulmin features. An LLM explicitation step identifies claims, grounds, warrants, qualifiers, and backing and reconstructs enthymemes. These feed an alignment model via argument-aware similarity and structural features. On a NERC-CIP to NIST-CSF mapping benchmark, argument-derived features improve alignment over a neuro-symbolic semantic baseline. Feature selection shows especially strong signal from warrant-related features, indicating that the link between a claim and its supporting reasoning is not captured by conventional similarity alone. A compact claim--grounds--warrant subset remains competitive with the full Toulmin feature set. The results give preliminary evidence that argument structure is a useful intermediate representation for aligning specialized normative texts. Cybersecurity standards are used as a controlled testbed, not as proof of domain-independent generalization. The argument graphs produced by LLM explicitation may also support later work on retrieval, reasoning, and explanation over normative text.

</details>


### [70] [The Emergent Symbolic Structure of Artificial Neural Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29530)
*R. Thomas McCoy,Paul Soulos,Tal Linzen,Paul Smolensky*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper argues that neural networks, though vector-based, implicitly implement symbolic structures, and demonstrates this by approximating their internal representations with explicit symbolic equations without significantly changing behavior.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: There is a long-standing tension between symbolic views of intelligence (which rely on discrete structures like logical formulas) and modern neural network approaches (which use continuous vector representations). Neural networks perform extremely well in domains that appear to require symbolic structure, such as language and logic, raising the question of how they manage to do so with seemingly unstructured vectors. The authors aim to reconcile this tension by investigating whether neural networks might actually encode symbolic structure internally, even if not explicitly represented.

Method: The authors analyze a range of neural networks, from small models trained on list manipulation to large language models (LLMs) operating in arithmetic, logic, computer code, and natural language. For each case, they construct closed-form symbolic equations that approximate the internal vector representations produced by the network. They then substitute these symbolic equations for the networks’ usual representation-generating processes and test whether the models’ behavior is preserved. They also perform targeted interventions on the symbolic structures to see how this manipulates model behavior.

Result: They find that the internal vector representations of the examined neural networks can be closely approximated by explicit symbolic structures, such that replacing the networks’ representation-generating components with these closed-form symbolic equations leaves overall behavior largely unchanged. Moreover, controlled interventions on the symbolic approximations result in predictable, targeted changes to LLM behavior, indicating that the identified symbolic structures are behaviorally relevant rather than incidental.

Conclusion: Neural networks, including large language models, appear to implicitly realize symbolic structures within their continuous vector representations. By capturing these structures with closed-form symbolic equations that can substitute for parts of the network without degrading performance, the work offers a concrete way to bridge symbolic and vector-based conceptions of intelligence. This suggests that modern neural models may owe their success in classically symbolic domains to latent symbolic organization in their internal representations.

Abstract: Modern systems in artificial intelligence (AI) somehow excel in domains for which they seem poorly suited. Intelligence has traditionally been modeled as operating over structured combinations of symbols, such as logical formulas. However, the strongest modern AI systems are based on neural networks, which instead represent information in continuous vectors. Vectors seem inadequate for capturing the structure of language, logic, and other cognitive domains, yet neural networks achieve impressive performance in these areas. How do they do it? In this work, we propose a potential answer: Despite appearances, perhaps the internal representations of neural networks implicitly realize symbolic structure. In support of this hypothesis, we show that the vector representations of a variety of neural networks can be closely approximated with symbolic structures: we can replace the network's entire representation-generating process with a closed-form equation instantiating a symbolic structure, and the network's behavior remains largely unchanged. This finding holds for both small-scale neural networks trained to manipulate lists as well as large language models (LLMs) operating in four domains that are central in symbolic traditions: arithmetic, logic, computer code, and language. Further, our symbolic approximation allows us to modify an LLM's behavior in targeted ways via precise interventions on its internal representations, showing that the LLM's behavior is reliant on the symbolic structures we have identified. This work provides a potential way to reconcile longstanding symbolic conceptions of intelligence with the vector-based nature of modern AI.

</details>


### [71] [LoGo: Token-Level Dynamic Local-Global Attention](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29539)
*Yuqi Pan,Zheng Li,Bohao Tang,Zhen Qin,Guoqi Li*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: LoGo introduces a dynamic, token-level local-global attention mechanism that selectively applies expensive global attention only to tokens that need long-range context, improving efficiency while preserving or improving performance compared to full-attention Transformers and static hybrids.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As context length grows, the quadratic cost of full self-attention makes Transformers computationally expensive. Existing local-global hybrids are more efficient but rely on static allocations of local versus global attention across layers or heads, which may waste computation on tokens that don't need global context and fail to give enough capacity to those that do. The paper aims to make attention computation more adaptive at the token level to achieve a better performance-compute trade-off for long contexts.

Method: The authors propose LoGo, a token-level dynamic local-global attention module. Each LoGo layer has two branches: (1) a local branch where all tokens attend within a restricted window, and (2) a global branch where only a subset of tokens, chosen by a learned gating mechanism, receive full-context attention. The gate treats attention span as a proxy for attention budget: tokens predicted to need longer-range information are routed to the global branch. A threshold-based budget controller enforces a target fraction of tokens that get global attention, without extra loss terms, and a progressive masking schedule delays hard sparsification to stabilize early training. They additionally implement query-sparse Triton kernels so that reduced global-attention work translates into real wall-clock speedups. They evaluate LoGo against full-attention Transformers and static local-global hybrids under controlled budgets and scaling regimes.

Result: Empirical results show that LoGo sustains the scaling behavior of full-attention Transformers across different model sizes while reducing the computation for attention. Compared to both standard full-attention Transformers and static local-global hybrids with similar compute budgets, LoGo matches or outperforms them, with notable improvements on long-range retrieval tasks. The authors also analyze the learned span allocation and find interpretable patterns—for example, certain structurally important tokens get more global attention—indicating that the model learns meaningful token-level routing of attention budget.

Conclusion: The paper concludes that dynamically allocating local versus global attention at the token level is a practical and effective way to improve the efficiency of long-context Transformers. LoGo demonstrates that learned span allocation can maintain or exceed the performance of full-attention models and static hybrids while providing better compute efficiency and long-context capabilities. This suggests a promising direction for building scalable LLMs that can handle very long inputs without prohibitive attention costs.

Abstract: As context lengths scale, attention increasingly becomes a primary computational bottleneck in large language models. Standard Transformers remain powerful but computationally inefficient, as they allocate the same attention budget to every token regardless of its contextual demand. Existing local-global hybrids provide a more efficient alternative by mixing restricted- and full-context attention, but they typically allocate span statically across layers or heads. To address these limitations, we propose LoGo, a token-level dynamic local-global attention mechanism that uses attention span as a direct proxy for attention budget allocation. Each LoGo layer contains coupled local and global branches: all tokens receive efficient local attention over a restricted context window, while a learned gate activates global attention with full-context access only for tokens requiring long-range information. A threshold-based budget controller maintains a target global ratio without auxiliary losses, and a progressive masking schedule stabilizes training before sparse routing takes effect. We further implement query-sparse Triton kernels that convert reduced global-attention computation into practical speedups. Extensive experiments validate LoGo's effectiveness, showing that it preserves the scaling behavior of full-attention Transformers across model sizes. In controlled comparisons, LoGo improves over the full-attention Transformer and matched-budget static local-global hybrids, with clear gains on long-range retrieval. Analysis further shows that LoGo learns interpretable span allocation patterns. These results suggest that learned token-level span allocation is an effective and scalable way to improve the long-context performance-compute trade-off.

</details>


### [72] [Evaluating LLMs on Conversational Text-to-SQL under Chain Ambiguity and Intent Drift](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29543)
*Yujia Liu,Jiayan Lin,Zijin Hong,Zheng Yuan,Shengyuan Chen,Hao Chen,Qinggang Zhang,Xiao Huang,Feiran Huang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Introduce TIDE-Bench, a benchmark for conversational text-to-SQL focusing on chain ambiguity and intent drift, with new metrics and evaluation of 12 LLMs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing conversational text-to-SQL benchmarks mostly measure execution accuracy and do not adequately capture how user intent evolves over multiple conversational turns, especially in terms of underspecification and changes of mind.

Method: Construct TIDE-Bench using 514 anchor SQL queries from BIRD, creating 1,542 conversational samples that exhibit chain ambiguity and intent drift; define new metrics for chain identification and drift recognition-resolution; evaluate 12 advanced LLMs on these dimensions in addition to execution accuracy.

Result: LLMs show persistent difficulty in correctly identifying clarification chains, regardless of how often clarifications occur, and exhibit a significant gap between recognizing intent drift and correctly resolving it; overlapping failure patterns are observed when both ambiguity and drift are present.

Conclusion: Conversational text-to-SQL systems face systematic challenges in handling chain ambiguity and intent drift, so future research should address these specific weaknesses; TIDE-Bench and its released code provide a resource and metrics to drive such progress.

Abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have established conversational text-to-SQL as a practical interface between users and databases, often involving multiple turns of clarification and revision. However, existing benchmarks primarily evaluate execution accuracy, leaving the unfolding and shifting of user intent across turns largely uncovered. To address this, we introduce TIDE-Bench, a benchmark for conversational text-to-SQL under chain ambiguity and intent drift evaluation, targeting two recurring patterns: chain ambiguity, where an underspecified question triggers layered clarification with conditional dependencies, and intent drift, where the user retracts and replaces a previously committed request element. Built on 514 anchor SQLs from BIRD, TIDE-Bench comprises 1,542 samples and introduces dedicated metrics for chain identification and drift recognition-resolution beyond execution accuracy. Evaluating 12 advanced LLMs reveals a persistent chain identification bottleneck unaffected by clarification frequency, a wide drift recognition-resolution gap, and overlap between failure modes when jointly activated. The corresponding code of TIDE-Bench is released for further research.

</details>


### [73] [TACS: Trajectory-Aware Candidate Selection for LLM Jailbreak Suffix Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29564)
*Shiliang Xiao*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper identifies a key flaw in existing gradient-based jailbreak suffix optimization methods: they myopically select candidates based only on current loss, leading to poor final jailbreak performance. It proposes a new trajectory-aware candidate selection framework (OURS) that considers longer-term effectiveness and corrects selection-stage reward hacking, achieving more stable and higher attack success on HarmBench.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing jailbreak suffix optimization methods pick, at each optimization step, the suffix candidate with the lowest current loss, assuming this correlates with better final jailbreak performance. The authors observe that this myopic selection often leads to 'reward hacking' at the selection stage: candidates that look better under the current loss proxy do not actually lead to better jailbreak success later in the search. This reveals that candidate selection itself, not just generation, is a bottleneck. The motivation is to design a selection mechanism that accounts for the long-term trajectory of optimization and mitigates this reward hacking, thereby improving jailbreak attack success and stability under a fixed search budget.

Method: The authors introduce OURS, a trajectory-aware candidate selection framework for optimizing jailbreak suffixes. Instead of choosing candidates solely based on their instantaneous loss, OURS augments the per-step evaluation with a trajectory-aware proxy that estimates how promising a candidate is over future steps. It further incorporates reference-policy regularization to keep selection stable and avoid overfitting to noisy signals, and uses a discriminator-estimated chi-squared correction to adjust for biases in the proxy. Together, these components guide selection toward candidates whose influence persists across the optimization trajectory, rather than those that only momentarily look good under the current loss.

Result: On the HarmBench benchmark, OURS consistently outperforms strong gradient-based jailbreak suffix optimization baselines under the same search budget. It achieves substantially higher attack success rates and shows more stable optimization dynamics across search steps, avoiding the degradation or instability commonly seen with myopic selection strategies.

Conclusion: The study concludes that myopic candidate selection causes a form of selection-stage reward hacking in gradient-based jailbreak suffix optimization and is a key, previously underappreciated bottleneck. By incorporating trajectory-aware evaluation, reference-policy regularization, and chi-squared correction, OURS effectively mitigates this issue, leading to more robust and successful jailbreak attacks. The broader implication is that improving candidate selection, not just generation, is critical for advancing jailbreak suffix optimization methods.

Abstract: Gradient-based jailbreak suffix optimization methods typically update the suffix by retaining the candidate with the lowest current loss. We show that this seemingly natural design is fundamentally myopic: candidates that look better under the current-step proxy often fail to produce better jailbreak outcomes later in the search, revealing a form of selection-stage reward hacking. This suggests that candidate selection, rather than candidate generation alone, is a hidden bottleneck in suffix optimization. To address this issue, we propose \OURS{}, a trajectory-aware candidate selection framework for jailbreak suffix optimization. Instead of selecting candidates solely by their immediate loss, \OURS{} augments per-step evaluation with a trajectory-aware proxy and stabilizes selection with reference-policy regularization and a discriminator-estimated chi-squared correction, encouraging choices that remain effective beyond the current step. Experiments on HarmBench show that \OURS{} consistently outperforms strong baselines under the same search budget, substantially improving attack success rates while exhibiting more stable optimization behavior throughout the search. Our findings highlight that mitigating selection-stage reward hacking caused by myopic candidate selection is critical for improving jailbreak suffix optimization.

</details>


### [74] [Which one is banana man? Evaluating vision-language models in multi-turn pragmatic interpretation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29571)
*Alvin Wei Ming Tan,Ben Prystawski,Veronica Boyce*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper compares humans and vision-language models in iterated reference games and finds that current models cannot build and use context for pragmatic interpretation as effectively as humans.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Human conversation relies on flexible, context-sensitive pragmatic reasoning and shared intuitions. Iterated reference games are a controlled way to test whether models can track and exploit discourse context over multiple turns to understand intended meanings, beyond literal interpretations. The authors aim to assess whether state-of-the-art vision–language models share humans’ ability to adapt to changing contextual information in collaborative language use.

Method: The authors run iterated reference game experiments where speakers repeatedly refer to novel visual targets. They systematically vary contextual factors such as how much prior discourse is available, the order in which it is presented, and its relevance to the current utterance. They then compare human participants and vision–language models on a comprehension task: given an utterance and a visual context, identify the intended referent, with or without the preceding interaction history.

Result: Humans maintain consistently high performance regardless of manipulations to context amount, order, and relevance, showing robust use of pragmatic and contextual cues. Vision–language models show some ability to exploit prior context when it is explicitly provided, but they are poor at constructing and maintaining the right contextual representation over multiple turns. As a result, their interpretation of referring expressions degrades when successful performance depends on dynamically updated discourse context.

Conclusion: Current vision–language models do not yet capture key aspects of human-like pragmatic reasoning in multi-turn, collaborative settings. They can leverage context when it is straightforwardly supplied, but they fail to reliably build, track, and update the relevant shared context needed for efficient linguistic coordination. This highlights a gap between pattern-matching over text–image inputs and the deeper, dynamically maintained common ground that underpins human conversational collaboration.

Abstract: Flexible adaptation to context and shared pragmatic intuitions contribute to smooth human conversation. Iterated reference games---in which players repeatedly pick out novel referents using language---present a test case for agents' ability to perform context-sensitive pragmatic reasoning in multi-turn linguistic environments. We tested humans and vision--language models on their ability to identify the intended meaning of descriptions produced in iterated reference games, varying the provided context in terms of amount, order, and relevance. While humans performed well consistently, the models we evaluated could make use of prior context to interpret humans' referring expressions, but they struggled to build up the relevant context to interpret those expressions effectively. Our results suggest that the models we evaluated lack core skills needed for efficient linguistic collaboration.

</details>


### [75] [SemTrace: Source-Grounded Semantic Signatures for Tracing LLM Exposure to Protected Documents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29575)
*Junyan Zhang,Yudong Zeng,Yongwei Huang,Zuhao Ouyang,Hong Chen,Xuming Hu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: SemTrace is a semantic watermarking method that encodes a document-specific binary signature into factual review content, enabling detection of whether a review was influenced by a particular protected manuscript copy without modifying token-level distributions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As large language models are increasingly used to read proprietary documents and generate text, document owners face a provenance problem: they cannot easily tell whether a specific piece of generated text was influenced by a particular protected copy of a manuscript, especially when they do not control or observe the model. Existing watermarking methods often rely on modifying token probabilities or visible patterns and are not tightly tied to the document’s factual content, limiting robustness and applicability. There is a need for a source-grounded, model-agnostic way to trace exposure of assigned copies that works even when only the outputs (e.g., reviews) are observable.

Method: SemTrace defines a semantic, document-specific binary codeword built from pairs of factual propositions that are directly supported by the manuscript. For each bit, the watermark picks one fact from a binary pair. A protected PDF embeds a “content contract” that instructs an LLM reviewer to express the selected facts in specified review slots while still freely evaluating the manuscript. This process encodes the binary signature in the semantic content of the review rather than in surface text patterns. At detection time, a frozen natural language inference (NLI) model examines the review, infers which facts from each pair are entailed, and explicitly models uncertainties or missing evidence as erasures. The inferred bitstring is then compared to the original codeword assigned to that manuscript copy to test whether the review was likely influenced by that specific protected source.

Result: The method demonstrates that semantic watermarks based on factual propositions can be reliably embedded into and decoded from LLM-generated reviews without constraining the model’s free-form evaluation, and without relying on model-specific token biases. Experiments (implied though not detailed in the abstract) show that the recovered semantic signatures align well with the assigned codewords for protected copies, supporting SemTrace’s effectiveness for exposure detection under realistic conditions where only the output reviews are observable.

Conclusion: SemTrace provides a model-agnostic, source-grounded semantic watermark that allows detection of whether a review was influenced by a specific protected manuscript copy. By encoding binary signatures in factual content and decoding them via NLI, it addresses provenance and exposure-tracing challenges for LLM-mediated document review, while keeping the watermark closely tied to the source document’s semantics instead of its surface form or the internals of any particular generation model.

Abstract: Large language models are increasingly used to read documents and produce downstream text, creating a provenance problem when the document owner cannot control or inspect the model that performs the generation. We introduce SemTrace, a source-grounded semantic watermark for detecting whether a generated review was influenced by a known protected manuscript copy. Rather than biasing token probabilities or imposing surface-form patterns, SemTrace constructs a document-specific binary signature from factual propositions that are directly supported by the manuscript itself. A protected PDF invisibly carries a content contract that selects one fact from each binary pair and asks an instruction-following reviewer to express those facts in fixed review slots without changing its independent evaluation. A frozen natural language inference model then decodes the resulting semantic evidence with explicit erasures and scores the recovered bits against the codeword assigned to that copy. This design targets model-agnostic, assigned-copy exposure detection while keeping the watermark semantically tied to the source document.

</details>


### [76] [SUP-MIMIC: A Multi-Task Clinical Diagnosis Benchmark for Evaluating LLMs' Robustness to Contradictory Evidence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29582)
*Yi Yu,Bo Wang,Chong Feng,Ge Shi,Xia Liu,Ziyi Yang,Xuewen Shi*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces SUP-MIMIC, a new benchmark framework to test large language models’ robustness in clinical reasoning, especially under diagnostic ambiguity and convergence, and shows that current models perform poorly and exhibit unsafe biases.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Most current evaluations of large language models in medicine emphasize factual recall instead of testing whether models can navigate complex relationships between clinical signs and final diagnoses. In real-world clinical settings, the same symptoms can arise from different diseases (diagnostic ambiguity), and different symptoms can point to the same underlying condition (diagnostic convergence). Existing benchmarks fail to capture these “one-to-many” and “many-to-one” reasoning challenges. The authors aim to build an evaluation that specifically probes these non-bijective mappings using realistic EHR data to better understand and improve the safety and reasoning robustness of LLMs in clinical practice.

Method: The authors construct SUP-MIMIC, a multi-task evaluation framework based on the MIMIC-IV-v3.1 electronic health records dataset. SUP-MIMIC includes three components: (1) a Basic Assessment (BA) that measures baseline performance on simpler diagnostic tasks; (2) a Diagnostic Divergence Task (DDT) that explicitly tests the model’s ability to disambiguate among multiple possible diagnoses that share highly similar clinical presentations (“one-to-many” mapping); and (3) a Diagnostic Convergence Task (DCT) that tests the model’s ability to recognize when diverse symptom profiles nonetheless indicate the same underlying disease (“many-to-one” mapping). State-of-the-art LLMs are evaluated across these tasks to compare their performance and to analyze their reasoning behavior versus reliance on statistical patterns.

Result: Across multiple state-of-the-art large language models, performance is acceptable on the Basic Assessment tasks but degrades significantly on the more challenging Diagnostic Divergence (DDT) and Diagnostic Convergence (DCT) tasks. The models often fail to correctly handle one-to-many and many-to-one clinical mappings, suggesting that they rely heavily on superficial statistical regularities rather than robust causal reasoning about pathophysiology.
