Additionally, the evaluation reveals a consistent conservative bias: when uncertain, models tend to predict “healthy” or under-diagnose, which may conceal true disease and translate into missed diagnoses in real-world use.

Conclusion: SUP-MIMIC provides a rigorous, clinically grounded benchmark for evaluating the robustness of LLM-based clinical reasoning under diagnostic ambiguity and convergence. The observed performance drop on DDT and DCT, along with the conservative “healthy” bias, indicates that current LLMs are not yet reliable for complex diagnostic decision support and could pose safety risks if used naively. The framework offers a structured way to measure and eventually improve these models’ causal reasoning and safety characteristics in clinical medicine.

Abstract: Current evaluations of large language models (LLMs) primarily focus on factual knowledge retrieval, overlooking the fundamental challenge of navigating the complex, non-bijective mappings between clinical indicators and diagnoses. Existing benchmarks fail to assess whether large language models truly possess the reasoning capability required for diagnostic ambiguity scenarios, where identical clinical presentations may correspond to different etiologies, and diagnostic convergence scenarios, where heterogeneous symptoms ultimately indicate the same disease. To address this issue, we propose SUP-MIMIC, a multi-task framework utilizing MIMIC-IV-v3.1 that comprises Basic Assessment (BA), Diagnostic Divergence Task (DDT), and Diagnostic Convergence Task (DCT). Specifically, DDT is designed to evaluate the model's "one-to-many" disambiguation capability among phenotypically similar cases, while DCT assesses the model's ability to identify "many-to-one" diagnostic patterns across different pathophysiological pathways. Comprehensive evaluation of state-of-the-art LLMs reveals substantial performance degradation on DDT and DCT compared to baseline tasks, exposing a systemic reliance on statistical shortcuts over genuine causal reasoning. Our findings further highlight a conservative bias toward "healthy" predictions, implying non-trivial risks for missed diagnoses in realistic medical settings. This work establishes a rigorous methodology for quantifying clinical reasoning robustness and provides a roadmap for enhancing the safety of language models in clinical medicine.

</details>


### [77] [How You Ask Shapes What You Get: A Theory-Seeded Measurement of Articulation in Advice-Seeking LLM Conversations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29591)
*Juneha Baek,Suhyeon Lee,Donghyuk Shin*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper studies how differences in how people phrase advice-seeking questions (articulation styles) form stable, measurable patterns that are distinct from topic, and how these patterns affect language-model responses.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Most research on language models and user prompts treats variation in how users ask questions as random noise, focusing instead on topics or tasks. However, users consistently differ in how specifically or vaguely they pose questions, which may systematically influence model behavior and is not captured by topic-based evaluation. The authors want to characterize this variation, understand its structure, and see how it affects model responses so evaluations can better reflect real-world usage.

Method: The authors compile 16,447 advice-seeking prompts from three public chat corpora (WildChat, LMSYS, ShareChat). They hand-design interpretable linguistic and structural features that capture how questions are articulated (e.g., length, specificity, detail, explicit constraints). Using these features, they perform latent factor analysis to recover underlying articulation dimensions. They check that these factors are stable across train/test splits and across different corpora, and they measure how the resulting articulation styles correlate with language-model responses such as answer length, vagueness, and whether the model asks clarifying questions. They also validate key contrasts with independent human annotators.

Result: They discover a small number of latent articulation factors that are robust across data splits and corpora and that are largely independent of topic. These factors cluster prompts into a few recurring articulation styles. One notable style is long-form but information-poor, comprising about one-sixth of prompts in the largest corpus. For this style, models systematically return shorter, vaguer answers and rarely ask for clarification, even though the prompts are under-specified. Importantly, this is not just about under-specification: another equally under-specified articulation style does elicit clarifying questions. The observed effects hold within each topic category and within length quantiles. Human annotators independently reproduce the distinction between these key articulation styles.

Conclusion: Articulation styles are stable, latent dimensions of advice-seeking prompts that are separable from topic and meaningfully affect how language models respond. Because these structures cut across topics, standard topic- or task-based benchmarks miss systematic disparities in model behavior across user populations. The authors argue that evaluation benchmarks should explicitly stratify by articulation style and they release their extracted factor structure as a measurement tool for doing so.

Abstract: Users articulate the same advice-seeking request in different ways: some specify detailed constraints, others gesture at a vague need. Prior work treats this variation as noise to be averaged away; we instead treat it as a stable, measurable structure in the input distribution. We ask whether articulation (how people ask) forms latent dimensions separable from topic (what they ask about), and whether it is associated with how language models respond. We extract interpretable features from 16,447 advice-seeking prompts pooled from public chat corpora (WildChat, LMSYS, and ShareChat) and recover a small set of latent articulation factors that replicate across train/test splits and across corpora. Because this structure is largely separable from topic, the populations it defines cut across topics and stay invisible to topic- or task-based evaluation. The factors define a handful of recurring articulation styles, one of which stands out: a long-form but information-poor style, roughly one in six prompts in the largest corpus, where models return shorter, vaguer answers and do not ask for clarification even though under-specification is exactly the condition that warrants it. The contrast holds within every topic group and length quintile, and is not under-specification alone -- a second, equally under-specified style does draw clarifying questions. Two independent human annotators reproduce this contrast. We argue that benchmarks should stratify on articulation, and we offer the extracted structure as a measurement instrument for doing so.

</details>


### [78] [Hindsight Memory-PRM: Supervising Memory Management with Auditable Hindsight Credit](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29605)
*Haoxuan Jia,Yang Liu,Yingguang Yang,Yancheng Chen,Chongyang Zhang,Hao Zheng,Qian Li,Yulin Huang,Jianshen Zhang,Yongzhi Qi,Shang Luo,Kefu Xu,Hao Peng,Junyu Lu,Du Cheng,Philip S. Yu,Bin Chong*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces Hindsight Memory-PRM, a method to train and supervise memory operations in long-horizon LLM agents using machine-readable evidence (retrieval hits, citations, and controlled deletions) instead of per-operation human labels.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long-horizon LLM agents rely heavily on external memory, but supervising which memory operations are useful is difficult because the true value of a memory operation is unobservable at the time it is taken. Existing approaches often require expensive human labeling, Monte Carlo rollouts, or very large contexts to track and evaluate memory usage. The authors aim to develop a scalable, label-efficient way to evaluate and improve memory operations using only artifacts already present in an agent’s trajectory.

Method: They propose Hindsight Memory-PRM, a preference-reward modeling approach that leverages an “audit trail” of memory usage. Offline, they train a memory-utility critic that is conditioned on memory operations, using retrieval hits and answer-time citations as evidence. Online, they use retrieval patterns, citations, and a controlled deletion-and-reanswer experiment for each probe to estimate a calibrated presence credit for memory entries. This credit is propagated along version chains of memory items and used as a proxy reward at the action level, without needing per-operation labels or Monte Carlo replay of full continuations.

Result: On the LoCoMo benchmark, a local 8B-parameter policy optimized with Hindsight Memory-PRM attains 77.5% accuracy under a fixed shared reader, outperforming its API teacher model (65.1%) and all reproduced external memory systems, while using only one-eighth the context length of Mem0’s official setting. On the LongMemEval benchmark, the method achieves 79.0% accuracy. Ablation studies indicate that the performance improvements come mainly from the causal calibration procedure rather than merely increasing the amount of training signal.

Conclusion: Hindsight Memory-PRM provides an effective and label-efficient way to supervise and improve memory operations in long-horizon LLM agents by exploiting the machine-readable traces of memory use. The approach yields strong empirical gains, enabling smaller local models to outperform larger teacher APIs and existing memory baselines while using significantly shorter contexts. The learned policy also converges to a structured, multi-version memory organization that open-loop alternatives fail to match, suggesting that intervention-calibrated credit assignment over memory versions is key to its success.

Abstract: Memory operations of long-horizon LLM agents are hard to supervise: an operation's value is unobservable when it is taken. But they are special -- they leave machine-readable evidence in the trajectory: retrieval hits and answer-time citations. Hindsight Memory-PRM exploits this audit trail twice: offline to train an operation-conditioned memory-utility critic, and online, where retrievals, citations, and one controlled deletion-and-reanswer per probe settle an intervention-calibrated entry-level presence credit, propagated along version chains as an action-level proxy reward -- no per-operation human labels, no Monte-Carlo replay of continuations. On held-out LoCoMo a local 8B policy reaches 77.5% under a fixed shared reader, surpassing its API teacher (65.1%) and all reproduced external systems, at one eighth the context of Mem0's official operating point; on LongMemEval, 79.0%. Ablations attribute the gain to causal calibration rather than signal density, and the policy converges to a multi-version memory organization whose gains no tested open-loop baseline reproduces.

</details>


### [79] [Agent Zero Memory: Provenance-Aware Long-Term Memory for LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29606)
*Ming Wu,Pengyuan Zhu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces Agent Zero Memory, a provenance-aware long-term memory system for LLM agents that uses three complementary memory representations with strict citation-based reading rules to reduce hallucination and achieve state-of-the-art results on long-term memory benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current memory systems for LLM agents typically rely on a single structure such as a fact store, vector index, or knowledge graph, each of which has intrinsic blind spots. LLM agents also need durable, faithful memory across all user conversations and stored data, without fabrications. The authors are motivated to design a memory architecture that is both comprehensive (capturing different facets of user history) and reliable (provenanced, citation-based, and structurally resistant to hallucinations), while being efficient across different backbone models.

Method: They propose Agent Zero Memory, which distills a user’s conversations, files, and connected sources into three parallel memory systems: (1) an episodic Memory Events timeline tracking when and what changed, (2) an associative entity-event knowledge graph linking people and projects across sessions, and (3) a semantic Hierarchical Documentary Memory (HDM) of curated, citation-locked durable facts. For each query, an intent gate decides if external memory is needed, then a source router and three concurrent agentic search loops (one per memory system) perform hybrid (embedding + lexical) retrieval with agent-controlled filters. Results from each system are grounded in cited sources and merged into a single answer with an overall confidence. The system enforces a strict reading discipline where each learned item includes provenance (origin, timestamp, evidence pointer), and every answer is generated under a citation lock that only allows citing sources that were actually retrieved and read, forcing abstention instead of guessing when evidence is lacking.

Result: On two public long-term memory benchmarks, LongMemEval and LoCoMo, Agent Zero Memory achieves new state-of-the-art performance: 95.60% on LongMemEval and 93.60% on LoCoMo, surpassing prior strongest systems by +0.73 and +1.10 points, respectively. In a controlled study across eight different backbone LLMs, the system exhibits a tight accuracy band (only 3.4 percentage points variation) while per-query cost spans roughly 30x, showing that high accuracy can be maintained even with cheaper models. They demonstrate near-state-of-the-art quality at up to 20x lower per-query cost, highlighting that improvements come primarily from the memory architecture rather than from using the largest or most expensive models.

Conclusion: The paper concludes that Agent Zero Memory provides a robust, provenance-aware long-term memory layer for LLM agents that significantly reduces hallucination risk via structural constraints like citation locking and provenanced items. By combining three complementary memory representations and an agentic retrieval pipeline, it attains state-of-the-art performance on long-context benchmarks while also enabling cost-efficient deployment across a range of backbone models. The results suggest that memory-centric design, rather than simply scaling model size, can be a primary driver of accuracy for tasks requiring reliable long-term memory.

Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents need durable, faithful memory of everything a user or organization has said and stored, yet most memory systems commit to a single organizing structure (a fact store, a vector index, or a knowledge graph) and inherit its blind spots. We present Agent Zero Memory, a provenance-aware long-term memory system that distils a user's conversations, files, and connected sources into three parallel memory systems, each capturing a different facet of the same history: an episodic Memory Events timeline that makes when and what changed first-class, an associative entity-event knowledge graph that links people and projects across sessions, and a semantic, curated, citation-locked Hierarchical Documentary Memory (HDM) of durable facts. A retrieval turn runs an intent gate (so self-contained turns add no latency), a source router, and three concurrent agentic searches, one per system, each a tool-using loop over hybrid (embedding + lexical) search under agent-controlled filters; their grounded, cited answers are integrated into one answer with a single confidence. We formalize the reading discipline: every learned item is a provenanced item carrying its origin, timestamp, and evidence pointer, and every answer is read under a citation lock, so it may cite only evidence its reader actually opened; fabrication is structurally excluded and the system abstains rather than guesses. On two public benchmarks the system sets a new state of the art: 95.60% on LongMemEval and 93.60% on LoCoMo, improving over the strongest prior systems by +0.73 and +1.10 points. A controlled study across eight backbone LLMs characterizes the accuracy-cost-latency frontier: accuracy varies by only 3.4 points while per-query cost varies by ~30x, with near-state-of-the-art quality at up to 20x lower cost per query, the signature of memory-driven, rather than model-driven, quality.

</details>


### [80] [Beyond Surface Alignment: Grounding the Dynamics of Situational Understanding and Generative Control in LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29610)
*Chenghao Yang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper argues current LLM alignment focuses on style and safety but not true grounding, and proposes a framework and tools for “grounded alignment” that better tie models’ use of context and generation to real situational needs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing alignment methods make LLMs sound safe, fluent, and consistent, but they can still misunderstand evolving situations, misuse long context, and generate confident yet incoherent outputs. This gap between surface behavior and underlying reasoning is dangerous in high‑stakes domains, motivating a deeper notion of alignment that ensures models track situations and their own generative process reliably.

Method: 1) Define two dimensions of grounding: Situational Grounding (how models track and update a mental model of context) and Generative Grounding (how models explore and evaluate possible continuations). 2) Build evaluation tools: SitTest for changing environments; ReCode for probing reliance on shallow heuristics vs syntactic/structural understanding; BF (Branching Factor) to quantify diversity/structure of generative trajectories; Hindsight to test whether models can interpret and assess their own outputs. 3) Design Dynamic Control techniques: AI Realtor as a context‑engineering protocol, Base‑Aligned Model Collaboration to split exploration from stylistic alignment, and Annealed Sampling to support verifiable RL. 4) Demonstrate the framework on an Addiction Support setting where rationalization is used as an interface for safe, grounded assistance.

Result: Empirically, the paper finds that state‑of‑the‑art LLMs with large context windows still fail to maintain consistent situational models across evolving scenarios (SitTest) and often rely on surface cues rather than deep structural dependencies (ReCode). The BF analysis shows that common alignment tuning narrows the model’s generative search space, causing premature convergence to a single stylistic mode. Hindsight reveals that models frequently misinterpret or fail to critically assess their own prior generations. The proposed Dynamic Control techniques partially mitigate these issues: context engineering improves situational grounding in AI Realtor; model collaboration allows more exploratory yet still aligned behavior; and annealed sampling supports more verifiable, controlled reinforcement‑learning‑style updates. Initial application to Addiction Support suggests improved suitability for high‑stakes interaction compared to purely surface‑aligned models.

Conclusion: Current alignment practices, though effective for friendly and safe chat, are insufficient for building robust, context‑reliable agents. Grounded Alignment—explicitly addressing how models represent evolving situations and structure their generative space—provides a more principled path forward. By diagnosing failures in situational and generative grounding and introducing dynamic control techniques, the work argues for alignment schemes that anchor models in both the context they process and the decisions they generate, especially for high‑stakes applications.

Abstract: The current alignment tuning paradigm for Large Language Models (LLMs) prioritizes surface-level behaviors -- fluency, safety, and tonal consistency. While effective for casual chat, this thesis argues that such surface alignment masks a lack of grounding, creating models that are stylistically confident but situationally brittle. We propose a framework of Grounded Alignment, analyzing how models process context (Input) and structure generation (Output), then aligning these grounded behaviors to human needs.
  First, we evaluate failures in Situational Grounding. SitTest shows that despite large context windows, state-of-the-art models struggle to maintain a consistent "mental model" of a changing environment. ReCode further shows that models rely on surface heuristics rather than deep syntactic dependencies: they "read" extensive histories without truly "understanding" the evolving situation.
  Second, we evaluate Generative Grounding. We introduce the Branching Factor (BF) to map LLM generation, finding that standard alignment tuning constricts this landscape into premature stylistic collapse. Hindsight further shows that models often fail to understand their own generations.
  Finally, we propose Dynamic Control for grounded interaction. AI Realtor demonstrates context engineering to compensate for poor situational grounding. Base-Aligned Model Collaboration decouples exploration from stylistic constraints. We also present Annealed Sampling for verifiable reinforcement learning and apply these ideas to Addiction Support, where model-generated rationalization offers a communication interface for high-stakes domains. Collectively, this work moves beyond surface alignment toward agents anchored in both context and generation.

</details>


### [81] [Cross-lingual Functional Vectors for Emotion Detection in Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29613)
*Jieying Xue,Phuong Minh Nguyen,Minh Le Nguyen,Shogo Okada*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper studies whether function vectors (FVs)—latent directions derived from in-context examples—can robustly steer LLMs across languages on a challenging semantic task and shows they work well for multilingual emotion recognition without needing demonstrations at inference time.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Function vectors were shown to steer LLMs on relatively simple, structured tasks, but it is unclear if they (1) work on semantically complex tasks and (2) generalize across languages rather than encoding language-specific patterns. Multilingual applications need lightweight, reusable steering mechanisms that avoid repeatedly feeding many in-context examples due to cost and latency. This paper addresses these gaps by testing FVs on cross-lingual, multi-label emotion recognition.

Method: The authors use multilingual multi-label emotion recognition as a benchmark and treat it as a cross-lingual zero-shot setting: they first extract function vectors from in-context demonstrations in a source language, then apply these FVs to steer model behavior in different target languages without providing demonstrations at inference. They test both clean and perturbed input conditions across several LLMs and systematically vary which attention heads are used to construct FVs, analyzing performance and stability of optimal head ranges. They also compare FV-steered performance with standard few-shot in-context learning to evaluate how much of the task-steering effect can be replicated using FVs alone.

Result: Across multiple cross-lingual setups, injecting FVs from a source language consistently and substantially improves emotion recognition performance in target languages, including under perturbed zero-shot conditions. The gains indicate that FVs encode language-agnostic task signals rather than relying on specific lexical patterns. Different LLMs show stable and model-specific optimal ranges of attention heads for building effective FVs, and these ranges remain similar across languages. Moreover, FVs recover a significant portion of the performance benefits of few-shot in-context learning while avoiding the need to process multiple demonstrations at inference.

Conclusion: Function vectors are an effective, lightweight, and transferable mechanism for steering LLMs on multilingual, semantically rich tasks. They demonstrate strong cross-lingual transfer, suggest that FVs capture language-independent task semantics, and can approximate few-shot in-context learning performance with substantially lower computational overhead. This makes FVs a practical tool for large-scale multilingual task adaptation and deployment.

Abstract: Function vectors (FVs) have recently emerged as a promising mechanism for steering the behavior of large language models (LLMs) by injecting task-specific latent direction representations derived from in-context demonstrations. While prior studies have shown that FVs can recover task behavior in structured in-context learning settings, their effectiveness on semantically complex tasks and their ability to generalize across languages remain underexplored. We investigate the cross-lingual transferability of FVs using multilingual multi-label emotion recognition as a challenging semantic classification benchmark. Specifically, we examine whether FVs extracted from a source language can steer task behavior in another language under both standard clean and perturbed zero-shot settings without providing demonstrations during inference. Across diverse cross-lingual settings, applying FVs substantially improves performance, suggesting that FVs capture language-agnostic, task-relevant signals rather than purely language-specific lexical patterns, and highlighting their potential as a lightweight and transferable mechanism for multilingual task adaptation. We observe that each LLM exhibits a relatively stable optimal range of attention heads for constructing effective FVs, and the pattern remains consistent across languages. In addition, FVs can partially replicate the task-steering effects of standard few-shot in-context learning while avoiding the computational overhead of processing multiple demonstrations, making them effective for large-scale practical applications. Our code is available at https://github.com/yingjie7/cross_lingual_fvs.

</details>


### [82] [JPO: Juris Policy Optimization for Structured Legal Reasoning in Criminal Judgment Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29616)
*Zhaolu Kang,Yantao Liu,Tailong Luo,Leqi Zheng,Lei Wei,Chenghua Zhu,Junhao Gong,Jiachen Qian,Eric Hanchen Jiang,Jiaxin Liu,Yuan Wang,Hao Zhang,Zixia Wang,Rong Fu,Zheng Lin,Richeng Xuan,Zhichao Hu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces Juris Policy Optimization (JPO), a post‑training framework that improves both accuracy and reasoning quality for Chinese criminal judgment prediction by enforcing a structured, four‑step legal reasoning process and optimizing it with a composite reinforcement learning reward.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Criminal judgment prediction is not just a flat classification task; it requires a logically structured chain: match facts to statutes, derive charges from statutes, and ensure sentencing is consistent with charges. Existing models mainly optimize for final labels and, when they do assess reasoning, they rely on indirect, often LLM‑generated rubrics that may not align with the true logic of legal adjudication. There is a need for a training and evaluation framework that directly targets and improves the internal legal reasoning structure, not just the final outputs.

Method: The authors propose Juris Policy Optimization (JPO), a post‑training framework for legal reasoning in Chinese criminal judgment prediction. JPO standardizes legal reasoning into a four‑step process, supervised initially with teacher‑generated rationales. After this supervised phase, it applies reinforcement learning, defining a composite reward that jointly captures: (1) quality of legal predictions (statutes, charges, sentencing), (2) completeness of the four‑step reasoning structure, and (3) logical cross‑step consistency. To better focus on key legal reasoning segments, JPO adds token‑level advantage reweighting and adaptive clipping, giving more precise credit assignment to legally salient parts of the generated rationale.

Result: Across several open‑source language models and three Chinese legal benchmarks, JPO yields consistent improvements over both standard supervised fine‑tuning and existing RL‑based baselines. The gains are seen not only in judgment prediction accuracy (for statutes, charges, and sentences) but also in metrics of reasoning quality and structure, indicating that the framework enhances both decision outcomes and the underlying justification process.

Conclusion: The study demonstrates that enforcing an explicit, multi‑step legal reasoning structure and directly optimizing it with reinforcement learning leads to better criminal judgment prediction and more coherent, law‑aligned rationales. JPO emerges as a general post‑training approach that can be applied to different language models and datasets to promote structured, legally faithful reasoning, addressing limitations of prior methods that either ignore internal reasoning or evaluate it only indirectly.

Abstract: Criminal judgment prediction requires models to infer statutory articles, charges, and sentencing outcomes from case facts. Unlike standard classification tasks, it involves a structured reasoning process in which statutes should be matched with facts, charges should be justified by statutes, and sentencing outcomes should remain consistent with charges. Existing approaches optimize final labels, and while some have attempted to evaluate reasoning quality, their evaluations are indirect, often relying on LLM-generated rubrics that reflect model-internal preferences rather than the inherent logical structure of legal adjudication. We propose Juris Policy Optimization (JPO), a post-training framework for structured legal reasoning in Chinese criminal judgment prediction. JPO first uses teacher-generated rationales to supervise a standardized four-step reasoning process, and then applies reinforcement learning with a composite reward over legal prediction quality, reasoning structure completeness, and cross-step consistency. JPO further introduces token-level advantage reweighting and adaptive clipping for legally salient reasoning segments. Experiments on multiple open-source language models and three Chinese legal benchmarks show that JPO consistently improves both judgment prediction and reasoning quality over supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning baselines.

</details>


### [83] [Memory-First Fact-Checking: A Knowledge-Graph-Grounded Multi-Agent System for Misinformation Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29617)
*Amelia Petrenciuc,Alexandru Lecu,Adrian Groza*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: A hybrid fact-checking framework combines a semantic-memory Knowledge Graph with adversarial multi-agent reasoning to detect misinformation accurately and explainably, updating its own knowledge over time.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing fact-checking systems either rely heavily on large language models, which can hallucinate and are hard to interpret, or on static knowledge bases, which have limited coverage and do not adapt quickly to emerging topics such as COVID-19. There is a need for a fact-checking framework that is both explainable and highly accurate, can prioritize trusted internal knowledge, minimize unnecessary web queries, and continuously expand its knowledge as new claims are verified.

Method: The paper proposes a memory-first, web-fallback fact-checking pipeline. First, claims are matched against a dual-index Knowledge Graph using Sentence-BERT-based semantic retrieval to find relevant nodes and edges, then evaluated with a Natural Language Inference (NLI) model. A graph-aware confidence mechanism, incorporating semantic similarity scores, NLI confidence, and structural graph evidence, decides whether internal knowledge suffices. If not, the system queries trusted web sources and sends retrieved evidence to an adversarial multi-agent tribunal: a support agent finds confirming evidence, a contradiction agent looks for refuting evidence, and a judging agent integrates their arguments to reach a verdict. Verified results are converted into triples and added back to the Knowledge Graph, enabling incremental semantic-memory growth.

Result: On a curated COVID-19 misinformation benchmark, the framework achieves 97.4% accuracy and a macro-averaged F1-score of 92.6% on resolved claims. It outperforms a strong Llama 3.3 70B baseline, which achieves 87.7% accuracy and 86.3% macro-averaged F1, demonstrating the effectiveness of combining KG-based semantic memory with adversarial multi-agent reasoning and confidence-aware decision-making.

Conclusion: Integrating a Knowledge Graph-based semantic memory with an adversarial multi-agent verification process yields a highly accurate and explainable fact-checking system that efficiently balances internal knowledge use with external web retrieval. The graph-aware confidence mechanism reduces unnecessary web queries, while continuous incorporation of validated information into the Knowledge Graph allows the system to adapt to evolving misinformation domains such as COVID-19. This architecture offers a promising direction for scalable, trustworthy misinformation detection beyond single LLM-based baselines.

Abstract: This paper introduces a hybrid fact-checking framework that integrates Knowledge Graph-based semantic memory with adversarial multi-agent reasoning for explainable misinformation detection. The proposed system follows a memory-first, web-fallback architecture, in which input claims are initially evaluated against a dual-index Knowledge Graph through Sentence-BERT-based semantic retrieval and Natural Language Inference. When the evidence retrieved from the graph is insufficient to support a reliable decision, the framework collects information from trusted web sources and assesses it using an adversarial tribunal composed of support, contradiction, and judging agents. A graph-aware confidence mechanism combines semantic similarity, NLI confidence, and structural graph evidence to determine whether internal knowledge is sufficient, thereby reducing unnecessary web retrieval. Following verification, validated information is transformed into structured triples and incorporated into the Knowledge Graph, supporting the incremental expansion of the system's semantic memory. Experimental evaluation on a curated COVID-19 misinformation benchmark demonstrates that the proposed framework achieves an accuracy of 97.4\% and a macro-averaged F1-score of 92.6% on resolved claims, outperforming a Llama~3.3~70B baseline, which obtains an accuracy of 87.7% and a macro-averaged F1-score of 86.3%.

</details>


### [84] [MI-Distillation: Selecting from Model-Interpolated Instruct-Reasoning Data Spectrum for Chain-of-Thought Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29623)
*Yangsong Lan,Renkai Hu,HongKai Zheng,Bo Zhang,Renzhi Wang,Hongliang Dai,Piji Li*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: They study why long chain-of-thought (CoT) traces from large reasoning models are hard to distill into smaller models, analyze it via gradients, and propose MI-Distillation plus SeqLSS to select better reasoning traces and improve small-model reasoning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long CoT from large reasoning models yields strong performance, but directly supervising small student models with these long traces brings only modest gains and can even underperform shorter CoT. The community lacks a clear understanding of why this happens and how to systematically exploit Long CoT for distillation. The authors want a principled way to leverage rich reasoning trajectories while keeping them learnable and aligned with the student model’s capacity.

Method: 1) Perform a gradient-centric analysis comparing Long vs Short CoT distillation, examining gradient magnitudes and concentration of update directions across model sizes. 2) Based on the insight that Long CoT causes larger, more focused gradients, design MI-Distillation: they interpolate between an instruction-following model and a reasoning-focused model to create a continuous spectrum of Instruct-Reasoning data/trajectories. 3) Introduce SeqLSS (Sequential Learnable Surprisal Score), a scoring scheme over reasoning steps that prefers trajectories that carry high information content but remain learnable for the student, and use it to select which interpolated trajectories to distill from.

Result: They empirically find that Long CoT supervision induces higher gradient magnitudes and more concentrated update directions than Short CoT, especially for larger student models, explaining why naive Long CoT distillation can be unstable or suboptimal. With MI-Distillation plus SeqLSS-based trajectory selection, small student models trained on CoT outperform strong baselines that use conventional Long CoT distillation on several reasoning benchmarks.

Conclusion: Long CoT is not inherently better for distillation; its effectiveness depends on how well the reasoning trajectories’ information density and distribution match the student model. By interpolating between instruction and reasoning behaviors and selecting trajectories with SeqLSS, one can obtain CoT signals that are both informative and learnable, leading to more effective distillation of reasoning capabilities into smaller models.

Abstract: Recent advances in large reasoning models (LRMs) have shown strong performance on complex problems through long chain-of-thought (Long CoT) reasoning. However, distilling such trajectories into smaller student models remains challenging: direct Long CoT supervision often provides limited gains and can be less effective than concise Short CoT rationales. In this work, we investigate this phenomenon from a gradient-centric perspective. Our analysis shows that Long CoT induces larger gradient magnitudes and more concentrated update directions than Short CoT, with this effect becoming more pronounced as student model capacity increases. These findings suggest that effective Long CoT distillation requires balancing the reasoning information density of reasoning trajectories with their distributional alignment to the student model. Motivated by this insight, we propose \textbf{M}odel \textbf{I}nterporlation \textbf{Distillation} (\textbf{MI-Distillation}), a framework that constructs a continuous Instruct-Reasoning data spectrum through model interpolation. To select suitable trajectories from this spectrum, we further introduce \textbf{Seq}uential \textbf{L}earnable \textbf{S}urprisal \textbf{S}core (\textbf{SeqLSS}), which favors reasoning paths that are both informative and learnable for the student. Extensive experiments on reasoning benchmarks show that MI-Distillation consistently improves small model CoT distillation over strong Long CoT baselines.

</details>


### [85] [PrivBench: A Holistic and Modular Benchmarking Platform for Evaluating Text-to-Text Privatization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29624)
*Stephen Meisenbacher,Andreea-Elena Bodea,Ahmet Bilal Akın,Alexandra Klymenko,Jana Diesner,Florian Matthes*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper presents PrivBench, a unified, extensible benchmarking platform for evaluating text-to-text privacy-preserving methods in NLP.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing work on text-to-text privatization uses many heterogeneous, often incompatible evaluation techniques and metrics, making it hard to compare methods and track progress. The authors want a standardized, holistic, and user-friendly way to assess how well privatization methods protect privacy while preserving utility.

Method: They design and implement PrivBench, a modular benchmarking platform. It defines a set of evaluation desiderata for text privatization and organizes them into modules (e.g., privacy, utility, fluency, etc.). The system is extensible so that new tasks, metrics, and modules can be added over time. It exposes a public interface with real-time evaluation and a live leaderboard so researchers can submit systems and compare results.

Result: PrivBench is deployed as a free, publicly accessible platform (https://privbench.com/) that operationalizes a unified evaluation scheme for text-to-text privatization methods. It offers real-time scoring along the defined desiderata and maintains a public leaderboard to promote comparison and competition. The abstract implies successful implementation and availability but does not provide numerical benchmarks.

Conclusion: PrivBench offers a holistic, modular, and extensible solution for evaluating text-to-text privatization methods, addressing fragmentation in current evaluation practices. By providing a standardized, publicly available benchmark with real-time feedback and leaderboards, it aims to catalyze more systematic development and comparison of privacy-preserving text transformation methods.

Abstract: Natural Language Processing methods have enabled novel solutions and advances in the field of privacy, particularly in the sub-domain of text-to-text privatization, where the goal is to transform a sensitive input text into a privatized output by ideally masking (in)directly identifiable or otherwise private information. The evaluation of text-to-text privatization, however, is not straightforward, and the extant literature has utilized a myriad of techniques and metrics to quantify the privacy-preserving capabilities of privatization methods. Seeking to unify the evaluation of text-to-text privatization, we introduce PrivBench, a holistic and modular benchmarking platform for researchers and practitioners working on text privatization. PrivBench is holistic in that it evaluates privatization on a series of defined desiderata, which are structured into modules. PrivBench is not only modular but also extensible, allowing for future updates and benchmark versions. PrivBench is user-centered and promotes competition via real-time evaluation and a live public leaderboard. The platform is free to use and openly accessible at https://privbench.com/.

</details>


### [86] [ACTD: Anchor-Based Cross-Tokenizer Distillation with Residual Regularization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29662)
*Huiyi Zhang,Zijian Li,Xiaocheng Feng,Weitao Ma,Xiaoliang Yang,Yichong Huang,Bing Qin*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes ACTD, an anchor-based cross-tokenizer knowledge distillation framework with residual regularization that enables effective reasoning transfer between heterogeneous language models and achieves state-of-the-art results, including in a multi-teacher setting.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Cross-tokenizer knowledge distillation is needed to transfer reasoning abilities from powerful but heavy LLMs to smaller models that use different tokenizers. Existing approaches struggle because token vocabularies and token sequences do not align, and naive or approximate alignment introduces noise that hurts distillation effectiveness. The paper aims to design a principled way to align vocabularies and sequences across model families while avoiding the noise and instability that current alignment strategies cause.

Method: The authors introduce ACTD (Anchor-Based Cross-Tokenizer Distillation with Residual Regularization). First, they construct an alignment between the teacher and student at both the vocabulary and sequence levels to bridge structural heterogeneity across tokenizers. Within this aligned space, they identify “anchors” (reliable alignment points) and define an anchor-based loss that guides the student to match the teacher on these stable regions. To counteract the noise from imperfect alignment, they add residual regularization, which constrains the discrepancy between the teacher and student predictions beyond the anchors, stabilizing training. They also generalize this framework to support multiple teacher models, combining information from different teachers while maintaining robust alignment and regularization across them.

Result: On five reasoning benchmarks and with three distinct teacher models, ACTD achieves state-of-the-art performance among cross-tokenizer distillation methods. The multi-teacher extension further improves over both the strongest single-teacher baseline and existing multi-teacher distillation methods, indicating that the approach scales well with multiple heterogeneous teachers and yields more robust and accurate student models.

Conclusion: ACTD provides an effective solution for cross-tokenizer knowledge distillation by jointly addressing vocabulary and sequence misalignment and mitigating alignment noise through anchor-based loss and residual regularization. The method not only advances the performance of distilled reasoning models but also proves robust and extensible in a multi-teacher setting, making it a strong candidate for practical deployment of compact yet capable models across diverse tokenizer architectures.

Abstract: Knowledge distillation effectively transfers reasoning capabilities from large language models to lightweight student models. To enable knowledge transfer across disparate model families, researchers increasingly explore cross-tokenizer distillation. However, cross-tokenizer distillation remains challenging due to vocabulary and sequence misalignment, while approximate vocabulary alignment can introduce additional noise into distillation. To address these challenges, we propose Anchor-Based Cross-Tokenizer Distillation with Residual Regularization (ACTD). ACTD bridges structural heterogeneity through vocabulary and sequence alignment, while mitigating alignment noise via a novel anchor loss with residual regularization. We further extend this framework to a multi-teacher setting. Evaluated across five reasoning benchmarks with three distinct teacher models, ACTD achieves state-of-the-art performance. Moreover, its multi-teacher extension outperforms the strongest single-teacher and multi-teacher baselines, further demonstrating the robustness of our method.

</details>


### [87] [A Hub of Short Rows Inflates Intrinsic Dimension Estimation of Token Embeddings](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29702)
*Alexandre Quemy*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper shows that a small cluster (“hub”) of short embedding vectors near the origin strongly biases nearest-neighbor intrinsic-dimension estimators in token-embedding spaces, artificially inflating measured dimension.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Intrinsic dimensionality (ID) of token-embedding tables is widely measured to understand model geometry and scaling, but observed IDs that grow with model size may be artifacts. The authors want to test whether the observed ID growth is real or caused by structural peculiarities of embedding spaces, such as hubs near the origin.

Method: They empirically analyze token-embedding tables across eleven language models (GPT-2, K3, GLM-4.7, Pythia variants, etc.), inspect distance patterns, and apply nearest-neighbor ID estimators like TwoNN per token and over vocabularies. They identify a central hub of short-norm vectors, then recompute ID estimates after (a) removing hub rows and (b) normalizing all rows, and compare with prior reported ID scaling (e.g., for Pythia). They also cross-reference hub membership with under-trained-token detectors and training-update statistics.

Result: They find a dense central hub of short-norm rows near the origin in token embeddings. Due to concentration of measure, tokens are closer to this hub than to other tokens, causing nearest neighbors to be hub rows at similar distances and heavily biasing estimators like TwoNN to overestimate ID. Per-token ID is heavy-tailed and vocabulary-level ID grows with model size only when the hub is present. Removing or normalizing the hub collapses the estimated ID into a narrow, low range (around 10–17) for all tested models and removes the heavy tail. In Pythia, the previously reported growth from 27 to 122 with parameter count disappears when the hub is removed, becoming a flat 10–17 instead. The hub rows are short but not untrained; they receive updates during training and are mostly characterized by low norm.

Conclusion: The apparent growth of intrinsic dimension in token-embedding tables with model size is largely an artifact of a small hub of short-norm vectors near the origin, which corrupts nearest-neighbor ID estimators. Accounting for or normalizing this hub reveals a stable, low intrinsic dimension across diverse models, calling into question prior claims of scaling ID and highlighting the need for care when applying nearest-neighbor ID estimators to embedding spaces.

Abstract: A token-embedding table holds a hub of short rows near its origin, and we show that this cluster biases what nearest-neighbor intrinsic-dimension (ID) estimators report. Because of the concentration of measure, a token is closer to the central cluster than to any other token, so its first two neighbors are both hub rows at nearly the same distance. As a result, the ID estimators such as TwoNN return a dimension far above the real ID. Measured one token at a time, dimension is a heavy-tailed distribution. Measured on the full vocabulary, it grows with the model's parameter count. However, when we remove the hub, the heavy tail disappears and the measured dimension collapses to a narrow range for eleven models, from GPT-2 to models such as K3 and GLM-4.7. The hub acts as a switch: a few hundred rows are enough to fully inflate the estimate. We reproduced an experiment stating that the intrinsic dimension (ID) of Pythia's token-embedding table grows with the parameter count, from $27$ to $122$ between 160M and 12B parameters. We show that this result disappears when the hub is removed: the table then reads $10$ to $17$ at every size. The hub contains a subset of the population that under-trained-token detectors flag, but on Pythia the hub that we detected and removed as a whole was updated during training: what seem to characterize these rows is simply their length, not an absence of updates. Finally, we show that normalizing the rows instead of removing them gives the same lower reading.

</details>


### [88] [The Depth Flow of Token Representations Is Nonlinear and Does Not Descend Its Own Density](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29706)
*Alexandre Quemy*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper models how token representations evolve through layers in transformer language models as a stochastic flow, finding that this flow is nonlinear, has significant rotational (non‑gradient) components, and preserves certain angular structure across layers.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To better understand and succinctly characterize how token embeddings transform across layers in large language models, beyond simple linear approximations, by treating the evolution of representations as a dynamical system or flow through representation space.

Method: They view the sequence of layer-wise token representations for the whole vocabulary as a flow and fit a discrete Langevin (stochastic differential equation) model to the corpus-mean trajectories in Pythia-160M and Pythia-410M. They compare linear vs quadratic drift terms as surrogate layer maps and validate them by scoring predicted next-layer representations on held-out tokens. They also use the Kramers–Moyal estimator to nonparametrically estimate drift, decompose the flow into gradient (potential-descending) and rotational components, and analyze how ranks of token properties (norm, angular position, concentration) change across the 13 layers.

Result: A quadratic drift model predicts layer transitions better than a simple linear map at every layer transition for both Pythia-160M and Pythia-410M, confirming substantial nonlinearity in the flow of token representations. The Kramers–Moyal estimator matches the quadratic model where locality assumptions hold. The drift field does not follow the gradient of the representation density (log-density); instead it descends another potential function. The flow contains a sizable rotational component, accounting for 4–45% of the explainable drift, and circulation patterns show that tokens largely preserve their angular rank across layers, while their norm rank is mixed and their “concentration” rank is inverted by the final block.

Conclusion: Layer-wise token dynamics in transformer LMs are better viewed as a nonlinear stochastic flow with both gradient and rotational components rather than as a simple sequence of linear maps or pure gradient descent on representation density. The presence of strong quadratic and rotational structure, along with preserved angular rank and reshuffled norm/concentration ranks, suggests new dynamical-systems-based ways to analyze, approximate, and potentially control representation evolution in language models.

Abstract: A token's representation is carried through the network layer by layer. The whole vocabulary carried together forms a flow. We fit this flow's equation of motion as a discrete Langevin model over corpus-mean trajectories of Pythia-160M and Pythia-410M, and score the predicted steps on held-out tokens. Linear maps are often used as cheap surrogates for a layer. The flow they summarize is not linear: a quadratic drift beats the linear linear map at every transition of both models, and the Kramers--Moyal estimator agrees wherever its neighborhoods stay local.
  We then characterize the flow further. First, we show that it does not descend its own log-density. The drift instead descends a potential that is not the density. Second, the rotational component is not negligible, $4$ to $45\%$ of the explainable drift, and the circulation shows in what the flow preserves: a token keeps its angular rank across all thirteen layers while its norm rank is shuffled and its concentration rank is reversed by the last block.

</details>


### [89] [DVBench: Benchmarking MLLMs for Understanding Dynamic Charts and Narratives in Data Videos](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29711)
*Bomiao Wang,Zekai Shao,Jiexiang Lan,Xiaoliang Fu,Xingchen Zeng,Siming Chen*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: DVBench is a new benchmark to evaluate multimodal large language models (MLLMs) on understanding data videos that combine dynamic charts and narratives.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing MLLM benchmarks focus separately on chart comprehension or video understanding and lack a way to evaluate models on temporally evolving structured visual information like data videos. The authors want to fill this evaluation gap.

Method: The authors construct DVBench, a benchmark of 300 real-world data videos and 1,000 human-verified question–answer pairs. They define data video understanding along five dimensions and curate the dataset via a semi-automated pipeline. They then evaluate nine MLLMs, including both proprietary and open-source models, and conduct fine-grained analyses and ablation studies on factors such as frame configurations and subtitle usage.

Result: Gemini-3.1-Pro achieves the best overall performance on DVBench, and among open-source models, Kimi-k2.5 performs best. Results show that open-source model performance does not monotonically improve with parameter size and that strong narrative understanding does not imply strong visual understanding. Dimension-wise analyses expose specific weaknesses of models and quantify the impact of different input configurations.

Conclusion: DVBench provides a focused benchmark for assessing MLLMs on data video understanding across multiple dimensions. The benchmark and analyses highlight current limitations of both proprietary and open-source MLLMs and offer guidance for designing models better suited for temporally evolving structured visual content. DVBench is publicly released for the community to drive further progress.

Abstract: While MLLMs have made significant strides in chart comprehension and video understanding, current evaluations largely isolate these capabilities, leaving a critical gap in understanding temporally evolving structured visual information. To address this gap, we introduce DVBench, a benchmark for evaluating MLLMs on data videos, a storytelling medium that integrates dynamic charts with structured narratives. We decompose data video understanding into five dimensions. DVBench comprises 300 real-world data videos and 1,000 human-verified QA pairs curated through a rigorous semi-automated pipeline. Extensive evaluations of nine MLLMs show that Gemini-3.1-Pro achieves the best overall performance, while Kimi-k2.5 is the strongest open-source model. We further identify two notable phenomena: open-source model performance does not scale strictly with parameter size, and narrative proficiency does not guarantee visual capability. Fine-grained analyses and ablation studies further reveal dimension-specific weaknesses and the effects of frame configurations and subtitle inputs, informing future MLLM development. DVBench is publicly available at https://bomiaowang.github.io/DVBench/.

</details>


### [90] [Evaluating the Capabilities of LLMs for Persuasive Dialogue](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29738)
*Jordan Robinson,Angus R. Williams,Katie Atkinson,Anthony G. Cohn*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces Persuasio, a dialogue platform based on formal argumentation theory, to compare how persuasive humans and LLMs are in debates. It finds that LLMs sound more persuasive to people but are worse than humans by formal logical standards, exposing a gap between rhetorical fluency and true argumentative strength.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs can produce fluent, convincing text, and many works evaluate their persuasiveness using subjective human judgments. However, it is unclear whether being subjectively persuasive actually corresponds to constructing logically strong, well-founded arguments. This creates a need for a principled framework to measure the quality of arguments and outcomes of debates beyond surface-level impressions, especially in sensitive domains like political discourse.

Method: The authors build Persuasio, a multi-agent dialogue platform grounded in a formal argumentation-based theory of persuasion dialogues that can adjudicate the winner of free-text debates based on logical criteria. They run 192 debates on a UK political topic between humans and various LLM-based interlocutors (single, multi-agent, and retrieval-augmented). They evaluate 22 different interlocutors using two lenses: (1) formal, automated adjudication derived from argumentation theory, and (2) 9,702 crowdsourced pairwise judgments across 1,386 annotated debate instances to capture subjective persuasiveness rankings.

Result: LLMs consistently rank higher than humans in subjective crowdsourced judgments of who is more persuasive. However, when debates are evaluated with the formal argumentation-theoretic adjudicator, LLMs perform substantially worse than humans, who remain competitive or superior. Multi-agent setups and retrieval-augmented LLM variants further increase the discrepancy: they sound even more persuasive to people but do not improve and may worsen their logical argumentative standing. This shows a systematic divergence between perceived persuasiveness and formally measured argumentative strength in LLM debates.

Conclusion: The study concludes that current LLMs excel at rhetorical fluency and can easily appear highly persuasive to human judges, but they do not reliably produce logically strong arguments when evaluated under formal argumentation criteria. Therefore, subjective persuasiveness metrics alone are insufficient and potentially misleading for assessing LLMs in deliberative or political contexts. The authors argue for integrating argumentation-theoretic tools like Persuasio into evaluation pipelines and caution against over-relying on crowd judgments when deploying LLMs in real-world decision-making or persuasive applications.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can generate apparently highly persuasive text, but does sounding persuasive mean arguing well? We introduce \textsc{Persuasio}, a multi-agent dialogue platform grounded in a formal argumentation-based theory of persuasion dialogues that adjudicates logical winners during free-text debates. Using this system, we generated 192 debates on a UK political topic between humans and LLMs, and evaluated 22 interlocutors through both automated adjudication and 9,702 crowdsourced pairwise judgements across 1{,}386 annotation instances. We observed a consistent decoupling between subjective and formal persuasiveness: LLMs dominated the subjective ranking yet performed substantially worse under argumentation-theoretic adjudication, where humans remained competitive. Multi-agent and retrieval-augmented variants further widened this divergence. These findings reveal a systematic gap between rhetorical fluency and formal argumentative strength in LLM-based persuasive dialogues.

</details>


### [91] [ReTrace: Rejected-Trajectory Conditioning for Speculative Decoding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29748)
*Luxi Lin,Zhanpeng Zeng,Shuang Peng,Songwei Liu,Rongrong Ji*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: ReTrace improves speculative decoding by reusing and refining rejected suffix information between rounds to speed up decoding without extra passes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In speculative decoding, once any token in a drafted block is rejected by the target model, the remaining suffix is discarded. This wastes computation and ignores the fact that parts of the rejected suffix may still be semantically or structurally aligned with the target model’s true continuation. The paper aims to exploit this overlooked information to increase token acceptance length and decoding speed while preserving lossless correctness and keeping inference cost low.

Method: The authors analyze DFlash and observe that tokens in rejected suffixes often still match the target continuation. Inspired by conditional diffusion, they propose ReTrace, a rejected-trajectory conditioning mechanism. Instead of regenerating future draft blocks purely from masked placeholders, ReTrace conditions each new draft block on the previous round’s rejected suffix. It preserves hidden states of the rejected suffix, aligns them with the next draft block, and refines them using target-aware correction signals computed during the same verification pass. These refined representations are fused into the drafter’s input embeddings through a gated residual connection, enabling the draft model to leverage information from prior rejected attempts without extra target model forwards or changes to the verification rule.

Result: On Qwen3-based setups evaluated on mathematical reasoning, code generation, and open-ended dialogue tasks, ReTrace yields higher average acceptance length per speculative step and faster end-to-end decoding compared to its DFlash baseline. The improvements are consistent across tasks, showing better throughput without harming model output quality or requiring additional inference passes from the target model.

Conclusion: ReTrace shows that rejected suffixes in speculative decoding contain reusable structural and semantic information that can be harnessed through cross-round conditioning. By conditioning new draft proposals on refined representations of previous rejected trajectories—while leaving within-round drafting and target-side verification unchanged—ReTrace preserves the lossless property of speculative decoding and provides speedups. Its design is largely orthogonal to other drafting optimizations, suggesting it can be combined with them for cumulative gains in decoding efficiency.

Abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates autoregressive language model inference by having a lightweight draft model propose multiple candidate tokens, which are then verified in parallel by a larger target model. However, after the first rejection, standard prefix-based verification discards the remaining draft suffix, so the computation spent generating and verifying those positions does not contribute to decoding progress. Focusing on DFlash, we show that rejected positions in a rejected suffix may still align with the target continuation, indicating that the draft model can retain useful semantic and structural information despite local token-level errors. Motivated by this observation and inspired by conditional diffusion, we introduce~\textbf{ReTrace}, a rejected-trajectory conditioning method that conditions each draft block on the rejected suffix from the previous round rather than generating it from fresh mask placeholders alone. ReTrace retains the hidden representations of the rejected suffixes, aligns them with the next draft block, refines them using target-aware correction signals from the same verification pass, and admits them into the drafter's input embeddings through gated residual fusion. Because rejected tokens are never committed and target-side verification remains unchanged, ReTrace preserves the lossless property of speculative decoding without requiring an additional model forward pass. Experiments with Qwen3 models across mathematical reasoning, code generation, and open-ended dialogue demonstrate that ReTrace consistently improves average acceptance length and end-to-end decoding speed over its DFlash backbone. By introducing cross-round conditioning without modifying within-round proposal generation, ReTrace is largely orthogonal to existing drafting improvements and might be combined with them for further gains.

</details>


### [92] [HiVe: Beyond Static Prompts for Multitask Learning via Hierarchy-based Vertical Mixture-of-Experts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29790)
*HyeonJik Bae,Minyeol Kim,Susik Yoon*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: HiVe is a prompt-tuning framework that builds a hierarchy of prompts and dynamically selects specialized prompts per input, outperforming prior prompt tuning methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods like prompt tuning often rely on flat or rigid hierarchical prompt structures, which prevents flexible, input-dependent specialization of prompts and underuses relationships between tasks.

Method: The authors introduce HiVe, which (1) learns a hierarchy of prompts by exploiting inter-task relationships during training, and (2) uses a vertical mixture-of-experts (V-MoE) at inference time to select and compose prompts from different levels of the hierarchy, allowing the model to adapt the degree of specialization to each input instance.

Result: Across a range of tasks, HiVe consistently achieves better performance than strong prompt-tuning baselines, demonstrating the benefit of hierarchical, input-dependent prompt specialization.

Conclusion: Modeling prompts hierarchically and enabling input-dependent prompt composition via a V-MoE leads to more effective parameter-efficient fine-tuning than traditional flat or fixed-structure prompt tuning approaches.

Abstract: As large language models (LLMs) continue to scale, parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) has become a practical alternative to full-parameter adaptation. Prompt tuning is effective, but existing approaches either use flat prompt structures or hierarchical structures with fixed prompt composition, limiting adaptive prompt specialization. To address this limitation, we propose HiVe, a prompt tuning framework that models prompts at multiple levels and enables input-dependent specialization. HiVe constructs a prompt hierarchy by leveraging inter-task relationships during training, and employs a vertical mixture-of-experts (V-MoE) mechanism at inference time to compose prompts up to the level of specialization required for each input. Experiments show that HiVe consistently outperforms strong prompt tuning baselines across diverse tasks.

</details>


### [93] [R$^2$A: Learning Persona Policies Through Persona Representation Learning and Runtime Alignment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29798)
*Mohan Zhang,Chengsong You,Xiaoyu Cao,Zhen Sun,Xiaohan Jia,Junwei Zhou,Yongchao Chen*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes a new framework and method (R^2A) to learn context-aware persona policies for AI systems, separating how a persona is selected from how it is realized in behavior, and shows it outperforms static persona prompts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Static persona prompts can make AI behavior inconsistent: the same persona traits can be helpful in one task and harmful in another. There is no clear way to reason about or fix these inconsistencies across different tasks and contexts. The authors want a principled framework and training procedure that produces persona behaviors that are both effective on tasks and aligned with high-level persona principles.

Method: They formulate behavior generation as arising from a latent Persona state and decompose it into two components: Persona Selection (which behaviors to activate in context) and Persona Realization (how those behaviors unfold in trajectories). They define Selection Gap and Realization Gap as mismatches between static persona elicitation and an ideal persona policy in each component. Based on this, they introduce R^2A, a two-stage method: (1) Persona Representation Learning, which encodes the persona via structured Who–How–What descriptions (persona objectives, conditional behavior principles, and trajectory-level examples); (2) Persona Runtime Alignment, which removes explicit persona prompts and uses task feedback to jointly adapt selection and realization so the model behaves according to the target persona while performing well on tasks.

Result: In 12 evaluation settings covering four principles of an Accountable-Professional Persona, R^2A yields better performance than both the base model without persona prompting and standard static persona elicitation. Ablation studies show that removing Persona Representation Learning harms stability and leads to behaviorally imbalanced policies during Runtime Alignment, indicating that the representation stage is essential for robust persona policy learning.

Conclusion: Modeling persona as a latent state with separate selection and realization components explains why static persona prompts can fail and provides leverage points to improve them. The R^2A two-stage approach, combining structured persona representation with feedback-based runtime alignment, produces more consistent, balanced, and effective persona-conditioned behavior than conventional methods, and the representation stage is crucial for stable learning of persona policies.

Abstract: The same Persona behavior can be beneficial in one context but harmful in another, causing static Persona elicitation to perform inconsistently across tasks. We introduce the Persona Selection--Realization Framework, which models behavior generation through a latent Persona state and decomposes it into Persona Selection and Persona Realization. The discrepancies between static Persona elicitation and an ideal Persona policy in these two components define the Selection Gap and Realization Gap, respectively. Building on this framework, we propose R$^2$A, a two-stage approach for learning Persona policies. Persona Representation Learning uses structured Who--How--What presentations to encode the target Persona's objective, conditional behavioral principles, and trajectory-level manifestations. Persona Runtime Alignment then removes the explicit Persona specification and jointly calibrates behavior selection and trajectory realization using task feedback. Across 12 evaluation settings covering the four principles of the Accountable-Professional Persona studied in this work, R$^2$A overall outperforms both the base model and static Persona elicitation. Ablation results further show that Persona Representation Learning is critical for preventing Runtime Alignment from producing behaviorally imbalanced policies and for achieving more stable Persona policy learning.

</details>


### [94] [A^2Agent: Action-Aware Reinforcement Learning for Repository-Level Code Localization Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29831)
*Doyeon Kim,Suyoung Bae,Yumin Lee,Jee-Hyong Lee*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes an action-aware reinforcement learning method to better localize issue-relevant code regions, using per-turn rewards and action-level credit assignment, achieving notable F1 gains over SOTA on SWE-Bench benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing automated software engineering methods for localizing issue-relevant code rely on sparse trajectory-level rewards, making it hard to know which individual actions were useful. As a result, agents may briefly discover the correct code regions during exploration but fail to commit to them, limiting performance.

Method: The authors introduce an action-aware reinforcement learning framework with two main components: (1) a per-turn reward sequence that explicitly rewards both discovering and then committing to gold (ground-truth) code regions, providing denser feedback; and (2) an action-level advantage estimation scheme that assigns credit to specific actions by grouping turns that share the same exploration context, thus isolating each action’s contribution to success. This is applied to code localization for software issues.

Result: On SWE-Bench Verified, the proposed method improves average F1 by 1.58% over the previous SOTA. On the more challenging SWE-Bench Pro, it yields an 8.55% F1 improvement. Their 4B-parameter model surpasses baseline systems that are up to 8 times larger, demonstrating both effectiveness and efficiency.

Conclusion: Action-aware reinforcement learning with per-turn rewards and context-aware action-level credit assignment helps agents both find and reliably commit to the correct issue-relevant code regions. This yields significant performance improvements over SOTA on SWE-Bench benchmarks while using a relatively small model, indicating a promising direction for more efficient automated software engineering agents.

Abstract: Localizing issue-relevant code regions is a critical step in automated software engineering. However, due to their reliance on sparse trajectory-level signals, existing methods cannot identify which per-turn actions are effective and often discover correct code regions during exploration but fail to commit them. To address these limitations, we propose an action-aware reinforcement learning method that combines a per-turn reward sequence rewarding both the discovery and commitment of gold code regions with an action-level advantage estimation scheme that isolates each action's credit by grouping turns sharing the same exploration context. Extensive evaluations show that our method improves the average F1 over the state-of-the-art (SOTA) by 1.58% on SWE-Bench Verified and 8.55% on SWE-Bench Pro, with our 4B model outperforming baselines up to 8x larger. Our code is available at https://github.com/donian00/A2Agent.

</details>


### [95] [You Know What I Mean: A Benchmark for Agentic Conversational Reference Grounding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29834)
*Karen Fuchs,Uri Katz,Yoav Goldberg*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces Conversational Reference Grounding (CoRG), the task of resolving indirect references in conversation to specific external items using tools, and studies it via RepoRef, a benchmark of multi-step, tool-based grounding tasks over GitHub artifacts, showing current agents still struggle.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In real collaborative work (e.g., software development chats), people often refer indirectly to artifacts like issues, pull requests, or commits (e.g., “the fix we discussed yesterday”), not by explicit IDs or URLs. Existing retrieval or grounding tasks typically assume direct mentions, single queries, or simple context windows, and don’t capture the multi-step, tool-using behavior needed to connect such conversational references to concrete external objects. There is a need to formalize and benchmark this more realistic grounding problem to understand and improve tool-using conversational agents.

Method: The authors formalize Conversational Reference Grounding (CoRG) as the task of using a set of external tools (APIs, UIs) to map a conversational reference to a unique intended external item. They construct RepoRef, a benchmark of 400 real developer chat segments linked to GitHub issues, pull requests, and commits across 92 repositories. Each instance requires using multiple cues—lexical, semantic, and temporal—from dialog plus repository state. They design scenarios where resolving the reference often needs multi-step tool use (search, inspect metadata/content, compare candidates). They then evaluate contemporary agents on RepoRef, measuring success at correctly identifying the intended target.

Result: On the RepoRef benchmark, agents demonstrate significant difficulty with CoRG. Even the strongest evaluated agent achieves only a 67.0% success rate in resolving references to the correct GitHub artifact, leaving about one third of examples unresolved or incorrectly grounded. The experiments highlight specific failure modes around multi-step reasoning, effective tool sequencing, and disambiguating close candidate items.

Conclusion: CoRG is a distinct and challenging problem that goes beyond simple retrieval or single-query grounding, requiring agents to coordinate conversational understanding with strategic, iterative tool use. RepoRef provides a concrete, realistic benchmark for studying how agents search, inspect, and verify information in multi-tool developer environments. The performance gap on RepoRef indicates substantial headroom for research on better planning, reasoning over heterogeneous signals, and robust multi-step tool use in conversational agents.

Abstract: Collaborative conversations frequently contain references whose targets are indirect rather than named: resolving "this looks like the fix discussed yesterday" requires combining conversational context with evidence from the surrounding workspace which is accessible through APIs or user interfaces. We formalize this problem as Conversational Reference Grounding (CoRG): using a given set of tools to resolve a reference in conversation to the unique external item intended by the speaker. CoRG is challenging because it combines lexical, semantic, and temporal cues distributed across the conversation and the external workspace. Agents must translate these heterogeneous signals into effective tool use: formulating strategies, discovering plausible candidates, inspecting their metadata and content, and ruling out close alternatives. We study CoRG through RepoRef, a benchmark of 400 developer-chat segments grounded in GitHub issues, pull requests, and commits across 92 repositories. Unlike single-shot retrieval tasks, RepoRef often requires multi-step tool use. Our results show that CoRG remains challenging for current agents, even the best agent reaches only 67.0% success rate, leaving one third of references unresolved. These findings position CoRG as a concrete benchmark for studying how agents search, inspect, and verify information in realistic multi-tool environments.

</details>


### [96] [EVAR: Evidence-Validated Hypothesis Admission for Budget-Aware Narrative Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29835)
*Peilin Liu,Zhiquan Ji,Jinglong Ping*
