Motivation: Despite NER being well studied for English, it remains largely unsolved for many Indic languages, leaving a major gap in the digital processing of these languages. With the rise of generative LLMs, it is unclear whether such models can replace or match classic encoder-based architectures for NER in low-resource, multilingual Indic settings. The paper aims to systematically clarify this by benchmarking both paradigms across many Indic languages.

Method: The authors perform a rigorous comparative study using the Naamapadam benchmark covering 11 Indic languages. They evaluate: (1) five encoder or sequence-to-sequence transformer model families, including multilingual encoders (mBERT, XLM-R); (2) four decoder-only LLMs fine-tuned with LoRA and 4-bit NF4 quantisation; and (3) nine generative models used in zero- to 5-shot inference setups. Performance is measured with strict CoNLL span-level F1 scores, and languages are analysed and grouped by outcome patterns.

Result: Encoder-based models such as mBERT and XLM-R achieve strong performance (e.g., F1=0.675 on Hindi) and consistently outperform all evaluated generative architectures in 10 of 11 languages. The strongest generative competitor (Gemma-2-2B) has an average F1 of 0.427, lagging 7.5–40 F1 points behind encoders depending on language. Few-shot generative setups reach at best about 28% of the encoder baseline, showing a large performance gap. The authors also identify three language clusters based on performance patterns: encoder-dominant, partial-coverage, and failure-zone.

Conclusion: In current form, generative LLMs—even when fine-tuned or used with few-shot prompting—are not competitive with encoder-based multilingual models for Indic NER. For practical deployments in Indic languages, encoder-based architectures like mBERT and XLM-R remain the preferred choice. The clustering analysis and guidelines suggest using transfer learning and low-resource NLP strategies tailored to language-specific characteristics, rather than relying on general-purpose generative models for NER in these settings.

Abstract: Language is humanity's most consequential technology, yet for over a billion speakers across India's twenty-two constitutionally recognised languages, its digital layer remains structurally incomplete. Named Entity Recognition (NER), the foundational step in transforming raw text into machine-interpretable knowledge, has been studied exhaustively for English but remains largely unsolved across most Indic languages. This paper presents a rigorous comparative study of generative and encoder-based neural architectures for NER on all eleven languages of the Naamapadam benchmark. We evaluate five classic model families spanning sequence-to-sequence transformers and multilingual encoders; four decoder-only large language models (LLMs) fine-tuned with LoRA and 4-bit NF4 quantisation; and nine generative models in zero-to-5-shot inference. Under strict CoNLL span-level evaluation, encoder-based models (mBERT and XLM-R, both F1=0.675 on Hindi) substantially outperform every generative architecture in ten of eleven languages, with gaps of 7.5-40 percentage points against the strongest competitor (Gemma-2-2B: avg F1=0.427). The best few-shot result reaches only 28% of the encoder baseline. We identify three language clusters--encoder-dominant, partial-coverage, and failure-zone; and provide actionable deployment guidelines grounded in transfer learning and low-resource NLP principles.

</details>


### [117] [DataFoundry: Evolving Data Preparators via Recursive Self-Improvement](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29966)
*Cehao Yang,Xiaojun Wu,Xueyuan Lin,Chengjin Xu,Xuhui Jiang,Hui Xiong,Jian Guo*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper presents DataFoundry, a framework that recursively improves data-preparation pipelines themselves—before large-scale data generation—to yield higher-quality domain adaptation data for LLMs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current domain adaptation for LLMs hinges on synthetic or curated training data whose quality strongly affects downstream performance. Existing pipelines mostly generate large datasets first and only then apply post-hoc filtering or quality checks, which cannot fix many issues that arise from the design of the data-preparation process itself (e.g., flawed prompts, weak decomposition, missing skills). There is a need for a principled way to optimize the data-preparation pipeline as a first-class object so that the generator of data becomes better over iterations, rather than just filtering its outputs.

Method: The authors propose DataFoundry, which treats a "data preparator" (the system that generates and processes training data) as an evolvable runtime specification. They implement this with a Skills-as-Modules architecture: a central Controller composes modular skills into executable runtimes for data preparation; it runs them on small pilot datasets, evaluates their outputs with domain-specific criteria, and diagnoses failure modes. Based on diagnostics, the system automatically creates adapters that modify individual preparation modules while keeping their interfaces stable, effectively evolving the pipeline. This recursive loop—compile runtime → run on pilots → diagnose → adapt—iteratively improves the data preparator before it is used for large-scale data creation.

Result: On the DataPrep-Bench benchmark spanning mathematics, finance, law, and medicine, evolved DataFoundry preparators generate training data that leads to better downstream performance than baseline data-preparation approaches. The gains hold across different model backbones, indicating that the improvements are not specific to a single LLM architecture. Additional analyses and case studies provide insight into the optimization dynamics, showing concrete examples of how modules are revised and how the preparator evolves over iterations.

Conclusion: DataFoundry demonstrates that treating data-preparation pipelines as objects that can recursively self-improve leads to higher-utility training data for domain adaptation. By modularizing preparation skills and closing the loop with diagnostic feedback on small pilots, the framework systematically refines the pipeline itself, outperforming traditional post-hoc filtering approaches and generalizing across domains and backbone models.

Abstract: Domain adaptation of large language models increasingly depends on constructing high-quality training data, yet existing data-preparation pipelines typically address quality only after generation through post-hoc filtering. This creates a fundamental mismatch: data-quality issues often originate from the construction process itself, while quality control is applied only to its outputs. We introduce \textsc{DataFoundry}, a framework for \textbf{evolving data preparators through recursive self-improvement} before large-scale data production. \textsc{DataFoundry} represents a data preparator as an evolvable runtime specification and instantiates its evolution with a \textsc{Skills-as-Modules} architecture, in which a central \textsc{Controller} orchestrates modular skills to compile executable runtimes, diagnose deficiencies on small pilot sets using domain-appropriate criteria, and translate diagnostic feedback into adapters that revise individual preparation components while preserving stable interfaces. We evaluate \textsc{DataFoundry} on DataPrep-Bench across mathematics, finance, law, and medicine, and find that recursively evolved preparators produce training data with higher downstream utility than baselines. Experiments across different backbones further demonstrate that these improvements are not tied to a particular model, while analyses and case studies further reveal the framework's optimization dynamics and illustrate how its evolution unfolds in practice.

</details>


### [118] [Evolutionary Soups: Evolving Mixture-of-Experts for Multi-Objective LLM Alignment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29978)
*Lingxiao Kong,Steffen Staab,Cong Yang,Oya Beyan,Zeyd Boukhers*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces Evolutionary Soups, a mixture-of-experts framework with evolutionary-trained gating networks to dynamically control trade-offs among multiple objectives in large language model generation at inference time, achieving better Pareto-front coverage and utility metrics than baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Large language models must often balance conflicting objectives (e.g., helpfulness vs. safety vs. style), and the best trade-off depends on both user preferences and the specific input. Existing methods typically require retraining or are limited in how finely they can control generation. There is a need for an inference-time, fine-grained, controllable method that can flexibly adjust the model’s behavior to different preference trade-offs while effectively exploring complex, non-convex Pareto fronts.

Method: The authors propose Evolutionary Soups, a mixture-of-experts (MoE) architecture equipped with per-layer gating networks. These gating networks take hidden-state representations as input and output coefficients to merge experts dynamically at each layer. Instead of standard gradient-based training of the gates, they use an evolutionary algorithm that optimizes these gating networks with a greedy hypervolume contribution objective, encouraging solutions that improve Pareto-front coverage and performance across multiple objectives under large, noisy training data.

Result: Across three different tasks involving multi-objective language generation, Evolutionary Soups outperforms baseline controllable-generation methods. It achieves higher hypervolume (indicating better and broader Pareto-front coverage) and improved scalarized utilities, including linear and Tchebyshev utility functions, with reported gains around 20% over competing methods on all evaluated tasks.

Conclusion: Evolutionary Soups enables fine-grained, inference-time control of multi-objective behavior in large language models without retraining, by using evolutionary-optimized per-layer gating in a mixture-of-experts setup. This approach yields more effective and diverse Pareto-optimal trade-offs and superior utility metrics compared to existing controllable generation techniques, demonstrating its promise as a general framework for dynamic multi-objective control in LLMs.

Abstract: Large language models are increasingly required to generate responses that satisfy multiple competing objectives. Since optimal trade-offs depend on both user preferences and input prompts, controllable multi-objective generation must dynamically adapt models at inference time without retraining. To address this, we propose Evolutionary Soups, a mixture-of-experts framework for fine-grained generation control, with gating networks trained via an evolutionary algorithm. The per-layer gating networks dynamically produce expert-merging coefficients from hidden-state representations, while the evolutionary algorithm incorporates greedy hypervolume contribution for effective evolution of these gating networks, achieving consistent improvements on large and noisy training datasets and broader coverage of the non-convex Pareto front. Experiments across three tasks demonstrate the effectiveness of Evolutionary Soups over baselines: it achieves the best hypervolume, linear utility, and Tchebyshev utility (~20% improvement) among controllable methods on all tasks.

</details>


### [119] [Beyond Fluency: A Rubric-Based Benchmark for Evaluating Saudi Dialect and Cultural Competence in Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29990)
*Ghassan Al-Sumaidaee,Sajjad Abdoli,Ahmed Rashad,Maxim Legg*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces a rubric-based benchmark that evaluates large language models’ competence in Saudi Arabic dialect, revealing that current state-of-the-art models perform poorly and often fail by mismanaging pragmatic nuance rather than hallucinating facts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing Arabic LLM benchmarks focus on Modern Standard Arabic and ignore dialectal and culturally grounded language use, despite dialects being central to everyday communication and social meaning. This creates a significant blind spot in assessing real-world performance of models in Arabic-speaking contexts, especially for the Saudi dialect.

Method: The authors design a benchmark of 31 expert-authored prompts covering idiomatic, pragmatic, lexical, and culturally embedded Saudi dialect phenomena. For each prompt, experts provide a ground-truth response and derive atomic, mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive (MECE) positive evaluation criteria in a model-agnostic phase. In a subsequent model-specific phase, four state-of-the-art LLMs (Claude Opus 5, Gemini 3.7, GPT-5.6, and Kimi K3) are evaluated against these criteria and penalized for additional errors, with all errors categorized into a nine-type taxonomy.

Result: From 124 model-prompt evaluations, the authors identify 466 error instances, with macro-average scores for the four models ranging from 42.7% to 53.1%, and no model surpassing 55%. Every model produces at least one negatively scored prompt. Ambiguous Framing emerges as the most common error type (37.3%), whereas Hallucination constitutes only 11.2% of errors. Distinct error profiles and a consistency-versus-ceiling trade-off are also observed across models.

Conclusion: Saudi dialectal competence remains an open problem for leading LLMs, which more often mishandle register and pragmatic nuance than invent false facts. The proposed rubric-based, model-agnostic evaluation framework, along with the released prompts, ground truths, and rubrics, offers a reproducible and fine-grained approach to assessing dialectal language ability and can guide future development and diagnosis of Arabic LLMs.

Abstract: Large language models are increasingly deployed in Arabic-speaking markets, yet standard benchmarks overwhelmingly reward Modern Standard Arabic (MSA) fluency while leaving dialectal and culturally grounded competence unmeasured. This gap is consequential: everyday Arabic is largely dialectal, and dialect encodes social meaning that MSA-centric evaluation cannot capture. We present a rubric-based benchmark for the Saudi dialect, comprising 31 expert-authored prompts spanning idiomatic, pragmatic, lexical, and culturally-embedded phenomena, each paired with an expert-established ground truth. Our methodology separates evaluation into a model-agnostic phase, in which atomic, MECE positive criteria are derived solely from the ground truth, and a model-specific phase, in which four state-of-the-art systems -- Claude Opus 5, Gemini 3.7, GPT-5.6, and Kimi K3 -- are scored against those criteria and penalised for errors they actively introduce. Across 124 model-prompt evaluations we catalogue 466 error instances under a nine-category taxonomy. The four systems cluster within a narrow macro-average band (42.7%-53.1%), with no model exceeding 55% and every model recording at least one negative-scoring prompt, confirming that Saudi dialectal competence remains broadly unsolved. Notably, Ambiguous Framing is the dominant failure mode (37.3% of errors) while outright Hallucination accounts for only 11.2%, indicating that models fail less by stating falsehoods than by distorting register and flattening pragmatic nuance. We further observe a consistency-versus-ceiling trade-off and model-distinctive error signatures. We release the full prompt set, ground truths, and scored rubrics to support reproducible dialectal evaluation.

</details>


### [120] [Generating Clinical Vignettes that Preserve Cognitive Formulations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29995)
*Amit Oren,Nimrod Hertz-Palmor,Dean Ariel,Guy Laban*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper presents FORMA, a framework that uses cognitive models of mental disorders to generate and validate structured, clinically faithful synthetic case vignettes, showing major improvements over zero-shot LLM generation in fidelity, expert ratings, and perceived human-likeness.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While large language models can create fluent clinical case vignettes, their outputs often lack fidelity to well-specified clinical structures and causal relations. This limits their usefulness for research, training, and evaluation, and raises concerns about hidden biases and unverifiable reasoning. The authors aim to create a method that embeds explicit, theory-based clinical formulations into text generation, enabling both high-quality synthetic data and auditable guarantees about what is represented in the text.

Method: The authors propose FORMA, a framework that: (1) compiles a cognitive model of a disorder into a directed, weighted “cognitive graph” encoding symptoms, mechanisms, and causal relations; (2) samples person-specific configurations on this graph to represent individual patients; (3) uses LLMs to generate vignettes conditioned on these configurations; and (4) validates whether the generated text preserves the specified components and causal links. They instantiate FORMA on PTSD using the Ehlers & Clark cognitive model, generating 16,500 vignettes across 500 personas, 11 LLM configurations, and three ablation conditions (including zero-shot). Evaluation uses an edge-recovery probe to see if the original graph can be reconstructed from text, two independent clinical experts’ ratings, a scaled LLM-as-judge, and a clinician user study with 100 licensed practitioners.

Result: From full-condition FORMA vignettes, the underlying cognitive graph is recoverable at moderate accuracy (MCC = 0.41, AUC = 0.70), whereas from zero-shot vignettes it is essentially unrecoverable (MCC = 0.01, AUC = 0.50, i.e., chance). Clinical experts rate FORMA-generated full-condition vignettes much higher in quality than zero-shot baselines. In the clinician user study, practitioners classify full-condition vignettes as human-written 85% of the time versus 22% for zero-shot texts. Moreover, FORMA reduces demographic disparities in perceived vignette quality by a factor of 1.5 to 7 compared with baselines.

Conclusion: Encoding clinical cognitive formulations as explicit graphs and conditioning LLM generation on these structures enables scalable creation of synthetic clinical vignettes that are both high-quality and auditable. FORMA improves fidelity to theory-based causal structure, enhances expert and clinician evaluations, and mitigates some demographic quality disparities relative to standard zero-shot generation. This suggests that cognitive-model-based specifications are a promising foundation for reliable synthetic clinical text generation, with open-source resources provided for further research and application.

Abstract: Large language models can generate fluent clinical case vignettes, but fluency alone does not ensure fidelity to a specifiable clinical structure. We introduce FORMA, a theory-grounded framework that compiles a cognitive model of a disorder into a directed weighted graph, samples a person-specific configuration of that graph, and validates whether the generated vignette preserves the specified components and causal links. We instantiate FORMA on Posttraumatic Stress Disorder using the Ehlers and Clark cognitive model, generating 16,500 vignettes across 500 personas, 11 generation models, and three ablation conditions. Evaluation combines an external edge-recovery probe, two clinical experts, a scaled LLM judge, and a clinician user study with 100 licensed practitioners. The cognitive graph is recoverable from full-condition vignettes (MCC = +0.41, AUC = 0.70) but not from zero-shot generation (MCC = +0.01, AUC = 0.50). Experts rate full vignettes substantially higher than zero-shot alternatives, and clinicians perceive them to be human-written 85% of the time, compared with 22% for zero-shot. FORMA also reduces demographic disparity in perceived quality by 1.5-7x. These results show that cognitive formulation can serve as an auditable specification for scalable synthetic clinical text generation. A repository with the data and code is available online: https://github.com/Amit-Oren/FORMA.

</details>


### [121] [Small Language Models as Judges for Rubric-Based Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30005)
*Fengyu Xie,Yilun Zhao,Bingsen Chen,Arman Cohan,Chen Zhao*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper investigates whether small language models can reliably act as rubric-based judges for reinforcement learning, offering a cheaper alternative to large LLM judges, and finds that probe-based small models perform surprisingly well.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Rubric-based reinforcement learning needs instance-specific scoring of model responses, which is typically done with large, expensive LLM judges or proprietary APIs. This high cost and latency limit practical training. The authors want to know if much smaller models can act as effective, low-cost rubric judges without sacrificing reliability, and to make this measurable they need datasets and methods tailored to criterion-level rubric evaluation.

Method: The authors construct two datasets, PointRubric and RaR-Science-Static, each containing instance-specific rubrics and item-level satisfaction labels. They evaluate three ways small models can perform criterion-level rubric judgments: (1) Generative verdicts where the model generates an explicit judgment, (2) Yes/No log-probability margins where binary satisfaction is inferred from logprobs, and (3) Probe judges where a separate probe is trained on model internal representations to predict criterion satisfaction. They run systematic comparisons of these methods across small models, especially Qwen3-1.7B, and measure agreement with ground truth labels. They then use the best-performing small-model judge as a reward model in GRPO RL training and run task/domain transfer experiments to test robustness of the learned reward structure.

Result: Across both PointRubric and RaR-Science-Static, the Probe judge based on Qwen3-1.7B achieves the highest agreement with the rubric labels, outperforming generative and logprob-based judging approaches at the criterion level. When used as a GRPO reward model on RaR-Science, this small probe judge improves a policy’s rubric score from 0.232 to 0.643, which is better than the 0.594 achieved using an 8B generative judge, while also being approximately 10.7 times faster in reward-judge compute time. Additional experiments indicate that probe judges better preserve fine-grained reward structure when transferred across tasks and domains.

Conclusion: Small language models, when equipped with probe-based judgment mechanisms, can act as efficient and reliable rubric-based reward models for reinforcement learning. They can match or exceed the performance of much larger generative judges while substantially reducing computation time and cost, and they appear to maintain consistent criterion-level reward structure across different tasks and domains. This suggests that lightweight probe judges are a practical and scalable alternative for rubric-based RL setups.

Abstract: Rubric-based reinforcement learning extends RL beyond tasks with exact answers or rule-based verifiers by scoring responses against instance-specific criteria. However, this makes reward computation expensive: training requires repeated rubric judging, often with proprietary APIs or local generative LLM judges with 7B parameters or more. We study whether smaller language models can serve as efficient and reliable rubric-based judges. To make this question measurable, we construct PointRubric and RaR-Science-Static, two pointwise rubric-based evaluation datasets with instance-specific criteria and itemwise satisfaction labels. We compare three ways of extracting criterion-level judgments from small models: Generative verdicts, Yes/No Logprob margins, and Probe judges. Across both datasets, the Qwen3-1.7B Probe judge achieves the strongest criterion-level agreement among these methods, outperforming Generative and Logprob judges. Used as a GRPO reward model, it trains a policy from 0.232 to 0.643 on RaR-Science rubric score, compared with 0.594 for an 8B Generative judge baseline, while the baseline requires 10.7$\times$ more reward-judge time. Task and domain transfer experiments further suggest that Probe judges preserve criterion-level reward structure across settings.

</details>


### [122] ["Act Like a 5th Grader" is Not Enough: Bounding Knowledge in LLM-Based User Simulators](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30033)
*Krisztian Balog,Arild Michel Bakken*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper shows that standard persona prompting makes LLMs unrealistically superhuman on children’s reading tasks, and proposes a cognitively constrained simulator (CBUS) that narrows this gap by modeling limited working memory and test-taking strategies.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs are being used as user simulators in education and HCI, but they tend to perform with unrealistically high accuracy and low variability compared with real humans, especially children. Persona prompts alone don’t make models faithfully reproduce human-like cognitive limits, which is problematic for designing and evaluating learning tools or assessments aimed at developing readers. The authors want a way to simulate young readers that reflects actual cognitive constraints and behavioral diversity, not just “acting like a child” in text style.

Method: The authors collect or use an existing large dataset of over 71,000 reading-comprehension answers from 2,359 students in grades 4–6. They first prompt LLMs with standard persona instructions (e.g., “You are a 10-year-old student”) to solve the same questions and compare performance patterns with human data, finding near-perfect, low-variance performance. They then propose CBUS, an architectural framework that imposes an episodic bottleneck representing bounded working memory. Within this framework, they define at least two explicit test-taking strategies (e.g., different ways of reading passages, selecting details, and answering) to mimic distinct reading behaviors. They instantiate CBUS on multiple LLM backbones and evaluate how well the simulated performance distribution (accuracy, variance, error patterns) matches that of real students.

Result: Persona-prompted LLMs achieve almost deterministic, near-ceiling scores on the primary-school reading tasks and fail to capture the diversity and error patterns of real children. In contrast, CBUS—with its explicit working-memory bottleneck and strategy models—produces performance distributions that more closely resemble human data across several backbone models. Quantitatively, the gap between simulated and real readers (in terms of accuracy levels and variability) is significantly reduced when using CBUS compared to simple persona prompting or scaling up model size.

Conclusion: The work argues that high-fidelity simulation of human users, especially children, requires architectural cognitive constraints rather than just instruction-level persona styling or larger models. By modeling restricted working memory via an episodic bottleneck and encoding explicit test-taking strategies, CBUS reduces the superhuman bias of LLMs and yields more realistic reading-behavior simulations. This suggests that future user simulators for education and HCI should integrate cognitive theories and structural limits into LLM-based systems, rather than relying solely on prompt engineering or model scaling.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to simulate human behavior but frequently fail to exhibit realistic cognitive constraints, suffering from a "superhuman bias." Using a dataset of over 71,000 reading comprehension responses from 2,359 primary-school students (grades 4--6), we demonstrate that standard persona prompting yields near-perfect, deterministic performance, failing to capture the natural variance of developing readers. To address this, we introduce the Cognitively Bounded User Simulator (CBUS), an architectural framework that explicitly models the restricted working memory of young readers through an episodic bottleneck. Within this framework, we formalize two distinct test-taking strategies to emulate different reading behaviors. Our evaluation shows that explicitly modeling cognitive bounds significantly narrows the simulation gap across multiple LLM backbones, demonstrating that enforcing architectural constraints is more effective for high-fidelity simulation than simply scaling raw model capabilities.

</details>


### [123] [Pak3H: Evaluating the Cost of Cultural Mismatch in LLM Alignment with a Human-Contextualized Urdu Benchmark](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30065)
*Abdullah Hashmat,Usman Naseem,Agha Ali Raza*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Introduces Pak3H, a human-validated, culturally contextualized Urdu benchmark suite to evaluate LLM alignment on Helpfulness, Harmlessness, and Honesty, revealing cross-lingual alignment gaps in current models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs are mainly aligned and evaluated in English, and existing multilingual 3H benchmarks often rely on automatic translation, which carries cultural and linguistic biases and fails to reflect local contexts, especially in low-resource languages like Urdu. There is a need for a culturally grounded benchmark that accurately assesses 3H alignment in such languages.

Method: The authors build Pak3H, an Urdu benchmark suite, by constructing three components: PakAlpaca for helpfulness, PakBeaverTails for harmlessness, and PakTruthfulQA for honesty. They employ a multi-stage pipeline that includes manual cultural adaptation by native speakers, dictionary-guided post-editing, and human validation to preserve semantic fidelity while ensuring cultural and contextual authenticity. They then conduct zero-shot evaluations of multiple open-source and proprietary LLMs on this benchmark.

Result: Across the evaluated models, performance in Urdu under culturally localized contexts shows systematic degradation compared to English or non-localized settings: helpfulness win rates drop, safety defenses fail more often on region-specific harms, and honesty metrics degrade when questions involve localized factual knowledge and constraints. These results empirically demonstrate a significant cross-lingual alignment gap in current LLMs.

Conclusion: Current LLM alignment methods do not transfer reliably to culturally distinct, low-resource languages such as Urdu. Human-guided, culturally aware localization—like that used to build Pak3H—is essential for fair, accurate multilingual evaluation of LLM helpfulness, harmlessness, and honesty, and future alignment work must explicitly address these structural cross-lingual limitations.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) demonstrate strong Helpfulness, Harmlessness, and Honesty (3H) alignment in English-centric settings, but these gains transfer poorly to low-resource languages due to cultural mismatches. Existing multilingual 3H benchmarks rely predominantly on automated translation or LLM based synthesis, propagating source-language biases while sacrificing local relevance. To address this gap, we introduce Pak3H1, the first human-validated, culturally contextualized Urdu benchmark suite for 3H alignment, comprising PakAlpaca (helpfulness), PakBeaverTails (harmlessness), and PakTruthfulQA (honesty). Our multi-stage pipeline integrates manual cultural adaptation and dictionary-guided post editing to prioritize native speaker judgment, ensuring both semantic fidelity and contextual authenticity. Zero-shot evaluations across multiple open and proprietary LLM architectures reveal systematic cross-lingual alignment gaps: helpfulness win rates decline under localized contexts, harmlessness guardrails break down against regional safety risks, and composite honesty metrics degrade substantially due to localized factual constraints. These findings expose structural limitations in current alignment approaches, underscoring the necessity of human-guided localization for equitable multilingual evaluation.

</details>


### [124] [Budget-Aware Compression Pipeline for Single-GPU LLM Inference: Methods, Trade-offs, and Coupling Effects](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30076)
*Hongyu Yu,Yifei Shen*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: They design and evaluate a practical compression pipeline (pruning, quantization, KV-cache compression) that allows a 70B LLM to run on a single NVIDIA GPU within strict memory and speed budgets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Running 70B-parameter language models on a single GPU is limited by memory capacity, long-context throughput, and engineering overhead. Existing works often optimize one axis in isolation, lack realistic end-to-end measurements, and don’t systematically explore how different compression techniques interact. There is a need for a principled, budget-aware design of single-GPU deployment that balances quality, memory, and speed together.

Method: Formulate single-GPU inference as a budget-aware design problem along three axes: memory footprint, long-context throughput, and engineering cost. Empirically study interactions between pruning, weight quantization, and KV-cache compression through controlled ablations. Evaluate layer-wise pruning’s effect on quantization robustness; analyze KV-cache sparsification and INT8 KV quantization; compare static vector quantization with dynamic caching. Based on these interaction findings and explicit resource tracking, build a practical compression pipeline for a 70B model and evaluate it end-to-end on a single NVIDIA A40 GPU with long prompts and multiple benchmarks.

Result: A 70B-parameter LLM is compressed to about 33 GB, fits on a single NVIDIA A40 GPU, and achieves around 57 tokens/s even for 10k-token prompts while preserving absolute accuracy within 5% on standard and reasoning benchmarks. The empirical ablations show that: (1) layer-wise pruning improves robustness of subsequent weight quantization; (2) KV-cache sparsification works well with INT8 KV quantization, reducing memory usage without harming decoding speed; (3) static vector quantizers often degrade performance when combined with dynamic KV caching.

Conclusion: A carefully co-designed pipeline combining pruning, quantization, and KV-cache compression can make 70B LLMs practically deployable on a single commodity GPU under realistic constraints, with modest accuracy loss. The paper offers design rules and a reproducible protocol to jointly report model quality, memory usage, and end-to-end speed, laying groundwork for future automated search of optimal compression pipelines for single-GPU deployment.

Abstract: Single-GPU deployment of 70B-parameter language models on an NVIDIA GPU is constrained by device memory, long-context throughput, and engineering integration cost. We cast single-GPU inference as a budget-aware design problem over these three axes and study how pruning, quantization, and KV-cache compression interact under realistic execution. Controlled ablations show that layer-wise pruning makes weight quantization more robust. KV-cache sparsification complements INT8 KV quantization by reducing memory without hurting decoding speed, while static vector quantizers often conflict with dynamic caching. Guided by these coupling results and explicit budget tracking, we assembled a practical pipeline and compressed a 70B model to about 33 GB, sustained about 57 tokens/s on 10k token prompts on a single A40, and kept absolute accuracy within 5% on common and reasoning benchmarks. We contribute design rules and a reproducible evaluation protocol that jointly report quality, memory, and end-to-end speed, and we provide a foundation for automated pipeline search under realistic single-GPU constraints.

</details>


### [125] [When Does a Classifier Help an LLM? Classifier-Guided Prompting and Hybrid Classifier-LLM Models for Credit-Default Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30086)
*Rishi Datta,Lavanya Prahallad*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper studies how to best combine large language models (LLMs) with traditional fitted classifiers (like random forests) for predicting credit-card defaults, and finds that using the classifier to guide the LLM’s prompt substantially improves performance, especially recall, without sacrificing ranking quality.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Credit-default prediction is central to financial risk management, but standard approaches (logistic regression, random forests) rely only on tabular features and do not exploit the potential of LLMs. Recent works prompt LLMs directly, but LLMs often lack strong probabilistic ranking ability compared with fitted classifiers. There is a gap in understanding how to systematically combine LLMs with traditional classifiers to leverage each model’s strengths for better credit-default prediction performance.

Method: The authors compare: (1) a few-shot prompted LLM, (2) traditional classifiers like random forests, and (3) several hybrid setups where the classifier and LLM are composed in different ways. They distinguish between (a) telling the LLM to imitate a classifier and (b) using the classifier to shape or augment the prompt. They run experiments on the Default of Credit Card Clients dataset, measuring recall, F1, and AUC for ROC and precision–recall curves, with bootstrap confidence intervals. They test prompt pruning to the classifier’s top features, adding the classifier’s predicted probability into the prompt, imitating the classifier with the LLM, reversing the composition (classifier using LLM output), and combining several classifiers.

Result: A few-shot LLM alone achieves the best recall (0.47) and F1 (0.50) among single models, but has worse ranking performance (AUC-ROC 0.72) than a random forest (0.79). Instructing the LLM to imitate the classifier does not significantly change performance. Using the classifier to guide the prompt works: pruning the prompt to the random forest’s eight most important features increases recall by 0.071 and F1 by 0.032. Adding the classifier’s predicted probability to the LLM prompt boosts the LLM’s AUC-ROC from 0.72 to 0.78, on par with the random forest’s ranking ability, while maintaining a recall that is 0.118 higher than the random forest’s. Reverse compositions and ensembles of multiple classifiers do not yield further gains.

Conclusion: The study shows that LLMs and fitted classifiers are complementary for credit-default prediction: LLMs offer strong recall and F1, whereas classifiers provide superior ranking. Directly imitating classifiers in the LLM is ineffective, but using classifier-derived information to structure and augment the LLM’s prompt significantly improves performance. A simple classifier-guided prompt—especially including the classifier’s top features and predicted probability—achieves near-classifier AUC while preserving higher recall. The authors recommend this straightforward classifier-guided prompting strategy for LLM-based credit-default prediction, and find that more complex compositions offer little additional benefit.

Abstract: Credit-default prediction is an important task in financial decision making. Traditional methods use fitted classifiers such as logistic regression and random forests on tabular features. Large language models (LLMs) have recently been applied to this task through prompting. In this work we study how a fitted classifier and an LLM can be combined for credit-default prediction. We distinguish telling the LLM to imitate a classifier from using the classifier to build the prompt. We hypothesize that a fitted classifier can supply the ranking ability that an LLM prompt lacks. We experiment on the Default of Credit Card Clients dataset, and report recall, F1, and the area under the ROC and precision-recall curves, with bootstrap confidence intervals. We observe that a few-shot LLM has the highest recall (0.47) and F1 (0.50) of any single model but ranks worse than a random forest (AUC-ROC 0.72 against 0.79). Instructing the LLM to imitate a classifier gives no significant change. Pruning the prompt to the classifier's eight most important features raises recall by 0.071 and F1 by 0.032. Adding the classifier's predicted probability to the prompt raises the LLM's AUC-ROC from 0.72 to 0.78, matching the random forest, while keeping 0.118 higher recall than it. The reverse composition, and the use of several classifiers, do not help. We thus recommend a simple classifier-guided prompt for LLM-based credit prediction.

</details>


### [126] [Arkios: An Open Bilingual English-Nepali Language Model Trained From Scratch, with a Devanagari-Aware Tokenizer](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30092)
*Sajal Regmi,Siddhartha Pudasaini,Chetan Phakami Pun*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Arkios is a 1B-parameter bilingual English-Nepali transformer trained on 150B tokens that outperforms similar-sized open models on ARC, reveals evaluation pitfalls in low-resource languages, introduces a manifest-gated tool-use protocol, and releases base and instruction-tuned weights under Apache-2.0.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To build a competitive, compact bilingual English-Nepali language model with efficient custom training infrastructure, to understand how evaluation setups can misrepresent small-model capabilities in low-resource languages, and to explore safer, more controllable tool-use behavior during instruction tuning.

Method: They pretrain a 1.04B-parameter dense transformer from scratch on 150B tokens of bilingual English-Nepali data using a custom single-file C/CUDA training stack and a Devanagari-aware byte-level BPE tokenizer. They then evaluate Arkios on standard benchmarks like ARC-Easy and ARC-Challenge, carefully comparing to similar-sized open models and analyzing differences in performance under two evaluation formats (letter-choice vs answer-text scoring). During instruction tuning, they implement a manifest-conditioned tool-use contract that only permits tool calls when a tool manifest is explicitly present in the prompt, and they empirically examine adherence to this contract. They release base and instruction-tuned weights and full evaluation protocols, but not the training code or most of the proprietary Nepali corpus.

Result: Arkios outperforms three similar-sized open models (Pythia-1.4B, TinyLlama-1.1B, OLMo-1B) on ARC benchmarks despite being trained on roughly 10x fewer tokens, likely due to pretraining data being well-matched to ARC’s educational-science domain rather than a broad capability gain. They find that standard multiple-choice-letter evaluation formats push Arkios to chance-level scores in both English and Nepali, masking its true reading comprehension ability; switching to answer-text scoring reveals non-trivial comprehension in both languages, with stronger English performance (0.306 Nepali vs 0.387 English). They also characterize when their manifest-conditioned tool-use contract is respected and where it breaks down.

Conclusion: Model performance can be significantly affected—and even misrepresented—by evaluation format, especially for small models and low-resource languages, so benchmark protocols must be chosen carefully. Domain-aligned pretraining data can let relatively small models with fewer tokens perform competitively against larger or more heavily trained peers. A manifest-gated tool-use scheme is a viable way to constrain tool invocation behavior, though it is imperfect and requires empirical validation. Arkios provides a practical, openly released bilingual base and instruction-tuned model for English-Nepali work, along with transparent evaluation details, even though the full training stack and most of the Nepali corpus remain closed.

Abstract: We present Arkios, a 1.04B-parameter dense transformer pretrained from scratch on 150B tokens of bilingual English-Nepali text, using a custom single-file C/CUDA training stack and a Devanagari-aware byte-level BPE tokenizer built for this project. On ARC-Easy and ARC-Challenge, Arkios exceeds three comparably sized open models (Pythia-1.4B, TinyLlama-1.1B, OLMo-1B) despite an order of magnitude fewer training tokens, likely aided by a match between our educational-web-text pretraining data and ARC's grade-school-science format rather than a general capability advantage. We report full evaluation results under standard protocols, including a correction to an earlier partial-sample estimate, and findings specific to evaluating small models in a low-resource language: the standard multiple-choice-letter prompt format used by common evaluation harnesses places this model at chance on Nepali reading comprehension, and simultaneously at chance on English in the same format, which would lead a naive benchmark run to conclude the model has no Nepali ability when in fact it does. Concretely, both languages score at chance in the letter-choice format (0.240 Nepali, 0.236 English, against a chance baseline of 0.250), while scoring the answer text directly reveals genuine, English-favoring comprehension (0.306 Nepali, 0.387 English). We describe a manifest-conditioned tool-use contract introduced during instruction tuning, where tool calls are permitted only when a tool manifest is declared in context and suppressed otherwise, and report where that contract holds and where it does not. We release both the base and instruction-tuned model weights under Apache-2.0. The training code and a small privately-sourced portion of the Nepali pretraining corpus are not released; everything needed to reproduce the reported numbers from the released weights is included here.

</details>


### [127] [AtlasNLP: A Country-Aware Atlas of Dataset Representation in NLP](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30107)
*Joan Nwatu,Tsedeniya Solomon Amare,Longju Bai,Bontu Fufa Balcha,Zayd Bashir,Angana Borah,Zara Burzo,Yubin Choi,Naihao Deng,Samika Gupta,Michel Faloughi,Claude Kwizera,Ziqiao Ma,Cynthia Yacel Fuertes Panizo,Ellie Seehorn,Hui Shen,Jiayi Tang,Zesen Zhao,Boyuan Zheng,Rada Mihalcea*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces AtlasNLP, a large country-aware atlas of NLP datasets, to make visible which countries’ data are represented and where datasets are produced.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Geographic information about NLP datasets is rarely documented, so it is hard to know which countries and populations are being represented, where datasets are created, where gaps exist, and how to design fair and country-aware AI and policy.

Method: The authors build AtlasNLP by aggregating and normalizing metadata from over 13,000 NLP dataset records, organizing them into standardized NLP task categories and adding country-level information for both represented populations and locations of dataset production. The resource has two components: AtlasNLP-Gold, a carefully human-curated subset, and AtlasNLP-Core, a large ACL-derived collection. They then analyze coverage patterns across countries, tasks, and languages.

Result: Analysis with AtlasNLP shows that (1) coverage across countries and tasks is highly uneven; (2) there is geographic asymmetry between where datasets are produced and which populations they represent; and (3) broad language coverage does not guarantee that many countries using that language are actually represented in the data.

Conclusion: Current NLP dataset documentation has serious geographic blind spots, and language-level claims can obscure country-level underrepresentation. The authors argue that more explicit and standardized geographic metadata is needed to support country-aware evaluation, identify gaps, and guide future data collection and policy.

Abstract: Understanding which countries are represented in NLP datasets is essential for identifying gaps, targeting data collection, measuring progress, and informing AI policy. However, geographic metadata is very rarely available, and country-level representation is often hidden behind broad language-level claims. We introduce AtlasNLP, a country-aware atlas of over 13,000 NLP dataset records across normalized NLP task categories, tracking both the populations represented and where datasets are produced. AtlasNLP includes AtlasNLP-Gold, a human-curated reference set, and AtlasNLP-Core, an ACL-derived large-scale collection. Using this resource, we show that (1) dataset coverage is highly uneven across countries and tasks; (2) dataset production and representation are geographically asymmetric; and (3) language coverage does not imply geographic representation. These findings reveal blind spots in current dataset documentation practices and motivate more explicit geographic metadata for country-aware NLP evaluation.

</details>


### [128] [COGTRL: Training LLMs for Scientific Discovery Assistance using Cognitive Traces via Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30109)
*Shrinidhi Kumbhar Santosh Mashetty Divij Handa Kevin Coutinho,Siddharth Sambhaji Ghule,Chitta Baral*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces COGTRL, a trajectory-level reinforcement learning framework that trains LLMs to generate explicit cognitive traces (constraints, alternatives, decisions) alongside scientific steps, leading to better performance as scientific discovery assistants than models trained only on standard scientific literature.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLMs trained on scientific papers lack access to the fine-grained cognitive processes—consideration of constraints, rejected alternatives, and iterative decisions—that real scientists use. Because research articles mostly present polished results, models trained solely on them struggle to emulate realistic, goal-directed scientific reasoning under constraints. The authors aim to bridge this gap so LLMs can act as more effective scientific discovery assistants, not just text generators.

Method: They propose COGTRL, a trajectory-level reinforcement learning (RL) framework that trains LLMs to jointly produce cognitive traces and the associated scientific steps in an interleaved sequence. Instead of optimizing only final answers or stand-alone methods, the model is optimized over full reasoning trajectories, where rewards reflect both the quality of the cognitive traces and the resulting methods. They evaluate this on two 3B-parameter models across two scientific domains (AI and Materials Science), comparing against similarly sized baselines and much larger (70B) models.

Result: COGTRL-trained 3B models produce higher-quality scientific methods than comparable 3B baselines, with an average improvement of 7.85 points on their method-quality metric. Their performance is competitive with that of 70B-parameter models, suggesting that cognitively grounded trajectory training can compensate substantially for smaller model size. Expert evaluations further indicate that domain specialists prefer the methods produced by COGTRL over baseline models’ outputs.

Conclusion: Embedding cognitively grounded reasoning—via explicit cognitive traces optimized at the trajectory level—improves LLMs’ effectiveness as scientific discovery assistants. COGTRL demonstrates that training models on structured reasoning processes, not just polished scientific text, yields better method quality and expert-preferred outputs, narrowing the gap between smaller and much larger models. This supports the broader view that aligning LLMs with human-like scientific cognition is a promising path for enhancing AI-driven research assistance.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) trained on extensive scientific research are increasingly integrated as assistants for scientific discovery. However, most research papers omit the fine-grained cognitive process of examining constraints, failed alternatives, and iterative decisions required to achieve the desired goal. Such cognitive processes are vital for real-world scientists working toward specific goals under constraints. In this paper, we show that LLMs, when trained to produce such cognitive traces, perform better as scientific discovery assistants than when trained solely on scientific literature. We propose COGTRL, a trajectory-level reinforcement learning framework that trains LLMs to emulate cognitively grounded reasoning by jointly optimizing cognitive traces and the scientific steps produced in an interleaved manner. Across two 3B-parameter models and two scientific domains (AI and Materials Science), COGTRL improves method quality by an average of 7.85 points over comparable 3B model baselines and achieves competitive performance relative to 70B parameter models. Moreover, analysis by domain experts shows a preference for methods generated by COGTRL over the baselines.

</details>


### [129] [Can LLMs Take the Pulse of the Economy? A Real-Time Evaluation of LLM Nowcasts on Macroeconomic Indicators](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30110)
*Xinyue Zhao,Ruiyi Zhang,Liqin Ye,Rui Cao,Pengtao Xie,Sudheer Chava*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces LiveMacroEval, a live benchmark to test whether LLM agents can nowcast major U.S. macroeconomic indicators in real time without data contamination, finding LLMs perform roughly on par with professional and institutional benchmarks overall.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Evaluating whether LLMs can nowcast macro indicators like GDP or CPI is important for monetary policy and financial markets, but historical backtests are contaminated because headline figures are likely memorized by models from pretraining. The authors want a clean, forward-looking way to see if LLM agents with web access can truly infer current macro conditions and add value relative to central-bank teams, Bloomberg consensus, and simple time-series models.

Method: They design LiveMacroEval, a live evaluation framework where LLM agents with web search produce hourly nowcasts for 16 key U.S. macroeconomic indicators during the embargo window before each official release. Performance is measured using two metrics: (1) a LiveMacro Score, based on how well the nowcasts explain equity returns around the announcement window, and (2) a LiveBetting Score, derived from simulated prediction-market style trading (Polymarket-like). They compare four state-of-the-art LLM agents configured with web search against Federal Reserve regional-bank nowcasts, Bloomberg ECOS professional consensus forecasts, and an auto-ARIMA statistical baseline over a six-month period.

Result: Over the six-month live evaluation, the ensemble of four web-enabled LLM agents achieves overall nowcast accuracy that is broadly comparable to both institutional (Fed regional banks) and professional (Bloomberg ECOS consensus) benchmarks, and better than or similar to an auto-ARIMA baseline in aggregate. However, performance is heterogeneous: LLM accuracy varies significantly across the 16 indicators, being stronger for some series and weaker for others.

Conclusion: LLM agents, when equipped with real-time web search and evaluated in a contamination-resistant live setup, can serve as reasonably competitive real-time estimators of macroeconomic conditions, on par with established institutional and professional forecasters in aggregate. Their uneven performance across indicators suggests substantial room for improvement and specialization, but the results demonstrate meaningful potential for LLMs in operational macro nowcasting and related financial applications.

Abstract: Nowcasting headline macroeconomic indicators, i.e., estimating an indicator's value for the current reference period before its official release, is critical for monetary policy and financial markets, and central banks devote dedicated teams of expert economists to producing such estimates. Large language model (LLM) agents are a promising candidate for this task, combining broad world knowledge with real-time web search and supporting queries at higher frequency than institutional nowcasts. Evaluating their nowcasting capability is, however, challenging: headline indicators such as GDP and CPI are widely reported and likely memorized during pretraining, so any evaluation on historical releases is vulnerable to data contamination. To address this, we introduce LiveMacroEval, a live, contamination-resistant benchmark in which LLM agents produce hourly nowcasts for sixteen major U.S. macroeconomic indicators over a pre-release window closing at each official release. Nowcast quality is assessed through a LiveMacro Score against announcement-window equity returns and a LiveBetting Score from simulated Polymarket-style trading, with Federal Reserve regional-bank nowcasts, the Bloomberg ECOS professional consensus, and an auto-ARIMA baseline as comparators. Over six months with four state-of-the-art LLM agents configured with web search, aggregate nowcast accuracy is broadly comparable to the institutional and professional benchmarks, with performance varying widely across individual indicators. This highlights LLM agents' potential as real-time estimators of macroeconomic conditions.

</details>


### [130] [Manacá-1B: An Open, Reproducible Brazilian-Portuguese Language Model and a Tokenizer-Aware, Paired Evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30114)
*Bruno Leonardo Santos Menezes,Carlos Leonardo Souza Cardoso,Fabio Andre Machado Porto*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Manacá-1B is a fully reproducible, 1.72B-parameter, Brazilian Portuguese decoder-only LLM with open logs, weights, and evaluation harness, achieving state-of-the-art sub-7B performance on last-word prediction and highlighting a tokenizer conversion pitfall.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Brazilian Portuguese lacks well-documented, reproducible open LLMs, and existing models are hard to reproduce and evaluated without uncertainty estimates; there is also a need to better understand and standardize evaluation practices and tooling (e.g., tokenizers) for Portuguese models.

Method: Train from scratch a 1.72B-parameter decoder-only language model focused on Brazilian Portuguese using a fully containerized, reproducible pipeline; log all training dynamics; evaluate the model alongside nine open baselines on four Portuguese benchmarks within a unified harness that reports standard errors and paired significance tests; investigate and quantify the impact of a tokenizer conversion bug from SentencePiece (with case-folding normalization) to HuggingFace fast tokenizers and propose a fix.

Result: Manacá-1B shows stable pretraining (no NaNs or skipped steps, self-recovering loss spikes) and achieves best-in-class performance under 7B parameters for last-word prediction in Portuguese, outperforming Tucano-1b1 and Tucano-2b4 on LAMBADA-PT by large margins; it is competitive on commonsense completion and near-chance on multiple-choice reasoning, like other small base models; the tokenizer bug is shown to severely degrade LAMBADA-PT accuracy from 45.3 to 25.0 by mis-handling capitalization.

Conclusion: Manacá-1B provides a strong, fully reproducible open Brazilian Portuguese LLM, complete with code, logs, predictions, weights, and a validated evaluation harness, enabling others to recompute all reported numbers; the work also surfaces a critical tokenizer conversion pitfall and offers a simple fix, thereby improving reliability and comparability of Portuguese LLM evaluations.

Abstract: Brazilian Portuguese remains under-served by open language models, and the few that exist are difficult to reproduce and are often compared without measures of uncertainty. We release Manacá-1B, an open decoder-only model of 1.72 billion parameters trained from scratch for Brazilian Portuguese with a fully containerized, reproducible pipeline. The pretraining is stable, with zero skipped or NaN steps and self-recovering loss spikes, and we release its full log and dynamics. We evaluate the model against nine open baselines on four Portuguese benchmarks under a single harness. Every comparison reports a standard error and a paired significance test, and the harness is validated against previously published numbers. On last-word prediction Manacá-1B is the strongest model below the 7B scale, exceeding both Tucano-1b1 and Tucano-2b4 on LAMBADA-PT with large paired margins; it is competitive on commonsense completion and near chance on multiple-choice reasoning, as are all small base models. Along the way we document a concrete evaluation pitfall: converting a SentencePiece tokenizer with case-folding normalization to the HuggingFace fast format silently drops the normalizer, routing every capitalized token to byte-fallback and depressing scores in a way that is invisible in aggregate metrics. The uncorrected tokenizer lowered LAMBADA-PT accuracy from 45.3 to 25.0; we quantify the effect and provide a one-line fix that reproduces the training tokenizer exactly. Code, raw training and evaluation logs, per-example prediction vectors, the model weights, and the corrected tokenizer are released so that every number in this paper can be recomputed.

</details>


### [131] [Verification-Aware Training for Speculative Decoding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30135)
*Geonmo Gu,Byeongho Heo,HeeJae Jun,Yoohoon Kang,Sangmin Lee,Sangdoo Yun,Dongyoon Han*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes Verification-Aware Training (VAT) to better align draft model training with the actual verification process in speculative decoding, yielding longer accepted sequences and faster inference.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing speculative decoding trains draft models with token-level imitation and fixed per-position weights, which ignore how verification sequentially discards tokens from the first rejection onward. This mismatch limits acceptance length and speedup.

Method: VAT modifies only the training objective using two components: (1) a verification head—a jointly trained lightweight binary classifier that predicts whether each token position will survive the sequential verification step; and (2) verification-adaptive weighting, which adjusts per-token loss weights to keep full weight up to the first rejected token and then restarts the decay from that point. VAT can be applied on top of existing speculative decoding approaches without altering architectures or inference procedures.

Result: On speculative decoding setups such as EAGLE-3 and DFlash with Qwen3-4B, Qwen3-8B, and LLaMA-3.1-8B as targets, VAT improves average verified (accepted) sequence length by up to 11.4% and end-to-end wall-clock speedup by up to 8.7%, with consistent gains across math, code, and chat benchmarks.

Conclusion: Aligning training with the actual verification dynamics through VAT leads to more verification-robust draft models, improving acceptance length and practical speedup for speculative decoding without requiring architectural or inference changes, and can be easily layered onto existing methods.

Abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates large language model inference by using a draft model to generate candidate tokens, which are verified by the target model in a single forward pass. Verification proceeds sequentially and discards every position from the first rejection onward, yet existing draft training relies on token-level imitation of the target with a fixed per-position weighting that reflects neither property. We introduce Verification-Aware Training (VAT), a plug-in framework that simulates verification at every training step and turns the resulting accept and reject patterns into supervision. VAT consists of two components: (i) a verification head, a lightweight jointly trained binary classifier that supervises the draft model on whether each position survives sequential verification; (ii) verification-adaptive weighting, which replaces the fixed weighting schedule by keeping full weight up to each sample's first rejection point and re-anchoring the decay to start there. VAT modifies only the training objective, so it can be layered on top of existing methods without changing the draft architecture, the target model, or the inference procedure. Applied to EAGLE-3 and DFlash on Qwen3-4B, Qwen3-8B, and LLaMA-3.1-8B, VAT improves average acceptance length by up to 11.4% and wall-clock speedup by up to 8.7%, with consistent gains across math, code, and chat benchmarks. Code will be available at https://github.com/naver-ai/vat

</details>


### [132] [CAST: Critique-Aware Supervision for Training Reliable Long-Horizon Tool-Calling Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30147)
*Amir Saeidi,Zehua Zhang,Rishitosh Singh,Naman Ahuja,Vivek Gupta,Ali Payani,Gaowen Liu,Jayanth Srinivasa,Chitta Baral*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: CAST is a critique-aware training framework that turns sparse task outcomes into action-level supervision, improving the reliability of LLM agents in long-horizon, tool-using environments.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM agents operating in long-horizon, interactive, and stateful environments can cause irreversible failures with a single wrong action, and such errors may only surface across repeated trials. Existing approaches (prompt-based critique agents and optimization-based methods) either lack reliability or cannot generate rich verification rationales needed for training. There is a need for a systematic way to improve step-wise reliability and provide interpretable, structured critiques about action validity under complex, domain-specific policies.

Method: The authors propose CAST, a critique-aware training framework. CAST analyzes full agent trajectories and converts sparse task-level success/failure signals into dense, action-level supervision. It synthesizes structured rationales explaining whether each action is valid under partial observability and domain constraints, training a critique model on these rationales. This critique model is then used to construct critique-aware training data that guides fine-tuning of the policy model (LLM agent), particularly in dynamic tool-calling environments.

Result: When fine-tuned on dynamic tool-calling benchmarks using CAST, Qwen3-family models achieve substantially higher reliability across domains. On Retail tasks, CAST-trained models outperform GPT-OSS-120B by over 10% in pass^4 metric, and on Telehealth tasks (an out-of-domain setting), they achieve an additional 9% improvement, indicating stronger generalization and robustness of the agents.

Conclusion: Critique-aware training with CAST effectively improves the robustness and reliability of LLM agents in realistic, dynamic, and partially observable environments. By converting sparse outcome signals into structured, action-level critiques, CAST enables better policy optimization than prompt-based critique agents or traditional optimization methods, leading to more dependable long-horizon tool-using agents across domains, including out-of-domain scenarios.

Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly deployed in long-horizon, interactive, and stateful environments. In these settings, a single wrong action, such as refunding the wrong purchase, can cause irreversible task failure and must be intercepted before execution. Such failures may not appear in every single run, but can emerge across repeated trials, making reliability across steps and trials critical. However, ensuring agentic reliability is challenging: even frontier LLMs struggle to explain why an action may be wrong, especially in long, intertwined trajectories governed by domain-specific policies. Much recent work relies on prompt-based critique agents, while optimization-based methods lack a systematic way to produce rich verification rationales for training. We address this gap with CAST, a critique-aware training framework that converts sparse task outcomes into action-level supervision for critique learning and policy optimization. CAST analyzes agent trajectories to synthesize structured rationales explaining action validity under partial observability. The resulting critique model is used to construct critique-aware training data for optimizing the policy model. Fine-tuning Qwen3-family models on dynamic tool-calling benchmarks, CAST improves reliability across domains, outperforming GPT-OSS-120B by over 10% pass^4 on Retail tasks and yielding an additional 9% improvement on Telehealth in an out-of-domain setting. These results demonstrate that critique-aware training improves the robustness of LLM agents in realistic dynamic environments.

</details>


### [133] [Reactivating Test-Time Scaling for Plane Geometry Problem Solving](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30156)
*Xiaoqiang Kang,Shengen Wu,Maizhen Ning,Xiaobo Jin,Kaizhu Huang,Yutao Yue,Xiaowei Huang,Qiufeng Wang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper enhances multimodal reasoning for plane geometry problems by diversifying symbolic reasoning traces and improving visual grounding, leading to more efficient and accurate test-time scaling.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Plane geometry problems are an important but challenging benchmark for multimodal models because they require both accurate perception of diagrams and multi-step symbolic reasoning. Existing test-time scaling works well for general math but not for plane geometry under the symbolic-program paradigm, mainly due to limited diversity in reasoning paths and weak explicit visual grounding. The authors aim to overcome these bottlenecks so that TTS can be effective for plane geometry reasoning.

Method: The authors introduce Multi-Trace Synthesis (MTS), which converts a single symbolic program into multiple heterogeneous reasoning traces, including executable Python scripts and chain-of-thought (CoT)-augmented variants, to increase reasoning diversity. They propose Perception-Augmented (PA) training that first parses geometry diagrams into structured semantic clauses to strengthen visual grounding before symbolic deduction. Finally, they design Consensus-Guided Multi-Trace Ensemble (CG-MTE), an inference scheme that adaptively combines multiple reasoning traces using consensus signals, enabling efficient and scalable test-time reasoning.

Result: Across three plane geometry benchmarks and multiple model scales, the proposed approach consistently improves the accuracy of plane geometry problem solving compared to both general-purpose multimodal LLMs and specialized geometry solvers. Under test-time scaling, the CG-MTE strategy achieves accuracy comparable to high-budget self-consistency methods while cutting the sampling cost by up to a factor of 8.

Conclusion: Diversifying symbolic reasoning traces and explicitly grounding visual information substantially improves multimodal plane geometry reasoning and enables more efficient test-time scaling. The proposed MTS, PA training, and CG-MTE ensemble together make symbolic-program-based geometry solvers more accurate and cost-effective, setting a stronger baseline for multimodal mathematical reasoning on plane geometry benchmarks.

Abstract: Plane geometry problem (PGP) solving has become a critical benchmark for multimodal reasoning because it requires accurate visual perception and precise multi-step symbolic deduction. Although test-time scaling (TTS) has demonstrated remarkable success in general mathematical reasoning, it fails to scale effectively under the symbolic-program paradigm for plane geometry. We identify two key obstacles: limited reasoning diversity induced by rigid symbolic programs and insufficient explicit visual grounding before symbolic deduction. To address these issues, we propose Multi-Trace Synthesis (MTS), which converts each symbolic program into heterogeneous reasoning traces, including executable Python scripts and CoT-augmented variants. We further propose Perception-Augmented (PA) training, which parses diagrams into structured semantic clauses before deduction, and Consensus-Guided Multi-Trace Ensemble (CG-MTE) for efficient self-adaptive inference. Experiments on three geometry benchmarks show that our method consistently improves PGP-solving across model scales and achieves strong performance against both general-purpose MLLMs and specialized geometry solvers. Under test-time scaling, CG-MTE achieves comparable accuracy to high-budget self-consistency while reducing sampling cost by up to 8x. Code and data are publicly available at https://github.com/Jason8Kang/ReTTS-PGPS.

</details>


### [134] [CPR for LLMs: Critical-Point Routing against Catastrophic Forgetting in Domain Adaptation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30158)
*Kwangmin Ki,Yunhun Nam,Jongheon Jeong,Jaehyung Kim*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: They propose CPR, a routing framework that dynamically decides per token whether to use a base LLM or its fine-tuned expert, preserving general abilities while improving domain performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard supervised fine-tuning improves domain performance but causes catastrophic forgetting of general capabilities, and loss-based mitigation methods are stuck in a trade-off between domain specialization and generality. The authors want a method that gets strong domain performance without sacrificing general capabilities.

Method: They keep both the original base model and a domain SFT expert and introduce CPR (Critical-Point Routing), which operates at token level. They identify critical tokens where the base model fails but the expert succeeds, then train a lightweight hierarchical router to predict, for each token, the probability of calling the expert. At inference they use a custom procedure with momentum smoothing and threshold gating to decide when to route tokens to the expert and when to stick with the base model.

Result: Across various models and domains, CPR outperforms the pure SFT expert by 1.4–5.5% on domain tasks, while almost completely recovering the loss in general capability (reducing drops from 3.4–14.5% down to at most 0.5%). It does this efficiently, needing the expert for only about one-third of tokens.

Conclusion: Decoupling general and domain-specific capabilities via token-level routing between a base LLM and its SFT expert avoids the usual domain–generality trade-off. CPR achieves better domain performance than standard SFT while essentially preserving the base model’s general abilities, with modest compute overhead.

Abstract: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) is the de facto standard for adapting large language models (LLMs) to target domains, but it often degrades the model's general capabilities, a phenomenon known as catastrophic forgetting. Existing approaches typically modify the SFT loss to mitigate forgetting, but they inevitably operate along a domain-generality trade-off. In this work, we step outside this trade-off by decoupling the two capabilities at the model level: we keep the original base model for general capability, and selectively invoke the SFT expert only when domain-specific knowledge is required. Specifically, we propose CPR (Critical-Point Routing), a token-level routing framework between a base model and its expert derivative, based on critical tokens where the base model fails but the expert succeeds. We train a lightweight hierarchical router that estimates the expert-call probability per token, and pair it with a tailored inference procedure that combines momentum smoothing and threshold gating. Across diverse model-domain configurations, CPR achieves state-of-the-art across all settings, surpassing SFT expert by 1.4-5.5% in domain performance while recovering its general-capability drop from 3.4-14.5% to at most 0.5%, with minimal overhead from invoking the expert on only one-third of tokens.

</details>


### [135] [GPAgentBench-2K: Benchmarking Large Language Model Agents in Complex Clinical Action Space](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30188)
*Boqi Chen,Xudong Liu,Yunke Ao,Heejin Do,Jianing Qiu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper presents GPAgentBench-2K, a new benchmark and environment to evaluate large language model agents for primary-care decision-making under explicit safety constraints, revealing a quality-safety gap and showing that constrained RL helps but is still not clinically safe.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing clinical benchmarks for LLMs oversimplify real-world workflows into static predictions or unconstrained MDPs with limited action sets, failing to capture realistic primary-care decision-making and safety constraints. There is a need to evaluate LLM agents in a setting that more faithfully reflects GP practice, including the full range of core actions, workflow structure, and safety-critical abstention behavior.

Method: The authors construct GPAgentBench-2K from expert-validated real-world general practitioner encounter records and formalize it as a Constrained MDP for primary-care decision-making. The environment includes six key clinical action types, a topological prior over possible workflows to constrain realistic action sequences, and explicit modeling of abstention as a safety-driven action. They then evaluate 16 state-of-the-art LLMs as agents within this environment and implement a constrained reinforcement learning baseline using Constrained Group Relative Policy Optimization (C-GRPO), comparing it to unconstrained RL approaches.

Result: The evaluation shows that as the clinical action space becomes larger and more complex, the performance of all tested LLMs degrades markedly. The authors identify a clinical quality-safety gap: even the best-performing frontier LLMs, which achieve relatively high diagnosis accuracy, still violate safety constraints in more than half of high-risk cases. C-GRPO, which explicitly accounts for constraints, outperforms unconstrained RL baselines but still falls short of clinically acceptable safety levels.

Conclusion: GPAgentBench-2K provides a more realistic and safety-aware benchmark for assessing LLM-based clinical agents in primary care. The findings demonstrate that current LLMs, even when optimized with constrained RL, are not yet safe enough for high-risk clinical use, and highlight the need for further research into safety-aware decision-making, constraint handling, and robust workflow modeling in clinical AI agents.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) show great potential as clinical agents, yet existing benchmarks reduce clinical workflows to static predictions or unconstrained Markov Decision Processes (MDPs) with coarse action sets. To address this, we introduce GPAgentBench-2K, the first Constrained MDP (CMDP) LLM-agent benchmark for primary-care clinical decision-making, constructed from expert-validated records of real-world GP encounters. Our environment models a full spectrum of six foundational clinical actions, imposes a topological workflow prior over the action space, and operationalizes safety-informed abstention as a first-class outcome. Evaluating 16 state-of-the-art LLMs reveals a significant performance degradation as the action space scales. Crucially, we uncover a clinical quality-safety gap: even frontier models with the highest diagnosis accuracy violate safety constraints in over half of high-risk cases.
