Finally, we establish a reference point using Constrained Group Relative Policy Optimization (C-GRPO), and show that while explicitly modeling constraints improves performance over unconstrained RL methods, it remains far from clinically acceptable safety.

</details>


### [136] [ALTSTEER: Selective Safety Steering for Moving Beyond Hard Refusals to Constructive Alternatives](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30197)
*Hoejoon Kwon,Byeonggeuk Lim,Kahyeon Kim,YoungBin Kim*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: ALTSTEER is an inference-time method that selectively steers LLM activations using refusal signals, turning blunt refusals into more constructive, safe responses while preserving helpfulness on benign queries.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing safety alignment for LLMs struggles to balance blocking harmful outputs and staying helpful on harmless requests. Activation steering is attractive because it is training-free and works at inference time, but current safety steering methods have two major problems: (1) their triggers for when to intervene are unstable across domains, and (2) they usually steer toward rigid refusals, which prevents models from giving constructive, safe guidance. There is a need for a more nuanced steering approach that decides more reliably when to intervene and that redirects responses toward safe, helpful completions instead of just saying no.

Method: The paper introduces ALTSTEER, an inference-time safety framework that operates via activation steering within a single decoding pass. It first extracts an internal refusal-relevant signal from the model to determine, token by token or step by step, when safety steering should be activated. Once triggered, ALTSTEER performs staged steering: it initially anchors the model around a refusal-oriented behavior to avoid unsafe compliance, then gradually redirects the generation toward constructive alternative content that is still safe. This design tightly couples selective intervention (when to steer) with a two-phase steering trajectory (from refusal to constructive guidance).

Result: Applied to Llama-3.1 and Qwen2.5, ALTSTEER improves the models’ ability to provide constructive safe completions on harmful prompts, especially for base models that otherwise default to short, unhelpful refusals. Quantitative evaluations show increased safety-compliant yet helpful responses while retaining utility on benign requests, indicating that the approach does not significantly degrade normal task performance.

Conclusion: ALTSTEER demonstrates that combining a refusal-sensitive trigger with staged activation steering can better control LLM behavior at inference time. It achieves a more favorable balance between safety and helpfulness by converting blunt refusals into constructive, safe alternatives, without retraining the underlying model and while preserving benign utility across evaluated architectures.

Abstract: Safety alignment is essential for deploying large language models, requiring systems to prevent harmful compliance while preserving helpfulness on benign requests. Activation steering offers a training-free inference-time approach to safety control, but effective safety steering requires addressing two coupled questions: when to intervene and how generation should be shaped after intervention. However, existing safety steering methods remain limited along both dimensions, as their triggering mechanisms can be unstable across domains and refusal-oriented steering often yields rigid refusals rather than constructive safe guidance. To address these limitations, we propose ALTSTEER, an inference-time framework that couples selective intervention with refusal-anchored constructive redirection within a single inference pass. ALTSTEER uses an internal refusal-relevant signal to decide when to steer, and applies staged steering to shift generation from refusal-oriented control toward constructive alternatives. Evaluations on Llama-3.1 and Qwen2.5 show that ALTSTEER preserves benign utility while improving constructive safe-completion behavior, especially on models that otherwise tend to produce short refusals for harmful requests.

</details>


### [137] [When Errors Become Memories: Causal Pathway Tracing in Multi-Turn Memory-Augmented LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30198)
*Shuyao Xiao,Shengling Wang,Xuan Chen,Ke Chao,Ming Cui,Feifei Qian,Fanlin Meng,Chaoyang Mei,Chaoyong Jiang,Qi Ouyang,Junxi Yi*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: They build a causal framework to study how mistakes in long-term-memory-augmented LLMs spread over multiple turns and how to fix them.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long-term memory can make LLMs more useful by allowing them to reuse information across conversations, but it also means that one incorrect piece of information can persist and affect many later interactions. Existing evaluations focus on whether memory is stored and retrieved correctly in a single step, not on how an early mistake can propagate through time and different system components. The authors want a principled way to characterize and measure this cross-turn error propagation so that memory systems can be made safer and more reliable.

Method: They propose a structural causal model (SCM) that treats user questions, LLM responses, and memory states as nodes in a dynamic causal process spanning multiple turns. Within this model, they identify two causal pathways by which an error can enter and spread: (1) internal memory updating (how responses write to and modify the memory store) and (2) external question feedback (how user questions, potentially based on earlier outputs, feed errors back into the system). Using causal interventions on these pathways, they define four counterfactual interaction trajectories that isolate the effects of each pathway and their interaction. They then design evaluation metrics at four levels—whether wrong info is retained in memory, whether it appears in natural responses, whether it can be elicited via targeted probing, and whether it has shifted underlying probability preferences—to quantify error influence over time and distance from the original error.

Result: Empirically, they find that the influence of an initial error tends to decay as the number of subsequent interactions grows, but the pathway through memory updates causes more persistent error effects than the question-feedback pathway. Even when natural responses stop explicitly mentioning the wrong information, latent error traces can remain, detectable through diagnostic probes and probability shifts. The patterns of propagation differ depending on what kind of information is stored (memory categories) and on the specific memory mechanism used. When they use their pathway decomposition to guide repair, they observe substantial reductions in residual error: repairing questions alone cuts residual error by 27.5%, repairing memory alone cuts it by 70.2%, and repairing both nearly eliminates it with a 98.3% reduction.

Conclusion: Cross-turn errors in memory-augmented LLMs can be systematically understood through a causal-process view that separates internal memory updates from external question feedback. Error influence is not simply about whether a wrong fact is currently being output; it can persist latently and differs by memory type and mechanism. Their SCM-based framework both reveals these propagation patterns and suggests effective mitigation strategies: by specifically repairing the memory-update channel and, to a lesser extent, the question-feedback channel, systems can substantially reduce or nearly eliminate long-range error propagation in long-term-memory LLM deployments.

Abstract: Long-term memory enables large language models (LLMs) to preserve and reuse information across interactions, but it can also turn localized errors into persistent risks. Existing work mainly evaluates whether memory systems store and retrieve information correctly, leaving limited understanding of how errors propagate across responses, memory states, and future interactions. We propose a structural causal model (SCM)-based framework for cross-turn error propagation in memory-augmented LLMs. We model user questions, model responses, and memory states as a dynamic causal process, and identify two entry pathways: internal memory updating and external question feedback. By intervening on these pathways, we construct four counterfactual trajectories and quantify their downstream effects and interaction. Error influence is evaluated at four levels: memory retention, natural responses, targeted diagnostic probing, and probability-level error preference. Experiments show that error influence generally decays with interaction distance, while the memory-update pathway contributes more persistent effects than question feedback; latent errors may remain even after disappearing from natural responses. Propagation patterns also vary across memory categories and memory mechanisms. Pathway-guided restoration further validates this decomposition: Question Repair reduces residual error by 27.5%, Memory Repair by 70.2%, and Joint Repair by 98.3%, nearly eliminating residual propagation.

</details>


### [138] [When Models Hear What They Expect: Diagnosing Prosodic Heuristics in Multimodal Sarcasm Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30204)
*Yongjian Chen,Pengfei Wei,Yiqun Sun,Zhu Li,Lawrence B. Hsieh*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper evaluates whether multimodal large language models truly use prosody for pragmatic understanding (sarcasm) or rely on superficial acoustic stereotypes, finding that they over-rely on a simplistic “expressive” prosody pattern that does not match real sarcasm cues.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Although multimodal LLMs can take both text and audio, it is unclear whether they meaningfully use prosodic information for pragmatic inference like sarcasm detection, or just overfit to shallow acoustic patterns. This gap matters because many claims about multimodal understanding assume robust use of prosody, yet there has been little systematic, cross-linguistic evaluation.

Method: They study sarcasm detection in Mandarin and English using Qwen2.5-Omni and Qwen3-Omni under five modality setups that tease apart lexical content, vocal semantic information, and prosodic structure. They compare performance with and without audio, diagnose acoustic error patterns, and then run targeted audio manipulations on pitch and pausing to test whether these dimensions causally drive model decisions. They also apply the same manipulation procedure to Gemini 3 Flash Preview to test whether the behavior generalizes beyond Qwen models.

Result: Adding audio increases false positives but does not improve detection of true sarcastic cases. Error analysis shows the models tend to equate elevated pitch and irregular pausing with sarcasm, despite these not being the real sarcasm cues in the data. When the authors artificially manipulate only pitch and pausing, false positive rates can be pushed as high as 60%. The same manipulation causes similar effects in Gemini 3 Flash Preview, indicating that the problematic heuristic is shared across different architectures.

Conclusion: Current MLLMs do not robustly use prosody for pragmatic inference in sarcasm detection; instead, they rely on a shallow stereotype of “expressive” prosody (high pitch, irregular pauses). This leads to many spurious sarcasm predictions when audio is present and suggests a systemic limitation in how these models integrate acoustic information, with implications for future design and evaluation of multimodal language understanding systems.

Abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) process speech and text jointly, yet whether they exploit prosodic cues for pragmatic inference or rely on surface acoustic patterns has received little systematic investigation. We address this through sarcasm detection, evaluating Qwen2.5-Omni and Qwen3-Omni on Mandarin Chinese and English under five modality conditions that decompose the contributions of lexical content, vocal semantics, and prosodic structure. Adding audio systematically inflates false positives without improving true positive detection. Acoustic error diagnosis reveals that model errors cluster on a shared stereotype of expressive prosody, namely elevated pitch and irregular pausing, that diverges from the actual cues marking sarcasm in both languages. Targeted manipulation of only these two dimensions causally confirms the heuristic, inducing false positive rates of up to 60%. Applying the same manipulation template to Gemini~3 Flash Preview without modification replicates the effect, suggesting that the stereotype extends beyond the Qwen Omni family rather than arising from a single model architecture.

</details>


### [139] [Label Semantic Expansion via Label Guided Neural Topic Modeling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30216)
*Haojia Zheng,Yuyin Lu,Juntian Huang,Fan Ou,Yanghui Rao,Haoran Xie,Fu Lee Wang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces a label-centered topic modeling framework that expands label semantics using corpus-grounded topics via a new Label-Guided Neural Topic Model, improving label-topic alignment and downstream tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional topic models discover latent, unordered topics, while many real applications require analysis centered around predefined labels (e.g., categories, tags). Existing label-aware topic models typically use labels as supervision to learn better topics (labels-for-topics), but the resulting topics are not directly aligned with labels nor ideal for label-centered analysis or label expansion. There is a need for models that directly enrich label semantics with corpus information and ensure a tight alignment between topics and labels.

Method: The authors invert the usual labels-for-topics view and propose a topics-for-labels framework called Label Semantic Expansion (LSE), where corpus-induced topics are used to enrich sparse label representations with descriptive words. They operationalize this via a Label-Guided Neural Topic Model (LGNTM) that: (1) learns topics that are explicitly aligned with labels, (2) jointly grounds these topics in lexical space (words) and document semantic space (embeddings), and (3) includes mechanisms to preserve structural consistency between the relationships among topics and the relationships among labels. The model is trained on labeled corpora to produce label-specific topic-word distributions and label representations.

Result: Through experiments on several tasks—label-topic alignment, label expansion, topic quality (e.g., coherence), and downstream text classification—the proposed LGNTM and LSE framework show strong performance. The model outperforms or is competitive with baselines across these complementary dimensions, indicating that it produces topics that are better aligned with labels, improves label semantic representations, maintains good topic quality, and positively impacts classification performance.

Conclusion: Focusing on a topics-for-labels perspective enables directly using topic modeling to enrich and analyze predefined labels. The proposed LSE framework and LGNTM achieve label-aligned topics that are well grounded in corpus semantics and consistent with label structures, leading to better label semantic expansion, higher-quality topics, and improved downstream task performance. This establishes a more effective way to integrate topic models into label-centered content analysis workflows.

Abstract: Topic models are widely used for content analysis, where users often analyze corpora around predefined labels rather than unordered latent topics. Existing label-aware topic models mainly follow a labels-for-topics perspective, using labels to guide topic learning, while the learned topics are not directly usable for label-centered analysis. We explore the reverse topics-for-labels perspective and instantiate it as Label Semantic Expansion (LSE), which enriches sparse label representations with corpus-grounded descriptive topic words. To exploit topics in LSE effectively, we propose a Label-Guided Neural Topic Model (LGNTM), which learns dedicated label-aligned topics, grounds them in lexical and document semantic spaces, and preserves consistency between topic structures and label structures. Experiments on label-topic alignment, label expansion, topic quality, and downstream classification demonstrate strong overall performance across complementary evaluation dimensions.

</details>


### [140] [The Differential Reasoning Router: Operationalizing Cost-Aware LLM Annotation in E-commerce](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30224)
*Cheng Lyu,Jingyue Zhang,Vinny DeGenova,Mengwei Li,Yuanli Pei*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Proposes a routing framework (DRR) that decides when to use direct LLM calls, heavier reasoning models, or humans to annotate e-commerce product data, reducing cost while keeping accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In e-commerce, structured product annotations must satisfy multiple business rules. At cold start, there are few labels, the benefit of costly reasoning models is unknown, and humans must review outputs. Existing confidence-based or simple fallback strategies either waste reasoning tokens or overuse humans, and do not reason at the level of individual business rules or anticipate both models failing. A more nuanced, cost-aware routing strategy is needed to make LLM-based annotation practical and economical from day one.

Method: Introduce the Differential Reasoning Router (DRR), which models separate success probabilities for a fast “direct” LLM and a more expensive “reasoning” LLM, at both sample-level and per-business-rule level. Using these estimates, DRR adaptively routes each item and rule: easy cases go to the direct model, difficult ones where reasoning is predicted to help go to the reasoning model, and cases with high chance of double failure or rule disagreement are escalated to humans. The framework is tuned for expected accuracy and token cost, and the human-reviewed escalations are then used as targeted ground truth for further improvement of prompts, fine-tuning, calibration, and rule design.

Result: In a production e-commerce annotation workflow, DRR achieves the same accuracy as the strongest baseline router that relies only on confidence scores, while reducing reasoning-token usage by over 60%, demonstrating substantial cost savings without sacrificing quality.

Conclusion: Cost-aware, probability-based routing between direct LLMs, reasoning LLMs, and human annotators can make cold-start deployment of LLM-based e-commerce annotation both accurate and efficient. By operating at the granularity of individual business rules and using escalated cases as focused training data, DRR enables a smooth transition from human-heavy workflows to high-confidence automated systems with significantly lower reasoning costs.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used to annotate structured product data in e-commerce, but early deployment often begins as a cold-start problem: only limited pre-launch labels are available, the value of expensive reasoning is unknown, and human review is needed before the system can be trusted at scale. This challenge is especially common in rule-based annotation workflows, where each item must satisfy multiple business rules and both model errors and ambiguous rule boundaries affect final decisions. We introduce the Differential Reasoning Router (DRR), a cost-aware framework for cold-start LLM annotation that jointly optimizes model selection and human escalation. Rather than treating a reasoning model as a default fallback, DRR estimates separate success probabilities for a direct model and a reasoning model at both the sample and business-rule levels, enabling adaptive routing: easy cases are handled directly, reasoning is reserved for cases where it is expected to improve the decision, and likely double-failure or rule-disagreement cases are escalated to human annotators. The resulting labels provide targeted ground truth for prompt engineering, supervised fine-tuning, calibration, and rule refinement, enabling a gradual shift from human-heavy cold-start annotation toward high-confidence automated routing. In a production e-commerce workflow, DRR reaches accuracy parity with the strongest confidence-based router while achieving more than 60\% reasoning-token cost savings.

</details>


### [141] [Quantifying and Mitigating Korean Jamo-Level Typographical Vulnerabilities in Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30229)
*Seojin Lee,Hwanhee Lee*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper studies how Korean-specific keyboard typos at the jamo (sub-character) level break tokenization and hurt LLM performance, then proposes a method to detect such typos from model representations and selectively trigger chain-of-thought reasoning to regain accuracy cheaply.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard character-level edit models and existing grammatical error correction pipelines fail to capture and reliably fix Korean typos that happen within a syllable block, because Korean characters are composed of smaller jamo units. These intra-syllabic perturbations can yield either different but valid syllables or exposed raw jamo, both of which disrupt sub-word tokenization and negatively impact LLMs. There is a need to systematically quantify LLM vulnerability to such errors and to develop an efficient way to mitigate their impact without incurring full-time chain-of-thought costs.

Method: The authors introduce five types of jamo-level perturbations that simulate realistic Korean keyboard typos and apply them to the KMMLU benchmark. They then evaluate four language models under varying perturbation intensities, measuring accuracy degradation. They analyze internal model representations to see how typo corruption changes them relative to ordinary incorrect answers, and train a simple linear probe on these representations to detect perturbed inputs, testing cross-perturbation generalization via AUROC. Finally, they propose Typo-Aware Chain-of-Thought (TACoT), which uses the probe to route suspected-typo inputs to chain-of-thought inference while leaving clean inputs to standard inference, and they measure the trade-off between recovered accuracy and additional inference cost.

Result: Accuracy on KMMLU decreases monotonically as the intensity of jamo-level perturbations increases, and increasing model size (parameter scaling) does not yield robustness to these intra-syllabic typos. Representation analysis shows that typo-induced errors cause distinct shifts not explained by generic answer incorrectness. The linear probe trained on internal representations successfully detects even unseen perturbation types with high AUROC, indicating a strong, generalizable typo signal. Using this probe in TACoT recovers a large portion of the accuracy gains normally obtained by always using chain-of-thought, while incurring only a fraction of the associated inference cost.

Conclusion: Korean jamo-level typos constitute a unique perturbation regime that standard tokenization and error correction methods handle poorly, leading to substantial LLM performance degradation. These typos leave a detectable signature in model representations that can be captured with a lightweight linear probe, which generalizes across perturbation types. By exploiting this signal, the proposed TACoT framework selectively activates chain-of-thought reasoning only for likely-typo inputs, achieving an effective robustness–efficiency trade-off. The work highlights the need for language-specific robustness analyses and suggests representation-level routing as a practical approach to mitigate keyboard noise in LLM deployment.

Abstract: Korean introduces an additional typographical perturbation level not captured by ordinary character-level edit models: because syllable blocks are internally composed of sub-character units called jamo, keyboard-level errors can occur within a syllable, either producing a valid but semantically altered character or exposing raw jamo on the surface. Both outcomes disrupt sub-word tokenization and are not reliably corrected by existing grammatical error correction pipelines, leaving LLMs directly exposed to corrupted inputs. To quantify this vulnerability, we apply five jamo-level perturbation types to the KMMLU benchmark and evaluate four language models, finding that accuracy declines monotonically with perturbation intensity and that parameter scaling does not confer robustness against intra-syllabic noise. We further show that typo-corrupted inputs induce a distinct shift in internal representations that is not reducible to ordinary answer incorrectness, and that a simple linear probe trained on these representations detects unseen perturbation types with high AUROC. Motivated by this signal, we propose Typo-Aware Chain-of-Thought (TACoT), which routes inputs to chain-of-thought inference only when the probe detects a likely typo, recovering a substantial portion of the CoT accuracy gain at a fraction of the inference cost.

</details>


### [142] [PaperBanana-Interact: Scientific Diagram Refinement with Multi-Turn Human Feedback](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30241)
*Xueqing Wu,Ashwin Balasubramanian,Bingxuan Li,Dawei Zhu,Kai-Wei Chang,Yale Song,Yiwen Song,Rui Meng,Tomas Pfister,Nanyun Peng*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: They build a benchmark and system for multi-turn, feedback-driven scientific diagram generation, diagnose common failure modes, and show their multi-agent method improves quality and reduces forgetting over turns.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Single-turn automatic diagram generation cannot fully satisfy authors’ nuanced visual and communicative preferences; users naturally want iterative refinement and existing work does not adequately support or evaluate this multi-turn workflow. Manual user studies to study this are expensive and not scalable.

Method: 1) Construct MTPaperBananaBench, a benchmark of 292 diagrams annotated with 3,518 fine-grained user requirements. 2) Build a user simulator that, at each turn, detects unmet requirements and surfaces k of them as natural language feedback to emulate multi-turn interaction. 3) Analyze baseline multi-turn systems under this setup to characterize failure modes like quality drift and forgetting. 4) Propose PaperBanana-Interact, a multi-agent system with an internal critique-and-refine loop that iteratively updates diagrams while aiming to preserve previously satisfied requirements and improve overall quality.

Result: On the new benchmark with simulated users, baseline multi-turn systems show two systematic problems: diagram quality tends to worsen over turns (quality drift) and previously implemented features are sometimes lost (forgetting). PaperBanana-Interact reverses this trend: it consistently improves quality over turns, achieves 11.9–18.6 higher quality scores than baselines, and reduces forgetting by 3.7–6.2 points.

Conclusion: Modeling diagram generation as a multi-turn, interactive process is both necessary and non-trivial. A benchmark plus user simulator enables scalable study of this problem, revealing quality drift and forgetting as key challenges. A multi-agent critique-and-refine approach like PaperBanana-Interact can systematically mitigate these issues, leading to higher-quality, more stable diagrams over iterative turns.

Abstract: Recent efforts have aimed to automate scientific diagram generation from paper content (Lin et al., 2026; Zhu et al., 2026a). However, fully satisfying an author's visual and communicative preferences in a single turn is challenging: in our formative user study (N = 14), all participants requested further revisions after viewing an initial draft, and 86% of them rated the refined diagrams as more satisfactory. Despite the clear demand, the multi-turn workflow remains largely underexplored. To bridge this gap, we present MTPaperBananaBench, a benchmark for multi-turn diagram generation containing 292 images annotated with 3,518 user requirements. To reduce expensive human studies and enable scalable benchmarking, we construct a user simulator that, at each turn, identifies unsatisfied requirements and converts k of them into natural language feedback. Evaluating both requirement satisfaction and overall diagram quality reveals two key failure modes shared across baseline multiturn systems: (1) quality drift, where diagram quality progressively declines over turns, and (2) forgetting, where previously implemented features are lost in subsequent turns. To address these issues, we introduce PaperBanana-Interact, a multi-agent system that refines diagrams via an internal critique-and-refine loop. PaperBanana-Interact consistently improves rather than degrades diagram quality across turns, outperforming baselines by 11.9-18.6 points in quality score and reducing forgetting by 3.7-6.2 points.

</details>


### [143] [Beyond Surface Forms: Symbolic Edits as a Test for Logical Reasoning with LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30256)
*Ramya Keerthy Thatikonda,Wray Buntine,Ehsan Shareghi*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: They build a tool-based pipeline that perturbs the logical structure of reasoning problems (at the symbolic level) and shows that LLMs often fail to update their answers consistently with these changes, revealing unreliable logical reasoning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Logical reasoning is important for LLMs, but current models behave unpredictably when minor wording or structural changes are made to problems. It is unclear whether they truly follow logical structure or rely on superficial patterns. Natural language makes it hard to systematically test this, so a controlled way to manipulate the underlying logic is needed to rigorously evaluate LLM reasoning robustness.

Method: They design a framework that starts from symbolic representations of first-order logic and constraint satisfaction problems, applies controlled, label-preserving edits (especially to logical operators and structural components), and then converts the edited problems back into natural language. They then use these systematically perturbed datasets to test a range of LLMs under cumulative and individual operator edits and compare how their predictions change.

Result: Across models of different sizes and families, reasoning under these controlled operator edits is inconsistent: models sometimes correctly adjust their conclusions when operators or structure change, but frequently fail to track the logically required consequences. Quantitative metrics and qualitative examples both show that performance degrades and behaves unreliably under such stress tests.

Conclusion: Even advanced LLMs do not robustly follow underlying logical structures; their answers are sensitive to controlled changes in logical operators and other symbolic elements. The proposed framework serves as an automated stress test that exposes these weaknesses and provides multidimensional evaluations of reasoning reliability, highlighting the need for better methods to achieve faithful logical reasoning in LLMs.

Abstract: Logical reasoning with large language models (LLMs) is a critical capability, as it reflects a system's ability to correctly deduce hypotheses from a given context using faithful deductive processes. However, LLM reasoning has often been shown to be sensitive to small surface-level variations in problem formulation, raising questions about whether models truly follow the underlying logical structure. Studying this behavior is challenging because the symbolic components of logical problems, such as operators and predicates, are difficult to systematically manipulate in natural language. We introduce a tool-driven framework for generating controlled, label-preserving edits to logical reasoning problems. Our method operates on symbolic representations of first-order logic and constraint satisfaction problem tasks, enabling targeted modifications to logical operators and other structural components before translating them back into natural language. Using this framework, we evaluate various LLMs under cumulative and individual operator edits and analyze their behavior in response to these changes. Our quantitative and qualitative analyses show that LLM reasoning behavior under controlled operator edits is inconsistent, regardless of model size or family: models sometimes adapt correctly to structural changes but often fail to track their logical consequences. The results from this automated stress test enable an evaluation of language models across different dimensions and help measure the reliability of their reasoning.

</details>


### [144] [Stratified Consistency Distillation for Natural Language Formalization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30258)
*Zhichao Hou,Ferhat Erata,Joe Lilien,MohamadAli Torkamani*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: They improve natural-language-to-logic translation for neurosymbolic reasoning by distilling consistent logical forms from an LLM into a smaller model using a stratified selection strategy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Neurosymbolic systems depend on accurate translation from natural language to logical formulas, but current approaches rely heavily on hand-crafted prompts, which are hard to scale and adapt to new domains or input formats. There is a need for a more systematic, data-driven way to improve translation accuracy and robustness.

Method: They propose Stratified Consistency Distillation. First, for each input, a strong LLM generates K candidate logical translations. These are clustered into equivalence classes based on semantic similarity. Then, depending on the entropy (disagreement) among candidates, different selection mechanisms are used: majority voting when entropy is low; an LLM-as-a-judge to choose the best cluster when entropy is medium; and logical unification or abstention when entropy is high. The selected outputs serve as pseudo-labels to fine-tune a smaller model specialized for logical translation.

Result: Experiments show that the fine-tuned smaller model substantially and consistently outperforms baselines on logical translation tasks. The gains are reflected in higher Pass@K scores and improvements in a new metric they introduce, Equivalent Logical Similarity, which captures semantic correctness of the translated formulas.

Conclusion: Stratified Consistency Distillation can effectively transfer the logical translation capabilities of a strong LLM into a smaller model by exploiting consistency across multiple candidate translations and entropy-aware selection strategies. This reduces reliance on brittle prompt engineering and offers a scalable route to more accurate neurosymbolic reasoning systems.

Abstract: Neurosymbolic reasoning has shown promising success in addressing complex reasoning tasks by combining large language models (LLMs) and symbolic solvers. While this approach shows promise, a fundamental challenge remains: improving the accuracy of translations from natural language to logical formulas. Current methods predominantly rely on prompt engineering, which is difficult to scale across different domains and input formats. Drawing inspiration from the success of fine-tuning in other model adaptation and alignment applications, we propose a fine-tuning-based Stratified Consistency Distillation approach: (1) We generate K logical translations per input using a frontier LLM and cluster them by semantic equivalence (2) Based on the entropy level, we apply majority voting (low entropy), LLM-as-a-Judge (medium entropy), or unification/abstention (high entropy), and (3) fine-tune a smaller model using the selected pseudo-labels. Our experiments show significant and consistent improvements in both Pass@K and our novel Equivalent Logical Similarity metrics, demonstrating the potential of advancing logical translation through consistency distillation.

</details>


### [145] [Using Prosody to Predict Syntactic Structure](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30260)
*Junghyun Min,Alex Warstadt,Tamar I. Regev,Tiago Pimentel,Ethan Gotlieb Wilcox*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper quantifies how much syntactic information is carried by prosody (timing features) using mutual information computed with multimodal language models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Although it is known that prosody (rhythm, pauses, lengthening) reflects syntactic structure, it is unclear how strong and systematic this relationship is, and how to compare it across corpora and features. Existing work is often theory-specific, limited in scale, or not easily comparable. The authors want a general, quantitative, and scalable way to measure how much syntactic information is encoded in prosody.

Method: They frame the syntax–prosody interface in information-theoretic terms, defining the interaction between prosody and syntax as mutual information. They propose a general framework that uses multimodal language models trained on aligned speech-text corpora to estimate how much prosodic features (e.g., word durations, inter-word pauses) reduce uncertainty about syntactic representations (e.g., parse structures or syntactic labels). The framework is modular (can swap in different syntactic formalisms) and structure-agnostic, allowing separate estimation for different prosodic cues and structural components. They apply this framework to large corpora of English read audiobooks and spontaneous conversations.

Result: Across both domains, they find that prosodic features indeed carry nontrivial syntactic information, with prosody reducing syntactic uncertainty in spontaneous conversations by as much as 10.2%. They also show differential contributions of specific features (word duration vs. pauses) and provide corpus-based quantitative profiles of the syntax–prosody relationship.

Conclusion: Prosodic timing cues contain measurable, non-negligible information about syntactic structure, and this information can be rigorously quantified using mutual information estimated via multimodal language models. The framework they introduce is general and extensible, offering a new empirical tool to evaluate theories of the syntax–prosody interface and to compare prosodic contributions across features, structures, and domains.

Abstract: While it is well-established that prosody carries crucial cues for syntactic structure, the degree and nature of correspondence between these two domains remains contested. We investigate the syntax-prosody interface through an information-theoretic lens, quantifying the interaction between prosodic features and syntactic representations as their mutual information. We provide a general-purpose framework for estimating this quantity over large speech-text corpora using multimodal language models. Our framework is structure-agnostic and modular, insofar as it can be used to measure the contributions of individual prosodic features or components of structure. We evaluate the syntax-prosody relationship for two features (word duration and inter-word pauses) across two domains--read audiobooks and spontaneous conversations--both in English. Our results demonstrate that prosody contains measurable syntactic information, with prosodic features reducing syntactic uncertainty in spontaneous conversations by up to 10.2%. Our findings offer new empirical support for several theoretical accounts of the syntax-prosody interface.

</details>


### [146] [Read the Room, Read the Image: Understanding Indirect Speech Acts in Multimodal Visual Contexts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30270)
*Jaehee Kim,Ji Hoon Chung,Seoyoon Park,Unsol Kim,Kyungwon Park,Ji Hak Kim,Yi-Jun Chen,Hansaem Kim*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces READI, a multimodal benchmark to test how well models understand indirect speech acts using both images and dialogue, especially in English and Korean.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing text and multimodal datasets mostly test either explicit context in language or basic visual recognition, but they rarely require models to do pragmatic reasoning about indirect speech acts that depend on nuanced context, which is particularly important in high‑context languages like Korean.

Method: The authors design READI as a vision-based pragmatic question answering (V-PQA) benchmark where indirectness is graded according to pragmatic theory. The tasks require integrated reasoning over visual scenes and dialogue to interpret indirect speech acts, and the dataset is constructed for cross-lingual use in English and Korean.

Result: State-of-the-art multimodal models perform poorly on the READI benchmark, especially as the level of indirectness increases, indicating that current architectures struggle with visually grounded indirect speech act interpretation.

Conclusion: READI exposes a significant gap in current multimodal models’ ability to handle context-dependent pragmatic reasoning, highlighting the need for new methods and benchmarks that directly target understanding of indirect speech acts in visually grounded, multilingual settings.

Abstract: Indirect speech acts (ISAs) require pragmatic reasoning over context, as directive intent can- not be inferred from surface form alone. Prior text-based studies and existing multimodal benchmarks largely overlook this requirement, focusing instead on explicitly encoded context or perceptual recognition, and thus underex- plore context-dependent pragmatic understand- ing, particularly in high-context languages such as Korean. We introduce READI, a multimodal benchmark for evaluating ISA understanding through integrated reasoning over visual con- text and dialogue. READI models graded in- directness grounded in pragmatic theory and formulates the task as vision-based pragmatic question answering (V-PQA), supporting cross- lingual evaluation in English and Korean. Ex- periments show that even state-of-the-art multi- modal models struggle with visually grounded indirect speech acts, with performance declin- ing as indirectness increases, underscoring the need for benchmarks that explicitly target con- textual pragmatic reasoning.

</details>


### [147] [AIA$^{2}$: Attribute-Agnostic Imbalance Augmentation for Subgroup Robustness](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30297)
*Hanshu Rao,Guangzeng Han,Xiaolei Huang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces AIA^2, a method to improve robustness on underrepresented data subgroups by automatically discovering and augmenting imbalance patterns without needing explicit subgroup labels.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Real-world datasets often have complex imbalance patterns not only in labels but also in latent attributes like topic or demographics. These imbalances create poorly performing subgroups, yet most existing methods only handle label imbalance and assume subgroup labels are known, which is rarely the case. There is a need for a practical approach that can improve worst-subgroup robustness without requiring explicit attribute or subgroup annotations.

Method: AIA^2 is a three-stage framework. First, it uncovers latent semantic distributions in the data to identify diverse imbalance patterns without using explicit attribute labels. Second, it defines data slices that jointly capture examples that are both hard to learn and underrepresented in those latent distributions, targeting the most vulnerable subgroups. Third, it uses a large language model to perform subgroup-aware data augmentation focused on these slices, effectively rebalancing the training data with respect to hidden subgroups.

Result: Across 5 popular, attribute-rich corpora, AIA^2 improves performance on the lowest-performing (worst) subgroups and achieves consistent gains over strong baselines designed for robustness and imbalance handling. Ablation experiments show that each component—latent-imbalance discovery, slice selection, and LLM-based augmentation—contributes complementary benefits to the final performance.

Conclusion: AIA^2 offers a practical, annotation-free way to increase robustness to hidden subgroup imbalances in text datasets. By automatically discovering imbalance patterns and using LLMs for targeted augmentation, it consistently improves worst-group performance and overall robustness, making it suitable for complex, attribute-rich domains where explicit subgroup labels are absent or incomplete.

Abstract: Attributes describing data content and context can induce diverse imbalance patterns that go beyond label imbalance alone. However, existing studies primarily address label imbalance while overlooking data attributes, such as topics and demographics, which can induce meaningful subgroup structure while causing model degradation on underrepresented subgroups. We propose Attribute-Agnostic Imbalance Augmentation (AIA$^{2}$), a framework for improving model robustness under varying subgroup imbalances without explicit subgroup annotations. AIA$^{2}$ automatically discovers varying imbalances via latent semantic distributions, obtains slices with both learning difficulty and subgroup imbalance deficits, and deploys a large language model (LLM) for subgroup-aware imbalance augmentation. We have evaluated AIA$^{2}$ on 5 popular corpora with rich domains and their attribute values, covering social issues and diverse topics. Results show improved performance on the lowest-performing subgroups and consistent gains over competitive baselines. Ablation studies confirm complementary contributions from each component, and additional analyses show that AIA$^{2}$ provides a practical and consistent way to improve worst-group robustness under data subgroup imbalance. Code is available at https://github.com/trust-nlp/AIA2-Subgroup-Robustness.

</details>


### [148] [Lazy Grounding: Attacking Search Agents with Factual Evidence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30303)
*Yulin Zhang,Yukun Huang,Sanxing Chen,Tianyi Lin,Ziang Yang,Xunjian Yin,Bhuwan Dhingra*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper studies a new failure mode of retrieval-augmented LLM agents called “lazy grounding,” where models incorrectly adopt answers supported by factual but off-target retrieved documents (for nearby questions), showing this can significantly reduce accuracy even without any misinformation in the corpus.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While search-augmented agents are used to reduce hallucinations by grounding responses in retrieved web evidence, they introduce a new vulnerability: if the retrieval returns misleading or poisoned content, agents may propagate errors. Existing work focuses mostly on overtly false or malicious documents, but the authors suspect that even fully factual evidence, when relevant to a neighboring but different question, may still systematically mislead agents. This gap motivates a study of how and when factual, off-target evidence can be misapplied and degrade performance.

Method: The authors define and operationalize “lazy grounding”: a failure where the model uses retrieved evidence that truthfully answers a different, nearby question, and then adopts that nearby answer for the original question. They construct nearby-evidence test cases by creating answer-changing rewrites of benchmark questions, such that each retrieved document correctly supports the rewritten question but is retrieved for the original question. They then evaluate 12 combinations of LLMs and benchmarks, measuring (1) overall accuracy drop when nearby evidence is present, and (2) the rate at which models adopt the nearby (incorrect for the current question) answer. They also analyze how the position of nearby evidence in the context and its “answer-shaped” nature affects the likelihood of lazy grounding.

Result: Across 12 model–benchmark combinations, the presence of nearby but off-target evidence reduces accuracy by an average of 5.9 percentage points, with degradation as high as 17.3 percentage points in some settings. In every evaluated configuration, models exhibit nearby-answer adoption, indicating that lazy grounding is a pervasive issue. The phenomenon becomes more pronounced when misleading nearby evidence is placed later in the context or is more “answer-shaped” (e.g., concise, declarative answer-like text), suggesting that models overweight such evidence during answer generation.

Conclusion: The authors conclude that retrieval alone is not sufficient to guarantee robust or truthful behavior in search-augmented agents: even fully factual evidence can be misapplied and cause systematic errors via lazy grounding. Therefore, robust search agents must incorporate defenses not just against misinformation and poisoned content, but also against the inappropriate use of factual, off-target evidence—for example through better question-evidence alignment checks, reasoning over evidence relevance, or architectural changes that reduce overreliance on answer-shaped snippets.

Abstract: Search agents reduce hallucination by grounding answers in retrieved web evidence. Yet reliance on retrieval also creates an attack surface: poisoned corpora with false or malicious documents can cause agents to reproduce misinformation. We show that falsehood is not necessary -- a search agent can be misled by factual evidence for a nearby question, adopting that nearby answer even when it does not answer the current question. We call this failure lazy grounding. We expose lazy grounding using nearby evidence from answer-changing rewrites of benchmark questions. Each document truthfully supports a neighboring rewritten question, but is surfaced for the original question. Across 12 model-benchmark pairs, nearby evidence reduces accuracy by 5.9 points on average and by up to 17.3 points, while inducing nearby-answer adoption in every setting. The effect is stronger when nearby evidence appears later or is more answer-shaped. Our results show that robust search agents must defend against not only misinformation but also the misapplication of factual evidence. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/frankyzha/lazy-grounding.

</details>


### [149] [Beyond Token-Level Guidance: Inference-Time Alignment of Specialized LLMs via Cross-Family Representation Steering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30319)
*Jin Gan,Xin Li,Jun Luo*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces CREST, an inference-time alignment method that improves the safety of specialized LLMs without harming their domain performance, by steering hidden states using safety directions from a guidance model and avoiding token-level interference problems.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Specialized LLMs fine-tuned for particular domains can lose safety safeguards, but existing inference-time alignment methods that use a separate safety or guidance model often degrade domain performance and suffer from unreliable guidance due to differing expertise between models. There is a need for a plug-and-play, computationally light method that reliably improves safety while preserving specialized capabilities.

Method: The authors identify a key issue called complementary expertise orthogonality between a specialized base model and a general-domain guidance model, which leads to failure modes such as stop token interference where the guidance model pushes for continuation beyond the base model’s correct stopping point. To overcome this, they propose CREST, which extracts safety directions from a separate guidance model and uses them to steer the hidden representations of the specialized base model directly at inference time, instead of combining token-level logits or relying on decoding-level interventions. CREST can use guidance models from any family and avoids token-structural constraints that cause interference.

Result: CREST improves safety on benchmarks by up to 22.2% compared with existing inference-time alignment baselines, especially in settings where finetuning for specialization has weakened safety. It preserves domain-specific capabilities of the specialized models and does not harm the safety of models that are already well-aligned.

Conclusion: Inference-time alignment can be made both safer and more reliable for specialized LLMs by operating in representation space rather than token space. CREST addresses guidance unreliability and stop token interference arising from orthogonal expertise between base and guidance models, offering a plug-and-play method that enhances safety while maintaining or even improving specialized capabilities, and generalizes across different model families.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) finetuned for specialized domains represent crucial high-impact applications. Inference-time alignment improves safety degraded from specialization finetuning without requiring substantial computational resources, complementing finetuning-based methods with an easy-to-use, plug-and-play solution. However, existing inference-time methods fail to reliably improve safety without disrupting domain capability. We identify the root cause as complementary expertise orthogonality: specialized base models and general-domain guidance models have orthogonal competencies, making the guidance signal unreliable for specialized generation. This primarily manifests as stop token interference, where the guidance model's tendency toward continuation overrides the base model's decision to stop, burying correct answers under guidance-induced continuation. To address this problem, we propose CREST, an inference-time alignment method that steers base model hidden representations using safety directions extracted from a guidance model of any family, avoiding token-level structural limitations entirely. CREST improves safety where specialization has weakened it while preserving both domain-specific capability and the safety of already well-aligned models, outperforming baselines by up to 22.2\% on safety benchmarks. Our code is available at: https://github.com/DecayingSeart/CREST.

</details>


### [150] [On the Design of Qwen3.8-Next Architecture: Evaluation, Efficiency, and Training Stability](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30320)
*Zihan Qiu,Zekun Wang,Xiao Li,Yanpeng Li,Yang Xu,Yixuan Wang,Huaqing Zhang,Rui Men,Bochao Mao,Chengruidong Zhang,Fan Zhou,Hao Luo,Haofeng Huang,Haoran Lian,Haoyan Huang,Hongqing Chen,Jianwei Zhang,Jing Xu,Junjie Wang,Langshi Chen,Liangyu Wang,Linlang Jiang,Man Yuan,Minmin Sun,Peng Jin,Siqi Zhang,Siyu Wang,Xingzhang Ren,Yakai Wang,Yi Zhang,Yiming Dong,Yizhong Cao,Yubo Ma,Yunfei Mao,Bo Zheng,Dayiheng Liu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Qwen3.8-Flash-Next is a 125B-parameter sparse MoE language model that matches or beats a much larger predecessor on many benchmarks while using far fewer active parameters, tokens, and FLOPs, via architectural changes, n‑gram embeddings, and an efficiency-focused optimizer recipe.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To build a large language model that is simultaneously more efficient, more capable, and more stable than its predecessor, reducing active parameters, training tokens, and FLOPs without sacrificing downstream performance, and to understand how architectural and optimization choices jointly affect loss, benchmarks, efficiency, and stability.

Method: Design a sparse mixture-of-experts model with 125B total parameters but only 6B activated per token plus 51B n-gram embeddings off-accelerator; employ a hybrid token-mixing scheme combining Gated DeltaNet with periodic full attention layers that are later replaced by Qwen Sparse Attention; widen the residual stream into four gated branches (Gated Residual); add capacity via a host-memory n-gram embedding layer; and co-design the architecture with the Muon optimizer, systematically ablating and evaluating each change along three axes: training and downstream loss, computational cost in training/prefill/decode, and impact on hyperparameters and training stability.

Result: On 14 pre-training benchmarks, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next outperforms the larger 397B-A17B predecessor on 8 tasks and is at most 2.6 points behind on the rest while using one-third the activated parameters and training tokens and roughly one-ninth the training FLOPs; it shows that increasing the n-gram vocabulary monotonically reduces loss but leads to saturated downstream accuracy, and the combined architecture–optimizer setup shifts optimal learning rate and batch size upward, removes the need for batch-size warmup, and significantly improves robustness in stress tests.

Conclusion: Jointly optimizing architecture, auxiliary capacity (n-gram embeddings), sparse attention mechanisms, and the Muon optimizer yields a sparse MoE model that is more efficient, competitive or superior in downstream performance, and more stable than a much larger baseline, demonstrating that loss, benchmarks, efficiency, and stability must be treated as a single integrated design problem.

Abstract: We describe the architecture and ablations of Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, a sparse mixture-of-experts model with 125B parameters, 6B activated per token, and additional 51B parameters of n-gram embedding tables held off the accelerator. On fourteen pre-training benchmarks the model leads the 397B-A17B predecessor on eight and trails it on the rest by at most 2.6 points, at 1/3 the activated parameters, 1/3 the training tokens, and roughly 1/9 the training FLOPs. Token mixing uses a layer-wise hybrid of Gated DeltaNet (GDN) and global attention, with one full-attention layer in every four; at continued-pretraining time those full-attention layers are replaced by Qwen Sparse Attention (QSA), which scores context at micro-block granularity with a compressed lightweight indexer. The residual stream is widened to four branches and read through an elementwise gate, a design we call the Gated Residual (GR). Capacity is added outside the backbone by a single n-gram embedding layer whose tables are prefetched from host memory. We evaluate every candidate change along three axes: loss together with downstream benchmarks; the cost of the change in training, prefill and decode; and its effect on the optimal hyperparameters and training stability. Loss and downstream accuracy do not always move together: enlarging the n-gram vocabulary lowers loss monotonically while downstream accuracy saturates. The architecture and the Muon optimizer together shift the optimal learning rate and batch size upwards, render batch-size warmup unnecessary, and substantially improve stability under stress tests. Loss, benchmarks, efficiency and stability form one design problem. Solved jointly, they yield a recipe that is simultaneously more efficient, more capable and more stable.

</details>


### [151] [Sequential Trajectories and Simultaneous Blending: Multi-Emotion Modeling for Instruction-Following TTS](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30325)
*Yan Zhou,Yun Hong,Yang Feng*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: HybridEmo is a post-training framework for TTS that enables controllable multi-emotion speech (emotion trajectories and blended emotions) using a hybrid, sample-aware reward and Group Relative Policy Optimization, outperforming prior emotional TTS systems without harming speaker similarity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing emotional TTS models typically assume a single, utterance-level emotion and are not designed to follow complex natural-language emotional instructions involving multiple emotions over time or blended affect. Standard supervised fine-tuning fails to explicitly optimize emotion realization, and single-emotion rewards cannot capture structure-aware feedback for trajectories or pair-aware feedback for blended emotions. There is a need for a method that can align TTS outputs with rich, multi-emotion instructions while preserving other qualities such as speaker similarity.

Method: The authors define two multi-emotion TTS tasks: (1) emotion trajectory, where speech must follow several ordered emotional stages; and (2) emotion blending, where multiple emotions co-occur throughout the utterance. They propose HybridEmo, a post-training framework that starts from supervised fine-tuned models and then performs policy optimization over speech tokens via Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). A sample-aware hybrid reward is designed: for trajectory samples, a segment-aligned consistency reward combines the average evidence over stages with the weakest-stage evidence, to ensure both global correctness and completeness of all stages; for blending samples, a GMM-based reward uses frame-level support from the union of target-emotion anchors in a precomputed emotion embedding space plus an utterance-level margin emphasizing the weaker target emotion. Both trajectory and blending branches share an ASR-based reward to maintain intelligibility and are optimized within a single unified policy.

Result: On the MultiEmo-Test benchmark, HybridEmo markedly improves metrics of trajectory correctness (how closely the produced emotional stages follow the prescribed sequence) and blending intensity (how strongly and distinctly multiple emotions are expressed) compared with baselines. These gains come without clear degradation in speaker similarity. Human listening tests show that raters prefer HybridEmo over CosyVoice 3 and EmoVoice-0.5B, and have nearly balanced preferences between HybridEmo and Qwen3-TTS, indicating competitive or superior perceptual quality and emotional control.

Conclusion: HybridEmo demonstrates that carefully designed hybrid rewards and GRPO-based post-training can effectively align TTS models with complex multi-emotion instructions, covering both temporal emotion trajectories and emotion blending within a single framework. The approach yields better control and perceived emotional expressivity while preserving speaker similarity and intelligibility, and sets a strong baseline for future research on fine-grained, instruction-following emotional TTS.

Abstract: Natural-language instructions enable flexible control of synthesized speech, yet emotional TTS systems primarily model a single utterance-level affect, leaving multi-emotion control underexplored. We study two complementary multi-emotion TTS tasks: emotion trajectory, which spans several ordered affective stages, and emotion blending, in which multiple emotions coexist throughout an utterance. These tasks expose a supervision mismatch: supervised fine-tuning (SFT) does not explicitly evaluate emotion features, while single-emotion rewards provide neither structure-aware feedback for trajectory completion nor pair-aware feedback for blending. We introduce HybridEmo, a post-training framework that initializes both tasks with SFT and then aligns the speech-token policy through Group Relative Policy Optimization using a sample-aware hybrid reward. For trajectory samples, segment-aligned consistency combines average and weakest-stage evidence to preserve the correctness and completeness of prescribed stages. For blending samples, a GMM-based reward combines frame-level support from the union of target-emotion anchors in an offline emotion space with an utterance-level weaker-target margin. Both branches share an ASR reward and are routed within a unified policy. On MultiEmo-Test, HybridEmo significantly improves trajectory correctness and blending intensity, without a noticeable degradation in speaker similarity. Human evaluation prefers HybridEmo to CosyVoice 3 and EmoVoice-0.5B, with nearly balanced preferences against Qwen3-TTS.

</details>


### [152] [Do Small Models Use the Law You Give Them? Measuring Context Use on a Bilingual Bangladesh Legal Benchmark](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30327)
*Moniruzzaman Mahadi,Abrar Mohammed Tanzim Alam,Sayma Siddika Monalisa,Mir Mohammad Asif Abdullah,Swakkhar Shatabda,Md Adnan Arefeen*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper investigates how fine-tuning affects legal QA models, showing that higher answer accuracy does not necessarily mean models better use the legal text provided in context.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To clarify what it actually means to “adapt” language models to law: does fine-tuning make them better at using the specific governing legal provisions supplied at inference time, or does it merely improve pattern-matching and scoring behavior? The authors focus on Bangladeshi bilingual legal QA, where errors may stem from scoring, retrieval, or misusing relevant law, and current evaluations often conflate these factors.

Method: They build a hierarchy-preserving statutory corpus for Bangladeshi law, curate 2,165 bilingual fine-tuning examples and a 150-item control set where the governing law is supplied. They evaluate six small instruction-tuned models (Llama-3.2 and Qwen3.5 variants plus Gemma-4-E2B), each with three LoRA fine-tuning seeds. To disentangle effects of scoring, retrieval, and model reasoning, they use: (1) constrained option-letter scoring; (2) cyclic rotation of answer options; and (3) controlled removal of the governing legal provision. They also apply an exact-line parser to attribute accuracy gains on Bar Council exam-style questions.

Result: For Bar Council-style questions, an exact-line parser suggests a large 50% accuracy gain for a Qwen3.5-2B adapter, but option-letter scoring shows only a 3% gain, revealing a big sensitivity to how scoring is done. For Gemma-4-E2B, different scoring methods even disagree on which system is better. When the governing provision is guaranteed present, most models and adapters gain 14.7–19.3 percentage points in accuracy; removing this provision reduces accuracy by 8.0–15.3 points for base models and 13.8–14.9 for adapters. Yet difference-in-differences analysis finds no increase in reliance on the governing provision after fine-tuning, despite higher headline accuracy.

Conclusion: Fine-tuning can boost legal QA accuracy without making models more dependent on or faithful to the specific legal provisions provided in context. Evaluation methods and metrics (scorer choice, retrieval setup, and treatment of governing provisions) critically shape perceived gains. Therefore, claims about “legal adaptation” of LMs must carefully separate scorer artifacts, retrieval quality, and genuine model reasoning over law. The authors release corpus, code, and data to support more rigorous future evaluation of legal QA systems.

Abstract: Fine-tuning can improve legal question-answering accuracy without improving how models use law supplied in context. We study this distinction in bilingual Bangladeshi legal QA, where observed errors can arise from answer scoring, retrieval, or failure to use relevant law. We construct a hierarchy-preserving statutory corpus, 2,165 reviewed bilingual fine-tuning examples, and a 150-item supplied-law control. We evaluate six instruction-tuned models: Llama-3.2-1B, Llama-3.2-3B, Qwen3.5-0.8B, Qwen3.5-2B, Qwen3.5-4B, and Gemma-4-E2B, with three LoRA seeds per model. To separate effects, we combine constrained option-letter scoring, cyclic option rotation, and controlled removal of the governing provision. On 398 Bar Council outputs, an exact-line parser attributes an accuracy gain of 50.0\% to the Qwen3.5-2B seed-42 adapter, whereas option scoring yields only $3.0\%$. For Gemma-4-E2B, the two scoring methods favor different systems. When the governing provision is guaranteed to be present, five of six reference models improve by $14.7\%-19.3\%$ under the four-order criterion. Removing that provision reduces accuracy by $8.0\%-15.3\%$ for models and by $13.8\%-14.9\%$ points for their adapters. However, difference-in differences estimates show no increase in reliance on the governing provision after fine-tuning. Results show that legal adaptation claims require separating scorer, retriever, and model effects. Our Code and data are available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/bangladesh-legal-qa-11E3

</details>


### [153] [Auditing MCQA Benchmarks through Probability Landscapes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30372)
*Minsoo Song,Chanjun Park*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper presents a probabilistic framework that uses language model output distributions to audit multiple-choice QA benchmarks at both the dataset and individual item level, helping detect structural issues and flawed questions more efficiently.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Performance of large language models on multiple-choice QA benchmarks is saturating, and new, harder datasets are costly to validate because manual question vetting and error analysis are labor-intensive. There is a need for scalable, quantitative tools to assess benchmark quality, understand residual difficulty, and automatically surface potentially flawed or low-quality items for human review instead of relying purely on accuracy metrics or exhaustive manual inspection.

Method: The authors propose a two-part probabilistic auditing framework based solely on model answer probabilities. (1) Benchmark-level analysis: they represent each question by two statistics derived from the model’s output distribution over answer options: the top prediction probability (P_top1) as a measure of confidence, and normalized residual entropy (H_norm) to capture how much probability mass is spread among non-top answers (residual option competition). They then summarize the overall ‘probability landscape’ of a benchmark using Mean Pairwise Distance (MPD) over these 2D points, enabling comparison of structural properties across datasets. (2) Item-level diagnostics: they introduce a noise-injection procedure that perturbs the answer distribution in a way that reduces real distractor competition. By comparing pre- and post-noise behavior, they flag items whose performance or probability patterns suggest issues (e.g., ambiguous keys, weak or misleading distractors) and categorize the remaining errors into residual failure types. This method produces ranked lists of suspect items for targeted human inspection.

Result: Applied to four MCQA benchmarks, the landscape analysis uncovers systematic differences among datasets in model confidence levels and how strongly distractors compete with the correct answer, as reflected in P_top1–H_norm distributions and MPD statistics. These structural differences are not visible from accuracy alone. At the item level, the noise-injection approach successfully highlights questions that experts had previously annotated as problematic in MMLU-Redux, indicating good alignment between model-based flags and human judgments. Overall, the framework surfaces both macro-level benchmark characteristics and micro-level items that merit human review without requiring additional labels.

Conclusion: Model probability distributions contain rich diagnostic signals that can be leveraged to audit MCQA benchmarks beyond simple accuracy. The proposed two-component framework—probability landscape analysis plus noise-based item diagnostics—offers a lightweight, scalable way to compare datasets’ structural properties and to prioritize specific questions for expert review. This can reduce manual auditing effort, guide benchmark design and revision, and help the community better understand where current MCQA resources still challenge or systematically mislead large language models.

Abstract: As Large Language Models rapidly advance, performance on standard multiple-choice question answering (MCQA) benchmarks is reaching saturation. While the community has responded by developing increasingly difficult datasets, validating question quality and filtering flawed items remains a labor-intensive process. To provide a scalable diagnostic approach, we propose a two-component probabilistic framework for auditing MCQA benchmarks using model output distributions. First, for benchmark-level analysis, we characterize the probability landscape using the top prediction probability ($P_{top1}$) and normalized residual entropy ($H_{norm}$), summarized globally by Mean Pairwise Distance (MPD). Second, for item-level diagnostics, we introduce noise injection to reduce meaningful distractor competition, enabling us to flag candidate items for targeted human review and categorize residual failure patterns. Across four MCQA benchmarks, our landscape analysis reveals benchmark-level differences in model confidence and residual option competition. Concurrently, our noise-injection method flags potentially actionable item-level issues, showing alignment with expert error annotations from MMLU-Redux. These results suggest that our probability-based framework provides a lightweight audit lens for comparing macro-level benchmark structure and prioritizing individual items for targeted human review.

</details>


### [154] [Beyond Consensus: Downward Bias and Role Asymmetry in Multi-Agent LLM Judges for Subjective Evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30373)
*Minsoo Song,Chanwoo Kim,Sugyeong Eo,Chanjun Park*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper tests whether multi-agent debate (MAD) improves LLM-based subjective scoring and finds that a simple single-judge setup aligns better with humans.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: MAD is popular for improving LLM evaluation by having multiple agents debate and reach consensus, but in subjective, rubric-based scoring tasks, it is unclear whether consensus between agents actually leads to better alignment with human judgments.

Method: The authors compare a single-judge baseline with a consensus-based MAD protocol on subjective evaluation tasks using six different LLM judge models. They design three ablations to separate the effects of role prompting (strict vs lenient judges), multi-round interaction, and explicit sharing of scores between agents. They then measure how closely each configuration’s scores align with human annotations and analyze biases and agreement patterns.

Result: Across six LLMs and two subjective tasks, the single-judge baseline achieves the best average alignment with human judgments. MAD degrades human alignment, mainly due to asymmetric role prompting that assigns a strict judge, which introduces a systematic downward scoring bias not corrected by consensus. The consensus score tends to be dominated by the strict stance and falls below the midpoint between strict-only and lenient-only conditions. Symmetric role prompting (no strict/lenient asymmetry) largely restores baseline performance, while hiding peer scores increases disagreement and further reduces human alignment.

Conclusion: Role-specialized, consensus-based MAD protocols can artificially enforce agent agreement while moving scores away from human ground truth. For subjective rubric-based scoring, single-judge setups or symmetric multi-agent designs may be preferable, and strict/lenient role asymmetry is a key structural source of misalignment rather than the debate interaction itself.

Abstract: Multi-Agent Debate (MAD) has been widely adopted to improve LLM-based evaluation by prompting multiple agents to negotiate and reach a consensus. However, for subjective rubric-based scoring, inter-agent agreement does not guarantee alignment with human judgments. In this paper, we compare a single-judge baseline against a consensus-based MAD protocol on subjective evaluation tasks and design three ablations to isolate the impact of role prompting, multi-round interaction, and explicit score sharing. Evaluations across six LLMs show that the single-judge baseline achieves the strongest human alignment on average across six judge models, whereas MAD shows degradation in human alignment on both tasks. Our ablations demonstrate that this performance drop stems primarily from asymmetric role prompting rather than the interaction itself. Specifically, assigning a strict judge role introduces a systematic downward bias that the consensus process fails to correct. The central finding is that this bias reflects strict-stance dominance beyond averaging: the consensus score falls well beyond the arithmetic midpoint of the standalone strict and lenient conditions, rather than averaging them out. Removing role asymmetry (Symmetric MAD) largely recovers baseline performance, while masking peer scores widens inter-agent disagreement on average and worsens average human alignment. These findings demonstrate that multi-agent consensus can enforce artificial agreement at the expense of true human alignment, revealing a structural limitation in consensus-style, role-specialized MAD protocols for subjective scoring.

</details>


### [155] [Kathleen Remembers: Length-Invariant One-Shot Recall Without Attention](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30376)
*George Fountzoulas*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper augments recurrent, attention-free sequence models with a lightweight holographic “notebook” memory that enables length-invariant, one-shot exact recall and interpretable operations like selective unlearning and attribution, improving rare-word repetition modeling over long contexts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard recurrent, attention-free sequence models struggle with exact recall of information seen once far in the past due to fading state, while attention mechanisms either fail to generalize beyond trained lengths or incur O(L^2) cost. The authors aim to provide an O(L) memory mechanism that supports exact, length-invariant recall, works as a small add-on to existing trunks, and offers interpretable operations like unlearning and provenance tracking, all under realistic compute constraints.

Method: They attach to an existing recurrent trunk a second memory layer called a “notebook,” implemented as a fixed-key holographic reduced representation (HRR) associative store with about 25K parameters. The notebook uses a learned local write gate to decide when to write, a self-gating raw read mechanism to retrieve information, and write-triggered forgetting to control interference. They evaluate it on (1) a controlled needle-in-haystack task for one-shot recall far beyond training sequence length, (2) real-text language modeling on WikiText-2 at the byte level focusing on repeated rare words and long-distance repetition, and (3) scaling experiments on WikiText-103 across dataset sizes from 8 MB to 512 MB. They compare against a parameter-matched attention head and analyze properties like length-invariant addressing, untrained-memory recall, selective unlearning via subtraction, and per-token attribution via counterfactual erasure.

Result: On the synthetic needle-in-haystack task, the notebook achieves ~80–82% one-shot recall at four times the training sequence length, whereas the bare trunk gets ~4% and a parameter-matched attention head gets 100% only within training length but 0% beyond it. The notebook’s addressing is length-invariant; the untrained memory alone recalls with ~90% accuracy at sequence lengths 512, 2048, and 4096 bytes. Due to linear superposition in the store, a single subtraction can selectively unlearn one fact without harming others, and counterfactual erasure identifies the originating fact for each correct byte with perfect provenance.
