On WikiText-2 bytes, the notebook improves prediction of repeated rare words by about +0.15–0.27 bits/byte, with gains increasing with mention distance and holding zero-shot at 4× the training length; write-triggered forgetting removes long-context pollution, turning the cost of first mentions at 8× length from +0.33 bits/byte to −0.004. On a WikiText-103 scale ladder (8 to 512 MB), the zero-shot repetition gain increases monotonically. All experiments are pre-registered, use reported seeds, and are reproducible on a single free-tier GPU.

Conclusion: The proposed notebook memory provides an efficient O(L) associative memory add-on that enables near-exact, length-invariant one-shot recall in recurrent, attention-free sequence models, outperforming both the bare trunk and a similarly sized attention head beyond trained sequence lengths. Its linear structure yields practical interpretability tools such as selective unlearning and perfect provenance attribution, and it delivers measurable gains on real-text long-range repetition, especially for rare words, with robust generalization well beyond training context lengths and modest compute requirements.

Abstract: Recurrent, attention-free sequence models share a structural weakness: a fading state cannot perform exact recall of something seen once, far in the past. We add to the Kathleen trunk a second memory layer -- a "notebook": a fixed-key holographic (HRR) associative store with a learned local write gate, a self-gating raw read, and write-triggered forgetting -- 25K parameters that attach to the logits of any trunk. (1) Mechanism: on a controlled needle-in-haystack task the notebook reaches 80-82% one-shot recall at 4x the training length, where the bare trunk scores ~4% and a parameter-matched attention head scores 100% inside its training length and 0% beyond it. Addressing is length-invariant by construction; the untrained memory alone recalls at 90% accuracy identically at 512, 2048 and 4096 bytes. Because the store is a linear superposition, two capabilities follow from arithmetic alone: selective unlearning (one subtraction erases one fact to chance, retained facts unharmed) and per-token attribution (counterfactual erasure names the source fact of every correct byte, 100% provenance). (2) Real text: on WikiText-2 bytes the notebook improves prediction of repeated rare words by +0.15-0.27 bits/byte, the gain growing with the distance between mentions and holding zero-shot at 4x training length; write-triggered forgetting eliminates memory pollution at 8x length (first-mention cost +0.33 -> -0.004). (3) Scope and scale: a parameter-matched attention head does generalize on natural-text repetition, so the notebook's claim is exact recall at O(L); on a WikiText-103 ladder (8 to 512 MB) the zero-shot repeat gain rises monotonically. All experiments are pre-registered, seeds reported, and reproducible on a single free-tier GPU.

</details>


### [156] [Using Grounded Theory for Agent Behavior Analysis at Scale](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30391)
*Zhuoran Lu,Yangyang Yu,Zhuoyan Li,Yibo Meng,Nan Jiang,Chengxi Zang,Jie Gao,Ziang Xiao*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces AutoTraceGT, an automated grounded-theory-based pipeline to discover and organize behavioral patterns in large collections of agent trajectories, achieving strong coverage of failure modes and improving downstream failure prediction over LLM baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing analysis of agent behavior does not scale to thousands of trajectories, struggles with long or unfamiliar tasks, and relies on pre-built classifiers that miss unanticipated behaviors. The authors seek a principled, scalable, and auditable way to extract, organize, and theorize about behavioral patterns—especially failure modes—from complex multi-agent trajectories.

Method: They adapt grounded theory, a qualitative social-science methodology, to agent trajectory analysis and implement it as an automated multi-agent pipeline called AutoTraceGT. The pipeline iteratively performs open coding (initial behavior labeling), axial coding (organizing labels into categories and relationships), and theoretical coding (building higher-level concepts and narratives) until a formal saturation criterion is met. The result is a task-specific behavioral taxonomy (codebook) that can also be used as a feature space for quantitative prediction tasks.

Result: Across six different trajectory corpora, AutoTraceGT produces codebooks that capture 73–91% of the failure modes present in human-designed taxonomies and additionally discovers novel patterns that humans missed. The high-level theoretical narratives derived from these codebooks are consistent with prior expert analyses. When the learned codebook is used as a feature representation for failure prediction, it outperforms zero-shot and few-shot large language model baselines.

Conclusion: Automated grounded theory, instantiated as AutoTraceGT, is an effective and scalable method for analyzing agent trajectories. It yields interpretable behavioral taxonomies with strong coverage of failure modes, uncovers new behaviors, and provides a powerful feature space for downstream prediction, indicating that grounded theory can serve as a practical analytic tool for ML researchers and agent developers investigating real agent behavior.

Abstract: Understanding agent behavior requires methods that scale to thousands of trajectories and surface new patterns in long, often unfamiliar tasks where pre-built classifiers fall short. We propose to bring grounded theory into agent trajectory analysis: a six-decade-old qualitative method from the social sciences, with a principled saturation criterion and an auditable trail from data to theory. We propose AutoTraceGT (Automated Trace analysis through Grounded Theory), the first multi-agent pipeline that automates grounded theory on agent trajectories. It iteratively performs open, axial, and theoretical coding until saturation, producing a behavioral taxonomy tailored to each task. Across six trajectory corpora, AutoTraceGT produces codebooks that recover 73-91 percent of the failure modes in human-annotated taxonomies and surface additional patterns that those taxonomies miss. The emergent theoretical narrative aligns with prior expert accounts. Used as a deductive feature space, the codebook outperforms zero-shot and few-shot LLM baselines on downstream failure prediction. These results suggest Grounded Theory offers a scalable analytic tool for ML researchers and agent developers studying what agents actually do.

</details>


### [157] [Quantitative Evidence Mining for Plausibility-Aware Biomedical AI](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30393)
*Negin Sadat Babaiha,Stefan Geissler,Marie-Christine Simon,Martin Hofmann-Apitius,Marc Jacobs*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper argues that biomedical AI must shift from extracting simple relations to mining structured, quantitative, and contextualized evidence units so that claims become auditable, verifiable, and trustworthy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current biomedical AI and text-mining systems, including LLM-based pipelines, often extract simplistic relations like Drug–TREATS–Disease, omitting crucial quantitative and contextual information such as dose, effect size, population, uncertainty, and experimental conditions. This leads to claims that appear actionable but are difficult to verify, compare, or reuse reliably, especially as AI is increasingly used for evidence synthesis, knowledge graph construction, and decision support. There is a need for representations that preserve the richness and uncertainty of scientific evidence so AI systems can support more trustworthy biomedical reasoning and decision-making.

Method: The paper is a perspective that conceptually proposes a shift from relation-centric text mining toward quantitative evidence mining. It outlines a framework in which AI systems extract and represent values, units, measured entities and properties, contexts, uncertainties, provenance, and plausibility as structured evidence objects. These objects populate evidence-aware knowledge graphs and are subjected to checks such as source grounding, unit consistency, completeness, and biological plausibility. Rather than running experiments, the work synthesizes existing challenges and articulates design principles for plausibility-aware AI.

Result: The main result is a conceptual framework and vocabulary for thinking about "quantitative evidence mining" and "plausibility-aware AI" in biomedicine. It identifies the limitations of current relation-centric approaches and specifies the richer types of information—quantitative details, context, uncertainty, provenance, plausibility checks—that should be captured and structured. The paper proposes representing extracted claims as evidence units that can be audited and validated, rather than as stand-alone facts, and discusses how such representations can better support evidence-aware knowledge graphs and downstream applications.

Conclusion: The paper concludes that the core risk in biomedical AI is not just incorrect extractions but structurally impoverished claims that look like evidence without containing the necessary quantitative, contextual, and provenance information to be trusted. To address this, AI systems must move beyond relation-centric extraction toward quantitative, context-rich evidence mining and plausibility-aware representations. Treating claims as auditable evidence objects—explicit about what was measured, how much it changed, under which conditions, with what uncertainty, and from which source—will enable more reliable evidence synthesis, knowledge graph construction, and decision support in biomedical domains.

Abstract: Biomedical artificial intelligence (AI) systems increasingly extract, organize, and reuse scientific claims from literature, clinical trials, and regulatory documents. But automatic extraction alone does not make a claim reliable evidence: a claim becomes useful only when it can be traced to its source, linked to the quantitative details that support it, and read within its biomedical context and uncertainty. This matters as large language models (LLMs) and increasingly autonomous systems drive evidence synthesis, knowledge graph (KG) construction, and decision support. Many text-mining and LLM pipelines remain relation-centric: they capture entities and relations such as Drug--TREATS--Disease, but drop the dose, effect size, population, comparator, uncertainty, and conditions under which a claim holds. Such relations can look actionable yet remain hard to verify, compare, or reuse. In this perspective, we argue for a shift toward quantitative evidence mining---extracting values, units, measured entities and properties, context, uncertainty, provenance, and plausibility as structured evidence units that populate evidence-aware KGs and can be checked for source grounding, unit consistency, completeness, and biological plausibility. We outline a framework for plausibility-aware AI that treats extracted claims not as final answers but as auditable evidence objects, making clear what was measured, how much it changed, in which setting, with what uncertainty, and from which source. The central risk is not only incorrect extraction, but claims that look like evidence while lacking the structure needed to trust them.

</details>


### [158] [When LLM Meets Tree Search: A Systematic View of Inference as Search in Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30395)
*Jiaqi Wei,Xiang Zhang,Yuejin Yang,Wenxuan Huang,Juntai Cao,Sheng Xu,Xiang Zhuang,Zhangyang Gao,Muhammad Abdul-Mageed,Laks VS Lakshmanan,Chenyu You,Wanli Ouyang,Siqi Sun*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Survey of test-time scaling via tree-search-based reasoning for language models, framing inference as search and proposing a unified design space and compute-reporting standard.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Pretraining scaling laws are saturating, so further gains from just training bigger models are diminishing. Test-time scaling—spending more compute during inference on a fixed model—has become key for improving reasoning. However, current methods like single-trajectory Chain-of-Thought limit exploration and error recovery, and the literature on tree-search-based reasoning is fragmented and inconsistent in how it reports compute and performance, making it hard to compare methods or understand design choices.

Method: The paper conducts a survey that reinterprets inference with language models as search over partial reasoning states, rather than simple left-to-right decoding. It systematizes methods that use tree search, tracing a progression from uninformed search strategies to more advanced Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) approaches. It introduces a Unified Design Space that categorizes methods along three axes: search topology (how the search tree is structured), evaluation signals (how partial states are scored), and control dynamics (how exploration vs. exploitation and compute allocation are managed). It also proposes a standardized abstraction for reporting inference-time compute and its relationship to accuracy.

Result: The survey organizes diverse test-time search methods into a common framework, clarifying how they differ and where they are similar. It shows that sampling-based control methods like MCTS allow more principled exploration-exploitation trade-offs compared to naive or single-trajectory approaches. The Unified Design Space and proposed compute-reporting abstraction reveal gaps and common patterns in existing work, providing a basis for more systematic comparison and design of tree-search-based reasoning algorithms.

Conclusion: Inference for reasoning tasks with language models is better viewed as an instance-specific optimization/search problem than as simple decoding. Tree-search-based methods, particularly those using sampling-based control like MCTS, offer a powerful way to implement test-time scaling by allocating additional inference-time compute for better reasoning. A unified design space and standardized compute-reporting scheme are necessary to make progress measurable and comparable, guiding future work in test-time scaling and search-based reasoning.

Abstract: As pretraining scaling laws approach saturation, Test-Time Scaling (TTS) has emerged as an important direction for improving reasoning by allocating inference-time compute to a fixed model prior. Viewed at a high level, TTS reframes inference as search over a space of partial reasoning states. While Chain-of-Thought (CoT) exposes intermediate steps, common instantiations rely on single-trajectory decoding, limiting recovery from early errors and exploration. This survey systematizes recent progress in tree-search-based reasoning, viewing inference as instance-specific optimization rather than decoding. We trace the evolution from uninformed search to Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS), highlighting how sampling-based control supports principled exploration-exploitation trade-offs. To unify a fragmented literature, we introduce a Unified Design Space spanning search topology, evaluation signals, and control dynamics, and advocate a standardized compute-reporting abstraction to make compute-accuracy trade-offs explicit and comparable.

</details>


### [159] [Co-Evolving Actor-Conditioned Critics for Non-Verifiable Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30397)
*Jinyoung Kim,Muhammad Khalifa,Lajanugen Logeswaran,Jaekyeom Kim,Moontae Lee,Honglak Lee,Lu Wang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces TAIScore, a metric to evaluate how useful natural-language critiques are for improving an LLM’s responses, and uses it to train a critic that co-evolves with the actor model, achieving better performance than larger or naively trained critics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing critique-guided refinement systems rely on natural-language feedback, but we cannot easily tell whether a critique is genuinely helpful for a particular model (actor). Final answer quality alone is ambiguous because an actor may improve without using the critique, or may fail to apply valid feedback due to its own limitations. There is a need for a supervision signal that explicitly measures whether a critique is targeted, actionable, and effective for a specific actor’s capabilities, and that can adapt as the actor improves.

Method: The authors conceptualize critiques as actor-conditioned revision guidance and define TAIScore (Targeted Actionable Improvement Score), a reward function that jointly evaluates the instruction, the actor’s initial response, the critique, and the revision. TAIScore measures: (1) whether the critique identifies a real weakness; (2) whether the actor follows the critique; and (3) whether the targeted aspect improves. They train a critic model with this reward using GRPO (a policy optimization method). Then, using the critic’s feedback and the actor’s refinements, they construct preference pairs and train the actor with DPO. This forms a co-evolving loop where the critic is continually updated to remain well-matched to the actor’s current abilities.

Result: An 8B-parameter critic trained with TAIScore significantly outperforms a zero-shot 120B critic and critics trained with only outcome-based rewards or only critique-quality rewards, across benchmarks of critique usefulness and refinement quality. When the critic and actor are co-trained (co-evolving), the actor’s performance improves further compared to baselines without this adaptive critic supervision.

Conclusion: Useful critique supervision must be actor-specific and adaptive. By explicitly rewarding critiques that are both well-targeted to the actor’s weaknesses and actually followed to yield improvements, TAIScore enables training of an efficient critic that can outperform much larger generic models. Co-evolving critics and actors via TAIScore-based training and DPO leads to better refinement and suggests a promising direction for scalable, natural-language-based supervision of LLMs.

Abstract: Natural-language critiques provide supervision beyond scalar rewards for non-verifiable generation, which lacks deterministic verifiers. In critique-guided refinement, a critic gives feedback on an initial response and an actor revises it. However, final revision quality does not reveal whether the critique was actually useful: a capable actor may improve without following the feedback, while valid feedback may fail if the actor cannot execute it. We frame critique as actor-conditioned revision guidance, where usefulness depends on whether the feedback helps the target actor address the intended weakness. We introduce TAIScore (Targeted Actionable Improvement Score), a reward that evaluates the instruction, initial response, critique, and revision together, assessing whether the critique targets a real weakness, whether the actor follows it, and whether the intended aspect improves. We use this reward to train an actor-tailored critic with GRPO, and use critique-guided refinements to construct DPO preference pairs for the actor, forming a co-evolving critic-actor loop where the critic adapts to the actor's changing capability. Experiments show that an 8B critic trained with TAIScore outperforms both a zero-shot 120B critic and critics trained with outcome-only or critique-only reward signals. Co-evolving the critic and actor further improves performance, suggesting that effective critique supervision should adapt as the actor changes.

</details>


### [160] [Beyond Polarization: The Generative Constraint of Chain-of-Thought in Pointwise Reranking](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30398)
*Xiaoyang Chen,Jie Liu,Haijin Liang,Haibo Shi,Jin Ma,Ben He,Yingfei Sun,Dezhi Ye*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper investigates why Chain-of-Thought (CoT) models underperform direct scoring models for pointwise document reranking and shows that this deficit persists even after strong targeted training interventions, implying a fundamental bottleneck in routing relevance judgments through discrete text explanations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Although CoT reasoning often improves performance in many tasks, in pointwise document reranking CoT-based models underperform models that directly output a relevance score. Prior diagnostics suggest issues like poorer classification, polarized scores, or calibration problems, but it is unknown whether better or more targeted training could close this gap. Understanding whether this is just a training artifact or a deeper limitation is important for designing effective reranking systems and for knowing when CoT is beneficial versus harmful.

Method: The authors conduct an empirical study across models up to 32B parameters to check if scaling resolves the CoT vs. direct scoring gap. They then design and run a series of stress-test interventions: (1) reinforcement learning tailored to improve ranking behavior, (2) fine-grained supervision signals to refine the CoT outputs and associated scores, and (3) architectural decoupling that separates reasoning text generation from scoring, all with the aim of explicitly repairing known diagnostics such as classification errors, score polarization, and calibration issues. They then evaluate both absolute relevance classification accuracy and downstream ranking quality.

Result: Scaling up to 32B parameters does not remove the performance gap: CoT-based pointwise scorers continue to underperform direct scorers in ranking quality. The targeted interventions via RL, fine-grained supervision, and architectural decoupling successfully improve classification accuracy and calibration and make absolute scores better behaved, but they do not eliminate the relative ranking performance gap between CoT and direct scoring models.

Conclusion: The persistent underperformance of CoT models for pointwise document reranking, even after aggressive and diverse training interventions, indicates that the core issue is not just a fixable training bias or capacity limitation. Instead, using discrete natural language Chain-of-Thought as an intermediate for encoding relevance appears to constrain the granularity of ranking signals. Within the standard pointwise scoring framework, this creates a stable bottleneck in ranking resolution that is difficult to overcome with current methods, suggesting that alternative paradigms or architectures may be needed to fully exploit CoT for reranking.

Abstract: In pointwise document reranking, Chain-of-Thought models typically underperform direct scoring models. While existing diagnostics attribute this to inferior classification, score polarization, or calibration breakdown, whether targeted training can bridge this gap remains unclear. Our empirical study first confirms that this gap is stable across scales up to 32B parameters, ruling out model and data capacity confounders. We then apply stress tests utilizing reinforcement learning, fine-grained supervision, and architectural decoupling to explicitly repair these deviations. Although these interventions improve classification accuracy and absolute scores, the relative ranking gap persists. These findings suggest that, within the pointwise scoring paradigm, routing continuous relevance semantics through discrete text constrains ranking signal resolution, revealing a bottleneck that is stable and difficult to overcome under current standard methods, rather than an easily resolvable training bias.

</details>


### [161] [SemPOI-RL: Aligning LLM Semantic Reasoning for Interpretable Out-of-Town POI Sequential Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30399)
*Yunqi Liu,Yang Zhang,Ruixing Zhang,Liangzhe Han,Yi Qiao,Tongyu Zhu,Leilei Sun*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: SemPOI-RL aligns LLM semantic reasoning with structured, position-aware POI sequence generation for out-of-town travel recommendation, achieving better accuracy and interpretability than existing methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing OOT POI recommenders either use latent ID-based transfer, which lacks interpretability and struggles with cross-city interest drift, or directly apply LLMs for sequence generation without structurally grounding semantics. There is a need to connect LLMs' rich semantic reasoning about user travel intent with the rigid structural constraints of trajectory recommendation (order, positions, phases of a trip) in an interpretable and transferable way.

Method: SemPOI-RL is a multi-stage framework. (1) Fine-tune an LLM to infer users' destination-oriented travel styles from their hometown trajectories, using natural language descriptions as an interpretable semantic representation. (2) Introduce the Semantic POI Alignment Module (SPAM), which conditions a masked autoencoder on the inferred travel styles to generate position-aware POI trajectories under structural constraints. (3) Use reinforcement learning with recommendation-oriented rewards to further align the LLM-generated styles with downstream sequence quality and user-centric objectives.

Result: On two real-world datasets, SemPOI-RL outperforms both traditional recommendation models and LLM-based sequence generators that do not explicitly align semantics with structure. It also yields interpretable style attributions for different phases of a trip, showing which inferred styles drive which POI choices along the trajectory.

Conclusion: Aligning LLM semantic reasoning with structured sequence models via an interpretable style layer, a style-conditioned generator, and RL-based fine-tuning leads to more accurate and interpretable out-of-town POI recommendations. SemPOI-RL demonstrates that natural-language travel styles can serve as a useful bridge between user behavior in one city and trajectory generation in another.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit strong semantic reasoning and open-ended generation abilities, but aligning these abilities with structured sequential generation remains challenging. This challenge is particularly evident in out-of-town (OOT) POI sequence generation, where a model must infer transferable travel intent from a user's hometown behaviors, adapt to cross-city interest drift, and generate a coherent destination trajectory under structural constraints. Existing approaches either rely on latent ID-based transfer with limited interpretability or directly use LLMs for sequence generation without explicitly grounding inferred semantics into position-aware predictions. To address this gap, we propose SemPOI-RL, a framework that aligns LLM semantic reasoning with structured sequence generation for interpretable OOT recommendation. Specifically, we first fine-tune an LLM to infer destination-oriented travel styles from users' hometown trajectories, using natural language as an interpretable semantic intermediate. We then introduce a Semantic POI Alignment Module (SPAM) to ground these inferred styles into a style-conditioned masked autoencoder for position-aware trajectory generation. Finally, we apply reinforcement learning with recommendation-oriented rewards to align LLM-generated styles with downstream sequence quality. Experiments on two real-world datasets show that SemPOI-RL consistently outperforms both traditional recommenders and direct LLM baselines, while providing interpretable style attribution across different phases of a trip. The code is available at https://github.com/Wind-Flipped/SemPOI-RL .

</details>


### [162] [Generative Models Enhanced by Sequence Labelling and Aspect-Code Switching Improve Cross-lingual Aspect-Based Sentiment Analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30425)
*Jakub Šmíd,Pavel Přibáň,Pavel Král*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes SeqLab, a seq2seq-based framework with an auxiliary sequence labeling task and aspect-code switching to improve cross-lingual aspect-based sentiment analysis, achieving state-of-the-art results on multiple languages, domains, and tasks including TASD.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Cross-lingual aspect-based sentiment analysis is important for fine-grained sentiment understanding in languages without annotated data, but remains underexplored, especially for complex tasks like target-aspect-sentiment detection. Existing methods mostly focus on English as the source language and simpler E2E-ABSA tasks, leaving a gap in methods that robustly transfer knowledge across diverse language pairs and more demanding ABSA subtasks.

Method: The authors introduce SeqLab, a sequence-to-sequence framework whose encoder is augmented with an auxiliary sequence-labeling task to strengthen aspect term recognition and sentiment prediction. They further propose aspect-code switching (ACS), a translation-based data augmentation method that swaps aspect terms between original source sentences and their translations, producing additional cross-lingual training examples. The approach is instantiated with two backbone models and evaluated on multiple languages and domains.

Result: Across eleven languages, three domains, and two backbone models, SeqLab with aspect-code switching outperforms prior state-of-the-art approaches on the widely studied end-to-end ABSA task and performs well on the more challenging TASD task. The experiments also include a systematic study of different source-target language pairs, showing robust cross-lingual transfer benefits.

Conclusion: The combination of a seq2seq architecture with an auxiliary sequence-labeling objective and aspect-code switching effectively improves cross-lingual ABSA, including more complex tasks like TASD. The method generalizes across many languages and domains, surpassing existing state-of-the-art approaches, while the error analysis reveals remaining challenges and suggests directions for future work in cross-lingual fine-grained sentiment analysis.

Abstract: Cross-lingual aspect-based sentiment analysis (ABSA) transfers knowledge from a source language with annotated data to a target language, enabling fine-grained sentiment analysis without annotated target-language data. While monolingual ABSA has seen significant progress, cross-lingual ABSA remains underexplored, especially for complex tasks involving multiple sentiment elements like target-aspect-sentiment detection (TASD). In this paper, we propose a novel SeqLab framework that enhances cross-lingual ABSA using a sequence-to-sequence model with an auxiliary sequence-labelling task performed by the encoder, enhancing aspect term recognition and sentiment predictions. Additionally, we incorporate aspect-code switching (ACS), a translation-based technique that swaps aspect terms between source and translated sentences, generating additional training data to enhance the model's cross-lingual understanding. We evaluate our approach across eleven languages, three domains, and two backbone models, surpassing previous state-of-the-art results for the commonly studied E2E-ABSA task. Unlike most prior work that relies solely on English as the source language, we systematically assess different source-target language pairs and extend our evaluation to the more challenging, yet underexplored TASD task in cross-lingual settings. Finally, we provide a detailed error analysis highlighting key challenges and limitations.

</details>


### [163] [Learning to Reason and Use Tools through Unsupervised Fine-Tuning in Task-Oriented Dialog Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30426)
*Markel Ferro,Oier Lopez de Lacalle*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper adapts the ReAct framework to task-oriented dialogue, using unsupervised fine-tuning on LLM-generated reasoning trajectories to improve factuality and tool use, achieving better performance than larger in-context models on SIMMC.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing dialogue systems often hallucinate and fail to retrieve up-to-date or context-specific information because they cannot effectively combine reasoning with external tool/knowledge access. The authors aim to build a task-oriented dialogue system that can reliably use tools and external knowledge, improving factual accuracy without requiring expensive, manually annotated reasoning trajectories.

Method: They adapt the ReAct (Reason + Act) framework to task-oriented dialogue so that an LLM can iteratively reason, call tools, and respond. They introduce an unsupervised fine-tuning pipeline: (1) use in-context learning to have a strong LLM generate reasoning trajectories and tool calls for many dialogue instances; (2) evaluate and filter these trajectories using an LLM-based judge, retaining only high-quality samples; (3) fine-tune a smaller LLM on this curated dataset; and (4) run an unsupervised self-improvement loop where each improved checkpoint generates better trajectories that are again filtered and used for further fine-tuning. They evaluate on the SIMMC dataset, analyze error types, study the impact of scene complexity, and test cross-domain generalization.

Result: On the SIMMC benchmark, ReAct-based dialogue systems outperform baseline methods, with clear gains attributed to improved reasoning and more effective tool usage. A fine-tuned 8B-parameter model trained with the proposed pipeline surpasses a 70B-parameter model that only uses in-context learning, demonstrating that unsupervised trajectory distillation plus self-improvement can close and even reverse the size gap. Additional analyses highlight how performance varies with scene complexity and how well the approach generalizes across domains.

Conclusion: Adapting ReAct to task-oriented dialogue and training it via unsupervised trajectory harvesting and self-improvement yields more accurate, less hallucination-prone systems that use tools more effectively. Careful LLM-based filtering of trajectories and iterative refinement allow a relatively small fine-tuned model to outperform a much larger in-context system, suggesting that reasoning-plus-action training can be more valuable than sheer scale alone and can generalize beyond a single domain.

Abstract: Current dialogue systems struggle with dynamic information retrieval, often leading to hallucinations and lower response accuracy. We address this by adapting the ReAct framework for Task-Oriented Dialogue, enabling Large Language Models (LLMs) to access external knowledge and produce factual responses. Mainly, we propose an unsupervised fine-tuning pipeline that harvests reasoning trajectories via in-context learning inference. High-quality samples are filtered using an LLM-based judge to construct a robust training set. This is enhanced by a unsupervised self-improvement loop, where improved checkpoints generate increasingly better trajectories for subsequent fine-tuning iterations. Experiments on the SIMMC dataset demonstrate that ReAct-based systems outperform baselines due to superior reasoning and tool use. Notably, our fine-tuned 8B model surpasses a 70B in-context system. Finally, we present an error analysis, impact of scene complexity, and cross-domain generalization.

</details>


### [164] [Ceiling-Clipped Acceptance Histograms Indicate Stranded Speed-up in Block-Diffusion Speculative Decoding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30427)
*Ephrem Wu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper identifies and mitigates “stranded speed-up” in speculative decoding by extending block-diffusion drafters beyond their trained block size using a targeted post-training method called DBloom, improving committed length and speedup across multiple LLMs and benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Speculative decoding can greatly speed up large language model generation when a smaller drafter model proposes token blocks that the main model then verifies. High-acceptance block drafters like DFlash and DFlare often have entire proposed blocks accepted, but only up to their trained block size. When the target model would have accepted even longer blocks, the potential extra speedup is lost—termed “stranded speed-up.” Existing metrics like mean committed length obscure this issue, so there is a need both to diagnose unrealized speedups and to recover them without harming accuracy or the target distribution.

Method: 1) Analyze speculative decoding behavior with block-diffusion drafters and introduce the concept of stranded speed-up, showing that acceptance histograms expose unrealized gains better than average committed length. 2) Empirically demonstrate that simply widening the block at inference beyond the drafter’s training horizon degrades front-of-block verification due to distribution shift from bidirectional attention. 3) Propose DBloom, a post-training curriculum that extends a pretrained drafter to a longer block size by emphasizing training on the newly added positions, thus preserving quality on earlier positions while learning to propose further tokens. 4) Apply DBloom to expand DFlash and DFlare from block size 16 to 24 for several target models, with and without a preceding continuation fine-tuning stage, and benchmark against both their original versions and a tree-based drafter (JetSpec).

Result: Using DBloom to expand DFlash and DFlare from block size 16 to 24 for Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-4B targets increases per-prompt committed length on high-ceiling benchmarks by a median of +0.8 tokens (up to +1.1), and by up to 1.37 tokens when continuation fine-tuning is applied before expansion. For Gemma-4-12B-IT, the same block-size expansion improves committed length across seven benchmarks by a median of +0.41 tokens (Arm A), and the full continuation-plus-DBloom pipeline (Arm B) adds a further +0.29 to +0.98 tokens over the baseline block-16 drafter. In a prompt-matched comparison with JetSpec at tree budgets up to 64 nodes, DBloom-based drafters achieve higher committed lengths on every benchmark.

Conclusion: Stranded speed-up is a significant and previously under-quantified inefficiency in block-based speculative decoding, best diagnosed via acceptance histograms rather than average metrics. Simply increasing block size at inference is ineffective due to distribution shifts in bidirectional drafters, but DBloom—a focused post-training curriculum on extended positions—can safely enlarge the drafter’s horizon and recover much of the unrealized speedup. This approach consistently improves committed length across models and benchmarks and outperforms a contemporary tree-based drafter (JetSpec) under comparable computational budgets, making DBloom a practical path to faster LLM generation with speculative decoding.

Abstract: Speculative decoding speeds up generation with an efficient draft model (drafter) that proposes tokens for a target model to verify in one pass, preserving the target's output distribution. High-acceptance block-diffusion drafters such as DFlash and DFlare fill an entire block in one parallel pass. In many cycles, the target accepts the whole block, so the drafter exhausts its trained block horizon before verification fails. We call this unrealized acceptance stranded speed-up. A mean committed length, per prompt or per cycle, hides it, whereas the acceptance histogram exposes it as a spike in the ceiling bin, the fraction of cycles that accept the entire block. We recommend the histogram as a preflight check before spending training compute. Naively widening the block at inference does not recover the speed-up, because once the block outgrows its training size, the drafter's bidirectional attention shifts its distribution even at early positions and erodes front-of-block verification. Instead, we post-train the drafter on a longer block with a short curriculum that emphasizes the newly exposed positions, a method we call DBloom. Expanding the pretrained DFlash and DFlare drafters from block size 16 to 24 across Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-4B targets raises the per-prompt committed length on the high-ceiling benchmarks by a median of +0.8 tokens (up to +1.1). Once continuation fine-tuning precedes expansion, the increase reaches 1.37 tokens. The same expansion also lifts committed length on all seven benchmarks for Gemma-4-12B-IT, a different model family, by a median of +0.41 tokens (Arm A), and the full continuation-then-expand pipeline (Arm B) adds +0.29 to +0.98 tokens over the same B16 drafter. In a prompt-matched comparison against JetSpec, a contemporary tree-based drafter not used in our design, DBloom commits more tokens on every benchmark at tree budgets up to 64 nodes.

</details>


### [165] [Lies We Can See: Joint Verbal and Non-Verbal Deception by VLM Agents in Embodied Social Interactions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30428)
*Jaewoo Ahn,Junseo Kim,Hyunseo Kim,Heeseung Yun,Jaehyeon Son,Zsolt Kira,Gunhee Kim*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces MineAmongUs, a 3D multimodal social-deduction sandbox and the ARIA VLM-agent harness to study and quantify strategic deception by vision-language model agents, showing that non-verbal behavior is a key driver of successful deceptive play.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Strategic deception by large language and vision-language model agents is a major AI alignment and safety concern, but current evaluation testbeds are text-only, single-configuration environments that ignore non-verbal sensorimotor channels and blur whether deceptive behavior stems from the model itself or the experimental harness. The authors aim to build a more realistic, controllable, and measurable environment to study deception that includes embodied, multimodal behavior and enables precise attribution of deceptive strategies.

Method: The authors design MineAmongUs, a 3D Among Us–style sandbox where agents interact through both language and in-game actions, forcing imposters to coordinate verbal and non-verbal deception. They further develop ARIA, a configurable VLM agent harness with five cognitive-component ablation axes, allowing systematic removal or modification of agent capabilities. To analyze behavior, they create a detailed annotation scheme at the atom and arc levels, grounded in existing deception taxonomies, and scale labeling using an LLM-as-a-Judge, calibrated to achieve near-human agreement on atom-level deception labels. They then run empirical evaluations across multiple VLMs and ablation configurations to assess how agents use verbal vs. non-verbal channels to achieve imposter wins.

Result: Empirical experiments show that VLM agents actively employ both language and embodied action to deceive, with non-verbal channels (e.g., movement, actions in the 3D world) having a stronger impact on successful imposter wins than verbal strategies. Across harness ablations and different VLM backbones, non-verbal deceptive behaviors consistently emerge as more decisive for game outcomes, validating the importance of multimodal, embodied evaluation. The LLM-based annotation pipeline achieves near-human agreement at the atom level, supporting scalable, fine-grained deception measurement.

Conclusion: The paper concludes that embodied, multimodal environments are essential for realistic evaluation of strategic deception in VLM agents, as non-verbal channels play a dominant role in successful deception. MineAmongUs and the ARIA harness provide a configurable, taxonomy-grounded benchmark that disentangles model behavior from harness design and enables systematic alignment research. This framework opens a new path for studying and mitigating deceptive capacities in VLM agents in settings closer to real-world interaction, and establishes scalable annotation tools for fine-grained deception analysis.

Abstract: Strategic deception by LLM and VLM agents has emerged as a central AI alignment and safety concern. Social-deduction games (where each player holds a hidden role and communicates with others to deduce identities) serve as the canonical testbed, particularly in multi-agent settings. Existing testbeds, however, are text-only and run on a single fixed agent configuration, missing the non-verbal sensorimotor channels treated as core by deception taxonomies and leaving it ambiguous whether an observed behavior reflects the underlying model or the surrounding harness. We introduce MineAmongUs, a 3D multimodal Among Us sandbox where imposter agents must deceive crewmates through joint verbal and non-verbal action. We also propose ARIA, a configurable VLM-agent harness that exposes five cognitive-component ablation axes; and an atom- and arc-level annotation scheme grounded in deception taxonomies and operationalized at scale by an LLM-as-a-Judge reaching near-human atom-labeling agreement. Empirical results show that VLM agents pursue imposter wins through joint verbal and non-verbal deception, with non-verbal channels emerging as the more decisive winning contributors across both harness ablation and cross-VLM evaluation. Taken together, our work opens a new path for embodied VLM-agent alignment research.

</details>


### [166] [Graph Evidence Is Not Enough: Diagnosing Native Decoder Use in Graph-Augmented LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30437)
*Xiaoyu Guo,Pengcheng Chen,Jiong Yu,Yi Lu,Yaohua Wang,Ziyang Li*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper shows that simply feeding graph evidence into large language models (LLMs) does not guarantee that the models can use it for graph reasoning, and proposes an interface design (S^2GE) that makes such evidence more usable for shortest-path hop-count queries.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Many graph-augmented LLM methods assume that once graph-derived facts or subgraphs are placed into the input context, the native LLM decoder can effectively exploit them for reasoning. However, this assumption is rarely tested in a clean setting because most tasks involve open-ended text generation or fuzzy evaluation. The authors want a tightly controlled diagnostic to isolate whether the LLM actually uses graph structure, focusing on a purely topological, objective task: computing the shortest-hop distance between two nodes.

Method: The authors introduce HopQA, a diagnostic task where the model must output the shortest-hop distance between two query nodes in a graph. They design an "intervention triangle" with three conditions: (1) readable graph evidence (graph structured and ordered to be human/LLM-readable), (2) shuffled graph evidence (same content but order and structure scrambled), and (3) no-graph input (only the query nodes). This separates the effects of having any evidence, having structurally readable evidence, and the model’s ability to form usable topology from the input. Based on insights from this diagnostic, they propose S^2GE, an interface for presenting graph evidence using query-aware sampling (selecting relevant subgraphs), endpoint and proximity-based ordering (organizing nodes/edges relative to the query nodes), and structure-preserving alignment (keeping relational patterns coherent in text form). They evaluate S^2GE versus existing graph-augmented and native-generation baselines on four datasets: DBLP, Biomedical, GoodReads, and PubMed.

Result: Existing graph-augmented LLM baselines perform poorly on HopQA, even though the answer space is tiny (small integers) and the task is purely topological, showing that the models fail to exploit the provided graph evidence effectively. In contrast, S^2GE substantially improves performance, achieving strict exact-match scores of 36.5% (DBLP), 57.8% (Biomedical), 76.6% (GoodReads), and 52.0% (PubMed), with an average gain of 53.5 percentage points over the strongest native-generation baseline. The intervention triangle further reveals distinct behavioral regimes: some settings where shuffling the evidence is harmful (harmful-shuffle), some where performance is robust to shuffling (shuffle-robust), and others where having no graph already saturates performance (no-graph-saturated).

Conclusion: The paper concludes that merely injecting graph-derived evidence into an LLM’s context does not ensure that the model can perform graph reasoning such as shortest-path hop computation. Careful interface design—how graph structure is sampled, ordered, and aligned in text—substantially affects the decoder’s ability to use topological information. The proposed S^2GE approach, informed by a controlled diagnostic and intervention setup, can make graph evidence genuinely usable, leading to large performance gains and revealing different regimes of model sensitivity to graph structure and ordering.

Abstract: Graph-augmented large language models often assume that graph evidence produced by external computation and placed in the input can be used by the native decoder. We test this assumption with HopQA, a deliberately bounded diagnostic that asks for the shortest-hop distance between two query nodes. Because the answer is a small integer and the target is purely topological, failure cannot be dismissed as open-ended generation or ambiguous evaluation. Yet existing graph-augmented baselines still fail on this setting, showing that providing graph evidence is not the same as making it usable. We introduce an intervention triangle with three matched conditions: readable graph evidence, shuffled graph evidence, and no-graph input. This separates evidence inclusion, structural readability, and decoder-usable topology. Guided by this diagnosis, we present S$^2$GE as an instance showing that diagnosis-driven interface design can improve native decoder usability. S$^2$GE uses query-aware sampling, endpoint and proximity-based ordering, and structure-preserving alignment. Across DBLP, Biomedical, GoodReads, and PubMed, S$^2$GE achieves strict exact-match scores of $36.5\%$, $57.8\%$, $76.6\%$, and $52.0\%$, improving over the strongest native-generation baseline by $53.5$ points on average. The interventions further reveal harmful-shuffle, shuffle-robust, and no-graph-saturated regimes.

</details>


### [167] [From Final Artifacts to Trajectories: Retrospective Process Supervision for Evidence-Grounded Long-Form Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30461)
*Junjie Huang,Jiarui Qin,Di Yin,Weiwen Liu,Yong Yu,Xing Sun,Weinan Zhang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: RetroGen is a self-improving framework that reconstructs and verifies latent reasoning trajectories from existing high-quality expert artifacts, then trains models on these reconstructed trajectories to enhance grounding and long-form evidence-seeking abilities.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Trajectory data (step-by-step reasoning or action traces) is crucial for training agentic LLMs, but for open-ended tasks expert trajectories are scarce, expensive to annotate, and lack clear ground truth, unlike math or coding. However, there are many high-quality final outputs (e.g., literature reviews, analyst reports, legal judgments) that implicitly contain the underlying reasoning processes. The paper is motivated by leveraging these abundant expert artifacts to bypass the need for costly explicit trajectory supervision and stronger teacher models.

Method: They introduce RetroGen, a retrospective process supervision framework. RetroGen: (1) takes expert final artifacts and treats them as compressed evidence-seeking traces; (2) reconstructs multiple candidate latent trajectories (step-by-step reasoning/evidence chains) that could have produced the artifact; (3) verifies these trajectories both against the final artifact and the external supporting evidence; and (4) selects successful reconstructions and uses them as training data, enabling the model to learn from its own reconstructed trajectories without relying on stronger models for supervision.

Result: Experimentally, applying RetroGen leads to improved performance on tasks requiring grounding in evidence, faithful synthesis of information, and long-form evidence-seeking agents. The model trained with RetroGen shows better use of supporting evidence and higher-quality, more trustworthy long-form outputs compared to baselines without such retrospective trajectory reconstruction and supervision.

Conclusion: The paper concludes that abundant expert artifacts can be systematically converted into high-quality trajectory supervision via retrospective reconstruction and verification. RetroGen provides a scalable, self-improving approach to process supervision that does not depend on stronger teacher models, and it significantly enhances grounding and evidence-seeking capabilities for agentic LLMs in open-ended domains.

Abstract: Trajectory data is getting more vital for training large language models for boosting the agentic abilities. Unlike the verifiable domains such as coding or mathematics, scaling trajectory data for open-ended tasks is much more difficult because these tasks lack singular ground truth and are costly to annotate or verify. In this paper, we propose RetroGen, a self-improving framework of retrospective process supervision. Our key observation is that although expert trajectories are scarce, high-quality final artifacts such as literature reviews, analyst reports and legal judgments, are abundant in pre-training data and can be viewed as compressed traces of the evidence-seeking processes that produced them. RetroGen reconstructs candidate latent trajectories from expert artifacts, verifies them against both the artifact and supporting evidence, and trains models on their own successful reconstruction data, without requiring trajectory data from stronger models. Experiments show that RetroGen improves grounding, faithful synthesis, and long-form evidence-seeking agent tasks.

</details>


### [168] [Enhancing Low-Resource Language Reasoning via High-Resource Language Feature Transfer](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30462)
*Minju Song,Hyeon Hwang,Junhyun Lee,Jaewoo Kang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: They propose a causal/mechanistic method to identify and transfer task-relevant reasoning features from high-resource to low-resource languages in LLMs, showing that some cross-lingual gaps are due to elicitation failures, not lack of capability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs perform much better in high-resource languages than in low-resource ones on semantically equivalent tasks. Prior work mainly attributes this to data, tokenization, or benchmark differences and treats it descriptively. The authors want to test whether the gap is partly due to models not properly activating existing task-specific reasoning mechanisms in low-resource languages, and to develop a causal/mechanistic way to probe and mitigate this.

Method: They use mechanistic interpretability with sparse autoencoders trained on residual-stream activations of a model solving tasks in a high-resource language. The autoencoders learn sparse latent features. They then select features that are enriched when the model is successfully performing task-specific reasoning in the high-resource language, while explicitly filtering out features tied to the source language identity or generic text generation. From these selected features they construct linear steering directions that can be added to the residual stream at inference time. During inference on low-resource language inputs, they inject these directions (activate them) to see if reasoning improves. Symmetrically, they can suppress these features in the high-resource language to test whether they are causally implicated in good reasoning. They compare against random and non-task-specific control directions.

Result: They identify sparse latent features whose activation correlates with successful task-specific reasoning in the high-resource language and is not just generic language or style. Suppressing these features in the high-resource language degrades its reasoning performance, while injecting them during low-resource language inference partially closes the performance gap relative to baselines and control interventions. This shows that these features are functionally involved in the cross-lingual reasoning gap and that some reasoning competence can be transferred without translation or retraining.

Conclusion: Cross-lingual performance gaps in LLM reasoning are not solely due to missing capabilities or pretraining disparities; they can also arise from failures to elicit existing mechanisms in low-resource languages. By using sparse autoencoders over residual activations and causal steering interventions, one can identify and transfer task-relevant reasoning features from high- to low-resource languages. This provides a mechanistically grounded, causally testable framework for improving low-resource language performance without modifying training data, model weights, or the surface language of interaction.

Abstract: Large language models exhibit substantial performance variation across languages, even when solving semantically equivalent tasks. Existing analyses often treat this phenomenon as an observational disparity caused by differences in pretraining data, tokenization, or benchmark coverage. We study a complementary hypothesis: high-resource languages (HRLs) may more reliably elicit latent computations useful for task-specific (i.e. mathematical) reasoning, while lower-resource languages (LRLs) may under-activate those computations despite expressing the same task. To test this hypothesis, we introduce a mechanistic intervention framework for identifying and transferring task-relevant sparse latent features across languages. Using sparse autoencoders over residual-stream activations, we isolate features enriched in successful HRL task-specific reasoning while filtering out source-language and generic-generation features. We then construct steering directions from these features and inject them during LRL inference. The resulting interventions test whether the selected features are functionally involved in the observed reasoning gap: suppressing them should impair source-language reasoning, while activating them should partially recover target-language reasoning beyond random and non-task controls. Our framework reframes some cross-lingual reasoning gaps as failures of mechanism elicitation rather than capability absence, and offers a causally testable route to feature-mediated transfer without translation, fine-tuning, or changing the user-facing language.

</details>


### [169] [More Capable, Less Faithful: A Multilingual Analysis of Mathematical (Un)Solvability Detection in LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30463)
*Maria-Eleni Zoumpoulidi,Nikolaos Xiros,Georgios Paraskevopoulos*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper studies how large language models detect whether math problems are solvable, extending prior English-only work to French and Greek, and finds that solvability belief is mostly language-agnostic but is less faithfully used in high-resource languages like English.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Previous analyses of LLMs’ ability to judge whether math problems are solvable have been conducted only in English, leaving open whether multilingual errors come from the internal representation of solvability or from language-specific expression issues. There is a need for a multilingual benchmark and a deeper understanding of how solvability belief is encoded and used across languages.

Method: The authors extend the ReliableMath benchmark to create the first multilingual paired set of solvable and unsolvable math problems in French and Greek. They then train multilingual probes on model representations to predict an internal "Solvability Belief" signal, and they evaluate multiple state-of-the-art LLMs using three lenses: (1) behavioral performance on solvability detection, (2) representational analysis via probes, and (3) faithfulness, i.e., how reliably internal solvability belief correlates with the model’s final answers across languages.

Result: The study shows that LLMs encode a notion of Solvability Belief as a predominantly universal, language-agnostic feature in their internal representations. However, they also find that models’ faithfulness in using this internal belief to guide their explicit responses varies by language: higher-resource languages such as English, which have better raw math performance, paradoxically exhibit lower faithfulness in solvability detection than lower-resource languages like French and Greek.

Conclusion: Solvability detection in LLMs relies on an internal, largely language-independent representation of whether a math problem is solvable. Nonetheless, the degree to which this internal belief faithfully drives model outputs is not uniform across languages; it is weaker in high-resource languages such as English. This implies that improving mathematical reasoning performance alone does not guarantee faithful use of internal solvability signals, and that multilingual evaluation is necessary to understand and improve LLM reliability across languages.

Abstract: Solvability detection is one of the most challenging aspects of mathematical reasoning for Large Language Models (LLMs). While prior work has studied this capability extensively, these analyses have been limited to English. Consequently, it remains unclear whether multilingual failures arise from differences in internal Solvability Belief or from language-dependent failures to express it. To address this gap, we introduce the first multilingual benchmark of paired solvable and unsolvable mathematical problems, extending ReliableMath to French and Greek. Using this, we train multilingual probes predicting Solvability Belief and analyze the solvability detection capabilities of state-of-the-art LLMs behaviorally, representationally, and in terms of faithfulness. We find that Solvability Belief is encoded as a largely universal, language-agnostic feature, and that higher-resource languages such as English, despite achieving stronger mathematical reasoning performance, exhibit lower solvability-detection faithfulness.

</details>


### [170] [Hi-Q: Hierarchical Evidence-guided Query Refinement for Multi-Hop Question Answering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30468)
*Jueun Kim,Sungho Park,Wook-Shin Han*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Hi-Q is a hierarchical query refinement framework that dynamically decomposes multi-hop QA questions into evidence-aligned sub-queries based on corpus support, achieving substantial gains over strong iterative-retrieval and graph-based RAG baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multi-hop QA often suffers from a mismatch between how questions are phrased (complex, multi-step) and how evidence is stored and retrievable in large corpora. Existing approaches either fix a decomposition structure (graphs), repeatedly rewrite queries, or run generated programs, but they lack an explicit mechanism to decide when a sub-query is already supported by retrieved evidence versus when it must be further refined. This bottleneck in controlling the level of query granularity limits retrieval effectiveness and downstream QA accuracy, especially in full-corpus, open-domain settings with many distractors.

Method: The paper formalizes the core problem as retrievable granularity discovery and proposes Hi-Q, an evidence-conditioned hierarchical query refinement framework. Hi-Q incrementally builds a query tree whose structure is not predetermined but is determined by corpus support signals. At each query node, a resolution operator checks whether currently retrieved evidence is sufficient to support that query unit. If so, the node is marked resolved and not expanded further. If not, a dependency-preserving binary operator decomposes the query unit into finer-grained sub-queries, which are then validated by a semantic coverage verifier to ensure they collectively preserve the original intent. This process is repeated, effectively growing a query tree adapted to what the corpus can support, and guiding retrieval and reasoning over multi-hop evidence without relying on pre-built corpus graphs or rigid templates.

Result: Hi-Q is evaluated on three multi-hop QA benchmarks under two regimes: (1) full-corpus retrieval, where the system must find supporting evidence among large open-domain distractors; and (2) a restricted supporting/distractor setting used in prior work. In the full-corpus setting, Hi-Q achieves an average of 52.3 EM and 64.0 F1 over the three benchmarks, outperforming the iterative retrieval baseline IRCoT by 15.1 EM and 18.2 F1 and the graph-based RAG baseline PropRAG by 11.5 EM and 12.0 F1 on MuSiQue-full, while avoiding explicit corpus-wide graph construction. In the restricted setting, Hi-Q also attains the best performance, with 57.9 EM and 69.3 F1 on average, surpassing PropRAG by 5.6 EM / 3.9 F1 and IRCoT by 13.7 EM / 15.8 F1.

Conclusion: Hi-Q demonstrates that explicitly modeling retrievable granularity discovery—deciding when a query unit is sufficiently supported by evidence and when it should be further decomposed—substantially improves multi-hop QA. By growing a query tree driven by corpus support signals, Hi-Q avoids rigid decomposition templates and expensive corpus-wide graph construction while outperforming strong iterative and graph-based retrieval baselines in both full-corpus and restricted evidence settings. This shows that evidence-conditioned hierarchical query refinement is a powerful and scalable approach for complex, multi-hop reasoning over large text corpora.

Abstract: A central bottleneck in multi-hop Question Answering (QA) is that the granularity at which a question is expressed often differs from the granularity at which corpus evidence is retrievable. Existing methods address this mismatch by imposing fixed graph structures over the corpus, by iteratively reformulating the query, or by executing a generated program over it, but these strategies do not explicitly decide when a query unit is already supported by evidence and when it should be refined. We formulate this bottleneck as retrievable granularity discovery and introduce Hi-Q, an evidence-conditioned framework for hierarchical query refinement. At each query node, a resolution operator tests whether retrieved evidence supports the current query unit; resolved nodes terminate, while unresolved nodes are expanded by a dependency-preserving binary operator and checked by a semantic coverage verifier. Hi-Q therefore grows a query tree whose topology is determined by corpus support signals rather than by a fixed decomposition template or a pre-built graph. We evaluate Hi-Q on three multi-hop QA benchmarks, primarily under full-corpus retrieval, where dependent evidence must be located among open-domain distractors rather than within a small annotated pool. In this setting Hi-Q reaches 52.3 EM and 64.0 F1 averaged over the three benchmarks, ahead of the iterative retrieval baseline IRCoT by 15.1 EM / 18.2 F1 on that same average, and ahead of the graph-based RAG baseline PropRAG by 11.5 EM / 12.0 F1 on MuSiQue-full, without corpus-wide graph construction. In the restricted supporting/distractor setting used by prior work, Hi-Q likewise attains the best accuracy, with 57.9 EM and 69.3 F1 on average, ahead of PropRAG by 5.6 EM / 3.9 F1 and IRCoT by 13.7 EM / 15.8 F1. The project page is available at https://hi-q-project.github.io/.

</details>


### [171] [ImageEval 2026: Culturally Grounded Arabic Multimodal Evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30475)
*Samir Abdaljalil,Hunzalah Hassan Bhatti,Ahlam Bashiti,Farina Amir,Md Arid Hasan,Basel Mousi,Nadir Durrani,Fahim Dalvi,Zien Sheikh Ali,Erchin Serpedin,Hasan Kurban,Mustafa Jarrar,Shammur Absar Chowdhury,Firoj Alam*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Overview of ImageEval 2026 shared task on culturally grounded Arabic multimodal evaluation, including VQA, hallucination detection, and cultural accuracy of image generation, with datasets, evaluation, systems, and main findings released.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: There is a lack of comprehensive, culturally grounded benchmarks and evaluations for multimodal systems in Arabic, especially covering both speech and image-text reasoning as well as cultural aspects of text-to-image generation. This task aims to fill that gap and standardize evaluation.

Method: Organize a shared task (ImageEval 2026) with two components: AynVQA for spoken visual question answering and image-grounded hallucination detection in English and MSA, and CRAI-Bench for assessing cultural accuracy in text-to-image generation. Provide datasets, define tracks and metrics, collect systems from participating teams, and evaluate them under a common protocol.

Result: Fourteen teams participated in the test phase and twelve submitted system papers, employing methods such as zero-shot prompting, fine-tuning vision-language models, speech-recognition pipelines, ensembling, and score calibration. The paper reports comparative performance across tracks and analyzes system behavior, though detailed scores are not in the abstract.

Conclusion: The shared task establishes new resources and benchmarks for culturally grounded Arabic multimodal evaluation, demonstrates diverse methodological approaches, and reveals that Arabic speech and image-text cultural reasoning remain challenging, underscoring the need for further research in this space.

Abstract: We present an overview of the ImageEval 2026 shared task on culturally grounded Arabic multimodal evaluation. It includes two tasks: (i) AynVQA, covering spoken visual question answering and image-grounded hallucination detection in English and Modern Standard Arabic (MSA), and (ii) CRAI-Bench, evaluating the cultural accuracy of text-to-image generation. A total of 14 teams participated in the test phase, with 12 teams submitting system description papers. Participating systems used a range of approaches, including zero-shot prompting, fine-tuning of vision-language models, speech-recognition pipelines, ensembling, and score calibration. We describe the task setup, datasets, evaluation procedure, and participating systems, and summarize the main results across the different tracks. All datasets and evaluation scripts from the shared task are released to the research community. The shared task highlights the challenges of culturally grounded multimodal evaluation, particularly for Arabic speech and image-text reasoning.

</details>


### [172] [Agents in the Large: Perception-Centered Architecture for Persistent Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30478)
*Shihan Dou,Haoxiang Jia,Shichun Liu,Feng Chen,Chenhao Huang,Yujiong Shen,Shaofan Liu,Jiayi Chen,Jiahang Lin,Honglin Guo,Qianyu He,Minghao Guo,Ziyi Ye,Pluto Zhou,Tao Gui,Qi Zhang,Xuanjing Huang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes Pera, a perception-centered architecture for building long-lived, adaptive language agents that provide persistent assistance rather than just solving one-off tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Most current language-agent frameworks focus on short-lived, user-specified tasks and lack a unifying architecture for agents that persist over time, adapt to evolving user needs, and handle ongoing service contexts. There is no clear conceptual framework to describe, compare, and guide the design of such persistent agents.

Method: The authors introduce Pera (Perception-Centered Architecture for Persistent Agents), a conceptual architecture that organizes a persistent agent around perception and control components. These components continuously gather and interpret signals from episodic tasks, internal state, and environmental changes, and then formulate “lifecycle tasks” that shape the agent’s ongoing behavior and adaptation. They apply Pera to retrospectively categorize existing work, analyze a detailed case study, and derive design insights for future systems.

Result: Pera provides a structured way to decompose persistent agents into perception and control processes, clarifying how agents can transform low-level signals into higher-level lifecycle tasks that update service procedures. Using Pera, the authors show how various recent systems fit into this architecture, and demonstrate through a case study how it can guide the design and operation of a concrete persistent agent.

Conclusion: Pera reframes language agents from short-lived problem solvers into long-lived, adaptive service providers by emphasizing continuous perception and lifecycle task construction. This architecture serves as a conceptual bridge analogous to the shift in software engineering from “programming in the small” to “programming in the large,” and is intended to guide the development of more capable, robust, and persistent AI agents.

Abstract: Cognitive language agents have achieved substantial progress by equipping language models with memory, tools, and decision-making procedures, enabling agents to reason and act in interactive environments. Existing frameworks largely cast these agents as systems for solving user-specified, bounded tasks. An increasingly important goal is for language agents to provide persistent assistance in long-lived settings where user needs, context, and service procedures persist and change, and to remain useful across the broad range of tasks that arise over time. Yet we still lack a framework to characterize persistent AI agents, organize existing work, and guide future development. To this end, we propose a Perception-Centered Architecture for Persistent Agents (Pera). Pera describes a persistent agent organized around perception and control components that continually perceive service-relevant signals from episodic task executions, internal context, and changes in the surrounding environment, and use these signals to construct lifecycle tasks. These tasks drive the ongoing operation and adaptation of the agent's service procedures. We use Pera to retrospectively organize recent work, examine a detailed case study, and offer forward-looking insights for building more capable persistent agents. Just as software engineering moved from programming in the small to programming in the large, Pera frames the evolution of language agents as an analogous architectural transition toward long-lived, adaptive intelligence systems.

</details>


### [173] [Two Centuries of Sexism in British Parliament: A Computational Analysis of Women's Representation in the Hansard Corpus](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30485)
*Mohammad Omar Khursheed,Mandira Sawkar,Ashiqur R. KhudaBukhsh*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Study of 200 years of UK parliamentary debates shows that sexist language, including when supporting women’s rights, is systematically embedded in legislative discourse.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand how sexism manifests linguistically in formal political debates over women’s suffrage and representation, and how this has evolved over two centuries, using large-scale computational methods.

Method: Construct a large, metadata-rich dataset from the UK Hansard parliamentary corpus (1803–2005). Use large language models to (1) classify each speech’s stance toward women’s suffrage and representation, and (2) detect and categorize sexist content according to the Ambivalent Sexism Inventory, distinguishing hostile and benevolent sexism. Compare patterns across speakers’ gender and time.

Result: In 6,531 suffrage-related speeches, 54% of anti-representation speeches contain sexist content vs 21% of pro-representation speeches. Anti-suffrage rhetoric blends hostile and benevolent sexism, while pro-suffrage sexist rhetoric is predominantly benevolent. Female MPs support women’s political rights in 93% of their speeches versus 70% for male MPs, with this gender gap disappearing only after women are enfranchised. A broader 6.7M-speech dataset with high gender-matching coverage is released for research.

Conclusion: Sexist rhetoric is pervasive even in speeches supporting women’s rights and follows distinct patterns consistent with Ambivalent Sexism theory: hostile and benevolent sexism are deployed in different rhetorical contexts. Legislative language over two centuries encodes systematic sexism, and the released dataset enables further computational social science research on these dynamics.

Abstract: The language a legislature uses to debate women's rights, even in favour of them, encodes systematic patterns of sexism that persist across two centuries. In this work, we analyse 6,531 speeches over 200 years of UK parliamentary debate (Hansard, 1803-2005) by using large language models to classify a speaker's perspective towards women's suffrage and political representation, as well as analyse sexist speech in parliament from the lens of the Ambivalent Sexism Inventory. We also release this parliamentary dataset, an organized and metadata-enriched version of the publicly available Hansard Corpus optimized for computational social science research, with 6.7 million speeches across 1.2 million debates, with 89% gender-matching for speeches by MPs from the House of Commons. We find that 54% of speeches opposing women's representation contain sexist content, compared to 21% of speeches that are for the cause, and that the two sides use fundamentally different types of sexism: anti-suffrage rhetoric combines hostile and benevolent framing, while pro-suffrage sexism is overwhelmingly benevolent. Female MPs support women's political rights at 93% compared to 70% for male MPs, a gap that closes only after enfranchisement. Our findings are evidence that benevolent and hostile sexism are used in different rhetorical contexts in a manner consistent with the theory of Ambivalent Sexism.

</details>


### [174] [UTILMEM: Benchmarking Evidence Utilization in Long-Term Conversational Memory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30508)
*Peijun Qing,Fobo Shi,Soroush Vosoughi*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces UtilMem, a benchmark to test how well conversational agents actually *use* long-term memory, not just recall isolated facts, and shows that current systems often fail at integrating and filtering retrieved information.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Most existing long‑term memory benchmarks for conversational agents only evaluate pointwise factual recall (retrieving single facts or local details from past interactions). However, real-world conversations require agents to integrate scattered, implicit, and noisy information from long histories into coherent, task-driven outputs. There was no focused benchmark to measure this more complex ability, which the authors term memory utilization, nor a clear understanding of how current systems perform on it.

Method: The authors design UtilMem, a diagnostic benchmark with 1,717 instances across five domains. Each instance targets one or more of four aspects of memory utilization: (1) reasoning over dense, long histories; (2) identifying implicitly relevant information in memory; (3) synthesizing distributed evidence into summaries, analyses, or plans; and (4) resisting interference from semantically similar but irrelevant distractors. They evaluate a diverse set of retrieval-based and memory-augmented conversational systems on UtilMem, comparing their performance to conventional factual-memory benchmarks.

Result: Experiments show that systems which perform well on traditional factual-memory benchmarks do not necessarily perform well on UtilMem.
