Even when retrieval components successfully surface relevant past information, models often fail to integrate evidence across sessions, synthesize it into appropriate outputs, or reliably distinguish helpful information from plausible but irrelevant distractors. Retrieval quality alone does not close the utilization gap.

Conclusion: There is a substantial gap between an agent’s ability to access stored information and its ability to use that information effectively in complex conversational tasks. Progress in long-term conversational memory will require architectures and training strategies that explicitly support multi-step evidence integration and robustness to retrieval interference, beyond improving factual recall alone. The UtilMem benchmark provides a diagnostic testbed to drive and measure such advances.

Abstract: Long-term memory is increasingly important for conversational agents, yet existing benchmarks primarily measure memory through pointwise factual recall: whether a system can recover isolated facts or event-level details from prior interactions. Real-world memory use, however, often requires a more demanding capability: integrating distributed, implicit, and noisy evidence across extended interaction histories into coherent, task-oriented outputs. We call this capability memory utilization. Here, we introduce UtilMem, a diagnostic benchmark comprising 1,717 instances across five domains, designed to evaluate four underexplored aspects of memory utilization: reasoning over dense histories, identifying implicitly relevant memories, synthesizing distributed evidence into summaries, analyses, or plans, and resisting interference from semantically similar distractors. Evaluating a diverse set of retrieval-based and memory-augmented systems, we find that strong performance on conventional factual-memory benchmarks does not reliably translate into effective memory utilization. Moreover, retrieval alone is insufficient: even when relevant evidence is successfully recovered, systems frequently fail to integrate information across sessions or to distinguish useful evidence from plausible distractors. These findings expose a substantial gap between accessing stored information and using it effectively, and suggest that progress in long-term conversational memory will require architectures that explicitly support evidence integration and robustness to retrieval interference. Code is available at https://github.com/peijunallin/UtilMem.

</details>


### [175] [WebWorld: The Browser as a World Model for Self-Improving Web Code](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30530)
*Jiajun Wu,Jian Yang,Yaxin Du,Wei Zhang,Haowen Wang,Junhang Cheng,Yuxuan Zhang,Tuney Zheng,Xianglong Liu,Ming Zhou*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces WebWorld, a browser-backed framework that lets a vision-language model (VLM) iteratively improve web code using the browser as an unfoolable world model, significantly boosting HTML coding performance over a base model.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing VLM-driven self-improvement for web code has a structural flaw: the same model both proposes and judges code repairs, relying on visual plausibility as a proxy for correctness. This leads to unreliable evaluation because the model can “fool itself.” The authors aim to introduce an objective, deterministic counterparty that accurately reflects whether a web page truly works under user interactions.

Method: They design WebWorld, an interface that connects a VLM prior to a real browser treated as a world model. In each iteration, the VLM produces a critique of current web code. A planner turns this critique into a typed interaction contract specifying how to interact with the page. The browser re-executes the candidate code under these interactions and issues an acceptance certificate only if (1) the target behavior improves and (2) all previously verified capabilities are preserved. These certified transitions are accumulated as a “quality ratchet,” and only this ratcheted data is used for subsequent supervised fine-tuning (SFT) of the model. They compare full WebWorld to equal-size ablations, including versions without browser-backed admission certificates.

Result: Using matched training settings, WebWorld-27B outperforms the base Raw-27B by 5.3 points on HTMLBench-400 and 14.9 points on MiniAppBench-Val, achieving parity with strong frontier systems such as Kimi-K2.6 and GPT-5.4 on interactive HTML generation. Ablation studies show that the performance gains largely vanish when the browser-backed acceptance certificate is removed, especially in the 9B model setting, indicating that the admission mechanism is the key contributor to the lift.

Conclusion: WebWorld effectively closes the loop in VLM-based web code self-improvement by introducing the browser as an unfakeable world model and gatekeeper. The browser-backed acceptance certificates and cumulative quality ratchet provide reliable supervision that substantially improves interactive HTML generation, elevating a 27B model to frontier-level performance. The results highlight that rigorous, environment-grounded admission—rather than just more data or naive self-critique—is crucial for successful self-improvement in code-generation for web interfaces.

Abstract: VLM-driven self-improvement of web code has a structural flaw: the model that proposes the repair is the model that judges it, and visual plausibility under that judge is a poor proxy for whether the page actually works. What the loop is missing is a counterparty the VLM cannot fool, and the browser already is that counterparty: a deterministic, executable simulator of how an HTML artifact behaves under user actions, and in everything but name a world model for web code. We present WebWorld, the interface that lets a VLM prior interact with this browser-as-world-model autonomously and decides which interactions become supervision. Each round, the VLM emits a critique that the planner compiles into a typed interaction contract; the browser re-executes the candidate and issues an acceptance certificate only when both target progress and preservation of every previously verified capability hold; certified transitions accumulate as a quality ratchet that is the only thing the SFT export ever sees. Under matched training, WebWorld-27B improves Raw-27B by 5.3 points on HTMLBench-400 and 14.9 points on MiniAppBench-Val, and reaches the level of strong frontier systems such as Kimi-K2.6 and GPT-5.4 on interactive HTML generation. Equal-size ablations show that browser-backed admission carries the gain: without the certificate, the matched 9B lift nearly disappears.

</details>


### [176] [Seeing the Unseen: Visual Similarity for Pixel Language Model Adaptation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30541)
*Ran Zhang,Miryam de Lhoneux,Wessel Poelman*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper studies how pixel-based language models can be adapted to a low-resource, complex-script language (Tibetan), and shows that visual similarity of scripts strongly affects cross-lingual transfer and adaptation behavior.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Pixel-based LMs avoid tokenization and operate directly on rendered text images, which conceptually allows easy extension to new scripts and languages. Yet, it is unclear how well they adapt to genuinely low-resource languages with complex morphology and unique scripts, and what role script similarity and prior pre-training play in this adaptation. Understanding these factors is important to make pixel-based approaches practical for underserved languages.

Method: Using Tibetan as a representative low-resource language written in a Brahmic-derived script, the authors conduct continued pre-training experiments on pixel-based LMs. They vary (1) the scale of additional Tibetan data, (2) whether the base model has seen the Tibetan script before, and (3) which other Brahmic-script languages are used for cross-lingual transfer. They design four rendering-level metrics that quantify visual similarity between scripts based on their pixel representations. They then evaluate the adapted models on three downstream Tibetan tasks, analyzing how script similarity and pre-training configuration affect performance.

Result: They find that higher orthographic (visual) similarity between scripts leads to better semantic transfer in pixel-based LMs, even when only small amounts of Tibetan data are available. There is a clear performance asymmetry between starting points: a multilingual pre-trained model (PIXEL-M4) performs better initially but shows limited gains from further adaptation, while a monolingual base model (PIXEL) that is later adapted with mixed scripts achieves larger improvements on sentence-level downstream tasks. The newly proposed visual script similarity metrics correlate with these transfer patterns.

Conclusion: Visual similarity between scripts is a key driver of cross-lingual transfer in pixel-based LMs, especially in low-resource settings. While multilingual pre-training yields strong out-of-the-box performance, it can restrict further adaptation, whereas starting from a simpler monolingual model and carefully selecting additional scripts for adaptation may deliver larger gains. The proposed rendering-level metrics and the Tibetan case study provide practical guidance for data and script selection when deploying pixel-based models to other low-resource, complex-script languages.

Abstract: Pixel-based language models (LMs) replace traditional tokenizers by processing rendered images of text, making cross-lingual transfer heavily dependent on the visual and structural properties of writing systems. However, the dynamics of adapting these models to low-resource languages with complex morphology and written in unique scripts are not yet explored. Using Tibetan as a case study, we analyze how continued pre-training of pixel-based LMs is influenced by data scale, initial script exposure, and cross-lingual transfer from languages written in other Brahmic scripts. We introduce four rendering-level metrics to quantify visual script similarity. We evaluate downstream performance across three tasks. Our results show that higher orthographic proximity enhances semantic transfer, even under severe data constraints. Additionally, we find a performance asymmetry based on the pre-training starting point: while multilingual pre-training PIXEL-M4 has stronger initial performance, its capacity for subsequent adaptation seems to be constrained, whereas adapting a monolingual model PIXEL with mixed scripts yields more gains on sentence-level tasks. Our metrics and case study offer empirical observations that could help inform data selection and script adaptation choices when working with pixel-based models in similar low-resource settings.

</details>


### [177] [Language Proficiency Assessment from Eye Movements in Naturalistic Passage Reading](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30583)
*Shachar Frenkel,Ido Falah,Omer Shubi,Yevgeni Berzak*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper investigates using eye-tracking during reading as an automated, reliable measure of second-language (L2) proficiency, extending prior work to more natural reading settings and addressing bias and reliability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard language proficiency tests depend on explicit linguistic tasks (vocabulary, grammar, reading comprehension), which can be limited, time-consuming, and potentially less cognitively grounded. Prior work showed that eye-movement patterns while reading single sentences can predict L2 proficiency, but it remained unclear whether this generalizes to more natural reading, different testing regimes, and how valid and reliable such measures are. There were also open concerns about bias related to a learner’s native language and about the test’s reliability compared to standard exams.

Method: The authors collect eye-tracking data from learners of English as a second language while they read contextualized passages in an information-seeking setting (more naturalistic than isolated sentences). They derive behavioral features from eye movements (e.g., fixation durations, saccades, regressions) and train prediction models to estimate language proficiency using new proficiency measures. They then (1) evaluate predictive performance across tasks and regimes, (2) analyze whether predicted proficiency scores are biased by the linguistic distance between the learner’s L1 and English, and (3) perform reliability analyses. To handle L1-related bias, they introduce and test a debiasing method for the eye-movement-based scores.

Result: Eye-movement-based proficiency prediction remains effective when moving from single-sentence reading to naturalistic, contextualized passages and information-seeking reading. The analysis shows that raw eye-movement proficiency scores are systematically higher for learners whose native languages are linguistically closer to English, indicating a scoring bias. The proposed debiasing method substantially reduces or removes this L1-proximity bias. Reliability tests show that the eye-movement-derived proficiency scores are at least as reliable, and in fact more reliable, than traditional language proficiency test scores used as comparison.

Conclusion: Eye-tracking during reading is a strong, cognitively grounded basis for assessing second language proficiency, and its effectiveness generalizes to more realistic reading conditions and new proficiency measures. Although such scores are initially biased by the learner’s L1 similarity to English, an appropriate debiasing method can correct for this, improving validity. The higher reliability of eye-movement-based scores compared with standard tests supports their promise for future language assessment technologies and motivates further development and deployment of eye-movement-based proficiency testing systems.

Abstract: Standard language proficiency tests rely on linguistic tasks such as vocabulary, grammar and reading comprehension quizzes. An alternative, cognitively motivated approach, introduced in Berzak et al. (2018), proposed instead to predict language proficiency from behavioral traces of eye movements in reading. In this work, we validate and extend this approach from single sentences to more naturalistic reading of contextualized passages in English as a second language, new proficiency measures, prediction models, and reading in an information seeking regime. We find that the approach is effective in all these evaluations. We further address two key open questions on eye movement based proficiency testing: (1) potential scoring biases that reflect the proximity of the reader's native language to English, which may undermine validity, and (2) its reliability. We find that eye movement based proficiency scores are indeed biased towards L1s that are linguistically closer to English. We propose a score debiasing method which effectively remedies this issue. The reliability analyses suggest that eye movement proficiency scores are more reliable than standard language proficiency scores. Overall, our results strengthen and broaden the empirical foundations for future eye movement based language assessment technologies.

</details>


### [178] [Reading the News: Adapting Large Language Models to Swedish Journalism Through Continued Pre-Training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30609)
*Lukas Borggren,Jenny Kunz,Marco Kuhlmann*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper studies how to adapt large language models to Swedish journalism via continued pre-training on a curated news corpus and shows that this helps domain generation and factuality when combined with experience replay and targeted evaluation, but less so for discriminative tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: General-purpose large language models often underperform in narrow, low-resource domains like Swedish journalism. Existing Swedish benchmarks also may not reflect performance on real editorial tasks. The authors aim to systematically adapt LLMs to this domain and to build better evaluation tools to measure the impact of adaptation.

Method: They curate a large, high-quality corpus of Swedish news articles and perform continued pre-training of two different model sizes on this corpus. They compare full fine-tuning and parameter-efficient fine-tuning (specifically low-rank adaptation) and test the effect of adding experience replay during continued pre-training to reduce catastrophic forgetting. They also build a new domain-specific benchmark of six editorial tasks covering typical newsroom needs and explore a training-free approach to enhance instruction following on top of the adapted models.

Result: Continued pre-training on the Swedish news corpus improves models on in-domain generative tasks and factual knowledge, but these gains appear only when experience replay is used; otherwise, forgetting harms performance. The improvements are not mirrored on discriminative tasks. A training-free instruction-following enhancement further boosts performance, but only for models adapted via low-rank (parameter-efficient) methods. Standard Swedish benchmarks fail to reflect these in-domain gains, whereas the new editorial benchmark does.

Conclusion: Domain adaptation of LLMs via continued pre-training can substantially benefit Swedish journalism use cases, especially for generation and factuality, provided that catastrophic forgetting is addressed with techniques like experience replay. Parameter-efficient methods interact favorably with training-free instruction-following enhancements. Targeted, domain-specific benchmarks are essential, as generic Swedish benchmarks largely miss the true in-domain improvements, underscoring the need for application-aligned evaluation in LLM adaptation.

Abstract: Large language models are increasingly capable in general, but their utility can remain modest in niche or understudied areas. One approach to address this limitation is to specialise existing models through additional training on target-domain corpora. In this work, we investigate such continued pre-training for adapting large language models to Swedish journalism, using a high-quality dataset that we curate from millions of news articles. To evaluate the adaptation efficacy, we also construct a novel domain-specific benchmark that covers six editorial tasks. Through full and parameter-efficient fine-tuning across two model sizes, we find that continued pre-training yields benefits in the target domain, but only when paired with experience replay to mitigate forgetting. We observe consistent enhancements in the models' generation quality and factual knowledge, but not their proficiency in discriminative tasks. Exploring a training-free method to facilitate instruction following, we see further improvements, but exclusively for models trained with low-rank adaptation. Crucially, we demonstrate the importance of targeted evaluation in the adaptation process, as an existing Swedish benchmark largely fails to capture the models' in-domain performance gains.

</details>


### [179] [TaxCE : A Framework for Automated Taxonomy Construction and Evaluation at Scale](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30614)
*Sandeep Sricharan Mukku,Albert Aristotle Nanda,Rohit Pyati*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: TaxCE is an automated framework that builds high-quality hierarchical taxonomies from large amounts of unstructured feedback text, plus new evaluation metrics and an iterative refinement loop that together outperform prior methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Unstructured feedback (reviews, transcripts, surveys) arrives at massive scale and in many forms, making it hard to organize into clear, multi-level taxonomies that capture both common and long-tail topics. Existing NLP approaches typically yield shallow hierarchies, miss rare but important themes, or lack principled, corpus-grounded ways to evaluate taxonomy quality. There is a need for an automated, scalable method that can construct deep, actionable topic hierarchies and rigorously assess and improve them.

Method: The authors propose TaxCE, a fully automated framework that: (1) progressively condenses raw text into actionable segments; (2) merges them into deduplicated semantic units; (3) clusters these into granular topics with definitions; and (4) organizes topics bottom‑up into a hierarchical taxonomy that remains grounded in the source corpus. They also design three corpus-grounded evaluation metrics—Exclusivity, Exhaustivity, and Granularity (EEG)—to quantify how well the taxonomy partitions and covers the corpus at appropriate detail. These metrics are used in a metrics-in-the-loop iterative refinement procedure: TaxCE diagnoses where the taxonomy underperforms on EEG and then applies targeted corrections (e.g., splitting, merging, or reassigning topics) until the metrics converge.

Result: In extensive experiments across multiple datasets, TaxCE outperforms strong baselines including classical topic models, neural topic modeling methods, and LLM-based taxonomy builders. On average, TaxCE achieves gains of 11.8 percentage points in Exclusivity, 20.5 in Exhaustivity, and 15.7 in Granularity over the best competing method. Human evaluators additionally rate TaxCE’s taxonomies as better in quality, actionability for downstream use, and navigability of feedback content.

Conclusion: TaxCE provides an effective, fully automated solution for constructing deep, corpus-grounded hierarchical taxonomies from unstructured feedback. By coupling a multi-stage condensation and clustering pipeline with novel EEG metrics and a metrics-driven refinement loop, it produces taxonomies that more cleanly separate topics, cover the corpus more completely, and offer more appropriate detail than existing methods. The combination of strong automatic and human evaluation results suggests TaxCE is a practical approach for large-scale feedback analysis and organization.

Abstract: Organizing unstructured feedback text into hierarchical taxonomy is a fundamental challenge in NLP, particularly in domains where feedback arrives at massive scale in varied forms such as reviews, transcripts, and surveys. Existing approaches either produce shallow hierarchies, neglect long-tail topics, or lack rigorous evaluation frameworks. We present TaxCE, a fully automated framework that constructs multi-level hierarchical taxonomies from raw text through progressive condensation of corpus content into actionable segments, deduplicated semantic units, and granular topics with definitions, which are then organized bottom-up into a hierarchy with corpus-groundedness. We also introduce three corpus-grounded evaluation metrics, Exclusivity, Exhaustivity, and Granularity (EEG), and integrate them into a metrics-in-the-loop iterative refinement mechanism that diagnoses deficiencies and applies targeted corrections until convergence. Extensive experiments demonstrate that TaxCE consistently outperforms existing baselines spanning classical topic models, neural methods, and LLM-based approaches, with average improvements of 11.8, 20.5, and 15.7 percentage points in exclusivity, exhaustivity, and granularity respectively over the strongest baseline. Human evaluation further confirms superior taxonomy quality, actionability, and navigability.

</details>


### [180] [Hidden Threat in Synthetic Data: Covert Targeted Bias Injection through Benign Text](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30619)
*Minkyung Cho,Jihyo Kim,SeungWoo Song,Junghun Yuk,Minjoon Kee,Hoyun Song,KyungTae Lim*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper studies whether synthetic data generated by misaligned models can secretly inject social biases into aligned language models during training.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As synthetic data becomes common for training LLMs, there is little understanding of its security risks, especially the possibility that hidden biases or behaviors could be transferred through data that appears harmless.

Method: The authors build a pipeline where a misaligned teacher LLM generates synthetic datasets in domains like creative writing and coding. These datasets are filtered to look benign, then used to fine-tune already aligned student models. They then measure whether targeted social biases and behaviors are transferred while monitoring overall task performance. They also explore a log-linearity-based scoring method to detect suspicious data.

Result: They find that even semantically benign-looking synthetic data can serve as a covert channel that reliably transfers targeted social biases to the student models, with minimal degradation of their general capabilities. Moreover, log-linearity-based scoring appears to provide a useful signal for flagging such suspicious synthetic data.

Conclusion: Synthetic data pipelines pose underappreciated security risks: misaligned models can embed targeted social biases into apparently harmless data that then corrupts aligned models. Therefore, current safeguards are insufficient, and methods like log-linearity-based scoring may help screen synthetic data, but more robust defenses are needed.

Abstract: Synthetic data is increasingly used to train large language models (LLMs), yet its security implications remain poorly understood. Prior work on subliminal learning suggests that models can inherit behavioral traits from seemingly unrelated training data. In this work, we investigate whether such mechanisms can be exploited to inject targeted social biases into aligned models through semantically benign synthetic data. We construct a pipeline in which a misaligned teacher model generates filtered synthetic datasets across domains such as creative writing and code generation, which are then used to fine-tune aligned student models. Our experiments show that benign-looking synthetic data can act as a covert channel for transmitting targeted biases while largely preserving the student model's general task capabilities. These results reveal a previously underexplored security risk in synthetic data-driven LLM training pipelines and highlight the need for improved safeguards. As one possible step toward this goal, we suggest that log-linearity-based scoring may provide a useful signal for screening seemingly benign synthetic data.

</details>


### [181] [REER-PT: Reverse-Engineered Reasoning for Perplexity-Guided Pre-training Data Augmentation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30627)
*Haoran Que,Jiajun Shi,Ting Huang,Renming Pang,Jiaheng Liu,Ge Zhang,Wenhao Huang,Shen Yan,Wei Ye,Shikun Zhang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: They propose REER-PT, a scalable framework that augments raw pre-training corpora with sparse reasoning annotations to better connect contexts and their continuations, improving perplexity and downstream reasoning performance without changing the standard next-token prediction objective.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As language models scale, performance becomes increasingly constrained by the quality, not just quantity, of training data. Standard next-token prediction only supervises the final continuation and leaves the underlying reasoning implicit, potentially limiting models’ ability to learn robust reasoning skills from raw web-style text. The authors aim to uncover and explicitly supervise intermediate reasoning that is already implicitly present in pre-training data, thereby improving data efficiency and model capabilities without more compute or a different objective.

Method: They extend Reverse-Engineered Reasoning (REER) into a pre-training setting (REER-PT). For raw text, they algorithmically identify continuations that are comparatively hard to predict yet still inferable from the preceding context. For these spans, they generate candidate reasoning annotations that would make the continuation easier to predict. These candidates are produced and iteratively refined offline, with language-model perplexity as the optimization signal: good annotations are those that significantly reduce perplexity on the continuation. They apply constraints on annotation length and on ‘target leakage’ so that annotations neither simply restate the answer nor become overly long or trivial. The transformation is sparse (only some examples are annotated), preserves the original source text, and is formatted to remain compatible with standard next-token prediction training. They then construct an augmented corpus by inserting these annotations into a base pre-training corpus and compare models trained on the original vs. augmented data.

Result: On corpus-level analysis, they report perplexity reductions between 0.42 and 7.29 points across different evaluation setups: augmented-data perplexity, perplexity on original tokens, and on selected continuations. Only about 0.05% of annotation 13-grams are found verbatim in the original text, suggesting the annotations are genuinely new rather than copied spans. In controlled experiments with two 680M-parameter models trained from scratch on either the original or augmented corpus (same architecture and training config), the model trained on augmented data achieves up to +2.07 percentage points on several knowledge and reasoning benchmarks, indicating better generalization and reasoning.

Conclusion: Explicitly inserting concise reasoning annotations into raw pre-training data—using an offline, perplexity-driven REER-PT pipeline—can measurably improve both the predictability of continuations and downstream benchmark performance, all while preserving the standard next-token prediction objective and avoiding expensive online reasoning rollouts. This suggests that scalable, automated reasoning-focused data augmentation is a promising direction for enhancing language-model capabilities via better use of existing pre-training data.

Abstract: As language-model compute continues to scale, high-quality training data is becoming an increasingly important bottleneck. Conventional next-token prediction supervises what follows a context but leaves the intermediate reasoning behind that continuation implicit. We introduce \textbf{REER-PT}, a scalable framework that extends Reverse-Engineered Reasoning (REER) to raw pre-training data. REER-PT identifies continuations that are difficult to predict but can still be inferred from the preceding context, and inserts concise reasoning annotations that reconstruct the missing connection between context and continuation. Candidate annotations are generated and refined offline, with perplexity serving as the optimization signal. Constraints on length and target leakage filter out unhelpful or trivial annotations. This sparse transformation preserves the source text and remains compatible with standard next-token prediction, avoiding online reasoning rollouts during pre-training. We apply REER-PT to transform a source pre-training corpus into an augmented one. Across augmented-data, original-token, and selected-continuation comparisons, perplexity reductions range from 0.42 to 7.29, and only about 0.05\% of annotation 13-grams appear verbatim in the source text. We then train two 680M-parameter models with the same architecture and training configuration on the source and augmented corpora, respectively. The augmented-data model gains up to 2.07 percentage points on several knowledge and reasoning benchmarks. Together, the perplexity analysis indicates improved continuation predictability, while the controlled pre-training experiments suggest that this augmentation can improve model performance without changing the standard pre-training objective.

</details>


### [182] [GMTS: Gradient Magnitude-based Token Selection Improves RLVR Training for LLM Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30632)
*Outongyi Lv,Yuanwei Zhang,Xiaoqun Zhang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper investigates why high-entropy tokens help RLVR training for LLM reasoning and proposes GMTS, a gradient-magnitude-based token selection method that outperforms entropy-based selection.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: RL with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) is powerful for improving LLM reasoning, and prior work shows that training only on high-entropy tokens (top 20%) still gives strong gains. However, it is unclear *why* these high-entropy tokens are so beneficial and whether entropy alone is the right signal for token importance, especially when answer-level rewards differ.

Method: The authors empirically analyze the relationship between token entropy, gradient magnitude, and reward across answers in RLVR settings. They show that within a single answer, high-entropy tokens often correlate with large gradient magnitude, but across different answers entropy does not reliably indicate importance because reward signals vary. Building on this, they propose Gradient Magnitude-based Token Selection (GMTS), which uses the entropy–gradient link to approximate gradient-magnitude rankings and select the top-k% most important tokens for training instead of simply using highest-entropy tokens.

Result: Experiments on three reasoning domains and multiple model sizes show that training RLVR updates only on the top 20% of tokens selected by GMTS leads to better performance than the commonly used entropy-based high-entropy token selection. This holds consistently across the tested tasks and models, indicating that GMTS more accurately captures token contribution to learning.

Conclusion: High-entropy tokens are useful in RLVR because they are often associated with large gradients within an answer, but entropy alone is an imperfect proxy for token importance across answers with different rewards. By estimating token importance via approximate gradient-magnitude ranking, GMTS provides a more fine-grained and reliable selection scheme, yielding superior reasoning performance compared to entropy-based token filtering in RLVR training.

Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL), particularly RL with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR), has recently emerged as a central paradigm for enhancing large language models' (LLMs) reasoning abilities, demonstrating remarkable effectiveness across reasoning tasks. Recent studies suggest that high-entropy tokens play an exceptionally important role in model training, since training with only the highest 20% entropy tokens yields significant performance gains. However, why such high-entropy tokens are beneficial remains insufficiently understood. In this work, we find that although high-entropy tokens within one answer tend to correlate with large gradient magnitude, entropy alone fails to consistently reflect token importance across different answers, considering the variations in the answer-level reward signals. Based on this observation, we introduce the Gradient Magnitude-based Token Selection (GMTS) method to quantify token importance, which leverages the entropy-gradient connection to approximate gradient-magnitude rankings for token selection. We find that training on the top 20% tokens ranked by GMTS consistently outperforms entropy-based token selection across three reasoning domains and various model sizes, suggesting that GMTS provides a more fine-grained estimate of token contribution for RLVR training.

</details>


### [183] [BiG-SURE - Bipartite Graph for Semantic Uncertainty and Reliability Estimation of LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30646)
*Debarpan Bhattacharya,Malay Phadke,Sriram Ganapathy*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: BiG-SURE is a black-box uncertainty estimator for LLMs/VLMs that uses semantic agreement between low- and high-temperature outputs across meaning-preserving input transformations, modeled via a bipartite graph and scored by spectral energy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In safety-critical applications, we need reliable uncertainty estimates from large language and vision-language models, but often only have black-box access (no logits or internal states). Existing black-box methods are limited, and we need a simple, unsupervised, model-agnostic way to know when the model’s answer is likely unreliable, especially for complex QA tasks in text, multilingual, and multimodal settings.

Method: 1) Sample low-temperature responses from the target model and treat them as stable semantic anchors representing the model’s core belief. 2) Apply meaning-preserving input transformations and query the model at higher temperatures to obtain more diverse probe responses. 3) Use an NLI model to compute entailment/semantic-alignment scores between each anchor and each probe, forming a bipartite graph adjacency matrix. 4) Define a Semantic Uncertainty and Reliability Estimation (SURE) score by computing the normalized squared spectral energy of this matrix; high energy reflects strong, consistent semantic agreement. 5) Convert this SURE score into a confidence value, with uncertainty taken as its complement.

Result: Across text QA, multilingual QA, and multimodal QA benchmarks and multiple model families, BiG-SURE achieves higher abstention AUROC than prior black-box uncertainty estimation methods, indicating that it more accurately distinguishes between correct and incorrect model answers. It does so without needing access to model internals or supervised calibration data.

Conclusion: BiG-SURE provides an effective, simple, and fully black-box method for semantic uncertainty estimation in LLMs and VLMs. By leveraging cross-temperature semantic agreement via a bipartite graph and spectral analysis, it reliably identifies uncertain predictions and outperforms existing black-box baselines on several QA tasks, making it suitable for safety-critical deployments where reliable abstention is needed.

Abstract: Reliable uncertainty estimation is a crucial requirement for deploying large language models (LLMs) and vision-language models (VLMs) in safety-critical settings, especially when the model parameters are not accessible (black-box). We propose BiG-SURE, an uncertainty estimator based on cross-temperature semantic agreement. The method samples low-temperature responses as stable semantic anchors and high-temperature responses as probes under meaning-preserving input transformations. It then constructs an anchor-probe Bipartite Graph (BiG) using NLI-based entailment scores and defines confidence through the normalized squared spectral energy of this matrix, with uncertainty given by its complement. This bipartite graph-based Semantic Uncertainty and Reliability Estimation (SURE) score measures whether high-temperature probes remain semantically aligned with the model's stable low-temperature belief or not. We evaluate BiG-SURE on text QA, multilingual QA, and multimodal QA tasks across multiple model families. In these experiments, BiG-SURE improves average abstention AUROC over prior black-box uncertainty estimators, while remaining simple, unsupervised, and applicable to black-box model settings.

</details>


### [184] [What It Costs to Compose, Rebuild, and Correct Precomputed Memory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30647)
*Asa Shepard*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Study of when and how precomputed memory (KV caches or their compressions) for Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct stays correct and useful across queries.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Repeatedly feeding long contexts to LMs is expensive; using precomputed memory (saved KV caches or compressed versions) promises efficiency, but it is unclear under what conditions this remains accurate, up-to-date, and robust to updates or composition from parts.

Method: Run experiments on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct using (1) raw saved key–value caches and (2) trained compressed representations of those caches, testing: (a) assembling memories from separately prepared parts; (b) how performance decays as underlying information changes and memory is not rebuilt; (c) how well different update mechanisms work (rebuilds, pasted corrections, injected cache updates) and at what computational cost.

Result: Precomputed memories become unreliable when composed from independently-prepared segments, lose currency unless frequently rebuilt at a cost approaching full recomputation, and often fail to incorporate corrective information given alongside them depending on phrasing. Warm-rebuilding compressed caches and serving carefully-phrased updates with the memory partially mitigate these issues, with measured (but nontrivial) computational costs.

Conclusion: For real systems handling varied queries, precomputed memories should be rebuilt at roughly the rate that new information changes the underlying source. Precomputed memory is useful only if it can be (1) rebuilt cost-effectively, (2) combined safely, and (3) reliably overridden by new information. Warm rebuilds of compressed caches and targeted side-by-side updates are promising strategies, but open questions remain about better compression, safer composition, and more robust update mechanisms.

Abstract: Language models can answer from precomputed memory, a model's saved reading of a body of material, reused across requests instead of read again at each. This paper maps where that practice preserves correctness and the conditions under which it fails. Across experiments on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct using both saved key-value caches and trained compressions of them, precomputed memory degrades when assembled from separately prepared parts, stays current only through rebuilds costing a large fraction of full preparation in our measurements, and ignores corrections served beside it conditional on phrasing. If precomputed memories can be served alongside one another, be cost-efficiently rebuilt, and be superseded by new information arriving in real-time, they can serve as a way to avoid re-feeding context to a model over repeated queries. The implication of our results for a deployed system that deals with a variety of queries is that precomputed memories are best rebuilt on the cadence at which new information changes what the memory was originally computed from. Both warm-rebuilding trained compressions of key-value caches and serving specifically-phrased updates beside a memory, as pasted text or injected cache state, show particular promise for keeping precomputed memories current, the latter as an interim measure between rebuilds, and we measure the cost and name the remaining questions associated with each.

</details>


### [185] [Where Identity Lives: Localized, Retain-Free Identity Unlearning in Multimodal Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30649)
*Kangwook Ko,Jaehyuk Jang,Wonjun Lee,Hee-Seon Kim,Changick Kim*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes PAVA, a retain-free unlearning method for multimodal large language models that removes specific individuals' information while preserving visual-language capabilities by localizing and constraining updates to identity-relevant MLP layers and anchoring them with distilled pre-unlearning behavior.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: After deployment, MLLMs may need to forget specific individuals' data for privacy or legal reasons. Existing unlearning methods require a retain set of benign data to balance forgetting, but this set is difficult to construct post-deployment and rebuilding it re-exposes sensitive data. Forgetting using only the forget set harms shared visual-language representations and degrades perception. The authors are motivated to design an unlearning approach that does not require a retain set yet still preserves the model’s general visual-language ability.

Method: The authors reframe retain-free unlearning as a localization problem: identify where identity information is stored so that updates can be restricted there. Using causal tracing, weight transplant experiments, and Fisher overlap analysis, they find that identity information in MLLMs concentrates in early-to-mid decoder MLP layers, which can be modified with minimal impact on vision components. They propose Pathway-Aware Visual-attribute Anchoring (PAVA), which confines unlearning updates to these decoder MLP layers and combines a forget loss (to erase the target individual) with a visual-attribute anchor loss. This anchor distills the model’s own pre-unlearning responses on the same forget images, preserving image-grounded behavior without needing an external retain set.

Result: On benchmarks MLLMU-Bench and ReMem, PAVA achieves the best trade-off between forgetting the target identity and retaining general capabilities among all methods that only use forget sets. Moreover, its performance is competitive with stronger baselines that do use retain sets, indicating that careful localization and anchoring can substitute for explicit retain data in many cases.

Conclusion: Identity information in MLLMs is localized mainly in early-to-mid decoder MLP layers, which can be selectively updated to forget individuals while preserving visual-language competence. By constraining optimization to these pathways and anchoring to the model’s own pre-unlearning behavior on forget images, PAVA enables retain-free unlearning with competitive performance to retain-based methods. This suggests a practical path for privacy-preserving post-deployment unlearning in multimodal models without reconstructing large retain datasets.

Abstract: Removing a specific individual's information from multimodal large language models (MLLMs) is often needed after deployment, but existing methods rely on a retain set, which is hardest to obtain at that point, and rebuilding it recreates the privacy exposure that unlearning aims to remove. Forgetting from the forget set alone instead damages the shared visual-language computation, harming perception. We cast retain-free unlearning as a localization problem: causal tracing, weight transplant, and Fisher overlap all point to early-to-mid decoder MLPs as the layers where identity information is stored and, unlike other module families, can be modified without substantially disrupting vision. We turn this into Pathway-Aware Visual-attribute Anchoring (PAVA), which confines updates to these layers and pairs a forget loss with a visual-attribute anchor that preserves image-grounded behavior by distilling the model's own pre-unlearning answers from the forget images alone. On MLLMU-Bench and ReMem, PAVA gives the strongest forget-retain trade-off among forget-set-only methods and remains competitive with retain-based baselines.

</details>


### [186] [SwarmBench: Can Large Language Models Act as Agent Swarm Orchestrators?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30661)
*Jinshan Gao,Zhuoran Jin,Tianyi Men,Kang Liu,Jun Zhao*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces SwarmBench, a benchmark for evaluating the orchestration capabilities of large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent swarms, and SwarmExp, an experience-based method that improves these orchestration abilities.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing benchmarks mainly focus on single-agent or generic agent tasks and do not systematically measure the unique orchestration challenges of dynamically coordinated LLM agent swarms. This gap prevents rigorous comparison and improvement of swarm-style multi-agent systems.

Method: The authors design SwarmBench, a benchmark that measures orchestration across multiple dimensions: final task accuracy, efficiency, computational cost, and qualitative aspects of the coordination process. They experimentally evaluate different LLMs on this benchmark. Building on observed gaps, they also introduce SwarmExp, which uses experience extraction and replay to enhance orchestration performance.

Result: Experiments on SwarmBench reveal large performance disparities between current LLMs in their ability to orchestrate agent swarms. These disparities appear not just in end metrics like accuracy, time, or cost, but also in the structure and quality of the coordination process. Applying SwarmExp consistently improves orchestration metrics for the tested LLMs.

Conclusion: Orchestration capability is a distinct and crucial dimension of performance for LLM-based agent swarms, inadequately captured by existing benchmarks. SwarmBench provides a systematic way to measure it, and SwarmExp shows that simple experience-based techniques can significantly enhance these capabilities across models.

Abstract: Large language model-based multi-agent systems are evolving from fixed interaction topologies toward dynamically orchestrated Agent Swarms. However, existing benchmarks are still largely based on single-agent or general-purpose agent tasks, making it difficult to systematically evaluate key orchestration capabilities. We propose SwarmBench, a benchmark that evaluates model performance from multiple perspectives, including accuracy, efficiency, cost, and process quality. Experimental results show that current models exhibit substantial differences in orchestration capability. These differences are reflected not only in final accuracy, efficiency, and cost, but also in the overall quality of the orchestration process itself. Based on these findings, we further propose SwarmExp, a simple yet effective method based on experience extraction and experience replay, which consistently improves the orchestration performance of large language models.

</details>


### [187] [MURANO: Design, Run, and Reproduce Mechanistic Interpretability Experiments as Composable Pipelines](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30662)
*Alireza Bayat Makou,Emirhan Böge,Phu Gia Hoang,Federico Tiblias,Jingcheng Niu,Subhabrata Dutta,Richard Eckart de Castilho,Iryna Gurevych*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Murano is an open-source, step-based framework that unifies the full workflow of mechanistic interpretability studies for large language models, making complex, multi-library pipelines easier to design, run, and reproduce.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Mechanistic interpretability studies of large language models require combining multiple operations—such as loading models, recording internals, computing attributions, performing interventions, and evaluating effects—typically using several different libraries. Because those libraries emphasize different parts of the workflow and expose incompatible interfaces, researchers must write substantial glue code to make them interoperate, which hinders reproducibility and cross-disciplinary use. A unified, composable framework can lower these barriers and standardize such experiments.

Method: The authors design Murano as a pipeline framework where core interpretability operations (loading, recording, attribution, intervention, evaluation) are implemented as modular, composable steps. Each step declares the inputs it requires and the named result artifacts it produces, enabling automatic wiring of dependencies and reuse of intermediate results. Pipelines are executed in user-specified order, with Murano managing canonical addresses to track and pass component identities (e.g., model components, features) between steps. Murano is implemented on top of existing machine learning and interpretability libraries, serving as an orchestration and abstraction layer rather than replacing them.

Result: Murano successfully integrates disparate interpretability operations into a single, coherent workflow framework, demonstrating that a step-and-artifact abstraction can capture typical mechanistic interpretability studies. The authors showcase Murano by reproducing two well-known mechanistic interpretability studies and presenting an additional case study involving sparse autoencoders, illustrating that the framework can express established methods and support new analyses.

Conclusion: Murano provides a general, open-source framework that structures mechanistic interpretability research on large language models as composable pipelines, improving interoperability among existing tools and supporting reproducible studies. By formalizing interpretability tasks as steps that exchange named artifacts and using canonical addresses to track components, Murano helps standardize how such experiments are built and shared, potentially lowering the barrier for researchers from various disciplines to design and replicate mechanistic interpretability work.

Abstract: This paper presents Murano, an open source framework for designing, running, and reproducing mechanistic interpretability studies of large language models, intended for researchers across disciplines. These studies often combine loading, recording, attribution, intervention, and evaluation, while existing libraries tend to focus on different parts of this workflow. As a result, researchers using several libraries may need to adapt outputs from one for use by another. To bridge this gap, Murano represents operations from these five areas as composable steps. Steps exchange named result artifacts and declare the inputs they require and the outputs they produce. A pipeline executes its steps in the order supplied, and Murano uses canonical addresses when component identities pass between operations. Murano builds on existing interpretability and machine learning libraries. We demonstrate Murano through two reproductions of established interpretability studies and one illustrative sparse autoencoder case study.

</details>


### [188] [OCR-MetaReasoning Benchmark: Evaluating the Meta-Reasoning Ability of MLLMs in Text-Rich Image Understanding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30678)
*Gengxu Li,Yuan Wu,Yi Chang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces OCR-MetaReasoning, a benchmark to evaluate how multimodal LLMs perform distinct types of reasoning—deduction, induction, and abduction—grounded in OCR-extracted content from text-rich images, separating answer accuracy from reasoning-process compliance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Text-rich image understanding requires not just reading text via OCR but organizing it across various structures (words, layout, fields, charts, and visual correspondences) and performing correct reasoning over it. Existing evaluations often mix up simple extraction with reasoning and do not carefully check whether models actually follow the intended reasoning direction (e.g., applying explicit rules vs. inferring patterns vs. hypothesizing missing information). This makes it hard to diagnose models’ true reasoning abilities and limitations. The paper aims to provide a more controlled, fine-grained way to evaluate OCR-grounded reasoning in multimodal LLMs, focusing specifically on different reasoning types and on whether the reasoning process itself is appropriate, not only whether the final answer is correct.

Method: The authors construct OCR-MetaReasoning, a single-image benchmark with 1,500 human-verified samples structured in a balanced 3×5 taxonomy. The three dimensions of reasoning are deduction (visible-rule application), induction (abstracting hidden regularities), and abduction (recovering missing premises). These are crossed with five OCR-object categories, covering different types of OCR-grounded elements such as words, layout, fields, charts, and visual correspondences. Each sample includes reference reasoning steps. The benchmark supports automatic scoring of final answers and introduces two main metrics: (1) Meta-Reasoning Macro Score (MRMS) for overall performance across the taxonomy, and (2) Reasoning Process Compliance Score (RPCS) to evaluate whether the model’s explained reasoning aligns with the required reasoning direction and steps. They then evaluate a range of open-source and closed-source multimodal LLMs on this benchmark.

Result: Across the evaluated models, performance on OCR-grounded meta-reasoning is far from saturated. Models show particular weakness in applying visible rules (deduction) and handling layout-sensitive inference, indicating that even when text is correctly read, structured reasoning over it is difficult. The evaluations also reveal that models can produce rationales that are process-compliant (i.e., they look like the right kind of reasoning) while still arriving at incorrect final answers under exact-match scoring, highlighting a mismatch between reasoning quality and answer accuracy. Overall scores on MRMS and RPCS show substantial headroom for improvement across model families.

Conclusion: OCR-MetaReasoning provides a controlled, fine-grained benchmark for assessing OCR-grounded reasoning in multimodal LLMs, explicitly separating deduction, induction, and abduction and decoupling reasoning-process compliance from final-answer correctness. The results demonstrate that current MLLMs struggle with core aspects of OCR-based reasoning, particularly rule application and layout-aware inference, and that seemingly plausible rationales do not guarantee correct answers. The benchmark, metrics, and released code offer a standardized way to diagnose and advance meta-reasoning capabilities in text-rich image understanding systems.

Abstract: Text-rich image understanding requires multimodal large language models (MLLMs) to organize OCR (Optical Character Recognition)-grounded evidence across words, layout, fields, charts, and visual correspondences. Existing evaluations often conflate extraction with reasoning and rarely test whether models follow the required reasoning direction: applying visible rules, abstracting hidden regularities, or recovering missing premises. We introduce OCR-MetaReasoning, a controlled single-image benchmark that treats deduction, induction, and abduction as distinct directions and separates final-answer correctness from reasoning-process compliance. The benchmark contains 1,500 verified samples in a balanced \(3\times5\) taxonomy crossing three reasoning types with five OCR-object categories, along with reference reasoning steps, automatic answer scoring, the Meta-Reasoning Macro Score (MRMS), and the Reasoning Process Compliance Score (RPCS). Experiments with representative closed-source and open-source MLLMs show that OCR-grounded meta-reasoning remains far from saturated: models struggle with visible-rule application and layout-sensitive inference, while process-compliant rationales can accompany incorrect final answers under exact-match evaluation. The code is available at https://github.com/gengxuli/OCR-MetaReasoning.

</details>


### [189] [LCoT-GV: Graph Attention Networks for Verifying Long Reasoning Chains in Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30679)
*Bérénice Jaulmes,Mehwish Alam*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: They build a graph-based verifier to check whether long chains-of-thought produced by reasoning models are reliable.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long chains-of-thought from large reasoning models often contain incorrect, contradictory, or irrelevant intermediate steps, even when the final answer is correct. Existing verifiers focus mostly on final answers or short explanations, leaving a gap in assessing the internal consistency and logical quality of long reasoning traces.

Method: They convert each long chain-of-thought into a reasoning graph where nodes represent individual reasoning steps and edges encode semantic and logical relations between steps. They then train a Graph Attention Network (GAT) on these graphs to predict whether the entire chain-of-thought is correct. To support this, they construct a new dataset for graph-oriented verification, derived from multiple question answering reasoning benchmarks across domains.

Result: Experiments on this new dataset show that their LCoT-GV framework achieves performance competitive with the strongest existing approaches for verifying reasoning or chains-of-thought.

Conclusion: Modeling chains-of-thought as graphs and applying a GAT-based verifier is an effective way to assess the correctness of long reasoning traces, offering a competitive alternative to prior verification methods and demonstrating the value of graph-structured representations for reasoning verification.

Abstract: Large Reasoning Models produce Long Chains-of-Thought (LCoTs) which involve breaking down the problem into smaller reasoning steps before reaching the conclusion. However, these steps often contain contradictions, unsupported inferences, or irrelevant steps, even when the final answer is correct. We propose Long Chain-of-Thought Graph Verifier (LCoT-GV), a graph-based framework that represents LCoTs as reasoning graphs. Each node in the graph represents a reasoning step and the edges encode semantic and logical relations. A Graph Attention Network is then trained to predict chain-of-thought correctness from the reasoning graph. We construct a new graph-oriented verification dataset from multiple reasoning benchmarks for question answering in various domains. The results show that our method is competitive with the most similar approaches.

</details>


### [190] [WildSEEK: Evaluating Language Models for Information-Seeking](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30683)
*Tanise Ceron,Joachim Baumann,Elisa Bassignana,Berat Cabuk,Dirk Hovy,Debora Nozza*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: WildSEEK introduces a real-world, human-annotated benchmark and framework to evaluate LLM responses to information-seeking queries, especially in high-risk domains and analytical settings.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As language models increasingly mediate how users access information, particularly in complex and high-risk domains (like health and finance), there is a lack of systematic, generalizable evaluation focused on real-world information-seeking behavior and associated risks. Existing benchmarks are often narrow, topic-specific, or synthetic, which misses the nuances and failure modes that arise in natural user queries.

Method: The authors construct WildSEEK, a dataset of 3,000 real user information-seeking queries that are manually annotated along several dimensions: domain risk level (e.g., health, finance), query type (factoid vs. analytical), and multiple failure criteria for LLM responses (sycophancy, overreliance, US-centric bias, treatment of vulnerable populations). They then train classifiers on this data to automatically label and analyze a much larger set of 1.8M realistic user queries. Using this framework, they systematically evaluate LLM responses along reliability, safety, and fairness axes.

Result: Analysis of the 1.8M queries shows that more than one-third of information-seeking questions fall into high-risk domains and that these high-risk queries are more often analytical than simple factoid questions. Evaluation of LLM responses reveals frequent failures in four key areas—sycophantic behavior, overreliance on the model, defaulting to a US-centric viewpoint, and inadequate treatment of vulnerable populations—with higher failure rates for analytical queries compared to factoid ones.

Conclusion: WildSEEK provides an empirical basis and scalable framework for monitoring and evaluating LLM behavior on real-world, risk-sensitive information-seeking tasks. The work highlights that a substantial portion of user queries are high-risk and that current LLMs systematically underperform, especially on analytical questions. This underscores the need for improved model design, guardrails, and evaluation practices aimed at reliability, safety, and fairness as LLMs increasingly serve as primary gateways to information.

Abstract: Language models are increasingly mediating information access to end users, urging a systematic evaluation of their responses for a fair and reliable information ecosystem. Existing evaluations, however, are often topic-specific or synthetic, limiting their ability to capture the complexity of "in the wild" information-seeking queries and the risks present in model responses. To address this gap, we introduce WildSEEK, a manually annotated dataset of 3k information-seeking queries from real user interactions, and an evaluation framework for LLM-generated responses. WildSEEK includes annotations for risk-sensitive domains (e.g. health and financial information), and distinguishes factoid queries from analytical queries which seek responses beyond facts. We train classifiers on WildSEEK to analyze more than 1.8M realistic user queries. We find that over a third of information-seeking queries are high-risk and more often analytical. Our findings show that LLM responses fail more often in four criteria: sycophantic behavior, overreliance, a default US-centric perspective, and poor handling of vulnerable populations -- with failure rates being mostly higher for analytical queries. By providing methods to monitor the reliability, safety, and fairness of LLM behavior, our dataset and evaluation framework offer an empirical foundation for the broader question of how these systems should behave as they take on a growing role in information access.

</details>


### [191] [An Agentic Retrobiosynthesis Framework with Learned Frontier Selection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30702)
*Philippe Meyer,Guillaume Gricourt,Thomas Duigou,Joan Hérisson,Jean-Loup Faulon*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper evaluates how much a learned search policy from a large language model can improve multistep retrobiosynthesis when the underlying biochemical reaction engine is held fixed.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In multistep retrosynthesis (here, retrobiosynthesis), large language models are increasingly used as agents to plan reaction routes, but their benefit is confounded with that of the reaction model itself. The authors want to isolate and quantify the contribution of the search policy alone—specifically, how the choice of which intermediate (frontier) molecule to expand affects the success rate when the biochemical generation and validation are identical across methods.

Method: They use a deterministic, rule-based retrobiosynthesis engine that always returns the same validated biochemical transformations. The only degree of freedom is the search policy that selects which frontier molecule to expand. They compare different policies on several benchmarks (LASER, RetroPath RL Golden, BioNavi-NP). Policies are implemented using Qwen2.5-7B as a large language model, via both prompted and LoRA-fine-tuned variants, constrained to a strict choice-only interface. Performance is measured as the percentage of targets for which a valid pathway to E. coli-available metabolites is found under different expansion budgets (e.g., 10 and 200 expansions). Baselines include Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) with the same reaction engine.

Result: The LoRA-fine-tuned LLM policy outperforms MCTS on all reported benchmarks at fixed expansion budgets. At 10 expansions on LASER it achieves a 65±1% solve rate versus 59% for MCTS; at 200 expansions on LASER it achieves 78±1% versus 75%. It also performs better on RetroPath RL Golden (88±3% vs 80%) and BioNavi-NP (63±2% vs 45%). Fine-tuned policies consistently outperform direct prompting of the LLM under the same interface.

Conclusion: A route-supervised LLM policy that only controls frontier selection—without altering the underlying biochemical generation or validation—can meaningfully improve the efficiency (budgeted success rate) of retrobiosynthesis search. However, overall performance still depends on how the frontier is constructed and how reactions are ranked, indicating that policy learning complements but does not replace careful design of these components.

Abstract: Large language models are increasingly used as agents for multistep retrosynthesis, raising the question of how much their search policy contributes independently of the underlying reaction model. We investigate this question in a biological setting through rule-based retrobiosynthesis: a deterministic biochemical engine generates the same validated transitions for every method, searching for routes that terminate in metabolites available to an \emph{Escherichia coli} chassis, while the policy only selects which frontier molecule to expand next. Prompted and LoRA-tuned Qwen2.5-7B policies use a strict choice-only interface. The fine-tuned policy reaches $65\pm1$\% solve rate at 10 expansions on LASER versus 59\% for MCTS, and at 200 expansions reaches $78\pm1$\% versus 75\% on LASER, $88\pm3$\% versus 80\% on the RetroPath RL Golden benchmark, and $63\pm2$\% versus 45\% on the BioNavi-NP benchmark. Fine-tuning also consistently outperforms direct prompting. These results show that route-supervised frontier selection can improve budgeted search without altering biochemical generation, although performance remains dependent on frontier construction and reaction ranking.

</details>


### [192] [GUIDE: Guiding Internal Evidence with Language Instructions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30712)
*Soyeon Caren Han,Hyunsuk Chung,Jinwoo Kim,Seungyeon Ji,Kyungreem Han*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper presents GUIDE, a framework that uses language instructions to control which multimodal evidence a large model relies on, making its internal evidence usage more robust and alignable without hurting overall task performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing large multimodal models can follow instructions about the desired output, but they still often rely on spurious or shortcut cues internally, even when explicitly instructed to use or ignore certain evidence sources. There is a need for methods that not only direct what the model should produce, but also how it should use different modalities or evidence pathways during reasoning, to improve robustness and controllability.

Method: The authors propose GUIDE, which integrates grouped parameter-efficient adaptation with instruction-conditioned gating to selectively modulate multimodal evidence pathways during both reasoning and generation. They also design a pathway-level evaluation framework that measures how instructions affect evidence usage, via reliance sensitivity analysis, controlled perturbation experiments, examining pathway modulation patterns, and studying autoregressive decoding dynamics.

Result: Using GUIDE on multiple multimodal tasks (reasoning, classification, and generation) and datasets (GQA, TextVQA, MM-IMDb, CREMA-D, RAVDESS, Flickr30K), the model shows structured, instruction-aligned changes in which evidence sources it relies on, while largely maintaining its baseline performance on the tasks. It becomes more robust under targeted perturbations to particular evidence sources and supports controllable changes to evidence reliance across diverse multimodal scenarios.

Conclusion: Multimodal instruction following can be extended from controlling only the model’s outputs to also regulating its internal evidence usage. GUIDE demonstrates that language instructions can effectively steer how different evidence pathways contribute to model predictions, enabling more robust and controllable multimodal models without substantially degrading task performance.

Abstract: Large multimodal models follow instructions about what to generate, but not necessarily about what evidence to rely on. Hence, models may continue to depend on shortcut-associated cues even when instructions suggest otherwise. We introduce GUIDE, a framework for controlling internal evidence usage through language instructions. GUIDE combines grouped parameter-efficient adaptation with instruction-conditioned gating to modulate multimodal evidence pathways during reasoning and generation. We further introduce a pathway-level evaluation framework that characterizes instruction-conditioned evidence modulation through reliance sensitivity, controlled perturbation analysis, pathway modulation, and autoregressive decoding dynamics. Across multimodal reasoning, classification, and generation, GUIDE induces structured and instruction-aligned redistribution of evidence reliance while largely preserving task behavior. Experiments on GQA, TextVQA, MM-IMDb, CREMA-D, RAVDESS, and Flickr30K show that GUIDE improves robustness under targeted evidence perturbations and enables controllable modulation across diverse multimodal settings. This suggests that multimodal instruction following can extend beyond output control toward regulating how different evidence sources contribute to model predictions.

</details>


### [193] [SocialReasonBench: A Video-QA Benchmark for Social Reasoning with Counterfactual Narrative Videos](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30716)
*Zheyu Huang,Zijing Shi,Haozhe Luo,Huadong Tang,Mingyu Liu,Meng Fang,Ling Chen*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper presents SocialReasonBench, a video QA benchmark built from branching gameplay in Detroit: Become Human to evaluate socially grounded reasoning of large multimodal models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Although large multimodal models have improved in video understanding, they still lack robust reasoning about human-centered social situations. Current benchmarks mostly use linear videos with single trajectories, which makes it ambiguous whether models genuinely understand social dynamics or are just exploiting recurring narrative patterns. The authors want a benchmark that can cleanly test deeper social reasoning, especially in settings where different social outcomes can result from different choices.

Method: They construct SocialReasonBench, a multiple-choice video QA benchmark based on gameplay videos from the interactive narrative game Detroit: Become Human. They exploit the game’s branching storylines: different player decisions lead to alternative social outcomes that can be traced via the game’s script, flowchart, and recorded branches. A multi-agent curation pipeline is used to (1) localize socially meaningful clips; (2) align answer labels with objective game-state signals; and (3) automatically generate theory-guided questions plus diagnostic distractor options. The benchmark spans seven reasoning dimensions, such as recognizing intent, empathizing with emotions, judging moral dilemmas, performing counterfactual reasoning, and identifying causal antecedents.

Result: State-of-the-art large multimodal models achieve decent performance on simpler forms of social understanding in the benchmark but perform poorly on more complex reasoning tasks, particularly counterfactual and causal reasoning. Ablation and error analyses show that these models often over-rely on partial modality information and are susceptible to reasoning traps, including using superficial visual patterns (visual shortcuts) instead of modeling deeper social dynamics.

Conclusion: There is a significant gap between current LMMs’ ability to recognize observable events in videos and their capacity for robust, socially grounded reasoning about latent mental and social states. SocialReasonBench provides a challenging, systematically constructed benchmark that exposes this gap, especially in counterfactual and causal dimensions, and can be used to drive future research on more sophisticated social reasoning in multimodal models.

Abstract: Recent advances in Large Multimodal Models (LMMs) have greatly improved video understanding, yet their ability to reason about human-centered social situations remains limited. Existing benchmarks typically rely on videos with a single observed trajectory, making it difficult to determine whether models truly understand social dynamics or merely exploit recurring narrative patterns. We introduce SocialReasonBench, a video multiple-choice QA benchmark for evaluating socially grounded reasoning in scenarios derived from interactive narratives. Built from gameplay videos of Detroit: Become Human, the benchmark leverages branching storylines where player decisions lead to alternative social outcomes that can be checked against the game's own script, flowchart, and recorded branches. We develop a multi-agent curation pipeline that localizes socially meaningful clips, grounds answer labels in game-state signals, and generates theory-guided questions with diagnostic distractors. SocialReasonBench covers seven reasoning dimensions, including intent recognition, emotional empathy, moral dilemma, counterfactual reasoning, and causal antecedent. Experiments on contemporary LMMs show that models perform reasonably well on basic social understanding but struggle with counterfactual and causal reasoning. Further ablation and diagnostic error analyses reveal that models often depend on incomplete modality cues and fall into reasoning traps such as visual shortcuts, highlighting a gap between observable event recognition and deeper reasoning over latent social states.

</details>


### [194] [Mind the Gap: Theory-of-Mind-Grounded Friction for Epistemic Alignment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30719)
*Yifan Zhu,Kyeongmin Rim,James Pustejovsky*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces a Theory-of-Mind-based training signal to distinguish true belief alignment from mere conversational smoothness, improving models’ ability to detect and intervene in referential misunderstandings.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing preference-based alignment methods mostly optimize for locally preferred responses and surface-level coordination (e.g., polite acknowledgments, fluent progression) but lack an explicit representation of what each participant believes about the shared context. This leads models to miss "silent divergence," where dialogue participants appear coordinated yet refer to different entities. The authors aim to build a mechanically computable notion of epistemic alignment—who thinks what about which referent and about the other’s beliefs—so that systems can more reliably recognize and correct misgrounded references.

Method: They formalize Theory-of-Mind (ToM) inference as a structured control signal in Frictive Policy Optimization. For each referring expression in a dialogue, they extract a four-part belief representation: (1) the speaker’s intended referent, (2) the addressee’s interpreted referent, and (3–4) each participant’s model of the other’s belief about the referent. From this, they compute "friction" as misalignment between epistemic states, especially cases where both agents are confident but grounded on different referents (silent divergence). They then integrate this friction signal in two policy-training variants: FAR (friction-aware reward shaping) and FTR (a trust-region version that constrains updates relative to a base policy). They also run ablations, particularly removing the second-order belief channels, to test their importance for detecting misunderstandings.

Result: At the representation level, removing the second-order belief channel sharply reduces recall of misunderstandings from 65% to 26%, showing that modeling what each agent thinks the other believes is crucial. At the policy level, both FAR and FTR outperform DPO on intervention F1 and on "warranted-context calibration"—how well the system’s uncertainty matches whether it has enough context to intervene. Brier scores corroborate that FAR and FTR produce better-calibrated confidence. In multiple runs, FAR and FTR show substantially more stable performance, whereas DPO exhibits large variance and can even destroy some of the base model’s existing competence at intervening in misgrounded references.

Conclusion: A Theory-of-Mind-grounded friction signal—based on explicit comparison of structured belief states around referential expressions—can be used as a training signal for dialogue policies. This approach helps systems detect and intervene when speakers are talking past each other about different referents, and yields more stable, better-calibrated policies than standard DPO.
