Epistemic alignment, and especially second-order belief modeling, is therefore both practically useful and trainable for referential dialogue tasks.

Abstract: Productive dialogue alignment requires distinguishing \emph{surface coordination} (acknowledgments and smooth task progression) from \emph{epistemic alignment} (convergence of belief states); standard preference-based methods typically optimize response-level preferences without explicitly modeling the latter. We operationalize Theory-of-Mind (ToM) inference as a control signal within Frictive Policy Optimization by extracting, at each referring expression, a four-part belief structure: the speaker's intended referent, the addressee's interpretation, and each participant's model of the other's belief. This makes friction mechanically computable from epistemic-state comparisons, capturing \emph{silent divergence}, where both participants proceed confidently while grounding to different referents. We evaluate the signal at two levels. At the representation level, ablating the second-order channel reduces misunderstanding recall from $65\%$ to $26\%$. At the policy level, reward-shaping (FAR) and trust-region (FTR) variants improve intervention F1 and warranted-context calibration over DPO, with Brier scores independently supporting the calibration gains. Across three training runs, FAR and FTR remain substantially more stable, whereas DPO varies widely and can degrade intervention competence already present in the base policy. Thus, ToM-grounded friction provides a trainable signal for context-sensitive intervention under referential belief divergence.

</details>


### [195] [Where Do Multilingual Vision-Language Encoders Fail on Low-Resource Languages?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30725)
*Donghoon Han,SungHyun Moon,Aidyn Zhakatayev,Junghun Cha,SeungJae Lee*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper investigates why multilingual vision–language encoders perform much worse on low‑resource languages than on high‑resource ones, and finds that the problem is not a simple linear language direction at the output but a deeper, language‑specific divergence of the end‑of‑sequence hidden state through the network; by manipulating this trajectory and adjusting training, they substantially improve low‑resource retrieval without harming high‑resource performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multilingual vision–language models (e.g., CLIP-like encoders) claim to support hundreds of languages, but retrieval performance on low‑resource languages lags high‑resource languages by over 30 percentage points. Existing hypotheses blame a linear “language direction” at the model output that supposedly disrupts cross‑lingual and cross‑modal alignment, implying that debiasing this direction might fix the issue. The authors want to precisely locate what in the encoder architecture causes this low‑resource gap, test whether the linear-language-direction explanation holds in practice, and identify mechanisms that can be targeted to improve low‑resource language performance without degrading high‑resource languages.

Method: 1) Empirically probe two state-of-the-art multilingual vision–language encoders on image–text retrieval across language tiers (HRL vs LRL). 2) Apply linear debiasing methods (LEACE and iterated INLP) at the output representation to aggressively remove linear language information, then measure how much cross-lingual and cross-modal retrieval changes relative to random baselines. 3) Analyze internal activations along the encoders’ depth, focusing on the end-of-sequence (EOS) token hidden state, to track how its representation diverges by language as layers deepen. 4) Perform causal intervention experiments by substituting a non-English language’s EOS hidden state with its English counterpart a few blocks before the projection head, and measure the resulting retrieval performance shifts, while running control interventions to exclude trivial explanations (e.g., generic pooled-position effects or English being uniquely special). 5) Propose and train a modified architecture that includes a front-layer “trunk” designed to pull language-specific projections toward a centroid that reflects parallel content across languages, and then evaluate its effect on low- and high-resource language retrieval on benchmarks such as XM3600 (1,000-image subset) and three additional datasets.

Result: 1) Linear debiasing at the output layer is highly effective at removing explicit language information: LEACE reduces linear language classification accuracy from above 99% to near chance; iterated INLP lowers it to about 37–50%. 2) Despite this large reduction in linear language signal, low-resource language retrieval accuracy changes by at most ±1.5 percentage points, and the average performance across language tiers stays within 2.2 percentage points, closely matching random-control perturbations. This falsifies the hypothesis that a simple linear language direction at the output is the main cause of the low-resource gap. 3) Analysis of internal states reveals that the EOS hidden representation follows language-specific trajectories that increasingly diverge with network depth. 4) Directly intervening on this EOS trajectory by replacing a low-resource language’s EOS hidden state with its parallel English EOS three blocks before the projection head leads to dramatic improvements, e.g., Swahili retrieval jumps from 22.1% to 69.1% on one encoder, with similar behaviors observed on another model. Multiple control experiments rule out confounding explanations such as general pooled-position behavior or English having unique properties. 5) Training-time architectural modifications that introduce a front-layer trunk encouraging each language’s representation to move toward a shared parallel-content centroid lead to substantial improvements on low-resource XM3600 retrieval (+9.6 / +17.1 percentage points, depending on setup), with consistent gains on three additional benchmarks, while leaving high-resource language performance essentially unchanged.

Conclusion: The paper concludes that the primary cause of low-resource language underperformance in multilingual vision–language encoders does not lie in a linear language direction at the output space—this linear signal is better viewed as a symptom. Instead, the problem emerges along the model’s forward path, where EOS token representations for different languages diverge as depth increases, degrading alignment for low-resource languages. Causal interventions on this EOS trajectory can largely close the gap, and architecture/training changes that explicitly encourage convergence toward a shared, content-based centroid significantly improve low-resource retrieval without sacrificing high-resource performance. The findings refine our understanding of where multilingual alignment breaks down and point to practical strategies for designing better, more equitable multilingual vision–language models.

Abstract: Recent multilingual vision--language encoders cover hundreds of languages in a single model, yet on two state-of-the-art instances retrieval on low-resource languages (LRL; e.g. Swahili) trails high-resource ones (HRL; e.g. English) by $30^+$\,pp. We ask where in the trained encoder this gap is located. Prior modality-gap and cross-lingual subspace work suggests a linear language direction at the output crowds out alignment-relevant geometry. We falsify this: LEACE drives the linear language classifier from $>99\%$ to near chance and iterated INLP to $37$--$50\%$ while LRL retrieval moves within $\pm 1.5$\,pp and all tier means within $2.2$\,pp, tracking random controls. The linear bias is a \emph{symptom}, not the cause. Instead, the alignment-causal factor lies along the encoder's forward path: the EOS (end-of-sequence) hidden state's per-language trajectory diverges with depth. Substituting the EOS with its parallel English value three blocks before the projector lifts Swahili from $22.1\%$ to $69.1\%$ on one encoder (and reproduces on the other); three controls rule out pooled-position tautology and English specificity. A front-layer trunk that pulls each language's projection toward the parallel-content centroid corroborates the diagnosis at training time, recovering $+9.6$ / $+17.1$\,pp on LRL XM3600 retrieval (1{,}000-image subset), with consistent gains across three further benchmarks while preserving HRL performance.

</details>


### [196] [Calibrating Small Language Models for Claim Check-Worthiness Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30731)
*Pratuat Amatya,Venktesh Viswanathan,Vinay Setty*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: They introduce NN-PPI, a lightweight calibration layer that corrects claim check-worthiness predictions of small language models at inference time, boosting their accuracy to match larger LLMs while remaining cheaper and faster.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Fact-checking pipelines need to decide which claims are worth checking, but running expensive large language models on every claim is not feasible in production, and small models are not accurate enough. The authors want a method that keeps the low cost and latency of small models while achieving the high accuracy of large models, and that can be added on top of existing systems without retraining.

Method: They propose NN-PPI, a pointwise variant of Prediction-Powered Inference used as a post-hoc calibration layer on model outputs. NN-PPI adjusts the predicted probabilities of claim check-worthiness at inference time, without changing or retraining the underlying model. It is applied to both few-shot small language models and a fine-tuned production model to calibrate and improve their predictions.

Result: Using NN-PPI yields weighted F1 improvements between 12% and 33.8% across baseline models of different sizes and qualities, effectively elevating small language models to the performance level of much larger LLMs. It also provides additional gains on top of an already fine-tuned production model, indicating that residual calibration and supervised fine-tuning are complementary.

Conclusion: A lightweight, post-hoc calibration layer based on pointwise Prediction-Powered Inference can substantially improve claim check-worthiness detection for small and fine-tuned models, making it possible to achieve LLM-level accuracy at a fraction of the serving cost and latency. This enables more scalable and economical automated fact-checking pipelines.

Abstract: Assessing claim check-worthiness is an essential first step in automated fact-checking pipelines. This work is motivated by a real deployment challenge at an early-stage startup: running large language models (LLMs) over every incoming claim is cost- and latency-prohibitive, yet smaller models sacrifice accuracy. We propose NN-PPI, a pointwise extension of Prediction-Powered Inference (PPI) that calibrates model predictions at inference time as a lightweight post-hoc layer, without re-training the underlying model. NN-PPI achieves weighted F1 gains ranging from 12% to 33.80% depending on the size and performance of the baseline model, bringing SLMs on par with larger LLMs. Beyond few-shot SLMs, NN-PPI further improves a production-deployed fine-tuned model, demonstrating that residual calibration is complementary to supervised fine-tuning. By recovering LLM-level accuracy from models that are an order of magnitude cheaper to serve, it makes accurate check-worthiness detection substantially cheaper to operate at scale. Our code and data can be found at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/arr-claim-worthiness-F237.

</details>


### [197] [Not All Fallbacks Are Failures: Understanding and Recovering from Fallbacks in Mobile Voice Assistants](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30738)
*Phillip Schneider,Alexandre Mercier,Joshua Oehms,Kristiina Jokinen,Florian Matthes*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper analyzes fallback situations in a smartwatch health voice assistant, creates a taxonomy and dataset of real-world fallback-triggering utterances, evaluates different classifier models, and finds that lightweight embedding-based methods outperform larger generative models for classifying fallback types under deployment constraints.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Voice assistants in real-world environments frequently fail due to noisy input, ASR errors, ambiguous or incomplete user requests, and unintended activations. Current systems usually respond with generic fallback messages that do not help recover from these failures and can harm user experience. There is a need to better understand real fallback situations and design more effective, efficient handling strategies, especially under resource constraints like those of smartwatch-based assistants.

Method: The authors conducted an empirical study using six months of real-world interaction logs from a deployed smartwatch-based voice assistant for general health support, involving over 500 users and producing 3,030 anonymized utterances that triggered fallback. They built an operational taxonomy of fallback situations and annotated the collected utterances to create the VoxFallbacks dataset. They then implemented a classification pipeline and performed a comparative evaluation of different models—including lightweight embedding-based classifiers and larger generative models—under realistic deployment constraints such as computational resources and latency.

Result: The study produced the VoxFallbacks dataset and an operational taxonomy of fallback types in a real-world health assistant. Empirical results from the classification experiments showed that lightweight embedding-based classifiers outperform larger generative models on most of the classification tasks related to fallback handling, while also using significantly fewer computational resources, making them more suitable for constrained devices like smartwatches.

Conclusion: Effective fallback handling in real-world voice assistants can be substantially improved by using specialized taxonomies and datasets to understand interaction failures and by deploying lightweight embedding-based classifiers instead of relying on generic fallback messages or heavy generative models. These approaches yield better classification performance and are more cost-efficient, offering practical guidance for designing robust fallback mechanisms in resource-constrained, real-world voice assistant deployments.

Abstract: Robust understanding of user input is a core requirement for voice assistants deployed in real-world environments. In practice, these systems encounter heterogeneous fallback situations caused by noisy audio input, transcription errors, ambiguous requests, incomplete utterances, or unintended activations. Existing systems typically respond with generic fallback messages, which do not resolve the underlying interaction failure and can degrade user experience. We study fallback handling in a deployed smartwatch-based voice assistant for general health support in everyday environments. Our analysis is based on six months of real-world usage data from more than 500 users, yielding a dataset of 3,030 anonymized, naturally occurring fallback-triggering utterances. We contribute (1) an operational taxonomy and the annotated VoxFallbacks dataset of these interactions, (2) a comparative evaluation of different models within a classification pipeline under practical deployment constraints, and (3) practical lessons for designing robust and cost-efficient fallback mechanisms. Results show that lightweight embedding-based classifiers outperform larger generative models on most classification tasks while requiring substantially fewer computational resources.

</details>


### [198] [CLIN: an Objective Framework for Evaluating Creativity in Short Persian Literary Text](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30754)
*Mohammad Reza Modarres,Armin Tourajmehr,Yadollah Yaghoobzadeh,Mohammad Taher Pilehvar*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper studies how well LLMs can judge creativity of short Persian literary texts, finds that reliability depends heavily on the specific creativity dimension and prompt, and proposes a cheap proxy-based metric suite (CLIN) that matches or beats LLM judges on structured dimensions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Creativity is essential in text generation, but hard and costly to evaluate, especially in low-resource languages like Persian. Human evaluation is expensive and LLM-based judges are not yet well understood or fully reliable, particularly given creativity’s multidimensional, subjective nature. The authors want to understand when LLM judges work, where they fail, and whether simpler automatic metrics can replace them for some creativity dimensions.

Method: They test multiple LLM-based evaluation strategies and prompt designs for judging short Persian literary texts on several creativity dimensions, some structured (Originality, Fluency, Elaboration, from TTCT) and some more subjective (Emotion, Attractiveness). They measure agreement between LLM scores and human judgments, analyze sensitivity to prompting, and then design CLIN: a set of simple proxies—topic-aware novelty for Originality, contextual lexical clustering for Fluency, and lexical diversity for Elaboration—and compare their human alignment to that of LLM judges and their computational cost.

Result: LLM-human agreement is uneven: it is relatively strong for structured, TTCT-derived dimensions (Originality, Fluency, Elaboration), but poor for subjective, affective dimensions (Emotion, Attractiveness). LLM judgments depend strongly on prompt wording, and advanced prompting strategies (few-shot, ensembling, multi-agent debate) do not produce consistent improvements. The proposed CLIN proxy metrics reach parity with or outperform the best zero-shot LLM judge for the structured dimensions, at significantly lower evaluation cost.

Conclusion: LLMs are not uniformly reliable creativity judges: they are better aligned with humans on structured, well-operationalized dimensions than on subjective ones, and are sensitive to prompt choices. Simple, interpretable proxies like those in CLIN can effectively approximate structured creativity dimensions, matching or surpassing LLM-based judges while being cheaper and more transparent. For evaluating creativity in low-resource languages, automatic proxy metrics may be preferable to relying solely on LLM judges, especially for structured aspects of creativity.

Abstract: Evaluating creativity in large language model (LLM) outputs remains challenging because creativity is multidimensional and human-centered. We examine how reliably LLMs evaluate short literary text in Persian, a low-resource language, across multiple evaluation strategies and prompt formulations. We find that LLM-human agreement varies substantially across dimensions: alignment is stronger for structured TTCT-derived properties such as Originality, Fluency, and Elaboration, but considerably weaker for more subjective dimensions, particularly Emotion and Attractiveness. Judgments are also sensitive to prompt formulation, while few-shot prompting, ensembling, and multi-agent debate provide no consistent improvement. Motivated by this dimension-dependent behavior, we investigate whether structured creativity dimensions can instead be approximated using simple, interpretable proxy metrics. We introduce CLIN, which evaluates three TTCT-derived dimensions separately using topic-aware novelty for Originality, contextual lexical clustering for Fluency, and lexical diversity for Elaboration. These proxies achieve human alignment comparable to or better than the strongest zero-shot LLM judge in our setting while requiring substantially lower evaluation cost.

</details>


### [199] [TopoCompress: Long Context Compression via Graph-Wired Semantic Trajectories](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30811)
*Daniel Agyei Asante,Yang Li*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes TopoCompress, a training-free, model-agnostic framework that compresses long contexts for LLMs by selecting coherent semantic spans via graph-based relevance propagation, achieving better or comparable performance to strong baselines with less compression budget and time.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long-context processing in large language models is expensive in terms of cost and latency. Existing compression methods can break apart important evidence, need extra training or alignment, and often rely tightly on the target model to work well. There is a need for a more general, training-free, and model-agnostic way to compress long contexts while preserving coherent, relevant information for downstream tasks.

Method: TopoCompress operates in two main stages: (1) It segments the long context into spans and scores each span using a combination of dense retrieval relevance, lexical (token-based) query relevance, and a semantic acceleration signal to estimate importance with respect to the query; (2) It builds a hybrid graph where nodes are spans and edges capture both semantic similarity and original sequential adjacency. Query-guided relevance scores are then propagated over this graph (graph-based diffusion/propagation) to select a subset of coherent, high-utility spans as the compressed context, without any additional training or dependence on a specific LLM.

Result: On five long-context benchmarks (HotpotQA, 2WikiMQA, MuSiQue, Qasper, and MultiFieldQA-en), TopoCompress consistently outperforms strong compression baselines in task performance. It can match the performance of the strongest baseline while using only one quarter of the compression budget (4x smaller) and also achieves a 1.41x reduction in compression time compared to the fastest baseline, demonstrating both efficiency and effectiveness.

Conclusion: TopoCompress provides an effective, training-free, and model-agnostic approach for long-context compression by selecting coherent semantic spans through graph-based relevance propagation. It preserves important evidence better than existing methods, enabling LLMs to maintain strong task performance while significantly reducing context length and compression time. This makes it a practical solution for cost- and latency-sensitive long-context applications.

Abstract: Long-context compression is essential for reducing the cost and latency of large language model inference. However, existing methods can fragment important evidence, require additional training or alignment, and often depend on the target model for effective compression. We introduce TopoCompress, a training-free and model-agnostic framework that compresses long contexts by selecting coherent semantic spans. TopoCompress first scores each span using dense and lexical query relevance together with semantic acceleration. It then constructs a hybrid graph that connects spans based on semantic similarity and sequential adjacency, and propagates the query-guided relevance scores over the graph. Across five long-context tasks-HotpotQA, 2WikiMQA, MuSiQue, Qasper, and MultiFieldQA-en-TopoCompress consistently outperforms strong compression baselines. Notably, TopoCompress achieves performance comparable to the strongest baseline while using a 4x smaller compression budget, and provides a 1.41x smaller compression time over the fastest baseline.

</details>


### [200] [Error-Type-Aware Loss Reweighting for Robust Named Entity Recognition with Noisy LLM Labels](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30827)
*Elena Merdjanovska,Jonas Golde,Alan Akbik*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: They show that noise from LLM-generated NER labels hurts fine-tuning and propose an error-type-aware loss reweighting strategy that improves robustness and F1 under noisy annotations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs are increasingly used to synthetically annotate data for training smaller NER models, but these auto-generated labels are noisy. Standard fine-tuning assumes labels are correct and existing generic noise-robust losses are not well-suited to sequence labeling, where different error types (missing mentions vs. type errors) affect learning differently. There is a need for methods that explicitly account for heterogeneous annotation noise in NER when training with LLM-labeled data.

Method: They analyze how LLM-introduced annotation noise affects NER model training and evaluate existing noise-robust loss functions, showing their limitations for sequence labeling. They then introduce an error-type-aware loss reweighting approach: during training, tokens are categorized according to different potential error types, and the loss contribution of each category is reweighted with separate rules rather than a single global noise-robust weighting. This maintains useful supervision for some noisy tokens while down-weighting others likely to be incorrect, all without extra training resources.

Result: Across multiple NER benchmarks with synthetic noise levels between 15% and 40%, their error-type-aware reweighting consistently improves dataset-level average F1 scores by about 0.8–2.0 points over baselines. On the Wikigold dataset with 24.1% label noise, they report a maximum F1 improvement of 4.6 points, demonstrating that their method makes NER training substantially more robust to LLM annotation errors.

Conclusion: Annotation noise from LLM-generated NER labels is heterogeneous and cannot be effectively handled by generic noise-robust losses that treat all noisy tokens the same. A simple, efficient error-type-aware loss reweighting scheme tailored to different token error types can significantly mitigate the impact of such noise, improving NER performance under realistic noisy-label conditions without additional computational or annotation costs.

Abstract: Large language models are increasingly used to annotate datasets for training smaller, task-specialized models such as named entity recognition. While this method yields effective models, it assumes that the synthetic dataset is correctly annotated. In this work, we find that (i) current fine-tuning processes simply ignore LLM-introduced annotation noise, resulting in degraded performance and (ii) existing noise-robust losses are not transferable to sequence labeling because annotation noise in named entity recognition is heterogeneous: for example, missing mentions and type errors affect the training signal in different ways. Treating all noisy tokens equally in noise-robust losses and applying a single reweighing criterion for all may therefore remove useful supervision or reinforce incorrect labels. To address this limitation, we propose error-type-aware loss reweighting for NER, which introduces separate reweighing rules for different types of potentially erroneous tokens. Our approach is simple and efficient, does not require additional training resources, and improves F1 by 0.8 - 2.0 percentage points on dataset-level average for noise levels between 15% and 40%, with a maximum improvement of 4.6 percentage points with 24.1% noise on Wikigold.

</details>


### [201] [Opinionated, Hesitant and Stressed: Three Studies of How Politicians Speak in Four Slavic Parliaments](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30828)
*Ivan Porupski,Nikola Ljubešić*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Three large-scale phonetic studies of Slavic parliamentary speech show cross-lingual links between sentiment and acoustics, predictors of filled pauses, and systematic patterns in Croatian stress variation, proposing a broader research agenda for corpus-based phonetics and political speech.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Spoken parliamentary debates are rich, naturalistic data for understanding how linguistic form reflects affect, planning, and style, yet most phonetic and disfluency research is small-scale, single-language, and not based on large, aligned corpora. There is also limited cross-linguistic work on how sentiment influences acoustic realisation, how social and linguistic factors shape filled pause usage, and how prosodic features like stress vary within a single language in real political settings. Using a large, multilingual, time-aligned corpus can reveal robust, cross-lingual patterns that smaller or text-only studies cannot detect.

Method: The authors use the ParlaSpeech 3.0 corpus, containing over 6,000 hours of time-aligned parliamentary speech in four Slavic languages (Croatian, Czech, Polish, Serbian). Study 1 links utterance-level sentiment scores to acoustic measures (pitch, intensity, speech rate) to model how sentiment affects realisation. Study 2 models counts of filled pauses with negative binomial generalized estimating equations (GEE), examining predictors such as speech rate, age, sentiment, and gender, and comparing patterns across language groups. Study 3 focuses on Croatian, analysing lexical items across parts of speech to quantify primary stress position and its variability at the speaker level, asking whether speakers show consistent preferences across lexical categories.

Result: (1) Negative utterances are systematically produced with higher pitch, greater intensity, and faster speaking rate across all four parliaments, and at the most positive sentiment extreme there is an additional arousal-related acoustic upturn. (2) Filled pause frequency is well predicted by speech rate, age, and sentiment in all languages; gender patterns differ by language group: in South Slavic parliaments men produce fewer filled pauses, while in West Slavic parliaments there is no gender difference, a cross-lingual contrast that would be missed in single-language analyses. (3) In Croatian, individual speakers show stable preferences for earlier vs later primary stress that are coherent across verbs, adjectives, and nouns, but these preferences do not extend in the same way to adverbs and proper nouns, where stress behaviour diverges.

Conclusion: Large-scale, multilingual parliamentary corpora enable robust discoveries about how sentiment, social factors, and prosodic preferences shape spoken language in political settings. Sentiment has a consistent acoustic signature across Slavic parliaments, disfluency (filled pauses) is systematically conditioned by tempo, age, sentiment, and language-specific gender patterns, and Croatian speakers exhibit structured but category-sensitive stress preferences. The authors argue for a research program that integrates corpus phonetics, statistical disfluency modelling, and analysis of political rhetoric to better understand speech production and style in institutional discourse.

Abstract: We present three large-scale studies of spoken parliamentary speech across four Slavic languages (Croatian, Czech, Polish, Serbian), drawing on over 6,000 hours from the ParlaSpeech 3.0 corpus. The first study examines how utterance-level sentiment shapes acoustic realisation: negative speech is consistently produced with higher pitch, greater intensity, and faster rate across all four parliaments, with a secondary arousal-driven upturn at the most positive extreme. The second study models filled pause frequency using negative binomial GEE, finding that speech rate, age, and sentiment are robust cross-lingual predictors, while gender effects reverse between South Slavic (men produce fewer filled pauses) and West Slavic parliaments (no gender difference) - a pattern invisible to single-language designs. The third study investigates primary stress variation in Croatian, showing that speaker-level preferences for early versus late stress cohere across verbs, adjectives, and nouns but decouple for adverbs and proper nouns. We conclude with a research agenda spanning corpus phonetics, disfluency modelling, and political rhetoric.

</details>


### [202] [Thesis Proposal: Toward a Human-Centered and Perspective-Aware Framework for Reproducible ML Evaluation and AI Alignment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30842)
*Deepak Pandita,Christopher M. Homan*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper argues that human disagreement is intrinsic and important in AI, and proposes a human-centered, perspective-aware framework to make ML evaluation and alignment more reproducible and reflective of diverse values.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: AI systems rely heavily on human input—labels, feedback, and evaluations—but humans frequently disagree due to subjective opinions, identities, beliefs, and social context. Current evaluation practices collapse these disagreements into a single consensus label (e.g., via majority vote), erasing minority perspectives. This not only undermines reproducibility—since different samples of annotators or raters can yield different ‘consensus’—but also risks building systems that poorly reflect the plurality of human values, which is especially problematic in sensitive domains like AI safety, content moderation, and sentiment analysis. There is therefore a need for an evaluation and alignment framework that explicitly models and preserves disagreement and diverse perspectives.

Method: The paper proposes, at a high level, a human-centered and perspective-aware framework for ML evaluation and AI alignment. Rather than aggregating labels into a single consensus, the framework treats disagreement and perspective diversity as first-class objects. It involves collecting human feedback with explicit perspective metadata (e.g., annotator identity factors, belief systems, or social context), modeling label distributions instead of point labels, and designing evaluation protocols that quantify performance across perspectives and subgroups. For alignment, it suggests using multi-perspective human feedback signals to train and assess AI systems so they better reflect diverse human values instead of a monolithic consensus.

Result: As this is a thesis proposal, specific empirical results are not detailed in the abstract. The main contribution described is conceptual: a structured, perspective-aware approach to modeling human disagreement in evaluation and alignment, which is argued to improve reproducibility and the representativeness of AI systems’ value alignment.

Conclusion: The work concludes that ignoring human disagreement in AI evaluation and alignment leads to obscured minority views, weaker trustworthiness, and contributes to the reproducibility crisis. By adopting a human-centered, perspective-aware framework that preserves and leverages disagreement, ML evaluation can become more reproducible and AI systems can be aligned with a broader and more accurate spectrum of human values and perspectives.

Abstract: Humans play a vital role at every stage of AI development, from data collection and curation to model development and evaluation. However, humans often disagree with each other and sometimes with themselves over time. It is essential to take disagreement into account when building human-centered AI systems, especially in domains where it is prevalent, such as AI safety, content moderation, or sentiment analysis. Disagreement often arises from subjective human opinion and can vary with one's identity, beliefs, and social environment. Despite this, current LLM evaluation approaches frequently rely on aggregating labels (often via plurality voting) to represent consensus, thereby obscuring minority perspectives. By failing to account for human disagreement, these evaluation methods contribute to the reproducibility crisis in AI. Human feedback is also crucial for ensuring that AI systems align with human values. For these systems to be trustworthy, it is critical to ensure that they reflect diverse human values and perspectives. In this thesis proposal, we present a human-centered and perspective-aware framework for reproducible ML evaluation and AI alignment.

</details>


### [203] [Linguistic Distance Segregates Latent Representations in Automatic Speech Recognition Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30853)
*Ting-Hui Cheng,Line Katrine Harder Clemmensen,Sneha Das*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper examines how speakers' first-language (L1) distance from English affects English ASR performance and finds a systematic, statistically significant relationship: more distant L1s tend to incur higher ASR error rates, and model latent spaces show L1-based clustering.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Despite progress in ASR, systems still perform unevenly across speaker groups. Speakers whose native languages are typologically distant from English may be disadvantaged, but this relationship has not been rigorously quantified across models and datasets. The paper aims to understand and measure how L1 background influences English ASR performance and internal model representations.

Method: The authors empirically analyze multiple English ASR datasets and models, computing L1 distance (between speakers' first languages and English) and correlating it with ASR error rates (e.g., WER). They then use Tweedie mixed-effects models to control for dataset-level variation and test statistical significance of the association between L1 distance and errors. Additionally, they inspect latent acoustic representations across network layers to see whether speakers cluster in embedding space by L1 background, focusing on deeper layers.

Result: They find a systematic positive correlation between L1 distance and ASR error rates across datasets and models: speakers whose L1 is more distant from English exhibit higher error rates. This association remains statistically significant ($p<0.001$) in Tweedie mixed-effects models that account for dataset-level variability. Latent space analyses show clear L1-based spatial segregation in deeper acoustic layers for most evaluated architectures, indicating that models encode L1-related characteristics in their internal representations.

Conclusion: First-language background, particularly its distance from English, is an important factor in English ASR performance disparities. ASR models not only perform worse for speakers with more distant L1s but also internally represent speech in an L1-segregated manner. These findings highlight the need to design and evaluate ASR systems with cross-linguistic fairness in mind and to explore techniques that mitigate L1-related performance gaps.

Abstract: While automatic speech recognition (ASR) models have achieved remarkable improvements in recent years, performance disparities persist across different speaker populations. One such disparity is for speakers whose first languages (L1) are from families distant from English. This paper investigates the relationship between first language background and English ASR performance. Through empirical analysis, we observe that the correlation between speakers' L1 distance and ASR error rates yields a systematic effect on English Speech, with its strength varying across datasets and models. This association is statistically significant in a follow-up analysis accounting for dataset-level variation in Tweedie mixed-effects models ($p<0.001$ across evaluated models). In addition, analysis of the latent space reveals a L1-based spatial segregation across deeper acoustic layers in the majority of evaluated architectures

</details>


### [204] [You Shouldn't Have Asked: A Pragmatics-Inspired Taxonomy for Evaluating LLM Refusals](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30856)
*Ruoxuan Li,Pinqiao Wang,Sheng Li,Cameron Robert Jones*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper analyzes how LLMs refuse harmful requests, proposing a pragmatics-based taxonomy and showing current models often use explicit, moralizing refusals that may inadvertently harm or shame users.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Refusals are face-threatening in human interaction and can damage a requester’s self-image if handled poorly. LLMs are now trained to refuse unsafe or inappropriate prompts, but most prior work treats refusal only as a binary safety/alignment outcome (comply vs. refuse). There is little understanding or evaluation of *how* models refuse across different harm contexts, and whether the interactional and social consequences of refusals are appropriately managed. The authors aim to fill this gap by bringing pragmatic theory to bear on LLM refusals.

Method: The authors develop what they claim is the first pragmatics-grounded taxonomy of LLM refusal strategies. Using this taxonomy, they systematically annotate and compare refusal behaviors across 16 contemporary LLMs on prompts spanning 14 categories of potential harm. They analyze properties such as explicitness, moral evaluation, presence/absence of interactional repair, and the use of alternatives or facework in refusals.

Result: Across models and harm types, refusals tend to be explicit and strongly morally evaluative, relying heavily on negative framing. Interactional repair, when present, mostly takes the form of offering safer alternative actions or information rather than strategies focused on preserving the user’s face or mitigating interpersonal threat. There are notable differences in style across the 16 LLMs, but the overarching patterns are consistent.

Conclusion: Current alignment practices succeed at making LLMs non-compliant with harmful requests but often neglect the interactional costs of refusal. Overly explicit, moralizing refusals, especially in sensitive harm domains, can make users feel shamed or provoked and can undermine the goals of safety. The authors argue that safety evaluation should incorporate not just whether models refuse, but whether they refuse in contextually adaptive, socially accountable ways that manage the interpersonal consequences of saying no.

Abstract: Refusals are often treated as face-threatening acts in pragmatics because they can challenge the requester's socially claimed self-image. Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly trained to refuse unsafe and inappropriate requests, and these refusals may harm users when models fail to manage this interactional cost properly. While existing work has mainly approached LLM non-compliance as a safety-alignment outcome, it does not provide a way to evaluate whether LLMs refuse appropriately across different harmful contexts. To study this question, we propose (to our knowledge) the first taxonomy of LLM refusals that is grounded in pragmatic theory. Applying this taxonomy to responses from 16 modern LLMs across 14 harm categories, we find that although models differ in how they refuse, their refusals are overall explicit and strongly morally evaluative, with interactional repair occurring mainly through offering or providing safer alternatives instead of interpersonal facework. This pattern is especially consequential in sensitive harm contexts, where overuse of negative framing may make users feel shamed or provoked, undermining the purpose of safe non-compliance. We therefore call for alignment evaluation that considers not only whether models refuse harmful requests, but also whether they refuse in ways that are contextually adaptive and socially accountable for the interactional consequences of saying no.

</details>


### [205] [Beyond Good Intentions: When Does the Framing of Multilingual and Low-Resource NLP Research Become a Caricature?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30866)
*Nedjma Ousidhoum,Noopur Zambare,Mohamed Abdalla*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper critically examines how NLP/ML research on low-resource languages is framed, showing that claims about helping communities or decolonising are often rhetorically strong but weakly evidenced, and it offers a framework and recommendations for more accountable, equitable research narratives.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Recent NLP work on low-resource and underrepresented languages is often justified as addressing inequality, helping local communities, or contributing to decolonisation. However, there is growing concern that these claims may be more rhetorical than real, lacking evidence of genuine community benefit, accountability, or structural change. The authors are motivated to systematically analyse these framings, reveal patterns that may reinforce inequities or obscure power imbalances, and support more responsible research practices.

Method: The authors conduct a qualitative and quantitative analysis of recently published NLP and ML papers, especially those dealing with multilinguality, low-resource languages, and underrepresented cultures. They propose a framework for analysing research framings and use it to identify recurring rhetorical patterns around community benefit, participation, and decolonisation. They then examine the evidential basis of claims about community ownership and impact, and complement this with statistical analysis of publication trends using the ACL Anthology to see what types of outputs (e.g., resources, benchmarks) are actually prioritised.

Result: They find several recurring rhetorical patterns that present work on low-resource languages as inherently beneficial or decolonial while often lacking concrete evidence of community ownership, participation, or structural impact. Assertions about community benefit are frequently weakly supported or entirely unsubstantiated. Statistical evidence from the ACL Anthology indicates that, in practice, research outputs centre on resource creation and benchmarking, with far less documentation of broader social, institutional, or power-structure changes that would reflect deeper equity goals.

Conclusion: The paper concludes that current framings of low-resource NLP and multilingual research can obscure accountability and overstate community benefits, risking misleading narratives about equity and decolonisation. The authors argue that resource creation and benchmarking, while valuable, should not be conflated with structural change or community empowerment. They provide practical recommendations for authors, reviewers, and readers to more critically evaluate claims about impact and participation, and to adopt framings and practices that better support equitable, evidence-based knowledge production with underserved communities.

Abstract: Building language technologies and conducting NLP research for low-resource languages---particularly when led by native speakers or involving participatory research practices---are often framed as means of addressing inequality, serving local communities, and, at times, contributing to *decolonisation*. In this paper, we examine recently published NLP and ML papers, focusing on the narratives used to characterise multilinguality, low-resource languages, and underrepresented cultures. We propose a framework for analysing research framings and identify recurring rhetorical patterns that may hinder accountability and constrain equitable knowledge production for---and by---underserved communities. We further assess the evidential basis of assertions regarding community benefit and find that such statements are often weakly supported or left unsubstantiated. Although community ownership and participation are frequently presented as key objectives, our analysis, supported by statistics from the ACL Anthology, suggests that research outputs more often prioritise resource creation and benchmarking---important but distinct goals---over evidence of broader structural change. We conclude by offering practical recommendations to help authors, reviewers, and readers critically assess these assertions and avoid potentially misleading framings.

</details>


### [206] [Personas Differ from Native-Language Generation: Language Pathways Shape LLM Interpersonal Advice](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30873)
*Jinhee Won,Xinlan Emily Hu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper shows that two common ways of getting ‘cross-cultural’ advice from LLMs—using a native-speaker persona in English vs. generating in the native language and translating—produce systematically different results, so they are not interchangeable.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs are widely used for interpersonal advice and as proxies for human behavior across languages and cultures. Researchers and practitioners often want culturally or linguistically specific outputs, and a common shortcut is to prompt the model to answer "as a native speaker" in English. Another strategy is to have the model generate advice in the target language and then translate it back to English. It is unclear whether these two strategies are equivalent. If they differ, studies of cross-cultural behavior and deployed advice systems may be drawing misleading conclusions from their elicitation choices.

Method: The authors assemble 600 interpersonal advice questions and apply them across 13 languages using eight large language models. For each language and model, they compare two prompting strategies: (1) Native-Language generation (NL), where the model generates advice in the target language and that output is translated back into English, and (2) Native-speaker Persona prompting (NP), where the model is asked, in English, to respond as a native speaker of the target language or culture. They then systematically analyze and compare the resulting English texts along three dimensions: (a) linguistic style (e.g., lexical social cues, positive tone, concreteness, social attunement), (b) behavioral scaffolding in open-ended advice (how actionable and structured the guidance is), and (c) choices in forced-choice scenarios (which specific action the model recommends). Effect sizes are examined across languages, topics, and models.

Result: The two elicitation strategies, NP and NL, yield measurably different outputs. Native-speaker persona prompting (NP) tends to increase lexical markers of social connection and positivity (e.g., more affiliative and warmly toned language) but produces less concrete, less socially attuned content than NL. In open-ended advice, NP offers less actionable, less structured scaffolding. In forced-choice situations, NP systematically alters which actions are recommended, with a bias toward more confrontational responses instead of redirection. These differences are not uniform; they vary across languages, advice topics, and model architectures, but they are consistent enough to show that NP and NL are not equivalent approaches.

Conclusion: Cross-lingual elicitation strategy is itself a powerful and consequential methodological decision when working with LLMs. Asking a model to answer "as a native speaker" does not reproduce what the same model would generate in that native language and then translate; the two paths differ in tone, specificity, and even in the actions recommended. Therefore, researchers studying cross-cultural behavior with LLMs and practitioners designing multilingual or culturally targeted advice systems must be explicit and cautious about their elicitation strategy, as it can meaningfully change both the framing and substantive content of the advice.

Abstract: LLMs are increasingly used for interpersonal advice and as tools for studying social behavior across languages and cultures. A common shortcut for eliciting language- or culture-related variation is to ask a model to answer as a native speaker. We test whether this native-speaker persona reproduces the outputs obtained when models instead generate advice in the target language and translate the response back into English. Using 600 interpersonal advice questions across 13 languages and eight LLMs, we compare native-language generation followed by translation (NL) with native-speaker persona prompting (NP), measuring linguistic style, behavioral scaffolding, and forced-choice action recommendations. We find that NP and NL are not interchangeable. Compared to NL, NP often increases lexical social cues, including affiliation and positive tone, while reducing qualities such as concreteness and social attunement; NP also provides less actionable scaffolding in open-ended advice. In forced-choice scenarios, NP changes which action the model selects, favoring confrontation over redirection, with effect sizes varying across languages, topics, and models. Our results show that cross-lingual elicitation strategy is a consequential methodological choice that can change both how advice is framed and which actions models recommend.

</details>


### [207] [Evaluating and Mitigating Anti-LGBTQ Biases in German and Multilingual Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30884)
*Melina Morch,Daniel Braun*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper presents a German-English benchmark to evaluate anti-LGBTQ bias in language models, showing that models reproduce queerphobic stereotypes, that cultural adaptation matters for multilingual bias evaluation, and that fine-tuning can reduce but not eliminate such biases.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Research has focused mainly on gender and racial bias and predominantly in English, leaving anti-LGBTQ bias, especially in other languages, underexamined. Existing benchmarks fail to capture cultural and linguistic differences and tend to rely on gender-based representations, which are not sufficient to understand nuanced queerphobic bias. The authors aim to fill this gap with a culturally grounded, multilingual benchmark.

Method: The authors construct a benchmark dataset by combining: (1) community-sourced stereotypes gathered from German-speaking queer individuals and (2) a German translation of the WinoQueer dataset. They then evaluate eight language models of different sizes and architectures on this benchmark to quantify anti-LGBTQ bias. Finally, they explore bias mitigation by fine-tuning models on community content and progressive media, and they compare model behavior on the translated vs. community-based portions of the data.

Result: Language models were found to reproduce anti-queer stereotypes, and the extent and nature of this bias varied across LGBTQ identities and across different models. Comparisons between the translated WinoQueer and the community-sourced German data revealed notable discrepancies, indicating that a simple translation of English benchmarks does not adequately capture culturally specific forms of bias. Fine-tuning with community and progressive media content generally reduced measured bias, but the effect was inconsistent and depended on the particular model and identity category being evaluated.

Conclusion: Anti-LGBTQ bias is present in current language models and is sensitive to both identity category and model architecture. Culturally adapted, multilingual benchmarks are necessary for accurately assessing such bias; direct translation of English datasets is insufficient. While fine-tuning on community-informed and progressive data can mitigate bias on average, it is not a universal or uniform solution, underscoring the need for more robust, culturally aware bias mitigation strategies.

Abstract: While gender and racial biases in language models have been widely studied, anti-LGBTQ biases remain underexplored, particularly beyond English. Existing benchmarks often do not capture cultural and linguistic variation and rely on gender representations. This paper introduces a multilingual German-English benchmark dataset for the evaluation of anti-LGBTQ biases in language models. It combines community-sourced stereotypes from German-speaking queer individuals with a German translation of WinoQueer. The data is used to evaluate eight language models across sizes and architectures and explore mitigation through fine-tuning on community and progressive media content. Results show that language models reproduce anti-queer stereotypes, with variation across identities and models. Differences between the translated and community-based data highlight the importance of cultural adaptation for multilingual bias evaluation. Fine-tuning reduces bias on average, but not consistently across models and identities. Warning: This text contains examples of anti-queer hateful language and stereotypes.

</details>


### [208] [ECGQuest: Benchmarking and Fine-Tuning Language Models for Electrocardiography](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30893)
*Mohammadsina Hassannia,Matthew A. Reyna,Reza Sameni*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Introduces ECGQuest, a literature-grounded benchmark of 21,808 true/false Q&A pairs for evaluating and fine-tuning ECG-focused language models, showing that parameter-efficient fine-tuning makes mid-sized open-source models competitive with larger commercial ones on contextual ECG knowledge.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing language-model benchmarks in medicine mainly test broad medical facts or isolated ECG signal/image interpretation, not the rich contextual and multidisciplinary knowledge (cardiology, electrophysiology, clinical diagnosis, instrumentation, literature) needed for real-world ECG interpretation. There is no standardized, reproducible benchmark focused specifically on ECG-domain language understanding and reasoning, nor clear evidence on whether smaller open-source models can be adapted efficiently to reach competitive ECG performance.

Method: 1) Curate sources: Collect 23 ECG reference texts and Computing in Cardiology proceedings from 2003–2025. 2) Data generation: Use a GPT‑4o-based pipeline to automatically generate literature-grounded true/false questions from these texts, then create negated counterparts for each item, producing 10,904 unique questions and 21,808 Q&A pairs in total. 3) Model evaluation: Evaluate three commercial and 20 open-source LLMs on a held-out ECGQuest test set in zero-shot mode, measuring accuracy and bias (e.g., tendency to answer True). 4) Fine-tuning: Apply Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) to five open-source 7–14B models; include BERT and BiomedBERT as supervised encoder baselines. 5) Generalization: Convert ECG-related subsets of MedMCQA and MedQA into binary True/False form using their answer keys and test both base and fine-tuned models on these external datasets.

Result: 1) Zero-shot performance on ECGQuest ranged from 49.5% to 74.4% accuracy, with GPT‑5 achieving the best results. 2) General-purpose LLMs outperformed medically specialized ones, and several models exhibited significant True/False answering bias; encoder baselines (BERT, BiomedBERT) performed near random chance. 3) LoRA fine-tuning yielded consistent gains of 6.5–14.1 percentage points across all fine-tuned open-source models. 4) The best fine-tuned single model, DeepSeek‑R1‑Distill‑Qwen‑14B, attained 76.3% accuracy, while a five-model voting ensemble achieved 78.5% on ECGQuest. 5) On MedMCQA and MedQA ECG subsets, fine-tuning mostly helped weaker or biased models and did not reliably improve already strong base models, indicating some domain transfer limits.

Conclusion: ECGQuest establishes a reproducible, literature-grounded benchmark specifically targeting contextual ECG knowledge, filling a gap left by general medical QA and signal-focused tasks. The study shows that parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods like LoRA can substantially boost the ECG reasoning abilities of mid-sized open-source LLMs, making them competitive with, though not necessarily surpassing, much larger commercial systems. However, general-purpose models still tend to outperform nominally medical-specialized ones, and fine-tuning benefits do not consistently transfer to other ECG-related benchmarks for already strong models, highlighting ongoing challenges in domain-specific adaptation and generalization.

Abstract: Electrocardiogram (ECG) interpretation requires knowledge of cardiology, electrophysiology, clinical diagnosis, ECG waveforms, signal acquisition, and instrumentation. Existing language-model benchmarks, however, primarily assess broad medical knowledge or interpretation of individual ECG signals and images rather than the broader contextual knowledge required for ECG interpretation. We developed ECGQuest, a literature-grounded resource for evaluating and fine-tuning ECG-specific language models. A GPT-4o-based pipeline generated questions from 23 ECG references and Computing in Cardiology proceedings from 2003-2025. The final dataset contains 10,904 unique True/False questions paired with their negated forms (21,808 Q&A pairs). We evaluated three commercial and 20 open-source language models on a held-out test set in a zero-shot setting. Five open-source models with 7-14B parameters were fine-tuned using Low-Rank Adaptation, with BERT and BiomedBERT included as supervised encoder baselines. Generalization was assessed on ECG-related subsets of MedMCQA and MedQA converted to binary True/False questions using official answer keys. Zero-shot accuracy on ECGQuest ranged from 49.5% to 74.4%, with GPT-5 performing best. General-purpose models outperformed medically specialized models, several models showed strong True/False bias, and encoder baselines performed near chance. Fine-tuning improved all open-source models by 6.5-14.1%. Fine-tuned DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-14B reached 76.3% accuracy, while a five-model voting ensemble reached 78.5%. On MedMCQA and MedQA, fine-tuning mainly benefited weaker or class-biased models and did not consistently improve strong base models. ECGQuest provides a reproducible benchmark for contextual ECG knowledge and shows that parameter-efficient fine-tuning can make smaller language models competitive with substantially larger commercial models.

</details>


### [209] [Low-Resource Preference Adaptation of LLMs via Activation-Based Label Propagation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30902)
*Alessio Galatolo,Meriem Beloucif*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper shows that user preference signals are already encoded and separable in LLM activations, and that a small linear probe trained on <=500 labeled pairs can reliably label large datasets (50K+) for preference optimization, outperforming direct training under the same annotation budget and rivaling methods using vastly more labels.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Preference optimization for LLMs usually needs many human-labeled examples, which is expensive and infeasible for niche, cultural, or highly personal preferences that LLMs cannot reliably self-label. The authors aim to reduce the dependence on large-scale human annotation by leveraging internal representations of LLMs, enabling effective alignment for low-resource or non-mainstream user groups.

Method: They empirically analyze intermediate activations of LLMs when generating chosen vs. rejected responses and show these form separable clusters across layers, both in pretrained and aligned models. They then train a lightweight linear probe on at most 500 labeled preference pairs to distinguish preferred from non-preferred responses. This probe is applied to a large pool of unlabeled responses (~50K+) to pseudo-label them, and these pseudo-labeled data are used in downstream preference optimization. They systematically evaluate across multiple datasets, preference optimization algorithms, and model sizes, and compare against direct preference training and baselines with much larger labeled sets.

Result: They find that representations associated with preferred vs. rejected responses cluster distinctly across layers, and this structure is amplified by alignment on standard datasets but disappears when the target preferences conflict with those alignment priors. Using the learned linear probe, they can reliably annotate large unlabeled datasets, and the resulting preference models consistently outperform direct training that uses the same (small) number of human-labeled examples. In many experimental conditions, their method remains competitive with baselines that use 50–100 times more labeled data.

Conclusion: LLMs internally encode preference-relevant information in a linearly decodable way, and this structure can be harnessed via a simple linear probe trained on a small number of labeled examples to dramatically amplify limited annotation budgets. However, alignment on canonical datasets can bias models away from non-mainstream preferences, making them unreliable judges in such settings. Their probing-based annotation pipeline offers a practical path to preference optimization for underrepresented or low-resource user groups with minimal human labeling requirements.

Abstract: Adapting large language models to user-specific preferences is often constrained by the cost of human annotation, making preference optimisation impractical in low-resource settings where preferences cannot be reliably labelled by LLMs themselves, e.g., due to cultural, subjective, or personalised contexts. In this paper, we investigate how language models encode preference information in their intermediate representations, finding that activations from chosen and rejected responses form distinct clusters across layers, even in pretrained models. Strikingly, this structure is strengthened by alignment on canonical datasets but erased when the target preferences differ from those the model was aligned on, suggesting aligned LLMs are poor judges for non-mainstream populations. Exploiting this structure, we propose training a lightweight linear probe on a few labelled preference pairs ($\leq$500) and using it to annotate large unlabelled datasets (50K+) for downstream preference optimisation. We systematically evaluate this approach across different datasets, preference optimisation methods and model scales and find that our method consistently outperforms direct training given the same annotation budget, and remains competitive against baselines trained on $50-100\times$ more labelled data in the majority of our settings. Code is available at https://github.com/alessioGalatolo/activ-pref-probe.

</details>


### [210] [MMDS-Bench: Benchmarking Multimodal Large Language Models on Dynamic Stance in Social Media Interactions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30903)
*Yuzhe Ding,Kang He,Li Zheng,Shengwu Zheng,Teng Shi,Fei Li,Chong Teng,Donghong Ji*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces MMDS-Bench, a benchmark for multimodal dynamic stance classification in social media, showing that existing multimodal LLMs struggle with this task, especially when relational inference between parent and reply is required.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Most stance classification work treats stance as a post’s relation to a fixed topic and assumes text-only inputs, but real social media conversations use images, memes, and complex cross-modal references. Existing models and datasets do not adequately test how systems understand stance dynamically between a reply and its parent across modalities, nor do they diagnose specific reasoning challenges. This gap motivates creating a focused benchmark and evaluation protocol for multimodal dynamic stance understanding.

Method: The authors build MMDS-Bench, a dataset of 3,482 multimodal parent–reply pairs from social media, each labeled with a seven-class dynamic stance taxonomy. They carve out an 800-instance diagnostic subset specifically designed to require structured reasoning in three phases: understanding the parent, understanding the reply, and inferring the stance relation. Each instance is further annotated with five challenge-factor tags (multimodal fusion, parent framing, non-literal expression, interaction reasoning, label-boundary ambiguity) to enable fine-grained error analysis. They then evaluate 12 multimodal large language models (both open- and closed-source) on this benchmark and introduce a reference-grounded LLM-judge evaluation protocol to assess not just accuracy but also the quality of the models’ reasoning.


Result: Across the 12 evaluated multimodal LLMs, performance on MMDS-Bench is substantially below what would be expected for robust stance understanding, particularly on the diagnostic subset. The models struggle most when successful stance prediction requires reasoning about the relational dynamics between the parent and reply, beyond simply understanding each in isolation, and when challenge factors such as multimodal fusion or non-literal expression are present. The LLM-judge protocol reveals that even when models arrive at correct labels, their underlying reasoning is often brittle or partially incorrect.

Conclusion: MMDS-Bench exposes significant limitations in current multimodal LLMs’ ability to perform dynamic stance classification in realistic social media interactions. The fine-grained annotations and diagnostic subset highlight that key difficulties lie in relational and interactional reasoning, multimodal fusion, and handling nuanced, non-literal communicative strategies. The authors argue that MMDS-Bench and the proposed LLM-judge framework provide a much-needed testbed and analysis tool for developing future models with stronger multimodal discourse and stance reasoning capabilities.

Abstract: Dynamic stance classification models how a reply responds to its direct parent message, rather than how a post relates to a fixed topic. Existing work has mainly studied this problem in text-only settings, while social media interactions increasingly rely on images, screenshots, memes, reaction images, and cross-modal references. We introduce MMDS-Bench, a diagnostic benchmark for multimodal dynamic stance classification in social media parent-reply interactions. MMDS-Bench contains 3,482 multimodal instances annotated with a seven-label dynamic stance taxonomy, together with an 800-instance diagnostic subset that requires structured reasoning over parent understanding, reply understanding, and stance-relation inference. We further annotate each instance with five challenge factors covering multimodal fusion, parent framing, non-literal expression, interaction reasoning, and label-boundary ambiguity. We evaluate 12 closed-source and open-source multimodal large language models and propose a reference-grounded LLM-judge protocol for assessing reasoning quality. Results show that current MLLMs still struggle with multimodal dynamic stance understanding, especially in cases that require relational inference beyond separate parent and reply comprehension.

</details>


### [211] [TRIPPULSE: Multi-Agent Travel Planning with Review-Grounded Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30924)
*Priyanshu Karmakar,Borru Vijay Sai,Shubhojit Mallick,Abhik Jana,Shreya Ghosh,Manish Gupta*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces TRIPPULSE, a multi-agent, review-grounded LLM framework that generates travel itineraries satisfying hard constraints while better reflecting real human experiential preferences.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM-based travel planners typically rely on structured data and coarse, predefined personas, failing to capture nuanced experiential factors—like comfort, safety, crowding, and ambiance—that are mainly expressed in user reviews. This gap leads to itineraries that may be feasible but not realistically user-centric or aligned with how people actually choose accommodations, attractions, and transport.

Method: The authors design TRIPPULSE, a multi-agent architecture that decomposes trip planning into domain-specific agents (for accommodations, transportation, meals, attractions, and events). Each agent operates on a localized context rich in review data, while a global orchestrator coordinates them and enforces temporal and budget constraints via scheduling mechanisms. They extend the TRIPCRAFT benchmark with over 100K real-world reviews and propose Review-Grounded Persona Alignment (RGPA), an LLM-as-a-judge evaluation metric to assess how well generated itineraries align with human-centric, review-derived travel experiences.

Result: Across trips of varying lengths and using multiple proprietary and open-source LLMs, TRIPPULSE produces itineraries that keep strong adherence to constraints (time, budget, logistics) while significantly improving personalization and experiential grounding compared to baselines that do not use the multi-agent, review-grounded design.

Conclusion: Incorporating large-scale review data and a multi-agent design into LLM-based itinerary planners leads to more realistic and personalized travel plans without sacrificing constraint satisfaction. The proposed TRIPPULSE framework and RGPA metric offer a more human-centered paradigm for evaluating and generating travel itineraries, demonstrating that review-grounded, agent-based orchestration can overcome context and reasoning bottlenecks of monolithic planners.

Abstract: Travel itinerary generation requires balancing strict spatio-temporal constraints with human preferences. Existing LLM-based planners mainly rely on structured attributes and pre- defined traveler personas, but real travel deci- sions are often shaped by reviews that reveal experiential factors such as comfort, safety, ser- vice quality, ambiance, crowding, and hidden risks absent from structured databases. Incor- porating such review information is therefore critical to realistic, user-centric itinerary gen- eration. We propose TRIPPULSE1, a multi- agent framework for review-grounded travel planning. Instead of relying on a monolithic planner (and face context and reasoning bot- tlenecks), TRIPPULSE2 decomposes itinerary generation into specialized agents (each op- erating over localized contexts) for accom- modations, transportation, meals, attractions, and events, coordinated through a global or- chestrator with scheduling mechanisms that enforce temporal and budget feasibility. We augment TRIPCRAFT with 100K+ real-world reviews and introduce Review-Grounded Per- sona Alignment (RGPA), an LLM-as-a-Judge metric for evaluating alignment with human- centric travel experiences. Experiments across multiple trip durations and diverse proprietary and open-source models show that TRIPPULSE maintains strong constraint satisfaction while generating more personalized and experien- tially grounded itineraries.

</details>


### [212] [Annotated Surrogate Retrieval for Polish Statutory Law](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30929)
*Orkun Yiğit Cengiz*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes and evaluates three document-surrogate-based retrieval methods for Polish statutory law, showing strong rank-1 improvements over standard lexical and dense baselines, with trade-offs in depth performance, latency, and cost.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Legal retrieval for statutory law, especially in Polish, is challenging; existing lexical and dense retrievers struggle to reliably surface the exact governing provision at the top ranks for exam-style questions. The authors aim to improve high-precision retrieval (especially rank-1) for Polish statutes while balancing cost and latency, and to rigorously benchmark against realistic legal exam questions.

Method: They introduce document surrogates: language-model-generated annotations attached to statutory articles during indexing, and build three retrieval architectures over them. ASCR is a surrogate cascade with a reranking stage; ASCR-H adds fusion with a dense candidate list; DTF is a non-LM-at-query-time pipeline using three lexical/dense retrievers, weighted reciprocal rank fusion, and a deterministic rescoring prior. They evaluate on 300 questions from Polish bar and legal counsel exams (2024–2025), over a corpus of 82,508 statutory articles from 1,133 acts, comparing against 14 baseline systems and 4 controls. They run paired McNemar significance tests at several cutoffs and perform ablations on components like reranking, lemmatisation, PRF, and query rewriting.

Result: ASCR-H significantly improves rank-1 retrieval of the reference article compared to all non-oracle baselines except one ablation, achieving 72.3% vs. 61.7% (BM25) and 52.3% (dense). Its gains are concentrated at shallow depths: advantages are significant at cutoffs 1 and 5, vanish by 10, and by depth 20, DTF slightly leads in recall (86.0% vs. 84.5%) while being ~9x faster and less than half as costly. Reranking alone contributes 27.6 points of rank-1 accuracy. However, improvements in ranking do not translate to better citation accuracy, where DTF reaches the oracle ceiling. Lemmatisation, pseudo-relevance feedback, and query rewriting show negative or no benefit. Surrogate annotations cover 27% of the corpus yet include all benchmark reference provisions, creating an acknowledged asymmetry.

Conclusion: Surrogate-based retrieval, especially ASCR-H, can substantially boost top-rank retrieval performance for Polish statutory law, but its advantages are shallow and come with higher cost and latency. A cheaper, LM-free-at-query-time design (DTF) is highly competitive in deeper cutoffs and citation accuracy. The work also cautions about benchmark asymmetries (surrogates covering all gold articles) and reports that some common IR enhancements (lemmatisation, PRF, query rewriting) are not beneficial in this legal retrieval context. The paper releases benchmark data and detailed evaluation artifacts to support further research.

Abstract: We present a family of retrieval methods for Polish statutory law built on document surrogates: language-model annotations attached to statutory articles at index time. Three designs occupy different points on the cost-quality frontier. ASCR is a surrogate cascade with reranking; ASCR-H fuses a dense list into that cascade; and DTF replaces both language-model stages with three lexical and dense retrievers, weighted reciprocal rank fusion, and a deterministic re-scoring prior, using no model call before generation. We evaluate all three against fourteen lexical, dense, fused and ablated baselines plus four controls, on 300 questions from the 2024 and 2025 Polish bar and legal counsel entrance examinations (264 with their reference article in the corpus), over 82,508 articles from 1,133 acts. On paired McNemar tests, ASCR-H places the reference provision at rank one significantly more often than every other non-oracle configuration except one of its own ablations (eighteen of twenty comparisons significant in its favour at p < 0.005), reaching 72.3% against 61.7% for BM25 and 52.3% for dense retrieval. The advantage is concentrated at the head and does not survive depth: it is significant at cutoffs of one and five, disappears by ten, and by twenty DTF leads on point estimate (86.0% versus 84.5%) at one ninth the latency and less than half the cost. Ablation attributes 27.6 points of rank-one accuracy to the reranking stage alone. We further report that the ranking advantage does not extend to citation accuracy, where DTF matches the oracle ceiling, and three negative results on lemmatisation, pseudo-relevance feedback and query rewriting. Surrogate annotation covers 27.0% of the corpus but every reference provision in the benchmark, an asymmetry we disclose and discuss. Benchmark, per-question outputs and paired significance tests are publicly available.

</details>


### [213] [Detecting AI Impostors: How Do Middle Schoolers Identify LLM Agents in a Live Collaborative Setting?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30948)
*Dan Schumacher,Pragathi Durga Rajarajan,Haven Kotara,Roman Rendon,Kosi Atupulazi,Deepti Tagare,Ismaila Temitayo Sanusi,Fred G. Martin,Anthony Rios*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper presents DoppelBot, a social deduction game used to study how adolescents detect AI impersonation, showing that repeated play improves detection and deepens reflection on privacy and AI limitations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As LLMs become adept at mimicking human writing, there are growing worries about impersonation, erosion of trust, and difficulty of detecting AI in everyday social communication.
