These issues are acute for adolescents, who are heavy users of generative AI yet may lack robust detection skills and critical awareness of privacy risks. The authors aim to understand how young people notice and respond to AI impersonation and how to help them reflect on the associated social and ethical implications.

Method: The authors design DoppelBot, a cooperative social deduction game where players must identify an AI agent impersonating one of them. They conduct studies with middle school students who repeatedly play the game. During play, AI agents are progressively personalized to better mimic specific students. The researchers collect game transcripts, voting behavior, and qualitative reflections to analyze changes in detection accuracy, reasoning strategies, and attitudes toward privacy and AI impersonation over time.

Result: Students’ accuracy at identifying the AI impersonator improves with repeated exposure to the game. Their strategies shift from relying primarily on surface-level linguistic cues toward using shared social context, personal history, and other interpersonal signals to distinguish human peers from AI. Students also articulate an understanding of AI’s limitations, particularly around embodiment and lived experience, and discuss concerns related to data privacy.

Conclusion: A game-based, social deduction approach like DoppelBot can effectively help adolescents practice and improve AI detection skills while fostering reflection on AI impersonation, embodiment limits, and privacy. The findings suggest that emphasizing social and contextual cues, rather than only linguistic markers, is key for detecting AI in social communication. The released anonymized dataset of gameplay and voting offers a resource for further research on AI literacy and safety for young users.

Abstract: LLMs can imitate how people write, which raises concerns about impersonation, trust, and detection in social settings. These concerns are especially important for adolescents, who use generative AI frequently but may struggle to recognize it. We introduce \textit{DoppelBot}, a cooperative social deduction game designed to study how young people detect and respond to AI impersonation. Through studies with middle schoolers, we investigate whether a DoppelBot prompts reflection on privacy and impersonation, how repeated exposure affects AI-detection accuracy as agents become more personalized, and which strategies students use to identify AI doppelgängers. We find that students' detection accuracy improves over time, driven by a shift from relying on linguistic cues to leveraging shared social and contextual signals. Students also demonstrated an understanding of AI limitations such as embodiment and reflected on broader issues such as data privacy. To support future research, we release an anonymized dataset of game transcripts and voting behavior.

</details>


### [214] [CogEvol: Towards Efficient and Reliable Learning Environment Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30968)
*Shangqing Tu,Daniel Zhang-Li,Yucheng Wang,Shiyu Gan,Yanpeng Wang,Huiqiang Rong,Mofei Chen,Shen Yang,Yini Chen,Yinuo Duan,Haoxuan Li,Binglin Liu,Ye He,Danqi Zheng,Zhanxin Hao,Yuxuan Wu,Mengting Tao,Yuqiu Liu,Jifan Yu,Juanzi Li,Bin Xu,Lei Hou,Huiqin Liu,Yu Zhang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: CogEvol is a specialized model family that converts course briefs into full learning artifacts (slides or interactive HTML) in a single pass, achieving high quality and major speed/cost gains versus multi-turn scaffolding agents.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM-based content creation for education often uses slow, brittle multi-agent or multi-turn pipelines to build slides or interactive learning environments, and general-purpose coding models are over-parameterized and expensive for this use case. The authors want a fast, reliable, and cost-efficient model specifically optimized for generating structured educational artifacts at production scale.

Method: They build CogEvol models (4B and 27B) specialized for Learning Environment Generation. A production-grounded data pipeline converts real-world failures into 53k+ high-quality supervised fine-tuning examples. They then apply GRPO-based reinforcement learning with a hybrid reward: rule-based checks plus a vision-language model to assess visual/functional correctness, hardening it after detecting reward hacking where models produced visually good but non-functional games. They benchmark against external flagship models under an identical harness and deploy on both Ascend accelerators and A800 GPUs. They also introduce scaffold editing to reuse structure and cut generation costs for interactive pages.

Result: CogEvol-27B achieves 83.7 on a slide-quality benchmark and 63.7 on a 500-case interactive-HTML benchmark while using 26.9x fewer parameters than top coding models, and it is robust enough to serve live production traffic (e.g., for OpenMAIC). CogEvol-4B is open-sourced under Apache 2.0. Scaffold editing reduces interactive-page generation cost by about 76%. The system runs efficiently on domestic Ascend accelerators with performance comparable to A800 GPUs.

Conclusion: A domain-specialized LLM family, trained with production-grounded data and robust RL rewards, can reliably generate complex educational artifacts (slides and interactive HTML) in a single pass, substantially lowering latency and cost while maintaining high quality, and can be deployed at scale on diverse hardware. Open-sourcing the 4B model and standardized benchmarking demonstrate its practicality and reproducibility for AI-native education.

Abstract: We present CogEvol, a family of models trained specifically for Learning Environment Generation: turning a course brief into a finished learning artifact (structured-JSON slides or self-contained interactive HTML pages) in a single pass. Across 220k production requests, CogEvol completes a slide in a median of 17 seconds and an interactive page in 59, replacing minutes-long multi-turn agent scaffolding. Reliability is enforced rather than hoped for: a production-grounded data pipeline turns real failures into 53,687 verified SFT samples, and a hybrid rule-plus-VLM reward drives GRPO-based RL, hardened after we caught and fixed a reward-hacking episode that produced visually convincing but unplayable games. CogEvol-27B scores 83.7 on slide quality and 63.7 on a 500-case interactive-HTML benchmark with 26.9x fewer parameters than flagship coding models, and, in collaboration with the OpenMAIC team, serves their live production traffic. CogEvol-4B is released openly under the Apache 2.0 license at https://github.com/CogEvol/CogEvol-4B; external flagships are measured on the same suites under the identical harness. Scaffold editing cuts interactive-page generation cost by a further ~76%, and the full stack runs on domestic Ascend accelerators at application-level parity with A800 GPUs, lowering the unit cost of AI-native education at scale.

</details>


### [215] [Evaluating and Improving LLM Self-Modeling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30980)
*Siqi Zeng,Andre N. Assis,Rowan Wang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper investigates how well large language models (LLMs) can predict and describe their own behavior, introduces a benchmark to measure this 'self-modeling' ability, and explores improving it with synthetic data and reinforcement learning, finding gains but not clear genuine introspection.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As LLMs are deployed in high-stakes settings, it's important to know whether they can reliably reason about and predict their own behavior, for tasks like self-debugging, corrigibility, and human-AI collaboration. Existing work mainly looks at external behavior or internal representations, not at models explicitly answering questions about what they themselves would do under counterfactual prompts. This paper aims to fill that gap.

Method: The authors (1) define 'self-modeling' as answering verifiable questions about the model's own behavior (e.g., whether a small prompt change would flip its answer); (2) construct a benchmark of diverse self-modeling question types focused on counterfactuals and behavior prediction; (3) empirically evaluate multiple current LLMs on this benchmark to characterize their self-modeling skill and error patterns; and (4) design a scalable synthetic-data pipeline that generates self-modeling examples and use reinforcement learning on top of three open-source model families to train them on these tasks, then measure performance and transfer to held-out self-modeling tasks.

Result: Baseline models exhibit some self-modeling ability but fail systematically even on relatively simple counterfactual questions about their own answers. Training with the synthetic self-modeling data via reinforcement learning improves overall benchmark scores across three different open-source LLM families and yields some generalization to unseen self-modeling tasks. However, detailed analysis suggests that these improvements may often reflect pattern-learning from data rather than genuine introspective access to internal decision-making.

Conclusion: Self-modeling is a measurable but currently limited capability in LLMs. It can be improved using synthetic data and reinforcement learning, but these improvements do not clearly demonstrate true introspection or privileged self-knowledge—models may just be better at guessing their own behavior from surface patterns. Robust, genuine introspective self-modeling likely requires new techniques beyond scaling current approaches.

Abstract: We study self-modeling: an LLM's ability to answer questions about its own behavior. We focus on verifiable behavioral questions, such as whether a prompt edit would change the model's final answer. To measure this capability, we introduce a benchmark that tests diverse types of self-modeling questions. Current models show non-trivial but limited self-modeling skill, and make systematic mistakes on simple counterfactual questions about their own behavior. To improve self-modeling skill, we develop a scalable synthetic-data pipeline that produces self-modeling training data, and show that reinforcement-learning can improve aggregate self-modeling skill across three open-source model families with some transfer to held-out tasks. These gains, however, do not seem to constitute introspection consistently: improved self-modeling may not arise from privileged access to the model's internal decision process.

</details>


### [216] [Stick to What You Know: A Study of Knowledge-Aligned Supervised Fine-Tuning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30987)
*Arthur Becker,Jakob Kemmler,David Thulke,Christine Schäfer,Christian Dugast,Hermann Ney*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper investigates how supervised fine-tuning (SFT) can cause hallucinations when targets exceed a base model’s actual knowledge, and proposes “knowledge-aligned SFT” methods that restrict SFT targets to what the base model truly knows, significantly reducing hallucinations while preserving capabilities.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: SFT trains language models to mimic target responses, but the targets can contain facts the base model has not actually learned. When forced to imitate such targets, models may overfit superficially and later hallucinate similar content. There is a need to understand this mechanism and to design SFT procedures that do not push models to generate content beyond their robust parametric knowledge while still maintaining overall performance.

Method: The authors formalize and study “knowledge-aligned SFT,” where training targets are constrained to be consistent with the base model’s own knowledge. They compare existing knowledge-alignment approaches, grouped into generation-based and estimation-based methods, within a unified experimental setup. They also introduce two new generation-based variants: (1) Evidence Rewrite, which generates candidate answers with the base model, then verifies or corrects them using external evidence before using them as SFT targets; and (2) Recall Rewrite, which filters or modifies target claims so that only those that the base model can consistently recall (i.e., reproduce reliably) are kept as SFT training targets. They apply these strategies when fine-tuning Qwen 3 4B and OLMo 3 7B.

Result: Across benchmarks such as WildHalu and Biography, knowledge-aligned SFT substantially reduces factual hallucinations compared to standard SFT while largely preserving other general capabilities. Among the tested methods, Recall Rewrite provides the largest factuality improvements and also leads to better refusal behavior on UnknownBench, a benchmark probing responses to unknown or uncertain queries. These results empirically support the hypothesis that misaligned SFT targets—i.e., containing information outside the base model’s parametric knowledge—are a key driver of hallucination behavior.

Conclusion: Constraining SFT targets to be aligned with a model’s own knowledge base, rather than blindly imitating external target responses, is an effective way to reduce hallucinations without significantly harming general performance. The success of methods like Recall Rewrite shows that when SFT pressures a model to output information it does not truly know, hallucinations increase; conversely, aligning targets with internal knowledge improves factuality and appropriate refusals. This suggests that future SFT pipelines should explicitly incorporate knowledge-alignment checks to obtain safer and more reliable language models.

Abstract: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) trains a base language model to imitate target responses, and these targets may require knowledge the base model has not robustly internalized. We study this as a source of hallucinations and frame a group of mitigation methods as \emph{knowledge-aligned SFT}: constraining SFT training targets to the base model's parametric knowledge. Under a unified setup, we compare existing generation-based and estimation-based knowledge-alignment methods and introduce two new variants: Evidence Rewrite, which verifies base-model generations using external evidence, and Recall Rewrite, which retains claims only when they can be consistently recalled by the base model. Experiments with Qwen 3 4B and OLMo 3 7B show that knowledge-aligned SFT can reduce factual hallucinations on WildHalu and Biography while largely preserving general capabilities. Recall Rewrite yields the strongest factuality gains and improves refusal behavior on UnknownBench. It thereby confirms that SFT targets beyond the base model's knowledge drive hallucination behavior.

</details>


### [217] [Faithfulness Is Not Free: Auditing Offline KV-Cache Quantization in Retrieval-Augmented Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30996)
*Atta Ul Asad,Ahsan Bilal,Muhammad Ali,Muhammad Haseeb,Dean F. Hougen*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper studies how quantizing key-value caches in retrieval-augmented generation affects not just accuracy but also faithfulness to retrieved evidence, finding INT8 is safe while INT4 harms faithfulness even when answers stay correct.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: RAG systems often precompute and store key-value caches for retrieved documents to save computation, and quantization is used to reduce storage. However, prior work has not examined whether such compression harms faithfulness—whether model outputs remain grounded in the provided context—focusing mainly on accuracy. Since accurate answers can still be unfaithful to the given evidence, there is a need to separately evaluate faithfulness under cache quantization.

Method: The authors evaluate Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct with INT8 and INT4 quantization applied to key-value caches in RAG setups. They test on RGB and HotpotQA benchmarks, measuring both accuracy and faithfulness. Faithfulness is assessed using three approaches: an automatic hallucination detector, natural language inference (NLI) entailment checks between answers and context, and judgments from a large language model acting as a judge. They also analyze performance under noisy retrieval conditions and with varying numbers of retrieved chunks.

Result: INT8 quantization is nearly lossless in terms of both accuracy and faithfulness. INT4 quantization, in contrast, significantly reduces accuracy and, more importantly, degrades faithfulness even for answers that remain factually correct. Over 90% of changes in faithfulness under INT4 are negative, indicating that answers become less grounded in the retrieved evidence while still sometimes being correct. The negative impact of INT4 grows when retrieval noise increases and when more context chunks are retrieved.

Conclusion: Quantizing RAG key-value caches to INT8 appears safe, but aggressive compression with INT4 harms faithfulness in ways that are not captured by standard accuracy metrics. Because models can produce correct yet ungrounded answers, faithfulness must be explicitly audited—using tools like hallucination detection, NLI, or LLM judges—before deploying compressed caches in real systems, particularly under noisy retrieval and large-context settings.

Abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation systems can precompute and store key-value caches of retrieved documents to avoid re-encoding context at every query. Quantizing these caches further reduces storage, but no prior work asks whether compression damages faithfulness, whether responses remain grounded in the retrieved evidence. Faithfulness and accuracy are not equivalent: a model can produce a correct answer that is no longer supported by the context it was given. We evaluate Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct under INT8 and INT4 quantization on RGB and HotpotQA, measuring both accuracy and faithfulness with a hallucination detector, NLI entailment, and an LLM judge. INT8 is near-lossless across both metrics. INT4 reduces accuracy and, more critically, even among answers that remain factually correct, over 90% of faithfulness changes are negative, i.e., accuracy metrics are blind to this regression. The harm grows under noisy retrieval and with more retrieved chunks. Faithfulness must be audited before compressed caches are deployed.

</details>


### [218] [Evidence-Bounded Mental Health Reasoning from Heterogeneous Speech Protocols](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.31014)
*Chengyuan Gao,Jiang Wu,Tao Lu,Jiayan Guo,Mingkun Xu,Tianyi Zang,Shangyang Li*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes a protocol-aware, evidence-bounded framework (EviBound) and a new benchmark (Evidence Package Benchmark) for multimodal speech-and-text-based mental health screening to prevent models from making unsupported clinical claims while improving accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current multimodal mental health screening models treat all clinical speech protocols (e.g., free interviews, reading tasks) as equivalent evidence sources. This ignores that different protocols naturally support different types and strengths of clinical evidence. As a result, models may hallucinate symptoms from irrelevant content or overstate what the data can justify. Even powerful LLMs with long chain-of-thought reasoning can worsen this by expanding beyond what the evidence warrants. There is a need for systems that explicitly constrain reasoning to what each protocol and modality legitimately supports, in order to be safer and more clinically trustworthy.

Method: The authors reformulate multimodal mental health screening as an evidence-bounded reasoning problem. They introduce the Evidence Package Benchmark, consisting of 1,870 evidence packages drawn from six heterogeneous data sources, each annotated with modality masks and explicit evidence permissions that define what type of inferences are allowed. They then propose EviBound, a protocol-aware evidence control framework. EviBound uses: (1) a profile-aware planner that restricts the scope of reasoning according to the participant profile and protocol; (2) orchestration of evidence tools via a five-way acoustic consensus mechanism to robustly integrate multimodal cues; and (3) a boundary critic that detects and suppresses claims not supported by the permitted evidence. The approach is compared against direct omni-modal LLM prompting and other baselines.

Result: On held-out test data, EviBound achieves a Depression AUROC of 0.8658, outperforming the strongest direct omni-modal baseline by +0.0811 AUROC. At the same time, it maintains zero evidence-boundary violations, meaning it does not make any clinical claims that exceed what is licensed by the available evidence and protocol annotations. This demonstrates that evidence-bounded, protocol-aware control can improve both predictive performance and safety/consistency of clinical claims compared to unconstrained multimodal reasoning with LLMs.

Conclusion: The study shows that treating multimodal clinical screening as an evidence-bounded reasoning task, with explicit protocol- and modality-aware constraints, yields systems that are both more accurate and more trustworthy. The Evidence Package Benchmark enables evaluation of such behavior, and the EviBound framework illustrates how to operationalize protocol-aware planning, multimodal consensus, and boundary criticism. This work argues that future clinical NLP systems should move beyond maximizing raw accuracy toward ensuring that all generated clinical inferences are tightly aligned with and justified by the available, protocol-specific evidence.

Abstract: Computational mental health screening using multimodal speech and text has shown great promise. However, existing models often assume all clinical speech protocols carry equivalent evidentiary validity. In reality, heterogeneous protocols, from free interviews to fixed reading tasks, support fundamentally different evidence. Forcing uniform reasoning flattens these boundaries, causing models to hallucinate symptoms from irrelevant text or overclaim support. Even advanced long chain-of-thought LLMs fail to resolve this issue, as free-form reasoning can exacerbate boundary violations. To address this, we reformulate multimodal screening as an evidence-bounded reasoning problem. We introduce the Evidence Package Benchmark, integrating 1,870 packages across six heterogeneous sources with explicit modality masks and evidence permissions. We further propose EviBound, a protocol-aware evidence control framework. Unlike direct LLM prompting, EviBound uses a profile-aware planner to restrict reasoning scope, orchestrates evidence tools via five-way acoustic consensus, and enforces a boundary critic to suppress unsupported claims. Empirical results show EviBound achieves a held-out test Depression AUROC of 0.8658, exceeding the strongest direct omni-modal baseline by +0.0811 AUROC while maintaining zero claim violations. Our work moves beyond unconstrained accuracy toward evidence-consistent, protocol-aware systems for safer clinical NLP research.

</details>


### [219] [LLM Judges Verify Presence, Not Absence: Omission Blindness in AI Clinical Notes and What Recovers It](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.31016)
*Sebastian Fox,Luke Markham,Ryan Lail,Michael Karotsieris*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper studies whether LLM “judge” models can reliably detect omissions (missing facts) in AI-generated clinical notes, finds that standard judge setups largely fail at omission detection, and proposes a restructured, fact-extraction-based approach that substantially improves detection with low false alarms.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Ambient AI scribes that draft clinical notes often omit clinically relevant information, which is the dominant real-world error type. Existing evaluation relies on LLM judges comparing notes to encounter transcripts, but it is unknown whether these judges can reliably detect omissions because public datasets have poor alignment between reference notes and transcripts. This gap prevents rigorous measurement and improvement of omission detection, which is critical for clinical safety and trust in AI documentation tools.

Method: The authors construct a benchmark of 500 single-error note pairs derived from audited fact sheets: 298 with a specific fact omitted and 202 with added or altered facts as controls. They test eight different LLM judge designs on paired-note discrimination (errorful vs clean twin) and single-note flagging, analyzing performance separately on omissions vs added/altered errors. They then redesign the task: first have the model list all facts established by the transcript, then check whether each fact is present in the note. They implement this both as a multi-step per-fact pipeline and as a single-call prompt evolved using GEPA, measuring detection rates, false-alarm rates, cost, and agreement with clinicians. They also test transfer to real vendor notes via recalibration.

Result: Standard LLM judges perform well on added/altered content (paired discrimination AUC 0.79–0.94) but near chance on omissions (0.50–0.63). On single notes, none of the eight judge designs flags omissions more often than perfect notes, and changes in wording, voting, or GEPA-based prompt optimization only shift operating points without achieving usable omission detection. The restructured, fact-first approach works: the per-fact pipeline names missing facts and assigns severity with a 2.7% false-alarm rate and 24.6% omission detection, while the single GEPA-evolved call detects more omissions (36.9%, p=0.002) at a 6.2% false-alarm rate and roughly one-tenth the cost per note. A physician author validated 70 cases and preferred the pipeline’s judgment in all 10 disagreements (p=0.002); a second blinded clinician largely agreed with the severity grading. On real vendor notes, no benchmark threshold transfers directly, but after recalibration the single-call method outperforms the best of the eight standard judges at roughly half their false-alarm rate. Both methods fail on omissions where the missing fact is redundantly stated elsewhere in the note.

Conclusion: LLM-based judge systems that directly compare clinical notes to transcripts are notably poor at detecting omissions, the most prevalent and safety-critical error type in ambient AI scribing. Simple variants of the conventional judging paradigm do not fix this. Reframing judging as structured fact extraction followed by per-fact checking substantially improves omission detection with low false positives and manageable cost, and can generalize to real vendor notes after recalibration, though limitations remain for redundantly expressed facts. The authors provide a benchmark and prompts to support further research on safe and reliable omission detection in AI-generated clinical documentation.

Abstract: Ambient AI scribes draft clinical notes, and published audits find their dominant error is omission: information the encounter established that the note fails to record. The standard check is an LLM judge: a second model reads the note against the transcript and flags problems. We ask whether judges detect omissions. Public corpora cannot supply the answer key: their clinician reference notes and transcripts are materially discrepant. Our benchmark has 500 single-error note pairs from audited fact sheets, 298 with a named fact certainly absent and 202 added-or-altered controls. Across eight judge designs, paired discrimination (the flawed note below its clean twin, 0.5 a coin flip) reads 0.79-0.94 on added or altered content and 0.50-0.63 on omissions. On single notes, no design flags omissions reliably more often than perfect notes. Wording changes, voting and GEPA prompt optimisation move the operating point without creating usable detection. Restructuring the task recovers it: list the facts the transcript establishes, then check the note for each. Two methods reach it independently and trade off: a per-fact pipeline, and a GEPA-evolved prompt doing the same in one call. The pipeline's flags name the missing fact and its severity at 2.7% false alarms. The single call detects more (36.9% against 24.6%, p=0.002) at 6.2% false alarms and a tenth of the cost per note. A physician author validated 70 items and, where the two routes disagree, sided with the pipeline on 10 of 10 (p=0.002). A second clinician, not an author, graded the severity rubric blind and agrees to within a grade. On real vendor notes from a companion census no benchmark threshold transfers, but the re-calibrated single call detects more than the best of the eight at half its false-alarm rate. Omissions whose fact is restated elsewhere defeat both routes. We release the benchmark, prompts and judgements.

</details>


### [220] [One note in three: a verified census of three deployed AI scribes, and the instrument that counted it](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.31017)
*Sebastian Fox,Luke Markham,Ryan Lail,Michael Karotsieris*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Audits three commercial ambient AI scribe systems on 142 real and simulated clinical encounters, finding that about a quarter to a third of generated notes contain clinically important, verified errors, especially in medications, allergies, and misdocumented care, and shows that error rates appear highly sensitive to how auditing instruments and prompts are designed.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Ambient AI scribes are entering clinical practice under the assumption that clinician co-signing will catch serious errors, but there is little rigorous, transparent evidence about the nature and frequency of those errors, and prior audits report widely varying results, possibly due to differing methods. The authors want to systematically measure clinically meaningful failure modes across multiple commercial systems and understand how much the measured error rate depends on the evaluation setup itself.

Method: The authors collected 565 AI-generated notes from 142 consultations (UK primary care, US ambulatory, and crafted scenarios), produced by three commercial AI scribe products. They ran 12 iterative "discovery passes" using AI-based review prompts to surface 13,678 potential errors, then filtered these down to 5,898 candidates deemed potentially important. These were then adjudicated by an adversarial panel formed by two different LLM families, each instructed to refute the alleged error when possible. This process produced 618 verified failures. Two human clinicians, blind to authorship and working on disjoint subsets, independently validated the AI-adjudicated failures and refusals. The authors also performed ablation-like comparisons varying only the review prompt and the reviewing model family to see how these choices affect the proportion of candidates that are confirmed errors and the apparent per-note failure rate. They compare their taxonomy and measured error composition with prior scribe-audit studies.

Result: They found that 31.3% of notes contain at least one verified failure, especially errors in allergy and medication documentation, fabricated patient identity details, and misclassification of history as physical examination findings in telephone consults. When discounting identity and date errors that a real EHR would usually pre-populate, the rate is still 24.8%. They identified an additional failure pattern not covered by existing scribe-error taxonomies: treatments that the clinician retracts but which the AI scribe documents as delivered care. Human clinicians strongly agreed with the AI panel: 20/21 and 12/12 sampled failures were upheld, and all refusals to label an issue as an error were judged appropriate. They demonstrate that apparent failure rates are highly sensitive to the auditing instrument: with the same underlying models and data, changing only the review prompt moves the fraction of candidate issues that are verified from 9.3% to 79.0%, and changing the reviewing model family alters the share of notes flagged from about 27.8% to 54.8%. Depending on how stringent the standard, between 28% and 97% of sampled notes had at least one failure. They also show that prior audits’ dominance of omission errors (54–86% of all errors) contrasts with their own lower omission proportion (23.1%), suggesting methodological differences as a major source of disagreement. The authors release all 618 verified findings, associated transcripts, prompts, model versions, and the full evaluation pipeline for re-use.

Conclusion: Commercial ambient AI scribes, as currently evaluated, frequently produce clinically relevant documentation errors, particularly in high-risk areas like medications and allergies, and can misrepresent the care delivered. However, measured error rates are highly contingent on how audits are performed; instrument design, prompts, and reviewing model family alone can create large discrepancies between reported failure rates. This means that comparisons across published scribe audits are not straightforward, and that robust, transparent, and standardized evaluation pipelines are essential. By releasing a fully reproducible pipeline and detailed error corpus, the authors aim to establish a more reliable foundation for auditing AI scribes and guide safer deployment and oversight in clinical settings.

Abstract: Ambient AI scribes draft clinical notes under the reassurance that a clinician signs every note. We audited three commercial AI scribes on the same 142 consultations: 565 notes from recorded UK primary-care and US ambulatory encounters plus authored scenarios. Twelve discovery passes proposed 13,678 candidate errors; the 5,898 clearing an importance filter went to an adversarial panel of two models from different families, each told to refute what it could, and 618 survived. One note in three (31.3% [27.0, 35.6]) carries a verified failure, concentrated in allergy and medication information, invented patient identity, and history written up as examination on telephone consultations that can contain none. No product was given a patient record; setting aside the two classes a record would have prefilled, invented identity and dates, the rate is 24.8% [20.8, 29.0]. One failure mode did not fit our scheme, drawn from published scribe-error taxonomies: a treatment the clinician retracts, recorded as delivered care. Two clinicians adjudicated blind, disjoint samples: a physician author upheld 20 of 21 findings (95.2% [77.3, 99.2]) and an independent clinician, not an author, 12 of 12 ([75.8, 100]); both judged every sampled refusal genuine. A failure rate depends on the instrument as much as the scribes. With model, evidence and settings fixed, the review instruction alone moves the share of candidates verified from 9.3% to 79.0%, and the reviewing family moves it too: alone at that instruction the gentler flags 54.8% of notes against 27.8%. Between 28% and 97% of sampled notes carry a failure depending on the standard. Published audits disagree among themselves by a margin instrument differences alone can produce: omission is 54-86% of their errors against our 23.1%. We release all 618 findings with transcript-side evidence, every prompt and model version, and the re-runnable pipeline.

</details>


### [221] [When Does Predictor-Based RL Align with Human Perception? A Study of Subjective Rewards in Codec-Based Speech Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.31035)
*Joonyong Park,Jerry Li*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper investigates when learned, subjective reward models can be safely used with RL for codec-based TTS, and compares GRPO against Best-of-N reranking under a CER constraint.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Codec-based TTS allows applying language-model-style post-training to speech, but it is unclear whether perceptual predictors (for style, naturalness, likability, arousal) can be used as RL rewards without losing alignment with human preferences, especially due to transcript drift and miscalibrated subjective predictors.

Method: They use Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with learned reward models targeting anime-like speaking style, naturalness, likability, and arousal. They add a character error rate (CER) zone constraint to prevent optimizing perceptual rewards by drifting away from the transcript. They compare RL policy optimization against Best-of-N reranking under the same reward and CER gating. They run both single-reward and multi-reward experiments, perform multi-rater human A/B tests, and analyze reward gaps vs. human preferences and CER gaps to study transfer and calibration across different reward axes.

Result: Each subjective reward model mainly improves its own metric, with limited cross-metric gains, showing that these learned predictors are axis-specific and not general quality proxies. Human A/B tests reveal that improvements in predictor scores do not transfer uniformly to human judgments across axes. Reward-gap analysis shows that signed reward differences correlate with human choices overall, while residual CER differences do not, but the calibration quality varies per reward axis. Best-of-8 reranking is a very strong baseline and performs comparably to GRPO in human evaluations.

Conclusion: Learned subjective speech rewards should be treated as specific predictor-axis-base tuples, not generic quality surrogates. GRPO’s main value is to amortize the behavior that a reward model and reranking would select, rather than to consistently beat strong Best-of-N reranking in perceived quality. The paper offers diagnostics—such as reward-gap vs. human-choice correlations—for validating and choosing reward models before undertaking multi-reward post-training for speech generation.

Abstract: Codec-based text-to-speech (TTS) models make language-model post-training applicable to speech generation, but it remains unclear when learned perceptual predictors can serve as reinforcement learning rewards without losing alignment with human listeners. We study this question with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) using learned rewards for anime-like speaking style, naturalness, likability, and arousal. To prevent perceptual rewards from being optimized through transcript drift, we introduce a character error rate (CER) zone constraint and compare policy optimization with Best-of-$N$ reranking under the same reward gate. Across single-reward runs, each reward primarily improves its own target metric, showing that subjective predictors are not interchangeable quality surrogates. Multi-rater A/B tests further show uneven human transfer, while a reward-gap analysis separates average transfer from within-axis calibration: signed reward gaps significantly predict listener choices in the pooled analysis, whereas residual CER gaps do not, but per-axis calibration remains heterogeneous. Best-of-8 is a strong human-level baseline and is not clearly worse than GRPO perceptually, suggesting that GRPO should be viewed as amortizing reward-selected behavior into the policy rather than uniformly outperforming reranking. These results support analyzing subjective speech rewards as predictor-axis-base tuples and provide practical diagnostics for selecting rewards before multi-reward speech post-training.

</details>


### [222] [Language-Statistical Analysis of Neural Audio Codec Tokens Across Architectures, Corpora, and Noise Conditions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.31037)
*Joonyong Park,Shinnosuke Takamichi,David M. Chan,Shunsuke Kando,Yuki Saito,Hiroshi Saruwatari*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper quantitatively studies the ‘language-like’ statistics of tokens produced by different neural audio codec architectures under various noise conditions, and links these statistics to codec behavior and distortion.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Neural audio codecs output discrete token sequences that have been informally observed to follow language-like statistical laws (e.g., Zipf’s and Heaps’ laws), but prior work has not systematically compared these statistics across codec architectures, corpora, and acoustic conditions, nor clarified how these statistics relate to codec robustness and distortion. The authors want to establish a rigorous, architecture-aware framework for applying language-statistical analysis to neural audio codec tokens and to understand how different designs behave under noise.

Method: The authors analyze token sequences from 13 neural audio codecs representing three meta-categories: multi-codebook residual vector quantization (RVQ), single-codebook vector quantization (VQ), and non-VQ designs. They evaluate each codec on three speech corpora, each under three acoustic conditions: clean, white noise, and real-world DEMAND noise. From carefully matched token samples, they compute several statistical measures: Zipf and Heaps law parameters, unigram entropy, codebook occupancy statistics, and Jensen–Shannon divergence (JSD) between conditions. They use safeguards to ensure valid fits of statistical laws and select n-gram orders in a way that is conditional on codec family. They then perform variance analysis to see how much each factor (corpus, acoustic condition, codec meta-category) explains in each metric and relate JSD changes to mel-cepstral distortion under noise.

Result: They find that the identity of the speech corpus contributes very little to the variance of the token statistics. Instead, the acoustic condition (clean vs noisy) and codec meta-category (RVQ, single-codebook VQ, non-VQ) explain most of the variation, in a way that depends on the specific metric. Among all metrics, unigram entropy shows the strongest association with codec meta-category. When comparing clean to noisy conditions using JSD at a matched unigram order, they observe a clear relationship between JSD and mel-cepstral distortion, especially under DEMAND noise. The characteristic ‘collapse’ and ‘explosion’ degradation patterns previously reported for RVQ codecs appear concentrated within RVQ codebooks, with collapse being prominent under white noise and explosion under DEMAND noise. Explosion-like behavior is also seen in non-VQ codecs, while single-codebook VQ codecs do not show clear collapse or explosion signatures but instead exhibit shifts in occupancy and distribution shape.

Conclusion: The study shows that language-like token statistics in neural audio codecs are shaped more by codec architecture and acoustic conditions than by the speech corpus itself. It provides evidence that unigram entropy and JSD-based measures, interpreted in an architecture-aware manner, can characterize codec behavior and degradation under noise and correlate with perceptual distortion. The authors propose architecture-conditioned conventions for applying language-statistical analyses to neural audio codec tokens, making such analyses more reliable and interpretable across different codec designs and noise environments.

Abstract: Neural audio codecs (NACs) convert speech into discrete token sequences, and prior work has reported that these sequences follow language-like statistical laws. This paper analyzes the token statistics of 13 NACs spanning multi-codebook residual vector quantization (RVQ), single-codebook VQ, and non-VQ designs, evaluated on three corpora under clean, white-noise, and real-world DEMAND-noise conditions. Zipf and Heaps parameters, unigram entropy, codebook occupancy, and Jensen-Shannon divergence (JSD) are estimated from matched token samples with explicit fit-validity safeguards and family-conditional $n$-gram orders. Corpus identity explains little variance in any metric, whereas acoustic condition and quantizer meta-category dominate in a metric-dependent way, and unigram entropy is the metric most strongly associated with meta-category. Clean-to-noise JSD computed at a common unigram order is associated with mel-cepstral distortion most clearly under DEMAND noise. The collapse and explosion degradation signatures previously reported for RVQ codecs concentrate in RVQ cells under white and DEMAND noise, respectively; explosion also occurs in non-VQ codecs, and single-codebook VQ codecs shift in occupancy and distribution shape without either signature. These results provide architecture-conditioned conventions for applying language-statistical analysis to NAC tokens.

</details>


### [223] [Type-Balanced Contextual Learning for Incremental Named Entity Recognition](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.31038)
*Duzhen Zhang,Yahan Yu,Xiuyi Chen,Chenxing Li,Dong Yu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes a new method, Type-Balanced Contextual Learning (TBCL), to mitigate biased context and catastrophic forgetting in incremental named entity recognition, improving performance across multiple datasets and settings.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Incremental Named Entity Recognition must continually learn new entity types without forgetting previously learned ones, while also dealing with semantic shifts of the non-entity class. Existing pseudo-labeling approaches help but introduce a biased context problem, where contexts of old-entity tokens in new data become biased toward new entity types, worsening forgetting and overfitting. The authors aim to understand and solve this overlooked issue.

Method: The authors first analyze and identify the biased context phenomenon in pseudo-labeling-based INER. They then propose Type-Balanced Contextual Learning (TBCL), which includes (1) a sentence-duplet learning scheme that jointly considers old and new sentences to balance contextual information across entity types, and (2) a contextual consistency loss that regularizes the model so that contextual representations of entities remain consistent across incremental steps, alleviating bias and preserving old knowledge.

Result: Through extensive experiments under ten different incremental NER settings on three standard datasets, the proposed TBCL method outperforms prior pseudo-labeling-based INER approaches, demonstrating better retention of old entity types and improved learning of new ones, validating its effectiveness against the biased context problem.

Conclusion: The paper concludes that the biased context problem is a key but previously neglected factor behind catastrophic forgetting and overfitting in pseudo-labeling-based INER. The proposed TBCL framework, with sentence-duplet learning and contextual consistency loss, effectively mitigates this issue and provides a new context-focused direction for future INER research.

Abstract: Incremental Named Entity Recognition (INER) stands as a pivotal task in information extraction, emphasizing the successive identification of new entity types within unstructured text. Faced with the continuous influx of entity types, INER grapples with two significant challenges: the widespread issue of catastrophic forgetting and the unique shift issue of the non-entity type semantics. While pseudo-labeling-based INER methods have proven effective in addressing these challenges, a previously overlooked issue arises: the biased context problem. Our analysis shows that, in new sentences, the contextual associations of tokens representing old entity types exhibit a significantly stronger bias towards new entity types compared to their contexts in old sentences. This tendency intensifies the degradation of old knowledge while promoting the overfitting of new knowledge. To solve this biased context, we propose a Type-Balanced Contextual Learning (TBCL) method, featuring a sentence-duplet learning scheme and a contextual consistency loss. This approach offers a fresh perspective for INER through context analysis. Extensive experiments across ten INER settings on three highly recognized datasets showcase the efficacy of our TBCL method, highlighting its proficiency in resolving the biased context issue inherent in pseudo-labeling based INER approaches.

</details>


<div id='cs.AI'></div>

# cs.AI [[Back]](#toc)

### [224] [DS-Lighting: Making Agent Harnesses Explicit for Data-Science Automation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.28590)
*Fan Liu,Hao Liu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: DS-Lighting is a unified, explicit harness toolkit for LLM-based data-science agents that standardizes how tasks, workflows, execution, and evaluation are represented and run, improving reproducibility and reliability across benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current LLM data-science agents rely on ad-hoc, implicit agent harnesses: how tasks are encoded, how execution state is tracked, how outputs are constrained, and how evaluation is performed is often left underspecified or buried in code. This makes it hard to reproduce results, compare agents fairly, or attribute performance differences to models vs. system design. There is also unnecessary system fragility and avoidable failures in end-to-end workflows. The authors want a principled, unified way to define and share these harnesses so that experimental results on data-science automation become comparable, reliable, and extensible across heterogeneous tasks and agents.

Method: The authors design DS-Lighting, a toolkit that explicitly decomposes an LLM agent harness for data science into four modular layers: (1) data layer for task and dataset specification; (2) workflow layer for representing data-science processes; (3) execution layer for managing state and running agent/operator programs; and (4) evaluation layer for metrics and feedback. Agents are represented as executable operator programs that can implement either fixed pipelines or adaptive search strategies. They also convert and integrate multiple open-source data-science benchmarks into a unified, MLE-Bench-style task format, running them under a shared task interface, sandboxed runtime, and standardized metric protocol. They perform experiments varying agents, harness designs, models, and ablations to study the impact of explicit harness design on system-level behavior and performance.

Result: Under DS-Lighting, different LLM-based data-science agents and benchmarks can be run and compared within a single, standardized harness. Experimental results show that when harness design is made explicit and modular, end-to-end workflows suffer fewer system-level and execution failures, and results become easier to reproduce and compare across agents and models. Ablations indicate that the structure and choices in the harness layers significantly affect observed performance, confirming that a large part of variability in agent results stems from harness design rather than only from the underlying LLM.

Conclusion: Explicit, modular harness design is a key, previously under-specified component in building reliable LLM data-science agents. DS-Lighting provides a unified harness toolkit and benchmark integration that standardizes how tasks, workflows, execution, and evaluation are represented. This improves reproducibility, comparability, and robustness of data-science automation experiments, and offers a common substrate for future research on LLM agents. The released codebase enables the community to build, extend, and fairly evaluate data-science agents under shared, transparent system assumptions.

Abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) agents have shown promise for automating data-science workflows, yet their end-to-end performance depends critically on the agent harness that represents tasks, manages execution state, constrains output artifacts, and provides evaluation feedback. Existing data-science agents often leave this harness implicit, making results difficult to reproduce, compare, and attribute across heterogeneous tasks. We introduce DS-Lighting, a unified harness toolkit that makes harness design explicit for data-science automation. DS-Lighting decomposes the harness into four reusable layers: data, workflow, execution, and evaluation, and represents diverse agents as executable operator programs that support both predefined pipelines and adaptive search. We further integrate multiple open-source data-science benchmarks into an MLE-Bench-style task format, enabling controlled comparison under a shared task interface, sandboxed runtime, and metric protocol. Experiments across agents, harnesses, models, and ablations show that explicit harness design improves reproducibility, comparability, and reliability, while reducing avoidable system-level failures in end-to-end data-science workflows. Our code is available at https://github.com/usail-hkust/dslighting

</details>


### [225] [Expert-validated STEM QA](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.28591)
*Kihwan Han,Saurabh Patil,Chinmayee Shukla,Abhinav Sharma,Marko Pavlovic,Anshuman Lall,Mahesh Joshi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They introduce a new, expert-validated STEM QA dataset that fixes key flaws in existing benchmarks and is hard for current AI models, and they show it can both evaluate and improve models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing STEM evaluation datasets have several problems: models are already near-saturated on them, their topic coverage is skewed, they often use multiple-choice formats unlike real scientific use, and they contain inaccuracies due to rushed, contest-style collection and limited review. Meanwhile, frontier models have largely exhausted public web data, so there is a growing need for high-quality, human-created benchmarks that accurately capture expert STEM knowledge and provide meaningful headroom for evaluating and training advanced models.

Method: They created a new STEM QA dataset (N=398 public benchmark items, plus a larger private set) in physics, chemistry, biology, and mathematics, authored by 241 vetted domain experts. They (1) designed a balanced taxonomy of topics, (2) selected and incentivized contributors for quality, (3) ran multiple review and revision rounds with consensus-based expert validation of each item, and (4) used a verifiable Q&A format instead of standard multiple choice. They then benchmarked frontier AI models on this dataset and conducted post-training of an open-source model on a separate, private subset (N=2,000) to test training utility.

Result: Frontier AI models performed poorly on the new benchmark, achieving under 25% accuracy, which shows that the dataset is challenging and leaves headroom for improvement. When an open-source model was post-trained on a separate private version of the dataset (2,000 items), its performance on the STEM subset of the HLE-verified dataset improved by 15% relative to the baseline, with the improvement statistically significant (p=0.045). A portion of the dataset was released openly for the community.

Conclusion: The authors conclude that their expert-validated STEM QA dataset addresses key gaps in existing STEM benchmarks by being more accurate, balanced, realistic in format, and still challenging for state-of-the-art models. The dataset is useful both as an evaluation benchmark and as training data to boost model STEM capabilities, and the open-sourced portion provides a new resource for AI research in scientific domains.

Abstract: Recent advancements in AI are helping scientists achieve breakthroughs in fields such as mathematics, medicine, and materials sciences. New evaluation datasets for AI models contribute to such advancement in AI. In the STEM domain, frontier models have consumed most of the available online data, creating the need for human-created datasets that codify the knowledge of leading experts in the domain. There are several STEM datasets available for the research community in this field. However, there are some gaps in these datasets, leaving room for improvement. Examples of gaps include (1) saturation in model performance on these datasets, leaving no head-room for meaningful evaluations, (2) skewed taxonomy distributions, (3) multiple choice question format that is misaligned with how scientists use AI in the real world, and (4) inaccurate answers and rationales partially led by a contest-based data collection and a time-bound review process. In this study, we present 'Expert-validated STEM QA', a high-quality, expert-validated STEM dataset (N=398) in Physics, Chemistry, Biology, and Mathematics, created by 241 domain experts. We (1) carefully designed a taxonomy with balanced distribution, (2) vetted question contributors with quality-driven incentive, (3) conducted multiple rounds of reviews with revisions validated by domain experts based on consensus, and (4) created the dataset in verifiable question and answer format. Our study demonstrated low performance ($<25\%$) of frontier AI models on the dataset as a benchmark. Post-training on a separate, private version of the dataset (N=2,000) increased performance of the open source model by $15\%$ relative to the baseline model (p=0.045) on the STEM subset of HLE-verified dataset, indicating potential utility of the dataset for model training. We have open-sourced a portion of our dataset for the AI research community.

</details>


### [226] [A collective capability boundary in frontier large language models on guideline-conformant and case-specific oncology decision-making](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.28592)
*Zhang Sheng,Jinming Li,Wangyang Chen,Zhiwei Bao,Yu YoSean Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces the Oncology Decision Boundary Benchmark (ODBB) to test how well large language models (LLMs) make real-world oncology decisions, showing that many decision failures stem from meta-judgment and commitment under uncertainty rather than lack of factual knowledge, and arguing that safe deployment needs architectures that detect models’ competence limits and defer to clinicians.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current medical LLM benchmarks mostly test factual recall (e.g., exam-style questions), but real oncology practice is about making sequential, high-stakes decisions under uncertainty following guidelines and pathways. There is concern that even frontier LLMs may share systematic blind spots in these decision processes that cannot be solved by ensembling or combining models. The authors want to rigorously characterize these decision-path failures, quantify how often all models fail simultaneously, and understand whether tuning for decisiveness improves safety or merely increases unsafe commitments. They also aim to test the assumption that a single LLM can reliably serve as the sole decision engine in clinical settings.

Method: The authors construct the Oncology Decision Boundary Benchmark (ODBB), comprising 2,005 oncology decision points: 1,586 distilled from NCCN clinical practice guidelines and 419 from colorectal cancer cases. They evaluate nine state-of-the-art LLM families (four closed-source and five open-weight), all released between mid-2025 and early-2026. A fully deterministic, rule-based scoring system (no LLM-in-the-loop) classifies each model’s output into one of 14 predefined failure types. To validate the scoring taxonomy and implementation, two oncologists independently review a stratified sample of 225 items, and inter-rater agreement is quantified with weighted Cohen’s kappa. The analysis treats the nine models collectively as a “pooled super-model” to measure how often all of them fail on the same item, and examines patterns such as pathway-selection vs within-pathway reasoning, decisiveness vs caution, and cases where models verbalize the correct action but fail to commit to it.

Result: Across the 2,005 decision points, when treating the nine LLMs as a pooled super-model, 42.1% of items (Wilson 95% CI 40.0–44.3%) are answered correctly by none of the models. This includes 35.7% of NCCN-derived items and 66.4% of colorectal-cancer case items. Failures cluster around higher-level choices between guideline pathways—deciding which treatment or workup track to follow—rather than errors within a chosen pathway, indicating a shared deficit in clinical meta-judgment and decision boundary recognition. Two models explicitly tuned for decisiveness (GPT-5.5, Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview) make unsafe commitments three to five times more frequently than more cautious models, without achieving better overall accuracy. Additionally, in 3–9% of items, models correctly state the appropriate next step but refrain from clearly endorsing or committing to it, revealing that some errors are about decision-making and commitment instead of knowledge gaps. The scoring framework achieves high agreement with oncologist judgments (weighted κ = 0.939 and 0.790 across two comparisons), supporting the validity of the failure taxonomy.

Conclusion: The study concludes that improving raw model quality alone will not resolve the key safety bottlenecks for clinical deployment of LLMs in oncology. The main limitation is the assumption that a single model can act as a stand-alone decision-maker: frontier models frequently fail at recognizing and handling their own decision boundaries, particularly when selecting among guideline pathways, and can become overconfident and unsafe when tuned for decisiveness. Effective and safe clinical use of LLMs will require new system architectures that can detect when a model has reached its competence limits and then defer or route decisions to human clinicians, rather than relying on one model to autonomously commit to treatment choices. The ODBB provides a benchmark to measure such decision-boundary behavior and to guide the design of more robust, human-in-the-loop clinical AI systems.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) achieve high scores on medical knowledge examinations, yet real-world oncology is not a knowledge test--it is a sequence of guideline-pathway choices, escalation judgments, and commitments under uncertainty. Existing benchmarks largely measure factual recall, leaving open whether frontier LLMs share decision-path blind spots that combining models cannot fix. We built the Oncology Decision Boundary Benchmark (ODBB)--2,005 oncology decision points across NCCN guidelines and colorectal cancer cases--and evaluated nine frontier LLMs (four closed-source, five open-weight families) released between June 2025 and April 2026. A fully deterministic scorer (zero LLM inference) classified outputs into 14 failure types, independently validated by two oncologists (Cohen's weighted $κ$ = 0.939 and 0.790) on a 225-item stratified sample. Treating the nine as a pooled super-model, 42.1% (Wilson 95% CI 40.0--44.3%) of all items--35.7% of the 1,586 NCCN items and 66.4% of the 419 colorectal-cancer cases--were answered correctly by none, with failures concentrated in choosing between guideline pathways before reasoning within any: a consistent blind spot in clinical meta-judgment that likely requires architectural intervention rather than more training data. Two models tuned for decisiveness (GPT-5.5, Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview) made unsafe commitments three to five times more often than the seven cautious models without scoring higher. In 3--9% of items, models stated the correct next clinical step yet did not commit to it--failures of decision, not knowledge. Model quality is no longer the primary bottleneck for clinical LLM deployment; the binding constraint is the assumption that any single model can be the sole basis for a clinical decision. Progress requires architectures that detect when a model reaches its competence boundary and route the decision to a clinician.

</details>


### [227] [Statutory AI: Aligning Large Language Models With Legal Norms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.28593)
*Cindy Delage,Stéphane Canu,Marc Décombas,Jonathan Foureur*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes Statutory AI, a hybrid alignment method that uses specific legal texts as a constitutional framework to reduce harmful outputs from generative models more effectively and efficiently than standard Constitutional AI.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: AI regulatory frameworks are expanding, and there is a growing need to ensure that generative AI systems comply with legal and ethical standards. Existing alignment approaches have drawbacks: methods like Constitutional AI rely heavily on human-written constitutions and supervision, and broad value principles such as Good-for-Humanity are too abstract and vague for concrete governance. The authors want a more precise, actionable, and automatable way to align AI with established norms, grounded in existing law.

Method: They introduce Statutory AI, which uses human-authored legal principles drawn from a legal corpus as the AI system’s governing framework. The method has two chain-of-thought stages: (1) classify the user’s prompt into one of several predefined legal themes; (2) analyze the prompt together with relevant legal articles from that theme, then critique and revise the model’s output to comply with those norms. They evaluate this using 1,000 red-teaming prompts across five penal themes: discrimination, disclosure of confidential information, violence, fraud, and abuse of vulnerable persons, comparing against standard Constitutional AI on several generative models.

Result: Statutory AI reduces harmful content by 52–59 percentage points across tested models, which is roughly 10 percentage points better than standard Constitutional AI, while also cutting computation time by more than 50%.

Conclusion: Grounding AI alignment in theme-specific legal texts enables more effective and efficient governance of generative models than standard Constitutional AI. Statutory AI offers a practical, legally anchored framework that can better filter harmful content and do so at lower computational cost, suggesting a promising path for aligning AI behavior with existing regulatory regimes.

Abstract: With the increasing development of AI regulatory frameworks, ensuring that artificial intelligence systems, particularly generative models, operate in accordance with legal and ethical standards has become a critical priority. Existing proposals for AI alignment and value-guided behavior, however, face some limitations. Approaches such as Constitutional AI depend on human supervision, while broad normative frameworks like the Good-for-Humanity (GfH) principle may be overly general and ambiguous to provide actionable governance guidance. To overcome these limitations, we propose a hybrid approach called Statutory AI that employs pre-existing human-authored principles drawn from specific themes within a legal corpus. Specifically, Statutory AI uses legal texts as a constitutional framework, enabling AI systems to autonomously critique and revise their outputs according to established norms. It operates in two stages, both using Chain-of-Thought prompting. The first stage classifies the user prompt into one of the identified themes, while the second stage analyzes it in conjunction with relevant articles selected from the legal corpus of that theme. To illustrate the potential of our approach, we conducted an experiment involving 1,000 red-teaming prompts and five penal themes: discrimination, disclosure of confidential information, violence, fraud, and abuse of vulnerable persons. Statutory AI reduced harmful content by 52 to 59 percentage points across tested models, approximately 10 percentage points higher than standard Constitutional AI, while cutting computation time by over 50%.

</details>


### [228] [From Question-First to Analyst-First: Domain-Expert Skills and Verified Knowledge Compilation for Proactive Enterprise Analytics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.28594)
*Harmohit Singh,Rahul Sharma*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They present an enterprise conversational analytics system that shifts from user question-first to domain-analyst-first, using pluggable expert skills and offline knowledge compilation to pre-generate validated reports and suggested questions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Non-expert users struggle to form good questions over complex, unfamiliar enterprise schemas, and current proactive or recommender tools either rely on hand-curated metric layers or require historical query logs that new datasets do not have.

Method: They design an architecture with two key components: (1) a pluggable domain-expert 'skill' abstraction packaged as a deterministic, folder-based, database-free bundle that is auto-selected per client/dataset and injected across the agentic pipeline, schema explorer, and reporting; (2) an offline knowledge-compilation loop where an agent uses DuckDB on parquet data to explore tables, converge on schema understanding under critic gating with self-healing retries, validate joins via value overlap, and then generate durable schema knowledge, standing expert reports, and agenda-aligned suggested questions. Reports’ metrics are continuously re-verified by re-running their underlying SQL.

Result: They provide a formal model of this analyst-first architecture and show illustrative single-tenant production evidence that it can drive proactive reports, validated metrics, and suggested questions in a live analytics setting, all without relying on query logs or heavy production database load.

Conclusion: Reframing conversational analytics from question-first to analyst-first, powered by pluggable expert skills and offline knowledge compilation, offers a defensible and extensible architecture that can proactively guide users through complex datasets, though they stop short of formal user studies or benchmarks.

Abstract: Conversational analytics systems assume the user already has a well-formed question, leaving a non-expert facing a blank query box on an unfamiliar enterprise schema. Commercial 'proactive' tools narrow this gap only by detecting statistical anomalies over analyst-curated metric layers, and academic next-question recommenders depend on query logs that a fresh dataset lacks. We describe a production analytics system that inverts the interaction model from question-first to analyst-first through two coupled architectural ideas. First, a pluggable domain-expert 'skill' abstraction: a folder-based, database-free subject-matter pack (a manifest, per-stage prompt facets, keyword-routed references, report templates, and optional compute) auto-selected per (client, dataset) by deterministic schema matching and spliced as a cross-cutting concern into every stage of an agentic pipeline, the schema explorer, and the report engines, degrading to a strict no-op when absent. Because a skill is a self-contained folder resolved deterministically, the catalogue is open-ended: an extensible marketplace of domain experts. Second, an offline knowledge-compilation loop: an agent probes the dataset's parquet via DuckDB (zero load on production), runs critic-gated per-table convergence with self-healing retries, and data-validates joins by value overlap, producing durable schema knowledge that drives standing expert reports whose every published metric is re-verified by re-executing its evidence SQL, plus suggested questions that mirror the report agenda. These close a proactive loop: reports surface numbers, the numbers seed questions, and a click launches a verified deep dive, all before the query box is used. We give a formal model and report illustrative single-tenant evidence. We make no user-study or benchmark claims; the contribution is the architecture and its defensibility.

</details>


### [229] [The Signal in the Noise: An Auditable Reliability Layer for Biomedical Text Classification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.28595)
*Moustafa Yehia Hassan,Sharon Wong,Woh Kai Xuan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They propose a conservative, auditable spell-correction layer for noisy biomedical text that fixes many OCR-like errors while avoiding harmful edits, improving downstream classifier performance with high safety.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Biomedical NLP pipelines rely on clean text, but automated PDF parsing of large corpora introduces OCR-like noise, tokenization errors, and character corruption that degrade lexical signals and downstream classifiers. Existing spell-correction often aims for maximal correction and may introduce unsafe changes in sensitive medical contexts. There is a need for a safety-first, auditable preprocessing layer that can repair common noise without risking harmful edits to domain-critical terms.

Method: They design a fully deterministic spell-correction reliability layer that acts conservatively: when uncertain, it abstains from editing. The architecture uses bounded edit-distance candidate generation combined with corpus-based n-gram scoring to choose corrections. It includes biomedical safety gates that protect key medical terminology from being altered. They intrinsically evaluate it on a manually curated benchmark of 2,104 token-level instances including synthetic errors and negative controls, and extrinsically on a 3-class CORD-19 topic classifier (Prevention, Treatment, Epidemiology) over 10,000 examples under a four-condition protocol (Clean, Noisy, Restored, Safety). They also run a supplementary case study on 103 OCR-extracted abstracts classified by BioBERT.

Result: Intrinsically, the layer achieves 94.61% recall on fixing synthetic errors while making zero harmful edits on negative control cases. In downstream evaluation, it recovers about 80.45% of the macro-F1 loss caused by injected noise, raising macro-F1 from 0.7654 (Noisy) to 0.7717 (Restored) and maintaining nearly clean performance in the Safety setting (macro-F1 0.7721). The BioBERT case study shows that transformer encoders are relatively robust to mild noise, suggesting room for a more advanced, grey-box design that combines bounded neural cues and UMLS lexicons with determinism and auditability.

Conclusion: A conservative, deterministic spell-correction reliability layer can substantially mitigate noise from OCR-like artifacts in biomedical corpora while maintaining high safety and auditability. It recovers most of the performance lost to noise for topic classification without harming clean-text performance. The findings imply that deployment-ready biomedical NLP can benefit from artifact-driven, auditable preprocessing and that future work should explore hybrid grey-box models that incorporate neural and lexical resources under strict safety constraints.

Abstract: Biomedical NLP pipelines routinely presuppose clean input text, yet large-scale corpora assembled through automated PDF parsing harbour pervasive OCR-like artifacts, token splits and merges, hyphenation remnants, and character-level corruption, that systematically erode lexical evidence and degrade downstream classifiers. We introduce a conservative, fully auditable spell-correction reliability layer conceived as a safety-oriented preprocessing module rather than a maximal-accuracy corrector: under conditions of uncertainty, the system abstains from editing, in accordance with a medical do-no-harm philosophy. The deterministic architecture couples bounded edit-distance candidate generation with corpus-derived n-gram scoring and a suite of biomedical safety gates that protect domain-critical terminology. We evaluate the layer both intrinsically, on a manually curated benchmark of 2,104 token-level cases, and extrinsically, on a tri-class CORD-19 topic classifier (Prevention, Treatment, Epidemiology) spanning 10,000 examples under a principled four-run protocol (Clean, Noisy, Restored, Safety). Intrinsically, the layer attains 94.61% error-fix recall on synthetic errors with zero harmful edits on negative controls. Downstream, it recovers approximately 80.45% of the noise-induced macro-F1 degradation, elevating macro-F1 from 0.7654 (Noisy) to 0.7717 (Restored) while preserving near-clean performance (Safety: 0.7721). A supplementary case study on 103 real-world OCR-extracted abstracts classified with BioBERT confirms that transformer encoders appeared relatively robust to mild noise, motivating a future grey-box architecture that integrates bounded neural signals and UMLS lexicons without compromising auditability. The system is fully deterministic, artifact-driven, and designed with deployment and auditability in mind.

</details>


### [230] [Paper Pilot: A Human-in-the-Loop Expert System for Evidence-Traceable Scientific Manuscript Generation in Applied Sciences](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.28596)
*Nidhi Jha,Siddharth Chaudhary,Ajinkya Kulkarni*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Paper Pilot is a human-in-the-loop framework that uses gated approvals, traceable evidence, and audit logging to make LLM-assisted scientific writing transparent, verifiable, and tightly governed.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As LLM agents are integrated into scientific workflows for literature review and manuscript drafting, there is a growing risk that ideas, methods, and claims propagate without clear human accountability or traceable links to underlying evidence. Existing autonomous manuscript-generation systems focus on productivity and discovery but do not adequately solve governance issues such as hallucinated citations, unapproved claims, and loss of provenance for data and interpretations. The authors aim to create a structured, controllable process that keeps humans in charge and ensures every claim is backed by verifiable evidence.

Method: The authors design Paper Pilot, an expert-system-style framework that embeds LLMs inside a human-governed manuscript pipeline. They adapt the CARE (Collaborative Agent Reasoning Engineering) methodology to the scientific writing context, defining eight explicit approval gates from initial idea to final claims. At each gate, a manuscript owner must approve progress based on predefined no-pass criteria. The system distinguishes literature-grounded from artifact-grounded claims and enforces evidence-locked revision control so that numbers and interpretations must map to approved sources. Additional mechanisms include claim classification, audit logs, advisory LLM reviews rather than autonomous decisions, and a system prompt that can be deployed across major LLM platforms. For empirical validation, they create a controlled benchmark using real arXiv papers, two commercial LLMs as drafters, mechanical scoring, and no LLM-based judging to test citation grounding under pressure to maximize coverage.

Result: In the citation-grounding benchmark, baseline ungated LLM drafters, pushed for high coverage, fabricated up to 25% of citations and failed to identify any evidence gaps. When the same models operated under Paper Pilot’s evidence-locked rules and approval-gate structure, they produced zero fabricated citations and instead marked missing evidence as explicit placeholders. Early, non-exhaustive experiments on result-grounding behavior, revision dynamics, and adversarial robustness show a similar pattern of improved reliability and transparency, though these findings are presented as preliminary.

Conclusion: Paper Pilot demonstrates that structuring LLM-assisted manuscript writing as a human-in-the-loop, evidence-traceable workflow can sharply reduce citation fabrication and improve the surfacing of evidence gaps, without relying on LLMs as final authorities. The framework reframes LLM use in science from autonomous authorship to governed decision support, emphasizing auditability, claim–evidence linkage, and mandatory human approvals. While initial results are promising, the authors highlight that a full-scale evaluation—especially beyond citation grounding—is future work, positioning Paper Pilot as a foundational governance approach rather than a fully validated production system.
