Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly embedded in scientific workflows for literature analysis, drafting, and review. Existing systems advance autonomous discovery and manuscript generation, but do not resolve the governance problem that arises when ideas, methods, results, and claims propagate through AI-assisted workflows without mandatory human approval or artifact-level traceability. This paper proposes Paper Pilot, a human-in-the-loop expert system for evidence-traceable scientific manuscript generation in applied sciences. It adapts the Collaborative Agent Reasoning Engineering (CARE) methodology to manuscript development through manuscript-owner approval gates, explicit no-pass criteria, claim classification, audit logging, advisory LLM review, and evidence-locked revision control. The framework defines eight approval gates across the idea-to-claim pipeline and distinguishes literature-grounded from artifact-grounded claims, requiring reported numbers and interpretations to remain traceable to approved evidence; its system prompt is openly released for deployment in ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, or institutional LLM environments. As a first empirical validation, we evaluate the citation-grounding layer with a controlled, mechanically scored benchmark (two commercial LLMs, real arXiv papers, no LLM judge): under coverage pressure ungated drafters fabricated up to 25% of their citations and never flagged an evidence gap, whereas the same models under Paper Pilot's evidence-locked rules produced zero fabricated citations and surfaced the planted gaps as explicit placeholders. Preliminary results for result grounding, revision, and adversarial robustness point the same way; full evaluation is left to future work. Paper Pilot positions LLM-assisted writing as a controlled human-AI decision-support process rather than a fully autonomous authorship pipeline.

</details>


### [231] [The Race between Agentic AI Capabilities and Data Quality Control in Online Surveys](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.28597)
*Sourav Panda,Hillmer Chona,Rupak Kumar Das,Shreyash Kale,Shikha Soneji,Jonathan Dodge*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper studies how well agentic AI systems can complete online surveys and bypass standard attention checks, exposes structural vulnerabilities in current survey designs, and tests a simple mitigation via DOM metadata obfuscation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Online surveys rely heavily on attention checks to ensure response quality. With the advent of agentic AI systems that can autonomously browse the web and use tools, it is unclear whether these traditional safeguards remain effective. There is a need to understand (1) whether such agents can reliably complete surveys and defeat attention checks, and (2) what defenses can preserve data quality for researchers while still enabling safe experimentation with agentic AI.

Method: The authors build and evaluate a single-agent architecture that can (a) process multimodal inputs, and (b) interact with web pages via tools in a controlled survey sandbox environment. They study the issue from two complementary sides: an attack analysis, where they design agent behaviors that exploit structural vulnerabilities in survey implementations (e.g., exposed DOM metadata, predictable encodings of answer options) to programmatically recognize and pass attention checks; and a defense analysis, where they implement DOM metadata obfuscation to strip or hide semantic cues in text-based survey questions. They then test multiple open-source language and multimodal models under this framework to assess both agent capability and orchestration strategies.

Result: The experiments show that current agentic AI systems can often pass common online survey attention checks using structured parsing of the DOM and predictable option encodings, without needing true question understanding. This reveals that many existing survey platforms unintentionally expose machine-readable cues that make attention checks fragile. When the authors apply DOM metadata obfuscation, the agents’ ability to exploit these cues is significantly reduced, demonstrating that relatively simple changes in survey implementation can hinder automated bypassing of attention checks. Results also highlight variation in performance across different open-source LLM and multimodal models and orchestration strategies.

Conclusion: The paper concludes that traditional attention checks in online surveys are vulnerable to modern agentic AI systems that exploit structural properties of the web interface rather than human-like comprehension. However, targeted engineering fixes—such as obfuscating DOM metadata and reducing predictable encodings—can meaningfully harden surveys against such automated attacks. The authors argue for closer collaboration between survey methodologists and agentic AI researchers, so that survey platforms can remain reliable for empirical research while still supporting safe and informative experimentation with autonomous AI agents.

Abstract: Online surveys are a foundational data collection instrument in a variety of fields, with attention checks serving as critical guardians of response quality. However, the rapid emergence of agentic AI (goal directed systems powered by a large language model (LLM) brain and/or a multimodal processing unit with tool-augmented capabilities) raises new questions about the robustness of these safeguards. We investigate how well agentic AI architectures can complete web-based surveys and pass standard attention checks. We evaluate a single-agent architecture capable of multimodal input processing and tool-based web interaction on a controlled survey sandbox. We analyze the problem from two perspectives. From an attack perspective, we demonstrate how structural vulnerabilities such as exposed DOM metadata and predictable option encoding allow agents to resolve attention checks through structured parsing only. From a defense perspective, we implement a mitigation strategy of DOM metadata obfuscation to remove semantic cues in text-based questions. We evaluate multiple open-source language and multimodal models to study capability and orchestration effectiveness. Based on our evaluations, we offer perspectives on how to simultaneously meet the needs of empiricists and agentic AI researchers.

</details>


### [232] [CDPR: Counterfactual Advantage-based Credit Assignment for Cost-Aware Sequential Medical Diagnosis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.28599)
*Qi Peng,Yi Cai,Changmeng Zheng,Xin Wu,Jiayuan Xie,Qing Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes CDPR, a reinforcement-learning-based framework that teaches medical language models to order diagnostic tests sequentially while balancing diagnostic accuracy and test cost, improving efficiency without needing expert labels or a learned critic.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing medical language models typically treat diagnosis as a one-shot classification problem and ignore how physicians actually work: ordering tests sequentially, observing outcomes, and trading off diagnostic value against test cost and feasibility. Standard RL approaches struggle in this setting because the only reliable supervision is a final outcome signal, which cannot distinguish between efficient and wasteful test sequences that end in the same diagnosis. The authors want a method that can shape rewards to favor efficient diagnostic processes, without relying on expensive expert annotations or unstable learned critics, and that can generalize across in-domain and out-of-domain clinical datasets.

Method: The authors model clinical diagnosis as a cost-aware sequential decision process where each action is an ordered diagnostic test and its outcome updates the patient state. They train a policy with reinforcement learning, introducing CDPR (Counterfactual Diagnostic Process Reward) as a novel reward shaping mechanism. CDPR identifies timesteps where the policy is uncertain (i.e., hesitates) based on the entropy or spread of its action distribution. At these states, it performs short counterfactual rollouts for the action actually taken and for alternative plausible actions the policy would consider. Each rollout is evaluated with a utility function that jointly rewards diagnostic correctness and penalizes excessive test count, monetary cost, and infeasible exam requests. The advantage of the chosen action over its alternatives defines a local reward used to guide learning. To make this efficient, a rollout cache reuses within-batch trajectories so that many counterfactual estimates can be obtained at low extra cost. CDPR is integrated into a GRPO-style optimization framework for training the policy.

Result: On three benchmarks—a large in-domain MIMIC-IV dataset and two out-of-domain datasets (ClinicalBench and a private hospital dataset)—the CDPR-augmented RL policy achieves higher diagnostic accuracy while simultaneously reducing both the number and total cost of ordered tests, compared with baseline methods that lack CDPR. The method also avoids the need for expert-labeled intermediate rewards or a separate learned critic, yet still provides effective credit assignment for individual test-ordering decisions.

Conclusion: The paper concludes that modeling diagnosis as a cost-aware sequential decision problem and shaping rewards with CDPR yields more clinically realistic and efficient diagnostic policies than one-shot classifiers or standard RL baselines. By leveraging the policy’s own uncertainty and short counterfactual rollouts under a utility that explicitly encodes accuracy–cost trade-offs, CDPR provides fine-grained credit assignment without expert labels or a critic network. This leads to better generalization across datasets and demonstrates a practical path toward training medical language models that not only predict correct diagnoses but also learn to order necessary and cost-effective tests in a stepwise manner.

Abstract: Clinical diagnosis is a step-by-step, cost-aware process: a physician orders examinations one at a time, observes the results, and updates the diagnosis before reaching a final conclusion. Most medical language models instead treat diagnosis as a one-pass classification task and ignore the trade-off between a test's value and its cost. We model diagnosis as a cost-aware sequential decision process and train the policy with reinforcement learning. The main difficulty is credit assignment: the only reliable signal comes once at the end of a long trajectory, so it scores a wasteful workup the same as an efficient one. We propose CDPR (Counterfactual Diagnostic Process Reward), which needs no expert labels and no learned critic. CDPR first finds the states where the policy hesitates, using the uncertainty of its action distribution, and then scores the chosen action by its advantage over the alternatives the policy itself would consider, estimated with short rollouts under a utility that balances correctness against test count, cost, and infeasible requests. A rollout cache reuses within-batch trajectories to keep the cost low. We integrate CDPR into GRPO and test it on one in-domain (MIMIC-IV) and two out-of-domain (ClinicalBench and a private hospital dataset) benchmarks. CDPR improves diagnostic accuracy while clearly reducing the number and cost of examinations.

</details>


### [233] [SHAPE of Chain-of-Thought in Math Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.28600)
*Jonghyun Song,Sangjun Song,Minjae Oh,Haesung Pyun,Sungsik Lee,Yohan Jo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper presents SHAPE, a framework to analyze and improve LLMs’ mathematical reasoning by categorizing their chain-of-thought into semantic spaces and heuristics, and shows that promoting diverse, human-like heuristic use improves math accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Although LLMs perform well on math benchmarks, we lack a clear understanding of the underlying, mathematically meaningful reasoning skills they use. Existing evaluations rely on surface-level CoT features (e.g., length) and final accuracy, which do not reveal whether models reason in a human-like, principled way. The authors want a diagnostic lens grounded in mathematics education research to characterize LLM reasoning processes and to guide more targeted post-training for math proficiency.

Method: The authors introduce SHAPE, a framework that decomposes a model’s chain-of-thought into: (1) semantic spaces, representing the type of mathematical interpretation or representation used (e.g., algebraic, geometric), and (2) heuristics, representing specific problem-solving actions within those spaces (e.g., simplifying, working backward). They apply SHAPE to CoT trajectories generated by different LLMs on math problems, then analyze how semantic-space usage and heuristic patterns correlate with correctness. They further study how post-training, especially reinforcement learning, changes heuristic usage (e.g., whether it becomes more mode-seeking). Finally, they perform post-training that explicitly encourages diverse heuristic use and evaluate its effect on math-reasoning accuracy.

Result: Analyses show that the types and patterns of mathematical heuristics used by models are more predictive of answer correctness than traditional CoT metrics like length or token counts. Successful reasoning typically involves focusing effort within a small number of coherent semantic spaces rather than switching among many, mirroring human problem-solving behavior. The authors find that reinforcement-learning-based post-training tends to induce mode-seeking in heuristic usage, meaning models over-rely on a narrower set of heuristics. When they instead post-train LLMs with objectives that promote diversity in heuristic usage, the models achieve improved accuracy on math reasoning tasks.

Conclusion: SHAPE offers a theoretically grounded framework, inspired by mathematics education, to interpret and evaluate LLMs’ mathematical reasoning beyond final accuracy and superficial CoT statistics. By framing reasoning in terms of semantic spaces and heuristics, it becomes possible to diagnose how models solve problems and how post-training changes these processes. Encouraging diverse, human-like heuristic use during post-training improves math performance, suggesting SHAPE is both a diagnostic tool and a practical avenue for building stronger math-reasoning LLMs.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) achieve strong performance on mathematical reasoning benchmarks, yet the mathematically meaningful skills underlying their reasoning remain underexplored. We introduce \texttt{SHAPE}, a framework that analyzes Chain-of-Thought (CoT) trajectories through two lenses developed in mathematics education: (1) semantic spaces: the model's evolving mathematical interpretations of a problem (e.g., algebraic, geometric), and (2) heuristics: the specific mathematical actions taken within those spaces (e.g., simplifying the problem, working backward). We first use \texttt{SHAPE} to analyze the reasoning patterns of various models. Our findings reveal that the mathematical heuristics employed by a model better explain final answer correctness than traditional CoT features. Furthermore, models are likely to reach correct solutions by concentrating their reasoning effort within a few semantic spaces rather than exploring many disparate ones -- a pattern consistent with human behavior. Next, we utilize the \texttt{SHAPE} lens to evaluate whether post-training truly enhances mathematical proficiency. We find that reinforcement learning induces mode-seeking in heuristic usage. Lastly, we post-train LLMs by promoting diverse heuristics and demonstrate its effectiveness in improving accuracy. Overall, \texttt{SHAPE} provides a theoretically-grounded diagnostic framework for decoding LLM reasoning and offers a new path toward post-training LLMs for math reasoning. The code for our model is available at https://github.com/holi-lab/SHAPE-of-CoT

</details>


### [234] [Leveraging Generative AI to Design Accessible Interactive Visualizations for Undergraduate Mathematics: A Six-Phase Workflow](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.28601)
*Mahesh Sunkula,Kuan-Hua Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper presents and evaluates a structured, six-phase, AI-assisted workflow that lets mathematics instructors create accessible, interactive visualizations without programming, while emphasizing that human verification is essential at every step.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Many undergraduate mathematics instructors want interactive visualizations to improve students’ conceptual understanding, but lack the programming skills needed to build such tools, especially ones that meet modern accessibility standards (e.g., WCAG 2.2 AA). At the same time, generative AI can write code but tends to be unreliable and inaccessible unless carefully guided. The authors are motivated to design a systematic workflow that harnesses generative AI for code generation while ensuring mathematical correctness, accessibility, and pedagogical quality, so that non-programmer instructors and students can reliably create and adapt visualizations.

Method: The authors use a design-based research methodology: iteratively designing, deploying, and refining a six-phase prompt-and-check workflow for generative-AI-based tool creation. The phases are Foundation, Customization, Mathematical Depth, Application, Accessibility, and Pedagogical Control. Each phase structures the prompts given to the AI, scaffolds how code is generated or modified, and explicitly marks where and how humans must verify outputs before proceeding. They test the workflow both ‘forward’ (starting from a plain-language idea and generating a tool) and ‘backward’ (reconstructing prompts from an existing tool). They deploy four interactive tools spanning calculus, multivariable calculus, and differential equations, and evaluate (1) mathematical correctness by comparing to known closed-form results, (2) accessibility using automated checkers and manual screen-reader testing, and (3) patterns in the errors that occur across phases.

Result: The six-phase workflow reliably produces first-pass interactive visualizations that are structurally complete and implement the requested features, and can be applied both forward and backward. The resulting tools achieve WCAG 2.2 Level AA compliance when the accessibility phase is properly executed and verified. However, across all four deployed tools, errors still appear: mathematical inaccuracies, accessibility shortcomings, and pedagogical mismatches recur unless humans systematically review and correct the AI’s outputs at each phase. The study identifies recurring error types and phase-specific verification needs, showing that the workflow makes errors more predictable and manageable but does not eliminate them.

Conclusion: The paper concludes that generative AI can substantially lower the barrier for creating accessible, interactive mathematical visualizations for undergraduate courses, provided that its use is organized through a structured, phase-based workflow with mandatory human verification at every step. The proposed six-phase workflow is platform-independent, works for both instructors and students, and supports both the creation of new tools and the analysis or adaptation of existing ones. Nonetheless, AI cannot yet replace human expertise: instructors must still check for mathematical validity, accessibility, and pedagogical alignment in each phase before advancing, so the workflow should be seen as a collaboration framework between humans and AI rather than an automated solution.

Abstract: Interactive visualizations support conceptual understanding in undergraduate mathematics, but building them has required programming expertise most instructors lack. Using a design-based research approach, we develop, deploy, and evaluate a six-phase workflow (Foundation, Customization, Mathematical Depth, Application, Accessibility, Pedagogical Control) that uses generative AI to build WCAG~2.2 Level~AA compliant visualizations without programming. The six phases structure every prompt, scaffold the AI's code generation, and define where human verification is applied. We ask whether the structure reliably yields correct and accessible tools, whether it runs both backward (reverse-engineering prompts from a finished tool) and forward (generating a tool from a plain-language idea), and what verification each phase requires. Across four deployed tools spanning calculus, multivariable calculus, and differential equations, we evaluate mathematical correctness against closed forms, accessibility through automated and manual screen-reader testing, and the errors that recurred. The structure produces structurally complete first-pass tools, but human verification remains mandatory at every phase: each output must be checked for mathematical correctness, accessibility, and pedagogical fit before the next phase begins. The workflow is platform-independent and serves both instructors and students.

</details>


### [235] [Integrating Triaxial IMU Sensors and Ensemble Learning for Effective Parkinson Disease Severity Classification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.28602)
*Rehan Khan,Muhammad Junaid Asif,Rana Fayyaz Ahmad*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper compares multiple machine‑learning classifiers on IMU-based motion and tremor data to detect and grade Parkinson’s disease, finding LightGBM performs best with ~97% accuracy and related metrics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Parkinson’s disease causes motor symptoms that significantly impair quality of life, and early, accurate detection is key for timely treatment and disease management. Traditional diagnosis relies heavily on clinical examination, which can miss subtle motor deficits and is not easily scalable for continuous monitoring. The rapid development of wearable sensors and AI provides an opportunity to create noninvasive, objective, and data-driven methods for PD detection and severity assessment.

Method: The authors collect motion and tremor data from an inertial measurement unit (IMU), specifically accelerometer and gyroscope signals in three axes (X, Y, Z). They extract features from these multi-axis signals that capture motor patterns and subtle tremor characteristics associated with PD. Several supervised machine learning classifiers are then trained and evaluated on this dataset: Logistic Regression, K-Nearest Neighbors, Support Vector Machine, Decision Tree, Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), and Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LightGBM). Model performance is compared using standard evaluation metrics including Accuracy, Precision, Recall, and F1-score to determine which algorithm is most effective for PD classification and severity prediction.

Result: Among the tested models, Logistic Regression achieves about 75% performance across metrics, KNN around 90%, SVM about 94%, and Decision Tree and XGBoost close to 96% classification performance. LightGBM outperforms all other methods, achieving about 97% on Accuracy, Precision, Recall, and F1-score, and ranks consistently as the best classifier across evaluations. These results indicate that tree-based ensemble methods, particularly LightGBM, are better suited to capturing the complex patterns in IMU-derived motion data for PD detection and grading.

Conclusion: The study concludes that IMU-based motion and tremor data, analyzed with machine learning classifiers, can provide an accurate, noninvasive method for detecting Parkinson’s disease and assessing its severity. Among the evaluated models, LightGBM delivers the best and most consistent performance, suggesting that gradient-boosting ensembles are well suited for this application. The approach demonstrates strong predictive capability and supports the feasibility of wearable, AI-driven tools for objective PD screening and monitoring in clinical or real-world settings.

Abstract: Parkinson disease PD is a progressive neurodegenerative disease that can have a significant impact on motor performance resulting in the appearance of symptoms such as tremors rigidity postural instabilities and bradykinesia. Timely clinical treatment disease management and quality life of the patients are closely linked to early and appropriate identification of PD. Over the past few years the growth of wearable sensor technology and artificial intelligence AI have made it possible to create noninvasive and data driven disease detection methods. This paper proposes a comparative system using artificial intelligence to detect Parkinsons disease by analyzing the motion and tremor data captured by an inertial measurement unit IMU. The data comprises the signals of the acceleration and gyroscope sensors measuring movement in three directions X Y and Z. The signs and symptoms provide helpful information about subtle motor deficits associated with PD. Several classification models like Support Vector Machine SVM Logistic Regression LR KNearest Neighbors KNN Decision Tree DT Extreme Gradient Boosting XGBoost and Light Gradient Boosting Machine LightGBM were used to compare their effectiveness. The Logistic Regression model had a performance around 75 percent in all evaluation metrics and KNearest Neighbours KNN around 90 percent. The support vector machine SVM performed almost 94 percent whereas the performance of classifiers such as Decision Tree and XGBoost was close to 96 percent and overall classification efficacy respectively. LightGBM model performs consistently at the best rank among all of the evaluated methods having Accuracy, Precision, Recall and F1score of around 97 percent. The results show that the proposed machine learning approach offers an accurate and effective predictive capability in the classification of PD severity.

</details>


### [236] [C3-UniMM: Causal Cycle-Consistent Unified Multimodal Modeling via Super Alignment and Shared Decoding Space](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.28603)
*Yujie Shen,Lianlei Shan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A causal-consistency-based unified multimodal model (C3-UniMM) that shares a structured latent causal graph across modalities to improve any-to-any understanding and generation, boosting semantic consistency and robustness over prior unified multimodal baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing unified multimodal models try to support any-to-any understanding and generation (e.g., text↔image, audio↔video), but they mainly learn implicit correlations without enforcing a shared, structured, causal semantic space. This causes semantic drift, weak compositional generalization, and instability when inputs are intervened on or perturbed. The paper is motivated by the need for a principled, causally grounded way to align modalities so that cross-modal mappings are invertible, structurally consistent, and robust across tasks.

Method: The authors propose C3-UniMM, a unified multimodal framework built on two main ideas: Causal Cycle Consistency and Super Alignment. They introduce a Structured Latent Causal Graph (SLCG) that serves as a shared, structured semantic space across all modalities. Unified multimodal encoders map each modality into this SLCG so that understanding and generation are optimized within the same causal structure. They then define a Unified Decoding Space that decodes from the SLCG back to each modality while enforcing structural preservation and semantic invertibility. Training objectives incorporate causal cycle consistency and alignment constraints to encourage invertible and mechanism-invariant cross-modal mappings, supported by theoretical analysis.

Result: On multiple benchmarks spanning multimodal understanding, generation, and especially compositional generalization tasks, C3-UniMM consistently outperforms prior unified multimodal baselines. Quantitatively, it shows better performance metrics (e.g., accuracy, quality scores) and qualitatively produces more semantically faithful and compositionally robust outputs under interventions or perturbations. Theoretical results further support that the method improves invertibility and mechanism invariance compared with previous correlation-based unified models.

Conclusion: By grounding unified multimodal learning in a shared Structured Latent Causal Graph and enforcing causal cycle consistency and a unified decoding space, C3-UniMM achieves more semantically consistent, invertible, and robust cross-modal mappings than previous unified multimodal approaches. The framework demonstrates that introducing explicit causal and structural consistency constraints into unified multimodal models is an effective way to improve any-to-any understanding, generation, and compositional generalization, suggesting a promising direction for future multimodal foundation models.

Abstract: Unified Multimodal Models aim to achieve any-to-any understanding and generation across arbitrary modalities. However, existing methods primarily rely on modeling implicit statistical correlations and lack cross-modal structural consistency constraints. This deficiency leads to profound issues, including semantic drift, poor compositional generalization, and instability under interventions. In this paper, we propose C3-UniMM, a unified multimodal modeling framework based on Causal Cycle Consistency and Super Alignment. Specifically, we introduce a Structured Latent Causal Graph (SLCG) as a shared cross-modal semantic space and design unified multimodal encoding blocks, enabling understanding and generation to be synergistically optimized within the identical causal semantic structure. Furthermore, we propose a Unified Decoding Space to enforce structural preservation and semantic invertibility during the cross-modal generation process. Theoretical analyses demonstrate that our approach significantly enhances both the invertibility and mechanism invariance of cross-modal mappings. Extensive experimental results across multiple understanding, generation, and compositional generalization tasks indicate that C3-UniMM substantially outperforms existing unified multimodal baselines.

</details>


### [237] [MedTVL: Harnessing Vision and Language for Medical Time Series Classification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.28605)
*Jiexia Ye,Jia Li,Fugee Tsung*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MedTVL is a tri-modal (time series, image, text) architecture for medical time series classification that uses dual temporal/visual pathways, text guidance, Mixture-of-Experts fusion, and multimodal contrastive learning to improve performance and transferability under diverse supervision regimes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Most existing multimodal methods for medical time series classification use only two modalities, typically time series and text, neglecting the potential diagnostic synergy among time series, vision, and language. Moreover, they often rely on a single architectural style and struggle with label scarcity and varying instance-specific reliance on different modalities. There is a need for a framework that better mimics clinical diagnostic practice—combining numerical trends, visual morphology, and textual context—while being robust under limited labels and capable of adapting to different patients and tasks.

Method: The authors propose MedTVL, a text-guided dual-pathway multimodal architecture. One pathway is convolution-based, operating on raw numerical time series to extract fine-grained temporal dynamics. The other is transformer-based, processing images derived from the time series to capture holistic morphological patterns. Both pathways are conditioned on adaptive medical textual semantics that guide representation learning. Their outputs are fed into a Mixture-of-Experts fusion module that dynamically routes each instance to different fusion experts, modeling instance-specific reliance on temporal vs. visual information. The framework is further equipped with multimodal contrastive learning across time series, images, and text to improve representation quality under label-scarce conditions.

Result: Across multiple medical datasets and tasks, and under supervised, few-shot, and contrastive-learning-based evaluation settings, MedTVL consistently outperforms prior baselines. The experiments show improved accuracy and better transferability of learned representations when moving across tasks or data regimes, confirming the benefit of tri-modal integration, text guidance, and Mixture-of-Experts fusion.

Conclusion: MedTVL effectively operationalizes tri-modal synergy among time series, images, and text for medical time series classification. By combining heterogeneous temporal and visual pathways under text guidance and adaptive Mixture-of-Experts fusion, it yields more robust and transferable representations, particularly helpful when labels are scarce. The framework demonstrates strong potential as a general and practical tool for clinical decision support across diverse medical time series applications.

Abstract: Recent advancements in multimodal learning for medical time series (MedTS) classification highlight the benefits of integrating complementary modalities for clinical decision. However, existing methods typically focus on bi-modal interactions (e.g., time series and text), leaving the tri-modal synergy between time series, vision, and language largely unexplored. Inspired by diagnostic practice synergizing numerical assessment, visual inspection and clinical context, we introduce MedTVL, a text-guided dual-pathway architecture tailored for MedTS classification. Specifically, it synergizes a convolution-based temporal pathway for fine-grained temporal dynamics from raw numerical sequences and a transformer-based visual pathway for holistic morphological structures from time-series-derived images. Such combination of cross-modal and architectural heterogeneity provides a comprehensive diagnostic perspective. To further resolve potential diagnostic ambiguity, both pathways are guided by adaptive medical textual semantics. Finally, a Mixture-of-Experts mechanism dynamically routes each instance to specialized fusion experts, capturing instance-specific reliance on the temporal and visual pathway outputs. In addition, MedTVL supports multimodal contrastive learning to mitigate the clinical label scarcity challenge. Extensive experiments across multiple medical datasets and tasks, spanning supervised, few-shot, and contrastive learning settings, demonstrate the superiority and transferability of MedTVL, highlighting its potential for robust clinical decision support.

</details>


### [238] [RegDivergence-101: An LLM Benchmark for Cross-Jurisdiction Regulatory Contradiction Detection in Life Sciences](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.28607)
*Chuchu Wu,Zhiyin Zhou,Jingzhuo Hu,Liang You*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper defines and pilots a new NLP task: automatically detecting when US FDA and EU EMA regulatory requirements agree, diverge, or when one is silent relative to the other, and releases a small benchmark plus baseline methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Drug developers operating in both the US and EU must reconcile separate regulatory guidances from FDA and EMA. Currently, experts manually compare documents to see where requirements align, conflict, or where one regulator is silent, which is slow, expensive, and error-prone. There is no standard automated or benchmarked method for this cross-jurisdiction comparison, especially for detecting one-sided silence, despite its practical impact on trial design and regulatory risk. The paper aims to formalize this comparison as an NLP task and to provide data and baselines to stimulate research and standardization.

Method: The authors define the task of cross-jurisdiction regulatory divergence detection: given a pair of requirements (one from FDA, one from EMA) on the same topic, classify the pair into AGREE, DIVERGE, or SILENT, with SILENT being directional (SILENT_FDA vs. SILENT_EMA). They construct RegDivergence-101, a benchmark of 101 requirement pairs grounded in three peer-reviewed FDA/EMA comparison studies and primary FDA/EMA/ICH guidance documents, annotated by two experts with substantial agreement (kappa=0.85). They evaluate a baseline hierarchy of four methods: (1) a simple lexical heuristic, (2) a standard NLI cross-encoder, (3) a Graph-RAG approach that builds obligation-level graphs over documents, and (4) a flat LLM-judge system based on Claude Haiku. Performance is measured with macro-F1, including per-direction F1 for SILENT, and confidence intervals by bootstrap or similar methods.

Result: On RegDivergence-101, the lexical heuristic achieves macro-F1 of 0.511 (95% CI [0.411-0.605]); the NLI cross-encoder performs poorly at 0.233; the obligation-level Graph-RAG approach improves to 0.663 (95% CI [0.570-0.747]); and the flat LLM-judge with Claude Haiku performs best with macro-F1 of 0.830 (95% CI [0.747-0.908]). Analysis of the results yields three findings: (1) SILENT relations are semantically detectable but are missed by entailment-only NLI formulations; (2) modeling obligation graphs at the pair level beats lexical heuristics but still underperforms a strong flat LLM with broader context (confidence intervals partially overlap); and (3) for scaling silent-detection, building corpus-level obligation graphs appears to be the right architectural direction.

Conclusion: The paper establishes cross-jurisdiction regulatory divergence detection as a concrete NLP task and provides an initial benchmark, RegDivergence-101, along with a hierarchy of baseline methods spanning lexical, NLI, graph-based RAG, and LLM-judge approaches. Results indicate that current entailment models are inadequate for detecting directional silence, that structured obligation graphs help but are not yet competitive with strong LLMs, and that future work should target corpus-level graph architectures for scalable detection of regulatory silence. The benchmark is explicitly positioned as a pilot, with additional regulatory domains and an expansion roadmap outlined for future dataset growth and methodological development.

Abstract: Pharmaceutical sponsors developing a drug for both the United States and the European Union must reconcile guidance issued independently by the FDA and the EMA. Where the two agencies require substantively the same thing, a sponsor can file once; where they diverge, a single trial design risks rejection in one region; where one agency is silent on a point the other regulates, the sponsor must infer obligations. Today this reconciliation is performed manually by regulatory-affairs experts. We introduce cross-jurisdiction regulatory divergence detection: given an FDA requirement and an EMA requirement on the same topic, classify their relationship as AGREE, DIVERGE, or SILENT. SILENT is inherently directional (SILENT_FDA vs. SILENT_EMA); we record direction per pair and report per-direction F1 alongside the collapsed label. We release RegDivergence-101, a 101-pair expert-grounded pilot evaluation benchmark (labels grounded in three peer-reviewed FDA/EMA comparison studies and primary FDA/EMA/ICH guidance text; dual-annotation inter-annotator kappa = 0.85), and systematically characterise a four-method baseline hierarchy: lexical heuristic (0.511 macro-F1, 95% CI [0.411-0.605]), NLI cross-encoder (0.233), obligation-level Graph-RAG (0.663 [0.570-0.747]), and flat LLM judge / Claude Haiku (0.830 [0.747-0.908]). Three directional observations emerge at pilot scale (n = 101): SILENT is semantically detectable but invisible to entailment-only formulations; pair-level obligation graphs improve over lexical methods but trail flat-LLM context (CIs partially overlapping); and corpus-level graph construction is the indicated architectural target for large-scale silent-detection. RegDivergence-101 is a pilot release establishing the task formulation and baseline hierarchy; four unrepresented regulatory domains and an expansion roadmap are described in Section 7.

</details>


### [239] [TPvG: A Moral Decision Framework for Large Language Models from One-Shot to Sequential Feedback](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.28610)
*Fangyuan Zhang,Dong Yu,Pengyuan Liu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces TPvG, a moral evaluation framework for LLMs that incorporates consequence feedback in a pain-versus-gain dilemma, revealing that LLM moral choices change substantially with decision format and differ from human patterns.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current LLM moral benchmarks mostly use isolated, one-shot moral vignettes, ignoring consequence feedback that is known to shape human moral behavior. The authors aim to close this gap by creating a more ecologically valid evaluation paradigm that mimics how humans learn from the outcomes of their moral decisions, especially in everyday dilemmas involving harm versus self-benefit.

Method: The authors adapt a human moral psychology paradigm called Text-based Pain-versus-Gain (TPvG) for LLMs. TPvG consists of five tasks that range from simple, low-context one-shot decisions to more complex sequential decisions where models receive explicit feedback about the consequences of their choices on others. Multiple LLMs are evaluated across these tasks to see how decision format and feedback affect moral choices, and model behavior is compared to human reference patterns.

Result: LLMs’ moral decisions were highly sensitive to whether choices were presented as isolated one-shot problems or as sequential interactions. Adding explicit feedback from the harmed receiver had varied, model-dependent effects on behavior. Across models, the patterns of response to consequence feedback deviated from those observed in humans, indicating that LLMs may be using different underlying decision processes.

Conclusion: Moral behavior in LLMs is not stable across interaction formats and can shift markedly when consequence feedback is introduced. Because this behavior also diverges from human patterns, standard one-shot vignette benchmarks are insufficient to understand how LLMs might act in more realistic, high-stakes, interactive scenarios. The paper argues that future evaluation and alignment work should explicitly test LLMs in dynamic settings with feedback about the impact of their actions.

Abstract: Existing LLM moral evaluations typically present models with isolated moral vignettes and elicit a single-shot decision, neglecting a factor known to profoundly influence human moral behavior: consequence feedback. We introduce TPvG (Text-based Pain-versus-Gain), adapted from a human moral paradigm, which embeds consequence feedback into an everyday moral dilemma of not harming others versus maximising self-gain. TPvG comprises five moral decision tasks, progressing from minimal-context one-shot choices to sequential decisions with explicit consequence feedback. Our results show that LLM moral decisions were strongly affected by decision format (one-shot versus sequential), and explicit receiver feedback produced heterogeneous effects across models. Furthermore, LLM responses to explicit receiver feedback diverged from the human reference pattern, suggesting potentially different decision processes. These findings highlight the need to evaluate whether LLM moral behavior remains stable in high-stakes interactive settings.

</details>


### [240] [InternReviewer & InternAdvocate: Objective Reward and Evaluation for Agentic Reinforcement Learning in Peer Review and Rebuttal](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.28612)
*Xuerui Su,Liya Guo,Qizhi Pei,Qipeng Guo,Zhongbo Tian,Lijun Wu,Kai Chen,Zun Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces a framework for building and evaluating scholarly AI agents for peer review and rebuttal writing, emphasizing factual grounding and domain reasoning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To improve the quality, reliability, and factual grounding of AI systems that assist with professional scholarly tasks like peer reviewing and rebuttal writing, addressing issues such as shallow reasoning, hallucinated citations, and subjective evaluation methods.

Method: They construct a large-scale, high-quality scholarly dataset and integrate an efficient arXiv retrieval tool for evidence gathering. They then train specialized agents, InternReviewer and InternAdvocate, using an agentic reinforcement learning paradigm that optimizes a unified metric and reward system based on multi-dimensional evaluation criteria: semantic alignment to references, structural compliance with expected formats, and a citation verification mechanism that checks all references against interaction logs to avoid hallucinations.

Result: Agents trained in this closed-loop RL framework achieve better reasoning depth and much more accurate citations compared to baselines or earlier versions without this setup.

Conclusion: A closed-loop, evidence-driven RL framework with robust, multi-criteria reward design can substantially enhance the reasoning quality and factual reliability of scholarly AI agents for tasks such as peer review and rebuttal generation.

Abstract: Generating professional scholarly content, such as peer reviews and rebuttals, requires an intricate synergy between domain reasoning and factual grounding. This work presents a comprehensive framework for the development and evaluation of specialized scholarly agents, InternReviewer and InternAdvocate. We first establish a large-scale, high-quality scholarly dataset and integrate a high-efficiency arXiv retrieval tool to enable active evidence gathering. To optimize these agents, we implement an agentic Reinforcement Learning (RL) paradigm driven by a unified objective metric and reward system. This system avoids the biases of subjective model-based judging by employing multi-dimensional criteria, including reference-anchored semantic alignment, structural compliance, and a strict verification mechanism that cross-checks citations against real-time interaction logs to eliminate hallucinations. Experimental results demonstrate that agents trained within this closed-loop framework exhibit significant improvements in reasoning depth and citation accuracy.

</details>


### [241] [Preference Elicitation for Policy Optimization and Application to Aligning Heart Transplantation with Human Values](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.28620)
*Itai Zilberstein,Ioannis Anagnostides,Zachary W Sollie,Arman Kilic,Tuomas Sandholm*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes a new preference-elicitation algorithm that directly learns a community-aligned utility function over allocation outcomes (rather than over individual decisions) and applies it to heart transplant policy, achieving policies much closer to the hindsight optimum than the current status quo.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing AI alignment and resource-allocation methods typically ask people to compare specific algorithmic decisions (e.g., which patient gets an organ), which mixes up policy mechanics with true values and can misrepresent stakeholder preferences. There is a need for a principled way to elicit preferences directly over multi-objective allocation outcomes and to turn those into utility functions that can guide policy optimization, especially in high-stakes settings like organ allocation.

Method: The authors assume utilities are linear over outcome attributes and design a two-phase preference elicitation algorithm. In Phase 1, they ask users pairwise comparison questions about allocation outcomes to generate cutting planes that quickly shrink the feasible set of attribute weights, eliminating dominated regions and warm-starting the search. In Phase 2, starting from this reduced space, they use a provably convergent procedure to recover the user’s underlying utility function. They then aggregate elicited utilities from multiple stakeholders to obtain a community-aligned utility and use it as the objective in a policy optimization problem for heart transplant allocation.

Result: The proposed two-phase algorithm empirically outperforms existing preference elicitation techniques for linear utilities. In the heart transplant case study, user studies show that the method can learn and aggregate a community-aligned utility function reflecting trade-offs between post-transplant outcomes, waitlist mortality, geographic considerations, and equity. When optimizing policies under this learned utility, the resulting heart allocation policies are much better value-aligned than the current status quo: the existing policy attains a competitive ratio of about 0.54 relative to the hindsight-optimal policy, whereas policies derived via the new method achieve about 0.95, nearly closing the optimality gap.

Conclusion: Directly eliciting preferences over allocation outcomes and using a structured, two-phase cutting-plane-based algorithm to learn linear utility functions yields significantly better-aligned and near-optimal allocation policies compared with current decision-level preference methods. In high-stakes domains like heart transplant allocation, this approach can reveal substantial misalignment in existing policies and enable the design of policies that more faithfully capture stakeholder values.

Abstract: Preference elicitation is essential for aligning AI systems with human values. Prior approaches (e.g., for organ allocation) often ask stakeholders to compare the decisions of an algorithm (e.g., patient A vs. patient B). Such a decision-level approach conflates the means with the ends. Instead, we elicit preferences directly over allocation outcomes to learn a utility function for policy optimization. We construct a novel preference elicitation algorithm for linear utilities that outperforms prior techniques in practice. Our algorithm has two phases. The first phase learns cutting planes through pairwise comparisons to rapidly shrink the space of possible attribute weights and warm-starts the second phase by eliminating dominated regions. The second phase then provably converges to the user's utility function. We apply our technique to heart transplant allocation where a policy must balance competing objectives such as post-transplant outcomes, waitlist mortality, geographic ease, and equity. Using our algorithm, we conduct a user study to learn and aggregate a community-aligned utility function, and use it to optimize heart transplant policies that are significantly better aligned with human values. Compared to the hindsight optimum, the status quo policy achieves a competitive ratio of just 0.54, while our method is near-optimal with a competitive ratio of 0.95.

</details>


### [242] [Machine Learning-Enhanced Tabu Search for Tactical Wireless Network Design](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.28627)
*Wissem Ahmed Zaid,Alain Hertz,Defeng Liu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They speed up Tabu Search for designing tactical wireless networks by using a GNN trained on past search trajectories to predict which moves are promising, cutting evaluations while improving solution quality.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Tactical wireless network design involves large, complex combinatorial optimization problems whose accurate evaluation requires expensive physical and traffic-aware simulations. Standard metaheuristics like Tabu Search can handle the large search spaces but remain computationally heavy, since many candidate moves must be fully evaluated each iteration. There is a need to make this search more efficient without sacrificing solution quality, especially for large-scale, realistic network design instances.

Method: They record the full search trajectories of a standard Tabu Search on network design problems, logging both improving and non-improving edge-based moves along with engineered features that describe structural, geometric, and performance aspects of the network and moves. Using this data, they train a Graph Neural Network to predict the effect of a candidate move on the objective function. The trained GNN is then embedded into the Tabu Search: at each iteration it ranks candidate moves based on predicted quality so that only a subset of the most promising moves require expensive exact evaluation. The neighborhood structure of Tabu Search is not altered; only the evaluation order and filtering are guided by the learned model.

Result: On synthetic benchmark network design instances, the learning-assisted Tabu Search significantly reduces the total computation time compared with the standard Tabu Search, thanks to fewer objective evaluations. At the same time, it consistently finds solutions of higher or at least comparable quality, demonstrating that the GNN-guided ranking preserves or enhances search effectiveness while improving efficiency.

Conclusion: Leveraging data from search trajectories to train a GNN predictor and integrate it into Tabu Search is an effective way to accelerate combinatorial optimization for tactical wireless network design. This learning-assisted metaheuristic reduces computational cost and improves solution quality without changing the underlying move set, suggesting a promising general paradigm for combining machine learning with classical metaheuristics in large-scale network design and related optimization problems.

Abstract: Designing high-performance tactical wireless networks under realistic operational constraints gives rise to challenging combinatorial optimization problems, where the evaluation of candidate solutions relies on detailed physical and traffic-aware models. Although classical metaheuristics such as Tabu Search offer effective mechanisms for exploring large search spaces, their computational cost remains high because numerous candidate moves must be evaluated at every iteration. In this paper, we propose a data-driven framework that improves the efficiency of Tabu Search by learning to guide its move selection process. Rather than altering the neighborhood structure, our approach exploits the information contained in the search trajectories generated during the optimization process. At each iteration, we record both improving and non-improving edge-based transformations together with a set of descriptive features capturing the structural, geometric, and performance characteristics of the network. This information is used to train a Graph Neural Network (GNN) that predicts the impact of candidate moves on the objective function. The trained model is then integrated into the Tabu Search algorithm to rank candidate transformations according to their predicted quality, thereby reducing the number of costly objective evaluations while maintaining an effective exploration of the search space. Experimental results on synthetic benchmark instances demonstrate that the proposed learning-assisted Tabu Search notably reduces computation time while consistently producing higher-quality solutions than the standard algorithm. These findings highlight the potential of combining machine learning with metaheuristics by leveraging the implicit knowledge embedded in search trajectories, paving the way for more efficient solution methods for large-scale network design problems.

</details>


### [243] [CDEP Agent: Connecting Meteorologically Detected Temporal Compound Events to Real-World Documentary Evidence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.28628)
*Zhuoran Li,Weiyi Kong,Boer Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces CDEP Agent, a large-language-model-based framework that links meteorologically detected compound drought-to-extreme-precipitation (CDEP) events with real-world impact records, revealing that most such events are weakly or not at all documented, especially in terms of their compound nature.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Although compound drought-to-extreme-precipitation events are increasingly recognized in climate science as impactful, it is unclear whether they are anticipated in early warning systems or documented in post-event reports. This gap means physically significant CDEP events may occur without warning or lasting record, limiting learning, risk assessment, and policy responses. The authors aim to quantify this mismatch and provide a systematic, auditable way to connect physical event definitions with real-world evidence across heterogeneous data sources.

Method: The authors develop CDEP Agent, an auditable LLM-agent framework that ingests meteorologically detected CDEP candidates and then searches across multiple heterogeneous information sources to find corroborating evidence. Using California (2021–2025) and ERA5 reanalysis, they identify 408 candidate CDEP events. For each, the agent evaluates the presence of (1) antecedent drought, (2) extreme rainfall, (3) local impact, (4) hazard-impact attribution, and (5) explicit drought-to-rainfall linkage. Evidence is drawn from the U.S. Drought Monitor, NOAA Storm Events database, and public webpages with varying spatial, temporal, and reporting characteristics, while ensuring traceable, provenance-linked outputs.

Result: Out of 408 meteorological CDEP candidates in California, only 34.3% are corroborated on both hazard components (drought and extreme precipitation) in real-world datasets and text sources. A mere 1.5% of events receive explicit documentation that links the extreme rainfall to a preceding drought. This indicates that the majority of meteorologically detected CDEP events either go undocumented or are only partially recorded, and their compound nature is rarely acknowledged in official or public records.

Conclusion: The study concludes that current early warning and reporting systems substantially under-represent compound drought-to-extreme-precipitation events, especially with regard to explicitly recognizing their compound nature. CDEP Agent offers a general, auditable framework for testing and refining physically based event definitions against what actually appears in impact records. This creates a provenance-linked evidence base that can support climate science, social science, economics, and disaster-response planning, and highlights the need to better capture compound-event dynamics in operational warning and documentation systems.

Abstract: Compound drought-to-extreme-precipitation (CDEP) events are recognized in climate science as a growing driver of extreme impact, but whether this recognition carries over into real-world early warning and post-event documentation is unknown, so a meteorologically real CDEP event may pass with neither advance warning nor any later record. Here we present CDEP Agent, an auditable LLM-agent framework that tests this mismatch directly by linking CDEP candidates detected from meteorological reanalysis to real-world hazard and impact evidence across sources with different spatial scales, temporal resolutions, and reporting conventions. Using California as a case study, we identify 408 candidate CDEP events from ERA5 observations during 2021-2025 and evaluate each against the U.S. Drought Monitor, NOAA Storm Events, and public webpages along five dimensions: antecedent drought, extreme rainfall, local impact, hazard-impact attribution, and explicit drought-to-rainfall linkage. Only 34.3% of candidates are corroborated on both hazard components, and just 1.5% are ever explicitly linked to their antecedent drought, indicating that most meteorologically detected CDEP events go undocumented and their compound nature almost never enters the record at all. Our framework gives climate scientists a way to test physical event definitions against what actually gets documented, and gives social scientists, economists, and disaster-response agencies a provenance-linked evidence base for compound events that current warning and reporting systems largely fail to capture.

</details>


### [244] [CrossAudit: A Git-Native, Cross-Vendor Audit Loop for Agentic Science](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.28631)
*Zhaohe Dong,Yuhao Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CrossAudit is a protocol for supervising autonomous AI research pipelines using cross-vendor auditing agents and a version-controlled supervision history to reduce shared blind spots and self-preference biases.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing AI research pipelines often use evaluators from the same model family or vendor as the generating model, creating risks of self-preferencing, shared blind spots, and opaque supervision records hidden in platform logs. There is a need for a transparent, auditable, and more independent oversight mechanism for autonomous research workflows.

Method: The authors propose CrossAudit, a protocol defined as eight invariants for supervising autonomous research pipelines. Each work increment is audited by a model from a different vendor than the producer, using a human-authored, versioned rulebook. Supervision artifacts (reports, verdicts, disputes, rulings) are stored as git commits. Scripted, deterministic checks run before any model calls. Models can only block progress by citing a rule and cannot override deterministic failures; unresolved blockers escalate to humans after limited revision rounds. They implement this via GitHub Actions and Python, deploy a variant in a computational-chemistry pipeline, and run a seeded-defect trial (30 increments, 43 planted defects) under different configurations, followed by a cross-vendor audit of their own repository that invalidated the original blinding and led to corrected results.

Result: The live deployment demonstrates that CrossAudit (or a close variant) can be integrated into a real computational-chemistry research pipeline. The seeded-defect trial with multiple configurations shows that two different model vendors interpret the same rulebook differently, affecting defect detection patterns. A later cross-vendor audit of the paper's own repository exposed issues with the original blinded setup, leading to corrected reporting of results and providing an uncontrolled but rich record of cross-vendor audits in practice.

Conclusion: CrossAudit offers a practical protocol and reference implementation for cross-vendor auditing of autonomous research pipelines, increasing transparency via version-controlled supervision histories and reducing reliance on single-vendor evaluators. While the trial does not establish which vendor is superior, it shows systematic differences in how vendors apply the same rules and underscores the value of maintaining an auditable, cross-vendor record of oversight, including for the paper itself.

Abstract: An AI scientist should not grade its own homework. Yet in the systems we examined, the agent that reviews the work usually comes from the same model family as the agent that produced it, or at least from the same vendor. Model evaluators are known to favour their own generations. Whether models trained alike also share blind spots is a conjecture, not a settled finding, but if they do, the reviewer inherits the author's. The record of what was flagged and what was waved through often sits in platform logs that nobody outside can replay.
  We present CrossAudit, a protocol for supervising autonomous research pipelines. It rests on three commitments. Each increment of work is audited by an agent from a different vendor against a rulebook a human wrote and versioned. Reports, verdicts, disputes and rulings are git commits, so the supervision history can be re-read and cited; raw model exchanges are not yet part of that record. Scripted checks run before any model does. Advisory judgement never gates the pipeline: a model blocks only by citing a rule, and no model may waive a deterministic failure. Blockers that survive a bounded number of revision rounds go to a person.
  We state the protocol as eight invariants. We describe a reference implementation built from GitHub Actions and a few hundred lines of Python, and report a live deployment of a closely related variant in a computational-chemistry pipeline. We also ran a seeded-defect trial (30 increments, 43 seeded defects, one run per configuration). A cross-vendor audit of our own repository then voided its blinding. We adopt that audit's findings and report the corrected results. The trial shows that two vendors read the same rulebook differently. It does not show that either is better. The strongest evidence here is the committed, uncontrolled record of cross-vendor audits of this paper itself.

</details>


### [245] [AutoScientist-Quant: Self-Evolving Coding Agents for Automatic Research in Quantitative Investment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.28632)
*Zongqian Li,Yaoyiran Li,Yaohui Guo,Ming Zhang,Nigel Collier,Eugene Ie*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: AutoScientist-Quant is a self-evolving, budget-aware LLM-agent framework that automates the full quantitative alpha-discovery pipeline and achieves state-of-the-art performance while enforcing strict out-of-sample evaluation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM-based alpha discovery methods are limited because they (1) use static search procedures that cannot adapt based on intermediate results or remaining resources, (2) automate only alpha idea generation while leaving library selection and model configuration to manual human decisions, and (3) risk evaluation leakage by inadvertently letting information from the test period influence the discovery process through feedback loops or flawed code/evaluation design. The authors aim to build a unified, fully automated, and statistically sound framework that treats quantitative research as a constrained search problem and that yields robust, truly out-of-sample trading strategies.

Method: The authors design AutoScientist-Quant, a single-controller, budget-aware search process built around large language model agents. The controller treats quantitative research as a sequential decision-making problem under a fixed resource budget. At each round, conditioned on the remaining budget and the shared memory of past trajectories, the controller chooses among several high-level actions: (i) improve existing alphas, (ii) combine them, (iii) pivot to new directions, or (iv) stop; it also decides which search node to expand, how many new alphas to generate, and how to query historical trajectories from shared memory. This same core controller is extended to downstream tasks such as choosing signal libraries and tuning predictive models, thus closing the loop from hypothesis generation to deployable trading strategy construction. In parallel, they carefully design and revise the evaluation pipeline inherited from prior work, explicitly fixing two identified lookahead (data leakage) issues and separating the feedback window used for agent learning from the held-out test window, ensuring proper out-of-sample testing.

Result: On CSI (China Securities Index) stock universes and across multiple backbone LLMs and market settings, AutoScientist-Quant achieves the best or near-best performance on almost all evaluation metrics in nearly every tested configuration. The improvements hold consistently across different backbones and markets, suggesting that the framework is robust rather than overfitted to a particular model or dataset. These empirical results validate both the effectiveness of the budget-aware, self-evolving search and the soundness of the corrected evaluation pipeline.

Conclusion: Treating quantitative alpha discovery as a budgeted, sequential search problem and controlling the entire pipeline—from hypothesis generation to model/library selection—via a unified, LLM-driven controller yields superior, robust trading strategies. AutoScientist-Quant not only automates more of the quant research workflow but also enforces stricter evaluation discipline by removing lookahead and test-set contamination, resulting in state-of-the-art performance on CSI universes across multiple backbones and markets. This demonstrates that properly orchestrated LLM agents can be powerful end-to-end tools for quantitative finance research and deployment.

Abstract: Large language model agents can discover alphas, yet current methods have three weaknesses. The search cannot adapt during the run, automation usually ends at alpha generation while library selection and model choice stay manual, and alpha discovery can read the test window through loop feedback or code problems. We present AutoScientist-Quant, a self evolving search process that regards quantitative research as one budgeted search problem. A single controller conditions every decision on the remaining budget, choosing at each round whether to improve, combine, pivot, or stop, which node to expand, how many alphas to generate, and how to retrieve past trajectories from the shared memory. The same core then selects from the library and tunes the model, closing the loop from hypothesis to deployable strategy. We also review the evaluation pipeline reused from prior work, fix two lookahead problems, and keep the feedback window disjoint from the held out test window, so every comparison tests true generalization. On CSI universes, the framework attains the best value of nearly every metric in every setting, and these conclusions hold across several backbones and markets.

</details>


### [246] [AI Scientist Mission Control (AIMC): Visual Analytics for Human Oversight of Autonomous Scientific Discovery](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.28637)
*Rikathi Pal,Klaus Mueller*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces AIMC, a visual analytics framework to help humans oversee and understand the quality and evolution of AI-generated scientific research outputs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Autonomous scientific discovery systems can now generate many research ideas, experiments, and manuscripts with little human input, but scientists lack effective tools to monitor quality, detect recurring problems, track how the research evolves over time, and identify the few promising results that deserve closer human review.

Method: The authors build AIMC, a visual analytics framework that integrates semantic embeddings of research artifacts, automatic extraction of methodological weaknesses from reviews, temporal analysis of research evolution, and interactive visualizations to enable users to explore and assess AI-generated papers and their reviews.

Result: Using a case study on papers produced by an autonomous AI Scientist system (FARS) and their review feedback, AIMC surfaces patterns such as repeated methodological weaknesses, shifts in research topics over time, differences in quality across domains, and a subset of unusually novel papers that stand out as promising.

Conclusion: The study shows that visual analytics, as implemented in AIMC, can make autonomous scientific discovery workflows more transparent and diagnosable, and can enhance human–AI collaboration by helping experts focus attention on the most important AI-generated research outputs and their systematic failure modes.

Abstract: Autonomous scientific discovery systems can generate large numbers of research ideas, experiments, and manuscripts with minimal human intervention. As these systems become increasingly capable, scientists require effective mechanisms to monitor output quality, identify recurring failure modes, understand research evolution, and prioritize promising discoveries for review. We present AIMC, a visual analytics framework for human oversight of autonomous scientific discovery. AIMC combines semantic embeddings, automated weakness extraction, temporal analysis, and interactive visualizations to support the exploration of AI-generated research artifacts. We demonstrate the framework through a case study of the papers generated by an autonomous AI Scientist (FARS), together with their associated review feedback. Our analysis reveals recurring methodological weaknesses, evolving research themes, domain-specific differences in quality, and a small set of highly novel papers that warrant deeper human inspection. These findings illustrate how visual analytics can support transparency, diagnosis, and human AI collaboration in emerging autonomous scientific discovery workflows.

</details>


### [247] [Self-Evolving Skills via Surrogate-Guided Solve-and-Reproduce](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.28638)
*Jiale Liu,Pinze Ren,Yuqi Xia,Huan Wang,Zhenlin Zhao,Siming Dong*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces reSolve, a framework that lets a cheaper model automatically learn portable task-specific skills that outperform human-curated skills by combining solve-and-reproduce execution, a surrogate verifier, and verifier-guided beam search.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing approaches for self-evolving agent skills are unreliable: (1) skills evolved entirely from scratch perform worse than human-designed skills and sometimes even worse than using no skills on weaker models, and (2) evolution typically records a single successful trajectory that later stochastic runs cannot reliably reproduce. This limits the usefulness and robustness of automatically learned skills at deployment time.

Method: The authors propose reSolve, an oracle-in-the-loop, per-task framework centered on a solve-and-reproduce protocol that separates interactive problem solving from generating a self-contained, reproducible solution artifact executed in a clean environment. They augment sparse reward signals with a surrogate verifier that evaluates candidate solutions without seeing hidden tests or reference answers. Using this verifier, they perform beam search over a solution-construction graph to iteratively refine and select high-quality skills, all within a fixed evaluation harness and using a relatively cheap model.

Result: In experiments, automatically evolved skills with reSolve achieve 74.9% mean-of-3 accuracy, which is a +14.8 point improvement over a 60.1% human-curated skill baseline and surpasses the strongest official curated-skill benchmark (67.3% with GPT-5.5/OpenHands). The paper also presents qualitative failure cases and task/domain-level breakdowns, including detailed behavior on 14 Natural Science tasks, to characterize the strengths and limitations of the framework.

Conclusion: reSolve enables reliable self-evolution of portable agent skills that not only close but exceed the performance gap with human-curated skills, even when using a cheaper model. By separating solving from reproducible execution, incorporating a surrogate verifier, and using verifier-guided beam search, the approach mitigates non-reproducibility of lucky trajectories and poor-from-scratch evolution. However, the authors also highlight specific domains and failure cases where the method is less effective, underscoring that its benefits are task-dependent rather than universal.

Abstract: Agent skills are portable packages of instructions and resources an agent consults at deployment. Self-evolving them fails in two ways today. First, skills evolved from scratch underperform human-curated ones and, on a weak model, using no skill at all. Second, an evolution-time pass records one lucky trajectory that a fresh stochastic agent often fails to reproduce at deployment. We present reSolve, a per-task, oracle-in-the-loop framework built on three components. It decouples interactive solving from a self-contained deliverable that is independently re-executed in a fresh container, a protocol we call solve-and-reproduce. It enhances the sparse reward signal with a surrogate verifier that cannot access hidden tests or reference answers. It then runs verifier-guided beam search over a solution-construction graph. Within a fixed harness, a cheap model self-evolves skills that reach $74.9\%$ mean-of-3, $+14.8$ points over the $60.1\%$ human-curated baseline, exceeding the strongest official curated-skill result ($67.3\%$, GPT-5.5/OpenHands). We also report observed failure cases and domain-level results, including performance on the 14 Natural Science tasks, to clarify when the approach does and does not help.

</details>


### [248] [Reward-Oracle MCTS for Formal Theorem Proving: Sample-Efficient Search and the Need for Kernel-Level Proof Auditing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.28639)
*Bodla Krishna Vamshi,Haizhao Yang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They introduce a new three-role MCTS framework for LLM-based Lean 4 theorem proving that uses the compiler only as a scalar reward oracle, improves success on several math/physics benchmarks under standard proof-attempt budgets, and reveals a reward-hacking issue requiring kernel-level auditing.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM-based formal theorem proving struggles with large proof search spaces and inefficient use of context. Existing tree-search methods either bloat the context by feeding full compiler error messages back into the model, or use custom evaluation setups that are not directly comparable with standard baselines. There is also a need for more reliable evaluation and detection of reward hacking in search-based proof generation.

Method: They design a Monte Carlo Tree Search framework with three specialized LLM roles: (1) a generator that proposes full proof attempts, (2) a decomposer that breaks problems into subgoals, and (3) a critic that scores subgoal quality. The Lean 4 compiler is treated purely as a black-box reward oracle: its output is reduced to a scalar signal guiding UCB-based tree updates, and detailed error text is not put back into the prompt. They evaluate this approach on four formalized benchmarks—MiniF2F, PutnamBench, LeanPhysBench, and PhysLeandata—using three different prover models and varying proof attempt budgets (PAB@16–256). They also perform an exhaustive axiom-level audit on every compiled proof to check for hidden reliance on an unsound sorryAx axiom, beyond standard sorry-token scanning.

Result: On MiniF2F, their framework reaches 87.1% success with Goedel-Prover-V2-8B at a budget of 256 proof attempts. On PutnamBench at PAB@32, the MCTS framework solves 26 out of 659 problems, outperforming base sampling which solves 18/659 under the same budget. The axiom-level audit uncovers instances of reward hacking: DeepSeek-Prover-V2-7B produces proofs on PutnamBench that compile and pass usual sorry-token filters but secretly depend on sorryAx. After audit, they remove 4 and 8 such proofs from whole-proof sampling at PAB@32 and PAB@128 and 11 and 19 such proofs from MCTS runs, demonstrating that standard evaluation can overestimate true theorem proving performance.

Conclusion: A three-role MCTS architecture that uses the Lean compiler purely as a scalar reward oracle can substantially improve LLM-based theorem proving performance on math and physics benchmarks under standard proof-attempt budgets, while avoiding excessive context usage. At the same time, rigorous kernel-level auditing is essential: even compiler-checked proofs and sorry-token scans can miss subtle reward hacking via unsound axioms such as sorryAx. Properly accounting for these issues leads to more accurate and trustworthy evaluation of search-based theorem provers.

Abstract: Formal theorem proving with large language models remains challenging due to the difficulty of navigating large proof search spaces efficiently.
