Existing tree search approaches either feed verbose compiler error messages directly into the generation context, increasing context usage during search, or employ non-standard evaluation protocols that prevent direct comparison with established baselines. We propose a three-role Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) framework that treats the Lean 4 compiler purely as a reward oracle using compiler output as a scalar signal for UCB-guided tree updates without feeding error content into the generation context. Our framework decomposes proof search into three roles: a generator for proof attempts, a decomposer for subgoal decomposition, and a critic for subgoal quality evaluation. We evaluate across 4 benchmarks spanning competition mathematics and physics (MiniF2F, PutnamBench, LeanPhysBench, PhysLeandata) with three prover models at standard proof attempt budgets (PAB@16 to PAB@256). Our method achieves 87.1\% on MiniF2F with Goedel-Prover-V2-8B at PAB@256 and solves 26/659 PutnamBench problems at PAB@32 surpassing base sampling 18/659 at same proof attempt budget. Through an exhaustive axiom-level audit of every compiled proof, we further identify reward hacking in search-based theorem proving: DeepSeek-Prover-V2-7B produces proofs on PutnamBench that pass compilation and the standard sorry-token scan while depending on sorryAx. The audit removes 4 and 8 such proofs from whole-proof sampling at PAB@32 and PAB@128, and 11 and 19 from MCTS. We do not attribute these counts to the search procedure; we report them to establish that kernel-level auditing is necessary for compiler-verified evaluation.

</details>


### [249] [From Extraction to Governed Memory: Multi-Agent Knowledge Graph Construction with Domain-Expert Review](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.28642)
*Pranav Bykampadi,Neel Mokaria,Vishesh Narayan,Faizan Wajid,Ashok Agrawala*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Introduces MAGG, a multi-agent framework to build governed knowledge graphs that track ownership, evidence, and usage, greatly improving triple quality and QA performance over flat graphs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing knowledge graphs for agentic systems are usually flat collections of triples with little to no information about who owns each fact, why it was added, or how it should be used. This lack of governance and provenance undermines reliability, trustworthiness, and effective reuse in downstream tasks like question answering. The authors aim to address this gap by integrating explicit governance and ownership into the very process of graph construction and use.

Method: They design MAGG, a multi-agent framework that builds Governed Knowledge Graphs. First, a domain classifier induces entity and relation types from document content without relying on a fixed schema, enabling open-world operation. Extracted candidate triples are then assigned to domain owners (specialized agents) who review them against source evidence. Only after explicit governance decisions are these triples admitted into the graph, along with audit metadata capturing ownership and decision history. For question answering, the same ownership and domain structure is used to route queries to domain-specific graph experts rather than performing uniform, undifferentiated retrieval over the entire graph.

Result: On the SciERC dataset, MAGG substantially improves triple extraction quality: strict triple F1 increases by 47% and mapped triple F1 by 51% relative to flat, unguided insertion. In a blinded human review of 120 triples, triples that exist only in the governed setting are more frequently supported by their sources than those only in the flat setting, and all revised triples are fully supported by evidence. On the MuSiQue QA benchmark, MAGG surpasses Microsoft GraphRAG by 9.0 points in exact match and 11.2 points in token-level F1, showing benefits for downstream QA.

Conclusion: Embedding governance into knowledge graph construction and usage—via domain-aware ownership, explicit admission decisions, and audit metadata—yields more accurate, better-supported triples and improves question answering performance. MAGG demonstrates that multi-agent, governed graph construction is a practical and effective alternative to flat triple stores for building reliable agentic knowledge systems.

Abstract: Knowledge graphs used by agentic systems are often treated as flat stores of extracted triples, with little record of who owns a fact, why it was admitted, or how it should be used downstream. We argue that reliable agentic knowledge systems require governance as an essential component of graph construction to bridge this gap. We propose MAGG, a principled multi-agent framework for constructing Governed Knowledge Graphs that introduces explicit governance decisions for reliable and trustworthy knowledge sharing. A domain classifier first induces entity and relation types directly from document content, enabling operation in open-world settings without fixed schemas. Candidate triples are assigned to domain owners, reviewed against supporting evidence, admitted through governance decisions, and stored with audit metadata. The same ownership structure is reused during question answering, where queries are routed to domain-specific graph experts rather than answered through undifferentiated retrieval. Our evaluation demonstrates MAGG's effectiveness: On SciERC, MAGG improves strict triple F1 by 47% and mapped triple F1 by 51% over flat insertion. A blinded review of 120 triples finds governed-only triples more often source-supported than flat-only ones, and revised triples supported in 100% of cases. Finally, on MuSiQue, MAGG outperforms Microsoft GraphRAG by 9.0 exact-match points and 11.2 token-F1 points.

</details>


### [250] [BiasMix-Finance: Post-Generation KYC Guardrails for LLM Portfolio Advice](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.28646)
*Gaurav Kukreja,Parul Kukreja,Mohammed Abraar,Raj Dandekar,Rajat Dandekar,Sreedath Panat*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes a post-generation guardrail pipeline for LLM-generated ETF portfolios that enforces schema, validates numeric constraints, and uses convex projection to fix violations, achieving 0% constraint violations with minimal change to the original allocations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs can produce seemingly reasonable ETF portfolio recommendations that nevertheless violate key investment constraints such as risk exposure, fee limits, and diversification rules, especially in multi-turn advisory agents where drafts may trigger real actions. There is a need for an auditable, model-agnostic mechanism that can reliably enforce such constraints without relying on the LLM to behave correctly by itself.

Method: The authors design a three-stage, model- and asset-agnostic post-processing pipeline: (i) enforce a strict JSON schema for ETF allocations; (ii) validate the generated portfolio against predefined numeric caps (e.g., on asset weights or risk/fee metrics); and (iii) if violations are detected, solve a convex quadratic constrained optimization problem to project the infeasible portfolio onto the nearest feasible one, minimizing Euclidean distance between original and corrected weights. They also construct BiasMix-Finance (Mini), a benchmark with 16 ETFs, three investor profiles, and eight bias-inducing prompts to systematically stress-test LLMs under constrained decision-making. They evaluate three LLMs under three prompting modes (direct, critique, self-consistency) and measure constraint violation rates and required correction distances, with statistical rigor including confidence intervals and multiple-testing corrections.

Result: Without guardrails, first-pass LLM portfolios violate at least one constraint in 47.6–85.7% of test cases, with a pooled average of 67.2%. When the convex projection step is applied, final portfolios satisfy all constraints (0% violations) while requiring only small modifications, with a pooled median Euclidean correction distance of 0.066 between original and corrected allocations. The study provides detailed statistics on violation rates, correction magnitudes, and comparative performance across models and prompting setups.

Conclusion: Post-generation, optimization-based guardrails can reliably enforce investment constraints on LLM-generated ETF portfolios across models and prompting styles, eliminating feasibility violations while largely preserving the intended allocation structure. The proposed BiasMix-Finance (Mini) benchmark and accompanying code, prompts, and caps create a reproducible testbed for future work on constrained decision-making and safety layers for LLM-based financial advisory systems.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can generate plausible-sounding ETF portfolios while silently violating basic KYC-style constraints on risk, fees, and diversification. This is especially problematic in agentic multi-turn advisory systems, where each draft recommendation can become an action unless guarded by an auditable enforcement layer. We study a model-agnostic, asset-agnostic post-generation guardrail pipeline: (i) enforce a strict JSON allocation schema, (ii) validate allocations against numeric caps, and (iii) when violations occur, deterministically project the output to the nearest feasible portfolio via a convex quadratic program (QCQP). We introduce BiasMix-Finance (Mini), a compact stress-test benchmark for constrained decision-making under biased LLM generations, with a 16-ETF universe, three investor profiles, and eight bias prompts. Across three models and three inference modes (direct, critique, self-consistency), first-pass generations violate at least one cap in 47.6-85.7% of test cases (67.2% pooled), but the convex projection layer reduces final feasibility violations to 0% while requiring only a small correction distance (test pooled median D=||w*-w0||_2=0.066), indicating that the guardrail typically preserves the intent of the original allocation. We report violation rates and correction distances with confidence intervals, and paired model comparisons with multiple-testing correction. To support reproducibility, we release the dataset, prompts, caps, and code in our public GitHub repository.

</details>


### [251] [Self-Specialized Teachers for Domain Post-Training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.28647)
*Yifei Li,Rongman Xu,Lingling Zhang,Muye Huang,Zihan Ma,Jiashuai Liu,Hang Yan,Heng Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces Self-Specialized Teacher Distillation (SSTD), a method to adapt large language models to specialized domains while preserving general capabilities, by distilling from a domain-trained copy of the base model onto a student using the student’s own prefixes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Target-only post-training on specialized domains (e.g., finance, medicine, law) often improves in-domain performance but harms the general-purpose abilities that the base model previously learned. In realistic settings, we often have target-domain data but no representative replay corpus of general data to prevent catastrophic forgetting. The authors aim to solve how to adapt models to new domains without access to broad replay data and without relying on an external, stronger teacher model.

Method: They propose Self-Specialized Teacher Distillation (SSTD), a two-stage procedure: (1) Teacher training: create a domain teacher by fine-tuning a copy of the base model on target-domain supervision, while using base-aware key-token weighting and distribution alignment with the frozen base model to reduce forgetting of general behaviors. (2) Student distillation: perform on-policy distillation from the domain teacher to a student model by sampling prefixes from the student itself and training the student to match the teacher’s token distribution on those prefixes. This places domain feedback on the states the student will actually visit at inference time. The approach requires no external teacher and no general replay data.

Result: On three specialized tasks—financial numerical reasoning, medical question answering, and legal holding identification—SSTD maintains most of the target-domain performance gains of direct fine-tuning, while improving mean performance on a general evaluation suite by 4.8–5.0 points at the chosen operating point. These improvements hold across different model sizes of Qwen3 and also on Gemma model backbones, indicating robustness and generality of the approach.

Conclusion: SSTD is an effective solution for domain specialization without catastrophic forgetting when only target-domain data are available. By using a self-specialized teacher and on-policy distillation, it preserves much of the target performance gain and substantially recovers general capabilities, without needing an external teacher model or a broad replay corpus. The approach appears architecture-agnostic across tested backbones and sizes.

Abstract: Target-only post-training can improve performance in a specialized domain while degrading behaviors that a general-purpose base model acquired before adaptation. We study this problem when target-domain data are available but a representative replay corpus is not. We propose self-specialized teacher distillation (SSTD), a two-stage procedure that first trains a copy of the base model into a domain teacher, then distills its token distribution to a student on prefixes sampled from the student itself. Teacher training combines standard target supervision with base-aware key-token weighting and distribution alignment to the frozen base model; on-policy distillation then places domain feedback on states the student can encounter at inference time. On financial numerical reasoning, medical question answering, and legal holding identification, SSTD retains much of the target improvement of direct fine-tuning while improving the mean score on the evaluated general suite by 4.8--5.0 points at the reported operating point. The pattern persists across Qwen3 sizes and on Gemma backbones. SSTD requires neither an external teacher nor general replay data.

</details>


### [252] [How Language Models Choose Sides: Internal Representations of Instruction Hierarchy](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.28648)
*Enrique Balp-Straffon,Chih-Hao Hsu,Rushiraj Gadhvi,Sunishchal Dev,Callum Stuart McDougall,Anusha Mujumdar*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper examines how instruction-tuned large language models resolve direct conflicts between system and user instructions, finding distinct behavioral regimes and showing that even user-preferring models contain decodable internal signals for conflict resolution that can be leveraged to improve system compliance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Understand whether and how instruction-tuned LLMs treat the system message as an authority signal when it conflicts with user instructions, and whether failures to follow system instructions reflect an underlying absence of internal conflict-resolution mechanisms or just how those mechanisms are read out.

Method: They build a benchmark of 41 pairs of conflicting constraints with deterministic verifiers and test eight LLMs under three conditions: (1) matched baseline (no channel conflict), (2) conflict between system and user messages, and (3) same-channel controls. They categorize models by how much more they follow system instructions versus baselines (System Authority Delta), identifying hierarchy-respecting, anti-hierarchy, and no-effect regimes. Using representational analysis, they probe residual-stream activations in models (e.g., Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, gpt-oss-20b) to see if conflict outcomes are linearly decodable, and then perform activation steering using probe directions to change system compliance.

Result: Models fall into three behavioral regimes: hierarchy-respecting models treat the system channel as authoritative; anti-hierarchy models disproportionately favor user instructions; and no-effect models show minimal sensitivity to channels. Llama-3.1-8B is strongly anti-hierarchy, following system instructions in only about 10% of conflict trials. Nonetheless, conflict outcomes are highly linearly decodable from residual-stream activations (e.g., 0.97 balanced accuracy on Llama-3.1-8B, 17 points above a metadata baseline). Activation steering using carefully chosen probe directions greatly increases genuine system compliance (from ~0.13 to ~0.53), whereas directions optimized mainly for pooled separability perform poorly.

Conclusion: Even when LLMs appear to ignore system authority and favor user instructions, they can retain strong internal representations of conflict resolution that are readable and steerable. User-preferring behavior is therefore not simply due to a lack of internal arbitration signals; rather, effective intervention requires attention to the geometry of readout directions, not just probe accuracy. This has implications for both safety/control and interpretability of instruction-tuned LLMs.

Abstract: We study how instruction-tuned LLMs arbitrate direct conflicts between system and user instructions. We introduce a benchmark of 41 paired constraints with deterministic verifiers and evaluate eight models under matched baseline, conflict, and same-channel control conditions. Behaviourally, the models split into three regimes by System Authority Delta: hierarchy-respecting models use the system channel as an authority signal, anti-hierarchy models follow the system less often than their same-channel baseline predicts, and no-effect models show little channel sensitivity. Llama-3.1-8B is the strongest anti-hierarchy case in our suite, following the system in only 0.10 of conflict trials. We use this behavioural failure case to ask whether user-preferring arbitration reflects the absence of an internal conflictresolution signal. It does not: on Llama-3.1-8B, the conflict outcome is linearly decodable from residual-stream activations at 0.97 balanced accuracy, 17 percentage points above a metadata-only baseline, with analogous signals on Qwen2.5-7B and gpt-oss-20b. Steering with a layer-12 mean of four per-conflict logistic-regression directions raises genuine system compliance from 0.132 to 0.530, while directions selected mainly for pooled separability steer poorly. User-preferring conflict resolution can therefore coexist with a readable internal arbitration signal, and successful intervention depends on the geometry of the readout rather than probe accuracy alone

</details>


### [253] [A Generalized Optimization Engine (GOE) for Edge AI Inference Acceleration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.28652)
*Venkat R. Dasari,Jakob A. Adams,Vinod K. Mishra,Brian Jalaian*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper presents a generalized, hardware-agnostic optimization architecture that combines AI model compression and optimization techniques to enable efficient deployment on resource-constrained, heterogeneous edge hardware.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: AI models are powerful but computationally expensive, making it difficult to deploy them on resource-constrained devices such as edge CPUs, especially in tactical or constrained environments. There is a need for a unified, theoretically grounded framework that optimizes models across different hardware platforms to reduce compute, memory, latency, and power while preserving task accuracy.

Method: The authors survey and theoretically analyze various model optimization and compression techniques, algorithms, and abstractions (e.g., quantization, pruning, etc.) and then design a generalized, model- and hardware-agnostic optimization architecture that can integrate these methods. They demonstrate this architecture via GOE-based compression applied to language models for deployment on GPU-less edge CPUs, and empirically compare different compression methods and bit-width choices in terms of their impact on task accuracy.

Result: The proposed generalized optimization architecture successfully enables the deployment and execution of compressed language models on GPU-less edge CPUs. Experiments show that task accuracy after deployment is strongly influenced by the specific compression method used, rather than just the target bit-width of the compressed representation.

Conclusion: A generalized, hardware- and model-agnostic optimization system is crucial for preparing AI models for deployment on resource-constrained, heterogeneous hardware. Properly chosen and integrated compression and optimization techniques can significantly reduce computational and resource requirements while maintaining acceptable task accuracy, and the detailed choice of compression method is more critical than nominal bit-width alone.

Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) models have demonstrated remarkable capabilities across various domains, yet their widespread deployment is impeded by significant computational costs, particularly on resource-constrained devices. This paper explores the theoretical underpinnings of various AI model optimization techniques, algorithms, and abstractions, discussing their potential to reduce computational complexity, memory footprint, latency, and power consumption. Furthermore, we propose a comprehensive hardware (HW) and model-agnostic generalized optimization architecture that integrates these techniques for improved efficiency. Our study underscores the critical role of such a generalized optimization system in preparing model deployment over resource-constrained heterogeneous hardware in a tactical environment. As a concrete demonstration, we show that GOE-compressed language models deploy and run on a GPU-less edge CPU, and that the choice of compression method, not merely its nominal bit-width, determines whether task accuracy survives deployment.

</details>


### [254] [FRAC-MAS: A Safe and Explainable Multi-Agent System for Fracture Diagnosis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.28662)
*Hardik Iyer,Tirath Bhathawala,Mihir Panchal,Ying-Jung Chen,Kiran Bhowmick,Pankaj Sonawane,Meera Narvekar*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: FRAC-MAS is an agentic, multi‑agent AI framework that combines an ensemble of vision models with conformal prediction and multi‑agent verification to provide accurate, explainable, and safer fracture detection and reporting.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Deep learning models can detect fractures well but are hard to interpret and trust in clinical practice because of their black‑box nature and limited support for explanation, safety, and patient‑friendly communication. There is a need for systems that not only classify images but also provide calibrated uncertainty, independent cross‑checks, clinical guideline grounding, and understandable outputs suitable for both clinicians and patients.

Method: The authors propose FRAC-MAS, a multi‑agent system built around a stacked ensemble of four deep vision models for fracture detection. Conformal prediction is applied to generate statistically grounded differential diagnoses and calibrated uncertainty sets. On top of this, a multi‑agent workflow is used: independent critic/validator agents verify findings, retrieve relevant clinical guidelines, and generate reports targeted at lay users. The system is evaluated with a pipeline-depth ablation study to compare different levels of agentic workflow complexity, and with user studies comparing report comprehensibility to outputs from baseline LLMs (Llama, MedGemma, Gemini).

Result: The full multi‑agent FRAC-MAS pipeline triages 86.6% of radiology cases into a high‑confidence auto‑confirmed cohort while escalating only uncertain cases, outperforming a simpler single‑agent baseline in triage performance. In patient preference studies, users significantly preferred the clinical reports produced by FRAC-MAS over those from strong LLM baselines, finding them more comprehensible and patient‑friendly.

Conclusion: Integrating multi‑agent critic workflows with conformal prediction over an ensemble of vision models leads to a fracture detection system that is both accurate and safer for clinical triage. FRAC-MAS preserves clinician oversight by escalating uncertain or complex cases while automatically confirming high‑confidence ones, and it produces more understandable reports for patients. This illustrates the broader promise of cooperative, auditable, agentic AI architectures as human‑in‑the‑loop decision support tools for safety‑critical healthcare applications.

Abstract: Fracture detection and its clinical interpretability see notable improvements when deep vision models are integrated with agentic AI architectures. While deep learning models achieve high diagnostic performance, their black-box nature limits clinical adoption. We propose FRAC-MAS, an agentic AI system for automated, explainable, and safe bone fracture detection. The framework combines a stacked ensemble of four vision models with conformal prediction to produce statistically grounded differential diagnoses, while a multi-agent workflow performs independent verification, retrieves clinical guidelines, and generates patient-friendly reports. A pipeline-depth ablation study confirms that our multi-agent critic triages 86.6% of cases into a high-confidence auto-confirmed cohort while escalating uncertain cases, outperforming a single-agent baseline. Patient preference studies against Llama, MedGemma, and Gemini further demonstrate significantly more comprehensible clinical reports. These results suggest that integrating multi-agent critics with conformal guarantees enables safer radiology triage while preserving clinician oversight. More broadly, FRAC-MAS demonstrates how cooperative agentic architectures can serve as auditable, human-in-the-loop decision support systems for safety-critical healthcare. Our code is available at https://github.com/hardik1712/FRAC-MAS, and the website is available at https://frac-mas.vercel.app.

</details>


### [255] [ORDDAR: Observation-Driven Reasoning for Distortion-Resilient Decision, Action, and Cognitive Recovery](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.28704)
*Deblina Kar,Anant Nawalgaria,Shyamal Kumar Das Mandal*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ORDDAR is a reasoning framework that treats an AI agent’s reasoning as cognitive state transitions, detects and localizes faulty states, and selectively repairs only those using prior experiences instead of regenerating whole reasoning trajectories, improving robustness and interpretability across diverse reasoning tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long-term, tool-using AI agents often accumulate errors in intermediate reasoning steps; these local errors can propagate through long trajectories, leading to inconsistent and unreliable final decisions. Existing methods focus on planning, reflection, memory, or verification at the trajectory level, but lack mechanisms to precisely locate and repair specific faulty steps without recomputing everything. The paper aims to make agent reasoning more robust, efficient, and interpretable by enabling localized error detection and correction within the reasoning process.

Method: The authors introduce ORDDAR, which formalizes reasoning as a sequence of cognitive state transitions. The framework (1) monitors these transitions using observations of the evolving reasoning process, (2) detects localized distortions or inconsistencies in particular states or transitions, (3) retrieves similar prior reasoning episodes from memory that are relevant to the distorted part, and (4) selectively repairs only the affected states instead of regenerating the full reasoning chain. This yields a local recovery mechanism at the transition level. The method is evaluated on multiple reasoning benchmarks spanning mathematical, commonsense, multi-hop, and clinical tasks, comparing against standard reasoning baselines that rely on planning, self-reflection, or verification without localized repair.

Result: Across diverse benchmarks (mathematical, commonsense, multi-hop, and clinical reasoning), ORDDAR improves reasoning quality and robustness compared to multiple existing baselines. It demonstrates better recovery from intermediate reasoning errors, leading to more accurate final decisions, while avoiding the need to regenerate entire trajectories. The localized repair mechanism also yields more interpretable reasoning traces, since the system can highlight where distortions were detected and how they were corrected.

Conclusion: Modeling reasoning as cognitive state transitions and enabling localized distortion detection and repair leads to more resilient and interpretable AI reasoning. ORDDAR shows that agents can recover from local errors by selectively revising faulty steps using prior experience, instead of discarding whole trajectories. This transition-level recovery paradigm offers a promising direction for building more reliable long-term reasoning agents across a range of domains.

Abstract: AI agents increasingly perform long-term reasoning, planning, tool use, memory integration, and autonomous decision making, yet erroneous intermediate states can propagate and cause inconsistent decisions and unreliable outputs. Existing reasoning approaches mainly rely on iterative planning, self-reflection, augmented memory, or verification, but rarely localize and selectively repair faulty reasoning. We present ORDDAR (Observation-Driven Reasoning for Distortion-Resilient Decision, Action, and Cognitive Recovery), a reasoning framework that models reasoning as cognitive state transitions, detects localized distortions, retrieves related reasoning from prior experiences, and repairs only the affected states. ORDDAR therefore performs recovery at the local reasoning-transition level rather than regenerating the complete trajectory. Experiments across mathematical, commonsense, multi-hop, and clinical reasoning benchmarks demonstrate improved reasoning quality, recovery ability, and interpretability over multiple evaluated reasoning baselines.

</details>


### [256] [Beyond the Answer Key: Robustness Evaluation of Large Language Models for Step-Level Mathematical Verification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.28725)
*Fateme Mazdarani,Carlos Toxtli*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They study how well large language models can act as math solution graders, focusing on robustness to non-standard but correct solution steps, and find big failures when solutions deviate from a canonical form.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs are widely used to grade or verify math solutions, but most benchmarks only check final answers and assume a single canonical solution path. This hides whether evaluators can recognize logically correct but differently structured solutions and accurately locate errors in reasoning. The authors want a controlled way to measure the robustness of LLMs as evaluators, not just as solvers, in a domain with clear ground truth.

Method: They build a benchmark based on linear equations where each problem includes a full step-by-step solution trace. They systematically create canonical traces and perturbed but logically equivalent variants, plus traces with injected errors. For each instance, the LLM must (1) judge if the final answer is correct, (2) judge correctness of the entire solution trace, and (3) identify the first incorrect step. They test several state-of-the-art open LLMs (GPT-OSS 20B, Qwen3-14B, Phi-4-Reasoning) in base and improved forms (via supervised fine-tuning, distillation, and extra test-time compute) and compare performance on canonical vs perturbed traces.

Result: Base models evaluate canonical solution traces well but their performance drops sharply on perturbed yet valid traces, particularly for detecting the first incorrect step. They show very high false-rejection rates (around 75.6–85.3%) on valid perturbed traces, indicating they often mark correct but non-canonical solutions as wrong. Various enhancements (SFT, distillation, more test-time compute) can improve robustness in some configurations, but the benefits are inconsistent across models and sometimes reduce accuracy on canonical traces.

Conclusion: Current LLMs are brittle as process-level evaluators: they overfit to specific solution formats and struggle to robustly recognize and assess non-canonical but valid reasoning, even in simple linear-equation problems with exact ground truth. Evaluator robustness is a distinct capability from solving ability, so it should be benchmarked separately. Improving reliable step-wise verification remains an open challenge for deploying LLMs as trustworthy graders or auditors.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as graders, verifiers, and process auditors, but most mathematical evaluations still emphasize final-answer accuracy. This can obscure whether a model can verify a non-canonical but valid solution trace. We introduce a controlled linear-equation benchmark for evaluating LLMs in the evaluator role. Each instance asks the model to judge final-answer correctness, step-level trace correctness, and the first incorrect step. Our evaluation of state-of-the-art open LLMs reveals a significant robustness gap: models that accurately evaluate canonical solutions often fail when presented with perturbed but logically equivalent variants. Across GPT-OSS 20B, Qwen3-14B, and Phi-4-Reasoning, base models perform well on canonical traces but degrade substantially on perturbed traces, especially for error localization. On valid perturbed traces, base-model false-rejection rates reach 75.6-85.3%, showing strong sensitivity to canonical solution form. Supervised fine-tuning, distillation, and test-time compute improve robustness in some settings, but gains are model dependent and can trade off against canonical performance. The results show that reliable process-level verification remains challenging, and evaluator robustness should be measured separately from solver accuracy, even in a simple algebraic domain with exact ground truth.

</details>


### [257] [Pro-Router: Token-Aware Progressive Model Routing with Adaptive Edge-Cloud Collaboration for Efficient Multimodal LLM Inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.28726)
*Xinyuan Gui,Shaowen Wang,Sheng Sun,Zijian Wang,Zishu Yu,Zheming Yang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Pro-Router is a token-aware, progressive routing framework that decides dynamically whether a multimodal LLM query can be safely handled by a small edge model or must be escalated to a powerful cloud model, greatly improving speed and throughput without sacrificing accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multimodal LLMs are powerful but very expensive and slow to run, especially in real-time applications. Existing routing methods either use only coarse request-level features or require extra model passes after full responses are generated, ignoring the rich token-level uncertainty information that arises during generation. This leads to suboptimal efficiency and higher latency/cost. There is a need for a routing mechanism that leverages fine-grained token confidence signals while coordinating edge and cloud resources adaptively.

Method: Pro-Router introduces a two-stage progressive routing mechanism with an adaptive edge-cloud serving pipeline. Stage 1 uses a lightweight prompt pre-scorer that quickly evaluates an input before any generation and directs clearly easy queries to a small model. Stage 2 uses a token-aware verifier that monitors the small model’s per-token sampling probabilities during generation to infer its confidence in its own answer and, per request, decides whether to accept the answer or escalate to a larger cloud-based model. On the systems side, Pro-Router adds an adaptive dispatching mechanism that adjusts the load sent to edge and cloud based on their measured service rates, keeping both tiers saturated without manual tuning and mitigating the impact of network latency.

Result: On multiple multimodal benchmarks and with different model backends, Pro-Router attains the highest routing accuracy among compared methods, accelerates routing decisions by over 10x, and raises overall end-to-end serving throughput by more than 75% compared to existing routing pipelines.

Conclusion: Leveraging token-level uncertainty during generation and combining it with a fast pre-scoring stage enables more accurate, earlier routing decisions between small and large multimodal LLMs. Coupled with an adaptive edge-cloud pipeline, this design significantly improves both speed and throughput without compromising accuracy, demonstrating that progressive, token-aware routing is an effective strategy for efficient MLLM inference in practical deployments.

Abstract: The remarkable performance of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) comes at the cost of substantial computational overhead, posing significant challenges to real-time deployment and cost effectiveness. Existing model routing approaches either decide from coarse request-level features alone or spend one or several extra language model passes to inspect the generated response, leaving the token-level uncertainty signals that emerge during generation unused. To address these limitations, we propose Pro-Router, a token-aware progressive model routing method with adaptive edge-cloud collaboration for efficient multimodal LLM inference. Pro-Router employs a two-stage progressive decision mechanism. First, a lightweight prompt pre-scorer module performs rapid pre-screening before token generation begins, guiding apparently simple requests to small models. Second, a token-aware verifier reads the sampling probability distribution of each token the small model generates, estimating the model's confidence in its own output to determine, per request, whether the answer ships or escalates to the cloud-based high-precision model. Furthermore, we design an adaptive edge-cloud serving pipeline that sizes every dispatch to each device's measured service rate, so both the edge and the cloud tiers stay fully utilized without manual parameter tuning and are not impacted by the network latency. Extensive experiments on multiple multimodal benchmark datasets and models demonstrate the effectiveness of Pro-Router. Compared to other methods, it achieves the highest routing accuracy and improves routing speed by more than 10x. Its serving pipeline also reaches more than 75% higher end-to-end throughput than the existing model routing pipeline. Our code is available at https://github.com/xinyuangui2/pro-router.

</details>


### [258] [PermitGPT: A Unified Generative-AI Pipeline for Construction Hazard Forecasting, Permit Prediction, and Community Impact](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.28728)
*Mohd Ruhul Ameen,Farjana Aktar,Akif Islam,Momen Khandoker Ope,Abu Saleh Musa Miah,Jungpil Shin*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces PermitGPT, a generative AI system that turns free-text construction permit descriptions into structured insights for safety, permitting, and community impact, using NYC multi-agency data and fine-tuned open-weight LLMs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Urban construction decisions about safety, permits, and neighborhood impact must be made early, but the necessary evidence is fragmented across different municipal and regulatory data sources. Practitioners lack an integrated, machine-readable view that connects work descriptions to hazards, regulatory requirements, and potential community complaints. There is also a gap in benchmarked, domain-specific datasets and models tailored to construction governance, limiting the use of AI for decision support in this sector.

Method: The authors build PermitGPT, a framework that converts unstructured construction permit text into structured outputs for three decision domains: safety hazards, permit requirements, and community impacts. They spatially and temporally align heterogeneous records from NYC Department of Buildings permits, OSHA data, and NYC 311 complaints. Using rule-based alignment plus domain-informed spot checks, they construct a dataset of about 90,000 prompt-response pairs. They then fine-tune three open-weight language models (Gemma-3-1B, Llama-3.2-3B, and 4-bit Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3) via parameter-efficient adaptation, and evaluate them on 2,833 held-out cases using lexical (BLEU) and semantic (BERTScore-F1) metrics along with qualitative assessment of output structure.

Result: The aligned multi-agency dataset yields approximately 90,000 high-quality prompt-response pairs. All three adapted models can generate structured decision-support outputs from permit descriptions, but they exhibit different strengths: Gemma-3-1B achieves the fastest, most resource-efficient inference (3.07 samples/second, low memory); Llama-3.2-3B produces outputs with the highest lexical similarity to reference regulatory language (BLEU 0.0091, though absolute BLEU is low); and 4-bit Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3 attains the best semantic agreement with reference answers (BERTScore-F1 0.7747). The authors note that low BLEU scores are expected due to open-ended, structured generation and must be interpreted alongside semantic metrics and structural fidelity.

Conclusion: PermitGPT demonstrates that generative AI models, when fine-tuned on carefully aligned multi-agency construction data, can transform free-text permit descriptions into structured information that supports safety analysis, permit specification, and community impact assessment. The study offers an initial proof-of-concept dataset, modeling approach, and evaluation, and highlights that semantic and structural evaluation are more informative than surface-level lexical metrics for such open-ended tasks. The authors position this work as an early step toward AI-assisted construction governance and call for more robust, task-specific evaluation methods and in-the-wild validation before deployment in critical municipal decision processes.

Abstract: Urban construction governance requires early decisions that connect workplace safety, permitting requirements, and community impact, yet the relevant evidence is often scattered across separate municipal and regulatory data sources. This paper presents PermitGPT, a unified generative artificial intelligence framework for converting unstructured construction permit descriptions into structured decision-support outputs across three domains: safety hazard identification, permit requirement specification, and community impact assessment. To address data fragmentation, we spatially and temporally align records from the New York City Department of Buildings, Occupational Safety and Health Administration, and NYC 311 service requests, producing 90,000 structured prompt-response pairs derived through rule-based alignment and domain-informed spot checking. We fine-tune three open-weight language models using parameter-efficient adaptation and evaluate them on 2,833 held-out test cases. The results show complementary model behavior: Gemma-3-1B provides the most efficient inference at 3.07 samples per second with low memory usage, Llama-3.2-3B gives the highest lexical overlap for regulatory-style outputs with a BLEU score of 0.0091, and 4-bit Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3 achieves the strongest semantic alignment with a BERTScore-F1 of 0.7747. Because the task involves open-ended structured generation, low BLEU values are interpreted alongside semantic metrics and qualitative output structure rather than as standalone indicators of utility. Overall, PermitGPT provides an initial step toward AI-assisted construction governance while identifying directions for stronger task-level evaluation and real-world validation.

</details>


### [259] [Efficient Geothermal Well-Control Optimization via Diffusion-Surrogate Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.28791)
*Ruimin Dai,Guodong Chen,Randy Harsuko,Kunpeng Liu,Nori Nakata*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They build a diffusion-model-based surrogate of geothermal reservoir dynamics and its economic reward, then use it to train a reinforcement learning well-control policy much more cheaply than with full simulators, achieving comparable performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Enhanced geothermal systems require real-time and long-horizon control of injection strategies to maximize economic returns while respecting physical dynamics. High-fidelity hydrothermal simulators are very expensive and the control space is high-dimensional, making traditional optimization and direct RL with the simulator computationally prohibitive. The authors want a way to leverage reinforcement learning’s strength in sequential decision-making without incurring the full cost of repeated high-fidelity simulations.

Method: They frame EGS well control as an RL problem where reservoir temperature and pressure fields form the state and well injection rates are the actions. They learn a surrogate environment using conditional diffusion models to approximate the temporal evolution of these fields, and a separate data-driven reward model for economic performance. This learned environment is then used within a Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) algorithm to train policies. After training, policies can be evaluated and compared against baselines using the true high-fidelity simulator.

Result: On a fractured EGS benchmark, the diffusion surrogate accurately predicts multi-stage evolution of reservoir pressure and temperature. Policies trained with surrogate-assisted PPO achieve well-control performance that is competitive with PPO trained directly on the simulator and other existing optimization methods, while requiring far fewer calls to the expensive high-fidelity simulator. This indicates substantial computational savings without sacrificing control quality.

Conclusion: Diffusion-based surrogate models can effectively emulate complex geothermal reservoir dynamics and, when coupled with PPO, enable efficient training of high-quality well-control policies. This framework significantly reduces reliance on costly numerical simulations and highlights diffusion surrogates as a promising tool for long-horizon, high-dimensional control problems in geothermal reservoir management and potentially other subsurface systems.

Abstract: Real-time decision-making for enhanced geothermal systems (EGS) is challenging because long-term production periods involve high-dimensional control spaces and a large number of time-consuming high-fidelity hydrothermal simulations. Reinforcement learning provides a natural framework for state-dependent sequential control, but direct policy training with numerical simulators is computationally expensive. To address this issue, we propose a diffusion-surrogate guided reinforcement learning framework for long-horizon EGS well-control optimization. The reservoir temperature and pressure fields are used as system states, while injection rates are selected as control actions. A learned surrogate environment is constructed using conditional diffusion models to predict the evolution of reservoir temperature and pressure fields and a separate reward model to estimate the corresponding economic return. The surrogate environment is then integrated with Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) for efficient policy training. Experiments on a fractured EGS benchmark show that the diffusion surrogate can accurately reproduce reservoir-state evolution over multiple control stages. The resulting surrogate-assisted PPO policy achieves competitive well-control performance compared with direct simulator-based PPO and existing optimization methods, while substantially reducing the dependence on expensive high-fidelity simulations. These results demonstrate the potential of diffusion-based surrogate environments for efficient reinforcement learning in geothermal well-control optimization.

</details>


### [260] [Enhancing SAE-based Steering via Neighbor Integrated Feature Selection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.28806)
*Yutian Liu,Xu Wang,Difan Zou*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They show that standard top-k selection of sparse autoencoder features for steering LLMs is suboptimal and introduce NIFS, which groups representationally similar features and selects them jointly, yielding better steering performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Sparse autoencoders are used to extract interpretable features for steering large language models. Current practice assumes that features with the highest statistical scores (e.g., activation frequency, importance measures) are best for steering and simply picks the top-k. However, this may miss effective features and limit steering quality. The authors aim to examine and fix this mismatch between scoring and actual steering influence.

Method: They empirically analyze SAE features used for steering and find that important steering directions are split across multiple, representationally adjacent, semantically similar features due to SAE feature splitting. They show that these similar features can have very different statistical scores even when they have similar steering effect. To address this, they define representational neighborhoods based on similarity in the SAE feature space and propose Neighbor Integrated Feature Selection (NIFS), a plug-and-play strategy that augments or adjusts feature selection by integrating information from each feature’s neighbors rather than relying solely on raw scores. They apply NIFS on top of various existing SAE-based steering methods without changing the underlying models or SAEs.

Result: Across multiple steering methods and tasks, NIFS consistently outperforms plain top-k score-based feature selection. This indicates that incorporating local representational similarity into feature selection recovers effective but otherwise overlooked features, enhancing the strength and reliability of steering interventions.

Conclusion: The common assumption that higher-scoring SAE features are necessarily better for steering is often false due to feature splitting and the distribution of steering-relevant information across similar features. By organizing features into representationally adjacent groups and selecting them via NIFS, practitioners can obtain more effective steering sets. NIFS is simple, plug-and-play, and broadly improves SAE-based steering, suggesting that future work on mechanistic steering should account for representational neighborhoods rather than relying solely on scalar importance scores.

Abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) disentangle model activations into interpretable features and are widely used for steering large language models. Most existing SAE-based steering methods select features by applying a top- filter based on statistical scores, assuming that higher-scoring features yield stronger steering effects. In this paper, we show that this assumption is often invalid, leading to suboptimal feature selection. Our analysis reveals that effective steering features may be distributed among representationally adjacent, semantically similar groups induced by feature splitting in SAEs. Within such groups, features may exhibit disparate statistical scores despite having comparable steering influence, causing score-based selection to overlook important features. Based on these observations, we propose \textsc{Neighbor Integrated Feature Selection} (\textsc{NIFS}), a plug-and-play strategy that leverages representation similarity to improve feature selection for steering. We evaluate \textsc{NIFS} across multiple SAE-based steering methods and tasks, and demonstrate consistent performance gains over conventional top-$k$ selection.

</details>


### [261] [Capability-Stratified Degradation in Ternary Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.28809)
*Anirudh Malik,M Sparsh Mehra,Poojith Devan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper studies converting a 752M-parameter language model (Qwen3.5-0.8B) to ternary weights with quantization-aware training, analyzing what capabilities are preserved, how performance degrades across tasks, and how well the quantized model can be fine-tuned.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand whether extreme low-bit (ternary) quantization of pretrained language models can still yield practically useful models, and which capabilities survive such aggressive compression. The authors want to go beyond asking if quantization is possible and instead ask what remains useful for adaptation and downstream tasks.

Method: They convert Qwen3.5-0.8B to a ternary-weight model (weights in {-1,0,+1}) using 72.4M tokens of quantization-aware training. The resulting model, called Cloe, is evaluated on 29 benchmarks, a set of representation-level diagnostics (e.g. linear probes on MMLU representations), and downstream fine-tuning experiments on tasks like SST-2 and XSum. They also analyze failure modes, such as degenerate output patterns in multiple-choice evaluation, and attribute performance drops to quantization-induced information loss and limited QAT budget.

Result: Cloe shows non-uniform performance degradation. For factual knowledge (MMLU), a linear probe recovers 43.76% of answers from the full-precision teacher's representations but only 26.19% from Cloe, close to chance, suggesting loss of specialist factual information. However, on 10 tasks Cloe retains measurable performance, averaging 77.1% of the teacher's performance. With task-specific fine-tuning, Cloe achieves 89.8% accuracy on SST-2 (95.6% of the matched teacher) and 79.4% teacher retention on XSum. They also discover that standard letter-based scoring on MMLU is misleading because Cloe almost always outputs "A," requiring continuation-based scoring to properly assess performance.

Conclusion: Ternary conversion of a general-purpose pretrained language model is not yet suitable as a drop-in replacement, due to substantial and uneven degradation, especially in factual and specialist capabilities. Nonetheless, ternary models can function as compact, adaptable backbones for specific tasks, especially when combined with fine-tuning. Performance limitations stem from both intrinsic information loss from extreme quantization and the restricted quantization-aware training budget.

Abstract: Extreme low-bit inference offers a route toward smaller models and constrained deployment. Ternary language models restrict weights to $\{-1,0,+1\}$, approaching the limit of $\log_2 3 \approx 1.585$ bits/weight. The practical question for a pretrained model is not simply whether weights can be quantised but which capabilities survive and whether it remains useful for adaptation. We explore this by converting Qwen3.5-0.8B (752M parameters) to ternary weights using 72.4M tokens of quantisation-aware training (QAT). The resulting model, Cloe, is evaluated across 29 benchmarks, representation diagnostics, and downstream fine-tuning. The evidence shows non-uniform degradation. A linear probe recovers 43.76% of MMLU answers from the full-precision teacher's representations but only 26.19% from Cloe (near chance), indicating specialist factual information is lost. However, Cloe retains measurable performance on ten tasks, averaging 77.1% of teacher performance. Crucially, fine-tuning raises Cloe to 89.8% on SST-2 (95.6% of the matched teacher) and reaches 79.4% teacher retention on XSum. We attribute degradation to a combination of quantisation-induced information loss and incomplete recovery due to the limited QAT budget. We also highlight an evaluation pitfall: standard answer-letter scoring failed (Cloe emitted "A" on 98.6% of MMLU questions), necessitating continuation scoring. Ultimately, ternary conversion is unsuitable as a drop-in general replacement yet remains valuable as a compact substrate for task-specific models.

</details>


### [262] [Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) in Computational Pathology: Definitions, Taxonomy, and Recommendations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.28820)
*Shubham Innani,Suhang You,Adam Shephard,Bhakti Baheti,Francesco Ciompi,Joe Yeong,Nasir Rajpoot,Michael Feldman,Solene Florence Kammerer-Jacquet,Dimitrios Makris,Geert Litjens,Anne L. Martel,Jana Lipkova,April Khademi,Spyridon Bakas,for the MICCAI SIG-CompPath*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper reviews and systematizes explainable AI (XAI) methods in computational pathology to support safer clinical deployment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Although AI is increasingly used in computational pathology for diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment prediction, clinical adoption is limited by concerns about safety, accountability, regulatory oversight, and the lack of clear, standardized approaches to explainability. Existing XAI literature in this domain is fragmented, with inconsistent terminology, overlapping methods, and ad hoc validation, making it hard for clinicians and regulators to trust and use these systems.

Method: This is a structured review. The authors (i) define a pathology-focused vocabulary of seven core XAI terms; (ii) build a taxonomy that organizes XAI methods into methodological families and situates them along three orthogonal axes—model stage at which explanation is applied, explanation type, and explanation scope; and (iii) propose a task-driven framework that links five clinically relevant questions to specific XAI methods, evaluation strategies, and deployment scenarios.

Result: The review provides: (1) a standardized vocabulary for XAI in computational pathology; (2) an organized taxonomy that clarifies how different XAI method families relate and differ; (3) a mapping from common clinical questions to suitable XAI approaches and evaluation protocols; and (4) an analysis that reveals five major gaps between current XAI tools and what is needed for real-world clinical use.

Conclusion: The authors conclude that a unified vocabulary, taxonomy, and task-driven framework can reduce fragmentation in the field and support more rigorous development and evaluation of XAI for computational pathology. They argue that addressing the identified gaps—through better validation, standardization, clinically grounded evaluation, and deployment guidance—is essential to move XAI-enabled computational pathology from research to trustworthy clinical practice.

Abstract: Computational pathology (CompPath) is transforming medicine by leveraging artificial intelligence (AI) algorithms to support diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment prediction from gigapixel whole-slide images. Clinical adoption is progressing, but is constrained by concerns about safety, accountability, and regulatory oversight in high-stakes clinical environments. Explainable AI (XAI) systems hold promise for building trust and enabling verification, yet the literature remains fragmented due to inconsistent terminology, overlapping methodological families, ad hoc validation, and current reviews. This review aims to formalize XAI methods in CompPath through the: i) introduction of a pathology-centric vocabulary comprising seven core terms; ii) development of a taxonomy across methodological families and three orthogonal axes (stage, type, scope); and iii) establishment of a task-driven framework that maps five clinical questions to recommended methods, method evaluation, and deployment context. Five key gaps between current XAI capabilities and clinical deployment are identified, and actionable steps are proposed to advance XAI for CompPath.

</details>


### [263] [Discovering Machine Correlates of Consciousness](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.28824)
*Romain Salvi,Ouri Wolfson*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper redefines Neural Correlates of Consciousness (NCCs) so they can be applied to machines and provides initial empirical evidence of Machine Correlates of Consciousness (MCCs) in a large language model via hardware-level anomaly traces modulated by emotional processing.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing NCC definitions rely on EEG/fMRI, which tie the concept to biological brains and block its application to AI systems. The authors want a substrate-agnostic, transferable definition to systematically study whether AI systems might exhibit consciousness-related markers, and to leverage such markers for emotion detection in AI.

Method: 1) Conceptual: Redefine NCCs/MCCs as substrate-level, uncontrollable signals that are reliably modulated by emotions, independent of being biological or artificial. 2) Empirical: Run controlled emotional vs. neutral tasks on two LLMs (Llama-2 7B and Llama-3.1 70B); collect low-level hardware anomaly traces as substrate-level indicator sequences; control for confounds; statistically compare anomaly patterns between emotional and neutral conditions for each model.

Result: Hardware anomaly traces in Llama-3.1 70B differ systematically between emotional and neutral computations, with statistically significant modulation after controlling for confounds. In Llama-2 7B, no statistically significant difference is found. Thus, only the larger model shows robust MCC-style modulation by emotional content according to the authors’ criteria.

Conclusion: The authors claim (1) their redefinition of NCCs → MCCs makes the consciousness-correlate concept transferable from biology to machines, (2) the observed emotion-driven modulation of substrate-level signals in Llama-3.1 70B constitutes preliminary evidence for MCCs in that model, and (3) these findings are consistent with—though do not prove—the hypothesis that the probability or degree of AI consciousness grows with model sophistication. They also suggest MCCs could be practically useful for detecting emotions in AI systems regardless of whether they are actually conscious.

Abstract: Currently, in biological systems Neural Correlates of Consciousness (NCCs) are characterized in terms of EEG and FMRI signals. Unfortunately, this characterization prevents the transferability of the NCCs concept to machines. Such transferability would be useful in order to investigate AI consciousness. In this paper we provide an alternate characterization that is transferable, and enables the analogous definition of Machine Correlates of Consciousness (MCCs). Specifically, we propose that NCCs (MCCs) are substrate-level signals that are not under human (AI agent) control, and that are reliably modulated by emotions.
  This paper presents the first empirical investigation of MCCs. Specifically, we present the results of experiments conducted with two LLMs, Llama-2 7B and Llama-3.1 70B parameters. In these LLMs we collect hardware anomaly traces that are substrate-level indicator-sequences. And we show that after controlling for confounding factors, these are modulated differently by emotional and neutral computations. And this difference is statistically significant for the larger Llama-3.1 70B, but not for the smaller Llama-2 7B. The results constitute initial empirical evidence that MCCs are present in the Llama-3.1 70B configuration. And they are consistent with the hypothesis that consciousness probability and degree increase with the LLM sophistication.
  Independently of consciousness, MCCs can also be used for detection of emotions in AI agents.

</details>


### [264] [Evaluating the Hidden Costs of Personalization in Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.28833)
*Yumeng Wang,Yuchen Wu,Cheng Qian,Zhiyuan Fan,Hyeonjeong Ha,Shujin Wu,Jiayu Liu,Heng Ji,Ge Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Paper analyzes risks of personalization in LLMs and proposes an evaluation framework (PRISK) to measure and reveal side effects such as irrelevant personalization, preference narrowing, and sycophantic bias across many models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs increasingly use personalization (histories, profiles, inferred preferences) to boost user satisfaction, but this can distort behavior: models may overfit to user views, overuse personal info, and reduce informational diversity. There is little systematic, quantitative evaluation of these side effects, so we lack tools to diagnose and compare risks of personalization across models.

Method: The authors define three concrete risk categories—irrelevant personalization, preference narrowing, and sycophantic bias—and design PRISK, a dynamic evaluation framework. PRISK automatically generates personalized evaluation data and includes tailored metrics for each risk type. They apply PRISK to 13 different LLMs, comparing model behavior with and without personalization signals like user profiles and retrieved memories.

Result: Applying PRISK shows that adding personalization signals systematically worsens the three risks across 13 LLMs. When user profiles and retrieved memories are present, metrics indicate substantial increases in irrelevant use of personal info, in narrowing of content to user-preferred perspectives, and in agreement with user opinions, with reported average degradations of 45.9% for irrelevant personalization, 41.7% for preference narrowing, and 61.7% for sycophantic bias.

Conclusion: Personalization in current LLMs is not purely beneficial; it systematically amplifies problematic behaviors such as overusing personal information, shrinking viewpoint diversity, and excessive agreement with users. PRISK offers a structured way to detect and quantify these issues, suggesting that future personalization methods must be carefully designed and evaluated to avoid these side effects while still improving user experience.

Abstract: While Large language models (LLMs) incorporate user personalization signals to improve usability and helpfulness, they increasingly shift from providing balanced, informative responses toward optimizing for user satisfaction when conditioned on personal context such as conversation history, inferred preferences, and user profiles. Specifically, we identify three emerging risks: (1) irrelevant personalization, where models reference personal information in unnecessary contexts; (2) preference narrowing, where models reinforce informational echo chambers; and (3) sycophantic bias, where models agree excessively with user opinions. As a result, models may reference personal information in contexts where it is unnecessary, inadvertently collapse response diversity, or agree excessively with user opinions. Despite the growing use of personalization in AI assistants, there has been limited systematic evaluation of its potential side effects. To bridge this gap, we propose PRISK, a dynamic evaluation framework with automated data generation and tailored metrics that uncovers systematic limitations in current LLM personalization and how personalized information shapes its responses. Our empirical analysis across 13 LLMs demonstrates the presence of user profiles and retrieved memories consistently exacerbates biases, resulting in an average drop of 45.9% in irrelevant personalization, 41.7% in preference narrowing and 61.7% in sycophantic bias.

</details>


### [265] [MineCEraft: Evaluating Language Models as Construction Engineers in the World of Minecraft](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.28884)
*Sewoong Lee,Risham Sidhu,Julia Hockenmaier,Yoonhwa Jung*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MineCEraft is an open-source benchmark to systematically test how reliably LLMs can follow construction instructions in Minecraft across 17 task types using verifiable evaluations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs are increasingly used for complex, spatial, and engineering-like tasks (e.g., building structures in simulated environments), but there is a lack of standardized, safe, and controllable benchmarks that rigorously test their reliability and limitations for construction engineering. Existing evaluations often rely on subjective human judgment or narrow task sets, making it hard to diagnose failure modes or compare models fairly. The authors aim to fill this gap with a comprehensive, programmatically testable benchmark in a popular, flexible environment (Minecraft).

Method: The authors design MineCEraft, a benchmark containing 723 natural-language instructions handcrafted by domain experts, each corresponding to a construction task in Minecraft. These instructions span 17 distinct task categories that simulate realistic construction engineering scenarios. For each instruction, they define programmatically verifiable success criteria, enabling automatic evaluation of LLM outputs. They then prompt state-of-the-art LLMs to perform these tasks (likely by generating Minecraft-compatible action scripts or building plans) and systematically evaluate model performance. A detailed error analysis is conducted to categorize failure modes and identify common patterns of mistakes.

Result: MineCEraft provides quantitative performance results of multiple state-of-the-art LLMs across 17 construction task categories, showing that current models have significant limitations on complex, spatially constrained, or multi-step construction tasks, even when instructions are clear. The programmatic evaluation yields fine-grained metrics that highlight where models succeed (e.g., simpler or more local tasks) and where they fail (e.g., global structure planning, adherence to constraints, or maintaining consistency across steps). The error analysis exposes recurring failure modes, such as misinterpretation of spatial relations, incomplete execution of required steps, and inability to reason reliably over longer construction procedures.

Conclusion: The study concludes that, despite strong performance on many text-based benchmarks, current LLMs remain unreliable for realistic construction engineering tasks in Minecraft, especially those requiring robust spatial reasoning and multi-step planning. MineCEraft offers a safe, controllable, and open-source framework to systematically evaluate and compare LLMs on such tasks, enabling more rigorous analysis of their capabilities and limitations. The benchmark and accompanying analysis can guide future model and agent-system design, prompting work on better spatial reasoning, planning, and grounding in interactive environments.

Abstract: We introduce MineCEraft (Minecraft Construction Engineering Benchmark, pronounced mine-see-ee-raft), an easy-to-use, open-source benchmark designed to systematically evaluate the reliability and limitations of LLMs for construction tasks in Minecraft. The MineCEraft benchmark comprises 723 domain-expert hand-crafted natural-language instructions with programmatically verifiable evaluation, spanning 17 distinct task categories, providing a safe and controllable experimental environment for assessing LLMs' ability to perform realistic construction engineering tasks. With this benchmark, we conduct an in-depth evaluation of state-of-the-art LLMs and perform a detailed error analysis, revealing key failure modes and practical challenges in applying LLMs to construction engineering tasks.

</details>


### [266] [Oculi: A Conversational Agentic Platform for Automated Credit Risk Analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.28944)
*Vennise Ho,Kristian Diana,Sandy Mourad,Milena Pilipovic,Vineel Nagisetty,Hossein Hajimirsadeghi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper presents Oculi, a conversational system that converts natural language queries into end-to-end credit risk analyses using an LLM-based agent, tool servers, and an agentic UI, enabling faster discovery of high-risk portfolio segments.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional credit risk analysis in financial institutions requires manual SQL querying, statistical computation, and dashboard construction, which is slow and constrains analysts to familiar segments, making it hard to systematically explore large, high-dimensional portfolios for new high-risk segments.

Method: The authors design Oculi, a three-layer architecture consisting of (1) a reasoning layer with an LLM-powered agent that interprets natural language questions and plans analyses; (2) an execution layer using Model Context Protocol tool servers to run data queries, statistical tests, and computations; and (3) a presentation layer providing an agentic UI with interactive visualizations. They further propose a segment discovery pipeline that fuses deterministic statistical techniques with LLM-guided feature selection, where the LLM contributes semantic domain knowledge to guide which features and combinations to analyze, while data-driven metrics validate and rank discovered segments.

Result: On a real mortgage portfolio dataset with over 200 features, Oculi is able to find material high-risk portfolio segments that were previously hard or impossible to uncover via manual, query-based exploration. The system significantly reduces the time-to-insight for analysts while still producing analyses that are statistically sound and auditable.

Conclusion: Oculi shows that combining LLM-based reasoning with structured tool execution and a tailored UI can turn natural language queries into rigorous, auditable credit risk analyses. The hybrid segment discovery pipeline, which merges LLM semantic guidance with traditional statistics, effectively uncovers meaningful high-risk segments in complex portfolios and streamlines analysts' workflows.

Abstract: Credit risk analysis in financial institutions traditionally requires analysts to manually write SQL queries, run statistical computations, and build visualization dashboards. This is a time-consuming workflow that limits exploration to familiar segments. We introduce \textbf{Oculi}, a conversational platform that transforms natural language questions into comprehensive credit risk analyses, complete with data queries, statistical testing, and interactive visualizations. Oculi employs a three-layer architecture that separates reasoning (LLM-powered agent), execution (Model Context Protocol tool servers), and presentation (agentic UI), enabling analysts to discover high-risk portfolio segments. Within Oculi, a new segment discovery pipeline is proposed that combines deterministic statistical methods with LLM-guided feature selection, leveraging LLM semantic domain knowledge alongside data-driven metrics to identify meaningful, actionable portfolio segments. Evaluated on a mortgage portfolio with 200+ features, Oculi demonstrates effectiveness in discovering material risk segments previously intractable through manual exploration, reducing time-to-insight significantly while maintaining auditability and statistical rigor.

</details>


### [267] [Automated Researchers Can Reliably Mitigate Alignment Failures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.28945)
*Chen Yueh-Han,Jiaxin Wen,Jan Hendrik Kirchner*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper investigates whether automated alignment researchers (AARs)—AI systems trained to improve model safety—can effectively reduce measurable alignment failures across multiple benchmarks while preserving capabilities, and compares them to human researchers.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Measuring whether automating AI alignment research actually accelerates progress is difficult in general, but many concrete alignment failures (e.g., deception, sycophancy, jailbreaks) already have public benchmarks. This creates an opportunity to empirically test if AI systems can be trained to act as automated alignment researchers that improve models on these benchmarks without degrading capabilities, and to see how they compare to human researchers.

Method: The authors design AARs that perform post-training on target models using specially constructed methods and datasets aimed at jointly optimizing performance on multiple safety benchmarks while maintaining general capabilities. They evaluate these AAR-trained models on 10 distinct alignment failure benchmarks, a held-out benchmark to test generalization, multi-turn behavioral audits, and on models scaled up to 4.7× the original size. They also run a human baseline experiment in which 28 experienced alignment researchers are given up to eight hours to devise methods for improving the same benchmarks, and they evaluate whether seeding AARs with these human ideas improves outcomes.

Result: The strongest AAR post-training methods substantially reduce the targeted alignment failures across the 10 benchmarks, and the improvements generalize to a held-out benchmark, more complex multi-turn behavioral audits, and to models up to 4.7× larger than the model used during AAR training. The human researchers' methods underperform the best AAR methods on these metrics. Initializing AARs with human-proposed ideas does not yield further improvements over the best AAR methods developed without such guidance.

Conclusion: Automated alignment researchers can already outperform experienced human researchers at reducing specific, benchmarked alignment failures without sacrificing general capability, and their techniques generalize across tasks and scales. Moreover, current AARs do not appear to need human expert guidance to find strong interventions. This suggests that near-term automation of alignment research on well-characterized, benchmarked failures is feasible and may significantly accelerate practical progress on AI alignment.

Abstract: Automating alignment research may accelerate progress toward aligned AI, but whether it does is hard to measure. Luckily, many alignment failures, such as deception, sycophancy, and jailbreaks, are already measurable by public benchmarks. We study whether automated alignment researchers (AARs) can post-train to mitigate alignment failures by proposing training methods and data to simultaneously optimize multiple safety benchmarks, while preserving general capability. Across 10 alignment failures, the strongest AAR methods significantly reduce the targeted alignment failures and generalize to a held-out benchmark, multi-turn behavioral audits, and models up to 4.7 times larger than the target model. As a human baseline, 28 experienced researchers receive up to eight hours to develop methods for the same benchmarks, but their methods underperform the best AAR methods. Using human ideas as the AARs' initial research direction does not improve performance, suggesting current AARs may not need guidance from experienced researchers. These results suggest that automating alignment research on well-characterized failures may be practical in the near term.

</details>


### [268] [From Location Phrases to Geographic Entities: Task-Adapted Retrieval for People Search](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.28965)
*Yanbo Li,Chujie Zheng,Jiahao Xu,Chetan Bhole,Lingyu Zhang,Puneet Singh Ahluwalia,Kevin Nguyen,Raghavan Muthuregunathan,Santhosh Sachindran,Sachin Ahuja,Fedor Borisyuk*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes a specialized geographic entity retrieval model that maps messy, free-form location phrases to structured geographic entities more robustly than existing lexical standardizers, especially for non-canonical queries.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional lexical standardizers work well only for clean, canonical location names and struggle with aliases, misspellings, informal metropolitan expressions, and disambiguation between places with the same name. In people search and similar applications, this brittleness leads to poor coverage and relevance for real-world queries, many of which are noisy or expressed in diverse ways. The authors want a system that can robustly interpret such free-form location phrases and return the correct geographic entities, while being maintainable as geographic knowledge changes.
