Method: They reformulate location normalization as graded, set-valued entity retrieval over a fixed geographic ontology, rather than strict string matching. They then design a prompt-asymmetric bi-encoder architecture where queries and entities are encoded differently, add calibrated support for aliases, construct ambiguity-aware negative examples to avoid over-penalizing valid same-name entities, and represent entities as editable documents so that local knowledge updates can be made without retraining the whole model. The training uses specialized supervision signals tailored to these design goals, beyond standard task fine-tuning.

Result: On both an internal production-like development benchmark and a public GeoNames transfer task, the adapted model significantly outperforms frozen encoders and token-based baselines. Ablation studies indicate that the specialized supervision and architecture provide gains beyond just scaling or generic fine-tuning. On GeoNames, the model improves Recall@1 for known targets across zero-to-moderate character overlap, though character n-grams still have a slight edge in overall Target Recall@5. In a blinded human evaluation on a difficult, stratified production challenge set, the model increases relevant P@1 from 28.0% to 46.0% with statistical significance. In fixed-query and live experiments, it improves performance on non-canonical queries without harming user engagement or frequent-query behavior.

Conclusion: Task-adapted geographic entity retrieval using their bi-encoder architecture is a practical drop-in replacement for an existing taxonomy-based lexical standardizer. It yields especially large relevance improvements on messy, non-canonical location queries, remains competitive on frequent canonical queries, and supports maintainable updates to geographic knowledge without full retraining.

Abstract: People search must map free-form location phrases to geographic entities used as structured retrieval filters. Lexical standardizers handle canonical names well but are brittle to aliases, misspellings, metropolitan expressions, and same-name ambiguity. We formulate this task as graded, set-valued entity retrieval over a fixed ontology. We identify three coupled design requirements: distinguishing identity-preserving variation from knowledge-dependent aliases, controlling false negatives among valid same-name entities, and separating stable transformations from mutable entity knowledge. We realize them in a prompt-asymmetric bi-encoder with calibrated alias support, bounded ambiguity-aware negatives, and editable entity documents that support localized updates without retraining.
  Across a fixed production-derived development benchmark and a public GeoNames transfer task, task adaptation improves substantially over frozen encoders and standard token baselines. Controlled development ablations show that specialized supervision contributes beyond standard task fine-tuning and encoder scaling. On GeoNames, the adapted model improves known-target Recall@1 throughout zero-to-moderate character overlap, while character n-grams retain a small aggregate Target Recall@5 advantage. In a blinded human comparison on a stratified production challenge set, our model raises relevant P@1 from 28.0% to 46.0% (p=0.012). Fixed-query endpoint estimates improve on non-canonical queries and remain close to control on frequent queries; a randomized live experiment detects no engagement regression. These results support task-adapted geographic entity retrieval as a practical replacement for the incumbent taxonomy-based standardizer, with the largest relevance gains on non-canonical queries.

</details>


### [269] [Efficient GPU Retrieval for Semantic Search](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.28968)
*Dhritiman Das,Chujie Zheng,Ronak Kaoshik,Pratik Dixit,Vishal Shah,Yanbo Li,Jiahao Xu,Manika Agarwal,Chinmay Naik,Lingyu Zhang,Chetan Bhole,Chirag Bhanuprasad Mehta,Meng Zheng,Puneet Singh Ahluwalia,Shirisha Singh,Ping Jin,Manas Apte,Gokulraj Mohanasundaram,Tugrul Bingol,Raghavan Muthuregunathan,Fedor Borisyuk*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes a policy-aligned, facet-aware embedding and retrieval framework for LinkedIn semantic search, combined with a two-stage low-precision GPU serving stack, significantly improving precision and throughput while matching an existing LLM-based graded relevance policy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LinkedIn semantic search must handle natural-language queries that implicitly specify multiple non-negotiable facets (e.g., role, industry, location, domain experience) over hundreds of millions of profiles. The existing relevance policy is bottleneck-oriented—every active facet must be satisfied—and operationalized by an LLM Graded Relevance judge that aggregates facet grades via min/median. Standard embedding-based cosine similarity instead averages signal, letting strong evidence on one facet compensate for weakness on another. This mismatch between policy and similarity scoring harms recall in the first-stage retriever and limits end-to-end relevance, motivating a retrieval approach that is explicitly aligned with the graded, facet-wise relevance policy and that can scale efficiently on large GPU infrastructure.

Method: The authors design a policy-aligned representation where each embedding is partitioned into eight supervised segments, each corresponding to a semantic category (facet). At serving time, segment scores are combined using the same min/median aggregation rule used by the LLM Graded Relevance judge, ensuring alignment with the bottleneck-oriented policy. For multi-vector (multi-slot) document representations, they compute a segment score independently for each tagged document slot and then take the maximum across slots, capturing the best matching evidence per category. They introduce a lightweight single-slot Stage-1 scorer for high-recall candidate generation, along with scale-invariant relative-norm gating to keep facet activations stable across training, offline evaluation, and production serving. For serving, they deploy a two-stage GPU architecture: a first FP8 coarse ranker that scores the entire corpus, improving per-shard capacity and matrix-multiply throughput, followed by a second FP16 re-ranker that exactly re-scores an oversampled candidate subset, thus recovering near-FP16 recall at lower cost.

Result: On a held-out set of 21K queries, the proposed representation outperforms a capacity-matched baseline in offline relevance metrics, with improvements appearing across diverse facet combinations, indicating that the gains are not confined to a narrow query type. In live production, using a member-randomized A/B test and keeping the existing LLM Graded Relevance judge unchanged, exploratory-query Precision@10 increases from 63.7% to 79.0% and navigational Precision@1 from 65.5% to 74.7%. The two-stage FP8/FP16 GPU stack attains over 500 QPS per shard replica and recovers 99.6–99.8% of the recall of a full-FP16 system, while enlarging per-shard capacity by 71% and Stage-1 matmul throughput by 36%. A blinded human evaluation independently validates the Precision@10 improvement, supporting that the gains reflect true relevance improvements.

Conclusion: Aligning the embedding structure and retrieval scoring with an existing facet-wise, bottleneck-oriented graded relevance policy yields substantial gains in both offline and online relevance for LinkedIn semantic search. Category-supervised segmented embeddings with min/median aggregation respect non-compensatory facet requirements, enabling higher recall and better satisfaction of complex natural-language queries. The multi-vector slot-wise max aggregation and relative-norm gating provide robustness across training and deployment. Coupled with an efficient two-stage FP8/FP16 GPU architecture, this framework scales to hundreds of millions of profiles while maintaining near-FP16 recall and delivering large improvements in Precision@K and system throughput. The approach demonstrates that policy-aligned representation learning and hardware-aware serving can jointly unlock meaningful real-world search quality gains.

Abstract: Semantic Search on LinkedIn must retrieve relevant profiles from a corpus of hundreds of millions in response to natural-language queries such as "a fintech founder in Berlin who worked in payments." The deployed relevance policy is bottleneck-oriented: every active non-negotiable facet must be satisfied, and a pre-existing LLM Graded Relevance (GR) judge operationalizes this through a fixed min/median aggregation over facet grades. Cosine similarity instead averages evidence, letting a strong match on one facet mask failure on another, capping the recall of the first-stage (L0) retriever.
  We present a policy-aligned retrieval framework: embeddings are partitioned into eight category-supervised segments whose scores follow the same min/median rule at serving time; for multi-vector retrieval, this segment score is computed independently per tagged document slot and maximized across slots. A lightweight single-slot Stage-1 scorer generates high-recall candidates, while scale-invariant relative-norm gating keeps category activation consistent across training, evaluation, and serving. On 21K held-out queries, this representation improves offline relevance over a matched-capacity baseline, with gains broadly distributed across facet combinations.
  We serve this framework with a two-stage GPU architecture: an FP8 coarse ranker scores the full corpus, increasing per-shard capacity by 71% and Stage-1 matmul throughput by 36%, then an FP16 stage exactly re-ranks an oversampled candidate set, recovering 99.6-99.8% of full-FP16 recall at over 500 QPS per shard replica. In a member-randomized A/B test, exploratory-query Precision@10 under the unchanged GR judge rises from 63.7% to 79.0% and navigational Precision@1 from 65.5% to 74.7%, with a blinded human evaluation independently confirming the Precision@10 gain.

</details>


### [270] [From Analytics to Tumor Boards: An Evidence-Linked Multi-Agent Workflow for Oncology Feature Extraction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.28974)
*Daniel Kang,Michelle Hu,Soorya Ram Shimgekar,Shayan Vassef,Yufan Wang,Anit Kumar Sahu,Munmun De Choudhury,Vedant Das Swain,Christian Poellabauer,Li Yan Khor,Koustuv Saha,Robert Wojciechowski,Elliot Kidd,Piyum Zonooz,Navin Kumar*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper presents and evaluates Nimblemind Multi-Agent System (nMAS), an AI-driven, configurable workflow that accurately extracts structured oncology data from fragmented clinical documents, outperforming a strong comparator and showing promise for scalable cancer-registry abstraction.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Oncology information is scattered across many heterogeneous, longitudinal clinical documents (e.g., pathology reports, progress notes), making manual abstraction time-consuming (27.2 minutes per case) and error-prone, especially when maintaining correct attribution across specimens, tumors, biomarkers, and time points. There is a need for scalable, automated methods that can convert this fragmented narrative documentation into high-quality structured data while preserving clinical context and traceability to sources, to support cancer registries, analytics, and downstream clinical applications.

Method: The authors design and implement the Nimblemind Multi-Agent System (nMAS), a configurable information-extraction workflow tailored to oncology. Using a clinician-informed schema with 328 attributes (covering report metadata, diagnosis, staging, and cancer-type-specific data), nMAS separates clinician-defined field specifications from model execution. The workflow employs complexity-aware extraction strategies, consolidates data at the report level, and performs source-grounded validation (retaining links to original text). In a retrospective evaluation, they applied nMAS to 230 de-identified oncology documents from 40 patients and created 418 clinician-reviewed document–field pairs with 1,126 non-empty reference values. They focused annotation only on fields that clinicians confirmed were present, not the entire schema. Performance was compared to an independently implemented UMA-style MiniMax M2.5 system using value-level, rank-weighted precision, recall, and F1.

Result: On the curated set of 418 document–field pairs and 1,126 non-empty reference values, nMAS achieved a rank-weighted value-level precision of 82.6%, recall of 87.5%, and F1 score of 85.0%. The comparator system (UMA-style MiniMax M2.5) attained a substantially lower F1 score of 66.4%, indicating that nMAS provides markedly better extraction quality under the same evaluation framework.

Conclusion: The study demonstrates that a configurable, source-grounded multi-agent extraction workflow can effectively transform fragmented oncology documentation into reusable structured data with high precision and recall. By separating clinical schema design from model execution and incorporating complexity-aware extraction and validation, nMAS substantially outperforms a strong baseline and appears feasible for scaling and improving cancer-registry abstraction and other oncology data-use cases.

Abstract: Clinically relevant oncology information is distributed across heterogeneous, longitudinal documentation, creating substantial abstraction burden and requiring accurate attribution across specimens, tumors, biomarkers, and time points, while manual cancer-registry abstraction can require 27.2 minutes per case, highlighting the need for scalable methods that preserve clinical context while converting documentation into structured data. We evaluate the Nimblemind Multi-Agent System (nMAS), a configurable oncology information-extraction workflow which extracts clinically relevant structured fields from fragmented oncology documentation. The extraction task uses a clinician-informed schema of 328 attributes spanning report metadata, diagnosis, staging, and cancer-type-specific information. nMAS separates clinician-defined field specifications from model execution and combines complexity-aware extraction, report-level consolidation, and source-grounded validation. The retrospective evaluation included 230 de-identified oncology documents from 40 patients and 418 clinician-reviewed document-field pairs containing 1,126 non-empty reference values. Evaluation focused on fields identified by clinicians as present in the source documents rather than exhaustively annotating all 328 schema fields. nMAS achieved a rank-weighted value-level precision of 82.6%, recall of 87.5%, and F1 of 85.0%, compared with an F1 of 66.4% for an independently implemented UMA-style MiniMax M2.5 comparator. These findings support the feasibility of using a configurable, source-grounded extraction workflow to convert fragmented oncology documentation into reusable structured data.

</details>


### [271] [The Role of Network Topology and Opponent Information in Shaping Cooperation in Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.28977)
*Seongho Son,Stephen Hailes,Mirco Musolesi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Study of how graph topology and opponent information affect emergence of cooperation in multi-agent deep reinforcement learning playing Iterated Prisoner’s Dilemma.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Most prior work on networked cooperation assumes simple strategy imitation based on observed payoffs, which does not match modern learning agents that use reinforcement learning and local information. It is unclear how graph structure and informational cues (history, identity) shape cooperation when agents learn with powerful function approximators.

Method: Model each agent as a deep RL learner (for IPD) placed on a node of a graph. Neighbours are possible opponents. Vary graph topologies (and thus degree and average path length). Provide agents with different observation sets: action history only, or action history plus opponent identity. Run many training episodes, measure cooperation levels under each condition, and analyze how structural and informational factors impact emergent behaviours. Also include a partner-selection mechanism where agents can choose among neighbours, effectively reducing diversity of opponents.

Result: Across tested graphs, the most predictive structural properties for cooperation are the number of neighbours per node and the graph’s average path length. Denser local neighbourhoods and shorter/longer paths (as characterized in the paper) systematically modulate cooperation rates. Partner selection increases mutual cooperation by restricting the diversity of actual opponents. Conversely, when agents are given explicit opponent identities in their observations, cooperation spreads less and selfish strategies become more prevalent.

Conclusion: Graph topology critically shapes cooperative outcomes for deep RL agents in IPD, with degree and average path length being key features. Mechanisms that narrow the effective opponent set (partner selection) promote cooperation, while richer opponent-specific information (identity) can paradoxically undermine it. This indicates that, for learning agents, both structural and informational design choices substantially affect whether cooperative conventions emerge in multi-agent systems.

Abstract: Several works have investigated the influence of graph topology on cooperation among artificial agents, while the majority of the literature has focused on modelling agents' adaptation through strategy imitation, which relies solely on the cumulative payoffs of others. This paper investigates scenarios in which each agent learns to play the two-player Iterated Prisoner's Dilemma (IPD) using deep reinforcement learning. Each agent is represented as a node in a graph, where its neighbours constitute the pool of opponents with whom it can interact. During each IPD episode, agents are provided with different types of information about their opponent, consisting of action history and opponent identity. Experimental results across different graph topologies show that the number of neighbours per node and the average path length are the main factors affecting the emergence of cooperation. We also show that, while partner selection fosters mutual cooperation by limiting the diversity of the opponent pool, providing agents with the identity of their opponent hinders the proliferation of cooperative strategies.

</details>


### [272] [Selective Forgetting: A Graph-Based Memory Framework for Long-Term LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.28978)
*Theo Rusu,Sourena Khanzadeh,Manar Alalfi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper tests whether knowledge-graph-based long-term memory actually helps over flat vector retrieval, and finds that it does not on a standard benchmark, though a simple forgetting/pruning module works well.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Retrieval-augmented generation systems need effective long-term memory. Knowledge graphs are often proposed as a superior, structured memory compared to flat vector stores, but their assumed benefits for recall and reasoning have not been rigorously tested against strong vector baselines under matched retrieval budgets.

Method: They build a pipeline that: (1) converts each conversational turn into a set of typed entity nodes and attributed relation edges; (2) answers questions using information from a two-hop subgraph around a small set of retrieved root nodes; and (3) periodically prunes graph nodes according to a weighted score combining recency, access frequency, degree centrality, and age. They evaluate this graph-based memory system on the LongMemEval benchmark, comparing it to a flat vector retrieval baseline with the same candidate-generation budget, and perform statistical tests (paired bootstrap) to quantify performance differences and the impact of pruning.

Result: At the same retrieval budget (five roots), the knowledge graph underperforms the flat vector baseline: token F1 of 0.417 vs 0.468, with a paired bootstrap difference of -0.050 (95% CI [-0.085, -0.016]). The largest performance drop occurs on questions that need recalling an exact prior assistant turn: judged correctness drops from 0.911 to 0.607, indicating that turn decomposition into entities loses crucial surface-form information. In contrast, the forgetting/pruning module removes 9.8% of nodes and 9.5% of bytes from a 27,021-node persistent graph with essentially no degradation: token F1 changes by +0.001 (95% CI [-0.015, +0.016]) and judged correctness decreases by only 1.6 points, with the 95% CI limiting potential loss to 3.8 points ([-0.038, +0.006]).

Conclusion: For this specific extraction-based knowledge-graph pipeline, graph-structured conversational memory does not outperform a strong flat vector baseline at equal retrieval budgets and can be especially harmful when questions require verbatim recall of prior turns. However, a simple, graph-based forgetting mechanism can significantly shrink memory with negligible performance loss. These findings apply to the tested setup (a single small extractor model and one benchmark) and do not rule out benefits from alternative graph representations, extractors, or retrieval strategies; they mainly caution against assuming that naïve KG extraction automatically improves long-term agent memory over well-tuned vector retrieval.

Abstract: Knowledge graphs have been proposed as a structured alternative to flat retrieval-augmented generation for long-term agent memory, on the assumption that representing conversations as entities and relations improves recall. We evaluate that assumption directly. Our framework extracts each conversational turn into typed nodes and attributed edges, answers questions from a two-hop subgraph, and periodically prunes nodes that score low on a weighted combination of recency, access frequency, degree centrality, and age. On LongMemEval, the graph does not outperform a flat vector baseline at a matched candidate-generation budget of five retrieval roots: token F1 is $0.417$ against $0.468$, and a paired bootstrap over 500 questions gives
$Δ= -0.050$ (95\% CI $[-0.085, -0.016]$). The gap is widest on questions that require recalling a specific prior assistant turn, where judged correctness falls from $0.911$ to $0.607$, suggesting that decomposing a turn into entities discards the surface form these questions depend on. The forgetting module is more successful. Applied once to a persistent 27{,}021-node graph, it removes 9.8\% of nodes and 9.5\% of stored bytes; token F1 is unchanged ($+0.001$, 95\% CI $[-0.015, +0.016]$) and judged correctness falls by $1.6$ points, with the 95\% interval bounding any loss at $3.8$ points ($[-0.038, +0.006]$). Because our extractor is a single small model evaluated on one benchmark, these results characterise this extraction-based pipeline rather than graph-structured memory in general. Code: https://github.com/skhanzad/Selective-Amnesia

</details>


### [273] [Agentic AI uncovers conserved cross-tissue protein co-abundance programs inaccessible to single-dataset analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.28990)
*Runyu Guan,Dehao Wu,Qiqi Xie,Yang Li,Haohan Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They build an LLM-based agent pipeline to systematically compare protein co-abundance networks across 41 human tissues, discovering thousands of conserved protein clusters that suggest shared mechanisms and therapeutic targets across organs, including unexpected tissue relationships and mechanistic axes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Shared disease mechanisms and drug targets can be reflected in protein co-abundance patterns that are conserved across tissues, especially when organ-specific disease proteins show coordinated behavior in accessible tissues like blood or CSF. Prior work largely examined a few hand-picked tissue pairs, missing the broader landscape and non-obvious cross-tissue relationships. There is a need for a scalable, systematic, and evidence-grounded way to compare tissue-specific protein networks across many tissues and to interpret conserved clusters mechanistically.

Method: They design an LLM-agent framework that: (1) constructs tissue-specific protein co-abundance networks; (2) computes pairwise consensus co-abundance clusters between every pair of 41 human tissues/fluids (820 combinations); and (3) automatically integrates multiple evidence sources—expression atlases, protein–protein interaction and complex databases, pathway annotations, disease catalogs, and literature—so the LLM can interpret and label conserved clusters. The framework then ranks tissues and tissue pairs by the number and character of conserved co-abundance clusters and performs cluster-level functional/disease interpretation to generate mechanistic hypotheses.

Result: Across 820 tissue-pair comparisons, the framework identified 1,833 conserved co-abundance clusters across 406 tissue pairs. Certain tissues (colon, synovial fluid, blood, cerebrospinal fluid, bone marrow) exhibited broad connectivity, while bone marrow-dominated pairs had the most conserved clusters. Unexpectedly strong cross-tissue relationships emerged, such as skin–bone marrow being more cluster-rich than bone–bone marrow, and colon–breast sharing cancer-related clusters tied to extracellular matrix remodeling, lipid metabolism, and immune modulation. Cluster-level interrogation also produced specific mechanistic hypotheses, including a brain–gut axis involving extracellular vesicles, redox regulation, and serotonin cofactor biology, and a liver–bone marrow stress-response axis involving genes associated with white matter disease.

Conclusion: The study delivers a global, systematically derived map of conserved protein co-abundance relationships across human tissues, showing that an LLM-agent framework can integrate heterogeneous biological data to uncover both expected and non-obvious cross-tissue connections. This resource highlights tissues that are central in shared protein modules, proposes concrete axes linking distant organs, and provides a hypothesis-generating foundation for future mechanistic studies and therapeutic target discovery. Code and data are publicly available for reuse and extension.

Abstract: Protein co-abundance clusters preserved across tissues can reveal shared disease mechanisms and candidate therapeutic targets, particularly when proteins implicated in organ-confined diseases converge in peripheral or accessible tissues. However, previous cross-tissue studies have focused on biologically pre-selected tissue pairs, leaving most possible combinations and non-obvious relationships unexplored. We present an LLM-agent framework for large-scale, evidence-grounded comparison of tissue-specific protein co-abundance networks. The framework constructs tissue networks, derives pairwise consensus clusters, and integrates evidence from expression atlases, protein interaction and complex databases, pathway annotations, disease catalogues, and literature. Applied to all 820 pairwise combinations of 41 human tissues and fluids, it identified 1,833 conserved co-abundance clusters across 406 tissue pairs. Colon, synovial fluid, blood, cerebrospinal fluid, and bone marrow were the most broadly connected tissues, while the most cluster-rich pairs were dominated by bone marrow. The analysis also highlighted non-obvious relationships: skin-bone marrow exceeded the anatomically adjacent bone-bone marrow pair, while colon-breast contained cancer-relevant clusters involving extracellular-matrix remodeling, lipid metabolism, and immune modulation. Cluster-level analyses generated further mechanistic hypotheses, including a brain-gut extracellular-vesicle/redox/serotonin-cofactor axis and a liver-bone marrow stress-response axis involving genes linked to white matter disease. These results provide a global, comparable landscape of conserved protein co-abundance and a hypothesis-generating resource for mechanistic and therapeutic exploration. Code and data are available at https://github.com/Gry1005/AgenticAI-conserved-cross-tissue-protein-co-abundance.

</details>


### [274] [Verification abundance, adjudication scarcity: what happens to mathematical knowledge when proof checking becomes free](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.28997)
*Maher Kallel,Mohamed El Louadi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper analyzes how AI-produced, machine-checked proofs change the nature of mathematical verification, arguing that only low-level derivational validity is mechanizable while higher-level interpretation and significance remain scarce expert work.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Recent AI systems can generate formally verified mathematical proofs, as illustrated by high-profile 2026 results. However, one result with a full Lean 4 certificate still faced controversy about whether the formal statement captured the intended claim. This motivates a deeper examination of what kinds of "verification" are being automated and what remain intrinsically human bottlenecks.

Method: Conceptual and structural analysis of verification in mathematics: the authors distinguish three layers (derivational validity, representational fidelity, epistemic significance), analyze a concrete August 2026 corpus of ten AI-assisted results with Lean 4 certificates, measure proof vs. statement sizes and the number of bespoke definitions, and classify types of mismatch between formalizations and intended problems. They also propose a taxonomy and a disclosure schema for future machine-generated results.

Result: Empirically, the machine-checked proof terms are vastly larger than the human-auditable statements (20.6 MB vs. 55.6 KB, a ratio of 379:1), yet the latter include 218 custom definitions not grounded in well-established libraries. This shows that the remaining verification work concentrates in a small but technically deep surface. Conceptually, they show that kernel checking ensures only derivational validity; representational fidelity and epistemic significance remain non-mechanized and require expert judgment. They identify six categories of representational mismatch and propose structured disclosure for machine-generated claims.

Conclusion: Machine checking creates an abundance of low-level verification but does not solve the harder problem of judging whether a result answers the intended question or matters epistemically. Verification work shifts rather than disappears, from proof steps to the design and audit of formal statements and definitions. Because these tasks demand scarce expert attention, adjudication remains a bottleneck. The authors recommend explicit reporting about formalization choices, awareness of representational mismatch modes, and careful integration of machine-checked results in high-stakes domains like software, cryptography, and regulated decision systems.

Abstract: In May 2026 an OpenAI model produced a counterexample to the Erdős unit distance conjecture. Five mathematicians published a human-verified version the same day, and the result entered the literature within weeks. In August 2026 the same laboratory published ten mathematical and theoretical computer science results, each accompanied by a machine-checkable Lean 4 certificate with no unproved steps. Four weeks later, one remained the subject of an unresolved dispute over whether its formalization meant what it claimed.
  We argue that this difference is structural. We distinguish three layers of verification: derivational validity, which a kernel checks; representational fidelity, whether the formal statement means the intended question; and epistemic significance. Only the first is mechanizable. Making it effectively free therefore does not eliminate verification work but shifts the burden to layers dependent on scarce expert attention.
  Measurements of the August corpus illustrate the shift. The kernel-checked proofs total 20.6 MB, while the statements requiring human audit total 55.6 KB, a ratio of 379 to 1. Yet those statements contain 218 bespoke definitions rather than relying on community-vetted ones. The audit surface is therefore small in volume but irreducibly expert. We argue that machine checking produces verification abundance while leaving adjudication scarce. We propose a six-category taxonomy of representational mismatch, a disclosure schema for machine-generated mathematical claims, and implications for software, cryptography, and regulated decision systems.

</details>


### [275] [Multi-Step Forecasting of Grape Berry Temperature based on LSTM Model with Feed-Forward Attention](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29008)
*Srikanth Gorthi,L. G. Divyanth,Dattatray Bhalekar,Markus Keller,Lav Khot*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper develops and evaluates an attention-augmented LSTM model (FAM-LSTM) to forecast grape berry temperature at high temporal resolution for up to 72 hours, outperforming standard deep learning and Random Forest baselines and enabling better vineyard heat-stress management.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Grape berry temperature strongly affects vine physiology, berry composition, and heat stress risk. Vineyard managers need accurate, high-frequency forecasts of berry temperature to time interventions such as irrigation, shading, or spraying. Existing models either focus on air temperature, not berry temperature, or lack sufficient accuracy and horizon length for operational decision-making. There is also a need to understand whether cheap open-field weather-station data are sufficient, or if more costly in-vineyard microclimate measurements significantly improve forecasts.

Method: The authors design a FAM-LSTM architecture that integrates a feed-forward attention mechanism with an LSTM network for multi-step time-series forecasting of berry temperature (Tb). They train and test the model using multi-year environmental and microclimate data from a vineyard in Prosser, WA (training on 2023–2024 data, validating on summer 2025). Forecast horizons span 15 minutes to 72 hours (288 steps). They compare FAM-LSTM against standard LSTM, GRU, vanilla RNN, and Random Forest baselines under two input scenarios: (1) nearest open-field weather station variables and (2) in-vineyard microclimate measurements. Performance is evaluated using MAE and RMSE, and error characteristics are analyzed across time of day and forecast horizons.

Result: Across all forecast horizons and both input scenarios, the FAM-LSTM model achieves lower MAE and RMSE than LSTM, GRU, RNN, and RF, indicating superior predictive skill. With only open-field weather station inputs, FAM-LSTM yields MAE between 0.58–1.70 °C and RMSE between 0.65–2.07 °C over the 15 min–72 h horizons. When in-vineyard microclimate data are used, accuracy improves further, with MAE of 0.51–1.55 °C and RMSE of 0.71–1.87 °C. Error analysis reveals that forecast uncertainty is largest during daytime peak heating (11:00–18:00) and grows with increasing forecast horizon.

Conclusion: The FAM-LSTM architecture provides robust, high-resolution, multi-step forecasts of grape berry temperature and outperforms widely used deep learning and ensemble baselines. Including in-vineyard microclimate measurements improves performance, especially for longer horizons, though reasonable accuracy is still achievable with only open-field station data. The framework is therefore well-suited to support precision vineyard management, particularly proactive heat-stress mitigation strategies, and could likely be extended to other specialty crops and microclimate-sensitive applications.

Abstract: Accurate forecasting of grape berry temperature (Tb) is essential for enabling timely heat stress management in vineyards. In this study, a feed-forward attention mechanism integrated with a Long Short-Term Memory network (FAM-LSTM) was developed and evaluated for multi-step, high-resolution Tb prediction. Models were trained using environmental data from 2023 and 2024 at Prosser, WA, USA, and validated on 2025 summer data. FAM-LSTM was benchmarked against LSTM, GRU, RNN, and Random Forest (RF) across horizons ranging from 15 minutes to 72 hours (288 time steps). Two input scenarios were evaluated: nearest open-field weather station observations and in-vineyard microclimate measurements. FAM-LSTM consistently outperformed all benchmark models across all horizons and input scenarios. Incorporating in-vineyard microclimate data significantly improved forecasting accuracy at longer horizons. Using open-field data, FAM-LSTM achieved MAE and RMSE ranges of 0.58 to 1.70 deg C and 0.65 to 2.07 deg C, respectively. In-vineyard observations further improved performance, with MAE and RMSE in the ranges of 0.51 to 1.55 deg C and 0.71 to 1.87 deg C. Error analysis showed prediction uncertainty was highest during peak daytime periods (11:00 to 18:00) and increased progressively with forecast horizon. Overall, the FAM-LSTM framework offers robust Tb forecasting to support precision heat stress management in vineyards.

</details>


### [276] [Frequency Selective Neural Networks as a Foundation Architecture for Time Series Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29012)
*Hui Huang,Ye Sun,Shiyan Hu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces Frequency Selective Neural Networks (FSNN), a deep learning architecture that explicitly models frequency structure in time-series data using a differentiable filter bank, achieving state-of-the-art accuracy while providing physically interpretable frequency bands.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing deep learning models for time-series (CNNs, RNNs, Transformers) treat sequences in the time or token domain and are largely insensitive to the true oscillatory and spectral structure of physical signals. This leads to spectral entanglement, where important frequency modes are mixed in opaque latent features, limiting physical interpretability despite strong predictive performance. The authors are motivated to design a model that maintains deep learning’s expressive power but directly incorporates signal processing principles to preserve spectral interpretability and align predictions with physical reality.

Method: The authors propose Frequency Selective Neural Networks (FSNN), which embed advanced signal processing directly into the network architecture. FSNN uses a fully differentiable Wiener-like filter bank as the first stage, implemented in the complex domain and trained end-to-end via complex-domain backpropagation. This filter bank autonomously learns to separate the input signal into distinct, task-relevant frequency components. Subsequent neural layers then operate on these disentangled spectral representations for prediction, ensuring that the learned features correspond to specific physical frequency bands rather than arbitrary latent features.

Result: On experiments with standard multivariate time-series benchmarks, FSNN achieves 77.0% average accuracy on the 10 canonical UEA datasets, outperforming prior methods. On the highly imbalanced PTB-XL clinical ECG dataset, FSNN leads across all major evaluation metrics, indicating both strong predictive performance and robustness under class imbalance. The learned filters are shown to align with known physiological structures (e.g., ECG QRS complex frequency ranges), evidencing that the model’s internal representations are physically meaningful.

Conclusion: FSNN provides a new foundation architecture for time-series analysis that marries the expressiveness of deep learning with the rigor of classical signal processing. By resolving spectral entanglement via a differentiable filter bank, it yields state-of-the-art predictive performance while maintaining strong physical interpretability of its learned frequency bands. This makes FSNN a scalable and transparent paradigm for analyzing complex temporal data in physical and biological domains, with particular promise in applications like clinical ECG interpretation.

Abstract: Time-series data across physical and biological domains are fundamentally driven by complex, non-stationary oscillatory modes. While deep learning models, such as Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), Recurrent Neural Networks, and Transformers, have dominated sequential analysis, they remain fundamentally "spectral-blind". By mapping continuous physical waves into unconstrained spatial or discrete token spaces, these architectures suffer from severe spectral entanglement, acting as opaque black boxes that decouple predictive accuracy from physical reality. In this paper, we introduce the Frequency Selective Neural Network (FSNN), pioneering a foundation architecture guaranteeing physical interpretability without sacrificing expressive power of deep learning. FSNN addresses spectral entanglement by explicitly embedding the rigorous mathematics of advanced signal processing into its neural topology. Through a fully differentiable Wiener-like filter bank optimized via complex-domain backpropagation, FSNN autonomously discovers and isolates the precise physical modes of a given task. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that FSNN establishes state-of-the-art predictive performance, achieving $77.0\%$ average accuracy on the standard 10 multivariate UEA datasets and leading across all major metrics on the highly imbalanced PTB-XL clinical ECG benchmark. Crucially, in contrast to yielding abstract feature maps, FSNN converges directly on physically meaningful frequency bands, such as isolating the cardiac QRS complex, providing a highly scalable, interpretable paradigm for robust pattern recognition in complex temporal domains. Our code is available at: https://github.com/ad6174hhhh/FSNN.

</details>


### [277] [Disentangling Representation using Attributes-based Gaussian Estimation for Medical Sound Diagnosis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29026)
*Ke Zhao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Proposes AGEDR, a disentangled representation learning framework that maps known attributes into parts of a VAE’s latent space, disentangles them via mutual information minimization, and uses the resulting latent means for fairer and more accurate medical classification.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Deep learning excels at feature extraction but is often unfair and hard to interpret, which limits its use in sensitive domains like medicine. The authors want a representation where clinically meaningful attributes are explicitly and separately encoded, supporting both better fairness and interpretability while maintaining strong predictive performance.

Method: They design AGEDR, a framework built on a Variational AutoEncoder with Attribute Mapping Embedding (AME) modules. AMEs map given attributes (e.g., patient or clinical factors) to vectors and explicitly align them with a designated subset of latent dimensions in the VAE. They encourage these attribute-aligned latent variables to be statistically independent from the remaining latent variables by minimizing the mutual information between them. After training the VAE with this disentanglement objective, they take the mean parameters of the latent variables as features and train a classifier on top. They conduct extensive experiments and ablation studies to compare AGEDR with standard classifiers and existing disentangled representation methods.

Result: AGEDR achieves higher classification performance than conventional models and prior disentangled representation approaches on the evaluated datasets. Ablation studies confirm that explicitly aligning attributes to parts of the latent space and minimizing mutual information both contribute to disentanglement. The framework also shows improved fairness metrics, suggesting that its representations mitigate some biases.

Conclusion: By embedding attributes into specific, disentangled parts of a VAE’s latent space and separating them from other factors via mutual information minimization, AGEDR provides more interpretable and fair representations for medical prediction tasks while improving accuracy. The method is empirically validated through comparative and ablation experiments, and the released code facilitates further research and application.

Abstract: Deep learning has a powerful capability of feature extraction. However, the lack of fairness and interpretability in deep neural networks poses limitations to their adoption in the medical domain. This paper proposes a disentangled representation learning (DisenRL) framework, named the Attributes-based Gaussian Estimation for Disentangled Representation (AGEDR), which incorporates Attribute Mapping Embedding (AME) modules designed to map attributes into vectors and align them with a subset of the latent vectors in a Variational AutoEncoder (VAE). This part of the latent vector will be disentangled from the remaining latent vectors by minimizing mutual information. A classifier is then trained using the mean parameters of the latent vectors from the VAE. Extensive experiments demonstrate that AGEDR outperforms both conventional classification models and existing disentangled representation learning methods. The ablation experiments also indicate the disentangling capability and fairness of AGEDR. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/ZhaoKe1024/DisentangledRepr.

</details>


### [278] [Facts Without Rules: Boundary Metadata Collapse in Multi-Agent LLM Handoffs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29028)
*Yian Wang,Agam Goyal,Eshwar Chandrasekharan,Hari Sundaram*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper identifies and quantifies a privacy failure mode in multi-agent LLM systems where compressed handoff summaries preserve task-relevant facts but lose usage boundaries, causing unintended information leakage. It shows how boundary explicitness and audience modeling can mitigate this problem.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multi-agent LLM setups often pass information between agents using short summaries or artifacts that function as shared state. While this improves efficiency and coordination, it may inadvertently strip away or weaken the contextual and policy metadata (e.g., who may see what, under which constraints) that should govern how information is used. Current work largely focuses on factual fidelity and performance, not on how summarization affects privacy boundaries and compliance. The authors aim to systematically study whether and how this summarization step causes structured privacy leakage, and to identify design principles for safer coordination.

Method: The authors build a controlled multi-agent coordination testbed where an upstream interaction includes both operational facts and boundary markers (metadata describing usage constraints, audiences, or access rules). They then generate handoff artifacts of varying lengths (e.g., free-text vs. 25-word budget) using different LLMs such as GPT-5-mini and DeepSeek-R1-32B. Using a human-validated judging process (inter-annotator agreement κ=0.74), they measure survival rates of boundary markers (σ_b) and operational facts through the handoff. They compute correlations (Pearson r) between the two kinds of survival, evaluate how boundary explicitness (vague vs. explicit constraints) affects downstream leakage behavior across multiple models, and compare multi-agent handoffs to a single-agent, no-handoff control. They also test mitigations like prompt-only instructions, exact-string redaction, and a gold-derived audience allowlist to see how each affects leakage rates.

Result: They find that the summarization handoff is a structural source of privacy leakage. When summaries are constrained (e.g., to 25 words), boundary-marker survival drops substantially (σ_b from about 0.80 to ~0.57) while operational-fact survival remains near ceiling, and boundary-marker and fact survival are nearly uncorrelated (Pearson r ≈ 0) across models. Downstream tests show that vague boundary language leads to leakage in 73% of GPT and 50% of DeepSeek cases, while explicit constraints bring leakage under 15% for all tested models. The single-agent, no-handoff control still leaks more often than an operationalized handoff, indicating that the issue is not just multi-agent topology but how boundary information is represented. Prompt-only mitigation and string redaction only partially reduce leakage, whereas a gold-derived audience allowlist almost completely prevents leakage across models, highlighting the importance of correctly modeling audience boundaries.

Conclusion: The paper concludes that “summary collapse”—where compressed handoffs preferentially preserve operational content while discarding governing boundaries—is a fundamental privacy risk in multi-agent LLM systems. This risk is not adequately addressed by focusing only on factual accuracy or by simplistic mitigations like prompts or redaction. Instead, system designers must ensure that boundary information is explicit, resilient under compression, and grounded in accurate audience modeling. Mechanisms like audience allowlists that tie usage directly to intended recipients can nearly eliminate leakage, suggesting that robust boundary representation and enforcement should be a first-class design objective in multi-agent AI architectures.

Abstract: Multi-agent LLM systems often coordinate by compressing an upstream interaction into a handoff artifact that downstream agents treat as shared state. We show that this handoff step is a structural source of privacy leakage: summaries preferentially preserve operational facts while weakening the boundary metadata that governs how those facts may be used---a failure mode we call \emph{summary collapse}. On a controlled multi-agent coordination testbed we measure marker survival with a human-validated judge ($κ= 0.74$), where $σ_b = 1$ means every boundary marker survives verbatim and $σ_b = 0$ means all are lost. Boundary-marker and operational-fact survival are nearly uncorrelated at the handoff level on both GPT-5-mini and DeepSeek-R1-32B (Pearson $r$ near zero): uncompressed free-text handoffs preserve boundaries at $σ_b \approx 0.80$, whereas a $25$-word budget drops $σ_b$ to ${\approx}0.57$ while operational-fact survival stays near ceiling. Controlled downstream tests reveal that protection depends on \emph{boundary explicitness}: vague languages leak in $73\%$ of GPT and $50\%$ of DeepSeek cases, while explicit constraints reduce leakage to under $15\%$ across all three tested models. A no-handoff single-agent control further shows the failure is not reducible to multi-agent topology as direct full-marker access still leaks more often than the operationalized handoff. Prompt-only mitigation and exact-string redaction only partially address the problem, while a gold-derived audience allowlist nearly eliminates leakage across models, showing that correctly identifying audience boundaries is the key factor.

</details>


### [279] [Learning to Follow In-Context Watermark Instructions via Self-Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29030)
*Yepeng Liu,Tianyi Chen,Xuandong Zhao,Dawn Song,Yuheng Bu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper studies how well large language models can follow in-context watermarking instructions and proposes a training method that greatly improves watermark detectability without hurting answer quality.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In-context watermarking allows third parties to request watermarked LLM outputs just by adding instructions to the prompt, without needing access to model internals. However, its practical reliability depends on how consistently models follow such instructions while preserving answer quality. Before this work, there was no systematic benchmark or clear understanding of current models’ capabilities or limitations for in-context watermarking.

Method: 1) The authors build ICWBench, a benchmark with three families of verifiable in-context watermarking instructions, and define metrics that jointly consider watermark detectability and response quality. They evaluate 14 state-of-the-art proprietary and open-source LLMs on this benchmark. 2) To improve ICW ability, they introduce a two-stage training pipeline that is self-contained. In stage one, Self-Distillation with Logits Perturbation (SDLP), the base model plays both teacher and student: at decoding time, they perturb the teacher’s logits in an instruction-equivalent way so it tends to follow the ICW instruction, then train the student to match the teacher’s output distribution. In stage two, they apply reinforcement learning where an automatic verifier of the watermark signal is used as the reward signal, further aligning the model towards reliably embedding detectable watermarks while preserving general performance.

Result: The benchmark results show that none of the 14 evaluated frontier LLMs can simultaneously achieve strong watermark detectability and high answer quality across all three ICW instruction families. After applying the proposed two-stage training method to Qwen3-14B and GPT-OSS-20B, the models’ average true positive rate at 1% false positive rate (TPR@1%FPR) across the three ICW instructions improves dramatically: from 0.100 to 0.974 for Qwen3-14B and from 0.337 to 0.968 for GPT-OSS-20B. At the same time, evaluations using perplexity and LLM-as-a-judge indicate that answer quality remains high and is not significantly degraded by the watermarking capability.

Conclusion: Current large language models are not yet reliable at in-context watermarking when both detectability and response quality are required across diverse instruction types. The proposed ICWBench provides a standard way to evaluate this capability. The two-stage self-contained training approach (SDLP plus RL with an automatic verifier) can transform base models into ones that follow ICW instructions with near-perfect detectability at low false positive rates while preserving response quality, without needing stronger teacher models, manual labels, or pre-existing watermarking skill.

Abstract: In-context watermarking (ICW) prepends an instruction to a query asking the model to embed a statistically detectable signal in its response. It thus equips LLMs with a watermarking interface that third parties can invoke without access to model internals. Its reliability hinges on the LLM following the instruction without degrading answer quality, yet how well current LLMs do so has not been measured. We introduce $\mathsf{ICWBench}$, a benchmark of three verifiable ICW instruction families, each scored on both detectability and answer quality. Evaluating 14 frontier proprietary and open-source LLMs, we find that none of the evaluated LLMs achieves both objectives across all three families. To address this, we propose a self-contained two-stage training method, requiring no distillation from a stronger model, no manual annotation, and no pre-existing ICW IF ability. The first stage, self-distillation with logits perturbation (SDLP), uses the same base LLM as both teacher and student: an instruction-equivalent decoding-time logits perturbation makes the teacher follow the ICW instruction, and the student is trained to match the teacher's output distribution. The second stage applies reinforcement learning with the automatic verifier as the reward. Applied to Qwen3-14B and GPT-OSS-20B, our method raises average TPR@$1\%$FPR across three ICW instructions from $0.100$ to $0.974$ and from $0.337$ to $0.968$, respectively, while maintaining high response quality under both perplexity evaluation and LLM-as-a-Judge.

</details>


### [280] [EmoLASP: Emotion Recognition with Language Models and Answer Set Programming](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29035)
*Thao Le,Michael Thielscher*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces EmoLASP, a framework that combines large language models with Answer Set Programming to improve emotion recognition in conversations via VAD (Valence-Arousal-Dominance) prediction, especially when long dialogue histories and fine-tuning are costly or unavailable.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Emotion recognition in conversations typically relies on language models that need long dialogue histories and/or fine-tuning to be accurate, which can be unstable, expensive, and computationally intensive. There is a need for a method that maintains or improves performance while avoiding heavy dependence on long prompts and model fine-tuning, and that can enforce consistency in emotion predictions across turns in a dialogue.

Method: The authors propose EmoLASP, a hybrid framework that integrates a language model with a symbolic reasoner based on Answer Set Programming. The language model (either an LLM used via prompting or a fine-tuned PLM like BERT/RoBERTa) provides base predictions or cues, and the ASP component encodes declarative rules and constraints over Valence-Arousal-Dominance dimensions to reason about conversational context and enforce consistency. The framework is evaluated on the IEMOCAP benchmark with six open-source LLMs of various sizes (3B–120B parameters) and two PLMs, comparing EmoLASP-enhanced predictions to raw model outputs with and without dialogue history.

Result: Across the IEMOCAP experiments, EmoLASP consistently improves VAD prediction performance over using the language models alone, even when the models receive no dialogue history. The performance gains are most pronounced for prompt-only LLMs that are not fine-tuned. For fine-tuned PLMs, once these models have access to dialogue history, adding the ASP-based reasoner yields only marginal additional benefits.

Conclusion: EmoLASP shows that combining neural language models with declarative reasoning via ASP can increase accuracy, improve consistency of emotion predictions, and reduce dependence on costly fine-tuning and long context windows. The approach is particularly valuable in prompt-only LLM settings with limited or no access to dialogue history, highlighting the promise of hybrid neuro-symbolic methods for conversational emotion recognition.

Abstract: Emotion recognition in conversations is increasingly tackled with language models, but these models can be unstable and expensive to fine-tune or to prompt with long dialogue histories. We propose EmoLASP, a framework that combines a language model with declarative reasoning via Answer Set Programming (ASP) to predict VAD scores (Valence-Arousal-Dominance) in conversations. Experiments on a widely used benchmark dataset (IEMOCAP) across six open-source LLMs (3B-120B) and two PLMs (BERT, RoBERTa) show that EmoLASP improves prediction performance compared to using the language model alone, even when the LLMs/PLMs are given no dialogue history in their prompts or input vectors. The gains are largest for prompt-only LLMs, which EmoLASP uses without any fine-tuning. However, for fine-tuned PLMs, the reasoner adds little once dialogue history is available. EmoLASP's LLM pipeline demonstrates the potential advantages of using a reasoning approach to ensure emotion prediction consistency and to reduce both the cost of fine-tuning and the cost of prompting with long dialogue histories.

</details>


### [281] [Let Prompts Bridge Defense Knowledge: Transferable Graph Purification via Vulnerability-Aware GPL](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29054)
*Shuomin Xue,Jingyuan Li,Ju Jia,Jingxuan Yu,Xiaojun Jia*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes ProGAP, a transferable graph purification method that defends GNNs against adversarial perturbations via vulnerability-aware graph prompt learning, achieving better robustness and lower computation than existing methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing adversarial defenses for Graph Neural Networks are mostly domain-specific, trained per-graph or per-task, which results in limited structural/semantic diversity for learning robust defenses and high computational cost when training from scratch for each new domain. There is a need for a practical, transferable defense that can generalize across different graphs and tasks while remaining efficient.

Method: They introduce ProGAP, a transferable graph purification framework. First, they pretrain a perturbation-capture edge detector on data-rich source graphs, jointly modeling graph topology and node semantics to learn universal adversarial edge patterns. Then, in downstream (target) graphs, they design vulnerability-aware graph prompts that focus on biased or vulnerable nodes and inject targeted purification guidance. The pretrained detector is adapted to the new graph distributions via these prompts without heavy parameter updates, enabling efficient transfer of robustness knowledge.

Result: On multiple benchmarks, ProGAP outperforms state-of-the-art graph adversarial defense and purification baselines by 1%–9% in robustness metrics while reducing time consumption by up to 2.2x compared to those baselines.

Conclusion: Transferable, prompt-based graph purification is an effective and efficient way to defend GNNs against adversarial perturbations across domains. By capturing universal adversarial edge patterns and adapting them with vulnerability-aware prompts, ProGAP can improve robustness and reduce computational overhead relative to domain-specific defenses.

Abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have emerged as a cornerstone for representing complex relational dependencies in diverse multimedia tasks, particularly in cross-platform user interest modeling and cross-modal semantic alignment. In the real world, a practical defense against graph adversarial perturbations is needed. However, we observe that the prevailing adversarial purification methods are essentially domain-restricted defenses, which leads to the following shortcomings: (1) single-domain data provides insufficient structural and semantic diversity for learning robust purification criteria; (2) training of domain-specific defense strategies from scratch consumes substantial computational cost. To address the above limitations, we propose a transferable graph purification scheme, named ProGAP, to bridge adversarial defense knowledge via vulnerability-aware graph prompt learning. Firstly, to capture universal adversarial patterns, a perturbation-capture edge detector is pretrained on data-rich graphs by jointly modeling topological and semantic information. Subsequently, to achieve more knowledge transfer w.r.t. robustness, vulnerability-aware prompts are designed that inject targeted purification guidance into biased nodes, during which the pretrained detector adapts to distribution shifts in downstream graphs without parameter-laborious updates. Experimental results demonstrate that compared with state-of-the-art baselines, our ProGAP achieves 1%-9% improvement, and reduces the time consumption by up to 2.2x. The code for ProGAP is available at https://github.com/Lieyoufffff/ProGAP.

</details>


### [282] [Agent2UCB: Agentic System for Generative Engine Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29063)
*Sheldon Yu,Rui Wang,Tong Yu,Sungchul Kim,Doga Dogan,Junda Wu,Julian McAuley*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Introduces Agent2UCB, an agentic system for Generative Engine Optimization (GEO) that autonomously optimizes web content to be more visible in LLM-driven search engines, while monitoring traditional SEO quality.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As LLM-driven search engines (e.g., AI Overviews, Perplexity) increasingly mediate how users access web content, creators need methods to optimize for being cited or summarized by these generative systems, not just ranked by classic search engines. Existing SEO tools don’t target GEO behavior or account for feedback from generative systems, creating a gap for automated, adaptive optimization tailored to LLM-based retrieval and summarization.

Method: The paper proposes Agent2UCB, an agentic GEO system that operates per content item. It (1) applies and evaluates nine distinct GEO strategies; (2) uses online feedback about content visibility as rewards; and (3) employs a bandit-based Agent2UCB policy that combines LLM-based prior beliefs about which strategies will work with observed online rewards to quickly identify the best-performing strategy. In parallel, it runs a lightweight, text-only SEO readiness checker that scores readability, topical coverage, and EEAT-like credibility to track any negative SEO side effects. The system is demonstrated interactively, allowing users to choose target websites and observe optimization iterations and outcome comparisons.

Result: On the GEO-Bench benchmark, Agent2UCB yields consistent improvements in generative visibility—i.e., a higher likelihood that content is cited or summarized by LLM-driven search engines—while maintaining traditional SEO quality metrics according to the built-in readiness evaluation. The demo further illustrates how different GEO strategies and the Agent2UCB policy impact both GEO and SEO performance.

Conclusion: Agent2UCB effectively operationalizes Generative Engine Optimization by using an agentic, bandit-driven approach that leverages LLM priors and real-time feedback to improve content visibility in LLM-based search. It achieves these gains without degrading core SEO attributes such as readability, relevance coverage, and credibility, and the demo provides a practical interface for exploring GEO strategies and their trade-offs.

Abstract: Large language model driven search engines such as Google AI Overviews and Perplexity have created new opportunities for Generative Engine Optimization (GEO) the practice of refining content to increase its likelihood of being cited or summarized by generative systems. We demonstrate Agent2UCB, an agentic GEO system that autonomously improves content visibility through customized, feedback-driven optimization. For each content item, the system evaluates nine GEO strategies, identifies the most effective method, and accelerates selection using a bandit-based Agent2UCB policy that integrates LLM priors with online reward signals. To monitor side effects, the system also provides a lightweight, text-only SEO readiness evaluation covering readability, topical coverage, and EEAT-style credibility. Experiments on GEO-Bench show consistent visibility gains while preserving SEO quality. The demo allows users to choose the websites of interest, observe the optimization workflow, and compare GEO/SEO outcomes across methods.

</details>


### [283] [Revolutionizing Turn-by-Turn Navigation with Cloud-Edge Deep Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29073)
*Yiming Yang,Hao Fu,Fanxiang Zeng,Xikai Yang,Yue Liu,Ning Guo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes a deep-learning-based, multi-task framework using Transformers and Mixture of Experts to generate real-time, context-aware audio instructions for turn-by-turn driving navigation, significantly reducing route deviation compared with rule-based systems.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing turn-by-turn navigation systems typically use handcrafted, rule-based audio instruction policies that have difficulty balancing richness of information with driver cognitive load. In complex road environments, this leads to confusing or poorly timed instructions, causing missed turns and route deviations. There is a need for an intelligent, data-driven approach that can flexibly adapt instruction content and timing to the driving context while remaining scalable and real-time in realistic deployments.

Method: The authors reformulate navigation instruction generation as a multi-task learning problem by decomposing each audio instruction into modular content elements (e.g., maneuver type, distance, landmark cues, timing). They design a deep learning framework that combines: (1) Transformers to model spatiotemporal information from navigation context (road topology, vehicle state, upcoming maneuvers, etc.), and (2) a Mixture of Experts (MoE) architecture to support multi-task learning and specialization of different experts for different instruction sub-tasks or contexts. To meet latency and computation constraints in real driving, they deploy the model in a cloud–edge collaborative architecture, offloading heavy computation to the cloud while keeping time-critical components at the edge to maintain real-time response.

Result: In real-world experiments, the proposed system is compared against traditional rule-based navigation audio policies. The key quantitative metric is yaw rate, defined as the proportion of vehicles deviating from the planned navigation route. The deep learning–based method achieves a significant reduction in yaw rate, indicating that drivers are better able to follow directions and avoid missed or incorrect turns. Qualitative results suggest that the learned instructions are clearer and more effective in complex driving scenarios.

Conclusion: The study demonstrates that framing navigation audio generation as a multi-task learning problem and solving it with a Transformer+MoE architecture can materially improve driver adherence to routes. The cloud–edge deployment shows that such a model is feasible at scale and in real time. This work is presented as the first large-scale application of deep learning specifically for driving audio navigation, representing a notable step forward in intelligent transportation systems and driver assistance technologies, and suggesting future extensions such as personalization and broader contextual inputs.

Abstract: Turn-by-turn (TBT) navigation systems are integral to modern driving experiences, providing real-time audio instructions to guide drivers safely to destinations. However, existing audio instruction policy often relies on rule-based approaches that struggle to balance informational content with cognitive load, potentially leading to driver confusion or missed turns in complex environments. To overcome these difficulties, we first model the generation of navigation instructions as a multi-task learning problem by decomposing the audio content into combinations of modular elements. Then, we propose a novel deep learning framework that leverages the powerful spatiotemporal information processing capabilities of Transformers and the strong multi-task learning abilities of Mixture of Experts (MoE) to generate real-time, context-aware audio instructions for TBT driving navigation. A cloud-edge collaborative architecture is implemented to handle the computational demands of the model, ensuring scalability and real-time performance for practical applications. Experimental results in the real world demonstrate that the proposed method significantly reduces the yaw rate (the proportion of vehicles deviating from navigation routes) compared to traditional methods, delivering clearer and more effective audio instructions. This is the first large-scale application of deep learning in driving audio navigation, marking a substantial advancement in intelligent transportation and driving assistance technologies.

</details>


### [284] [Nested Convex-Body Chasing for Online Optimization with Evolving Feasible Sets](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29074)
*Dhruv Sarkar,Aprameyo Chakrabartty*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper studies online convex optimization when feasible sets shrink over time, designing algorithms that separate loss minimization from geometric movement and achieve near-optimal trade-offs between regret and movement, with improved dimension dependence via nested convex-body chasing.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Classical online convex optimization assumes either fixed or simply changing constraints; however, many applications involve nested, shrinking feasible regions where one must both maintain low regret and limit movement between decisions. Existing approaches can incur very large (even exponential in dimension) movement or rely on heavy projection analyses. The authors aim to understand the fundamental trade-offs between regret, constraint violations, and movement in such settings, and to replace the poor dimension dependence of prior work with polynomial dependence by leveraging advances in nested convex-body chasing.

Method: 1) Introduce two models: CONES (convex optimization with nested evolving feasible sets) and COCO (adversarial constrained online convex optimization). 2) Develop algorithms that cleanly separate two concerns: (a) loss control via constrained minimizers and cumulative-loss tests to preserve standard regret guarantees, and (b) geometric movement control via a deterministic, resettable nested convex-body chasing algorithm. 3) For CONES with G-Lipschitz, μ-strongly convex objectives over bounded domains, design a strategy that chases intersections of current feasible sets with adaptive sublevel sets of the objective, using the Euclidean nested convex-body chasing ratio O(√(d log(1+d))). 4) Analyze regret and movement bounds, deriving nonpositive prefix regret and movement scaling with √(d log(1+d) GD log(eT)/μ), and show matching lower bounds on the horizon dependence in 2D. 5) Under additional structural assumptions (linear growth away from the constrained minimizer set), use Steiner-point tracking to obtain movement bounds that do not depend on T. 6) Extend the framework to general convex COCO via one-step-delayed chasing combined with online regularized-leader style resets, and analyze regret and cumulative constraint violations. 7) Compare the resulting bounds against prior work, emphasizing the improved polynomial (rather than exponential) dependence on dimension coming from nested convex-body chasing results.

Result: For the CONES setting with a G-Lipschitz, μ-strongly convex objective on a domain of diameter D, the proposed algorithm achieves: (i) nonpositive regret at every time prefix, meaning the algorithm never does worse cumulatively than the best constrained sequence up to that time; and (ii) total movement bounded by O(√(d log(1+d) GD log(eT)/μ)). This movement bound adapts to how much the constrained optimum value increases over time. In two dimensions, they prove that any randomized algorithm achieving terminal expected regret O(T^β) for any β<1 must incur expected movement at least Ω(√(log T)) on some deterministic nested feasible sequence, showing their horizon dependence is optimal. With an additional linear growth condition around the constrained minimizer set, using Steiner-point tracking yields movement bounds independent of the time horizon T. For general convex COCO, one-step-delayed chasing plus regularized-leader resets gives regret O(G_f D √(d log(1+d) T)) and cumulative constraint violation O(G_g D √(d log(1+d) T)). For strongly convex losses in COCO, both regret and constraint violation improve to O(d log(1+d) log(eT)) (for fixed other parameters). Across these settings, the new reductions replace the exponential-in-d projection-path factor O(d^{d/2}) from prior analyses with the substantially better polynomial dimension dependence arising from Euclidean nested convex-body chasing.

Conclusion: The paper shows that online optimization with nested, shrinking feasible regions can be handled by decoupling loss control from geometric movement and importing tools from nested convex-body chasing. This yields algorithms that guarantee low regret and controlled movement, with provably near-optimal dependence on the time horizon and only polynomial dependence on dimension. In CONES, they obtain prefix-wise nonpositive regret and near-optimal movement bounds, with dimension-2 lower bounds establishing the sharpness of the horizon dependence and additional assumptions enabling horizon-free movement via Steiner-point tracking. In the broader COCO framework, their reductions provide unified algorithms with sublinear regret and constraint violation, and logarithmic guarantees under strong convexity, while dramatically improving on the dimension dependence of earlier projection-based methods. Overall, the work clarifies the trade-offs between regret, constraint violations, and movement in constrained online convex optimization with nested feasible sets, and connects this area to geometric chasing problems to obtain more efficient algorithms.

Abstract: We study online optimization with nested shrinking feasible regions in two settings: convex optimization with nested evolving feasible sets (CONES) and adversarial constrained online convex optimization (COCO). Our algorithms separate loss control from geometric movement: constrained minimizers and cumulative-loss tests preserve regret guarantees, while a deterministic resettable nested convex-body chaser limits movement.
  For CONES with a $G$-Lipschitz, $μ$-strongly convex objective on a diameter-$D$ domain, we chase intersections of the current feasible set with adaptive objective sublevel sets. Using the Euclidean chasing ratio $O(\sqrt{d\log(1+d)})$, we obtain nonpositive regret at every prefix and movement $O(\sqrt{d\log(1+d)\,GD\log(eT)/μ})$. The bound adapts to the increase in the constrained optimum value. In dimension two, with all other parameters fixed, every randomized algorithm with terminal expected regret $O(T^β)$, $β<1$, suffers $Ω(\sqrt{\log T})$ expected movement on some deterministic nested sequence, proving optimal horizon dependence. Under linear growth away from the constrained minimizer set, Steiner-point tracking yields movement independent of $T$.
  For general convex COCO, one-step-delayed chasing with regularized-leader resets gives regret $O(G_fD\sqrt{d\log(1+d)T})$ and cumulative constraint violation $O(G_gD\sqrt{d\log(1+d)T})$. For strongly convex losses, both are $O(d\log(1+d)\log(eT))$ when other parameters are fixed. These reductions replace the $O(d^{d/2})$ projection-path factor in prior analyses by the polynomial dimension dependence of Euclidean nested convex-body chasing.

</details>


### [285] [HANIA: Planner-Guided Multimodal Graph Evidence Selection for Grounded Question Answering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29088)
*Zafar Ali,Asad Khan,Nimbeshaho Thierry,Nabila Amir,Adam A. Q. Mohammed,Pavlos Kefalas*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Introduces HANIA, a planner-guided multimodal graph framework that builds a compact, grounded evidence set from images and text to improve robustness and accuracy in multimodal question answering without task-specific fine-tuning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing multimodal QA systems struggle with long, noisy, and weakly grounded contexts. Long unstructured inputs lead to redundancy and hallucinated answers, while simple (flat) retrieval often misses the relational and multi-step reasoning structure required for complex questions. There is a need for a method that can: (1) extract only question-relevant evidence from multimodal inputs, (2) explicitly decide when visual information is insufficient, and (3) organize evidence in a structured way that supports multi-hop reasoning, all while remaining efficient and not requiring fine-tuning on each target dataset.

Method: HANIA uses a frozen vision-language model to process the given image and text and extract concise, question-focused visual evidence while allowing abstention when evidence is missing or uncertain. It then builds an input-grounded multimodal graph whose nodes and edges represent entities, concepts, and relations across both text and image. A two-group finite-state planner coordinates descriptive evidence (what is present) and relational evidence (how elements are related) over this graph.
