A coverage-aware pruning stage selects a small but informative subset of evidence based on multiple signals: relevance to the question, graph-based confidence, coverage of important concepts, and diversity of modalities (text vs. vision). The final pruned set of text passages, visual statements, and graph triples is fed into a frozen instruction-tuned language model decoder to generate the answer.

Result: On the ScienceQA benchmark, HANIA is evaluated along several dimensions: answer accuracy, the quality of its evidence filtering, robustness to different evidence budgets (how much evidence is allowed), and computational efficiency. The experiments show that HANIA achieves competitive performance in multimodal QA compared to existing methods, even though it does not use fine-tuning on the target dataset and avoids iterative retrieval loops.

Conclusion: Structured evidence planning via a multimodal graph and planner, combined with coverage-aware pruning, enables a compact, high-quality evidence set that improves grounding and robustness in multimodal question answering. HANIA demonstrates that a pipeline of frozen vision-language and instruction-tuned models, orchestrated through explicit graph-based planning rather than heavy fine-tuning or iterative retrieval, can achieve strong performance on ScienceQA. This suggests that graph-guided, planner-based evidence selection is a promising direction for reliable, efficient multimodal QA.

Abstract: Multimodal question answering remains sensitive to noisy, incomplete, and weakly grounded evidence. Long unstructured contexts can introduce redundancy and encourage unsupported generation, while flat retrieval may overlook relations needed for multi-step reasoning. We present HANIA, a planner-guided multimodal graph framework for evidence-grounded question answering. HANIA processes the supplied image and text using a frozen vision-language model to extract concise question-relevant visual evidence with explicit abstention. It then constructs an input-grounded multimodal graph and applies a two-group finite-state planner to coordinate descriptive and relational evidence. Coverage-aware pruning retains a compact evidence set based on relevance, graph confidence, concept coverage, and modality diversity. The selected passages, visual statements, and graph triples are provided to a frozen instruction-tuned decoder. We evaluate HANIA on ScienceQA using answer accuracy, evidence-filtering quality, evidence-budget sensitivity, and efficiency. The results show that structured evidence planning and compact graph-guided retrieval can support competitive multimodal question answering without target-dataset fine-tuning or iterative retrieval. The code is available at https://github.com/Zafar-southeast/HANIA.

</details>


### [286] [EviAnchor: Mitigating Hallucinations in Large Vision-Language Models via Regional Visual Evidence Compensation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29092)
*Sihang Jia,Shuliang Liu,Songbo Yang,Xuming Hu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes EviAnchor, a training-free inference framework to better preserve and reuse visual evidence in large vision-language models, improving visual grounding and reducing hallucinations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Large vision-language models often hallucinate, generating answers that are not supported by the image. Preliminary analysis shows that visual information strongly affects earlier decoder layers but its influence fades in later layers, causing the model to rely too much on textual context instead of visual evidence. The authors want a way to keep visual evidence accessible and influential throughout the whole generation process, without retraining the base model.

Method: The authors introduce EviAnchor, a training-free, single-branch inference framework. They add Regional Evidence Anchor (REA) slots that progressively aggregate dense visual tokens into spatially-structured representations, acting as compact visual memory. During generation, they apply decision-conditioned evidence routing so that the current decoding state selectively attends to the most relevant visual anchors, thereby reactivating visual evidence and reducing overreliance on language-only context. After this routing step, the model resumes its usual Transformer decoding to integrate the retrieved visual evidence with the question semantics and the generation history.

Result: On benchmarks focused on hallucination and visual grounding—POPE, CHAIR, and MMHal-Bench—the EviAnchor framework consistently improves visual grounding metrics compared to the baseline LVLMs, indicating fewer unsupported generations and better alignment between answers and image content.

Conclusion: Maintaining and reactivating structured visual evidence throughout decoding mitigates the attenuation of visual signals in LVLMs and leads to more visually grounded outputs. EviAnchor achieves these gains without extra training or architectural branches, providing a practical plug-in inference method for existing vision-language models.

Abstract: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) frequently generate content unsupported by visual inputs. Preliminary experiments show that visual evidence is primarily incorporated into answer-side representations in early-to-middle decoder layers, while its direct influence progressively weakens in later layers. This attenuation suggests that visual evidence acquired earlier may be insufficiently utilized during subsequent generation. Based on this observation, we propose EviAnchor, a training-free and single-branch inference framework that preserves and reactivates visual evidence throughout generation. EviAnchor introduces Regional Evidence Anchor (REA) slots to progressively aggregate dense visual tokens into spatially structured representations. It then strengthens the current decision state's access to these visual anchors through decision-conditioned evidence routing, mitigating excessive dependence on textual context. Finally, the model resumes its native Transformer computation to integrate the retrieved visual evidence with question semantics and generation history. Experiments across POPE, CHAIR, and MMHal-Bench demonstrate consistent improvements in visual grounding.

</details>


### [287] [SafeAtlas-VL: Beyond Binary Multimodal Safety with Large-Scale Data and Guard Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29098)
*Zongrui Wang,Xiangyang Zhu,Sicheng Wang,Han Wang,Dingyi Rong,Zeyu Zhang,Chunyi Li,Yue Shi,Kaiwei Zhang,Zicheng Zhang,Yuan Tian,Qi Jia,Yan Teng,Wei Sun,Ning Liu,Guangtao Zhai*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper presents SafeAtlas-VL, a large-scale multimodal safety dataset with fine-grained, multi-level risk labels and associated guard models that outperform prior state-of-the-art in safety detection.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current multimodal safety moderation systems usually make only binary safe/unsafe decisions and are trained for a single target (image, request, or response). This makes it hard to compare risk across components of an interaction and obscures borderline or ambiguous cases. There is a need for fine-grained, multi-target, and better-calibrated safety assessment in multimodal AI systems.

Method: The authors build SafeAtlas-VL, a 1.5M-instance dataset labeled at the image, request, and response levels on a five-level ordered safety scale across 15 harm categories and 55 subcategories. They aggregate data from real and synthetic sources and use a disagreement-aware annotation process to better capture ambiguity. They also create SafeAtlas-Bench, a 5,000-instance evaluation set for both discrete five-level predictions and continuous risk scoring. On top of this data, they train the SafeAtlas Guard models using target-conditioned tuning and a soft cumulative ordinal classification head that outputs both discrete classes and continuous safety scores.

Result: The resulting guard models demonstrate strong generalization, achieving competitive or superior results on multiple external benchmarks without training on those benchmarks’ datasets. The 8B-parameter model achieves the best reported performance, surpassing the previous state of the art by about 4 F1 points. The dataset and models support both discrete five-way classification and continuous risk estimation.

Conclusion: Fine-grained, multi-target, and ordinally structured safety labels substantially improve multimodal safety moderation. Models trained on SafeAtlas-VL can robustly generalize to diverse safety benchmarks and outperform existing systems, showing that ordinal, target-conditioned training is an effective approach for multimodal safety detection. The released code, data, and models aim to facilitate further research in this direction.

Abstract: Multimodal safety moderation requires distinguishing risks arising from visual content, user intent, and assistant behavior. Existing safeguards, however, are typically trained for a single judgment target and reduce safety assessment to a binary decision. Consequently, risk becomes difficult to compare across a multimodal interaction, and ambiguous cases are obscured. We introduce SafeAtlas-VL, a dataset of 1.5M training instances that places image-, request-, and response-level judgments on a five-level ordered scale. We curate a broad collection of safety-relevant data from both real-world and synthetic sources and apply a disagreement-aware annotation procedure. The resulting dataset spans 15 harm categories and 55 fine-grained subcategories, covering a broad range of multimodal safety scenarios. We also construct SafeAtlas-Bench, a held-out set of 5,000 instances for evaluating five-level predictions and continuous risk scores. Upon this dataset, we train the SafeAtlas Guard series of models via target-conditioned tuning for multimodal safety detection. Our models not only perform five-way classification of safety levels but also map safety to continuous scores through a soft cumulative ordinal head. Experimental results demonstrate that guard models trained on our dataset exhibit strong generalization: even without using the training sets of other benchmarks, they achieve competitive performance on the corresponding test sets. Notably, our 8B model attains the overall best performance, outperforming the previous SOTA by approximately 4% in F1 score. Code, data, and models are released to support further research. Warning: this paper contains example data that may be offensive, harmful, graphic, or disturbing.

</details>


### [288] [Clustering as Approximation by Constrained Projectors: Theory and Guarantees](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29102)
*Angshul Majumdar*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Unifies many clustering methods as structured low-rank projection problems on a signal-derived matrix, yielding common optimization form, geometric properties, stability bounds, and exact recovery conditions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Clustering algorithms like k-means, fuzzy c-means, kernel and spectral clustering appear different and are studied separately, making it hard to compare them theoretically, understand their relationships, or derive general guarantees. A unified mathematical formulation can clarify their connections, highlight what truly differentiates them, and enable shared theory about their geometry, stability, and recovery properties.

Method: Show that various clustering methods can be written as minimizing a Frobenius norm objective of the form min_{B in C} ||M - M P_B||_F^2, where M is a signal-derived matrix and P_B is a structured low-rank projector determined by B. Different clustering families correspond to different constraint sets C (e.g., hard assignments, fuzzy memberships, kernel feature spaces, orthonormality). Within this abstract projector framework, the paper analyzes the geometry of the projection manifold, proving geodesic convexity properties, derives perturbation bounds under noise, and establishes exact recovery results in idealized block-structured data models. It also studies conditions under which distinct clustering formulations yield the same optimal subspace or diverge under small violations like inter-cluster leakage.

Result: Derives a common optimization template that represents k-means, fuzzy c-means, kernel k-means, kernel FCM, and spectral clustering as special cases of structured low-rank projection problems. Proves geodesic convexity on the manifold of such projectors for the given objective, obtains perturbation bounds that characterize robustness of the learned subspace to noise in M, and provides exact recovery guarantees when the data follow an ideal block model. Identifies regimes where different clustering methods converge to an identical optimal subspace and characterizes how and when their solutions start to differ as inter-cluster leakage or departures from the ideal model increase.

Conclusion: Many seemingly different clustering algorithms can be interpreted in a single theoretical framework as structured low-rank projectors that best approximate a signal-derived matrix. This unification clarifies their algebraic and geometric relationships, provides general tools to analyze their stability and recovery properties, and explains when their outputs coincide or differ. The framework offers a theory-first perspective that can guide both the understanding and design of clustering methods via properties of projection operators rather than ad hoc algorithmic formulations.

Abstract: This paper develops a unified theoretical framework showing that a broad family of clustering methods, including k-means, fuzzy c-means, kernel k-means, kernel FCM, and spectral clustering, can all be expressed as structured low-rank projectors acting on a signal-derived matrix. By formulating each method as an instance of min over B in C of ||M - M P_B||_F^2, with different constraint sets C, we establish a common optimization template that clarifies the algebraic links among hard, fuzzy, kernel-induced, and orthonormal projections. Within this framework, we derive non-trivial theoretical results, including geodesic convexity properties on the projection manifold, perturbation bounds quantifying stability to matrix noise, and exact recovery guarantees under ideal block-model conditions. The analysis further explains when different clustering families collapse to the same optimal subspace and how deviations arise under small inter-cluster leakage. Overall, the work provides a coherent, theory-first foundation for understanding clustering through structured projectors.

</details>


### [289] [Emergent Misalignment Is Not Magical](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29118)
*Mingxuan Li,Qirun Dai,Heran Wang,Chenhao Tan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper studies “emergent misalignment” (LLMs becoming broadly harmful after being fine‑tuned on narrowly harmful data) and shows it is a predictable, representation-driven generalization effect rather than a mysterious global misalignment or evil persona.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Emergent misalignment (EM) is a safety concern: fine‑tuning LLMs on limited harmful data can make them behave misaligned in a wide range of contexts. Prior work treats EM as surprising and explains it vaguely (e.g., global misalignment direction, evil personas) without a clear mechanistic account. The authors aim to clarify what actually causes EM and how to predict when and where it will occur.

Method: They analyze how the base model represents the harmful training data and the evaluation prompts in its embedding space. Specifically, they compute the centroid of the EM training data representations and measure the representational distance of evaluation prompts to this centroid. They then correlate these distances with the “evilness” of outputs after EM fine‑tuning across 12 model–dataset combinations. They also vary training data formats, probe for a shared misalignment direction across EM models, compare EM to persona prompting, and extend the scalar distance metric into a dataset-specific generalization direction that can handle semantics-preserving prompt perturbations.

Result: Evil behavior after EM fine‑tuning is strongly predictable from representational distance in the base model: prompts closer to the harmful-data centroid elicit more evil outputs, with an average Spearman correlation of about -0.73 across 12 settings. EM’s impact depends strongly on the format of training data, there is no single misalignment direction that transfers across EM models, and EM-induced behavior differs qualitatively from persona changes. Their generalized “directional” metric continues to predict EM behavior under semantics-preserving perturbations (e.g., appending random tokens, paraphrasing) where alternative methods fail.

Conclusion: Emergent misalignment is not a mysterious global failure mode but a structured, data-dependent generalization pattern that can be predicted from internal representations of training data and prompts. EM depends heavily on how harmful data is formatted, does not arise from a universal misalignment direction, and is distinct from simple persona changes. A representation-based generalization direction offers a robust way to anticipate EM behavior even under prompt perturbations.

Abstract: Fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) on narrowly harmful datasets can lead to misalignment broadly, a phenomenon known as emergent misalignment (EM). EM poses a challenge for AI safety and our understanding of LLMs. Prior work often frames EM as an unexpected behavior, and explains it by appealing to general misalignment directions or anthropomorphizing it as acquiring an evil persona. However, the mechanisms behind these framings remain obscure. In this work, we show that EM is a predictable and data-dependent generalization phenomenon. By examining the base model's representation of EM training data and evaluation prompts, we find that evilness after EM training is highly predictable from representational distance: the closer an evaluation prompt is to training data centroid, the more evilness it elicits from EM models after training (with an average Spearman correlation of -0.73 across 12 model-dataset settings). Building upon this analysis, we further demystify EM by showing that (1) its effectiveness changes significantly based on training data format; (2) there is not a general misalignment direction that transfers across different EM models; (3) the effect of EM is fundamentally different from persona changes. Furthermore, we extend the EM generalization metric from a scalar distance to a dataset-specific generalization direction, which robustly predicts EM models' evilness under semantics-preserving prompt perturbations including appending random tokens and paraphrasing, where other methods do not reliably generalize.

</details>


### [290] [Beyond Correctness: Validity-Oriented Evaluation of Biomedical LLM Judges](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29127)
*Rodrigo de Oliveira,Federico Pittino,James Gwinnutt,Jay Nanavati*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A pipeline to evaluate biomedical LLM judges using metric-based synthetic preference pairs and multi-dimensional metrics, showing SFT followed by RL works best for Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct on decomposable medical tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Evaluating biomedical LLMs as judges is hard due to scarcity of reliable human annotations and the need for trustworthy, robust, and format-compliant evaluations in safety-critical medical settings. Existing benchmarks and aggregate metrics don’t capture robustness or structural correctness for tasks like PICO extraction and clinical calculations.

Method: 1) Augment existing human-labeled biomedical benchmarks with deterministic, metric-grounded mutations that create auditable preference pairs for evaluation. 2) Evaluate LLM judges along three axes: correctness against metric-derived gold labels, robustness under repeated stochastic sampling, and compliance with requested output formats. 3) Apply this pipeline to Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct under four training regimes: base instruct, supervised fine-tuning via distillation (SFT), reinforcement learning via GRPO (RL), and sequential SFT followed by RL (SFT→RL). Compare their performance, particularly on structured biomedical tasks like PICO extraction and medical calculations.

Result: Base and single-stage regimes (SFT-only, RL-only) perform poorly on structured medical discrimination tasks (e.g., PICO extraction, clinical calculations). The combined SFT→RL regime achieves the best overall scores in correctness, robustness, and format compliance. Performance gains are especially strong on decomposable tasks such as PICO and MedCalc, with SFT→RL sometimes matching or exceeding the performance of larger frontier models.

Conclusion: A validity-oriented, mutation-based evaluation pipeline can effectively assess biomedical LLM judges even with limited human labels, capturing dimensions beyond aggregate accuracy. For Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, a combined SFT followed by RL training regime yields the most reliable and compliant judge behavior, particularly on decomposable biomedical tasks, and can reach or surpass frontier-level performance in these settings.

Abstract: We propose a scalable, validity-oriented pipeline for evaluating biomedical LLM judges when high-quality human judgments are scarce. First, we augment existing human-labelled biomedical benchmarks with deterministic, metric-grounded mutations that produce auditable preference pairs. Second, we evaluate judges beyond aggregate correctness using three deployment-relevant dimensions: correctness against metric-derived gold labels, robustness under repeated stochastic sampling, and compliance with the requested output format. We use this pipeline to assess Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct under four regimes: (1) base, using the instruct model as is; (2) SFT, distillation-based supervised fine-tuning only; (3) RL, GRPO-based reinforcement learning only; and (4) SFT$\rightarrow$RL, SFT followed by RL. The base and single-stage regimes struggle on structured medical discrimination such as PICO extraction and clinical calculations, whereas SFT$\rightarrow$RL performs best across correctness, compliance, and robustness; gains concentrate on decomposable tasks (PICO, MedCalc), at times matching or outperforming frontier models.

</details>


### [291] [APIFlow-Bench: Measuring Whether Agents Survive Long, Dependent API Workflows](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29128)
*Zelin Wan,Arash Nourian,Xiaoxiao Li,Nihar Nandan,Kamalakannan Nandagopal*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Benchmark for evaluating tool-using AI agents on complex REST-API workflows, decomposing performance into detailed capabilities and auditing full call paths.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing evaluations judge tool-using agents with a single success/failure bit for the whole workflow, which misses where and why failures occur (e.g., auth, payload, or delivery issues). A more diagnostic, auditable benchmark is needed for long, dependent API workflows.

Method: Design APIFlow-Bench: synthetic multi-step REST-API “worlds” built forward subtask-by-subtask, each validated via automated self-tests and oracle solvability checks. Deploy deterministic, provenance-sensitive grading using canary tracing through API calls and typed answer cards. Release full answer keys and over 44k execution transcripts. Evaluate 19 models under a shared scaffold, measuring seven distinct engineering capabilities and requiring answers be grounded in the actual API call path.

Result: On individual subtasks, models reach 93% success, but performance drops on longer API chains to 74% on clean 20-step chains and 61% including hard trials that no model passes. Reliability metrics show large spread across models: best-of-five scores vary modestly (7 points), but requiring all-five-of-five success exposes a 44-point gap. Failure patterns contradict a simple independent-error compounding model: 20-step chain success is 33 points higher than multiplying per-subtask rates would predict, and on the clean subset, 77% of failed runs reach the correct final state but fail only at the answer-delivery stage.

Conclusion: APIFlow-Bench provides a fine-grained, auditable way to evaluate and compare tool-using agents on long-horizon REST-API tasks. It reveals that (a) longer dependency chains significantly hurt performance, (b) reliability over multiple runs is a key differentiator between models, and (c) many failures occur at the final response-delivery step rather than in achieving the correct underlying state, challenging simple independent-error models of compounding failure.

Abstract: Tool-using agents are commonly evaluated by a single bit: whether an end-to-end workflow completed. This metric fails to distinguish failures that matter in production, such as expired credentials, malformed payloads, or correct execution followed by incorrect final delivery. We introduce APIFlow-Bench, a fully auditable benchmark for long-horizon, dependent REST-API workflows that decomposes performance into seven engineering capabilities and requires agents to produce answers supported by the actual call path. We generate synthetic API worlds forward, subtask by subtask; each subtask is admitted only after a zero-LLM self-test triad verifies its grader and an oracle establishes solvability, and an adversarial audit identified and fixed six grader exploits. Grading is deterministic and provenance-sensitive: a state check traces a mock-minted canary through the API data flow to the response the answer must originate from, and a typed answer card is verified field by field. We release all answer keys and 44,362 unredacted execution transcripts. Across 19 frontier and open-weight models under one neutral scaffold, we find: (1) longer dependency chains degrade success, from 93% on individual subtasks to 74% on clean 20-subtask chains and 61% when including the 8% of chain trials that a model-consensus screen flags as passed by no model; (2) reliability separates models more than best-case capability, with best-of-five spanning seven points but all-five-of-five reliability spanning 44 points; (3) the independent-error account of compounding failure does not fit the data: pass rates on 20-subtask chains are 33 percentage points above the product of subtask-level rates, and on the clean slice 77% of failing runs reached the correct final state and failed only at delivery.

</details>


### [292] [More Perspectives, Stronger Signals: Multi-Perspective Enhancement and Progressive Fusion for Multimodal Entity Representation Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29139)
*Chenyi Xiong,Yan Zhang,Jing Hu,Ziyue Qin,Kui Xiao,Xiaopan Lyu,Xiaoju Hou,Zhifei Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper presents PrismF, a framework for learning stronger multimodal entity representations by combining multi-perspective intra-modal enhancement with progressive cross-modal fusion, achieving state-of-the-art results on multimodal knowledge graph completion benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing multimodal KGC methods struggle with semantic over-smoothing within each modality and with filtering noisy or unreliable information across modalities, especially when data is sparse or ambiguous. The authors aim to design a representation learning framework that can both refine fine-grained semantics within each modality and more effectively integrate information across modalities, improving robustness and performance on MMKGC tasks.

Method: The authors propose PrismF, which has two key components: (1) a multi-perspective intra-modal enhancement mechanism that decomposes each modality (e.g., text, image) into several complementary semantic views and applies a decoupling loss to prevent these views from collapsing into redundant representations, thereby preserving fine-grained distinctions; (2) a progressive fusion strategy that dynamically calibrates interactions between modalities in stages, so that informative cross-modal signals are amplified while noisy or unreliable signals are down-weighted. The entire framework is trained end-to-end for multimodal knowledge graph completion.

Result: On three public multimodal KGC benchmarks, PrismF achieves state-of-the-art or strongest overall performance. On the KVC16K dataset in particular, it improves Mean Reciprocal Rank (MRR) by 4.04% and Hits@1 by 11.17% relative to prior methods, demonstrating better link prediction accuracy under multimodal conditions.

Conclusion: By decomposing each modality into complementary semantic perspectives and fusing modalities progressively with dynamic calibration, PrismF mitigates intra-modal over-smoothing and cross-modal noise issues in multimodal KGC. The empirical gains across multiple benchmarks indicate that this multi-perspective plus progressive fusion design leads to more informative and robust multimodal entity representations, and offers a promising direction for future MMKGC research.

Abstract: Learning effective multimodal entity representations is fundamental for reasoning tasks such as multimodal knowledge graph completion (MMKGC). However, existing methods often suffer from semantic over-smoothing within modalities and ineffective noise filtration across modalities, particularly under sparse or ambiguous conditions. To overcome these limitations, we propose PrismF, a unified framework that synergizes multi-perspective enhancement with progressive fusion to extract stronger signals from diverse inputs. PrismF enhances fine-grained intra-modal semantics through a multi-perspective mechanism that decomposes each modality into complementary views and constrains them with a decoupling loss to reduce representation collapse. Furthermore, it improves cross-modal integration through a progressive fusion strategy that dynamically calibrates inter-modal interactions, enabling the model to emphasize informative signals while suppressing noisy or unreliable ones. Extensive experiments on three public benchmarks show that PrismF achieves the strongest overall performance, including relative improvements of 4.04% in MRR and 11.17% in Hits@1 on KVC16K. Our code can be found at https://github.com/HubuKG/PrismF.

</details>


### [293] [JudgePanel: A Compact Judge with Panel Deliberation via Adaptive Multi-Reward Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29168)
*Yiyue Qian,Shinan Zhang,Huan Song,Hannah Marlowe*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They introduce JudgePanel, a compact LLM judge that imitates multi-agent panel deliberation, plus an adaptive RL scheme (AdaReward) and quick domain-specialization for strong, cheap LLM-based evaluation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM-as-a-Judge is scalable but flawed: single judges are biased, while multi-agent judging is accurate but too expensive. The authors want a judging system with the robustness of diverse panel deliberation but the efficiency of a single compact model, and that can be quickly adapted to new domains.

Method: 1) Collect and train on panel deliberation traces produced by an ensemble of strong evaluator models so a single compact Judge model can internally emulate multi-agent discussion, disagreement, and resolution. 2) Apply AdaReward, an adaptive multi-reward reinforcement learning algorithm that automatically re-weights different reward components over training as they saturate at different speeds, to further refine the judge. 3) Add a lightweight domain specialization module that can be fine-tuned with only a few hundred labeled examples for new evaluation domains.

Result: A 14B-parameter JudgePanel model surpasses specialized judge models up to 70B parameters on four evaluation benchmarks, maintains strong positional consistency (e.g., robust rankings under paraphrase/order changes), and can be rapidly specialized to new domains with a few hundred labels.

Conclusion: JudgePanel shows that a single compact LLM can effectively emulate multi-agent panel deliberation and, with AdaReward and a light specialization module, achieve reliable, sample-efficient, and computationally cheap LLM-as-a-Judge performance that rivals or exceeds much larger specialized judges.

Abstract: The LLM-as-a-Judge paradigm has emerged as a scalable alternative to human evaluation. However, single-model judges are limited by their inherent model biases, while multi-agent evaluation protocols that mitigate this through diverse deliberation are prohibitively expensive at inference time. To this end, we propose \textbf{\modelname}, which equips a compact \underline{Judge} model with multi-agent \underline{Panel} deliberation capability. Specifically, we first train on panel deliberation traces from an ensemble of strong evaluators, capturing structured patterns of discussion, disagreement, and resolution. To further improve judgment quality beyond SFT, we introduce \textit{AdaReward}, an adaptive multi-reward RL algorithm that dynamically rebalances reward component weights as different objectives saturate at different rates during RL training. For practical deployment, we further design a lightweight domain specialization module for rapid adaptation to new evaluation domains with few hundred labeled samples. As a result, (i) \textit{Novel}: the first framework to equip a single compact judge with multi-agent panel deliberation capability at single-model inference cost; (ii) \textit{Effective \& Reliable}: JudgePanel with a 14B backbone outperforms judge-specialized models up to 70B across four evaluation benchmarks, demonstrates strong position consistency, and rapidly specializes to new domains with few hundred samples.

</details>


### [294] [An Explainable Coherence Score for Detecting Temporal Inconsistencies in Political News](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29175)
*Marius Nicusor Pantea,Adrian Groza*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes Temporal Coherence Score (TCS), a metric and system to detect temporal inconsistencies in political news articles by building and verifying a temporal knowledge graph, achieving high-precision detection of time-related disinformation and providing interpretable explanations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing fake news detectors rely heavily on lexical or stylistic cues, which fail when disinformation is limited to subtle temporal inconsistencies like wrong dates or impossible event sequences in otherwise well-written text. There is a need for a method that can capture these temporal incoherences and provide interpretable, fine-grained feedback suitable for human fact-checkers, prioritizing precision over recall.

Method: The authors design a four-stage pipeline: (1) extract temporal facts from an article (events, entities, time intervals); (2) build a temporal knowledge graph encoding these facts; (3) verify this graph using hierarchical checks: eight internal consistency checkers based on Allen’s interval algebra rules and a five-level external hierarchy of reference sources, from a local curated KB of 1,256 political facts up to live Wikidata SPARQL queries; (4) aggregate verification outcomes into a continuous Temporal Coherence Score (TCS) and automatically generate explanations specifying inconsistency types, involved entities, and contradicting sources.

Result: On a benchmark of 100 political news articles where temporal errors were artificially injected, the system achieves a precision of 0.909 at the operating threshold chosen, leaving only one false positive. The system is tuned for high precision, accepting more missed detections in order to minimize false alarms, which is suitable for human-in-the-loop fact-checking contexts.

Conclusion: The Temporal Coherence Score provides an interpretable, fine-grained measure of temporal coherence and effectively detects temporal disinformation that is invisible to traditional lexical or style-based fake news detectors. By combining internal temporal reasoning with external knowledge sources and by outputting explanations rather than just binary labels, the approach better supports human fact-checkers and suggests a promising direction for combating time-related misinformation in news content.

Abstract: Temporal inconsistencies, such as mandates attributed outside their real interval, events presented as past before they occurred, or inverted causal sequences, are a form of political disinformation that evades style-based fake news detectors: a well-written article with a single wrong date carries no lexical signal of falsehood. This paper introduces the Temporal Coherence Score (TCS), a continuous, intrinsically interpretable metric that quantifies the temporal coherence of a news article, computed by a four-stage pipeline: extraction of temporal facts, construction of a temporal knowledge graph, hierarchical verification against internal consistency rules and external reference sources, and score aggregation with automatically generated explanations. Verification combines eight internal checkers derived from Allen's interval algebra with a five-level external hierarchy ranging from a locally stored reference knowledge base of 1{,}256 curated political facts to live Wikidata SPARQL queries. On a benchmark of 100 political news articles with injected temporal errors, the system reaches a precision of 0.909 at the selected operating threshold, with a single residual false positive, a profile deliberately tuned for human-in-the-loop fact-checking assistance, where false alarms are costlier than missed detections. Unlike lexical baselines that output only a binary label, every flagged article is accompanied by the inconsistency type, the entities involved, and the reference source that contradicts the claim.

</details>


### [295] [How Identity and Opinion Shape Political Sycophancy in LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29198)
*Li-Ni Fu,Chang-Chih Meng,Chien-Hua Chen,Hen-Hsen Huang,I-Chen Wu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper investigates how large language models change their political stances in response to users’ opinions and identities, showing that political alignment is context-dependent and steerable, not fixed.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As LLMs increasingly ask for personal and demographic information to enable personalization, there is growing concern that they may mirror users’ political opinions (sycophancy) or stereotype based on identities, potentially amplifying bias or polarization. Existing political benchmarks mostly use static, closed-ended questions, failing to capture how models adapt their views dynamically during real interactions. The authors aim to better characterize this interactive political behavior and the specific roles of user opinion and identity cues.

Method: The authors propose a framework separating two triggers of political sycophancy: (1) opinion-based sycophancy (agreeing with explicit political narratives provided by the user) and (2) identity-based sycophancy (shifting stance based on demographic labels, even without explicit opinions). They create a set of 450 manually-verified political dilemmas as controlled test cases and use these to probe 13 instruction-tuned LLMs. They systematically vary user-provided context—opinions, identity cues, and combinations thereof—as well as system-level personas, then quantify how the models’ political stances change across conditions.

Result: Across the 13 LLMs, the authors find that a model’s tendency to mirror explicit user opinions is not strongly predictive of its tendency to respond differently based on user identity labels, indicating a dissociation between opinion- and identity-based sycophancy. When both cues (opinion and identity) are present, their influence on the model’s stance tends to be sub-additive, meaning their combined effect is weaker than the sum of their separate effects. System-level persona prompts shift the overall baseline political stance of models but have relatively little impact on how much the models’ stances move in response to users’ expressed opinions or identities.

Conclusion: LLMs’ political stances are not stable traits but are strongly context-dependent and can be steered by interaction signals such as user opinions and demographic identities. Personalization mechanisms that leverage user profiles risk amplifying these context-conditioned shifts, potentially increasing political sycophancy or stereotyping. The paper argues that evaluations and safeguards must therefore focus on interactive, personalization-aware settings rather than only static benchmarks of political alignment.

Abstract: As Large Language Models (LLMs) increasingly encourage users to disclose personal profiles for tailored assistance, measuring their political alignment becomes increasingly important. However, many existing benchmarks for assessing political behavior rely on closed-ended questions and do not fully capture how a model's stance may adapt to user-provided context during interaction. We introduce a framework that disentangles two distinct triggers of political sycophancy: opinion (aligning with explicit narratives) and identity (stereotyping based on demographic labels). Using 450 manually-checked political dilemmas as controlled probes, we evaluate 13 instruction-tuned LLMs. We uncover a dissociation: a model's susceptibility to explicit opinions does not necessarily predict its susceptibility to identity cues, and vice versa. When both signals are present, their effects are generally sub-additive rather than simply additive. Additionally, system-level personas primarily shift a model's baseline stance while having limited effect on the stance shift caused by user opinion or identity. Ultimately, our results suggest that LLM political stance is interactively and steerably vulnerable rather than being a fixed trait, highlighting how personalization may amplify identity- or opinion-conditioned shifts in the model's behaviors.

</details>


### [296] [Benevolent Bias in Multi-Turn Human-Agent Dialogue](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29206)
*Qianqi Liu,Jin Huang,Fethiye Irmak Dogan,Hatice Gunes*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces BENEVDIAL, a large dialogue dataset designed to study and detect benevolent bias—unequal but positively framed treatment—in human-agent interactions, and shows that current safety detectors and LLM judges struggle to reliably identify it without high false positives.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing work on bias in human-agent interaction focuses mainly on clearly hostile or negative expressions (overt bias). However, unequal treatment can also appear as benevolent bias: interactions that sound supportive or positive but still treat different demographic groups differently. This type of bias is harder to detect automatically yet can still cause harm and unfairness. The authors aim to (1) formally define benevolent bias in dialogue, (2) create a controlled benchmark to evaluate it, and (3) assess whether current safety tools and LLM-based judges can detect it fairly across demographics.

Method: The authors operationalise benevolent bias along two dimensions: tone (e.g., warm/positive vs neutral/negative) and treatment (equal vs unequal). Crossing these dimensions yields three classes for dialogue turns: neutral support, overt bias (clearly negative and unequal), and benevolent bias (positive tone but unequal treatment). Using these definitions, they construct BENEVDIAL, a class-balanced dataset of 362,880 multi-turn support dialogues that systematically vary user and agent demographics, roles, and underlying generators. They then evaluate two detector families on this corpus: (1) existing off-the-shelf safety and toxicity detectors; and (2) large language models prompted as judges with different levels of explicitness in the bias-detection instructions. They analyze detection performance by bias type and examine how demographic context affects error rates, especially false positives on neutral support.

Result: Off-the-shelf safety detectors perform well on overt bias—they tend to reliably flag clearly hostile or negative unequal treatment—but they largely fail to detect benevolent bias, missing many instances where treatment is unequal but framed in a positive tone. Prompted LLM judges, when given more explicit detection criteria, identify more benevolent bias cases than off-the-shelf detectors. However, as the criteria become more explicit or sensitive, these LLM judges increasingly misclassify neutral support as benevolent bias, leading to substantial false positives. Furthermore, the presence of demographic context in the dialogue amplifies these misclassifications, with detectors more likely to raise false alarms when demographics are salient, regardless of whether actual bias is present.

Conclusion: Current monitoring tools for human-agent dialogue are insufficient for fair bias detection when unequal treatment is expressed benevolently rather than overtly. Surface-level cues like hostile words or sentiment are not enough; systems must assess whether the agent’s treatment differs across demographic groups, even under a supportive tone. The BENEVDIAL corpus provides a controlled benchmark to study this phenomenon, and the observed trade-off—missing benevolent bias versus over-flagging neutral support—highlights the need for more nuanced models and evaluation criteria that can distinguish genuine benevolent bias from fair, neutral support across demographic contexts.

Abstract: Bias in human-agent interaction can manifest not only through hostile language but also as benevolent bias, whereby unequal treatment hides behind a warm, positive tone. To make it detectable, we operationalise benevolent bias along two dimensions, tone and treatment, yielding three classes: neutral support, overt bias, and benevolent bias. Building on these definitions, we construct BENEVDIAL, a class-balanced corpus of 362,880 multi-turn support dialogues spanning user and agent demographics, roles, and generators, to support controlled evaluation. We then test two detector families on it: off-the-shelf safety detectors and prompted large language model (LLM) judges. Our results reveal a detection gap: off-the-shelf detectors reliably flag overt bias yet largely miss benevolent bias, while LLM judges catch more under more explicit detection criteria but increasingly misclassify neutral support as benevolent bias, and demographic context amplifies the false alarms. These findings suggest that fair monitoring of human-agent dialogue must look beyond surface cues to whether the agent's treatment is disparate.

</details>


### [297] [Hyper-Fold: Exploring the Expressive Limit of Sequence-Geometry Learning for Proteins via Hypergraph Modeling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29207)
*Yifan Feng,Guanjie Cheng,Shihui Ying,Shaoyi Du,Yue Gao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper studies the expressive limits of geometric GNN layers for protein structures and proposes Hyper-Fold, a more expressive yet efficient 3D backbone that approaches the theoretical ceiling and achieves strong empirical performance on multiple structure-based protein tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current protein structure models rely on geometric GNNs whose message-passing layers may be fundamentally limited in how they couple amino-acid identity (sequence content) with 3D geometry. These limitations may explain why many models need large sequence language models or evolutionary information. The authors want to understand the theoretical expressive ceiling of such layers and design a practical architecture that approaches this ceiling without high computational cost.

Method: They formally analyze the layer class describing interactions between residue content and 3D geometry, showing that the complete bilinear operator over content-geometry outer products is the expressive upper bound. They prove that standard additive message-passing GNNs cannot capture full content-geometry binding. Based on this, they design Hyper-Fold, a rank-K separable convolutional backbone. For each residue, they build two hyperedges (sequence neighborhood and 3D contact neighborhood) and apply an edge-conditioned matrix-valued operator, factorized into K learned basis operators with coefficients generated from geometry. They also define Hyper-Fold-Deep, a hierarchical version, and Hyper-Fold-Pocket, a set-prediction head specialized for pockets.

Result: Hyper-Fold and Hyper-Fold-Deep outperform other protein-specific 3D encoders on enzyme function prediction, fold classification, and ligand binding site detection. Hyper-Fold-Pocket exceeds UniSite-3D on the UniSite-DS benchmark and two zero-shot tests, without using sequence language model features, while having 68x fewer parameters and 4.8x lower latency.

Conclusion: The expressive ceiling for content-geometry interactions in protein structure modeling is the full bilinear operator over content-geometry outer products. Mainstream geometric GNNs fall short of this, but the proposed Hyper-Fold architecture provides a practical approximation with message-passing cost. Its strong performance, even without sequence LM features, indicates that a sufficiently expressive 3D structural backbone can recover information that previous models needed evolution-scale sequence pretraining to supply.

Abstract: Protein structure modeling rests on a single computational primitive: the interaction between what a residue is (sequence content) and where it sits (three-dimensional geometry). What is the expressive limit of this layer class? We show that the complete bilinear operator over content-geometry outer products--the sufficient statistic of all second-order interactions--is the expressive ceiling, while the additive message passing of mainstream geometric GNNs is provably blind to content-geometry binding. We then introduce Hyper-Fold, a rank-K separable convolutional backbone approaching this ceiling at message-passing cost: each radius neighborhood is organized into a sequence hyperedge and a contact hyperedge, modulated by an edge-conditioned matrix-valued operator factorized into K learned basis operators with geometry-generated coefficients. Across enzyme function prediction, fold classification, and ligand binding site detection, Hyper-Fold and its hierarchical variant Hyper-Fold-Deep achieve the best results among protein-specific structure encoders; Hyper-Fold-Pocket, an anchored set-prediction head, surpasses UniSite-3D on UniSite-DS and two zero-shot benchmarks with no sequence language model features, 68x fewer parameters, and 4.8x lower latency--suggesting that a sufficiently expressive 3D backbone recovers information that fusion architectures previously borrowed from evolution-scale pretraining.

</details>


### [298] [Imag-Eval: a language-grounded framework for interpretable Text-to-Image instruction following evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29210)
*Ibrahim Mohamed Serouis,David Jaramillo Duque*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Imag-Eval is a controlled benchmark for evaluating how well text-to-image models follow compositional natural language instructions, separating true compositional difficulty from superficial prompt complexity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing T2I benchmarks are hard to interpret and not sufficiently diagnostic. They often miss important failure modes like global incoherence (missing parts, impossible configurations) and usually control prompt difficulty only along a single axis, such as length or number of elements, which conflates linguistic complexity with compositional difficulty.

Method: The authors design Imag-Eval, a benchmark that systematically varies (1) the number of instances to be generated and (2) the number and combinations of constraints or rules applied to those instances. They keep these factors independent to avoid error propagation and to disentangle compositional complexity from surface linguistic complexity. The benchmark consists of 1,140 prompts and 8,842 rule combinations, and is used to evaluate several state-of-the-art text-to-image models.

Result: Experiments across multiple state-of-the-art T2I models, along with an auxiliary analysis of more than 2,000 prompts from another benchmark, show clear patterns in how models fail at following structured, compositional instructions. The analysis enables pinpointing where models break down with respect to global coherence and rule grounding.

Conclusion: For structured skills in text-to-image generation, the main driver of compositional difficulty is the number of grounded rules and how they are bound to specific instances, not prompt length or surface linguistic complexity. Imag-Eval provides a more interpretable, fine-grained way to analyze cross-modal instruction-following failures in T2I models.

Abstract: Text-to-Image (T2I) models have recently achieved impressive visual fidelity, yet their evaluation remains constrained by benchmarks that are often difficult to interpret and insufficiently diagnostic. Existing skill-based evaluations tend to overlook critical failure modes that strongly impact usability but fall outside standard taxonomies, such as global incoherence arising from missing parts or physically implausible configurations (e.g., floating objects). In addition, prompt difficulty is typically controlled along a single dimension; either prompt length or the number of elements to generate. To address these limitations, we introduce Imag-Eval, a controlled benchmark designed to assess how T2I models ground compositional natural-language instructions into visual outputs. Unlike prior work that conflates surface linguistic complexity with compositional difficulty, Imag-Eval explicitly seeks to disentangles these factors by independently varying both the number of instances and the combination of constraints (rules), while avoiding error propagation. This design enables fine-grained and interpretable analysis of where cross-modal instruction following fails. Our benchmark comprises 1,140 prompts and 8,842 combined rules, and we evaluate it on several state-of-the-art models. Complementing this analysis with an additional study of over 2,000 prompts from a concurrent benchmark, our results suggest that, for structured skills, compositional difficulty is primarily governed by the number of grounded rules and their binding to instances,, rather than by prompt length alone.

</details>


### [299] [Computational Depth Measurement in Thermographic Video: Overcoming Spatial Overfitting via Spatio-Temporal Decoupling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29223)
*Zain Ul Abidin,Habeeban Memon,Junaid Ahmed*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes a spatio-temporal decoupling and feature-based learning framework to robustly estimate subsurface delamination depth in CFRP from optical pulsed thermography, mitigating spatial memorization and achieving high cross-specimen accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In CFRP structures, knowing not just the presence but the through-thickness depth of delaminations is critical because depth determines which load-bearing plies are compromised. Optical pulsed thermography naturally gives 2D thermal videos rather than full 3D data, so depth must be inferred indirectly from temporal thermal responses. Existing learning-based depth regressors often train on specimens with defects arranged on regular grids; as a result they may overfit spatial patterns (pixel positions) instead of learning the underlying physics of heat diffusion, causing calibration failure when evaluated on specimens with different defect layouts. The paper is motivated by the need for robust, cross-specimen depth estimation that generalizes beyond a specific calibration geometry.

Method: The authors introduce a spatio-temporal decoupling architecture. First, defect areas are localized via image segmentation to obtain defect masks. Within each mask, thermal responses over time are spatially averaged, removing explicit spatial coordinates from the regression input. From these averaged signals, sixteen physics-informed temporal, energy-related, statistical, and geometric features are extracted to capture the essentially one-dimensional through-thickness heat conduction behavior. These feature vectors are used as inputs to several regression models—Random Forest, Gradient Boosting Machine, an advanced multi-layer perceptron (Adv-MLP), and XGBoost. The models are evaluated with specimen-level cross-validation to test generalization across different defect geometries. The study also investigates the effect of tree and network regularization (L1/L2 penalties, column sampling) on mitigating spatial memorization and preserving calibration across specimens. Finally, predicted depths are combined with defect masks and reconstructed into 3D defect surfaces using Delaunay triangulation.

Result: Unregularized tree-based methods (e.g., standard Random Forest, unregularized Gradient Boosting) and an over-parameterized Adv-MLP suffer from “calibration collapse” when the defect geometry shifts between calibration and test specimens, leading to depth prediction errors larger than 0.5 mm. In contrast, a regularized XGBoost model incorporating L1/L2 penalties and column sampling maintains robust calibration under specimen-level cross-validation. It achieves a mean absolute error of 0.056 mm and a root mean square error of 0.085 mm in depth estimation. The entire pipeline, including segmentation, feature extraction, regression, and 3D reconstruction via Delaunay triangulation, can generate 3D defect models in about 3–5 seconds per specimen.

Conclusion: Separating spatial localization from temporal depth estimation and using physics-informed temporal features effectively constrains the learning problem to a one-dimensional heat-conduction relationship, which in turn mitigates spatial memorization biases present in thermal-video regression. When combined with strong mathematical regularization (as in XGBoost with L1/L2 penalties and column sampling), this framework yields accurate and robust cross-specimen depth predictions for subsurface delaminations in CFRP. The work suggests that carefully designed feature engineering and regularization are key to achieving generalizable, geometry-agnostic depth calibration in optical pulsed thermography, enabling fast 3D reconstruction of internal defects suitable for structural assessment workflows.

Abstract: Accurate through-thickness measurement of subsurface delamination depth in Carbon Fiber Reinforced Polymer (CFRP) is important for structural assessment because defect location determines affected load-bearing layers. Optical pulsed thermography (OPT) provides a two-dimensional thermal video rather than volumetric measurements, so depth must be inferred from temporal heat-diffusion responses. A challenge is spatial dataset bias: when calibration defects follow regular grids, regression models may memorize their geometry instead of learning physical relationship between thermal decay and depth. This work introduces a spatio-temporal decoupling architecture that separates spatial defect localization from temporal depth measurement. Defect regions are first localized using segmentation methods, after which thermal responses are spatially averaged and converted into sixteen physics-informed temporal, energy, statistical, and geometric features. These features expose the one-dimensional heat-conduction relationship while withholding pixel coordinates from the depth model. Four regression models are evaluated using specimen-level cross-validation: Random Forest (RF), Gradient Boosting Machine (GBM), Advanced Multi-Layer Perceptron (Adv-MLP), and XGBoost. Unregularized trees and over-parameterized Adv-MLP exhibit calibration collapse under geometric shifts, with errors exceeding 0.5 mm. In contrast, regularized XGBoost with L1/L2 penalties and column sampling maintains cross-specimen calibration, achieving a mean absolute error (MAE) of 0.056 mm and root mean square error (RMSE) of 0.085 mm. Predicted depths are merged with masks to generate Delaunay-triangulated three-dimensional defect models in three to five seconds per specimen. Results show that mathematical regularization and spatio-temporal decoupling reduce spatial memorization in thermal-video depth regression.

</details>


### [300] [Localizing Emergent Failures in Agentic AI: Recovering Minimal Repair Families via Counterfactual Replay](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29228)
*Bingjie Li,Yumeng Song,Zhongming Yao,Tianyi Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces a method to precisely identify minimal sets of events in multi-agent LLM systems whose correction would fix a failure, while greatly reducing the number of expensive replays needed compared to exhaustive search.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Agentic AI systems often involve multiple LLM agents exchanging many messages. When the overall system fails, it is hard to attribute the failure to specific events, especially when the cause is a combination of events rather than a single one. Existing pointwise attribution approaches usually look at one event at a time and cannot detect jointly necessary sets of events that must be changed together to repair the failure. This motivates a principled way to recover all minimal combinations of events whose correction would make the system succeed, within a reasonable search effort.

Method: The authors formalize the Minimal Repair Family Recovery (MRFR) problem: given a failed execution, find all inclusion-minimal sets of events (within a bounded size) such that, if these events were repaired, the system would succeed when counterfactually replayed. They propose Graph-Constrained Joint Replay (GCJR), which uses the execution dependency graph of the system to restrict the search. GCJR first slices out failure-relevant events from the dependency DAG. It then constructs graph-feasible candidate repairs consisting of single events and pairs of events that are consistent with the graph structure. These candidates are tested via counterfactual replays where each event is replaced with a clean version. By operating within a fixed graph domain, GCJR provides exact recovery of the minimal repair families while requiring far fewer replay calls than an exhaustive search over all event subsets.

Result: On a controlled benchmark built from 120 execution DAGs, with 90 cases falling within the method's assumed graph domain, GCJR recovers the true minimal repair families exactly (Family Exact Match of 1.000). Compared with exhaustive search, it reduces the average number of replay calls from 56.3 to 25.3, a 55.1% reduction. In a pilot study on a four-agent LLM setup with 24 failure cases, GCJR again achieves perfect Family Exact Match (1.000) and cuts the average number of model calls from 21.0 to 10.0 (52.4%). The authors also show that simple single-event replays fail to capture jointly necessary repairs that involve multiple events, highlighting GCJR's advantage.

Conclusion: The paper concludes that analyzing failures in multi-agent LLM systems requires moving beyond pointwise attribution to reasoning about joint event sets. Their MRFR formulation captures this need, and the GCJR algorithm provides an exact and practical solution within a dependency-graph-defined domain. Empirically, GCJR maintains perfect accuracy in identifying minimal repair families while reducing the number of expensive replay/model calls by roughly half compared to exhaustive approaches. The results suggest that structured, graph-based search is an effective way to diagnose and repair complex failures in agentic AI systems, and that relying solely on single-event attributions will miss important multi-event failure modes.

Abstract: Failures in agentic AI systems can arise from interactions among messages exchanged by multiple large language model (LLM) agents. Pointwise attribution cannot distinguish a jointly necessary repair from alternative singleton repairs. We formulate Minimal Repair Family Recovery (MRFR): recovering all inclusion-minimal event sets whose counterfactual replay restores task success within a declared size bound. We propose Graph-Constrained Joint Replay (GCJR), which slices failure-relevant events from an execution dependency graph, constructs graph-feasible singleton and pair candidates, and verifies them by replay with paired clean counterparts. For fixed replay outcomes, GCJR is exact within its declared graph domain. On 90 in-scope cases from a 120-DAG controlled benchmark, GCJR achieves 1.000 Family Exact Match while reducing mean replay calls from 56.3 to 25.3 (55.1%) relative to exhaustive search. On a 24-case, four-agent LLM pilot, it again achieves 1.000 Family Exact Match and reduces mean model calls from 21.0 to 10.0 (52.4%); single-event replay misses jointly necessary repairs.

</details>


### [301] [Validating FKG.in: Soundness Assessment in LLM-Augmented Indian Food Knowledge](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29249)
*Saransh Kumar Gupta,Armaan Shah,Lipika Dey,Partha Pratim Das,Ramesh Jain*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes a semi-automated workflow to check and correct LLM-generated structured recipe data, ensuring it is structurally and semantically sound for use in a food knowledge graph.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM-generated recipes, though fluent, can include hallucinated ingredients, wrong quantities, or culturally implausible combinations, making them unreliable for downstream applications like knowledge graph construction. There is a need for systematic validation and correction of such LLM-augmented culinary data.

Method: The authors design a multi-stage soundness assessment pipeline for structured recipe data within the FKG.in Indian food knowledge graph. The workflow uses formal grammars to enforce structural constraints, vocabulary-based checks to validate ingredient and cooking term usage, statistical heuristics to detect anomalies, Set Transformer-based models to assess recipe coherence, and retrieval-based verification to compare against original source texts, identifying and mitigating structural, semantic, logical, and fidelity-related errors.

Result: Applied to Indian recipes in FKG.in, the pipeline successfully identifies common LLM failure modes such as structural inconsistencies, semantic/logical incoherence, and deviations from source text. The evaluation indicates that the approach improves the reliability and soundness of the resulting structured recipe data, making it more suitable for knowledge graph integration and downstream applications.

Conclusion: The paper concludes that the proposed semi-automated, auditable, and application-agnostic workflow provides an effective way to validate and improve LLM-augmented recipe data. Although demonstrated on Indian recipes, the methodology generalizes to multilingual and multicultural culinary domains, thus offering a robust foundation for building machine-readable food knowledge infrastructures in an era dominated by LLM-generated content.

Abstract: The online culinary ecosystem is increasingly populated by recipe content generated, modified, or summarized by Large Language Models (LLMs). While often plausible, such outputs may contain hallucinated ingredients, misrepresented quantities, or culturally implausible combinations, limiting their suitability for downstream applications and knowledge graph construction. In this paper, we present a semi-automated soundness assessment workflow for validating structured recipe data extracted and augmented by LLMs from informal culinary sources. Developed as part of FKG.in, a knowledge graph of Indian food, the pipeline identifies and addresses common failure modes, including structural inconsistencies, semantic and logical incoherence, and deviations from the source text, through a multi-stage process combining formal grammars, vocabulary-based checks, statistical heuristics, Set Transformer-based coherence modeling, and retrieval-based verification. Although evaluated on Indian recipes, the proposed methods are applicable to broader multilingual and multicultural culinary domains. We provide a practical, auditable, and application-agnostic framework for validating LLM-augmented recipe data, thereby strengthening the foundations of machine-readable food knowledge infrastructures in the era of LLM-generated content.

</details>


### [302] [GuardianAgent: Policy-Conditioned Risk-Adaptive Anonymization with Verified Adversarial Escalation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29251)
*Ruiyi Yang,Gayathri Lihinikaduarachchi,Rahat Masood,Flora D. Salim,Salil S. Kanhere*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: GuardianAgent is an agent-side, policy-aware anonymization system that scores disclosure risk and adaptively rewrites text, outperforming prior methods in privacy-utility trade-offs across several benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM-based privacy tools mostly detect and mask PII spans in isolation, ignoring the target site's policy, the context and purpose of sharing, and the varying sensitivity of information. Directly asking an LLM to judge risk can be unreliable and inefficient, and over-aggressive anonymization harms utility. The authors want a principled way to decide when and how much to rewrite outgoing text, conditioned on the actual privacy policy and contextual factors, while avoiding hallucinated risk estimates.

Method: They design GuardianAgent, which separates policy-based risk scoring from LLM rewriting. Risk is computed via AMRSF, an explicit multi-factor formula combining: (1) likelihood of policy violation, (2) data sensitivity, (3) recipient characteristics, (4) purpose legitimacy, (5) contextual legal/contractual basis, and (6) transparency of the destination policy. This numeric risk controls allow/transform/deny decisions and the anonymization level. For efficiency, there is an evidential fast path for low-uncertainty policy matches; only ambiguous cases go to an LLM slow path. Rewriting uses a five-level anonymization hierarchy (e.g., light redaction to heavy generalization) driven by a verified adversarial guesser: anonymization escalates only if the attacker model can correctly infer hidden data from the remaining text using evidence present in the original, thus avoiding hallucinated over-redaction.

Result: On three benchmarks—legal text (TAB), Reddit posts (SynthPAI), and synthetic PII records (PII-Masking-300k)—GuardianAgent outperforms prior anonymization baselines in the privacy-utility trade-off and is uniquely able to exceed 0.90 privacy across all domains. Its performance remains strong even when the LLM backbone is changed, indicating robustness. Stress tests with varying recipients, purposes, legal bases, and transparency show that the framework meaningfully changes decisions and anonymization strength based on context, as intended.

Conclusion: GuardianAgent demonstrates that policy-conditioned, formula-based risk scoring combined with adaptive adversary-verified rewriting can provide stronger and more contextually appropriate privacy protection than span-based or purely LLM-judged approaches. It yields high privacy with better utility across diverse domains and remains robust under model changes, suggesting a viable blueprint for deployable, context-aware privacy guards for web agents and automated systems.

Abstract: Privacy protection for live web traffic requires more than detecting private spans. Agent-based privacy protection systems must determine whether an outgoing action complies with the destination site's privacy policy, then apply only the level of rewriting or sanitisation justified by the residual disclosure risk. We present GuardianAgent, a policy-conditioned anonymization framework that couples structured risk assessment with verified adaptive rewriting. GuardianAgent computes risk through AMRSF (Adaptive Multi-factor Risk Scoring Formula), an explicit controller that combines policy-violation likelihood with data sensitivity, recipient transmission, purpose legitimacy, contextual basis, and policy transparency, rather than relying on an LLM to assign risk directly. This risk score determines both the allow/transform/deny decision and the initial anonymization level. For efficiency, GuardianAgent uses an evidential fast path for low-uncertainty policy matches and invokes an LLM slow path only for uncertain cases. For rewriting, it applies a five-level hierarchy driven by a verified adversarial guesser: guesses trigger escalation only when supported by the original text, preventing hallucinated attacker confidence from causing unnecessary over-anonymization. Experiments across three benchmarks spanning legal text (TAB), Reddit posts (SynthPAI), and multi-format synthetic PII records (PII-Masking-300k) show that GuardianAgent achieves the strongest privacy-utility trade-off among published baselines and is the only method to reach more than 0.90 privacy in all three domains, remaining robust under a backbone switch. Action-context stress tests further show that the same outgoing text receives different decisions and anonymization strengths under different recipients, purposes, action bases, and policy-transparency conditions.

</details>


### [303] [Dynamic Important Example Mining for Reinforcement Finetuning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29252)
*Haoru Tan,Sitong Wu,Yanfeng Chen,Shizhen Zhao,Yang-Tian Sun,Tianjia Liu,Chirui Chang,Shaofeng Zhang,Samm Sun,Xiuzhe Wu,Ruobing Xie,Xiaojuan Qi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces DIEM, a dynamic data selection and reweighting framework for reinforcement fine-tuning that improves reasoning performance of large models by prioritizing training samples based on their estimated contribution to policy improvement at each optimization step.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing reinforcement fine-tuning (RFT) methods for improving large models’ reasoning rely on static or heuristic sample selection, implicitly treating each sample’s training value as fixed. This ignores the fact that as the model (policy) changes over time, the usefulness of each sample also changes, leading to suboptimal learning efficiency and weaker final performance. The authors aim to create a principled, automated way to adaptively focus on the most beneficial examples throughout training, matching the non-stationary nature of policy learning.

Method: They propose Dynamic Important Example Mining (DIEM), which is plugged into each RFT optimization step. DIEM has two key components: (1) a gradient-alignment importance estimator that efficiently approximates each sample’s marginal contribution to improving the current policy by estimating how well its gradient aligns with the target improvement direction; and (2) a constrained batch reweighting scheme that adjusts example weights within each batch to maximize total estimated utility while constraining the overall gradient norm, so that the update remains stable and comparable in magnitude to standard training steps. This yields an adaptive, fully-automated procedure that changes which samples are emphasized as training progresses.

Result: On multiple reasoning benchmarks, models trained with DIEM during RFT outperform both strong static data selection approaches and other dynamic baselines. This indicates that DIEM’s gradient-based importance estimation and constrained reweighting lead to better data utilization and more effective policy improvement.

Conclusion: The study concludes that accounting for the non-stationary value of training samples is important in reinforcement fine-tuning. By dynamically estimating per-sample contribution and reweighting batches under stability constraints, DIEM provides a principled and automated way to improve reasoning-focused RFT, consistently yielding better performance than existing selection strategies. The authors plan to release the implementation for broader use and further research.

Abstract: Reinforcement fine-tuning (RFT) is increasingly used to strengthen the reasoning abilities of large models, yet its effectiveness is bound by how training data are selected and used. Most data-centric RFT methods rely on static or heuristic sample selection, implicitly assuming a sample's value is fixed over training. This overlooks the non-stationary dynamics of policy learning and can lead to suboptimal updates. We propose Dynamic Important Example Mining (DIEM), a principled and fully automated framework that makes data utilization adaptive throughout RFT. DIEM integrates two components into each optimization step: (i) a gradient-alignment importance estimator that efficiently approximates each sample's marginal contribution to policy improvement; and (ii) a constrained batch reweighting scheme that maximizes aggregate utility while preserving the update's gradient magnitude to stabilize optimization. Across several reasoning benchmarks, DIEM consistently outperforms strong static and dynamic baselines. The code will be released via https://github.com/hrtan/DIEM.

</details>


### [304] [RACER: Reinforced Agent Collaboration for Explainable Reasoning on Knowledge Graphs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29263)
*Yuwei Lou,Hao Hu,Yuzhou Jiang,Zongfei Zhang,Liang Wang,Jincai Liu,Jidong Ge,Xianping Tao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: RACER is a multi-agent, reinforcement learning-based framework that integrates large language models with knowledge graphs to improve explainable multi-hop reasoning and reduce hallucinations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs hallucinate and perform poorly on complex, multi-hop reasoning tasks that require reliable domain knowledge. Existing KG-enhanced LLM approaches typically use a single agent to extract paths and fixed prompts, which are not adaptive and suffer from large, inefficient search spaces and brittle, single-path reasoning. There is a need for a more efficient, adaptive, and interpretable way to leverage KGs for LLM reasoning.

Method: RACER introduces a Reinforced Agent Collaboration framework operating over knowledge graphs. It uses semantic-aware action pruning and teacher-guided reinforcement learning to efficiently explore and extract high-quality reasoning paths from large KGs. To avoid relying on a single reasoning path, it builds a cross-task accumulated shared memory graph and an attention-driven multi-path knowledge refinement module. These are coordinated through four collaborating agents—GraphAgent for KG reasoning, TemplateAgent for prompt construction, AnswerAgent for answer generation, and CriticAgent for evaluation and feedback—forming a closed-loop, adaptive reasoning process.

Result: On CommonsenseQA and OpenBookQA benchmarks, RACER achieves about 5% average performance gains over state-of-the-art KG-enhanced LLM baselines, while providing more robust and interpretable reasoning via explicit multi-hop paths and multi-agent collaboration.

Conclusion: RACER demonstrates that combining multi-agent collaboration, reinforcement learning, and structured KG reasoning can substantially improve LLM performance on complex reasoning tasks. Its semantic pruning, shared memory graph, and multi-path refinement yield more efficient KG exploration and more reliable, explainable answers than prior single-agent, fixed-prompt approaches.
