This limitation restricts reasoning quality and adaptability, especially when useful information is distributed across the graph or when the best neighbours are not obvious beforehand. The paper aims to make neighbour selection an integral, learnable component of the reasoning process, enabling proactive, topology-aware exploration of the graph.

Method: The authors propose Call Neighbours Yourself (CNY), a framework where an LLM interacts with a TAG via topology-constrained graph-walk actions. The model sees lightweight previews of candidate neighbours and can choose to "expand" specific neighbours to fetch full textual content as additional evidence. Neighbour selection is thus integrated into multi-step reasoning. To effectively train this exploration behavior, they introduce destination-conditioned on-policy self-distillation: after expanding a neighbour and revealing its content, they retrospectively measure how this new evidence changes the model's action preferences and convert this into an action-level training signal, addressing the delayed credit assignment problem in exploration.

Result: On standard TAG reasoning benchmarks, evaluated in a unified raw-text setting (without task-specific feature engineering), CNY consistently outperforms post-training baselines that rely on fixed contexts. The learned exploration policy demonstrates robustness and generalization: it transfers successfully to unseen graphs and to a new, graph-level task that was not part of the training data.

Conclusion: Integrating neighbour exploration into the reasoning loop over TAGs, rather than treating it as a static pre-processing step, leads to better reasoning performance and more generalizable LLM behaviours. The CNY framework shows that lightweight neighbour previews and a principled self-distillation strategy can effectively train LLMs to proactively and adaptively explore graph neighbourhoods, improving both accuracy and transfer to new graph settings and tasks.

Abstract: Reasoning over text-attributed graphs (TAGs) requires large language models (LLMs) to combine a node's text with evidence distributed across its neighbourhood. Existing methods fix the set of accessible neighbours before generation, forcing reasoning to operate over a static context and preventing the model from acquiring missing evidence during inference. We argue that neighbour selection should itself be part of the reasoning process. To this end, we propose Call Neighbours Yourself (CNY), a framework that enables LLMs to proactively explore graph neighbourhoods through topology-constrained graph-walk actions. Instead of reasoning over a pre-selected neighbour set, CNY exposes lightweight neighbour previews and learns when to expand candidate neighbours for additional evidence. To address the delayed-credit challenge of neighbour exploration, we introduce destination-conditioned on-policy self-distillation, which retrospectively evaluates a selected neighbour after its content is revealed and converts the resulting change in action preference into an action-level training signal. Experiments on standard TAG reasoning benchmarks under a unified raw-text setting show that CNY consistently outperforms fixed-context post-training baselines. Furthermore, the learned exploration policy transfers to unseen graphs and to a graph-level task not encountered during training. Code is available at https://github.com/superallen13/CNY.

</details>


### [325] [Not Safe for All: Auditing the Dialect Penalty in Text-to-Image Safety Pipelines](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29589)
*Minkyu Kim,Juhwan Choi,YoungBin Kim*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper shows that current text-to-image (T2I) safety systems are unfair to speakers of non-standard English dialects, over- or under-flagging their prompts due to surface linguistic features rather than actual harmful content, and proposes balanced retraining to reduce this "dialect penalty."


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As T2I models are widely deployed with safety guardrails, it is critical that these systems work equitably across different user populations. However, most safety evaluations focus on standard English and aggregate metrics, which can hide systematic failures for minority dialect speakers. The authors are motivated to quantify and understand whether T2I safety filters unfairly penalize or neglect content written in non-standard English dialects, and to identify where in the pipeline this bias arises and how to mitigate it.

Method: The authors construct a dataset of 23,080 paired prompts spanning five English dialects, carefully controlling for semantic equivalence across dialect variants. They evaluate multiple T2I safety components—text-level filters like NSFW-T, LatentGuard, and the OpenAI Moderation API, as well as the image generator and post-hoc guardrails—on these prompts. They define and measure a "dialect penalty" as differential flagging rates across dialects, and run a controlled typo ablation to separate dialect-specific flagging from generic out-of-distribution reactions. They analyze which stage of the T2I pipeline introduces bias and relate it to the training data distribution. Finally, they apply group-balanced retraining and GroupDRO to assess which mitigation strategies effectively reduce the dialect penalty, using ablations to pinpoint the mechanism behind improvements.

Result: The study finds that text-level safety filters exhibit substantial dialect penalties: NSFW-T disproportionately flags benign prompts from non-standard dialects, LatentGuard over-flags toxic prompts in those dialects, and the OpenAI Moderation API under-detects harmful content when expressed in them. Bias gaps reach up to +28.29 percentage points. The typo ablation indicates the penalty is driven by dialectal linguistic markers rather than a general sensitivity to out-of-distribution text. The image generator itself is largely insensitive to dialect variation, but biased text processing causes uneven behavior that propagates to downstream guardrails. Empirical analysis links the observed bias to imbalanced training data, and group-balanced retraining significantly reduces the dialect penalty, with improvements attributable mainly to balanced exposure rather than the GroupDRO objective per se.

Conclusion: The paper concludes that current T2I safety pipelines systematically and inequitably fail speakers of non-standard English dialects, and that standard, mean-accuracy benchmarks obscure this equity failure. The primary source of bias lies in text-level safety components that misinterpret dialectal features as signals of (or against) toxicity. Since this penalty is tied to training data imbalance, it can be meaningfully mitigated through group-balanced retraining rather than more complex distributionally robust optimization objectives. The authors argue that equitable safety in generative systems requires explicit dialect-aware evaluation and debiasing, and they release code and data to support further work in this area.

Abstract: Text-to-image (T2I) safety guardrails fail to generalize equitably to non-standard dialects. Evaluating 23,080 paired prompts across five English dialects, we formalize this failure as the dialect penalty, where filters trigger based on linguistic surface features rather than semantic intent. Text-level filters fail in opposing directions: NSFW-T over-flags benign dialect prompts and LatentGuard over-flags toxic ones (bias gaps up to +28.29 pp), while the OpenAI Moderation API under-detects them. A controlled typo ablation confirms this penalty originates from flagging dialectal features, not generic out-of-distribution sensitivity. The pixel-level generator is largely dialect-agnostic; the penalty enters at text processing and cascades unevenly to post-hoc guardrails. We show this bias tracks training data imbalance and is mitigable via group-balanced retraining, with an ablation attributing the gain to balanced exposure rather than to the worst-group objective of GroupDRO (group distributionally robust optimization). Current pipelines systematically fail dialect speakers, an equity failure masked by mean accuracy benchmarks. Our official code and dataset are publicly available at https://github.com/minguinho26/dialect-penalty-t2i.
  Content Warning: This paper contains offensive, toxic, or disturbing text prompts and generated images.

</details>


### [326] [Towards a Systems Foundation for Agentic Skills: Architecture, Lifecycle, and Security](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29596)
*Sanket Badhe,Deep Shah,Priyanka Tiwari,Nehal Kathrotia*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes a unified systems and architectural framework for “agentic skills” – modular, reusable procedural capabilities for autonomous LLM agents – and outlines their lifecycle, infrastructure, and open challenges.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Autonomous LLM agents tackling complex, long-horizon tasks face limitations in reliability, context window usage, and stable execution. Current approaches such as large monolithic prompts and simple stateless tool calls do not scale well as tasks grow in complexity. The community is informally converging on "agentic skills" (modular, reusable capabilities), but there is no unified formalization, architecture, or lifecycle model for how such skills should be represented, discovered, stored, composed, executed, evaluated, and governed. The paper aims to provide this missing systems foundation and common reference architecture so that future agent systems can be more scalable, robust, and interoperable.

Method: The authors conceptually formalize "agentic skills" as externalized procedural knowledge that connects high-level cognitive planning of LLM agents with deterministic execution environments (e.g., tools, code, robots). They then decompose the agentic skills ecosystem into a nine-stage lifecycle: (1) autonomous discovery of skills; (2) authoring and representation formats; (3) memory and storage infrastructures; (4) dynamic retrieval and routing mechanisms; (5) composition and orchestration of multiple skills; (6) execution monitoring and repair; (7) lifelong adaptation and updating; (8) empirical evaluation methodologies; and (9) security and governance. They also analyze marketplace and registry structures for sharing skills, identify adversarial threat models, and survey runtime verification and defense strategies. Finally, they map and categorize existing system implementations across several application domains to illustrate the framework.

Result: The paper yields a reference architecture and lifecycle model that describes how agentic skills should be discovered, represented, stored, retrieved, composed, executed, adapted, evaluated, and secured. It organizes the fragmented work on LLM tools, functions, and agents into a coherent framework and taxonomy. It also provides an analysis of marketplace and registry dynamics, outlines adversarial vectors and corresponding defenses, and categorizes existing systems for software engineering, operating systems interaction, robotics, and scientific discovery according to the proposed framework. The main concrete result is this unifying conceptual and systems-level blueprint rather than a single empirical benchmark or model performance gain.

Conclusion: The authors conclude that agentic skills—modular, externalized procedural capabilities—are a foundational paradigm for scalable, reliable, and verifiable autonomous LLM agents. By treating skills as first-class, shareable artifacts with a well-defined nine-stage lifecycle and security model, developers can overcome reliability, context, and stability bottlenecks of monolithic prompts and naive tool use. The paper argues that adopting this unified systems view will enable more robust ecosystems of skills, foster marketplaces and registries, and guide research on continual learning, realistic benchmarks, and defenses against adversarial threats in agentic systems.

Abstract: Autonomous large language model (LLM) agents increasingly face reliability, context consumption, and execution stability bottlenecks when deployed on complex, long-horizon tasks. While monolithic prompt engineering and stateless tool-calling paradigms struggle to scale, the field is rapidly converging toward \emph{agentic skills}: modular procedural abstractions that externalize execution knowledge into reusable, executable, and portable artifacts. This paper establishes a unified systems foundation and reference architecture for the agentic skills ecosystem. We formalize skills as externalized procedural knowledge bridging high-level cognitive planning with deterministic execution environments, and systematically delineate the architecture across a nine-stage lifecycle: autonomous discovery, authoring and representation formats, memory storage, dynamic retrieval and routing, composition and orchestration, execution and repair, lifelong adaptation, empirical evaluation, and security governance. We further examine marketplace dynamics, public registries, and emerging adversarial threat vectors, alongside runtime verification and defense mechanisms. Finally, we categorize system implementations across software engineering, operating system navigation, embodied robotics, and scientific discovery, while highlighting critical open challenges in continual learning and benchmark realism. This work establishes agentic skills as a foundational paradigm for building scalable, robust, and verifiable autonomous language agents.

</details>


### [327] [LLMs Interpret, Embeddings Organize, Graphs Emerge: Agent-Driven Compilation of Scientific Knowledge](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29612)
*Shi-Ju Ran,Kun Zhang,Xi Wu,Liu-Si Yang,Wen-Jun Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces ASKS, an agent-driven system for compiling scientific knowledge into a persistent, inspectable knowledge graph and wiki, demonstrated on 56 papers from a tensor-network-focused research program.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Scientific research produces large volumes of literature, but it is hard to maintain a coherent, evolving knowledge base that links interpretations, structured representations, and original evidence over time and across projects. The authors want a way to compile scientific knowledge so it can be reused, traced back to sources, and analyzed as a living, evolving structure rather than as isolated papers.

Method: They define “scientific knowledge compilation” and implement it in ASKS, an Agent-Driven Scientific Knowledge System. For each source paper, an LLM generates (1) a human-readable Wiki-style summary and (2) machine-oriented semantic representations. Deterministic validation converts those semantics into a document-local GraphDelta, describing proposed updates to a global knowledge graph. A combination of embedding-based similarity and explicit graph rules is then used to integrate each GraphDelta into a persistent graph state. Each ingestion is treated as an explicit, inspectable state transition that links back to the original source, with synchronized wiki and graph representations. They test this pipeline by incrementally ingesting 56 papers from a single research program and measuring graph dynamics such as branch survival, cross-paper support, lineage, coverage, and churn.

Result: The system successfully compiles 56 related papers into a unified, evolving knowledge graph and wiki. Analysis of the resulting graph reveals a structured research portrait centered on tensor-network methods and branching into quantum many-body physics, tensor-network-based machine learning, and quantum-AI-related directions. The higher-level organizational hubs in the graph remain stable with low churn over time, while most canonical nodes grow in an additive way, indicating that new papers generally extend rather than radically revise existing knowledge. The graph-level metrics and navigation paths maintain explicit links back to the underlying source papers used in compilation.

Conclusion: ASKS demonstrates that LLM-assisted, agent-driven scientific knowledge compilation can maintain a persistent, source-traceable knowledge substrate over a sequence of research publications. The compiled graph and wiki views provide a stable, inspectable structure that captures the evolution, branching, and support relationships within a research program, while preserving direct paths back to original evidence. This suggests a viable approach to building living scientific knowledge bases that support both human interpretation and machine reasoning.

Abstract: Sustained scientific work requires a knowledge substrate that carries interpretation across tasks and preserves paths to source evidence. We call this process \emph{scientific knowledge compilation} and implement it in ASKS, the \emph{Agent-Driven Scientific Knowledge System}. For each source, an LLM produces a readable Wiki view and machine-facing semantics. Deterministic checks convert the latter into a document-local GraphDelta, and embedding geometry together with explicit graph rules integrates the proposed changes into persistent state. Each ingest is an inspectable state transition over accumulated knowledge, with compiled Wiki and graph views linked to the preserved source record. We examine this process by chronologically compiling 56 published papers from one research program. Branch survival, cross-paper support, lineage, coverage, and churn yield a source-traceable author research portrait centered on tensor-network methods, with branches into quantum many-body research, tensor-network machine learning, and quantum-AI-oriented directions. In this run, higher-level Hub organization remains stable and low-churn. Canonical-node growth is predominantly additive. Graph-level measurements and navigation paths retain links to the source records from which they were compiled.

</details>


### [328] [Detect Before You Attribute: Cascade Failure Attribution for Multi-Agent Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29646)
*Jiayi Zhang,Zexin Wang,Degang Sun,Changhua Pei,Fei Sun,Gaogang Xie,Jingjing Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: DUOTRACE is a plug-and-play detection module that improves failure attribution for LLM-based agents by first detecting anomalous execution steps with a VAE-based trajectory model, then passing focused evidence to LLM-based attribution methods, yielding substantial gains in attribution accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM-based agents can perform complex multi-step reasoning but frequently fail during execution. To improve their reliability, we need to accurately identify which steps or components caused a failure. Existing topology/spectrum-based attribution focuses on structural patterns and misses semantic nuances, while purely LLM-based attribution uses semantics but struggles with long trajectories due to context-length and degradation issues. There is thus a need for a method that (1) is sensitive to both semantic and structural signals, (2) scales to long and hierarchical trajectories, and (3) can operate in data-scarce failure regimes to support better, more precise failure attribution.

Method: The paper introduces DUOTRACE, a detect-before-attribute framework used as a plug-and-play detection filter in LLM-based agent pipelines. DUOTRACE first represents agent trajectories as heterogeneous, hierarchical execution graphs/trees. It builds dual-view node embeddings that capture both semantic content and structural information. A Tree-LSTM-based encoder is then applied to these trajectories to obtain representations suitable for anomaly detection. A variational autoencoder (VAE) is trained on these representations to model normal executions; anomalous steps or sub-trajectories are detected by reconstruction error or latent likelihood. To enhance robustness under limited failure data, the method uses prefix-chain data augmentation (generating partial trajectories as training samples) and LLM-based augmentation for more diverse trajectory variants. Once anomalies are detected, DUOTRACE filters and highlights these suspicious segments and passes them as compact, focused evidence to downstream LLM-based attribution models, mitigating long-context issues.

Result: In experiments across multiple LLM-based agent settings, DUOTRACE is combined with six existing LLM-based attribution baselines. It consistently improves attribution performance: agent-level failure attribution accuracy increases by 8.7% on average, and step-level attribution accuracy increases by 7.0%. These gains show that using DUOTRACE as a pre-filter to detect anomalous executions leads to more precise and reliable identification of failure causes than either structural or pure LLM-based methods alone.

Conclusion: DUOTRACE demonstrates that separating failure detection from attribution—by first using a VAE-based detector over dual-view, Tree-LSTM-encoded trajectories and then passing only anomalous segments to LLM-based attribution—significantly improves attribution accuracy for LLM agents, especially on long and hierarchical trajectories. The method is plug-and-play, compatible with various attribution systems, and effective even with limited failure data, suggesting a practical path to more reliable and interpretable LLM-based decision-making agents.

Abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based agents have shown strong potential in solving complex tasks through multi-step reasoning, yet they remain vulnerable to execution failures. Accurate failure attribution is therefore critical for improving agent reliability. Existing topology- and spectrum-based methods exploit trajectory structures but often overlook fine-grained semantics, while LLM-based attribution methods capture semantic cues but suffer from long-context degradation over lengthy trajectories. To address these challenges, we propose DUOTRACE, a plug-and-play detection filter for LLM-based failure attribution. DUOTRACE follows a detect-before-attribute paradigm: it first detects anomalous executions and then supplies focused trajectory evidence to downstream LLM-based attribution methods. For effective VAE-based anomaly detection on agent trajectories, DUOTRACE integrates dual-view semantic-structural node representations, a Tree-LSTM-based trajectory encoder, and prefix-chain- and LLM-based data augmentation to handle heterogeneous nodes, hierarchical execution structures, and limited failure data. Experiments with six LLM-based attribution baselines show that DUOTRACE improves agent-level and step-level attribution accuracy by 8.7% and 7.0%, respectively.

</details>


### [329] [Ideation Arena: Evaluating LLM Generated Research Ideas with Battle-style Human Expert Assessment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29696)
*Zhiyu Chen,Keyu Zhao,Jigao Fu,Dong Liang,Yanbiao Wu,Jiaoyang Li,Haidong Xue,Xinhua Zeng,Yuanyi Zhen,Fengli Xu,Yong Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces Ideation Arena, a battle-style, pairwise-comparison platform to evaluate research ideas generated by LLMs and research agents, and finds large differences in ideation quality across models and agent frameworks while showing that current LLM judges only partially align with expert preferences.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Evaluating research ideas produced by LLMs is hard because scientific value is subjective, context-dependent, and lacks a single correct reference answer. Existing automatic metrics and evaluations are insufficient to capture nuanced expert judgments about what constitutes a promising research idea. The authors seek a systematic, scalable, and reliable way to compare LLMs and agentic systems on research ideation quality, grounded in real expert preferences rather than proxy metrics or synthetic judgments.

Method: The authors design Ideation Arena, a battle-style evaluation platform based on double-blind pairwise human comparisons of research ideas. They construct shared literature contexts from papers already familiar to participating researchers to give all LLMs and agents a common starting point. They evaluate ideas produced by 14 frontier LLMs and 5 research agent architectures (built on 2 base models). Using 6,000+ pairwise comparisons from 105 active computer science researchers, they estimate an Elo rating for each system, forming a leaderboard of proposal-stage idea quality under a shared closed-context protocol. They validate the ranking via interrater agreement and robustness checks (e.g., varying annotator subsets and domain coverage). They also build Ideation Arena Eval, a benchmark that tests how well automated LLM evaluators ("judges") can reproduce human preference rankings.

Result: The platform yields a stable Elo-based leaderboard of LLMs and research agents for research ideation quality in computer science. There is substantial variation among agent frameworks: some significantly improve ideation quality relative to their base models, while others offer limited gains or even degrade performance. Robustness and agreement analyses indicate that the ranking is reliable to changes in annotators and domains. For automated evaluation, current LLM judges do not fully match expert preferences: the best-performing judge achieves 72.56% Soft Accuracy on Overall Quality, leaving a notable alignment gap.

Conclusion: Ideation Arena provides a principled, expert-driven framework to evaluate LLM-based research ideation through pairwise human preferences under a shared, closed-context setup. It reveals meaningful differences among LLMs and agent architectures and highlights that current LLM judges are not yet reliable proxies for expert evaluation, as they only partially align with human preferences. The released code, data, and leaderboards establish a reusable testbed and benchmark (Ideation Arena Eval) for future work on research ideation systems and automated evaluators.

Abstract: Evaluating research ideas generated by LLMs is difficult because their scientific value cannot be fully determined by objective criteria, and no single reference answer specifies what counts as a good idea. To address this challenge, we introduce Ideation Arena, a battle style platform that evaluates research ideas through pairwise human assessment. Ideation Arena evaluates ideas generated by 14 frontier LLMs and 5 research agent architectures built on 2 base models. To ensure a common starting point, Ideation Arena builds shared literature contexts from papers familiar to the participating researchers and provides the same contexts to all LLMs and agents. We collect over 6,000 double blind pairwise comparisons from 105 active computer science researchers and construct an Elo rating leaderboard of proposal-stage expert preferences in computer science under a shared closed-context protocol. We validate the rankings through interrater agreement and robustness analyses, showing that the leaderboard remains stable under changes in annotator composition and domain coverage. Our results show substantial variation in agent effectiveness, with some frameworks improving ideation quality over their backbones and others offering little benefit or even underperforming their base models. We further construct Ideation Arena Eval, a benchmark for assessing whether automated evaluators align with human preferences in research ideation. Experiments with current LLM judges show that they still cannot reliably reproduce expert preferences, with the best judge reaching 72.56% Soft Accuracy on Overall Quality. Our code, data, and leaderboards are available at https://github.com/foss12138/Research-Ideation-Arena.

</details>


### [330] [PAGE-RAG: Provenance-Aware Graph Evidence Promotion for Fixed-Budget Multi-hop Retrieval-Augmented Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29753)
*Haokun Deng,Xunkai Li,Hongchao Qin,Rong-Hua Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces PAGE-RAG, a provenance-aware graph-based selection layer that builds a temporary query-local graph over retrieved candidates to better select multi-hop evidence for RAG, improving both support and answer accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In multi-hop QA for RAG, simply retrieving a small number of top documents risks missing necessary hops, while broad retrieval brings many distractors. Existing methods across different knowledge-base formats lack a query-aware selection layer that can leverage relational structure among candidates to pick truly supportive evidence before generation. There is a need to bridge the gap between being graph-connected and actually supporting the answer, in a way that can plug into various retrieval/RAG backends.

Method: The authors construct, for each query, a temporary graph over retrieved candidate items instead of assuming a fixed graph KB. Edges capture why candidates are related (e.g., lexical or entity-level connections), treating each edge as a support hypothesis. They identify the connectivity-support gap—connected items may not truly support the answer—and address it with PAGE-RAG, a Provenance-Aware Graph Evidence promotion method. PAGE-RAG scores paths in the graph using multiple signals: relevance to the query, provenance/source-tracing metadata, specificity, hubness (to avoid generic hubs), noise indicators, and coherence. Using these scores, it performs minimal sufficient selection to choose a compact set of supporting facts for the reader, forming a complete retrieval-to-reading pipeline or a plug-in stage after existing retrievers or RAG systems.

Result: On three multi-hop QA benchmarks under a fixed final context budget, PAGE-RAG improves support F1 by 10.4 points and answer F1 by 3.3 points on a weighted average over a strong baseline retriever. When integrated as a plug-in after various RAG backends—including reasoning-focused, compression-based, graph-based, and document/chunk-level systems—PAGE-RAG yields additional gains across all of them.

Conclusion: Using a temporary, provenance-aware graph over retrieved candidates and promoting only minimally sufficient evidence based on rich path-level signals effectively narrows the connectivity-support gap in multi-hop RAG. PAGE-RAG improves both evidence quality and answer accuracy, works as an end-to-end retrieval-to-reading pipeline, and can be seamlessly added on top of diverse existing RAG architectures to enhance their performance.

Abstract: Multi-hop question answering in retrieval-augmented gener?ation (RAG) often benefits from retrieving beyond the few candidates that will finally be read: narrow retrieval can miss an indispensable hop, while expanded retrieval introduces topical distractors. This challenge is not tied to a particu?lar knowledge-base format. Candidate pools may come from standalone retrievers, standard RAG backends, or graph-based retrieval pipelines. What is needed is a query-aware selection layer that can use relational structure to filter candidates be?fore generation. PAGE-RAG addresses this setting by using a graph as a temporary selection structure, rather than assum?ing a graph-structured knowledge base. It builds a query-local graph over retrieved candidates, records why candidates are connected, and treats each connection as a support hypothe?sis rather than support itself. We identify the resulting failure mode as a connectivity-support gap: connected candidates do not necessarily support the answer. We propose PAGE-RAG, a Provenance-Aware Graph Evidence promotion method that scores candidate paths with relevance, source-tracing meta?data, specificity, hubness, noise, and coherence signals, and applies minimal sufficient selection to promote supporting facts into a compact reader context. PAGE-RAG can serve as a complete retrieval-to-reading pipeline, and the same promo?tion stage can be inserted after existing retrieval or RAG sys?tems without replacing their upstream retrieval logic. Across three multi-hop QA benchmarks under the same final bud?get, PAGE-RAG improves support F1 and answer F1 by 10.4 and 3.3 points on a weighted average over a strong retriever. As a plug-in, PAGE-RAG further improves all reported RAG backends, including reasoning-oriented, compression-based, graph-based, and document/chunk-level systems.

</details>


### [331] [FRAMEWORKERS: A Dynamic Multi-Agent Framework for AI-Generated Video Production](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29814)
*Zhendong Li,Lei Sun,Letian Shi,Deheng Zhang,Ruibo Ming,Mengshun Hu,Dannong Xu,Jian Wang,Danda Paudel,Luc Van Gool,Jinjin Gu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A multi-agent framework, FRAMEWORKERS, for end-to-end video production that uses a central Director and execution Assistant to dynamically manage tasks and sub-agents, improving orchestration reliability and video quality over existing methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing video generators can create single clips but cannot manage the full, long-horizon, multi-step video production workflow, which requires scripting, storyboarding, generation, editing, asset management, and robust handling of changing execution states. Current automated systems use rigid pipelines that don’t generalize to diverse workflows, and general LLMs are unreliable for long-horizon orchestration and multimodal asset routing. There is a need for a flexible, reliable orchestration framework that can coordinate multiple specialized tools and adapt to evolving tasks in open-ended video production.

Method: They propose FRAMEWORKERS, a task-centric, workspace-grounded multi-agent framework. A central Director agent formulates video creation as dynamic task management by continuously editing a Task Stack (deciding what subtask to run next and which sub-agent to call). An Assistant agent acts as the execution layer, grounding tasks in a shared Workspace, fetching needed assets and context, invoking the chosen sub-agent, and saving outputs. Execution tools are modular sub-agents with registered descriptors so new ones can be plugged in without changing the orchestration logic. The Director is first supervised-fine-tuned and then optimized with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) for reliable, descriptor-conditioned task routing and orchestration. They evaluate routing accuracy, robustness to failures, generalization to new sub-agents, and end-to-end video quality and task coverage.

Result: FRAMEWORKERS achieves higher routing accuracy than strong LLM-based planners, reliably recovers from runtime failures, and generalizes to unseen sub-agents without additional training. In end-to-end evaluations, it produces higher quality videos and supports a broader range of video-production tasks compared with fixed pipelines, single-agent LLM systems, and previous multi-agent baselines.

Conclusion: Task-centric, workspace-grounded multi-agent orchestration with a trained Director and modular sub-agents yields more reliable, flexible, and higher-quality open-ended video production than existing rigid pipelines or generic LLM planners. FRAMEWORKERS demonstrates that fine-tuned orchestration agents and explicit task/asset structures are effective for long-horizon, multimodal creative workflows and can be extended by plugging in new capabilities without retraining the orchestration logic.

Abstract: Modern video generators excel at synthesizing individual clips, but complete video production requires coordinating a long sequence of interdependent creative steps, including scripting, storyboarding, generation, and editing. It further demands persistent asset management and dynamic task orchestration as intermediate outputs, dependencies, and execution states evolve over time. Existing automated systems typically rely on rigid pipelines that are difficult to adapt to diverse inputs and changing workflows, while general-purpose large language models (LLMs) remain unreliable for long-horizon orchestration and multimodal asset routing. We introduce FRAMEWORKERS, a task-centric and workspace-grounded multi-agent framework for open-ended video production. A central Director formulates video creation as dynamic task management, continuously editing a Task Stack to determine which subtask to execute next and which sub-agent to invoke. An Assistant serves as the execution layer, grounding each selected task in a shared Workspace, retrieving the required assets and context, invoking the assigned sub-agent, and persisting the resulting artifacts. Execution capabilities are exposed through modular sub-agents with registered descriptors, allowing new sub-agents to be integrated without redesigning the orchestration workflow. To improve orchestration reliability, we fine-tune the Director via supervised fine-tuning (SFT) followed by Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) for descriptor-conditioned task routing. Experiments show that FRAMEWORKERS outperforms strong LLM planners in routing accuracy, recovers reliably from runtime failures, generalizes to unseen sub-agents without retraining, and achieves higher end-to-end video quality and broader task coverage than fixed pipelines, single-agent systems, and prior multi-agent approaches.

</details>


### [332] [Perceive to Hypothesize, Verify to Ground: An Agentic Reasoning Framework for Open-World Geo-Localization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29880)
*Yutian Jiang,Ruijie Li,Sisuo Lyu,Xixuan Hao,Qingxiang Liu,Yongzi Yu,Yuxuan Liang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They propose GeoPAVE, an agent-based perceive-then-verify framework for open-world visual geo-localization, and release PAVED, a dataset with rich reasoning traces for rigorous evaluation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Open-world geo-localization is challenging because models must interpret ambiguous visual signals and use external knowledge through multi-step reasoning. Current large vision-language approaches, although strong at multimodal reasoning, still hallucinate locations or drift in context because they lack explicit, evidence-grounded verification of their hypotheses. There is also a lack of benchmarks that capture realistic multi-hop reasoning and tool use needed for this task.

Method: They recast geo-localization as a human-like perceive-then-verify process. The proposed GeoPAVE framework is a bi-level agentic system: (1) a perception stage that generates location hypotheses via single-pass rollouts, and (2) a verification stage that grounds decisions in external evidence and outputs one of three actions—support, refute, or refine the current hypothesis. They also construct PAVED, a dataset built from real user check-in data that includes multi-hop queries, multi-round tool calls, and structured traces of perception and verification steps to support training and evaluation.

Result: GeoPAVE operationalizes explicit hypothesis generation and verification for geo-localization, addressing hallucination and context drift observed in prior LVLM-based approaches. PAVED provides a challenging, realistic benchmark with detailed reasoning trajectories, enabling more rigorous quantitative and qualitative assessment of geo-localization reasoning systems. (Concrete numerical performance gains are not given in the abstract.)

Conclusion: Formulating geo-localization as a perceive-then-verify reasoning problem leads to a bi-level agentic solution, GeoPAVE, which better aligns the model’s decisions with explicit supporting evidence. The accompanying PAVED dataset fills an evaluation gap by capturing realistic, multi-step reasoning and tool use, laying groundwork for developing and benchmarking more reliable open-world geo-localization systems.

Abstract: Open-world geo-localization requires models to reason over ambiguous visual cues through multi-step reasoning and external knowledge grounding. While recent large vision-language models exhibit strong multimodal reasoning capabilities, existing approaches still suffer from perceptual hallucination and context drift due to the lack of explicit evidence-grounded verification. In this work, we reformulate geo-localization as a human-like perceive-then-verify reasoning problem and propose GeoPAVE (Geo-localization Perception-and-Verification-Engine), a bi-level agentic framework that contains perception-based hypothesis generation via single-pass rollouts and verification-based evidence grounding for decision actions: support, refute, and refine. To support rigorous evaluation, we further introduce PAVED, a novel dataset derived from real-world user check-in data, equipped with comprehensive reasoning trajectories featuring multi-hop queries, multi-round tool invocations, and structured perception-verification traces. The dataset and code are available at https://github.com/Arandinglv/GeoPAVE.

</details>


### [333] [On the Instance Hardness as a Decision Criterion in TinyML Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29913)
*Tobiasz Puslecki,Krzysztof Walkowiak*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper explores using a tree-depth-based pruning method (instance hardness pruning) in TinyML to trade off accuracy for lower computational cost and energy consumption during inference on resource-constrained devices.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: TinyML targets running ML models on devices with constrained memory and compute. As AI models grow larger and more computationally demanding, there is a need for methods that make inference more energy efficient and environmentally sustainable, especially on small devices. The paper is motivated by the need to reduce computational costs and energy consumption while maintaining acceptable classification performance.

Method: The authors apply a tree depth prune instance hardness method to TinyML models. By controlling a pruning threshold based on tree depth and instance hardness, they effectively remove or simplify parts of the model used in inference. This threshold acts as a tunable parameter that allows trading off model accuracy against computation and energy use. The work is presented as a preliminary, proof-of-concept study rather than a fully developed system.

Result: Initial experiments show that adjusting the pruning threshold can significantly affect energy consumption while only slightly impacting classification quality. The results confirm that there is a controllable trade-off between accuracy and computational/energy cost in TinyML using this method.

Conclusion: The study concludes that tree depth prune instance hardness is a promising technique for controlling the trade-off between classification accuracy and energy consumption in TinyML systems. The method enables dynamic adjustment of computational complexity at inference time and offers a path toward more energy-efficient, environmentally sustainable TinyML deployments. However, the work is still in progress, and the current findings are preliminary proof-of-concept results.

Abstract: TinyML includes the implementation of machine learning on devices with limited memory and computing resources. With the development of technology, AI systems continue to scale in terms of size and computational requirements. This forces researchers to adapt methods to be environmentally sustainable by designing techniques for reducing computational costs and energy consumption in inferring AI models, even in small devices. In this work, we present preliminary findings on a novel application of the tree depth prune instance hardness method to the TinyML system. The results indicate that threshold control can change energy consumption with limited classification quality changes. This method allows us to adjust classification accuracy, thereby influencing computational complexity and energy consumption for inference. We present a work in progress with initial results as a proof of concept.

</details>


### [334] [AcrossWAM1.0:A Modular Latent World-Action Stack for Compact Robot Policies](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29937)
*Yafei Zhang,Nan Wu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: AcrossWAM1.0 refactors latent world‑action models (like LaWAM) into a modular, auditable stack that supports more compact backbones while preserving nearly all task performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Previous latent world‑action work (LaWAM) coupled the world model, vision‑language backbone, and deployment checkpoint into a monolithic system, making it hard to swap components, audit what runs at inference, or scale models up/down. The authors want a clean, verifiable software boundary so practitioners can change the backbone size or family, understand exactly which parameters are used at inference, and measure what performance is retained when compressing policies.

Method: They design AcrossWAM1.0 as a modular stack with explicit components: (1) a policy adapter that takes the multimodal backbone output and produces latent actions plus an action‑generation context; (2) a retained latent world decoder that grounds predicted latent transitions in the current scene; and (3) a flow‑matching expert that outputs continuous action chunks. They separate training‑only teacher components from the final inference graph and provide a deployment export where all retained tensors are bitwise identical to the source checkpoint. They empirically compare different backbones (Qwen3‑VL‑2B vs Qwen3.5‑0.8B) on 2,000 paired LIBERO episodes using a McNemar test and predefined retention criterion; they also run a smoke‑test adapter with a MiniCPM‑V backbone to check cross‑family execution.

Result: Swapping the original 2B Qwen3‑VL backbone for a smaller Qwen3.5‑0.8B backbone yields 97.45% vs 98.00% success on 2,000 paired LIBERO episodes, a −0.55 percentage‑point difference that is not statistically significant by an exact McNemar test (p=0.266). This satisfies a pre‑specified “within 2 points” retention criterion. The resulting deployment‑ready checkpoint has 1,472.6M unique parameters, 42.4% fewer than the original 2B policy, while all tensors that are kept remain bitwise identical to those in the original model. Cross‑family execution with a MiniCPM‑V adapter works in a smoke test, but closed‑loop performance for such cross‑family transfer is not yet fully evaluated.

Conclusion: AcrossWAM1.0 is not a new latent‑subgoal algorithm but a principled modularization and scaling framework for latent world‑action models. It defines a clear, auditable boundary between backbone, policy adapter, world decoder, and action generator; separates training‑only teachers from inference components; and provides a verifiable deployment export. Experiments show that a more compact backbone can retain almost all performance with substantially fewer parameters, while enabling future work on cross‑family backbones and more rigorous transfer evaluations.

Abstract: Latent world-action models avoid rendering future pixels by predicting an action-relevant visual subgoal in feature space. LaWAM established this formulation, but its original presentation left the world model, multimodal backbone, and deployment checkpoint tightly coupled. We introduce AcrossWAM1.0, a modularization and scaling study of this latent world-action stack. Rather than presenting latent subgoals as a new algorithm, we make the module boundary explicit: a policy adapter produces latent-action and action-generation contexts; a retained latent world decoder grounds the predicted transition in the current scene;and a flow-matching expert generates continuous action chunks. We further separate training-only teachers from the inference graph and provide a verifiable deployment export. On 2,000 paired LIBERO episodes, replacing a Qwen3-VL-2B backbone with Qwen3.5-0.8B yields 97.45% success versus 98.00% for the 2B model (a-0.55percentage-point difference; exact McNemarp=0.266). This does not prove equivalence, but it meets a prespecified two-point retention criterion. The compact, inference-reachable checkpoint contains 1,472.6M unique parameters, 42.4% fewer than the original 2B policy, while all retained tensors are bitwise identical to the source checkpoint. Cross-family execution is additionally checked with a MiniCPM-V adapter smoke test; closed-loop cross-family transfer remains an open evaluation. AcrossWAM1.0 therefore contributes an auditable software and evaluation boundary for compact latent world-action policies, distinct from LaWAM's original latent-subgoal contribution.

</details>


### [335] [Spatial Matryoshka Training for Multi-Granularity Visual Document Retrieval](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29951)
*Trishan Singha Roy,Arkadeep Acharya,Vishwajeet Kumar,Jaydeep Sen,Sachindra Joshi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ColSNAP is a training method that enables multi-modal late-interaction retrievers to flexibly trade off accuracy and storage by producing multiple compression levels from a single encoding.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multi-modal late-interaction retrievers for visually rich documents use per-patch embeddings, leading to high storage costs. Existing compression methods fix one compression level at indexing time, reducing flexibility in adapting to different storage budgets. There is a need for a method that supports multiple compression levels without retraining or architectural changes.

Method: ColSNAP (Spatial Nested Average Pooling) builds a nested hierarchy of compression tiers from the backbone's patch grid via spatial average pooling. These tiers range from fine to coarse resolutions. The model is trained so that all tiers are optimized simultaneously, allowing a single backbone to support multiple compression levels. A single encoding pass generates embeddings for all tiers, and ColSNAP can be applied as a lightweight adaptation on top of pre-trained late-interaction retrievers.

Result: Models trained with ColSNAP preserve retrieval quality close to full-resolution performance even under heavy compression. The approach generalizes across several late-interaction backbones and gains most of its benefits from a small adaptation stage on existing pre-trained retrievers, demonstrating strong transferability and practical applicability.

Conclusion: ColSNAP enables flexible, storage-efficient multi-modal retrieval on visually rich documents by jointly training a hierarchy of spatially pooled embedding tiers. This allows practitioners to choose an appropriate accuracy-storage trade-off at indexing time using a single, unified model that transfers well across backbones and requires only lightweight adaptation to pre-trained systems.

Abstract: Multi-modal late-interaction retrievers achieve strong retrieval on visually rich documents by representing each page as per patch embeddings and matching at the token level. However, this approach incurs high storage costs. Existing compression methods typically fix a single compression level at indexing time, limiting flexibility. We present ColSNAP (Spatial Nested Average Pooling)1, a training method that generates a nested hierarchy of compression levels directly from a backbone's patch grid. By spatially pooling patch embeddings into pro- gressively coarser tiers and training all tiers simultaneously, a single model learns to support retrieval at multiple compression levels without architectural changes. Crucially, a single encoding pass yields every tier, enabling the accuracy-storage trade-off to be configured at indexing time to match avail- able storage budgets, rather than being fixed during training. We demonstrate that models trained using ColSNAP maintain near full-resolution retrieval performance under substantial compression and that ColSNAP transfers effectively across multiple late-interaction backbones, and achieves most of its improvements via a lightweight adaptation stage applied to a pre-trained retriever.

</details>


### [336] [SearchWiki: Learning to Build and Navigate Knowledge Wikis for Active Information Seeking](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29953)
*Guransh Singh,Vishwajeet Kumar,Arkadeep Acharya,Adnan Qidwai,Jaydeep Sen,Sachindra Joshi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes SearchWiki and an RL-trained agent, WikiResearcher-9B, that navigate a hierarchical wiki-style corpus for retrieval-augmented generation, outperforming flat retrieval approaches and larger models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems typically use flat retrieval over chunks, ignoring document hierarchy and cross-document structure, which can lead to missed or suboptimal information retrieval, especially for complex or long-context tasks. There is a need for a principled way to structure corpora and to train agents that can navigate this structure effectively.

Method: The authors build SearchWiki, a harness framework that converts a corpus into a hierarchical wiki with three layers: document overviews, cross-document topic pages, and page-level source records. They then train an agent, WikiResearcher-9B (based on Qwen 9B), to query this structured corpus using multi-turn tool use. The agent’s navigation policy is optimized via on-policy reinforcement learning with a multi-component reward that balances answer correctness, retrieval quality, and trajectory efficiency.

Result: On benchmarks including ViDoRe-V3 (8 domains), FinanceBench, and long-memory benchmarks like LoCoMo, LongMemEval, and PersonaMem-v2, the RL-tuned WikiResearcher-9B significantly outperforms same-sized untrained baselines and matches or surpasses larger external models in retrieval-augmented generation tasks.

Conclusion: Hierarchical, wiki-style structuring of corpora combined with RL-learned navigation policies yields superior retrieval-augmented generation performance compared to traditional flat retrieval systems. SearchWiki and WikiResearcher-9B demonstrate that agents can effectively learn to navigate structured knowledge sources to improve answer quality and efficiency.

Abstract: Flat retrieval-augmented generation treats a corpus as a bag of chunks, discarding document hierarchy and cross document structure. We introduce SearchWiki, a harness framework that synthesizes a corpus into a hierarchical, typed, navigable wiki and trains an agent, WikiResearcher-9B, to retrieve information through multi-turn tool use. The wiki organizes knowledge into three layers - document overviews, cross- document topic pages, and page-level source records; enabling progressive refinement of retrieval when initial lookup misses. We optimize the agent's navigation policy with on-policy reinforcement learning with a multi-component reward function balancing answer correctness, retrieval quality and trajectory efficiency. Evaluation on ViDoRe-V3 (8 domains), FinanceBench, and memory benchmarks (LoCoMo, LongMemEval, PersonaMem-v2) shows that WikiResearcher- 9B which is our RL-tuned Qwen 9B model, significantly outperforms same-size untrained baselines and exceeds or matches larger external models. SearchWiki paired with WikiResearcher-9B demonstrates that learned navigation over structured corpora is a superior alternative to flat retrieval.

</details>


### [337] [Review Before Trust: Source-Grounded Integrity Gates for AI-Assisted Personal Health Records](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29965)
*Nora Girda,Adrian Groza*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They propose and implement a safeguard framework so LLM‑extracted data from medical documents can only become part of a longitudinal health record when it is explicitly and uniquely supported by evidence in the source document.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs are good at extracting structured data from medical documents but can hallucinate or overgeneralize. If their unverified output is stored in longitudinal health records, it can corrupt downstream analytics, summaries, and care decisions because later computations might treat those data as ground truth. The authors want to maintain record integrity by ensuring that generated content cannot silently authorize its own reuse without verifiable provenance from the original document.

Method: They define an “evidence-gated trust-promotion” model: LLMs generate candidate structured fields from documents, but these candidates remain provisional until an independent, deterministic monitor validates them. The monitor enforces strict rules: (1) each candidate must have a unique supporting quotation in the original document, (2) all required fields must co-occur in the same lab table row, and (3) provenance links back to the specific source snippet must be preserved. The generator cannot self-approve its own outputs. Ambiguous, missing, or conflicting evidence leads to refusal, but refused candidates are surfaced for human review instead of being discarded. They implement this architecture in Medical DataCloud and test it via automated conformance/mutation tests and a replay study using real lab PDF reports with manual row labels.

Result: All 22 automated conformance and mutation tests for the implementation pass. In the replay study over 9 historical lab PDFs with 102 manually labeled rows, the system generates 97 numerical candidates. Schema checks accept all 97, a more basic evidence check accepts 94, and the strict quotation- and row-level policy admits 72 candidates while holding 25 for human review. This shows the system can reliably distinguish well-supported extractions from those needing oversight, with no silent promotion of weakly supported data.

Conclusion: The proposed evidence-gated model provides a technically feasible way to enforce data provenance and integrity when using LLMs for medical-document extraction into longitudinal health records. By requiring independently verified textual evidence and row-level consistency, and by preventing the generator from approving its own outputs, they create a robust boundary that blocks unverified generated claims from being automatically reused. The work focuses on integrity engineering rather than clinical accuracy but demonstrates that enforceable safeguards against self-authorizing LLM outputs are practical in real personal health-record applications.

Abstract: Large language models can convert medical documents into structured data, but plausible output may still be unsupported by the source. Persisting such output in a longitudinal health record, a record that accumulates patient information over time, therefore creates an integrity risk: unverified data may influence later summaries, trends, or preventive-care computations. We introduce an evidence-gated trust-promotion model that keeps generated data provisional until a deterministic monitor verifies it against the source document. The monitor admits a candidate for a specified downstream use only when the source contains a unique supporting quotation, the relevant fields occur within the same laboratory row, and the required provenance is preserved. The generator cannot approve its own output, missing or ambiguous evidence causes refusal, and refused candidates remain available for human review rather than being silently discarded. We implement the model in Medical DataCloud, a personal health-record application, and evaluate it through automated tests and a replay of saved extraction outputs. All 22 conformance and mutation tests pass. The replay covers nine historical laboratory PDF reports containing 102 manually labelled rows. The reports produce 97 numeric candidates: schema validation accepts all 97, an earlier packet-level evidence check accepts 94, and the hardened quotation- and row-level policy admits 72 while retaining 25 for review. The study evaluates system integrity rather than clinical correctness or clinical safety. The results demonstrate the technical feasibility of an enforceable boundary that prevents generated claims from authorizing their own reuse in a longitudinal health record.

</details>


### [338] [EDGE: Engine for Deterministic Graph Evaluation through Conversation Simulation from Graph Structured DSL Configuration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29971)
*Ram Kulathumani,Regunathan Radhakrishnan,Anupam Tripathi,Xiangbo Mao,Roshanak Omrani,Keshav Somani,Shwet Kamal Mishra,Shayna Lurya*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They propose a graph-based, exhaustive testing framework to measure how deterministic and behaviorally consistent multi-agent orchestration systems are, using AgentGraph/LangGraph-style planners and new reliability metrics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As multi-agent workflows get more complex, their behavior becomes harder to predict and reproduce. Current evaluation methods are ad hoc and don’t systematically cover an agent’s full behavioral space or quantify how deterministic and reliable the agent is. The authors want a principled way to measure whether agent systems behave consistently with their design specifications and to compare different orchestration frameworks.

Method: They use AgentGraph, where an agent’s reasoning is encoded as a domain-specific language (DSL) forming a dynamically adjustable directed graph. They apply graph traversal algorithms to exhaustively enumerate all conversational paths allowed by this graph, creating a comprehensive set of test trajectories. These trajectories are then replayed to observe actual outputs and state transitions, which are compared against the DSL specification. They define new metrics for: (1) response determinism, (2) trajectory determinism, (3) structural adherence (following the intended graph), and (4) semantic consistency, evaluated on exact replays and paraphrased/linguistic variants of the conversations.

Result: Using their framework and metrics, they evaluate agents built with structured graph-based planners (AgentGraph, LangGraph) against agents without explicitly controlled node transitions. The structured agents show higher determinism and reliability according to their determinism, adherence, and consistency metrics.

Conclusion: A graph-based, DSL-specified representation of agent behavior enables exhaustive path enumeration and reproducible trajectory replay, which in turn supports rigorous measurement of behavioral determinism and consistency. Frameworks with explicit, structured node transitions (like AgentGraph and LangGraph) yield more deterministic and reliable agent behavior than less structured approaches, and the proposed metrics provide a systematic way to evaluate and compare such systems.

Abstract: As agentic systems evolve into complex multi agent orchestration workflows, there is a growing and critical need for systematic frameworks that measures an agent's behavioral consistency and determinism. In this paper, we introduce a formal evaluation methodology that is grounded in AgentGraph, a planner powered by a domain specific language that represents agent reasoning through a dynamically adjustable directed graph. We leverage this structural formalism and utilize graph traversal algorithms that exhaustively enumerate conversational paths, forming a comprehensive evaluation set that captures the agent's complete behavioral space. We then systematically replay these reproducible trajectories to compare observed outputs and state transitions against the intended DSL specification. To quantify reliability, we define novel metrics that measure response and trajectory determinism, structural adherence and semantic consistency across both exact replays and their linguistic variants. Our system's results demonstrate that agents configured using frameworks like AgentGraph and LangGraph with explicitly structured node transitions show superior determinism over agents that are not configured with controlled transitions.

</details>


### [339] [An Open-Source, Event-Driven Pipeline for Cryptocurrency Market Data: Ingestion, Forecasting, and On-Chain Fraud Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29973)
*Basil Sajid Shaikh,Melrick Mascarenhas,Nuzhat Faiz Shaikh*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Open-source Kafka-Spark-PostgreSQL pipeline for high-frequency crypto data plus example forecasting and fraud-detection models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Working with high-frequency, multi-source cryptocurrency data is costly without commercial cloud streaming and warehousing infrastructure. The authors want a low-cost, fully open-source way to reproduce cloud-native, event-driven data engineering patterns on commodity hardware.

Method: They design an event-driven pipeline using Apache Kafka and a filesystem-watching poller to mimic cloud triggers. Historical Gemini exchange data is partitioned into hourly and minutely files and ingested via two Kafka consumer groups: one for audit logging and one to trigger Spark-based ETL. Cleaned data are stored in a PostgreSQL warehouse with both historical/aggregated schemas and asset-specific data marts. On this infrastructure, they build and compare: (1) seasonal ARIMA vs a single-layer LSTM for Bitcoin price forecasting; and (2) Random Forest vs Gradient Boosting classifiers, using additional engineered features, on the Ethereum fraud detection benchmark by Farrugia et al.

Result: The pipeline successfully processes and warehouses high-frequency exchange data using only open-source tools and commodity hardware. The authors obtain forecasting and fraud-detection performance metrics for the tested models and discuss how the architecture supports these workloads. They also identify issues in comparing models across different forecast horizons and in assessing fraud classifiers on static labeled data.

Conclusion: A fully open-source Kafka–Spark–PostgreSQL stack can effectively replicate key behaviors of cloud-native, event-driven data pipelines for cryptocurrency analytics. It supports practical modeling tasks such as price forecasting and fraud detection, but care is needed when interpreting performance metrics across different forecast horizons and static fraud benchmarks.

Abstract: Cryptocurrency markets generate high-frequency, multi-source data that is expensive to work with unless a team already has commercial-grade streaming and warehousing infrastructure in place. This paper describes a fully open-source pipeline that reproduces the behavior of a cloud-native, event-driven system -- file arrival triggering a message, a message triggering compute -- entirely on commodity hardware, using Apache Kafka and a filesystem-watching poller in place of managed cloud triggers. The pipeline partitions historical Gemini exchange data into hourly and minutely files, ingests them asynchronously through two independently grouped Kafka consumers (one for audit logging, one for Spark-triggered ETL), and lands cleaned output in a PostgreSQL warehouse with historical and aggregated schemas plus asset-specific data marts. We use the resulting Bitcoin data mart to compare a seasonal ARIMA model against a single-layer LSTM network for price forecasting, and separately apply Random Forest and Gradient Boosting classifiers, with additional engineered features, to the public Ethereum fraud detection benchmark introduced by Farrugia et al. We report the architecture, the modeling methodology, and the resulting metrics, and we are explicit about the limitations of comparing forecasts issued at different horizons and of evaluating fraud detection on a static, already-labeled dataset.

</details>


### [340] [AutoCRAT: Within-trajectory Joint Control of Stochasticity and Compute for LLM Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29988)
*Hanjun Luo,Qiushi Liu,Jingya Zhang,Haihong Pang,Jiaheng Wen,Yifei Ma,Yu Yao,Chengxi Zhang,Hanrong Zhang,Yankai Chen,Hanan Salam*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes AutoCRAT, a decoder-side controller that adaptively adjusts both sampling stochasticity and reasoning budget during a single LLM reasoning trajectory, improving accuracy while reducing inference tokens.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM inference is usually governed by static, one-size-fits-all decoding policies that cannot adapt to different tasks or evolving reasoning stages within a single generation. Recent adaptive methods only tune either sampling randomness or reasoning compute separately, ignoring their interaction and limiting efficiency and performance. There is a need for a unified, within-trajectory control mechanism that can jointly manage how much the model explores and how long it reasons, using only information observable during decoding.

Method: The authors introduce AutoCRAT, a decoder-side controller that sits on top of a frozen LLM backbone. During generation, AutoCRAT observes signals available at decoding time and, at selected semantic boundaries, chooses actions from a discrete control space that jointly specify (a) the level of sampling stochasticity and (b) the remaining reasoning budget or compute allocation. Control decisions are updated only at these semantic checkpoints to balance stability and responsiveness. The controller thus performs joint within-trajectory control of exploration (via decoding randomness) and reasoning length (via token or compute budget) without modifying the underlying model parameters.

Result: Across six reasoning benchmarks, AutoCRAT reduces inference tokens by 13.8–52.7% compared to recommended static decoding settings, while also achieving 1.5–4.5% higher relative accuracy than both static and existing adaptive baselines. Additionally, the learned control policy exhibits strong cross-backbone transfer, meaning that it generalizes well when applied to different underlying LLMs than those it was tuned on.

Conclusion: Joint, within-trajectory control of both sampling stochasticity and reasoning budget can substantially improve the efficiency-accuracy trade-off in LLM reasoning. A decoder-side controller like AutoCRAT, which operates over a discrete action space and updates only at semantic boundaries, can reduce token usage while improving accuracy and can transfer across different LLM backbones, offering a practical way to enhance inference-time reasoning without retraining the base model.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) achieve strong reasoning performance, which depends critically on inference-time decisions. Yet these decisions are commonly handled by static, one-size-fits-all policies, limiting adaptation to diverse tasks and reasoning stages. Recent adaptive methods partially address this limitation, but they primarily adapt either decoding stochasticity (how the model explores) or reasoning compute (how long the model reasons) in isolation, leaving their interaction within a single reasoning trajectory unmodeled. To address this challenge, we shift toward a within-trajectory joint control view, and instantiate it in AutoCRAT, a decoder-side controller for frozen backbones. Using only signals available during decoding, AutoCRAT jointly adjusts sampling stochasticity and reasoning budget during generation. AutoCRAT operates over a discrete action space and updates control decisions only at semantic boundaries, improving stability while remaining responsive to the evolving reasoning process. Comprehensive evaluation across 6 benchmarks demonstrates that AutoCRAT (I) uses 13.8-52.7% fewer inference tokens on average than recommended static configurations, (II) surpasses recommended static and adaptive baselines by 1.5-4.5% in relative accuracy, and (III) enjoys strong cross-backbone transferability.

</details>


### [341] [Automatic Conversion of NICE Guidelines to an Executable Computational Model Using Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30022)
*Ashvin Gupta,Denys Prociuk,Alessandra Russo,Brendan C. Delaney*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper presents an LLM-based pipeline that automatically converts unstructured NICE cancer guidelines into executable, interpretable clinical decision models, showing high alignment with expert interpretations and strong performance on patient vignettes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Clinical practice guidelines like those from NICE are written in natural language, making them hard to use directly in clinical decision support systems. Existing efforts to encode them are labor-intensive, typically disease-specific, and do not scale, limiting the broad deployment of guideline-based, patient-specific recommendations. There is a need for a scalable, less manual method to transform textual guidelines into computable, executable formats.

Method: The authors design an end-to-end, stepwise transformation pipeline driven by large language models. Using in-context examples, the pipeline converts narrative NICE guidelines into a series of human-readable intermediate artifacts that ultimately yield executable rule-based models. The process is applied to NICE pancreatic and lung cancer guidelines. Domain experts review the resulting rule sets to assess their fidelity to the original guidelines, and the pancreatic cancer model is tested on 20 synthetic or curated patient vignettes to evaluate recommendation accuracy.

Result: Expert review found high concordance between the original NICE guidelines and the generated executable models. Most differences involved partial omissions or missing detail, rather than incorrect or fabricated logic, and hallucinated or fundamentally wrong rules were uncommon. When run on 20 pancreatic cancer patient vignettes, the executable model reached an F1 score of 82.5% in generating appropriate recommendations relative to an expert-derived reference standard.

Conclusion: The study shows that large language models can reliably translate natural-language NICE cancer guidelines into transparent, executable decision models that maintain guideline structure and can be inspected and edited by humans. The demonstrated performance and expert-aligned logic suggest that scalable, semi-automated generation of computable clinical guidelines is feasible, potentially enabling broader and more efficient deployment of guideline-based decision support in clinical practice.

Abstract: Introduction: NICE guidelines provide evidence-based recommendations for clinical care but remain largely in unstructured natural language. Existing approaches to converting them into computable representations often focus on individual diseases, require substantial manual encoding, and do not scale. Large language models (LLMs) may enable much of this translation to be automated. Methods: We present an end-to-end approach that converts textual clinical guidelines into executable models capable of generating explainable, patient-specific recommendations. A stepwise LLM-based transformation with in-context examples produces human-inspectable intermediate artifacts. We apply the approach to NICE pancreatic and lung cancer guidelines, use expert review to assess rule alignment, and evaluate the executable pancreatic cancer model on 20 patient vignettes. Results: Expert review showed strong alignment between the source guidelines and generated executable models. Most discrepancies were partial omissions rather than incorrect logic, while hallucinated or fundamentally incorrect rules were rare. On the patient vignettes, the executable model achieved an F1 score of 82.5%. Conclusion: LLMs can transform natural-language NICE guidelines into interpretable, executable models that preserve guideline structure, support transparent inspection and modification, and generate patient-specific recommendations. These findings demonstrate the feasibility of scalable automated generation of computable clinical guidelines.

</details>


### [342] [Interpreting and Steering for Safe and Correct Code Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30025)
*Hao Yan,Ziyu Yao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper investigates how large language models internally differentiate between safe and vulnerable code, builds a contrastive dataset of safe/vulnerable Python pairs, and proposes a mechanistic steering method (DuoSteer) that reduces vulnerabilities and improves correctness during code generation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs often emit code with security vulnerabilities, but existing work mainly treats models as black boxes, focusing on prompting or fine-tuning rather than understanding or controlling the internal mechanisms that lead to unsafe code. The authors want a mechanistic understanding of where and how code safety vs. vulnerability is represented in model components so that they can directly steer models toward safer generations at inference time, without costly retraining.

Method: They first construct CodeSec-Pairs, 9,342 Python contrastive pairs where each pair contains a safe and a vulnerable version of the same code, sampled from Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. Using this dataset, they perform mechanistic interpretability analyses to localize layers and attention heads that correlate with safety versus vulnerability. Based on these findings, they evaluate various steering techniques that adjust the activations of the identified components at inference. Their main method, DuoSteer, is a double-steering scheme that concurrently applies a safety-steering vector and a code-correctness-steering vector to selected attention heads to bias the model toward safer and more correct outputs.

Result: On five classes of vulnerabilities, DuoSteer reduces the rate of vulnerable generations by an average of 26.9% while simultaneously improving functional correctness by 7.5%. It outperforms other steering strategies as well as prompting-based methods and supervised fine-tuning baselines. The approach generalizes beyond the original model: applying the same methodology to Qwen-2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct with an additional 2,500 contrastive pairs yields similar advantages.

Conclusion: Mechanistic analysis of LLM internals can reveal components that encode code safety signals, and directly steering these components at inference time is an effective way to reduce vulnerabilities while improving correctness, without full retraining. The proposed DuoSteer method, supported by the CodeSec-Pairs dataset, offers a practical and more effective alternative to prompt engineering and fine-tuning for safer code generation across different models.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) frequently generate source code containing vulnerabilities, yet little work studies the internal mechanisms that distinguish safe from vulnerable generation in them. In this work, we systematically perform a mechanistic interpretation of LLMs, aiming at both understanding how code safety-vs-vulnerability is represented or driven by components in an LM and turning the insights into actionable steering strategies to encourage safer code generation. To this end, we introduce CodeSec-Pairs, a dataset of 9,342 Python safe-and-vulnerable contrastive code pairs, sampled from Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. Utilizing the dataset, we explore approaches to localize layers and attention heads that relate to code safety, and further experiment with different steering strategies for inference-time vulnerability reduction. In particular, we propose DuoSteer, a double-steering approach that simultaneously applies safety and code-correctness steering to attention heads. In experiments over five vulnerability types, DuoSteer leads to an average of -26.9% vulnerability rate reduction and +7.5% functional correctness improvement, which outperforms not only other steering variants but also prompting and supervised fine-tuning baselines. The advantage also replicates on Qwen-2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct with another 2,500 contrastive pairs sampled from that model.

</details>
