To further enhance the system's capability, we introduce a two-stage supervised tuning strategy and a verification-guided hierarchical reinforcement learning stage to jointly optimize coordination and tool-use policies. Experiments on Earth-Agent Benchmark and ThinkGeo show that HiRS-Agent substantially improves long-horizon tool-use capability and final-task correctness, demonstrating the effectiveness of structured multi-agent collaboration for reliable RS agents. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/IntelliSensing/HiRS-Agent.

</details>


### [382] [MedAgent-R1: Faithfulness-Aware Reinforcement Learning for Evidence-Grounded Medical Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30676)
*Jiangwang Chen,Chenghao Zhang,Hengxing Cai*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper shows that standard RL training for medical retrieval-augmented agents increases answer accuracy but makes their explanations less faithful, and proposes a new reward design that drastically reduces fabricated citations while keeping strong accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In medical settings, AI systems are increasingly expected not just to provide answers, but to explain their reasoning and cite supporting evidence. However, large language models can hallucinate: they generate plausible-sounding explanations and citations that are not truly grounded in retrieved evidence. When such hallucinated reasoning appears confident and well-referenced, clinicians may trust unsafe recommendations. Existing RL training for retrieval agents typically optimizes outcome-only rewards like answer correctness, ignoring whether the explanation is actually supported by evidence. This can incentivize models to rely on internal parametric memory and then fabricate justifications, creating a critical safety risk in healthcare applications. The paper is motivated by the need to systematically understand this failure mode and to design training methods that explicitly promote faithful, evidence-grounded reasoning, not just correct final answers.

Method: The authors first empirically study RL-trained retrieval-augmented medical agents optimized with outcome-only rewards (primarily answer correctness). They analyze how these agents generate answers and accompanying justifications with citations to retrieved documents. They measure citation fabrication, where cited passages do not actually support the claims, and overall faithfulness metrics. Finding that RL increases accuracy but worsens faithfulness, they term this pattern confident hallucination. To address it, they design a faithfulness-gated reward structure. In this scheme, the agent only receives accuracy reward if its answer is demonstrably grounded in retrieved evidence, implemented via a hard gate that conditions correctness credit on evidence grounding. They further add auxiliary rewards related to retrieval validity (ensuring relevant documents are retrieved and used) and conciseness (discouraging verbose, exploitative behaviors in the agentic retrieval loop). They then train a new system, MedAgent-R1, under this reward design and evaluate it on metrics including citation fabrication rate, evidence completeness, answer accuracy, and safety benchmark scores, as well as human-assessed faithfulness dimensions such as factual support and overclaiming, comparing against both a supervised baseline and GPT-4o under the same retrieval setup.

Result: With conventional outcome-only RL, citation fabrication rates in the medical retrieval agent nearly double (from 16.5% to 31.8%) even while answer accuracy increases by 5 percentage points over a supervised baseline, illustrating confident hallucination. After introducing the faithfulness-gated reward with retrieval validity and conciseness components, the resulting agent, MedAgent-R1, shows a large improvement in faithfulness metrics: citation fabrication drops sharply from 31.8% to 4.7%, and evidence completeness rises from 58.7 to 82.6. At the same time, MedAgent-R1 maintains strong answer accuracy at 75.1% and achieves a 13.2-point improvement on HealthBench Safety, indicating safer clinical recommendations. When compared to GPT-4o under an identical agentic retrieval configuration, MedAgent-R1 achieves higher scores on faithfulness-oriented human evaluation dimensions (Factual Support 4.55 vs. 4.25; Overclaiming 4.40 vs. 4.15), although GPT-4o still surpasses it in overall accuracy, highlighting a trade-off between raw accuracy and explicit faithfulness training.

Conclusion: The paper concludes that standard RL approaches that reward only answer correctness can be actively harmful for medical retrieval agents because they encourage confident hallucination: models rely more on internal memory and fabricate seemingly well-supported explanations and citations. To build safe medical AI systems, training objectives must explicitly incorporate faithfulness to retrieved evidence, not just accuracy. The proposed faithfulness-gated reward, supplemented with retrieval validity and conciseness signals, demonstrates that it is possible to substantially reduce citation fabrication and improve evidence completeness while preserving competitive accuracy and enhancing safety metrics. MedAgent-R1’s superior faithfulness compared to a stronger general model (GPT-4o) under the same retrieval framework suggests that targeted faithfulness optimization can yield grounding benefits beyond what scaling alone provides, and that future medical AI development should prioritize such designs for trustworthy, verifiable clinical reasoning.

Abstract: When medical AI systems hallucinate clinical reasoning, the consequences extend beyond incorrect answers: fabricated justifications that superficially reference retrieved evidence can mislead clinicians into unsafe treatment decisions. Medical reasoning agents must therefore produce not only correct answers but also faithful justifications that clinicians can verify against cited evidence. We identify a systematic failure mode in RL-trained retrieval agents: outcome-only rewards improve accuracy while degrading faithfulness, a phenomenon we term confident hallucination. The agent learns to answer from parametric memory and backfill plausible but unsupported justifications; citation fabrication rates rise from 16.5% to 31.8% even as accuracy improves by 5 points over the supervised baseline. We address this with a faithfulness-gated reward design: accuracy credit is conditioned on evidence grounding via a hard gate, complemented by retrieval validity and conciseness signals that close exploitation paths unique to agentic retrieval. The resulting system, MedAgent-R1, reduces citation fabrication from 31.8% to 4.7% and raises evidence completeness from 58.7 to 82.6 while maintaining 75.1% accuracy, with 13.2-point gains on HealthBench Safety. Under the same agentic retrieval setup, MedAgent-R1 outscores GPT-4o on faithfulness-specific dimensions (Factual Support 4.55 vs. 4.25; Overclaiming 4.40 vs. 4.15) while remaining below GPT-4o in overall accuracy, suggesting that explicit faithfulness training yields evidence-grounding gains not achieved by scaling alone.

</details>


### [383] [ATLAS: Dual-Horizon Diagnostic Evaluation for Industrial Tool-Use Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30685)
*Wei Chen,Peilun Zhou,Zhaoyu Hu,Jiajun Chai,Zhongni Hou,Yufei Zhang,Derong Xu,Guojun Yin,Wei Lin,Zhi Zheng,Tong Xu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ATLAS is a dual-horizon diagnostic evaluation framework for industrial LLM tool-use agents that provides fine-grained trajectory-level and longer-term interaction-level signals, implemented via calibrated LLM judges and distilled models, and validated on large-scale production traffic showing both offline and online gains.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Industrial LLM agents for tool use operate in complex, dynamic, multi-step interactions where performance depends on both individual request trajectories and longer-term user interactions. Existing evaluations that focus mainly on final outcomes fail to pinpoint where in a trajectory deficiencies occur or whether the agent remains aligned with evolving user context across multiple turns. There is a need for a diagnostic evaluation framework that can reliably expose specific capability gaps, connect errors to execution steps, and measure sustained service quality in a way that can directly guide policy improvement in production systems.

Method: The authors introduce ATLAS, a dual-horizon evaluation framework. At the request horizon, they design trajectory-wise diagnostic signals that annotate specific locations in the tool-use execution and map them to capability concerns. At the interaction horizon, they define user-wise signals to measure whether the service remains responsive and context-aligned across continued interactions. These signals are instantiated as executable evaluation components with clearly defined evidence scopes and decision boundaries. LLM-based judge interfaces are calibrated using high-confidence labels derived from real business logs. Where latency or cost matter, the authors distill LLM judge behavior into lighter diagnostic models. The framework is then used to generate feedback for policy optimization. They test ATLAS on Meituan Xiaotuan’s production traffic, using both offline replay experiments and online A/B testing.

Result: In offline experiments on Meituan Xiaotuan production logs, ATLAS’s diagnostic signals demonstrate high fidelity, meaning they reliably track true execution deficiencies and correlate with improved policies in replay-based optimization. When ATLAS-generated feedback is used for policy tuning, the replay studies show clear gains in agent behavior compared with baselines. In online A/B experiments on live traffic, deploying policies improved under ATLAS leads to simultaneous improvements in user engagement metrics, downstream business outcomes, and the quality of sampled sessions as judged by human auditors, indicating that the diagnostic framework effectively drives real-world performance gains.

Conclusion: The paper concludes that ATLAS provides a practical and effective diagnostic evaluation framework for industrial LLM tool-use agents by combining request-level and interaction-level perspectives. Its calibrated LLM-judge-based signals, along with distilled low-latency models, offer actionable, fine-grained feedback that both characterizes where and why agents fail and enables policy optimization that translates into measurable online benefits. This dual-horizon, executable-signal design is argued to be a scalable approach for maintaining and improving complex agent services in dynamic production environments.

Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly deployed in user-facing services that require iterative tool use under dynamic business conditions. Reliable evaluation is essential for sustained improvement: it must reveal capability deficiencies, inform priorities, and assess interventions. Yet industrial agent service unfolds both through the iterative trajectory of a current request and through continued user interaction. Final-outcome assessment can therefore obscure where deficiencies arise and whether later service remains aligned with context from earlier exchanges. We propose ATLAS, a dual-horizon diagnostic evaluation framework for industrial tool-use agents. At the request horizon, trajectory-wise diagnostic signals relate deficiencies to execution locations and capability concerns. At the interaction horizon, user-wise signals assess whether service remains responsive across continued interaction. Together, these views provide structured diagnostic evidence for analyzing execution deficiencies and sustained service behavior. ATLAS instantiates them as executable signals with explicit evidence scopes and decision boundaries. LLM judge interfaces are calibrated against high-confidence references from real business logs; when needed, their decision behavior is distilled into efficient diagnostic models for lower-latency, lower-cost evaluation. The resulting feedback supports policy optimization. We evaluate ATLAS on Meituan Xiaotuan production traffic. Offline experiments assess diagnostic-signal fidelity and replay-based policy improvement, while online A/B experiments show concurrent gains in user engagement, downstream business outcomes, and sampled human-audit quality.

</details>


### [384] [Multimodal Adaptive Expert Selection with Text Routing and Ordinal Prototype Optimization for Sentiment Analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30726)
*Xiaode Chen,Jiakang Yu,Hongtao Deng,Huina Qu,Xun Zhu,Yinxia Lou*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes MAESTRO, a new multimodal sentiment analysis framework that dynamically routes text-guided multimodal experts and uses ordinal-aware prototype contrastive learning to better capture sentiment intensity, achieving state-of-the-art results on CMU-MOSI and CMU-MOSEI.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing multimodal sentiment analysis methods struggle with two issues: (1) static computation graphs treat all samples equally, failing to adapt to varying semantic complexity and diverse emotional/contextual patterns; and (2) standard contrastive objectives ignore the ordered nature of sentiment intensity (e.g., very negative to very positive), leading to latent spaces that do not respect ordinal relationships between sentiments.

Method: The authors propose MAESTRO, which has two key components. First, a Text-Guided Hybrid Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) module uses linguistic content as a routing signal to dynamically select and combine specialized audio-visual experts, enabling adaptive multimodal fusion instead of static feature combination. Second, an Ordinal-aware Prototype Contrastive Learning (O-PCL) objective learns sentiment prototypes and adds distance-based penalties so that latent representations and prototypes reflect the ordinal structure of sentiment intensities, enforcing ordered margins between sentiment levels in the representation space.

Result: On the CMU-MOSI and CMU-MOSEI multimodal sentiment benchmarks, MAESTRO achieves state-of-the-art or superior performance compared to prior disentanglement-based and other baseline models. Ablations show the contributions of the text-guided MoE routing and the ordinal-aware prototype contrastive loss, and qualitative analyses indicate that the dynamic expert selection is interpretable, with different experts activated for different emotional and contextual patterns.

Conclusion: Dynamic, text-routed expert selection and ordinal-aware prototype contrastive learning collectively address key shortcomings of prior multimodal sentiment analysis methods. By adaptively fusing audio-visual cues based on linguistic context and structuring the latent space to respect sentiment intensity order, MAESTRO delivers improved accuracy and interpretability on standard benchmarks, suggesting a promising direction for more nuanced and scalable affective computing models.

Abstract: Multimodal Sentiment Analysis (MSA) is a fundamental component of affective computing that aims to decipher complex emotional states by integrating verbal content with non-verbal cues including vocal intonation and facial micro-expressions. While recent disentanglement-based approaches have advanced the field, their potential is hindered by two methodological challenges. First, static computation graphs process all samples indiscriminately regardless of semantic complexity, which leads to suboptimal representation for diverse emotional expressions and contextual scenarios. Second, generic contrastive objectives often neglect the intrinsic ordinal hierarchy of sentiment intensities. To systematically address these limitations, we introduce Multimodal Adaptive Expert Selection with Text Routing and Ordinal prototype optimization (MAESTRO), a novel framework designed to dynamically orchestrate and refine multimodal representations. Drawing inspiration from an orchestra conductor, we design a Text-Guided Hybrid Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) mechanism. Unlike static fusion, this module utilizes linguistic context as a routing signal to dynamically activate specific audio-visual experts, thereby resolving cross-modal ambiguity through adaptive feature enhancement. Furthermore, to capture fine-grained sentiment gradations, we propose an Ordinal-aware Prototype Contrastive Learning (O-PCL). By incorporating distance-based penalties into the prototype learning objective, O-PCL enforces a structured latent space that preserves the natural order of emotion. Extensive experiments on the CMU-MOSI and CMU-MOSEI benchmarks demonstrate that MAESTRO achieves state-of-the-art performance, and qualitative analysis further confirms the interpretability of our dynamic routing paradigm.

</details>


### [385] [Autoregressive Mosaics: Probing 2D Spatial Reasoning in Text-Only Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30751)
*Ashwin Nedungadi,Stefan Oehmcke,Stefan Lüdtke*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces AM-Bench to test whether text-only LLMs truly represent 2D spatial layout, showing that models can translate fully specified layouts into code but differ widely when layouts are underspecified, and that both model choice and output medium (e.g., SVG vs. code) strongly affect spatial performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Text-and-code–trained LLMs sometimes write code that produces recognizable images, but it is unclear whether this reflects genuine internal 2D spatial understanding or merely strong code translation skills. Existing evaluations conflate these factors and often do not isolate the role of the output medium. The authors want a principled way to distinguish between (1) understanding or planning spatial layouts and (2) just generating correct code from explicit spatial descriptions, and to probe how the medium and internal planning behavior affect spatial performance.

Method: The authors propose Autoregressive Mosaics (AM-Bench), a benchmark with two main tasks. (1) A translation task: the model receives a prompt containing a fully specified geometry for an image described in words, and must output code that reproduces that exact picture. This isolates pure translation from description to code. (2) A layout task: the model is given an underspecified prompt that leaves room for design choices, and must compose a plausible image layout, revealing its spatial planning ability. They evaluate eight open-weight LLMs trained on text and code on both tasks, and perform an output-medium ablation by changing the format of the output from procedural drawing code to raw SVG. They also conduct activation probing: inspecting internal representations during generation to see whether the model forms an initial layout plan and how it tracks geometry as code is produced.

Result: All tested models perform reliably on the translation task, successfully converting fully specified geometric descriptions into corresponding code. However, they vary greatly on the open-ended layout task, showing that high code-generation capability does not guarantee strong 2D layout ability. The output-medium ablation reveals that when models output raw SVG instead of procedural drawing code, their layout performance improves consistently across all models. Probing of model activations shows that models do encode a coarse layout plan early on, but that this plan only reflects what is explicitly implied by the prompt; as generation proceeds, the models dynamically track and update the geometric state rather than simply executing a fixed precomputed plan.

Conclusion: 2D spatial performance in text-only, code-capable LLMs cannot be reduced to code-generation skill alone. Differences across models in open-ended layout tasks reflect genuine variation in how they handle spatial composition. Moreover, the medium of expression—such as using SVG rather than procedural code—systematically impacts performance, making the interface a key design variable. Internally, models appear to maintain a prompt-driven, coarse spatial plan and to update a representation of the evolving geometry during generation. AM-Bench therefore provides a more precise framework for dissecting and evaluating spatial reasoning in autoregressive LLMs.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) trained only on text and code can sometimes generate programs that draw recognizable images. However, it is unclear whether this reflects an internal representation of 2D spatial layout or simply the ability to translate spatial descriptions into code. We introduce Autoregressive Mosaics (AM-Bench), a benchmark that separates these factors: First, a translation task gives a model a fully specified geometry of a picture in words as a prompt and asks for the code that produces it. Second, a layout task requires the model to compose an image from an underspecified prompt. Across eight open-weight text-and-code-only models, all models reliably translate specified geometry into code, but their open-ended layout performance differs substantially, indicating that these differences are not explained by code-generation ability alone. An output-medium ablation further shows that the interface or medium of expression that the model uses matters: replacing procedural code with raw SVG improves layout scores across all models. Finally, probing model activations shows that a coarse layout plan is present before generation, but reflects only the layout implied by the prompt. During generation, models track the evolving geometric state instead of executing an initially fixed plan. Overall, these results show that 2D spatial performance in text-only LLMs depends on both the model and the output medium, and is not explained by code-generation ability alone.

</details>


### [386] [Which Rules Matter Now? Policy-Centroid Routing Before an Intelligent System Acts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30757)
*Thomson D. Nguy*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes policy-centroid routing, a pre-adjudication mechanism that maps proposed actions and policy texts into a shared semantic space and routes relevant policy regimes for human review, focusing on attention rather than final judgment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Intelligent systems face difficulty determining which rules apply to a proposed action because policies are expressed in complex natural language across multiple overlapping regimes while actions are underspecified. Current systems struggle not with making final judgments, but with attending to and identifying the relevant policies efficiently and reliably before adjudication.

Method: Introduce policy-centroid routing: compress each policy regime into one or more semantic centroids; embed proposed actions in the same space; use a declared similarity or distance measure and threshold to route all regimes whose centroids are sufficiently close to the action for authoritative review. The paper then formulates six falsifiable propositions and seven planned studies to compare this approach against baselines such as structured workflows, lexical/semantic retrieval, hierarchical and direct classification, and selective prediction, under matched review effort, focusing on when geometry helps or fails, particularly for rare/overlapping obligations and abstention cases. It also provides a synthetic worked example, but no empirical efficacy evaluation yet.

Result: No empirical performance results are reported. The main results are conceptual: a formalization of policy-centroid routing, a set of six testable propositions about its behavior, a comparative experimental design with seven follow-on studies, and analysis identifying potential strengths (recovering applicable regimes via geometry) and weaknesses (compression losses, especially for rare or overlapping obligations, and the need for principled abstention).

Conclusion: Policy-centroid routing is proposed as an attention mechanism that precedes legal or policy judgment, generating a review agenda by geometrically routing potentially applicable policy regimes rather than issuing determinations like permission or compliance. The approach is framed as falsifiable and is positioned for future empirical testing against existing retrieval and classification methods to understand when policy geometry is beneficial, when it fails due to compression, and when the system should abstain.

Abstract: Before an intelligent system can decide whether an action is allowed, it must first know which rules the action has approached. A single proposed action can implicate several policy regimes at once. Their requirements may stack, overlap, or qualify one another, yet many remain written in natural language while the action itself arrives as an incomplete description of intent. The first problem is not judgment. It is attention.
  Policy-centroid routing creates a layer before adjudication. It compresses expressions within each policy regime into one or more representative centroids, places the proposed action in the same semantic space, applies a declared measure, and routes every regime crossing a declared threshold to authoritative review. Several regimes may trigger at once. The output is a review agenda, not permission, prohibition, legality, breach, compliance, certification, or enforcement.
  The paper develops six falsifiable propositions and seven follow-on studies comparing the hypothesis with structured workflows, lexical and semantic retrieval, hierarchical and direct classification, and selective prediction under matched review burden. The studies are designed to identify where policy geometry recovers applicable regimes, where compression loses rare or overlapping obligations, and where the mechanism should abstain. The paper includes a synthetic worked example and reports no empirical efficacy result.

</details>


### [387] [SkillZip Pro: Execution-Aware Dynamic Compression of Progressively Loaded Skills for Self-Evolving Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30785)
*Xiaofan Bai,Chao Liu,Hongqiang Lin,Di Wu,Mingli Song,Xuan Jin,Xipeng Cao,Yuhong Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Summary generation failed


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Motivation analysis unavailable

Method: Method extraction failed

Result: Result analysis unavailable

Conclusion: Conclusion extraction failed

Abstract: Production agent skills are directory bundles, not isolated prompts. The root is loaded at activation; references, schemas, scripts, assets, and nested subskills are loaded only when an execution path needs them. Compressing only the root misses most deployment cost and may move branch-specific details into the always-loaded context. Flattening instead destroys progressive-loading boundaries.
  We introduce \method, an evaluation-free compressor for complete, progressively loaded skill bundles. It leaves the agent harness unchanged and emits an ordinary directory. The method combines two safeguards. First, it compresses \emph{across files}, removing content from a reference or subskill when the root or a declared environment contract already provides it. Second, it preserves routing, so every required file and directly callable entry remains reachable after rewriting. Users can configure \method along two independent axes. \emph{One-Shot} mode rebuilds the full bundle; \emph{Continual} mode reuses state and applies Zip-on-Write after each evolution patch. \emph{Persistent} compression rewrites the shipped bundle to reduce storage and runtime context. \emph{Transient} compression keeps that bundle byte-identical and builds a task-specific view, reducing only per-run context after build cost. Entry contracts mark private, public, and conditional resources; a multi-entry audit preserves standalone public subskills.
  On a production content-moderation skill evaluated by our industrial multi-round harness, \method removes \hl{38\%} of skill bundle tokens and \hl{10.4\%} of end-to-end per-run tokens with no quality loss, while an unprotected 71\% configuration loses up to 26 accuracy points to one-sided false positives. On a multi-entry bundle, \method effeciently reduces token cost while near-perfectly preserving every route and public entry.

</details>


### [388] [HSRM: Hidden-State Reward Models for Test-Time Verification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30841)
*Xianzhi Li,Xiaodan Zhu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They propose a very small reward model that reads a language model’s hidden states to judge which of several math solutions is correct, avoiding expensive text-based verification.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current test-time reasoning with LLMs in math requires verifying many candidate solutions using separate text-based verifiers that re-read each solution, which is computationally costly. Yet internal activations of LLMs already contain signals about correctness and uncertainty. The authors aim to exploit these existing internal representations to build a cheaper, still-accurate verifier that does not need human process labels or large verifier models.

Method: They freeze a generator LLM and, at reasoning-step boundaries in its chain-of-thought, extract its hidden states. These hidden states form trajectories for each candidate solution. A compact ~2M-parameter Transformer encoder—the hidden-state reward model (HSRM)—is trained on self-generated trajectories labeled only with the final outcome (correct/incorrect). At test time, HSRM reads the hidden-state sequences and assigns scores to rank candidate solutions, reusing the generator’s already-computed representations instead of re-processing text.

Result: On four mathematical reasoning benchmarks and across 16 combinations of generators and datasets, HSRM matches or surpasses a much larger 55M-parameter text-only energy-based verifier in 15 settings. It achieves comparable or better solution selection accuracy with significantly fewer parameters and no extra text encoding cost, since it operates purely on cached hidden states.

Conclusion: Internal representations of LLMs can be effectively leveraged by a tiny reward model to verify candidate math solutions, providing an efficient alternative to traditional text-based verifiers. This approach reduces computational overhead, avoids dependence on human process supervision and large verifier models, and demonstrates that correctness-related signals are richly encoded in hidden states at reasoning-step boundaries.

Abstract: Large language models can often generate plausible mathematical reasoning traces, but reliably identifying the correct solution among multiple candidates remains a key challenge. Existing test-time reasoning pipelines typically rely on text-based verifiers that re-read each generated solution, making verification an expensive component of inference. Prior work has shown, however, that LLMs often encode correctness-related signals in their internal representations, including awareness of when their own answers are likely to be wrong. Building on this observation, we introduce HSRM, a lightweight hidden-state reward model that verifies candidate solutions by directly reading the generator's internal representations rather than re-processing its text. HSRM extracts hidden states from a frozen generator at reasoning-step boundaries and uses a small Transformer encoder to rank candidates. It is trained from self-generated trajectories with outcome labels, requiring neither human-written process supervision nor a large pretrained verifier. Across four mathematical reasoning benchmarks, HSRM matches or outperforms a 55M-parameter text-only energy verifier in 15 of 16 generator--dataset settings while using only about 2M parameters, providing an efficient alternative to text-only verification by reusing representations already computed during generation.

</details>


### [389] [VFR-Audit: Verdict-Level Reliability for Fairness Audits in Hospital Length-of-Stay Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30846)
*Md Jannatul Rakib Joy,Viet Vo,Caslon Chua*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces VFR-Audit, a framework that quantifies the stability of fairness audit verdicts for clinical AI models by measuring how often pass/fail decisions would flip under resampling and across settings.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Clinical AI fairness audits currently convert continuous fairness metrics into binary pass/fail decisions using thresholds. These audits are repeated over time and across hospital sites, which can cause verdicts to flip between pass and fail. Existing uncertainty quantification methods operate on the continuous metric level, not directly on the binary verdict, and require manual interpretation to assess verdict stability, which does not scale across many models, metrics, and demographic attributes. Moreover, it is unclear how bias mitigation methods affect the stability of passing verdicts relative to performance metrics like AUROC and AUPRC. A systematic, scalable way to directly quantify and report verdict stability is missing.

Method: The authors propose VFR-Audit, a framework centered on a new scalar metric called the Verdict Flip Rate (VFR). VFR is defined on [0, 0.5] and estimates the probability that a fairness verdict (pass vs fail) would reverse under stratified bootstrap resampling of the evaluation data. The framework reports VFR together with three additional reliability dimensions: (1) within-cohort resampling stability, which reflects how verdicts vary under resampling within a single cohort; (2) audit-size sensitivity, which examines how verdict stability changes as the sample size of the audit varies; and (3) cross-hospital verdict agreement, quantified using Fleiss' kappa to summarize how consistently different hospital sites reach the same fairness verdicts.

Result: VFR-Audit produces a direct, interpretable measure of how likely fairness decisions are to flip, and augments it with diagnostics on within-cohort stability, sensitivity to audit size, and cross-site agreement. This allows users to distinguish between verdicts that are reliably stable and those that are highly sensitive to sampling variability, audit design, or hospital context. It also enables systematic comparison of how bias-mitigation strategies affect not just fairness metrics but the robustness of the resulting pass/fail verdicts, in relation to standard performance measures such as AUROC and AUPRC.

Conclusion: The paper concludes that verdict-level stability is a critical but previously under-addressed dimension of clinical AI fairness audits. By introducing the Verdict Flip Rate and the VFR-Audit framework, the authors provide a scalable way to quantify and communicate the reliability of pass/fail fairness decisions across metrics, attributes, and hospital sites. This can better inform governance boards, payers, and regulators about when fairness verdicts are trustworthy enough to act upon and how mitigation strategies impact both fairness and verdict robustness.

Abstract: Fairness audits in clinical Artificial Intelligence convert continuous fairness metrics into binary pass-or-fail verdicts against operational thresholds, where hospital governance boards, payers, and regulators act on the resulting verdicts. Such audits are repeated over time and across hospital sites, thus the same verdict can flip between pass and fail across audits. Existing uncertainty methods such as Bayesian posteriors, bootstrap confidence intervals, and permutation tests address verdict instability only at the continuous-metric level. Converting metric-level uncertainty into a verdict-stability claim remains a manual step that scales poorly across the (model, metric, attribute) cells an audit covers. Existing uncertainty methods also leave open whether bias-mitigation steps, such as reweighing or per-group threshold shifts, yield a stable passing verdict at the cost of model discrimination measured as AUROC or AUPRC.To address this verdict-stability gap, we propose VFR-Audit, a framework built around the Verdict Flip Rate (VFR), a scalar bounded between 0 and 0.5 that measures the probability of verdict reversal under stratified bootstrap resampling. VFR-Audit reports VFR alongside three reliability axes, namely within-cohort resampling stability, audit-size sensitivity, and cross-hospital verdict agreement via Fleiss' kappa.

</details>


### [390] [Predicting Residential Rents in Dakar Using Machine Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30865)
*Amadou Tidiane Kassa Diallo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper builds and evaluates a full machine-learning pipeline to predict residential rents in Dakar, producing an interpretable benchmark model and discussing methodological issues with target encoding and feature importance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Dakar has a large rental sector (over half of households rent) but its rental market is under-documented, limiting informed decisions by policymakers, investors, and residents. There is a need for a robust, transparent pricing model tailored to this context and for methodological insights on how to handle location information and categorical variables in hedonic rent models.

Method: The authors systematically scraped 1,507 online rental listings for Dakar, cleaned the data with a documented pipeline, and engineered four additional features, including a luxury score and a keyword-based quality score. They encoded location using leakage-free KFold target encoding, then trained and compared several models: linear regression, Random Forest (as baseline), XGBoost, and LightGBM. Hyperparameters for the gradient boosting models were tuned with Bayesian optimization via Optuna. Model performance was evaluated using R^2, MAE, and RMSE. They interpreted the best model (XGBoost) using both native gain-based feature importance and SHAP values for more nuanced attribution.

Result: The optimized XGBoost model outperformed the others with an R^2 of 0.847, a mean absolute error of 210,902 XOF, and a root mean squared error of 324,195 XOF. Engineered features such as luxury and quality scores contributed meaningfully to performance. Feature importance analysis showed a discrepancy: XGBoost’s native gain metric suggested location was relatively unimportant, while SHAP values indicated that location was actually the second most influential predictor after the top feature(s).

Conclusion: The study demonstrates that a carefully designed ML pipeline, including bespoke feature engineering and robust encoding of location, can accurately predict residential rents in Dakar. It warns that native gain-based feature importance can underestimate the role of target-encoded categorical variables like location, and argues for the use of SHAP or similar methods in hedonic pricing studies. The work delivers a transparent benchmark dataset and model for Dakar’s rental market and suggests future enhancements such as incorporating richer geospatial features and applying conformal prediction for calibrated uncertainty estimates.

Abstract: Dakar's residential rental market remains poorly documented despite its economic and social importance: 54.4% of households are renters, compared to 23.3% nationally. This study develops a complete machine learning pipeline to predict residential rents in Dakar, from data collection to model interpretation. An original dataset of 1,507 rental listings was built through systematic web scraping and a documented cleaning pipeline, then enriched with four purpose-built features, including a luxury score and a keyword-based quality score. Five models were compared: linear regression, Random Forest (baseline), XGBoost, and LightGBM optimized through Bayesian optimization with Optuna, using leakage-free KFold target encoding for location. The optimized XGBoost model achieved the best performance with an $R^2$ of 0.847, an MAE of 210,902 XOF, and an RMSE of 324,195 XOF. Feature importance was assessed using native XGBoost gain and SHAP values, revealing a substantial difference in the ranking of location, which appears as a minor predictor by gain but as the second most influential variable by SHAP. This result carries methodological implications for hedonic studies using target-encoded categorical variables. This study provides an interpretable benchmark for Dakar's rental market and highlights several avenues for improvement, including the integration of geospatial features and conformal prediction.

</details>


### [391] [CAER: Causal Action Effect Reweighting for World Model Training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30897)
*Jianjie Fang,Xvyuan Liu,Ziyou Wang,Rongze Tang,Zhaolu Wang,Zhuohang Li,Xin Zhang,Haisheng Su,Chen Gao,Wei Wu,Xinlei Chen,Yong Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes CAER, a training paradigm for action-conditioned video world models that reweights loss toward action-affected regions, improving physical consistency, controllability, and visual quality.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing world models for embodied intelligence are typically trained with uniform mean squared error over space and time. This causes the loss to be dominated by abundant, mostly static background pixels or tokens, while the relatively sparse, dynamically changing regions where agent actions actually have an effect are under-optimized. As a result, models tend to prioritize reconstructing appearance rather than accurately modeling how actions causally influence the future state of the world. The authors aim to address this imbalance so that world models better capture action-driven dynamics crucial for control and planning.

Method: The authors introduce Causal Action Effect Reweighting (CAER), a general training paradigm that adaptively redistributes supervision during training. For each training sample and step, the model produces two predictions of the future: one conditioned on the agent's action and one without that conditioning. By contrasting these two predictions, CAER estimates an "effect map" that highlights which tokens (e.g., spatial-temporal video tokens) are causally affected by the action. This effect map is then normalized into a set of weights that preserve the total loss magnitude but reallocate it toward action-affected tokens and away from unaffected background tokens. The procedure is performed online, integrated into training without external annotations or offline preprocessing, and is designed to scale with both model and dataset size. The reweighted loss replaces conventional uniform MSE during optimization.

Result: Across multiple heterogeneous tasks involving action-conditioned world models, CAER-trained models converge to better solutions than those trained with standard uniform MSE. The improvements manifest in several aspects: stronger physical consistency of predicted dynamics, better controllability of the generated video with respect to actions, and higher visual quality of the predicted frames. These gains are reported as consistent across the evaluated settings, indicating robustness of the approach.

Conclusion: Reweighting supervision toward regions of a video that are causally affected by actions leads to more effective learning of action-conditioned world models than uniform error minimization. CAER offers a simple, annotation-free, and scalable way to implement this idea by using the model’s own contrasting predictions to infer where actions matter and then shifting loss weight accordingly. This improves the practical usefulness of world models for embodied intelligence by enhancing their ability to produce physically consistent, controllable, and visually compelling future predictions.

Abstract: World models are becoming core infrastructure for embodied intelligence, with action-conditioned video generation providing controllable predictions of how scenes evolve after agent interventions. Yet existing models are commonly trained with space-time-uniform mean squared error, allowing abundant background tokens to dominate the gradient while sparse interaction dynamics remain under-optimized; such uniform fitting rewards reconstructing appearance rather than learning how actions change the world. We introduce Causal Action Effect Reweighting (CAER), a general training paradigm that redistributes supervision toward the tokens whose predicted future is causally affected by the action. CAER contrasts the model's own predictions with and without action conditioning to localize these tokens online, then normalizes the resulting effect map into a weight that preserves the total coefficient mass and changes only where it is spent. This online signal requires no external annotations or offline preprocessing, avoids additional data-processing time, and scales naturally with model and dataset size. Experiments across heterogeneous action-conditioned world-model tasks show that CAER converges to better solutions than uniform MSE training, with consistent improvements in the physical consistency, controllability, and visual quality of generated videos.

</details>


### [392] [Responsible Integration of AI in Cancer Genomics: Barriers, Risks, and Pathways to Trustworthy Clinical Translation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30912)
*Bahar İlgen,Yiannos Tolias,Denise Kühnert,Paraskevi Papadopoulou,Magnus Westerlund,Dominik Heider,Katharina Ladewig,Georges Hattab*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Review of how AI/NLP support cancer genomics and a roadmap to make them trustworthy in routine oncology practice.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Although AI and NLP can already mine biomedical literature and genomic data at scale, they are not yet reliably embedded into everyday clinical oncology workflows. The authors are motivated by this implementation gap: powerful tools exist, but clinicians hesitate to rely on them because of concerns about trust, reliability, governance, and integration. They aim to clarify why this translational failure happens and how to systematically overcome it.

Method: This is a conceptual review. The authors survey current uses of NLP and AI across the cancer genomics pipeline (literature mining, variant interpretation, clinical trial matching, knowledge graphs, multimodal integration). From this landscape, they synthesize and categorize key obstacles into four interacting ‘failure domains’: evidence inconsistency, explainability/uncertainty, data governance/reproducibility, and interoperability. They then propose a systems-level conceptual framework and a roadmap, emphasizing validation, uncertainty-aware methods, interoperable infrastructure, regulatory alignment, and continuous human oversight across the AI lifecycle.

Result: The paper’s main results are: (1) a structured mapping of where and how AI/NLP are currently used in cancer genomics; (2) identification and articulation of four interrelated translational failure domains that hinder routine clinical adoption; and (3) a systems-level framework that links these domains across the full translational pathway, showing that failures in one domain can propagate or interact with others. They also outline specific technical, organizational, and regulatory strategies to mitigate these issues.

Conclusion: The authors conclude that further gains in raw AI/NLP capability are not the main bottleneck to clinical adoption in cancer genomics. Instead, progress requires systematically addressing evidence inconsistency, explainability and uncertainty, data governance and reproducibility, and interoperability in an integrated way throughout development, deployment, and post-deployment monitoring. With rigorous validation, uncertainty-aware modeling, interoperable and well-governed infrastructures, regulatory alignment, and sustained human oversight, AI and NLP can be more safely and effectively translated into routine oncology practice.

Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) and natural language processing (NLP) are increasingly used to extract, integrate, and interpret biomedical knowledge relevant to cancer genomics, yet their translation into routine clinical oncology has been comparatively slow. The central challenge is not computational capability alone, but trustworthy integration into clinical workflows. This review examines how NLP and AI support the cancer genomics pipeline, from literature mining and automated variant interpretation to clinical trial matching, knowledge graph construction, and multimodal data integration. We identify four interrelated translational failure domains: evidence inconsistency, explainability and uncertainty, data governance and reproducibility, and interoperability. Rather than considering these challenges in isolation, we take a systems-level view, focusing on their interaction across the translational pathway. We propose a conceptual framework and roadmap for addressing these domains through rigorous validation, uncertainty-aware methods, interoperable infrastructures, regulatory alignment, and human oversight across the AI lifecycle. Progress toward routine clinical use will depend less on further improving model capability than on systematically addressing these interacting failure domains from development through deployment and post-deployment monitoring.

</details>


### [393] [CARVE: Verified Expansion for Variable-Length Generation in Diffusion Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30922)
*Wail Bouhedja,Amr Mohamed,Guokan Shang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes CARVE, a training-free algorithm that allows masked diffusion language models to dynamically adjust response length during decoding, improving accuracy and reducing FLOPs versus fixed-length decoding.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Masked diffusion language models currently require a fixed number of answer tokens to be chosen before decoding. Picking this length is hard: if it is too short, the model’s reasoning or code can be truncated; if it is too long, computation is wasted and the extra canvas can destabilize the denoising process. There is a need for a method that can adaptively adjust sequence length during inference without retraining the model while maintaining or improving quality and efficiency.

Method: CARVE (Counterfactual-Aware Reveal with Verified Expansion) starts decoding on a relatively short response canvas with some positions masked. During decoding, it proposes to expand the canvas by inserting additional [MASK] positions. To decide whether to accept these insertions, CARVE performs a counterfactual test: it compares the model’s token prediction distributions on the unresolved positions in the original (short) canvas with those obtained when the candidate expanded canvas is used. It measures similarity using Jensen–Shannon divergence between aligned token distributions. If the divergence is low (indicating stable predictions), the additional masks are kept, thereby lengthening the canvas; otherwise, the expansion is rejected. This algorithm is training-free and can be applied to both full-canvas and blockwise masked diffusion decoders.

Result: On code generation and mathematical reasoning benchmarks, CARVE consistently improves average performance compared to fixed-length masked diffusion decoding for all tested model families. In addition to accuracy gains, CARVE reduces inference cost, achieving up to a 2× reduction in FLOPs relative to fixed-length decoding in some settings.

Conclusion: Variable-length decoding for masked diffusion LMs can be achieved without retraining by using counterfactual stability checks to decide when to expand the response canvas. CARVE provides a principled, JS-divergence–based criterion for verified sequence-length growth, yielding better accuracy and, in many cases, substantially lower inference cost than fixed-length baselines across diverse models and tasks.

Abstract: Masked diffusion language models predict tokens from a partially observed response canvas, enabling bidirectional conditioning and parallel token refinement. Yet standard masked-diffusion decoders use a rigid inference interface: the number of masked positions allocated to the answer is fixed before generation begins. Choosing this length is difficult. A short canvas can truncate reasoning or code, while a long canvas wastes computation and can perturb denoising. We introduce CARVE (Counterfactual-Aware Reveal with Verified Expansion), a training-free variable-length algorithm for masked diffusion LMs. Starting from a shorter canvas, CARVE can grow the response during decoding by inserting additional [MASK] positions. Rather than keeping every insertion, CARVE tests a candidate expanded canvas and asks a counterfactual question: would the model make similar predictions for the unresolved positions in the original canvas if the extra masked space were present? The inserted masks are kept only when they induce low Jensen-Shannon (JS) divergence on aligned unresolved positions. This makes length growth a verified stability decision rather than a pure confidence heuristic. CARVE applies without retraining to both full-canvas and blockwise diffusion decoders. Across code generation and mathematical reasoning benchmarks, CARVE consistently improves average performance over fixed-length baselines across all evaluated model families. Crucially, CARVE achieves these accuracy gains while reducing inference cost, reaching half the FLOPs of fixed-length decoding in some settings.

</details>


### [394] [Learning Action Models with Conditional and Quantified Effects via Uncertainty-Guided Exploration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30955)
*Jeffrey Jewett,William Solow,Sandhya Saisubramanian*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes OHCAM, an online, hypothesis-driven algorithm for learning complex action models with conditional and quantified effects efficiently and robustly from limited, noisy interactions, outperforming baselines and working on real robots.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Accurate and expressive action models are vital for automated planning, especially in realistic domains that involve conditional and quantified effects. However, most existing learning methods either assume overly simple action representations or become computationally infeasible when extended to such complex effects. There is a need for an approach that can learn rich action models online from few, potentially noisy observations while remaining scalable and practically applicable, including on physical robots.

Method: The authors introduce OHCAM (Online Hypothesis-Driven Conditional Action Model Learning), which maintains a belief distribution over different hypothesized action models. It actively selects actions that are expected to be most informative by maximizing the disagreement among the competing hypotheses, thereby reducing uncertainty in the learned model. The method is robust to noisy observations. To address scalability, OHCAM starts from a compact hypothesis space consisting of simple action models and only grows to include more complex conditional structures when simpler hypotheses become inconsistent with observed data. Learning proceeds online through interaction with the environment.

Result: On six benchmark planning domains, OHCAM learns action models that can successfully solve many more tasks than baseline methods, and it does so with higher sample efficiency, even when the observations are noisy. Additionally, the authors demonstrate the approach on two real-world tasks using a Kinova Gen3 robot, showing that the learned models enable successful planning and execution beyond simulation settings.

Conclusion: OHCAM provides an effective and scalable solution for online learning of expressive action models with conditional and quantified effects. By combining hypothesis-driven active exploration with a progressive increase in model complexity, it achieves strong sample efficiency and robustness to noise. Empirical results in simulated benchmarks and on a real robot validate that OHCAM can acquire practical action models that significantly outperform existing baselines in terms of the range of tasks solvable by the resulting planners.

Abstract: Accurate action models are critical for effective planning. Existing action-model learning methods largely assume simple action representations or become computationally intractable when learning conditional and quantified effects. We present Online Hypothesis-Driven Conditional Action Model Learning (OHCAM), an online approach for learning action models with conditional and quantified effects from limited interactions with the environment. OHCAM maintains a belief over hypothesized action models and actively selects informative actions to reduce uncertainty by maximizing disagreement among competing hypotheses, while being robust to noisy observations. To enable scalability, OHCAM begins with a small set of simple action model hypotheses and expands to more complex conditions only when the current hypotheses become inconsistent with the data. Experiments on six benchmark planning domains demonstrate that OHCAM is sample efficient in learning action models that solve substantially more tasks than baselines, even with observation noise. We validate OHCAM on two tasks using a Kinova Gen3 robot, demonstrating the real-world applicability of our approach.

</details>


### [395] [MNIST-PRO: MNIST is Back as a Partially Observable World for AI Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.31022)
*Vernon Toh,Navonil Majumder,Zhengyuan Liu,Nancy F. Chen,Soujanya Poria*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces MNIST-PRO, a benchmark that turns digit recognition into a sequential, partially observable task to study how AI agents build and update perceptual state from glimpses and memory.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing benchmarks for AI agents in partially observable environments often mix perception with physical control and environmental complexity, making it hard to isolate and evaluate the core ability of constructing and updating a perceptual state over time. The authors want a clean, controlled setting focused purely on agentic perception: how agents coordinate active sensing with working memory to maintain and revise an internal representation of the world.

Method: They convert standard MNIST digit recognition into a sequential, glimpse-based search task with constraints on how agents can look back at past observations. Using this new MNIST-PRO benchmark, they test ten multimodal models under four different memory representations: storing raw visual histories, textual descriptions of state, structured metric grid maps, and a consolidated visual canvas. They compare performance under full versus partial observability.

Result: Under full observability, models perform very well, but partial observability significantly degrades performance and reveals systematic weaknesses. The study identifies three bottlenecks: (1) difficulty in constructing and interpreting a coherent perceptual state from disjoint glimpses; (2) a tendency to stop exploring too early, before collecting enough evidence; and (3) failure to revise initial incorrect beliefs even when presented with later contradictory observations.

Conclusion: The findings demonstrate that strong performance under full observability does not translate to robust perception in partially observable settings. Simply collecting more visual evidence is insufficient; agents must be able to actively coordinate sensing with memory, integrate fragmented observations into a coherent state, and flexibly update that state when new evidence conflicts with prior beliefs. MNIST-PRO provides a focused benchmark to study and improve these capabilities.

Abstract: AI agents in partially observable environments need to coordinate active sensing with working memory to maintain an evolving perceptual state. However, existing benchmarks struggle to isolate this perceptual-state construction and interpretation capability because they introduce physical and control complexities. We address this with MNIST-PRO, a benchmark that isolates agentic perception by converting MNIST digit recognition into a sequential, glimpse-based search task with lookback constraints. We evaluate ten multimodal models across four memory representations, including raw visual history, textual states, structured metric grid maps, and a consolidated visual canvas. While models excel under full observability, partial observability exposes a clear performance gap. We identify three distinct bottlenecks. First, perceptual-state construction and interpretation present a challenge, as agents struggle to integrate fragmented glimpses. Second, agents often stop exploring before they see the full sequence. Third, models often fail to revise early, incorrect beliefs even when faced with subsequent contradictory evidence. These results show that simply acquiring visual evidence is not enough. Agents must also be able to build and update a reliable perceptual state.

</details>


### [396] [Measure Before You Manage: Evaluating Agent Working Memory in Coding Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.31057)
*Le Chen,Zishen Wan,Baixi Sun,Xiaolong Ma,Chih-Hsuan Yang,Feng Yan,Sheng Di,Franck Cappello,Rajeev Thakur*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper analyzes how different types of objects in coding agents’ working memory behave differently and argues that memory management and evaluation must be semantically aware, not just based on token budgets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing agent memory systems largely treat all context tokens uniformly, even though real coding agents store heterogeneous items like instructions, code, intermediate tool outputs, and internal notes that differ in importance, persistence, and structure. This mismatch can lead to suboptimal compression, retrieval, and evaluation of memory strategies. The authors are motivated to understand and exploit this semantic heterogeneity to design better working-memory policies and more realistic evaluations.

Method: The authors empirically study 55 archived coding-agent trajectories, categorizing working-memory contents into semantically distinct object types (e.g., instructions, artifacts, tool outputs, agent state). They measure how each type is retained, compressed, and used over time, and then design and test two semantically informed memory-management strategies: (1) an object-aware compression policy that treats different object types differently, and (2) a retrieval-based policy that selectively brings objects into context. They compare these to baseline approaches under equal token budgets and also run a real-system replay to examine serving behavior and system limits.

Result: They find that different semantic object types in working memory show distinct retention and compression patterns, confirming strong heterogeneity. Semantically informed strategies alter how much meaningful context is actually delivered under the same nominal token budget and incur different management costs. Calibration improvements seen during development do not consistently transfer to held-out tasks. Real-system replays reveal serving and system constraints that are not apparent from token-budget accounting alone.

Conclusion: Semantic structure is crucial for both the design and evaluation of agent working memory. Memory-management strategies must account for object type and usage patterns, not just token counts. Evaluations based only on nominal token budgets are misleading; instead, they should consider four levels: what is stored, what is actually delivered as context, the management work required, and the resulting task or process outcomes. This multi-level, semantically aware perspective is needed to properly assess and improve working-memory mechanisms for coding agents.

Abstract: Agent working memory is heterogeneous. Objects such as instructions, artifacts, tool outputs, and agent-generated state play different semantic roles and exhibit different size, retention, and representation profiles. Recent work has begun to explore memory-management mechanisms that account for such heterogeneity. This work focuses on semantic heterogeneity and studies how it should shape the management and evaluation of working memory in coding agents. Across 55 archived coding-agent trajectories, we find that semantically different working-memory objects exhibit distinct retention and compression behavior. This heterogeneity motivates semantically informed memory management. We study two semantically informed strategies: an object-aware compression policy and a retrieval-based policy. Their evaluation shows that calibration gains may not transfer to held-out tasks, and that equal token budgets do not imply equal delivered context or management cost. A real-system replay further exposes serving limits that nominal budgets alone do not capture. Together, these results show why semantic structure matters for agent working memory and why evaluating memory-management strategies requires more than a nominal token budget. We organize these lessons into four levels: stored state, delivered context, management work, and task or process outcome.

</details>


### [397] [Wrong Prediction, Right Answer: Recovering Evidence from Collapsed LLM Sequence Scores](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.31068)
*Qiyao Yan,Chenpeng Wang,Liangming Pan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper shows that large language models often internally compute correct reasoning but fail to express it in their final answers, and that a tiny output-level correction can recover much of this hidden capability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Benchmark failures are usually interpreted as true reasoning weaknesses in LLMs, but this may conflate two issues: whether the model can form correct internal logic, and whether it can express that logic in its outputs. The authors want to disentangle these and test if hidden states already contain correct answers even when the output layer fails, which would change how we interpret zero-shot reasoning deficits and benchmark scores.

Method: First, they probe hidden states of LLMs on diverse reasoning benchmarks to see if linear probes can decode the correct answers where normal generation fails, revealing a “readout gap.” Then they design a diagnostic protocol: a minimal additive correction applied to the model’s output logits that does not use target labels (target-label-free). This correction has only two parameters and is fitted using very few unlabeled examples (as few as 25). They test this on Qwen3.5 models and then examine transfer to other models like OLMo-2-1B and Llama-3.1-8B. They also compare against baselines like count-preserving permutations and lexical-overlap heuristics.

Result: They find a consistent readout gap: simple probes can decode correct answers from hidden states even when standard sequence scoring fails due to structural biases. The two-parameter additive correction, trained on just 25 unlabeled samples, recovers between 9 and 34 percentage points of accuracy on reasoning benchmarks for Qwen3.5 models, and this fix transfers well to OLMo-2-1B and Llama-3.1-8B. The recovered improvements hold on harder cases that are not solvable by trivial lexical overlap and clearly beat permutation-based baselines that preserve token counts but scramble structure.

Conclusion: A substantial portion of what appears as zero-shot reasoning failure in LLMs is actually an expression or readout problem rather than a lack of internal reasoning. Correct, instance-specific logical information often exists in hidden states but is lost in the final decoding stage. Simple, low-parameter, label-free corrections at the output level can recover much of this performance, so benchmark evaluations should be interpreted more narrowly and not automatically equate output errors with absent reasoning capabilities.

Abstract: When a large language model fails a reasoning task, it is often assumed to lack the underlying capability. However, this conflates a genuine absence of reasoning with a late-stage output bottleneck. We observe a consistent readout gap across diverse reasoning benchmarks: hidden-state probes successfully decode correct answers even when native sequence scoring completely collapses due to structural biases. To test whether instance-specific logic survives this collapse, we introduce a diagnostic protocol using a minimal, target-label-free additive correction. Fitting just two parameters on as few as 25 unlabeled examples recovers 9--34 accuracy points for Qwen3.5 models, transferring successfully to OLMo-2-1B and Llama-3.1-8B. Crucially, these recovered decisions persist on hard instances unresolved by simple lexical overlap and significantly exceed count-preserving permutation baselines. Our results show that many apparent zero-shot reasoning deficits are expression failures masking intact internal logic, urging a narrower interpretation of benchmark evaluations.

</details>


### [398] [Scaling Large Reasoning Models beyond Human Supervision: A Path toward Superintelligence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.31075)
*Zhiqin Yang,Jingwen Fu,Yuhan Liu,Hengyu Liu,Yonggang Zhang,Kainan Cao,Zizhuo Zhang,Chenxin Li,Ruibin Yuan,Jiahao Pan,Jiankai Sun,Zhenyuan Zhang,Yibo Li,Yunlong Lin,Jing Xiong,Sida Lin,Bo Han,Wei Xue,Yike Guo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper analyzes how large reasoning models (LRMs) can keep improving when direct human supervision becomes sparse, proposing a framework for rewards, data generation, risks, and evaluation as models move toward more autonomous learning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) works well for math and code because outcomes are easily checked, but it does not directly extend to open-ended, agentic tasks where reliable rewards and scalable supervision are difficult to obtain. There is a need to understand how to keep improving LRMs as human supervision becomes less frequent and less central to the learning loop.

Method: The authors conceptually analyze two axes: (1) the reward axis, describing a progression from dense, per-instance human judgments toward reusable verifiers and fully automated rewards; and (2) the experience axis, describing a progression from human-curated datasets and environments toward self-generated curricula, constructed environments, and autonomous co-evolution. They integrate these into a five-level ladder (L0–L4) that categorizes how much of the learning process is still controlled by humans at each stage. They also characterize key risks and propose a three-part evaluation scheme for policies, feedback, and experience.

Result: They provide a structured framework (the L0–L4 ladder) that situates current and future approaches to scaling LRMs beyond human supervision, identify major risk modes such as reward hacking, feedback drift, curriculum collapse, and environment errors, and define three complementary evaluation targets: policy capability, feedback fidelity, and experience quality. They also release and maintain an evolving GitHub repository cataloging recent work in this area.

Conclusion: Scaling LRMs beyond intensive human supervision requires systematically transitioning from human-dependent to increasingly autonomous rewards and experience generation, while rigorously monitoring and mitigating new risks. The proposed ladder, risk taxonomy, and evaluation dimensions offer a roadmap for building more self-sustaining learning systems that may eventually approach superintelligent performance, and the accompanying repository helps track progress in this rapidly changing landscape.

Abstract: Recent advances in large reasoning models (LRMs) have shown that reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) can substantially improve reasoning in mathematics and code, where outcomes can be checked automatically. Extending this progress to open-ended and agentic tasks remains difficult because reliable rewards are harder to obtain and direct human supervision cannot keep pace with the scale and complexity of model-generated experience. This paper studies how LRMs can continue to improve as human supervision gradually recedes from the learning loop. We examine two connected dimensions of this problem. The reward axis traces the development from per-instance human judgments to reusable verifiers and rewards that operate even without human feedback. The experience axis examines how learning can progress from human-curated tasks and environments toward self-generated curricula, constructed environments, and autonomous co-evolution. We connect these dimensions through a five-level ladder from L0 to L4 that identifies which parts of the learning process remain under continued human control. Our analysis further highlights the risks introduced by increasingly autonomous rewards and experience generation, including reward hacking, feedback drift, curriculum collapse, and environment errors. Consequently, we also provide the evaluation around three complementary objects: policy capability, feedback fidelity, and experience quality. This analysis provides a structured account of current approaches to scaling LRMs beyond human supervision and the open problems involved in developing self-sustaining learning systems toward superintelligence. Furthermore, we maintain a continuously updated \href{https://github.com/visitworld123/Awesome-Scaling-LRM-Beyond-Human-Supervision}{GitHub repository} to track the latest advances.

</details>


### [399] [Reconciling Process Supervision with Outcome-Based Credit in Agentic Policy Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.31077)
*Jingxiao Yang,Wangjie Gan,Yingxuan Zhuang,Wenqi Zhang,Jintao Chen,Xuhong Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces TASPO, a method that turns outcome-based and privileged-information-based supervision into fine-grained, action-level credit assignments for language-model agents, improving long-horizon reinforcement learning performance and stability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing outcome-based RL for language-model agents gives only trajectory-level credit, so every decision in a long interaction gets the same advantage, which is too coarse. On-policy self-distillation with privileged information (PI) offers token-level supervision, but this supervision doesn’t map cleanly into how much each executable action should be credited for the final verified outcome. This creates a gap between available supervision and effective credit assignment, especially when PI is irrelevant to the current state, misaligned with action granularity, or not directly tied to task outcomes.

Method: The authors propose TASPO, a framework that converts PI-based supervision into outcome-grounded, action-level credit. TASPO (1) extracts decision-relevant privileged information from previously verified successful trajectories, (2) aggregates the resulting PI-induced likelihood changes at the level of executable actions instead of tokens, and (3) uses these aggregated shifts to reweight the original trajectory-level advantage into positive, bounded, mean-preserving per-action weights. This way, the final task outcome still defines the overall direction and magnitude of the update, while PI only redistributes that fixed total credit across actions within the trajectory.

Result: On three benchmarks involving agentic language-model behavior, TASPO outperforms GRPO by 10.6% on average and exhibits better generalization to unseen tasks. Empirical studies further show that TASPO narrows the mismatch between supervision and credit assignment and leads to more stable policy optimization dynamics.

Conclusion: TASPO provides a principled way to bridge the supervision-credit gap in outcome-based RL with privileged information for language-model agents. By grounding PI-driven refinements in verified outcomes and applying them at the action level, TASPO achieves better performance, generalization, and training stability than baseline methods such as GRPO. The work highlights the importance of aligning supervision granularity with decision-making granularity in long-horizon LLM agents.

Abstract: Outcome-based reinforcement learning provides verified feedback for language-model agents, but assigns trajectory-level advantage uniformly to all decisions, yielding coarse credit over long-horizon interactions. On-policy self-distillation offers finer supervision by re-evaluating sampled behavior with privileged information (PI) available only during training. However, fine-grained supervision is not necessarily fine-grained credit: PI-induced likelihood changes describe how additional information alters policy preference, but do not directly determine how an executable action should inherit the verified task outcome. This creates a supervision-credit gap. Privileged signals may be irrelevant to the current interaction state, operate at a token granularity misaligned with executable decisions, and lack the outcome semantics required for reinforcement. We introduce TASPO, which converts privileged supervision into outcome-grounded action credit. TASPO constructs decision-applicable PI from verified successful experience, aggregates PI-induced likelihood shifts at the executable-action level, and converts relative action support into positive, bounded, mean-preserving weights on the original trajectory advantage. Thus, the verified outcome determines the update direction and average scale, while PI only redistributes credit across actions. Across three agentic benchmarks, TASPO improves over GRPO by 10.6\% and generalizes better to unseen tasks. Further analysis indicates that TASPO reduces supervision mismatch and that action-level assignment stabilizes the policy optimization process. These findings offer the community another interesting perspective.

</details>


### [400] [Token-Efficient Data Reasoning Agents via Adaptive Structuring of Unstructured Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.31082)
*Milad Rezaei Hajidehi,Qitong Wang,Stratos Idreos*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces 'agentic data cracking', a method that incrementally structures unstructured enterprise data as a side-effect of LLM agents’ reasoning, drastically cutting token cost while preserving accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Enterprise LLM agents must reason over large unstructured corpora (web pages, PDFs, filings, transcripts, etc.), which is extremely expensive because each query re-reads large documents and consumes many tokens. If the data were structured, answering the same questions would be as cheap as database lookups. However, pre-structuring everything is infeasible: unstructured documents contain far more potential structure than queries will ever use, and it is unknown in advance which structure and documents will matter. The paper is motivated by this cost-accuracy gap and seeks a way to approach the efficiency of structured querying without paying the upfront, exhaustive structuring cost.

Method: They propose 'agentic data cracking', where a main LLM agent answers user questions over unstructured data, while a secondary 'cracking' sub-agent is spawned whenever a document is opened. This sub-agent, using the already-loaded context, extracts grounded structured representations (e.g., facts, fields, or relations) that are likely to be useful for future, related questions.
