Structuring is driven by observed queries (adaptive) and goes beyond the immediate question to anticipate related needs (speculative). The extracted structure is stored in a shared structured store so that future queries can often be answered via cheap lookups instead of re-reading documents. The approach is evaluated on the FanOutQA benchmark, including an extension with additional related questions.

Result: On FanOutQA, reasoning over an ideal, fully pre-structured store is shown to be 28× cheaper than reasoning directly over documents, with the cost gap growing superlinearly as questions span more documents. Using their proposed agentic data cracking, and extending FanOutQA with only one additional related question per original question, they achieve a 53% reduction in token/cost usage while maintaining essentially the same accuracy as standard RAG-style document-based reasoning.

Conclusion: Agentic data cracking demonstrates that it is possible to substantially reduce the cost of LLM agent reasoning over unstructured data by opportunistically and incrementally building structured representations as a byproduct of normal query answering. Over time, more queries can be served directly from the accumulated structured store, bringing costs closer to those of querying a database while preserving agentic accuracy. The authors position this as an early step toward a new kind of data infrastructure for LLM agents, where knowledge discovered during reasoning is retained in a shared structured substrate rather than being repeatedly re-extracted from raw documents.

Abstract: Valuable data remains embedded in unstructured sources: web pages, reports, contracts, filings, earnings calls, and PDFs. The big bet in enterprise AI is deploying LLM agents that reason over this data to answer complex questions for every knowledge worker. Agents can do this today, but at prohibitive cost. Each question repeatedly opens large documents to recover scattered evidence, consuming up to a million tokens. However, if the data were already structured, the same question would reduce to a cheap database lookup. For example, on FanOutQA benchmark, reasoning over an ideal pre-structured store is 28X cheaper, and the gap grows to orders of magnitude as questions fan out over more documents. Yet structuring everything in advance is not viable: documents hold vastly more possible structure than any workload will use, and the useful structure and documents are unknown until queries arrive. We propose agentic data cracking, a method that structures unstructured data adaptively and speculatively as a byproduct of reasoning itself. Structuring is adaptive because observed queries decide when it happens and what matters, and speculative because it goes beyond the current question. Whenever the agent opens a document to answer, a cracking sub-agent forks from the already-loaded context at marginal cost and extracts grounded structure likely to serve related future queries. Over time, an increasing share of queries is fully covered by structured data and answered without opening a document, keeping agentic accuracy at close to RAG cost. On FanOutQA, extended with merely one related question per test question, cracking cuts cost by 53% while preserving accuracy. Agentic data cracking is a first step toward next-generation data infrastructure for agentic reasoning over unstructured data: a shared substrate beneath the model where knowledge that reasoning already paid to uncover accumulates.

</details>


### [401] [Cross-Regional Grapevine Cold Hardiness Prediction via Learned Multimodal Latent Representations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.31097)
*William Solow,Paola Pesantez-Cabrera,Markus Keller,Lav Khot,Sandhya Saisubramanian,Alan Fern*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They propose a model that predicts daily cold hardiness in woody plants and can transfer well to new regions and cultivars using embeddings from text descriptions and limited data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Accurate daily prediction of cold hardiness is vital because freezing temperatures can damage dormant buds and reduce seasonal yield. Current accurate models are mostly site-specific and need substantial local data, which restricts their use in new or data‑scarce regions. There is no principled way to transfer cold hardiness predictions across regions and cultivars, limiting broader adoption in practice.

Method: They design a prediction framework that learns a transferable latent representation of cold hardiness. The framework uses learned embeddings to capture region-specific variation. For unseen regions, it infers embeddings from (1) textual descriptions of cultivars and growing regions and (2) small amounts of historical observations, enabling both zero-shot and few-shot prediction transfer. The model is evaluated against biophysical, hybrid, and deep learning baselines.

Result: On datasets from six North American regions, the proposed approach consistently outperforms existing state-of-the-art cold hardiness prediction methods. It achieves higher predictive accuracy and significantly better transfer performance in regions with little or no local cold hardiness data.

Conclusion: Learning transferable latent representations with region-specific embeddings, informed by text descriptions and limited historical data, allows accurate cold hardiness prediction even in new or data‑scarce regions. This approach overcomes the site-specific limitations of prior models and can enhance the practical utility and scalability of cold hardiness prediction in woody plants.

Abstract: Accurate daily predictions of cold hardiness in woody plants are critical in regions where freezing temperatures can damage dormant buds and reduce seasonal yield. Existing biophysical, hybrid, and deep learning models have shown high predictive accuracy when trained on local data but remain largely site-specific. The limited availability of cold hardiness data, coupled with the lack of principled methods for transferring cold hardiness predictions to new regions and cultivars, has limited the broader adoption and practical utility of these approaches, particularly in data-scarce regions. To address these limitations, we propose a cold hardiness prediction framework that learns a transferable latent representation by capturing region-specific variation through learned embeddings. To enable prediction in previously unseen regions, we infer embeddings from (1) text descriptions of the cultivar and growing region, and (2) limited historical observations, supporting both zero-shot and few-shot transfer. Experiments on datasets from six regions across North America demonstrate that our approach consistently outperforms state-of-the-art cold hardiness prediction methods, yielding more accurate predictions and substantially improving transfer to data-scarce regions.

</details>


### [402] [BLOOM-WILT: Logit Tilting for Behaviour Elicitation in Automated LLM Auditing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.31105)
*Adrians Skapars,Edoardo Manino*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces BLOOM-WILT, an auditing pipeline that efficiently elicits rare, risky behaviors from deployed language models without extra training or internal access, outperforming baseline auditors and changing safety rankings.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Deployed language models exhibit problematic behaviors that standard testing rarely reveals because deployment involves vastly more and more diverse interactions than evaluations. Automated auditors can explore many behaviors cheaply but are sample-inefficient since they lack optimization pressure to focus on rare events. There is a need for an auditing method that is both scalable and sample-efficient, able to uncover low-probability but important behaviors without requiring additional training or privileged access to the model.

Method: The authors propose BLOOM-WILT, a full auditing pipeline. On the input side, WILT uses an auditor model that conducts multi-turn conversations with the target model and revises its strategy over rounds based on scored past interactions, effectively learning how to better elicit the target behaviors. On the output side, WILT leverages the target model’s own next-token distribution under a specialized elicitation prompt to adaptively reweight decoding, prioritizing behavior-relevant outputs over equally likely but irrelevant ones, without modifying or retraining the target. The approach uses only black-box next-token access and no training cost on the target model.

Result: Across 4 target language models and 8 types of problematic behaviors, WILT outperforms a baseline automated auditor in 30 out of 32 model–behavior combinations and even reverses prior safety rankings between models. For a particularly challenging case—eliciting self-harm encouragement from the Qwen3.5-4B model—WILT increases the observed presence of the behavior from 51% to 100%, at equal compute, beating all other elicitation methods ported into the same pipeline while maintaining output probabilities comparable to the baseline (i.e., without resorting to unlikely, contrived generations).

Conclusion: BLOOM-WILT significantly improves the sample efficiency and effectiveness of automated auditing for language models, enabling discovery of rare, safety-critical behaviors using only black-box access and no additional training. Its success across multiple models and behaviors, and its ability to change model safety rankings, suggest that more powerful, optimization-driven auditing pipelines are necessary and feasible for reliable safety evaluation in real-world deployments.

Abstract: Users of a deployed language model routinely encounter behaviours that testing almost never surfaces, since deployment puts the model through orders of magnitude more interactions than any evaluation can simulate. Automated auditors make testing cheap to scale and flexible enough to cover almost any specified behaviour, yet their lack of optimisation pressure makes them sample-inefficient. To address this shortcoming, we introduce BLOOM-WILT, a full auditing pipeline that elicits natural multi-turn instances of rare behaviours, without training cost or access beyond the target's next-token distribution. On the input side, WILT's auditor model revises its conversational strategy across rounds, learning from previous scored interactions. On the output side, WILT adaptively reweights the target's decoding using the model's own distribution conditioned on an elicitation prompt, so that behaviour-relevant generations are sampled ahead of others it finds equally probable when unprompted. We evaluate WILT across 4 target models and 8 behaviours, where it beats the baseline auditor in 30 of the 32 settings and overturns the previous model safety rankings. WILT raises average behaviour presence from 51% to 100% when eliciting self-harm encouragement from Qwen3.5-4B, beating every elicitation method we port into the same pipeline at matched compute, without pushing output probability below the baseline's.

</details>


### [403] [When Does Bigger Help? A Controlled Study of LLM Scale for Ontology Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.31118)
*Hamed Babaei Giglou,Sören Auer,Jennifer D'Souza*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper systematically evaluates how scaling different LLM families affects ontology learning performance and finds that bigger is not always better, with gains highly task- and architecture-dependent.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Ontology learning is important for structuring domain knowledge in areas like biomedicine and materials science, but we lack clear, controlled evidence on how LLM size and architecture actually affect performance on concrete OL tasks. Practitioners often choose models mainly by parameter count or brand (e.g., largest open model vs. latest proprietary model), which may be suboptimal or irreproducible. The authors aim to provide a rigorous, apples-to-apples comparison of multiple open and proprietary LLMs for key OL subtasks, to understand whether model scale really helps and under what conditions.

Method: The authors use a controlled OntoLearner retrieval-augmented generation pipeline and evaluate 13 LLMs, including dense and Mixture-of-Experts Qwen3.5/Qwen3.6 variants and proprietary GPT releases. They fix the embedding model, retrieval setup, prompts, decoding, datasets, and evaluation metrics to isolate the effect of the generative model. They then benchmark each model on three core ontology learning subtasks—term typing, taxonomy discovery, and non-taxonomic relation extraction—across four ontologies in biomedical and materials science/engineering domains. Performance is analyzed as a function of parameter count, architecture (dense vs MoE), and lineage (Qwen vs GPT).

Result: Within the dense Qwen3.5 series, larger models mainly improve precision rather than recall, with the biggest jump between 9B and 27B parameters. Scaling effects are inconsistent: performance does not increase monotonically with size and differs by task and domain. Dense 27B models beat much larger sparse (MoE) models on term typing, while larger MoE models yield the best open-weight results on taxonomy discovery. Non-taxonomic relation extraction remains challenging at all scales, especially in the Materials Data Science ontology. Comparisons between closely matched Qwen variants and GPT versions show that architecture and training lineage can have more impact than raw parameter count.

Conclusion: Model size alone is a poor predictor of ontology learning performance. Different OL subtasks and domains benefit from different model configurations, and architectural choices and model lineage can be more important than nominal scale. The study provides empirical, reproducible evidence to guide selection of LLMs for ontology engineering and suggests that careful benchmarking on target tasks should replace naive “bigger is better” assumptions when choosing models for OL workflows.

Abstract: The effect of Large Language Model (LLM) scale on ontology learning (OL) performance remains insufficiently characterized. We present a controlled evaluation of 13 models spanning dense and Mixture-of-Experts variants from the Qwen3.5 and Qwen3.6 lineages, together with proprietary GPT release variants, using the OntoLearner retrieval-augmented generation pipeline. All models are evaluated with the same embedding model, retrieval configuration, prompt templates, decoding settings, datasets, and metrics on term typing, taxonomy discovery, and non-taxonomic relationship extraction across four biomedical and materials science and engineering ontologies. Within the dense Qwen3.5 lineage, increasing parameter count primarily improves precision rather than recall, with the largest gains occurring between 9B and 27B parameters. However, the effect of scale is neither monotonic nor uniform across tasks and domains. Dense 27B models outperform substantially larger sparse models on term typing, whereas larger Mixture-of-Experts models achieve the strongest open-weight results on taxonomy discovery. Non-taxonomic relationship extraction remains difficult across model scales, particularly for the Materials Data Science ontology. Performance differences across matched Qwen variants and proprietary GPT releases further indicate that architecture and model lineage can outweigh nominal parameter count. These findings show that model size alone is an insufficient selection criterion for OL and provide empirical guidance for reproducible LLM-assisted ontology engineering.

</details>


### [404] [OntoAligner-Ensemble: Voting-Based Fusion across Heterogeneous Ontology Alignment Techniques](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.31137)
*Hamed Babaei Giglou,Sören Auer,Peio Popov,Mahsa Sanaei,Jennifer D'Souza*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces OntoAligner-Ensemble, a modular framework that ensembles different ontology aligners to systematically fuse their outputs, improving precision–recall trade-offs over individual methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Ontology alignment methods come from diverse paradigms—lexical, structural, KGE-based, and LLM-based—and often produce complementary but conflicting correspondences. Existing OA frameworks integrate multiple aligners but lack principled, configurable mechanisms to reconcile their outputs. The authors aim to address this gap with a systematic, reproducible ensemble strategy that can exploit heterogeneity among aligners and provide guidance on configuring ensembles for different alignment goals.

Method: They design OntoAligner-Ensemble, a modular, aligner-agnostic framework operating in two stages: (1) voting-based fusion, where candidate correspondences from arbitrary aligners are combined via configurable voting strategies; and (2) post-fusion selection, where policies decide which fused correspondences to keep, trading off precision vs recall. The framework plugs into OntoAligner and can use any aligner that outputs candidate correspondences. The authors instantiate it with three paradigms: lightweight string-based aligners, KGE-based aligners, and Retrieval-Augmented Generation aligners driven by both open-weight and API-based LLMs. They then configure different ensemble compositions (heterogeneous vs homogeneous) and run systematic evaluations across standardized OAEI benchmarks from multiple tracks and domains.

Result: Across eight benchmark tasks in five OAEI tracks (including biomedical and beyond-equivalence settings), ensemble configurations generally outperform most standalone aligners. The fusion strategies consistently yield a better balance between precision and recall, and particular ensembles surpass the best single aligners in F1-score. The experiments also reveal patterns: heterogeneous ensembles that mix paradigms (e.g., string + KGE + LLM) tend to increase precision, while ensembles composed solely of LLM-based aligners tend to deliver higher overall F1-scores, indicating stronger overall alignment quality.

Conclusion: The study concludes that systematic ensemble learning is an effective, robust, and reproducible approach for ontology alignment. By providing a configurable two-stage fusion and selection framework that is aligner-agnostic, OntoAligner-Ensemble enables practitioners to exploit the complementary strengths of diverse OA paradigms. The observed precision–recall behaviors of different ensemble compositions translate into practical guidance: use heterogeneous ensembles when precision is critical, and prefer homogeneous LLM ensembles when maximizing F1 is the priority. This establishes ensemble-based OA as a promising direction for future research and deployment.

Abstract: Ontology alignment (OA) has evolved through several methodological paradigms, ranging from lexical and structural aligners to knowledge graph embedding (KGE) models and, more recently, Large Language Model (LLM)-based approaches. Although modern OA frameworks provide unified ecosystems for deploying these heterogeneous aligners, mechanisms for systematically reconciling their complementary and sometimes conflicting predictions remain relatively underexplored. We present OntoAligner-Ensemble, a modular and aligner-agnostic framework that combines candidate correspondences through a configurable two-stage process comprising voting-based fusion strategies followed by post-fusion selection policies. The framework supports any aligner implemented within OntoAligner that produces candidate correspondences, enabling diverse alignment paradigms to be integrated through a unified decision process. To demonstrate its effectiveness, we instantiate the framework using representative lightweight string-aligner, KGE-based, and Retrieval-Augmented Generation aligners powered by both open-weight and API-based LLMs. We evaluate individual aligners and ensemble configurations across eight benchmark tasks from five OAEI tracks spanning biomedical to beyond-equivalence. The results show that ensemble fusion consistently improves the balance between precision and recall and frequently outperforms standalone aligners across diverse domains. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that ensemble composition directly affects the precision-recall trade-off: heterogeneous cross-paradigm ensembles generally improve precision, whereas homogeneous LLM ensembles more often achieve higher overall F1-scores. These findings demonstrate that systematic ensemble learning offers a robust and reproducible strategy for OA while providing practical guidance for selecting ensemble compositions under different alignment scenarios.

</details>
